intro: Chapter 1 introduces the two great threads that will wind through Samuel: the theme of divine reversal — the barren woman made fruitful, the lowly raised up — and the figure of Samuel himself, given to YHWH before he draws breath. The wordplay on his name seeds an irony that runs across the whole book.

notes.original: ha-Ramatayim Tzofim — the double-heights of the Zuphites
notes.rendering: Ramathaim-zophim, from the hill country of Ephraim
notes.why: The place-name is a compound of ramah (height, high place) and a gentillic of Zuph. By verse 19 it is simply Ramah — the hill, the home Samuel always returns to. The double form may be honorific or geographical; the Zuphites are the clan Elkanah belongs to, as the genealogy confirms.

notes.original: lo ya’aleh mora’ al rosho — no razor shall come upon his head
notes.rendering: no razor shall ever come upon his head
notes.why: The language is unmistakably Nazirite (cf. Numbers 6:5). The text never applies the word Nazirite to Samuel, but the dedication echoes Samson’s birth narrative (Judges 13) and marks Samuel as a man set apart from the womb. The vow is Hannah’s, not God’s — which is itself remarkable: a mother volunteers her son to divine service before he exists.

notes.original: ki me’YHWH sh’iltiv — because I asked him of YHWH
notes.rendering: Because I asked him of YHWH
notes.why: Shemu’el (Samuel) is linked to sha’al (to ask, request). The etymology is approximate — the name more likely derives from shama’ El (God has heard) or shem El (name of God) — but the text is not offering philology. It is offering theology: this child is the embodied answer to Hannah’s prayer. The sha’al wordplay returns in chapter 8 when Israel asks (sha’al) for a king, and again when Saul (Sha’ul — the asked-for one) is given. The name Samuel anticipates and ironises the entire monarchy.

intro: Chapter 2 is the theological axis of the book’s opening movement. Hannah’s Song lifts the child’s birth into a cosmic frame — YHWH the overturner of all human calculus — and then the narrative descends into the contrast that will drive the plot forward: the boy Samuel growing in grace beside the sons of Eli sinking into corruption.

notes.original: qarni ramah b’YHWH — my horn is exalted in YHWH
notes.rendering: my horn is lifted high in YHWH
notes.why: The horn (qeren) is the image of animal power and dignity — a bull lifting its horns in strength. For Hannah to say her horn is raised is to say her standing, strength, and honor have been restored. The image recurs at the song’s end: YHWH will exalt the horn of his anointed (v.10). The song frames the anointed king as the large-scale fulfilment of what Hannah experienced in miniature.

notes.original: tzur — rock
notes.rendering: there is no Rock like our God
notes.why: Tzur (rock, crag) is one of the oldest divine titles in Hebrew poetry — appearing across Deuteronomy 32, the Psalms, and here as Hannah’s climax of incomparability. The Rock is not merely strong; it is the immovable ground beneath the feet of those who would otherwise slip. The image will reappear in David’s own song in 2 Samuel 22.

notes.original: mashicho — his anointed one
notes.rendering: exalt the horn of his anointed
notes.why: The song ends on the word that will define the rest of the Samuel narrative: mashiach, the anointed one. No king yet exists in Israel. The word is prospective, even prophetic. Hannah’s personal experience of reversal is here transposed into a political key: the God who flips barrenness and fullness will raise up a king — and the book of Samuel is the story of what that means when it collides with human ambition. Mary’s Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55) is the New Testament echo of this song, almost line for line.

notes.original: ki chafetz YHWH lahamitam — for YHWH had resolved to put them to death
notes.rendering: for YHWH has resolved to put them to death
notes.why: The verb chafetz (to take pleasure in, to delight in, to will, to purpose) is unusually strong for divine intention toward death. The text is not saying YHWH hardens their hearts (as in the Exodus narrative); it is saying their refusal to listen is itself the sign of a judgment already sealed. They cannot hear their father’s voice because the outcome is already determined. The theological edge is sharp: Eli’s words are correct, but they come too late.

intro: Chapter 3 is one of the great vocation narratives of the Hebrew Bible — spare, tender, and inexorable. The triple call and triple misunderstanding prepare for the fourth moment when the word finally lands. Eli’s role is quietly moving: the failing priest who cannot see (literally, 2:1) is still able to recognise the divine voice and direct the boy toward it.

notes.original: dabar YHWH hayah yaqqar — the word of YHWH was rare
notes.rendering: The word of YHWH is rare in those days
notes.why: Yaqqar means rare, precious, costly — the same word used for precious stones and for a life that is valued. The word of YHWH is not merely infrequent; it is absent in the way that something precious is absent when it has been squandered. The sentence is a diagnosis of the Eli era: a house of worship where the sacred word no longer speaks is a temple in name only.

notes.original: v’Shemu’el terem yada’ et YHWH — Samuel did not yet know YHWH
notes.rendering: Samuel does not yet know YHWH
notes.why: Yada’ (to know) carries the full relational weight it bears elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible — the knowledge of covenant intimacy, not mere information. Samuel has been in the temple since childhood, has served before YHWH, but has not yet had the relational encounter that constitutes prophetic knowledge. The word of YHWH has not been revealed (niglah — uncovered, unveiled) to him. What is about to happen in vv.10–14 is not instruction but unveiling.

notes.original: lo hipil mikol devarav artza — he did not let any of his words fall to the ground
notes.rendering: letting none of his words fall to the ground
notes.why: The image is of words as things thrown or dropped — a word that ‘falls’ is a prophetic word that fails to come true, a pronouncement that lands without effect. The phrase is the Hebrew idiom for prophetic reliability: what Samuel says, happens. It implicitly contrasts with Eli’s house, where words were spoken (the man of God in ch.2, YHWH himself in ch.3) and not heeded. Samuel is the prophet in whom word and fulfilment are joined.

notes.original: mi-Dan v’ad Be’er Sheva — from Dan to Beersheba
notes.rendering: All Israel from Dan to Beersheba
notes.why: The standard idiom for the whole land, measuring it from its northern limit (Dan, near the Hermon headwaters) to its southern edge (Beersheba, on the edge of the Negev) — a span of roughly 150 miles. The phrase signals that Samuel’s prophetic standing is not local or tribal but national. He belongs to all Israel, not just to the sanctuary at Shiloh.

intro: Chapter 4 is the first movement of what scholars call the Ark Narrative (chapters 4–6). The ark, brought to the battlefield as a guarantee of divine presence, is captured. The dual tragedy — Eli’s death and the birth of Ichabod — closes the chapter on a note of total desolation. The two sons whose deaths were prophesied in chapter 2 fall in a single verse (v.11).

notes.original: aron berit YHWH — ark of the covenant of YHWH
notes.rendering: the ark of the covenant of YHWH
notes.why: The aron (ark, chest, box) is introduced here for the first time in the Samuel narrative, though the reader knows it from Exodus and Joshua. The elders’ reasoning is theologically flawed but not absurd: if YHWH’s throne is with the ark, bring the throne to the battle. What they have not reckoned with is that YHWH is not bound to the ark — as the Philistines will discover, the ark is not a talisman but a testimony. Bringing the ark without repentance simply puts the covenant in danger.

notes.original: vayishpot et Yisrael arba’im shanah — he judged Israel forty years
notes.rendering: He has judged Israel forty years
notes.why: The obituary formula closes the Eli era. Forty years (arba’im shanah) is the standard biblical period for a generation or a complete era — Moses in the wilderness, Israel’s wandering, Solomon’s reign. The number may be historical or it may be schematic; either way, the era is over. Eli’s death from a broken neck (literally, his neck broke — vayishaver) echoes the ‘breaking’ (shever) of Eli’s house promised to the man of God in 2:31.

notes.original: i-kavod — no glory; kavod — glory, weight, presence
notes.rendering: The glory has departed from Israel
notes.why: Kavod (glory) is the great word for the weighty, substantial, visible presence of YHWH — the same word as in the Sinai theophany, in Ezekiel’s vision of the departing glory, in the temple dedication. I-kavod negates it: no-glory, the un-presenced. The dying woman’s last act is to name her child as a theological statement. The glory has not merely gone absent; it has been taken. The word also carries the connotation of honor and reputation — Israel’s honor is gone with the ark. The name anticipates Ezekiel 10–11, where the glory literally departs from the temple by stages.

intro: Chapter 5 is deliberate comedy with a theological edge. The narrative of Dagon twice prostrating before the ark is staged with the precision of a parable: the god of the conquerors falls before the god of the conquered, losing first his posture, then his extremities. The chapter works by means of repetition and escalation — city to city, panic to greater panic — as the ark makes its terrible progress through Philistine territory.

notes.original: Dagon — the Philistine deity
notes.rendering: the house of Dagon
notes.why: The name Dagon connects to either dagan (grain) or dag (fish) — the older grain interpretation is more likely, making Dagon the deity of agricultural fertility. The house of Dagon is his temple at Ashdod, a major Philistine cult site. Placing the captured ark beside the cult statue is a statement of victory theology: the captured god serves the conquering god. What happens next subverts that entirely — it is Dagon who prostrates, as a worshipper falls before YHWH.

notes.original: raq Dagon nish’ar alav — only the stump of Dagon was left to him
notes.rendering: Only the stump of Dagon is left
notes.why: The dismemberment is precise and ironic: the head (the seat of authority and speech) and the hands (the instruments of action and power) are severed at the threshold. What remains is a torso — helpless, voiceless, incapacitated. The detail about the threshold (v.5) becomes an etiology: the priests dare not step on the place where their god’s dignity was destroyed. The ark has done to Dagon what Dagon could not do to Israel’s God.

notes.original: yad YHWH nikhbedah — the hand of YHWH was heavy
notes.rendering: The hand of YHWH is heavy against the people
notes.why: Yad YHWH (the hand of YHWH) is the great Exodus phrase — the divine hand that struck Egypt is now at work in Philistia. Nikhbedah (was heavy, was weighty) shares the root with kavod (glory, weight) — the same root as Ichabod in chapter 4. The glory has ‘departed’ from Israel in the sense that the kavod-weight is now falling on the Philistines. YHWH’s hand moves, even in captivity.

intro: Chapter 6 closes the Ark Narrative with a double irony: the Philistines, by their own practical theology, send the ark home with the correct sacrificial vocabulary (asham — guilt offering), while Israel at Beth-shemesh, on receiving the ark back, are struck down for irreverence. The ark is equally dangerous to those who disrespect it on either side of the border.

notes.original: asham — guilt offering, reparation offering
notes.rendering: a guilt offering
notes.why: The asham is the specific Levitical offering prescribed for offenses that damage the holy or the neighbor — requiring restitution plus twenty percent (Leviticus 5–6). The Philistine priests use the correct Hebrew cultic term, apparently without knowing it. They are reasoning from pragmatic precedent (Egypt) toward a form of atonement that the Mosaic law would recognize. The golden tumors and mice are asham in kind: reparations for the damage done by the divine hand.

notes.original: mikreh hu lanu — it happened to us by chance
notes.rendering: it happened to us by chance
notes.why: Mikreh (chance, accident, what befalls) is the same root used in Ecclesiastes for the random events that fall equally on wise and fool. The Philistine diviners are designing a test that will distinguish between divine causation and mere coincidence: if the unmothered cows resist nature and walk straight to Israel, that is not chance. If they wander, it is mikreh. The cows go straight. The diviners have, unwittingly, set up a falsifiable theological experiment — and YHWH passes it.

notes.original: mi yukhal la’amod lifnei YHWH ha-Elohim ha-qadosh haze — who is able to stand before YHWH, this holy God?
notes.rendering: Who is able to stand before YHWH, this holy God?
notes.why: The question of Beth-shemesh is not rhetorical despair but the central theological problem of the ark narrative: YHWH’s holiness (qadosh — set apart, other, dangerous to the profane) is not suspended for Israel’s benefit. The Philistines could not contain the ark; Israel cannot casually handle it either. The question ‘to whom shall he go up?’ drives the ark toward Kiriath-jearim and a twenty-year waiting period (7:2) before it moves again — setting the stage for David’s later attempt to bring it to Jerusalem.

intro: Chapter 7 closes the Ark Narrative and opens the era of Samuel as judge. The movement is from public ceremony (the water-pouring repentance) to public battle (YHWH’s thunder) to the Ebenezer stone — which quietly corrects the geography of chapter 4. Israel’s first Ebenezer was a camp before a defeat; this one is a stone of help after a victory.

notes.original: ha-Asherot — the Ashtaroth
notes.rendering: put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth
notes.why: Ashtaroth (plural of Ashtoreth) is the Canaanite fertility goddess, the female counterpart to Baal. The pairing of Baals and Ashtaroth is the standard synecdoche for all Canaanite religious practice — a shorthand the narrator uses throughout Judges and Samuel. Samuel’s call to put away these gods echoes Joshua’s farewell address (Joshua 24:14). The choice is always the same: serve YHWH only.

notes.original: shafat — judged, administered justice
notes.rendering: Samuel judges the people of Israel at Mizpah
notes.why: Shafat (to judge, to rule, to administer right) is the defining verb of the period between Joshua and the monarchy. The shofet (judge) is not primarily a legal officer but a deliverer-ruler raised up by YHWH for a crisis. Samuel is the last of these figures — and the transitional figure who will crown the first king. That he judges at Mizpah, the very site of Israel’s repentance assembly, is deliberate: governance flows from covenant renewal.

notes.original: Even ha-Ezer — Stone of Help
notes.rendering: He calls it Ebenezer — Stone of Help
notes.why: The name reverses the geography of disaster. In 4:1, Israel camped at a place already called Ebenezer and was defeated there — a place named for help at the site of catastrophe. Now Samuel names a new stone Ebenezer after a victory: the same name, a different stone, a different story. The narrative is not subtle about the contrast. The Ebenezer of chapter 7 is the theological answer to the Ebenezer of chapter 4.

intro: Chapter 8 is the pivot of the entire book — the moment when the political structure of Israel changes forever. YHWH’s response to Samuel is both gracious and devastating: he grants the request while naming it for what it is. Samuel’s speech about the ways of the king is the Bible’s most sustained critical analysis of monarchy before the institution exists.

notes.original: k’chol ha-goyim — like all the nations
notes.rendering: appoint for us a king to judge us — like all the nations
notes.why: The phrase ‘like all the nations’ (k’chol ha-goyim) is the theological problem in four words. Israel’s entire vocation since Sinai has been to be unlike the nations — a kingdom of priests, a holy nation (Exodus 19:6). To ask to be like the nations is to ask to undo the covenant distinction. The elders frame this as a practical request about succession and governance; YHWH hears it as a rejection of theocracy. Both are correct.

notes.original: ki oti ma’asu — for me they have rejected
notes.rendering: they have rejected me from being king over them
notes.why: YHWH’s self-interpretation is startling in its directness. Samuel feels the rejection personally; YHWH reframes it: this is not about Samuel, it is about YHWH’s own kingship. The verb ma’as (to reject, spurn, despise) is a strong word of covenant abandonment — it is what Saul later does to YHWH’s command (15:23, 26), and what YHWH then does to Saul (15:23). The vocabulary of rejection runs through the whole book like a thread.

notes.original: mishpat ha-melekh — the way/right of the king
notes.rendering: This is what the king who reigns over you will do
notes.why: Mishpat ha-melekh — literally the justice, the custom, the right of the king. The word mishpat (justice, judgment, right, custom) is the same word used for the justice Samuel administered (7:6) and the justice Israel’s courts were supposed to uphold. The king’s mishpat, according to Samuel’s speech, is a relentless taking: sons, daughters, fields, tithes, servants, flocks. The list is precise and prophetic — it describes the Solomonic state before Solomon exists.

intro: Chapter 9 is one of the most artfully constructed introduction scenes in the Hebrew Bible. Saul enters the narrative looking for donkeys and stumbles into his destiny. The narrator keeps the reader ahead of the character: we know from verse 15 what Saul does not know until verse 20. The gap between YHWH’s advance word and Saul’s bewilderment is the space in which the whole first portrait of the king is drawn.

notes.original: mishichmo va’maalah — from his shoulders upward
notes.rendering: From his shoulders upward he is taller than anyone
notes.why: The first description of Saul is entirely physical — handsome (tov — good, beautiful) and tall. The narrative says nothing about his character, his wisdom, his faithfulness. The contrast with YHWH’s later instruction to Samuel (16:7 — ‘do not look on his height or the height of his stature; YHWH does not see as man sees’) is retrospective but deliberate. The book introduces its first king by the criteria that will later be explicitly rejected.

notes.original: ha-navi / ha-ro’eh — the prophet / the seer
notes.rendering: the one now called a prophet was formerly called a seer
notes.why: The parenthetical gloss is the narrator’s oldest comment in the book — a lexical note explaining that ro’eh (seer, one who sees visions) is the archaic term for what is now called navi (prophet, one who speaks forth). The note signals antiquity: this story is told from a later vantage point when terminology has shifted. It also quietly establishes that Samuel belongs to both categories — he sees (9:15–17) and he speaks (9:19–20). The prophet who anoints kings is the seer who was also a judge.

notes.original: nagid — prince, designated leader
notes.rendering: Anoint him as prince over my people Israel
notes.why: YHWH’s word to Samuel uses nagid — not melekh (king). Nagid means the one designated, the one in front, the designated leader — a title that implies accountability to the one who designates him. When Israel asked for a king (melekh) in chapter 8, YHWH gives them a nagid — a subtle but significant adjustment. The nagid is a leader; the melekh is a sovereign. The first royal title in the Samuel narrative is one degree below what Israel demanded, and one degree more dependent on YHWH.

notes.original: ha-shevet ha-qatan — the smallest tribe
notes.rendering: Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of Israel’s tribes?
notes.why: Saul’s humility here — invoking Benjamin’s smallness and his clan’s obscurity — echoes the pattern of the called-but-reluctant figure found in Moses (Exodus 3–4) and Gideon (Judges 6). The reader who knows Judges 19–21 will also recall that Benjamin was nearly annihilated in the civil war over the Gibeah atrocity. To say I am a Benjaminite is to invoke a tribe that barely survived. That the first king comes from this tribe is itself a statement about divine reversal.

intro: Chapter 10 moves from the intimacy of private anointing to the awkwardness of public selection. The three signs confirm Samuel’s word; the Spirit transforms Saul; and then, at the moment of his public coronation at Mizpah, the chosen man is found hiding in the luggage. The narrator does not comment. He does not need to.

notes.original: nagid — prince, designated leader (not melekh — king)
notes.rendering: Has not YHWH anointed you to be prince over his people Israel?
notes.why: As in 9:16, Samuel uses nagid — the designated one, the one put forward — rather than the melekh Israel demanded. The anointing (mashach — to smear, to anoint with oil) is the moment the relationship between Saul and YHWH is formalised. The oil is a flask (pak — a small vial, distinct from the large horn used for David’s anointing in 16:13), a detail that later readers may have noticed: the smaller vessel for the smaller beginning.

notes.original: tzalach — to rush, to fall powerfully upon
notes.rendering: the Spirit of YHWH will rush upon you
notes.why: Tzalach al (to rush upon, to overpower) is the specific verb for the Spirit’s sudden and overwhelming arrival — used for the Spirit coming on Samson in Judges 14:6, 19 and 15:14. It implies not a gentle inspiration but a violent divine empowerment. Saul will experience this twice more in Samuel (11:6; then the darker echo in chapter 18 when ‘an evil spirit from God’ rushes upon him instead). The same verb, the same mechanism — different spirit.

notes.original: ba-kelim — among the equipment, baggage, gear
notes.rendering: he has hidden himself among the baggage
notes.why: Kelim (vessels, equipment, baggage) is what armies carry and what households store. The chosen king of Israel, on the day of his public coronation, is crouching behind the gear. The narrator offers no explanation — modesty? fear? reluctance? — and the ambiguity is deliberate. The hiding will be read differently as the story unfolds: what looks like humility here will look like evasion later. Saul’s instinct to conceal himself runs through his entire reign.

intro: Chapter 11 gives Saul the best possible beginning — the one chapter in his story where everything works. The Spirit arrives, the muster is overwhelming, the battle is decisive, and his response to victory is magnanimous. “Not a man shall be put to death today” is Saul at his finest. It will not last. But the narrative preserves it, fully and without irony.

notes.original: v’niqart lachem kol ayin yemin — I will gouge out every right eye
notes.rendering: I will gouge out every man’s right eye
notes.why: The right eye is the fighting eye — soldiers held their shield on the left, leaving the right eye exposed to aim and to see the enemy. To lose the right eye was to lose military usefulness. Nahash’s demand is a calculated humiliation: the men of Jabesh would survive as a living disgrace, a warning to Israel about the cost of Ammonite enmity. The 4Q Samuel Dead Sea Scroll adds a preface explaining that Nahash had been doing this throughout Gad and Reuben — making his threat here the culminating outrage.

notes.original: pachad YHWH — the terror/dread of YHWH
notes.rendering: the terror of YHWH falls on the people
notes.why: Pachad YHWH (the terror or dread of YHWH) is a holy fear that overrides ordinary human calculation — the same force that drives Canaan’s inhabitants to paralysis before Joshua’s advance (Exodus 15:16; Joshua 2:9). Here it mobilises Israel instead of defeating her enemies. Saul’s action with the oxen echoes the Levite’s dismemberment of the concubine in Judges 19:29 — a gruesome summons by body-part that signals total-war intent. The echo is deliberate: Benjamin was the tribe almost destroyed by that episode; now a Benjaminite king summons all Israel to rescue.

notes.original: ki hayom YHWH asa teshuah b’Yisrael — for today YHWH has worked deliverance in Israel
notes.rendering: today YHWH has worked deliverance in Israel
notes.why: Teshuah (deliverance, salvation, victory) — the same root as yeshuah (salvation, Joshua, Jesus). Saul’s attribution of the victory entirely to YHWH is theologically correct and personally generous. He refuses the revenge his supporters want and deflects all credit upward. This is the Saul the book wants us to see before it shows us the other Saul. The contrast with his later self-monument (15:12) and his self-justification before Samuel (15:20–21) is the measure of how far he will fall.

intro: Chapter 12 is Samuel’s farewell address — one of the great speeches of the Hebrew Bible. Its structure is classical: integrity established, history recited, warning issued, sign performed, grace extended. Samuel does not leave quietly. He leaves with thunder in harvest season and a promise to keep praying for the people who no longer wanted him.

notes.original: u-miyyad mi laqachti kofer — from whose hand have I taken a bribe
notes.rendering: From whose hand have I taken a bribe to look the other way?
notes.why: The legal terminology is precise. Kofer (ransom, bribe — from kafar, to cover, to atone) is the payment made to cover over a wrong or blind a judge’s eyes. Samuel lists the entire inventory of corrupt leadership — taking livestock, oppression, bribery — and invites Israel to testify against him. The challenge is a formal legal procedure before YHWH and the anointed king as witnesses. His sons failed this test (8:3); Samuel passes it. The implicit contrast with the king the people have chosen is unmistakable.

notes.original: hagashem b’yom qatzir chitim — thunder and rain in the wheat harvest
notes.rendering: I will call on YHWH to send thunder and rain
notes.why: The sign is meteorologically precise. Wheat harvest in the central hill country falls in late May or early June — the driest part of the year, when rain is essentially unknown. Thunder and rain in harvest season was not merely unusual; it was catastrophic for crops. Samuel’s sign is not a gentle wonder but a violent disruption of the natural order, timed to make Israel feel in their bodies what it means to act against YHWH. The same authority that commands the weather has been judging their request for a king.

notes.original: chalilah li me-cheto l’YHWH — far be it from me to sin against YHWH
notes.rendering: far be it from me that I should sin against YHWH by ceasing to pray for you
notes.why: Chalilah (far be it, God forbid — from chalal, to profane, to desecrate) is a strong oath of repudiation. Samuel frames the cessation of intercessory prayer as a sin against YHWH, not merely a failure of duty. Prayer for the people is his covenantal obligation as a prophet — as fundamental as Moses interceding after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11–14) or Abraham pleading for Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32). Even when the people reject his leadership, he will not stop praying for them. This is the definition of prophetic faithfulness.

notes.original: ki ho’il YHWH la’asot etchem lo l’am — because it pleased YHWH to make you his people
notes.rendering: because it has pleased YHWH to make you his people
notes.why: The grounds of YHWH’s faithfulness are not Israel’s merit but his own prior choice — the same logic as Deuteronomy 7:6–8 (not because you were great, but because YHWH loved you). The word ho’il (it pleased, it was good in the sight of) grounds the relationship entirely in divine initiative. Israel’s failure does not undo YHWH’s commitment because that commitment was never conditional on Israel’s worthiness in the first place. Samuel says this to people who have just been terrified by harvest thunder. Grace arrives through the storm.

intro: Chapter 13 springs the trap that was set in chapter 10: Samuel told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal. Saul waits seven days. Samuel arrives — and arrives at the worst possible moment, one step too late for Saul to claim innocence. The chapter’s theological verdict is delivered in a single phrase that will echo across the rest of the book.

notes.original: ben-shanah Sha’ul b’molko — [lit. ‘a son of a year’ was Saul in his reign]
notes.rendering: Saul is [---] years old when he becomes king
notes.why: The verse is one of the most famous textual corruptions in the Hebrew Bible. The formula ben-X shanim (a son of X years) requires a number before shanah, but none survives in the MT. The Septuagint omits the verse entirely. Various manuscripts supply thirty, forty, or other numbers. The honest translation preserves the gap rather than silently filling it. The two-year reign figure that follows may itself be a minimum — Saul’s reign was certainly longer by any historical reckoning.

notes.original: ish k’levavo — a man according to his heart
notes.rendering: YHWH has sought out a man after his own heart
notes.why: The phrase that defines David before David appears. Levav (heart, will, inner person) — YHWH is looking for a man whose inner orientation matches his own. The contrast with Saul is implicit: Saul acted from his own calculation (I forced myself — v.12) rather than from trust in YHWH’s word. The ‘man after God’s own heart’ is not a morally perfect man (David’s biography will make this clear) but a man whose fundamental orientation is toward YHWH rather than away from him.

notes.original: charash barzel lo yimmatzei b’chol eretz Yisrael — no blacksmith was found in all the land
notes.rendering: not a sword or a spear
notes.why: The iron monopoly is a precise historical detail. Philistine military superiority in the early Iron Age rested partly on control of ironworking technology — they could produce iron-tipped weapons while Israel fought with bronze or stone. The detail that Israelites had to go to the Philistines just to sharpen their farming tools explains the military desperation of chapters 13–14. Jonathan’s attack on the garrison with no sword among the people is not bravado; it is the only available theology.

intro: Chapter 14 is the high-water mark of Jonathan’s story and the most sustained portrait of his character in the book. His theology is simple and audacious: ‘nothing holds YHWH back.’ The contrast with his father is the chapter’s whole argument. Saul’s oath, intended to consecrate the battle, nearly destroys his best soldier and silences the divine voice he most needs.

notes.original: ulai ya’aseh YHWH lanu — perhaps YHWH will act for us
notes.rendering: Perhaps YHWH will act for us — for nothing holds YHWH back
notes.why: Jonathan’s theology is compressed into two clauses. Ulai (perhaps, maybe) is the honest modal: Jonathan does not presume on YHWH’s will but opens the possibility. The second clause grounds the risk: ein michtsar l’YHWH l’hoshi’a b’rav o b’me’at — there is no restraint (michtsar — hindrance, obstacle, limitation) for YHWH to save by many or few. This is the theology of Gideon’s three hundred applied without Gideon’s hesitation. Jonathan is betting his life on the freedom of God.

notes.original: vata’ornah einav — his eyes became bright
notes.rendering: his eyes light up
notes.why: The honey detail is told with the narrator’s most precise and tender observation: Jonathan’s eyes become bright (or’ — to be bright, to give light). In a story about men exhausted and blinded by his father’s oath, Jonathan’s brightened eyes are a small beacon. He immediately interprets what he sees: if the people had eaten freely, the victory would have been greater. The honey is not just sustenance; it is the symbol of what Saul’s compulsive oath-taking denies his own army.

notes.original: ki im Elohim asa hayom haze — for he has worked with God this day
notes.rendering: for he worked this day with God
notes.why: The people’s ransom of Jonathan is framed in explicitly theological terms: Jonathan acted im Elohim — with God, alongside God. The preposition im (with) is the covenantal word of accompaniment — ‘YHWH was with him’ is the standard narrator’s verdict on those whom the book approves. The people read the day’s events correctly: the victory was God’s, worked through Jonathan. Saul’s oath, which nearly executed the instrument of the victory, is implicitly indicted.

intro: Chapter 15 is the hinge of the entire Saul narrative. The verdict of chapter 13 is confirmed and made final. Saul’s disobedience follows a precise pattern: he partially obeys, then misnames what he has done, then shifts blame, then confesses — but confesses too late, and confesses to the wrong thing (the people’s opinion) rather than the right one (his own will). Samuel’s poetic oracle and the torn robe are the two images that carry the chapter’s weight.

notes.original: cherem — the ban, devotion to destruction
notes.rendering: put everything under the ban
notes.why: Cherem (the ban, devotion to destruction) is the most theologically contested practice in the Hebrew Bible — the total destruction of an enemy and their property as an act of sacred dedication to YHWH. Nothing from a cherem-d city or army may be kept; everything belongs to YHWH by destruction. Saul’s sin is not military disobedience but sacred theft: keeping what was consecrated to YHWH. The sparing of Agag and the best livestock is cherem-violation. This is why Samuel’s accusation uses the language of divination and idolatry (v.23) — keeping the spoil is functionally equivalent to worshipping a foreign god.

notes.original: shamo’a mi-zevach tov — to obey is better than sacrifice
notes.rendering: to obey is better than sacrifice, to listen than the fat of rams
notes.why: The verse is the prophetic critique of cult in its most concentrated form — earlier even than Amos 5:21–24 or Isaiah 1:11–17. Shama (to hear, to obey, to heed) is set against zevach (sacrifice, slaughter-offering). The parallelism is exact: listening versus fat rams. The next verse’s equation of rebellion with divination and presumption with idolatry is the theological explanation: a man who substitutes his own judgment for YHWH’s word is already practising a form of self-worship. Saul’s offering of the Amalekite livestock as a gift to YHWH is not piety — it is an attempt to redefine obedience on his own terms.

notes.original: Netzach Yisrael — the Glory/Eternity of Israel
notes.rendering: the Glory of Israel does not lie and does not relent
notes.why: Netzach (eternity, enduring permanence, victorious strength) is a rare divine title — used here as a name for YHWH: the Enduring One of Israel, the Eternal Victor. The verb nacham (to relent, regret, be moved to compassion) appears in the same chapter for YHWH’s regret about making Saul king (vv.11, 35). The apparent contradiction is the point: YHWH’s emotional response to Saul (grief, regret) is real, but his covenantal decisions are irrevocable. He grieves the loss; he does not reverse the sentence. The Glory of Israel does not lie — the word given in v.28 stands.

notes.original: vayit’abel Shemu’el el Sha’ul — Samuel grieved over Saul
notes.rendering: Samuel grieves for Saul
notes.why: The closing verse is one of the most quietly devastating in the book. The final word on the Saul-Samuel relationship is not condemnation but mourning. Avel (to grieve, to mourn — the word used for mourning the dead) is what Samuel does for a living king. The political verdict is irrevocable; the personal grief is real and ongoing. YHWH shares the grief: the same verse says YHWH regrets (nacham again) that he made Saul king. The book refuses to let Saul’s rejection be clean or cold. He is mourned before he falls.

intro: Chapter 16 turns on two anointings that rhyme but diverge: the public ceremony at Mizpah in chapter 10 and this hidden one in Bethlehem. The anointing of David is private, unexplained to his family, never announced to Israel. It is also immediately followed by the most theologically unsettling sentence in the chapter: the Spirit that rushes on David simultaneously departs from Saul — replaced by something darker.

notes.original: YHWH yireh lalev — YHWH looks at the heart
notes.rendering: man looks on the outward appearance, but YHWH looks on the heart
notes.why: The contrast is between einayim (eyes, the visible surface) and lev (heart, the inner person, the seat of will and character). The verse is Samuel’s explicit retrospective correction of the criteria by which Saul was introduced in 9:2: tall, handsome, head-and-shoulders above everyone. Now YHWH announces those criteria are not his. David will be described as ruddy and handsome in v.12 — but the verse insists the physical description is incidental to the choice, not its basis.

notes.original: admoni im y’feh einayim v’tov ro’i — ruddy, with beautiful eyes and good-looking
notes.rendering: He is ruddy, with bright eyes and a handsome face
notes.why: Admoni (ruddy, red-complexioned) is a detail that will reappear when Esau is described — a word associated with vitality and outdoor life. David’s eyes are yafeh (beautiful, bright). The physical description comes after YHWH’s instruction not to judge by appearance, which is not a contradiction but a literary wink: David is beautiful, but that is not why he is chosen. The narrator gives us the looks and then refuses to let us rest on them.

notes.original: ruach ra’ah me’et YHWH — a harmful spirit from YHWH
notes.rendering: a harmful spirit from YHWH torments him
notes.why: The phrase is one of the most theologically difficult in Samuel. Ra’ah (bad, harmful, evil) modifies the spirit (ruach), and the spirit is attributed directly to YHWH: me’et YHWH, from YHWH. Ancient Hebrew theology did not yet develop the robust angelic/demonic intermediary structures of later Judaism; the distressing spirit that comes on Saul is not the devil but a divine affliction. The narrator will not soften it. Saul’s psychological disintegration is presented as YHWH’s active withdrawal — a darkness that falls where the Spirit once was.

intro: Chapter 17 is the book’s great set piece — the story the whole world knows. Its theology is not subtle, and that is its power. David’s speech before Goliath is not bravado; it is prophetic declaration. The battle is framed as a theological contest before the first stone flies: whose God will be known? David’s answer is given before the outcome, which is what makes it faith rather than confidence.

notes.original: maarchot Elohim chayyim — the armies of the living God
notes.rendering: the armies of the living God
notes.why: Elohim chayyim — the living God — is the title that distinguishes YHWH from the gods of wood and stone who do not live, do not act, do not speak. David uses it twice (vv.26, 36). The phrase implies that Goliath’s defiance of Israel’s army is defiance of their God, and that Israel’s God is alive to respond. It is also the first time in the chapter that anyone invokes YHWH in relation to the battle. The Israelite army is silent; the boy from Bethlehem is the only one who names the contest correctly.

notes.original: anochi ba elecha b’shem YHWH tzvaot — I come to you in the name of YHWH of hosts
notes.rendering: I come to you in the name of YHWH of hosts
notes.why: The formal contrast is between Goliath’s weapons (sword, spear, javelin) and David’s authority (the name of YHWH of hosts). YHWH tzvaot — YHWH of armies/hosts — is the great military title of the Ark Narrative (4:4) and of Hannah’s prayer (1:11). David is not fighting alone; he is fighting in the authority of the one who commands all armies. The speech is a formal legal challenge in YHWH’s name: what Goliath has done to Israel’s army is an offense against the God who commands them.

notes.original: ki l’YHWH ha-milchamah — for the battle is YHWH’s
notes.rendering: The battle belongs to YHWH
notes.why: The declaration ki l’YHWH ha-milchamah is the theological key to the whole narrative. The battle is not David’s achievement or Israel’s victory — it is YHWH’s battle, given into human hands as an act of grace. The same conviction underlies Gideon’s three hundred (Judges 7), Deborah’s war (Judges 4–5), and Jonathan’s solo assault in chapter 14. Hebrew battle theology consistently locates the decisive agency with YHWH while using human instruments. David’s speech makes this explicit before the sling is ever raised.

intro: Chapter 18 sets two movements in counterpoint: David rising (every verse confirms his success and love from all sides) and Saul falling (every verse confirms his fear, his murderous intent, his growing isolation). Between them stands Jonathan — the prince who gives away his own inheritance to the man who is about to take it, and calls the act love.

notes.original: nefesh Yonatan niqsherah b’nefesh David — the soul of Jonathan was bound to the soul of David
notes.rendering: the soul of Jonathan is bound to the soul of David
notes.why: Niqsherah (was bound, was knit, was tied — from qashar, to bind, to tie, to conspire) is used elsewhere for physical binding and for political alliances. Here it describes something more absolute than alliance: a soul-binding. The word nefesh (soul, life, breath, self) is used four times in two verses, insisting on the personal depth of what happens. Jonathan’s love for David is then stated three times in the chapter (vv.1, 3, 20) — the same word, ahavah, used for the covenant love YHWH shows his people.

notes.original: vayitpashet Yonatan et ham’il — Jonathan stripped himself of his robe
notes.rendering: Jonathan strips off the robe he is wearing and gives it to David
notes.why: The robe Jonathan removes is the royal heir’s robe — the garment of his inheritance and status. By giving it to David, Jonathan performs a wordless abdication. The gesture echoes the torn robe of chapter 15 (YHWH tearing the kingdom from Saul) but inverted: there the robe was taken; here the heir gives it freely. Jonathan adds his armor, his sword, his bow, and his belt — everything that marks a warrior and a prince. He empties himself of his future and places it on David.

notes.original: vayehi Sha’ul oyen et David — Saul was eyeing David
notes.rendering: Saul eyes David
notes.why: The verb ayin (to eye, to look at with suspicion, to keep a hostile watch on) is used only here in the Hebrew Bible. Its root is ayin — the eye — and the connotation is the evil eye, the malevolent gaze, the surveillance of a threatened man. Samuel told Saul in chapter 13 that YHWH was looking for a man after his own heart; now Saul looks at David and sees his replacement. The chapter’s refrain — YHWH was with David — is the direct cause of Saul’s fear. He is not afraid of David’s skill. He is afraid of YHWH’s presence.

intro: Chapter 19 is a chapter of escapes: three attempts on David’s life, three survivals. The final scene is the strangest in the Saul narrative — the Spirit of God disabling the king’s murder attempts by turning his messengers and then the king himself into naked prophets. The proverb from chapter 10 returns, but its tone has completely inverted.

notes.original: terafim — household gods, idols, figurines
notes.rendering: Michal takes a household idol
notes.why: Terafim (household gods, oracular figurines) are the small divine images kept in Israelite homes despite repeated prohibitions — Rachel steals her father’s terafim in Genesis 31; they appear in Judges 17–18 as objects of illicit domestic cult. Their presence in David’s house is mentioned without editorial comment, which is itself notable. Michal uses one to buy David the night he needs. The narrator does not ask whether David knew it was there. The idol that deceives Saul’s men saves YHWH’s anointed.

notes.original: vayitpashet gam hu bigadav — he too stripped off his clothes
notes.rendering: He strips off his robes and prophesies before Samuel, and lies naked
notes.why: The scene is the darkest reprise of the ‘Is Saul also among the prophets?’ proverb (first coined in 10:11). In chapter 10 the Spirit’s arrival on Saul was a sign of divine calling — Saul transformed into a new man. Here it is an undoing: the king arrives to commit murder and is stripped, thrown to the ground, and held there naked for an entire day. The Spirit that once empowered him now immobilises him. Nakedness in the Hebrew Bible is exposure, vulnerability, and shame. Saul lies naked before the prophet he tried to circumvent.

notes.original: dam naki — innocent blood
notes.rendering: why would you sin against innocent blood?
notes.why: Dam naki (innocent blood, clean blood) is the covenant legal category that makes murder of the guiltless a uniquely heinous offense — it defiles the land (Numbers 35:33), and YHWH himself is the avenger of it (Deuteronomy 19:10). Jonathan’s intercession is not merely tactical; it is a formal legal accusation: what Saul is planning is not execution but murder, and the blood of an innocent man will be on the king’s hands. Jonathan uses the full moral and covenantal weight of the phrase.

intro: Chapter 20 is Jonathan’s great chapter — the fullest portrait of a man who sees clearly what is coming and chooses loyalty over self-preservation. His father hurls a spear at him in verse 33, using on his own son the weapon twice aimed at David. The farewell at the field’s edge is one of the most quietly devastating scenes in the Hebrew Bible.

notes.original: ki f’sa bein’ u-vein ha-mavet — but a step between me and death
notes.rendering: there is barely a step between me and death
notes.why: The phrase is one of the great compression achievements of Hebrew prose — six words that make the reader feel the narrowness of the gap. Pesa (a step, a pace — from pasa, to step over) is the smallest unit of distance between two points. David is not saying his life is in danger; he is saying the margin between living and dying has shrunk to a single footfall. The word has an echo in Psalm 18:36 (you gave me a wide place for my steps) — the opposite image, the expansive safety YHWH provides.

notes.original: b’ahavato oto ki k’ahavat nafsho ’ahevo — his love for him, for he loved him as his own soul
notes.rendering: for he loves him as he loves his own soul
notes.why: The phrase ahavat nafsho — the love of his soul, the love of his self — is used three times across chapters 18 and 20 to describe Jonathan’s love for David. It is the love-language of covenant: the same formula used of the great commandment (you shall love your neighbor as yourself — Leviticus 19:18). Jonathan’s love is the model of covenantal love: freely given, costly in its consequences, directed toward someone who will receive what Jonathan has given up.

notes.original: vayivku yachdav — they wept together; David higgdil livkot — David wept the most
notes.rendering: They kiss each other and weep together — David weeping the most
notes.why: The narrator’s final measurement: David wept more. The comparison is not competitive; it is a measure of understanding. Both men know what this farewell means. David’s greater weeping may be because he knows more completely what he is losing — or what Jonathan is sacrificing. The covenant Jonathan speaks (YHWH between me and you, and between my children and your children, forever) will be fulfilled in 2 Samuel 9 when David finds Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth and restores everything to him. The oath survives the man who swore it.

intro: Chapter 21 is a chapter of desperate improvisations. David lies to the priest of Nob, is recognised at the Philistine court, and saves himself by feigning madness before the king whose champion he killed. The chapter plants two seeds: Doeg the Edomite watching in silence, and Goliath’s sword in David’s hand — both will matter in chapter 22.

notes.original: lechem ha-panim — bread of the face, bread of the Presence
notes.rendering: the Bread of the Presence
notes.why: Lechem ha-panim (bread of the face, bread of the Presence) is the twelve loaves placed weekly before YHWH in the sanctuary — a standing offering representing the twelve tribes (Leviticus 24:5–9). It is removed on the Sabbath and replaced with fresh bread; the old loaves are eaten by the priests alone. Ahimelech’s willingness to give it to David’s men — in an emergency, with the caveat about ritual purity — becomes the exegetical example Jesus cites in Mark 2:25–26 when challenged about Sabbath law: human need as the interpretive key to sacred regulation.

notes.original: Doeg ha-Edomi — Doeg the Edomite
notes.rendering: a man named Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul’s herdsmen
notes.why: Doeg is mentioned in a single verse, without dialogue or action. He is simply there, detained before YHWH — possibly completing a vow, possibly undergoing ritual purification — and he sees everything. The narrator notes his presence with the economy of a writer who knows the reader will need to remember it. When Saul cannot find anyone willing to kill the priests of Nob in chapter 22, Doeg steps forward. The watcher at Nob becomes the executioner of Nob. His name means ‘anxious’ or ‘fearful’ — a name the story earns.

notes.original: vayitholel b’yadayim — he feigned madness in their hands
notes.rendering: he disguises his sanity — acting deranged in their hands
notes.why: Vayitholel (he acted the madman — from halal, to be mad, to rave, to behave wildly) is the root of Hallel (praise) run through a dark register: ecstatic behavior that here means self-degradation rather than worship. David scratches the doors and lets spittle run — the marks of the ancients’ conception of madness. The irony is precise: the man who will be the greatest king in Israel’s history saves his life by convincing the Philistine king he is useless. The sword of Goliath is in his belt. He drools on the doorpost to stay alive.

intro: Chapter 22 is the darkest chapter in Samuel so far. Saul’s paranoia becomes massacre. The servants who would not kill now give way to the informer who will. Doeg does what four hundred soldiers refused to do: he kills eighty-five priests, then the whole city. David’s self-accusation in verse 22 is the most anguished line he speaks in the fugitive years.

notes.original: kol ish matzor... kol ish asher lo noshi... kol mar nefesh — every man in distress, in debt, bitter of soul
notes.rendering: everyone in distress, in debt, bitter in soul
notes.why: The three categories define the social base of David’s first army: the economically desperate (noshi — one who has a creditor, one under debt pressure), the politically threatened (matzor — in straits, hemmed in), and the spiritually broken (mar nefesh — bitter of soul, the same phrase used of Hannah in 1:10). The Adullam cave is a refuge for Israel’s losers and outcasts. That this is the nucleus from which the Davidic kingdom grows is a sustained irony the book does not explain.

notes.original: lo avdu avdei hamelech — the king’s servants would not raise their hands
notes.rendering: the king’s servants will not raise their hands to strike the priests of YHWH
notes.why: The refusal of Saul’s own soldiers is a moral data point the narrator records without comment. They will not kill priests — even under direct royal command. It takes Doeg, the Edomite outsider, to do it. His foreignness is part of the horror: the most sacred bloodshed in the book is carried out not by an Israelite soldier following orders but by a man who volunteers. The narrative does not call him a monster. It simply names what he does, and how many, and moves on.

notes.original: anochi sachoti b’nefesh kol beit avicha — I have brought about the death of all your father’s house
notes.rendering: I am responsible for the deaths of every person in your father’s house
notes.why: Sachoti (I have occasioned, I have brought about — from savav, to turn, to go around; here in the Hiphil: to cause to turn, to bring around) is a rare causative confession. David does not say he killed them; he says he caused their deaths. The distinction is precise and morally serious: he lied to Ahimelech, was seen by Doeg, and left the priest’s household exposed. He owns the chain of causation. This kind of moral clarity — taking responsibility for consequences he did not intend but should have foreseen — is one of the marks that distinguishes David’s character at its best.

intro: Chapter 23 is held together by the theme of inquiry — David asks YHWH twice before going to Keilah, then uses the ephod twice more to probe the loyalty of the very people he saved. The answer is always honest and never comfortable. Jonathan’s visit at Horesh is the last time the two men will see each other alive. He speaks David’s future plainly and asks nothing for himself.

notes.original: vayish’al David b’YHWH — David inquires of YHWH
notes.rendering: He inquires of YHWH
notes.why: The verb sha’al (to ask, to inquire) — the same root as the name Saul — marks a recurring contrast between the two men. Saul is the king Israel asked for (sha’al); David is the man who asks (sha’al) of YHWH before every major move. The inquiry via ephod (v.9–12) gives binary yes/no answers, but David asks the right questions: not ‘will I win?’ but ‘will Saul come?’ and ‘will the men of Keilah surrender me?’ He consults YHWH about the actual shape of his situation, not to solicit reassurance.

notes.original: vayechazek et yado b’Elohim — he strengthened his hand in God
notes.rendering: He strengthens David’s hand in God
notes.why: Chazak (to be strong, to strengthen, to grip firmly) — the word is physical as well as spiritual: Jonathan grips David’s hand and holds it fast in relation to God. The scene is the last of the Jonathan-David encounters. Jonathan says three things: do not be afraid; you will be king; I will stand at your side. Then he goes home. He will die at Jezreel in chapter 31 without seeing the first of those things fulfilled. His prophecy is his gift to David. His going home is his last act of integrity.

notes.original: Sela ha-Machlekot — Rock of Escape / Rock of Divisions
notes.rendering: that place is named the Rock of Escape
notes.why: Machlekot (divisions, partings, separations — from chalaq, to divide, to apportion) names the geography of the near-miss: Saul on one side of the mountain, David on the other, one man circling to catch the other. The Philistine raid that interrupts Saul is not presented as miraculous deliverance — the narrator simply records it, matter-of-factly. YHWH’s protection in the fugitive years rarely announces itself. It tends to arrive as a Philistine raid, an unexpected message, a step between pursuit and capture.

intro: Chapter 24 is the first of two cave-and-conscience scenes (the second is chapter 26). David holds Saul’s life in his hands, cuts one thread of his robe, and then is struck by what he has done. The restraint is theological, not tactical: Saul is the anointed of YHWH, and David will not be the instrument of his removal. Saul’s weeping confession is real — and will last exactly as long as it takes him to get home.

notes.original: vayak lev David oto — David’s heart struck him
notes.rendering: David’s heart strikes him
notes.why: The idiom is striking in its physicality: the heart (lev — the inner person, the moral center) does not merely trouble him but strikes him, beats him — as one strikes a blow. The verb nakah (to strike, to smite) is used elsewhere for violent physical attack. David’s conscience is described in the language of assault. He has cut one corner of a robe — not killed a man — and his heart hammers him for it. The scene establishes the moral texture that will define David throughout the fugitive years.

notes.original: meshiach YHWH — the anointed of YHWH
notes.rendering: He is the anointed of YHWH
notes.why: Meshiach YHWH (the anointed of YHWH, the one set apart by oil as YHWH’s designated agent) is the ground of David’s refusal — stated twice in one verse for emphasis. David does not say: Saul is innocent, or Saul was once a good man, or Saul may reform. He says: Saul is the anointed of YHWH, and that status is not revoked by Saul’s behavior. YHWH chose to anoint Saul; YHWH must choose when and how to remove him. The theology is rigorous: the office confers a protection the officeholder does not deserve and cannot forfeit by his own failure.

notes.original: achar mi yatza melech Yisrael... achar kelev met... achar parosh echad — after whom... a dead dog... a single flea
notes.rendering: A dead dog! A single flea!
notes.why: The self-deprecating images are precisely chosen. A dead dog (kelev met) is the most contemptible object in the ancient Near East: not merely an inferior creature but a worthless corpse. A single flea (parosh echad) is both microscopic and parasitic. Together they ask: why does the king of Israel mobilize three thousand men to hunt something so negligible? The rhetorical self-abasement also performs innocence: a man planning regicide does not describe himself as a flea. David’s smallness is the argument for his harmlessness.

intro: Chapter 25 is the book’s great wisdom story, and Abigail is its wisest figure. The chapter opens with Samuel’s death in a single verse and then gives its full attention to the woman who stands between David and a massacre he would have regretted the rest of his life. Her speech is the longest by a woman in the entire book of Samuel — and the most theologically rich.

notes.original: Naval — fool, senseless one; u-naval ma’asav — and his deeds were churlish
notes.rendering: Nabal is his name, and folly is with him
notes.why: Naval (fool, senseless, morally depraved — from a root meaning to wilt, to be worthless) is not merely a nickname but a character verdict the text endorses. The name is glossed in Abigail’s speech (v.25): k’shmo ken hu — as his name is, so is he. The naval in Hebrew wisdom literature is not the naive or the unintelligent but the person who lives as though there is no God, no consequence, no covenant obligation. Nabal’s refusal to honor the social contract of hospitality is naval behavior in its purest form.

notes.original: tzror ha-chayyim — the bundle of the living
notes.rendering: bound up in the bundle of the living in the care of YHWH your God
notes.why: Tzror ha-chayyim (bundle of the living, knot of life) is Abigail’s image for the security of the God-protected life — precious things tied up and kept safe, as valuables were carried in a bundle close to the body. The contrasting image is equally precise: the lives of David’s enemies YHWH will sling out (qela’ — the hollow of a sling). The sling that brought down Goliath becomes the image of divine judgment. Abigail speaks prophetically without being called a prophet.

notes.original: vayamot libo b’qirbo vayehi l’aven — his heart died within him and he became like a stone
notes.rendering: his heart dies within him and he becomes like a stone
notes.why: The medical picture is a sudden catastrophic event — almost certainly a stroke or cardiac arrest triggered by the shock of learning how close he came to annihilation. The heart (lev) that was ‘merry’ with wine in v.36 is dead in v.37. He turns to stone (even — a stone, a rock), the most inert thing in the world, the opposite of the living, moving, speaking man of v.10–11. He does not die for ten days, which the narrator notes without comment. He lives in that stone for ten days before YHWH strikes him.

intro: Chapter 26 is a deliberate echo of chapter 24 — the same temptation, the same refusal, the same confession from Saul, and then the same quiet parting. Scholars debate whether the two stories are variants of one event or two separate incidents; the text presents them as separate and the differences are theologically significant. Here David does not waver at all. The spear and the water jar are taken as proof, not the robe. And Saul’s confession is noticeably shorter.

notes.original: o yomo yavo v’met — or his day will come and he will die
notes.rendering: YHWH will strike him — or his day will come to die, or he will go down in battle
notes.why: David articulates three possible ends for Saul: divine strike, natural death, or death in battle. The third is exactly what happens in chapter 31. What is remarkable is what David excludes: my hand. He is not merely tactically cautious; he is theologically convinced that timing and agency belong to YHWH. The anointed can only be removed by the one who anointed. David’s restraint is not patience but theological conviction about how YHWH’s world works.

notes.original: tardematah YHWH — a deep sleep from YHWH
notes.rendering: a deep sleep from YHWH has fallen over them
notes.why: Tardemah (deep sleep, stupor, supernatural slumber — the same word used when YHWH caused Adam’s deep sleep in Genesis 2:21) is not ordinary exhaustion but divinely induced unconsciousness. The whole camp is given over to it. The narrator is explicit: this is from YHWH. David’s ability to walk through three thousand sleeping soldiers, take the king’s spear and water jar, and depart unseen is not stealth — it is miracle. YHWH arranges the scene and then holds everyone asleep while David makes his choice.

notes.original: lech avod elohim acherim — go, serve other gods
notes.rendering: Go and serve other gods
notes.why: David’s theological complaint is precise: to be driven from the land is to be cut off from the presence of YHWH, and to be cut off from YHWH’s presence is to be handed over to foreign gods by default. The land is YHWH’s territory; the gods of Philistia are the default deities of Philistine land. David is not tempted toward idolatry — he is describing what exile means in the ancient theological geography. His cry anticipates Psalm 42 (my soul thirsts for God… where shall I go?) and the exilic Psalms of disorientation.

intro: Chapter 27 is the most morally uncomfortable chapter in the fugitive narrative. David, the man after God’s own heart, calculates his survival prospects, defects to the enemy, and conducts raids he deliberately conceals from his Philistine host through systematic deception. The narrator records it without comment. The theological problem does not resolve — it simply continues into chapter 29.

notes.original: vayomer David el libo — David said to his heart
notes.rendering: David says to himself
notes.why: El libo (to his heart, within himself) is the marker of interior monologue — the rare moment when the narrator gives us David’s unguarded reasoning. The thought is not prayerful and not theological: it is a cold probability calculation. One day I will die by Saul’s hand. Therefore: defect. The man who twice refused to kill Saul because YHWH would handle it now reaches a conclusion with no YHWH in it at all. The contrast with David’s constant inquiry (sha’al) of YHWH in chapter 23 is stark. This decision is made without asking.

notes.original: Tziqlag — the narrator’s aside
notes.rendering: This is why Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day
notes.why: The parenthetical note is the narrator’s only aside that addresses the reader directly in the fugitive section. It anchors the story in a later reader’s geography: whoever is reading this knows where Ziklag is and who owns it. The detail also quietly validates David’s kingship: a Philistine gift to a refugee becomes a permanent holding of the Davidic crown. The fugitive years are not wasted years. Even a desperate defection leaves something behind.

notes.original: vaya’amen Achish b’David — Achish trusted David
notes.rendering: Achish trusts David completely
notes.why: The chapter ends on an irony so sharp it barely needs comment: the Philistine king fully trusts the man who is systematically deceiving him. Aman (to trust, to believe — the root of amen) is covenantal language for reliable faithfulness. Achish extends it to David in good faith; David is exploiting it in bad faith. The text does not resolve this. David is the hero of the book — and in this chapter he is also a liar whose lies preserve him to become king. The narrator holds both facts without flinching.

intro: Chapter 28 is the most haunted scene in the book. YHWH’s silence drives Saul to the very practice he suppressed. The dead prophet speaks once more — and says nothing that has not already been said. The woman’s final act of anonymous kindness is one of the great quiet moments of the narrative: the king who came to consult the dead eats bread and goes out into his last night.

notes.original: v’lo anahu YHWH gam b’chalomot gam b’urim gam b’nevi’im — YHWH did not answer him
notes.rendering: YHWH does not answer him — not by dreams, not by Urim, not by prophets
notes.why: The triple silence is a formal verdict. The three channels of divine communication — dreams, Urim, prophets — are the complete list available to an Israelite king. YHWH has closed all three. The silence is the answer. Saul’s frantic turn to the forbidden medium is not apostasy so much as desperation: he has exhausted every legitimate channel and finds only absence. The irony is that the dead prophet, when he comes, says nothing new — only confirms what was already said in chapters 13 and 15.

notes.original: elohim olim min ha-aretz — divine beings / a god coming up from the earth
notes.rendering: I see a divine being coming up out of the earth
notes.why: The woman’s description uses elohim (a divine being — here singular in function, referring to a single figure with divine status). What exactly she sees, and whether Samuel’s ghost is literally present, is the great exegetical question of the passage. The text does not explain the mechanism; it presents the event as real. Samuel speaks, Samuel knows, Samuel pronounces. Whether this is divine permission, demonic deception, or something the ancient world understood more readily than we do, the narrator does not say. He simply reports what happens.

notes.original: machar atah u-vanecha imi — tomorrow you and your sons will be with me
notes.rendering: Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me
notes.why: The verdict is exact and soon fulfilled. Samuel says ‘with me’ (imi) — in the place of the dead, in Sheol. It is the most precise death sentence in the book. And the final clause — YHWH will give the army of Israel into Philistine hands — expands the catastrophe beyond Saul’s own death to the nation he has failed. The battle of Jezreel in chapter 31 is not a surprise. Samuel has announced it in the dark, the night before it happens.

intro: Chapter 29 resolves the problem chapter 28 created: how does David fight alongside the Philistines against Israel? The answer is that he doesn’t — not because he refuses but because the Philistine commanders refuse him. The reader notices that YHWH does not appear in the chapter. The solution to David’s impossible position is arranged through Philistine politics, not divine intervention. The result is the same.

notes.original: v’lo yered iman’u ba-milchamah — he shall not go down with us to the battle
notes.rendering: He must not go down to battle with us
notes.why: The commanders’ reasoning is precisely correct, and the narrator knows it. David cannot fight against Israel. He has sworn loyalty to YHWH, been anointed king over Israel, and built his entire identity on service to Israel’s God. The Philistines’ suspicion — that he would turn against them to win back Saul’s favor — is the right instinct for the wrong reason. They think he is loyal to Saul; he is loyal to YHWH. Either way, he cannot be their weapon against Israel.

notes.original: chai YHWH ki yashar atah — as YHWH lives, you are trustworthy
notes.rendering: As YHWH lives, you have been reliable
notes.why: For the second time in the narrative, a Philistine king swears by YHWH — Israel’s covenant God, not a Philistine deity. Achish has absorbed enough of David’s world to use his oath form. The irony is layered: Achish swears by YHWH to affirm David’s reliability, while it is precisely YHWH’s claim on David that makes him unreliable as a Philistine soldier. The oath form and its content point in opposite directions.

intro: Chapter 30 is built around two pivots: David’s strengthening himself in YHWH (v.6) and the equal-shares ruling (v.24). The first is the great interior moment of the fugitive years — a man at the bottom of everything turning toward God rather than away. The second is one of the founding acts of Davidic leadership: a just distribution that becomes statute.

notes.original: vayitchazek David b’YHWH Elohav — David strengthened himself in YHWH his God
notes.rendering: David strengthens himself in YHWH his God
notes.why: The verb chazak (to be strong, to grip firmly — the same word Jonathan used when he ‘strengthened David’s hand in God’ in 23:16) here is reflexive: David strengthens himself. Jonathan is gone; there is no one to grip his hand. The men who have been his army for years are speaking of killing him. In the most isolated moment of the fugitive years, David turns to YHWH alone. The next verse is immediate: he inquires of YHWH, and YHWH answers. The strengthening is both theological act and practical pivot.

notes.original: k’cheleq ha-yored ba-milchamah u-k’cheleq ha-yoshev al ha-kelim yachdav yechallequ — as the share of the one who goes down to battle, so the share of the one who stays with the supplies — they shall share alike
notes.rendering: The share of the man who goes into battle shall be the same as the share of the man who stays with the supplies
notes.why: The ruling is just and it is remembered. The word cheleq (portion, share, lot) is the same root as the territorial allotments given to Israel’s tribes — everyone’s portion in the land is YHWH’s gift, not earned by fighting power. David’s principle extends the same logic to plunder: the victory belongs to YHWH, not to the strongest soldiers. The two hundred exhausted men who stayed behind are as entitled to the rescue as those who fought. This becomes statute (chuqah) — the first law David gives Israel.

intro: The book closes on a hillside, with the king who was chosen for his height lying dead alongside the son who was worth more than he was. Samuel’s prediction is exact to the detail: Saul and his sons on the same day. The last act of the book belongs not to David or to YHWH but to the men of Jabesh-gilead — the people Saul saved in his finest hour, repaying the debt twenty years later under cover of darkness.

notes.original: vayipol Sha’ul al charbo — Saul fell upon his sword
notes.rendering: Saul takes his own sword and falls on it
notes.why: The armor-bearer’s terror — he fears greatly (ki yare me’od) — echoes the terror that has surrounded Saul since chapter 18 but has never touched him correctly. His own men fear him; YHWH’s spirit has left him; he has lain naked on the ground at Ramah; he has spoken with the dead. Now, at the end, he chooses his own death rather than Philistine hands. The death has a kind of pride in it — and also a kind of theological precision: Saul’s fall is by his own sword, on the mountain, on the day Samuel predicted. He is not murdered; he is not even killed by the enemy. He ends himself.

notes.original: vayamot Sha’ul u-sh’loshet banav v’nose kelav v’chol anashav ba-yom ha-hu yachdav — Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on that day together
notes.rendering: Saul dies, along with his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men — together, on that day
notes.why: The verse is the book’s final accounting. Yachdav (together, as one) — the same word used for Jonathan’s soul bound to David’s, for Israel going out as one man. Here it gathers the dead: king, sons, servant, army — all together, all on the same day. Samuel said tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The exactness of the fulfillment is the book’s last theological statement: the word of YHWH spoken through a dead prophet, in a room the king was not supposed to enter, on the night before a battle he could not win, came true.

notes.original: vayyelchu kol ish chayil — all the valiant men arose
notes.rendering: all their fighting men rise and travel through the night
notes.why: The last act of the book is an act of loyalty — performed in darkness, for a dead king, by the people he saved twenty years earlier. In chapter 11 Saul rose to rescue Jabesh-gilead from Nahash’s threat of mutilation. Now Jabesh-gilead rescues Saul’s mutilated body from the wall of Beth-shan. They travel all night; they burn the bodies; they bury the bones; they fast seven days. The covenant of chapter 11 holds. The book ends not with David’s triumph or Saul’s disgrace but with faithfulness — the small, unglamorous, costly faithfulness of ordinary people who remembered.

intro: The Chronicler opens not with a narrative but with a list — and the list is the argument. Beginning from Adam, the genealogy sweeps through all humanity before narrowing to Israel, then to Judah, then to David. The structure is funnel-shaped: the whole earth is in view, and from it God draws one people and from that people one line. The Edomite king list (vv. 43–54) is remarkable for its candour: Edom has kings before Israel does. The Chronicler records the fact without embarrassment.

notes.original: Adam, Shet, Enosh... Noach — Shem, Ham, Yapheth
notes.rendering: Adam, Seth, Enosh... Noah — Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
notes.why: The opening ten names are presented without verbs — no 'begat,' no lifespans. The Chronicler strips the genealogy to pure lineage. The effect is stately and deliberate: these names are not biography but foundation. The list reprises Genesis 5 but without Genesis's interest in longevity. What matters is the chain, not the length of each link.

notes.original: hu hechel lihyot gibbor ba'aretz — he began to be a mighty man in the earth
notes.rendering: the first on earth to become a mighty warrior
notes.why: Hechel — began (chalal, to begin, but also to profane or pierce). The same root underlies the name Nimrod, which tradition connects with marad — to rebel. The Chronicler retains this loaded figure from Genesis 10 without commentary. Nimrod is simply noted as the first warrior-king — a prototype whose lineage runs through the very nations Israel will contend with.

notes.original: ki v'yamav niphlegah ha'aretz — for in his days the earth was divided
notes.rendering: for in his days the earth is divided
notes.why: Niphlegah — was divided (palag — to split, divide; the root of Peleg's name). The verse is its own etymology. The Chronicler does not explain what the division was — the Table of Nations in Genesis 10–11 provides the context. The name becomes a fixed historical marker: Peleg's generation is the generation of dispersal.

notes.original: u'v'nei Yisrael lo-malakh — before any king reigned over the Israelites
notes.rendering: before any king reigns over the Israelites
notes.why: The Edomite king list is one of the oldest pieces of historical data in the Bible. Its formula — 'when X died, Y reigned in his place' — differs significantly from Israel's dynastic pattern because Edomite succession is not hereditary but electoral or military. The Chronicler includes the list without ideological comment: Israel is younger as a kingdom. The Chronicler's readers after the exile would have felt the irony — the kingdom that once was is now a memory like Edom's kings.

intro: Chapter 2 narrows the genealogical lens from all humanity to the twelve sons of Israel, then immediately narrows further to Judah — the tribe from which David comes. The Chronicler's interest is not neutral: Judah is the first tribe treated at length. The genealogy is not merely historical; it is theological prioritisation in list form.

notes.original: Er b'chor Yehudah ra be'einei YHWH — Er the firstborn of Judah was evil in the eyes of YHWH
notes.rendering: Er, Judah's firstborn, is wicked in the sight of the LORD, and he puts him to death.
notes.why: The Chronicler mentions Er's death with stark brevity — three words where Genesis 38 gives a full narrative. This is characteristic of the Chronicler's genealogical method: moral information is registered but not elaborated. The reader is expected to know the story. The purpose here is to establish that Perez, not Er, carries the Judahite line forward — and Perez is the ancestor of David.

notes.original: Achar okher Yisrael asher ma'al ba'cherem — Achar who troubled Israel by violating the devoted thing
notes.rendering: Achar, who troubles Israel by violating the devoted thing
notes.why: Achar — literally 'trouble' (achar — to make turbid, to disturb). In Joshua 7 the man's name is Achan; Chronicles preserves Achar, a name that is itself a judgment. Ma'al ba'cherem — he acted unfaithfully against the devoted thing (cherem — that which is placed under the ban, devoted to destruction; to take it for oneself is a grave sacrilege). The brief note is a reminder that the genealogy is not sanitised: violation and judgment are part of the lineage.

notes.original: David ha'shvi'i — David the seventh
notes.rendering: David the seventh.
notes.why: In 1 Samuel 16, Jesse presents seven sons before David — making David the eighth. Chronicles gives him as the seventh, which may reflect a different tradition, the death of one son before the census, or the Chronicler's theological schematisation. Either way, the placement of David at the end of the list, after six brothers, is the culmination: the list has been building to this name since verse 1.

notes.original: v'l'Sheshan ein banim ki im banot — Sheshan had no sons, only daughters
notes.rendering: Sheshan has no sons, only daughters. Sheshan has an Egyptian slave whose name is Jarha.
notes.why: The Sheshan-Jarha arrangement — a free Israelite woman given in marriage to an Egyptian slave to continue the family line — is striking evidence of social flexibility in pre-monarchic Israel. The line continues through this union for thirteen generations (vv. 36–41), ending in Elishama. The Chronicler records it without comment. Lineage, however it is established, is what matters.

intro: Chapter 3 is the Davidic spine of Chronicles — the chapter to which everything before has been leading and which gives everything after its legitimacy. The list of David's sons establishes the dynasty; the post-exilic tail of the genealogy (vv. 17–24) carries it down into the Chronicler's own era. The fact that the line continues past the exile is itself a theological statement: the covenant with David has not ended.

notes.original: b'nei David asher noldu lo b'Chevron — the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron
notes.rendering: the sons of David born to him in Hebron
notes.why: The Chronicler lists six sons born in Hebron and nine in Jerusalem — fifteen in total from the wives, plus sons from concubines and the daughter Tamar. The parallel in 2 Samuel 3 and 5 has minor variations; Chronicles shows signs of independent tradition. The theological point is abundance: David's house is fruitful, the dynasty is established, the royal line is wide.

notes.original: arba'ah mi'Bat-shua bat Ammiel — four by Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel
notes.rendering: four by Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel
notes.why: 2 Samuel 11:3 gives Bathsheba's father as Eliam; Chronicles gives Ammiel — the same consonants in inverted order (both mean 'my kinsman is God'). Chronicles also uses the name Bath-shua rather than Bathsheba. Among Bath-shua's four sons is Nathan (v. 5), whose line, not Solomon's, becomes significant in later genealogical tradition (Luke 3:31 traces Jesus through Nathan rather than Solomon).

notes.original: b'nei Yechonyah ha'asur — the sons of Jeconiah the captive
