notes.rendering: the sons of Jeconiah the captive
notes.why: Ha'asur — the captive, the prisoner (asar — to bind, to imprison). Jeconiah (also called Jehoiachin) was taken to Babylon in 597 BCE, where he remained for decades before being released by Evil-merodach (2 Kings 25:27–30). The epithet 'the captive' is not merely biographical; it marks the turning point of the entire dynasty. Everything that follows — Shealtiel, Zerubbabel — emerges from exile. Zerubbabel is the governor who leads the return; his name anchors the post-exilic community to the Davidic line.

notes.original: b'nei Zerubavel... u'vnei Eliyo'einai — the sons of Zerubbabel... the sons of Elioenai
notes.rendering: Zerubbabel and the post-exilic generations down to Anani
notes.why: The genealogy extends six or seven generations beyond Zerubbabel, placing its final composition well into the Persian period (fifth or fourth century BCE). The last name, Anani, has been connected by some interpreters with 'anani — 'my cloud,' and read messianically (cf. Daniel 7:13 — one like a son of man coming with the clouds). Whether or not that reading is intended, the genealogy ends with the promise still open: the line has not died. The booth of David may be fallen (cf. Amos 9:11), but it is not extinct.

intro: Chapter 4 continues through Judah's sub-clans before turning briefly to Simeon. Embedded in the genealogy is one of the most unexpectedly personal passages in Chronicles — the prayer of Jabez (vv. 9–10), a name-etymology and petition that interrupts the list of names to remind the reader that behind every name is a life, a cry, an answer.

notes.original: Yabetz nichbad me'echav — Jabez was more honoured than his brothers
notes.rendering: Jabez is more honoured than his brothers. His mother names him Jabez, saying, 'I bore him in pain.'
notes.why: Yabetz — Jabez; the name is here connected to otsev — pain, sorrow. His mother named him after her suffering. The prayer that follows is a fourfold petition: blessing, enlarged territory, divine presence, and protection from harm. Each element maps onto the ancestral promises (Genesis 12; 26; 28). The remarkable thing is that God answers: va'yave Elohim et asher sha'al — God granted what he asked. The prayer is not commentary on the genealogy; it is a window through it.

notes.original: ha'osei vad — those who work linen
notes.rendering: the linen workers' guild at Beth-ashbea
notes.why: The guild of linen workers at Beth-ashbea is one of several craft-community notices in this genealogy (cf. potters at Netaim, craftsmen of Ge-harashim in v. 14). The Chronicler is interested in how Judahite clans occupy their social and economic roles. These craft guilds pass their trades down within the family — the genealogy is also an occupational record.

notes.original: v'achehem lo hirbu — but his brothers did not multiply
notes.rendering: his brothers do not have many children, and all their clan does not multiply as much as the sons of Judah
notes.why: The explicit comparison with Judah is the Chronicler's way of marking Simeon's lesser significance. Simeon's territory was eventually absorbed into Judah; the tribe effectively disappears as a distinct entity. The genealogy preserves the memory of a tribe that was historically overshadowed. The Chronicler does not erase Simeon but notes the demographic reality.

intro: Chapter 5 covers the Transjordanian tribes — Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. The Chronicler opens with an explanation for why Reuben, the firstborn, does not hold the position of honour: his sin with Bilhah (Genesis 35:22) costs him the birthright. The chapter ends with exile — the definitive consequence of covenant infidelity.

notes.original: ki chilel yetzu'ah aviv — because he defiled his father's bed
notes.rendering: because he defiles his father's bed, his birthright is given to the sons of Joseph
notes.why: The Chronicler explains the structure of Israelite primogeniture with unusual candour: Reuben is the firstborn but is disqualified. Judah produces the ruler (David), and Joseph receives the double portion through his two sons Ephraim and Manasseh. The division of the birthright is the theological key to understanding why Chronicles places so much weight on Judah and Joseph — both are inheritors of what Reuben forfeited.

notes.original: va'ye'azru aleihem — and they received help against them
notes.rendering: they receive help against them... because they cry to God in the battle, and he grants their plea, because they trust in him
notes.why: Va'ye'azru — they were helped (azar — to help, to support; the same root in Ezra's name). The theological mechanics are explicit: they cry (za'aq — to cry out urgently), they trust (batach — to rely upon, to lean on), God grants. This is the Chronicler's consistent formula: military success is not the result of troop numbers or tactics but of covenantal fidelity. The same formula governs the wars of David and the kings of Judah throughout Chronicles.

notes.original: vayiznu acharei elohei amei ha'aretz — and they whored after the gods of the peoples of the land
notes.rendering: they break faith with the God of their ancestors, and whore after the gods of the peoples of the land
notes.why: Ma'al — to break faith (the same ma'al used of Achan in 2:7; of Saul in 10:13). The verb carries the force of sacrilegious breach of trust. The consequence is exile — not as punishment from an angry deity but as the logical result of abandoning the relationship on which everything depended. The Assyrian kings (Pul = Tiglath-pileser III) are instruments of a divine purpose: the God of Israel stirs their spirit.

intro: Chapter 6 is the Levitical heart of the genealogical section — the longest chapter of the nine. The Chronicler traces the high-priestly line from Aaron to the exile, establishes the lineages of the three great Levitical families, and devotes special attention to the musicians David appoints. The chapter closes with the list of Levitical cities — a reminder that the Levites' inheritance is not land but dispersal throughout the people.

notes.original: hu asher kohen ba'bayit asher banah Shlomoh b'Yerushalayim — he who served as priest in the temple which Solomon built
notes.rendering: he is the one who serves as priest in the temple that Solomon builds in Jerusalem
notes.why: The parenthetical identification of Azariah is one of the Chronicler's historical anchors: the high-priestly line passes through this man who serves in Solomon's temple. The Chronicler is tracing not an abstract lineage but an institutional continuity — the line of Aaron who serves the altar runs from Phinehas (son of Eleazar, son of Aaron) through the generations to Jehozadak, who goes into exile. The chain is unbroken even in catastrophe.

notes.original: b'haghlot YHWH et Yehudah v'Yerushalayim — when the LORD sent Judah and Jerusalem into exile
notes.rendering: Jehozadak goes into exile when the LORD sends Judah and Jerusalem into exile by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar
notes.why: The exile is presented as the LORD's own action — not merely a military defeat but a divine deportation. B'yad Nevuchadnetzar — by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar: the Babylonian king is the instrument. The priestly line does not end at the exile; it is carried into Babylon. The implication is crucial for the Chronicler's post-exilic community: the priests who serve in the restored temple are the legitimate heirs of Aaron's line.

notes.original: asher higid David al yad shir — whom David stationed for the service of song
notes.rendering: the men whom David puts in charge of the service of song in the house of the LORD after the ark rests there
notes.why: The establishment of the temple musicians is one of the Chronicler's signature interests. Where Samuel-Kings barely mentions the Levitical singers, Chronicles traces their genealogies across three families (Heman / Kohath, Asaph / Gershom, Ethan / Merari) and grounds their appointment in David himself. The music of the temple is as much David's legacy as the building plans. The ark's rest (nuach — to rest, to settle; the same root as Noah and Canaan's 'rest') is the moment the liturgical music begins.

notes.original: v'Aharon u'vanav maqtirin — but Aaron and his sons were the ones who burned offerings
notes.rendering: Aaron and his sons make offerings on the altar of burnt offering... and to make atonement for Israel
notes.why: The distinction is important: the Levites serve and sing, but Aaron's sons alone make the offerings and the atonement. The verb kipper — to make atonement (literally to cover, to wipe clean) — reserves to the Aaronic priesthood the sacrificial function at the centre of Israel's worship. The Chronicler inserts this priestly charter precisely between the Levitical genealogy and the city list, to ensure the distinction is not blurred.

intro: Chapter 7 sweeps through the remaining northern tribes with varying degrees of detail. Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Asher are each given space — though notably Dan and Zebulun are absent, for reasons scholars still debate. The Ephraim section (vv. 20–29) contains an extraordinary embedded story: a family raid gone wrong, a father's grief, and a daughter who builds cities.

notes.original: vayit'abel Ephrayim avihem yamim rabbim — and Ephraim their father mourned many days
notes.rendering: Ephraim their father mourns many days, and his brothers come to comfort him
notes.why: The grief of Ephraim over his sons killed in the Gath raid is one of the few moments of personal anguish in the genealogical section. Va'yavo el ishto — and he went in to his wife: the text uses the same verb as in Genesis for conjugal intimacy. The son born from this grief is named Beriah — connected to be'ra'ah — in calamity, in disaster. The name is a scar. The Chronicler does not smooth this out.

notes.original: u'vito She'erah — and his daughter was Sheerah
notes.rendering: His daughter is Sheerah, who builds both Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah
notes.why: Sheerah is one of a very small number of women in the Hebrew Bible credited with building cities. The two Beth-horons are important towns on the main road from the coast to Jerusalem; they appear in Joshua's campaigns, in Solomon's building programme, and in the Maccabean wars. A woman's name is on their foundation. The Chronicler records this without comment — which is its own kind of emphasis.

notes.original: Nun bno, Yehoshua bno — Nun his son, Joshua his son
notes.rendering: Nun his son, Joshua his son
notes.why: The genealogy of Ephraim arrives at Joshua — the great general who leads Israel into the land — in verse 27. He appears at the end of a nine-generation chain from Ephraim. The placement is deliberate: Joshua belongs to the family that received Joseph's double portion, and his conquest of the land fulfils the promise given to that family. His appearance here, embedded in a list, is understated; his story is told elsewhere. The Chronicler notes the lineage and moves on.

intro: Chapter 8 returns to Benjamin — the tribe already covered briefly in chapter 7 — with far greater detail. The reason becomes clear at the chapter's end: this is the genealogy that leads to Saul. The Chronicler is setting up the transition from Saul to David that will dominate chapter 10 onwards. Benjamin matters because it is the tribe of the first king, whose failure makes way for the second.

notes.original: Ner holid et Kish, v'Kish holid et Sha'ul — Ner fathered Kish, and Kish fathered Saul
notes.rendering: Ner fathers Kish, and Kish fathers Saul, and Saul fathers Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal
notes.why: The appearance of Saul's name arrives without fanfare — he is simply a node in the genealogical chain. The Chronicler is not interested in Saul's heroism or his tragedy; he is interested in the dynasty. Jonathan's son appears in verse 34 as Merib-baal — the same person called Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel (the name was changed, likely to remove the element 'baal' from a proper name). Chronicles preserves the older form without editorial comment.

notes.original: u'ven Yonatan Merib-ba'al — and the son of Jonathan was Merib-baal
notes.rendering: the son of Jonathan: Merib-baal; and Merib-baal fathers Micah
notes.why: Merib-baal — 'Baal contends' or 'Baal is my advocate.' In 2 Samuel 4:4 and 9:6 he appears as Mephibosheth — 'from the mouth of shame' (a polemical replacement using bosheth, shame, for baal). Chronicles uses the original theophoric form without alteration. This is one of several places where Chronicles preserves names that later tradition found theologically uncomfortable. The Chronicler's interest is genealogical accuracy, not theological sanitising.

intro: Chapter 9 is the hinge of the book. The genealogies end; the narrative is about to begin. But before the story of David starts, the Chronicler pauses to list the returned exiles — the community to whom the book is addressed. The great genealogical arc from Adam (chapter 1) arrives here, in Jerusalem, in the generation after the exile. The names in this list are not ancient; they are the names of the Chronicler's neighbours. Then, at the end of the chapter, the Saulide genealogy reappears — preparing the reader for chapter 10 and the death that clears the way for David.

notes.original: u'Yehudah hoglah l'Bavel b'ma'alam — and Judah was carried away captive to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness
notes.rendering: Judah is carried away into exile in Babylon because of their unfaithfulness
notes.why: Ma'al — unfaithfulness (the recurring Chronicler's word: used of Achan, Saul, the Transjordanian tribes). The exile is not a geopolitical accident; it is the consequence of a broken covenant. The Chronicler does not dwell on this; he states it and immediately moves to restoration. The first word of verse 2 is v'harishoniym — 'and the first ones,' the returnees. The exile is a clause; the return is the sentence.

notes.original: v'hayoshviym harishoniym ba'achuzatam b'areihem — and the first who lived in their possessions in their cities
notes.rendering: the first to live again in their possessions in their cities are Israel, the priests, the Levites, and the temple servants
notes.why: The fourfold order — Israel, priests, Levites, temple servants — is the Chronicler's hierarchy of the restored community. The nethinim (temple servants, from natan — to give, to assign) appear here for the first time in Chronicles; they will be prominent in Ezra-Nehemiah. The community that returns is structured around the temple and its service. This is what it means to be Israel after the exile: a people organised around worship.

notes.original: David u'Shemu'el haro'eh yissadum bi'emunatasam — David and Samuel the seer established them in their office of trust
notes.rendering: David and Samuel the seer establish them in their office of trust
notes.why: The Chronicler reaches back to Samuel — not a figure he has discussed in the genealogies — to establish the antiquity of the gatekeeper office. Bi'emunatasam — in their office of trust (emunah — faithfulness, reliability; the same root as 'amen'). The gatekeepers are not minor functionaries; they are trusted custodians of the threshold between the holy and the common. David's organisation of the temple service is being anticipated: this verse looks forward to chapters 23–27.

notes.original: hem b'lishakhot p'turim — they are in the chambers, exempt from other service
notes.rendering: these are the singers... who live in the chambers of the temple free from other service, for they are on duty day and night
notes.why: The singers are exempt from other Levitical duties because their service is continuous — day and night. The image of unceasing song in the temple is one of the Chronicler's most characteristic contributions to biblical theology. The temple is not a building that opens for services; it is a place where worship never stops. This vision of perpetual liturgy shaped the later Jewish practice of daily prayer and the early Christian practice of the liturgy of the hours.

intro: The Chronicler's narrative begins here — not with Saul's anointing, his early victories, or his gradual corruption, but with his death. Chronicles has no interest in the long arc of Saul's story as Samuel tells it; Saul matters only as the foreground against which David appears. The two-verse theological verdict (vv. 13–14) is the most concentrated statement of the Chronicler's interpretive method: history is explained by faithfulness or its absence.

notes.original: va'yamot Sha'ul u'shloshet banav u'chol beito yachdav metu — thus Saul died and his three sons and all his house died together
notes.rendering: Thus Saul dies — he and his three sons and all his house dies together
notes.why: The Chronicler adds 'all his house' to the 1 Samuel 31 account, which mentions only the three sons. This expands the scope of the dynastic collapse: the Saulide house is extinguished in a single day. The addition is not careless; it serves the Chronicler's purpose of showing that there is no rival claimant remaining when David comes to the throne.

notes.original: va'yamot Sha'ul b'ma'alo asher ma'al ba'YHWH — so Saul died in his unfaithfulness which he committed against the LORD
notes.rendering: So Saul dies for his unfaithfulness. He is unfaithful to the LORD in that he does not keep the command of the LORD, and also consults a medium
notes.why: Ma'al — unfaithfulness (the term that began in 2:7 with Achan, then 5:25 with the Transjordanian tribes). The Chronicler uses it twice in verse 13. Saul's consultation of the medium (1 Samuel 28) and his failure to keep the command (1 Samuel 13, 15) are given equal weight. The real failure is in verse 14: lo darash ba'YHWH — he did not seek from the LORD. Darash — to seek, to inquire, to pursue (the same root as midrash — the seeking that produces exposition). Not seeking YHWH is, for the Chronicler, the root of all failure.

intro: Chapter 11 opens the Davidic narrative with three deliberate moves: the national covenant (all Israel gathers), the capture of the capital (Jerusalem becomes the city of David), and the roster of warriors (the men who make the kingdom possible). The Chronicler omits the seven-year reign in Hebron and the slow consolidation of power — David is king of all Israel from the start.

notes.original: attah hotze'ta v'heveta et Yisrael — you were the one who led out and brought in Israel
notes.rendering: it was you who led out and brought in Israel
notes.why: The idiom 'lead out and bring in' (hotzi ve-hevi) is the standard biblical description of military leadership — the general who takes the troops to battle and brings them home. The people are appealing to David's proven record: you have been our de facto king for years. The Chronicler omits David's history of service to Saul; this verse is all the people need to say. The transition is presented as a recognition of what has already been true.

notes.original: va'yit'aveh David va'yomar — and David longed and said
notes.rendering: David says longingly, 'Oh that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem'
notes.why: The water episode is one of the great vignettes of warrior loyalty. David's longing is casual — a soldier's nostalgia for home. The three warriors take it as a command and break through enemy lines to fulfil it. David's response — he pours it out to the LORD — turns an act of loyalty into an act of worship. The water becomes blood; the blood becomes offering. David refuses to drink the gift because its cost is too high for personal consumption. This moment reveals David's character more than any military victory.

notes.original: Uriah ha'Chitti — Uriah the Hittite
notes.rendering: Uriah the Hittite
notes.why: Uriah appears in the list of David's thirty mighty warriors — one of the king's most loyal soldiers. The Chronicler places this name in the list without comment. The reader of Samuel knows what happened to Uriah; Chronicles says nothing. The inclusion of his name in the roll of honour is, in its silence, a kind of testimony: this man was among the finest warriors David had. What was done to him stands against everything the list celebrates.

intro: Chapter 12 is the Chronicler's great mustering scene. Warriors come from every tribe — even from Saul's own tribe of Benjamin, even from Manasseh — to join David. The chapter builds to the feast at Hebron, where all Israel eats together in joy. This is the Chronicler's vision of Israel as it ought to be: united, fed, and celebrating its king.

notes.original: asher peneihem k'fnei ha'aryeh — whose faces were like the faces of lions
notes.rendering: whose faces are like the faces of lions, and who are swift as gazelles upon the mountains
notes.why: The double simile — lion faces, gazelle speed — is the Chronicler's most vivid piece of martial poetry. The lion's face suggests ferocity, resolve, and the threat that stops an enemy in their tracks; the gazelle's speed suggests the kind of warrior who cannot be caught or escaped. The Gadites who cross the Jordan in flood season (v. 15) and rout the valley-dwellers are presented as elemental forces rather than merely skilled soldiers.

notes.original: v'Ruach lavsha et Amasai — and the Spirit clothed Amasai
notes.rendering: Then the Spirit comes upon Amasai
notes.why: Lavsha — clothed (lavash — to put on, to be clothed with). The Spirit does not merely descend on Amasai; it dresses him, envelops him like a garment. This is the language used in Judges 6:34 for Gideon and 2 Chronicles 24:20 for Zechariah son of Jehoiada. The speech Amasai delivers — a lyrical pledge of loyalty — is therefore not his own composition but the Spirit's. The Chronicler marks the moment of David's legitimacy with a prophetic endorsement.

notes.original: m'vnei Yissachar yod'ei vinah la'itim — from the sons of Issachar, men who knew understanding of the times
notes.rendering: men who have understanding of the times to know what Israel ought to do
notes.why: Binah la'itim — understanding of the times (binah — insight, discernment; eit — time, season, moment). This brief notice has had an outsized influence: the sons of Issachar become in Jewish tradition a byword for wisdom about history and timing. The phrase implies not merely calendrical knowledge but political and theological discernment — knowing when to act, what the moment requires. Only two hundred of them come, but they bring all their kinsmen under their command.

notes.original: ki simchah b'Yisrael — for there was joy in Israel
notes.rendering: for there is joy in Israel
notes.why: The feast at Hebron — food carried on camels and mules from Zebulun and Naphtali, three days of eating and drinking — is the Chronicler's image of shalom. Simchah — joy (not merely pleasure or contentment, but the active, outward expression of wellbeing). The same word will govern David's bringing of the ark to Jerusalem (15:25) and Solomon's dedication of the temple (2 Chr 7:10). Joy, for the Chronicler, is the measure of a community in right relationship with God and with itself.

intro: The first attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem ends in disaster. The Chronicler presents this not as a story of divine caprice but as a lesson in the proper ordering of worship — the point will be made explicit in chapter 15. What matters here is that David begins with consultation, with communal decision-making, with proper intent. The problem is not his heart but his method.

notes.original: v'nashivah et aron Eloheinu eleinu ki lo d'rashnuhu bimei Sha'ul — let us bring back the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul
notes.rendering: let us bring back the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul
notes.why: D'rashnuhu — we sought it (darash — to seek, inquire; the same root used of Saul's failure in 10:14). The ark has been sitting at Kiriath-jearim since the Philistines returned it (1 Samuel 6–7). Saul reigned without seeking the presence it embodied. David's first major act as king of all Israel is to remedy this: to make the ark — and therefore the LORD — central to the national life.

notes.original: va'yichar af YHWH b'Uzzah vayakkeihu al asher shalach yado al ha'aron — and the anger of the LORD burned against Uzzah and he struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark
notes.rendering: the anger of the LORD is kindled against Uzzah, and he strikes him down because he put out his hand to the ark
notes.why: The death of Uzzah has troubled readers for millennia. The Chronicler does not explain or mitigate it. The ark is holy — qadosh, set apart, charged with divine presence. The cart is wrong (the law requires Levites to carry the ark on poles, Numbers 4:15); the touch is wrong. David's anger and then his fear in verses 11–12 are the appropriate human responses. The story teaches that holiness is not managed; it is approached on its own terms.

notes.original: va'yivarekh YHWH et beit Oved-Edom — and the LORD blessed the household of Obed-edom
notes.rendering: the LORD blesses the household of Obed-edom and all that he has
notes.why: The same presence that is dangerous in the wrong hands becomes a source of blessing in the right ones. Obed-edom the Gittite — an outsider, from Gath (a Philistine city) — receives what Israel's king cannot yet receive. The reversal is characteristic of the Chronicler's theology: the blessing of the ark waits not on ethnicity or status but on whether the one who receives it is in right relation to holiness.

intro: Chapter 14 is positioned between the two ark narratives (chapters 13 and 15) as an interlude that shows the Davidic blessing flowing outward. The palace, the family, the military victories — all are consequences of the divine favour established in chapter 13's closing verse. The Philistine campaigns bracket the chapter and end with David's fame reaching all nations.

notes.original: va'yeda David ki hechino lo YHWH l'melekh al Yisrael — and David knew that the LORD had established him as king over Israel
notes.rendering: David knows that the LORD has established him as king over Israel, and that his kingdom is highly exalted for the sake of his people Israel
notes.why: Ki nisa malkhuto ma'alah ba'avur amo Yisrael — because his kingdom is lifted up on high for the sake of his people Israel. The Davidic kingdom is not established for David's own honour but for Israel's sake. This is the Chronicler's consistent corrective: the king's greatness is instrumental, not terminal. The exaltation serves the people.

notes.original: va'yish'al David b'Elohim — and David inquired of God
notes.rendering: David inquires of God
notes.why: Va'yish'al — and he asked, inquired (sha'al — to ask, to inquire; the root of Saul's name, sha'ul — the asked-for one). The contrast is pointed: Saul (sha'ul) consulted a medium rather than asking YHWH (10:13–14); David (chapter 14) consults God directly before both Philistine engagements. The king who asks and receives divine direction is the model the Chronicler sets against the king who sought guidance elsewhere.

notes.original: b'shmoa'kha et qol hatsead b'rashei hab'ka'im — when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees
notes.rendering: when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then go out to battle, for God has gone out before you
notes.why: The sound in the balsam trees is one of the most arresting images in Chronicles: the divine army moves through the treetops, and its rustling is the signal to advance. God goes before — panah — to face, to go forward; the same root as panim, face. The battle is already won in the unseen realm before David's army moves. The Chronicler's warfare is consistently theophanic: the human army follows where the divine army leads.

intro: Chapter 15 is the correction of chapter 13. David now knows what he did not know before: the ark must be carried by Levites on poles, not by oxen on a cart. The Chronicler's explanation in verse 13 is explicit and theological: the first attempt failed because they did not seek God according to the rule. The second attempt succeeds because order is restored. The celebration that follows is one of the most elaborately described liturgical events in the Hebrew Bible.

notes.original: ki rak ha-Leviyim yis'u et aron ha-Elohim — for only the Levites may carry the ark of God
notes.rendering: No one is to carry the ark of God but the Levites, for the LORD has chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD
notes.why: The Chronicler's David articulates the principle the first attempt violated: the Levites are chosen (bachar — elected, set apart) for this specific task. This is not legalism; it is order. The Chronicler is writing for a post-exilic community rebuilding its liturgical life and needs to establish that worship has proper form — that not everything is interchangeable.

notes.original: ki lo d'rashnuhu kamishpat — because we did not seek him according to the rule
notes.rendering: because we did not seek him according to the rule
notes.why: Ki lo d'rashnuhu — because we did not seek him (darash again — the word that governs the entire theology of Chronicles). The mishpat — the rule, the ordinance, the right procedure — was written in Torah (Numbers 4:15). David's confession here is one of the most theologically significant moments in Chronicles: the king admits the mistake was his, identifies its source (failure to consult Torah), and corrects it. This is what repentance looks like in Chronicles: not sackcloth but inquiry.

notes.original: va'tere et ha'melekh David m'pazzez um'chakel — and she saw King David leaping and dancing
notes.rendering: Michal the daughter of Saul looks out of the window and sees King David dancing and celebrating, and she despises him in her heart
notes.why: The Chronicler retains this detail from 2 Samuel 6 — Michal's contempt — but omits the confrontation that follows (2 Samuel 6:20–23). What is retained is the contrast: David in linen, dancing before the ark; Michal watching from behind glass, despising. She is identified here as 'daughter of Saul' rather than wife of David — a genealogical judgment. The house of Saul cannot celebrate what the house of David embodies.

intro: Chapter 16 is the liturgical climax of the opening section of Chronicles. The ark is in place; the Levites are appointed; the psalm is sung. The great psalm of verses 8–36 is a composite drawn from Psalms 105, 96, and 106, assembled by the Chronicler to mark this founding moment. Its themes — thanksgiving, covenant memory, universal praise, the prayer for the exiles — are perfectly suited to the post-exilic community the Chronicler is addressing.

notes.original: va'yechalek l'khol ish Yisrael — and he distributed to every man of Israel
notes.rendering: he distributes to all Israel, both man and woman, to each a loaf of bread, a portion of meat, and a cake of raisins
notes.why: The royal feast distributed to every Israelite is David's first act after installing the ark. The addition 'both man and woman' (ish u'ishah in some textual traditions, reflected in 2 Samuel 6:19) emphasises the radical inclusiveness of the celebration. The three gifts — bread, meat, raisins — are a full meal. The king who brings the ark feeds the people. Worship and provision are inseparable.

notes.original: oz v'chedvah bimqomo — strength and joy are in his place
notes.rendering: Splendour and majesty are before him; strength and joy are in his place
notes.why: This verse adapts Psalm 96:6, which reads 'strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.' The Chronicler changes 'beauty' (tif'eret in some traditions) to chedvah — joy, gladness (from chadu — to rejoice; rare in biblical Hebrew, concentrated in Chronicles and Ezra). Joy is the Chronicler's signature note: it is what characterises authentic worship. The presence of YHWH does not produce merely awe but chedvah.

notes.original: hodu la'YHWH ki tov ki l'olam chasdo — give thanks to the LORD for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever
notes.rendering: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Say also: Save us, O God of our salvation, and gather and deliver us from among the nations
notes.why: The psalm closes by pivoting to the exile: the prayer to be gathered and delivered from among the nations is the prayer of the diaspora. The Chronicler has woven this petition into the inaugural psalm of the ark — making the worship of David's era speak directly to the concerns of the restored community. The song of thanksgiving for past covenant faithfulness becomes simultaneously a prayer for present rescue. The steadfast love (chesed — covenant loyalty, the love that does not let go) is the ground of both.

intro: The Davidic covenant is the theological summit of 1 Chronicles. Everything from Adam to David has led here; everything from David to Solomon will flow from here. The Chronicler follows 2 Samuel 7 closely but with one crucial difference: he removes the conditional element of punishment (2 Sam 7:14b — 'when he commits iniquity, I will discipline him'). In Chronicles the covenant is unconditional. The throne is established forever.

notes.original: u'vniticha YHWH bayit — the LORD will build you a house
notes.rendering: I declare to you that the LORD will build you a house
notes.why: The wordplay is the theological core of the chapter. David wants to build God a house (bayit — house, temple). God refuses — but tells David that God will build David a house (bayit — dynasty, lineage). The one who planned to be the builder becomes the recipient. Human initiative is redirected by divine prerogative. The temple will be built — but by Solomon, not David, and on God's terms, not David's schedule.

notes.original: ani ehyeh lo l'av v'hu yihyeh li l'ven — I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son
notes.rendering: I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. I will not take my steadfast love from him
notes.why: The father-son language of the Davidic covenant becomes one of the most productive theological formulas in the Bible. It is quoted in Psalm 2:7, alluded to in 2 Samuel 7, and applied to Jesus in Hebrews 1:5 and the Gospel accounts of the baptism. The crucial difference from 2 Samuel 7:14 is the omission of the discipline clause. Chronicles' version of the covenant has no 'when he sins'; the steadfast love (chesed) is permanent and unconditional.

notes.original: va'yavo ha'melekh David va'yeshev liphney YHWH — and King David went in and sat before the LORD
notes.rendering: Then King David goes in and sits before the LORD
notes.why: David sits before the LORD — a posture of reception and contemplation rather than petition or prostration. The prayer that follows is one of the most theologically dense in the Hebrew Bible: it moves from personal humility (who am I?) to cosmic uniqueness (there is none like you) to the particularity of Israel (who is like your people?) to the permanence of the promise. David does not pray for more; he prays for the word already spoken to be kept.

intro: Chapter 18 is a rapid survey of David's imperial expansion — Philistines, Moab, Aram-Zobah, Edom, Amalek. The Chronicler follows 2 Samuel 8 closely, adding the note in verse 8 that the bronze captured from Hadadezer becomes the raw material for Solomon's temple furnishings. David's wars are therefore not merely military achievements but temple-building in disguise.

notes.original: va'yosha YHWH et David b'chol asher halakh — and the LORD saved David in all that he went
notes.rendering: the LORD saves David wherever he goes
notes.why: This refrain — repeated in verse 13 — is the Chronicler's interpretive frame for the entire military narrative. David's success is not tactical brilliance but divine accompaniment. The same formula governs the victories of Joshua ('the LORD gave them into his hand'), of Hezekiah, and of Jehoshaphat. When the Chronicler says 'the LORD saves', he is identifying the real agent behind every sword stroke.

notes.original: min Tivchath u'miKun — from Tibhath and from Cun
notes.rendering: from Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadadezer, David takes very much bronze. With it Solomon makes the bronze sea and the pillars and the vessels of bronze
notes.why: This single verse is one of the Chronicler's most characteristic additions. The parallel in 2 Samuel 8:8 says David took bronze and leaves it at that. The Chronicler connects David's military spoils directly to Solomon's temple furnishings — the bronze sea (the great laver), the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the vessels. David is not merely a warrior; he is the temple's inadvertent supply chain.

notes.original: va'yishpot David mishpat utzedaqah l'chol amo — and David administered justice and righteousness to all his people
notes.rendering: David reigns over all Israel, and he administers justice and equity to all his people
notes.why: Mishpat utzedaqah — justice and righteousness (the same paired terms Amos demands like rolling water in Amos 5:24). The Chronicler's David is not just a military conqueror but a just king — the model of what sovereignty should look like when it is rightly ordered. The administrative list that follows (vv. 15–17) gives the justice a human face: specific officials, specific responsibilities, the machinery of a righteous state.

intro: The Ammonite war begins in diplomatic insult and ends in decisive victory. The Chronicler follows 2 Samuel 10 closely but omits the Bathsheba episode entirely — 2 Samuel 11 does not exist in Chronicles. The reader who knows Samuel feels the gap; the Chronicler is not unaware of it. The omission is interpretive: David as the Chronicler presents him is a man of genuine piety, whose failures do not define him the way Samuel presents them.

notes.original: a'aseh chesed im Chanun ben Nachash — I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash
notes.rendering: I will deal kindly with Hanun son of Nahash, for his father dealt kindly with me
notes.why: Chesed — the great covenant word, here used in a diplomatic context: David's chesed toward Hanun mirrors Nahash's chesed toward David (whatever that earlier kindness was; it is not recorded in Chronicles). The word is deliberately chosen: David approaches international relations with the same posture of covenantal faithfulness he uses before God. The Ammonites misread the gesture as espionage. What appears as chesed is received as threat — a study in the gap between intent and interpretation.

notes.original: chazaq v'nit'chazaq — be strong and let us strengthen ourselves
notes.rendering: Be strong, and let us use our strength for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the LORD do what seems good to him
notes.why: Joab's pre-battle speech is a small masterpiece of Chronicler theology: it combines human resolve (be strong) with divine submission (may the LORD do what seems good). This is not fatalism; it is the proper ordering of initiative and trust. The same formula governs David's entire career in Chronicles: act with full strength, and leave the outcome to God. The cities of our God — ha-arei Eloheinu — is a remarkable phrase: Jerusalem and the other Israelite cities belong not to Israel but to God.

intro: Chapter 20 is the briefest chapter in this section — three verses on Rabbah and five on the Philistine giants. The Chronicler's omission of the Bathsheba narrative (2 Samuel 11–12) is felt most acutely in verse 1: 'David remains at Jerusalem' — the very detail in Samuel that introduces the temptation. In Chronicles it is simply a logistical note. The Chronicler is not naive; he is selective.

notes.original: b'et tshuvat hashana l'et tzet ham'lachim — at the turn of the year, at the time of kings going out
notes.rendering: In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, Joab leads out the army... But David remains at Jerusalem
notes.why: These are the most loaded words in the chapter. In 2 Samuel 11:1 the same phrase — 'the time when kings go out to battle' — introduces Bathsheba. In Chronicles, David staying behind in Jerusalem leads to nothing but the eventual coronation of Ammon's conquered king. The parallel is exact; the sequel is entirely different. The reader who knows Samuel understands that the Chronicler has chosen a different David — not a falsified one, but the one who matters for the post-exilic community's needs.

notes.original: va'yak Elhanan ben Ya'ir et Lachmi achi Golyat haGitti — and Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi the brother of Goliath
notes.rendering: Elhanan son of Jair strikes down Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite
notes.why: The parallel in 2 Samuel 21:19 says 'Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite killed Goliath the Gittite' — which contradicts the David-and-Goliath story. Chronicles resolves the contradiction by making Lahmi Goliath's brother rather than Goliath himself, and by restructuring the name Jaare-oregim. Whether this is textual harmonisation or an independent tradition, the Chronicler clearly knew the tension existed and addressed it.

intro: Chapter 21 is the shadow that makes the temple's light shine more brightly. The census, the plague, the angel's sword — these are the darkness out of which the altar emerges. The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite is where the angel sheaths his sword, and that spot becomes the temple mount. The Chronicler's genius is this: the site of the temple is not found by a pleasant survey — it is identified by catastrophe halted by grace.

notes.original: va'ya'amod satan al Yisrael vayaset et David — and Satan stood against Israel and incited David
notes.rendering: Then Satan stands against Israel and incites David to number Israel
notes.why: The parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says 'the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he incited David.' Chronicles replaces YHWH as the inciter with the satan — the adversary. This is not Satan as the later theological figure but ha-satan, the adversarial one who operates within the divine court (as in Job 1–2). The Chronicler makes the change to protect the theological coherence of his portrait of David: God incites to sin, in the Chronicler's reading, only through an intermediary agent.

notes.original: niphla rachamav me'od — his mercies are very great
notes.rendering: Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is very great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man
notes.why: David chooses divine judgment over human judgment — not because divine punishment will be lighter but because divine mercy is greater. Rachamav — his mercies, his compassions (racham — the word related to rechem, the womb; the instinctive, bodily mercy of a parent for a child). This is an extraordinary act of faith: David chooses pestilence knowing that its administrator is the one whose mercy is deeper than any human clemency.

notes.original: lo ekach asher l'kha la'YHWH v'ha'alot olah chinnam — I will not take what is yours for the LORD and offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing
notes.rendering: I will not take for the LORD what is yours, nor offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing
notes.why: David's refusal of Ornan's gift is one of the most famous lines in Chronicles. The principle — worship must cost something — underlies the entire temple project. The altar on Ornan's threshing floor bought at full price becomes the altar of the temple built with the full wealth of David's kingdom. Offering that costs nothing is not offering; it is performance. The price of the site sanctifies what is built on it.

notes.original: va'ya'an lo ba'esh min hashamayim — and he answered him with fire from heaven
notes.rendering: the LORD answers him with fire from heaven upon the altar of burnt offering
notes.why: Divine fire from heaven is the sign of accepted sacrifice — from Elijah on Carmel (1 Kings 18:38) to Solomon's temple dedication (2 Chr 7:1). The fire here ratifies the altar before the temple exists. It is the LORD's stamp of approval on the site: this is the place. The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, bought at full price, where David built in penitence, is the ground on which the house of God will stand.

intro: Chapter 22 is the pivot of the entire book. Here David formally transfers the temple-building mandate to Solomon — with the same 'be strong and courageous' language that Joshua received from Moses. The Chronicler frames David's reign not as military achievement but as temple preparation. This is his crowning work.

notes.original: na'ar v'rak v'habayit livnot laYHWH l'hagdil l'ma'lah — the boy is young and tender, and the house to be built for the LORD must be exceedingly great
notes.rendering: Solomon my son is young and inexperienced, and the house... must be exceedingly magnificent
notes.why: Na'ar v'rak — young and tender — is almost maternal language. David's enormous preparations are an act of love for both his son and his God. The Chronicler's David is not diminished by not building the temple; rather, his preparation is presented as equal or greater to the act of building itself.

notes.original: v'shemo yihyeh Shlomo u'shalom va'sheket eten al Yisrael — his name shall be Solomon and I will give peace and quiet to Israel
notes.rendering: his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days
notes.why: The name Shlomo (Solomon) is derived from shalom (peace). The wordplay is deliberate: the man of rest (ish menukhah, v.9) builds the house precisely because he is not a man of war. This is not a demotion of David but a theological division of labor. Every war David fights is clearing the ground, financially and politically, for the temple.

notes.original: chazaq ve'ematz al tira ve'al techat — be strong and courageous, do not fear and do not be dismayed
notes.rendering: Be strong and courageous. Fear not; do not be dismayed
notes.why: This four-part charge — chazaq / ematz / al tira / al techat — echoes God's words to Joshua in Joshua 1:6-9 and Moses' charge to Joshua in Deuteronomy 31:7-8. The Chronicler is deliberately casting Solomon as a new Joshua: one who receives a promised land (the temple site) and must complete what his predecessor began. The covenant continuity is unmistakable.

intro: Chapter 23 begins the great organizational sequence that runs through chapter 26. David's final act is not a military campaign or a political treaty — it is the ordering of Israel's worship. For the Chronicler, this is the most important thing a king can do. The precision of the lists reflects the seriousness of the calling.

notes.original: v'arba'at alafim m'hallalim laYHWH — and four thousand praising the LORD
notes.rendering: four thousand shall offer praises to the LORD with the instruments that I have made for praise
notes.why: This is the only place in the Bible where a king explicitly says 'I made instruments for worship.' David's musicianship is not incidental — it is structural. The four thousand singers and musicians become a permanent feature of the temple liturgy. The Chronicler traces every subsequent moment of musical worship back to this organizational decree.

notes.original: l'hakdish kodesh kodashim — to consecrate the holiest of holies
notes.rendering: set apart to dedicate the most holy things
notes.why: The phrase kodesh kodashim — holiest of holies — is used of both the inner sanctuary and the holiest category of offerings and persons. Aaron's line is consecrated to the same degree as the most sacred space. The distinction between Aaron (priest, offering, sanctuary) and Moses (teacher, intercessor, tribe of Levi) is theologically significant: even Moses' sons are Levites, not priests.

notes.original: natan menukhah l'ammo — he has given rest to his people
notes.rendering: the LORD... has given rest to his people
notes.why: Menukhah — rest — is the theological counterpart to temple-building throughout Chronicles. The tabernacle was for a people in motion; the temple is for a people at rest. David's organization of the Levites (they no longer carry the ark) signals that the wilderness era is truly over. A new stage of Israel's story begins.

intro: The twenty-four priestly divisions established here become one of the most historically consequential organizational decisions in all of Israelite history. These divisions are still referenced in Luke 1:5 when Zechariah, 'of the division of Abijah' (the eighth course), serves in the temple and receives the annunciation of John the Baptist. The lot system ensures divine impartiality.

notes.original: va'yamut Nadav va'Avihu lifney avihem — and Nadab and Abihu died before their father
notes.rendering: Nadab and Abihu die before their father
notes.why: The shadow of Leviticus 10 falls over this list. Nadab and Abihu offered 'strange fire' and were consumed. The Chronicler mentions their death matter-of-factly — it is not editorialized — but the absence of their line shapes the entire priestly organization that follows. Aaron's legacy runs through Eleazar and Ithamar only.

notes.original: va'yachlekem b'goralot — and he divided them by lots
notes.rendering: they divide them by lot, all alike
notes.why: The lot (goral) is not random chance in the Hebrew worldview — it is the mechanism by which God's will is disclosed without human favoritism. By casting lots to determine priestly divisions, David removes any possibility of political patronage in the assignment of sacred duties. All courses are equal in dignity; only God decides their order.

notes.original: l'Abiyah — to Abijah
notes.rendering: the eighth to Abijah
notes.why: The division of Abijah is the eighth course. Luke 1:5 identifies Zechariah as a priest 'of the division of Abijah.' The twenty-four courses rotate through the year, each serving one week at a time, twice a year. Scholars use this to calculate the probable birth dates of John the Baptist and Jesus. What seems like a dry administrative list carries extraordinary narrative freight.

intro: The twenty-four musical divisions mirror exactly the twenty-four priestly divisions of chapter 24. This is not coincidence — it is the Chronicler's theology in structural form. Music and sacrifice are coordinate acts of worship. The musicians 'prophesy' with their instruments: this is not metaphor but a serious theological claim that Spirit-filled music is a form of divine communication.

notes.original: v'yavdilu... l'nevuah b'chinorot b'nevalim uv'metziltayim — and they set apart... for prophecy with lyres, harps, and cymbals
notes.rendering: who prophesy with lyres, with harps, and with cymbals
notes.why: The word nevuah — prophecy — applied to instrumental music is striking. These musicians are not performers; they are prophets. Their music mediates divine presence in the same way prophetic speech does. Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun are each called 'seers' (chozeh) elsewhere in Chronicles. The Chronicler understands worship music as a form of revelation.

notes.original: al yedey divrey ha'Elohim l'harim keren — by the word of God to exalt the horn
notes.rendering: according to the promise of God to exalt him
notes.why: The phrase 'to exalt the horn' (l'harim keren) is idiomatic for divine blessing and elevation. The fact that Heman has fourteen sons and three daughters — the largest family of the three chief musicians — is itself read as divine favor and a fulfillment of promise. His sons' names, which form the musical divisions 4–17, may contain a hidden acrostic prayer in the Hebrew, though scholars debate this.

notes.original: va'yapilu goralot mishmarot k'katon kagadol maskil im talmid — and they cast lots for watches, small as great, teacher alongside pupil
notes.rendering: they cast lots for their duties, small and great, teacher and pupil alike
notes.why: The lot system here mirrors chapter 24. Notably, the lot makes no distinction between teacher (maskil) and pupil (talmid) — both are assigned by divine lot, not by seniority or skill. This radical equality in sacred vocation is consistent with the Chronicler's vision of an all-Israel worship community where rank does not determine calling.

intro: The gatekeepers receive a full chapter because the Chronicler treats them as a genuine order of sacred ministry, not a servant class. To stand at the gate of the house of God is a high calling — a theme echoed in Psalm 84:10. The treasure-keepers and regional administrators complete the picture of a fully organized sacred commonwealth.

notes.original: ki berakhahu Elohim — for God had blessed him
notes.rendering: for God blesses him
notes.why: The note that God blesses Obed-edom with eight sons is remarkable given what the reader knows: Obed-edom is the man in whose house the ark rested for three months and who was blessed because of it (1 Chr 13:14). His sons and grandsons now become gatekeepers — sixty-two in total. The blessing of the ark becomes a dynasty of temple servants. Sacred proximity bears institutional fruit.

notes.original: v'Zechariah bno yo'etz b'sekhel — and Zechariah his son, a counselor with insight
notes.rendering: a shrewd counselor
notes.why: The word sekhel — insight, discretion — is used sparingly in Chronicles and always as high praise. That a gatekeeper's son is commended for wisdom, not just strength or lineage, reflects the Chronicler's conviction that all temple roles require not merely physical capacity but godly intelligence. The gate is a place of judgment as well as security.

notes.original: min hamilchamot u'min hashalal hikdishu — from wars and from the spoil they dedicated
notes.rendering: From the spoil won in battles they dedicate gifts
notes.why: The chain from military victory to temple treasury is explicit: David's wars are not ends in themselves but means of provisioning the house of God. The Chronicler lists Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab as contributors alongside David — a remarkably inclusive picture. Even those who died in conflict or disgrace contributed to the temple's endowment.

intro: Chapter 27 presents Israel's civil and military administration as a parallel structure to the sacred administration of chapters 23–26. The twelve rotating monthly divisions (each of 24,000 men) reflect the same orderly beauty as the twenty-four priestly and musical courses. David's kingdom is organized as a totality: no domain is outside the scope of divine ordering.

notes.original: ki amar YHWH l'harbut et Yisrael k'chokhvey hashamayim — for the LORD had promised to multiply Israel like the stars of heaven
notes.rendering: the LORD has promised to make Israel as many as the stars of heaven
notes.why: The reason David stops his census at age twenty is theologically motivated: to count those younger would be to imply a ceiling on God's promise. The stars-of-heaven promise goes back to Abraham (Gen 15:5). The Chronicler inserts this note to rehabilitate the census narrative — David's error was not in counting per se but in counting as if God's promise were already exhausted.

notes.original: va'yachel Yo'av lispor v'lo chillah — and Joab began to count but did not finish
notes.rendering: Joab begins to count, but does not finish
notes.why: The contrast with chapter 21 is instructive: there the census is completed and the plague follows. Here, in the administrative summary, the census is noted as incomplete — and the wrath that came on Israel is referenced as past and resolved. The Chronicler's editorial hand is visible: the disgraceful episode is acknowledged but not dwelt upon. The organizational life of Israel moves forward.

notes.original: v'Chushay ha'Arki re'eh ha'melekh — and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend
notes.rendering: Hushai the Archite is the king's friend
notes.why: The title re'eh — friend — is an official court title, not merely a description of personal intimacy. It appears in Egyptian and Canaanite court documents as a specific advisory role: the king's confidant who speaks freely and without agenda. Hushai's famous role in countering Ahithophel's advice during Absalom's revolt (2 Sam 15–17) shows the office carried real power.

intro: Chapter 28 is the theological and rhetorical summit of 1 Chronicles. David's final public speech recapitulates the entire narrative logic of the book: divine election, the transfer of responsibility, the architecture of worship, and the charge to seek God. The transfer of the written building plan (tavnit) is a moment charged with Moses-Joshua typology.

notes.original: darshehu v'yimmatze lach — seek him and he will be found by you
notes.rendering: if you seek him, he will be found by you
notes.why: The verb darash — to seek, inquire — is the Chronicler's governing theological word. It appears more in Chronicles than in any other book of the Bible. Here it reaches its most personal expression: not a cultic command but a relational invitation. The counterpart — 'if you forsake him' (azavtanu) — completes the conditional structure that defines the entire Davidic covenant in its Solomonic application.

notes.original: v'kol asher hayah b'ruach imo — all that was with him in spirit / in his mind
notes.rendering: the plan of all that he has in mind
notes.why: The Hebrew is ambiguous: b'ruach imo can mean 'in his spirit' (divinely inspired) or 'in his mind' (mentally conceived). Most translations choose 'mind,' but the LXX and Vulgate favor a stronger sense of divine inspiration. Given verse 19 — 'all this he makes clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD' — the plans are explicitly attributed to divine origin, not merely human genius. David is not an architect; he is a recipient.

notes.original: ha'kol bikhtav miyad YHWH alay hiskil — all in writing from the hand of the LORD, upon me he caused to understand
notes.rendering: all this he makes clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD
notes.why: This verse explicitly parallels David's reception of the temple plans with Moses' reception of the tabernacle plans (Exodus 25:9, 25:40). Just as Moses received the exact pattern on the mountain, David receives the exact pattern by divine revelation. The temple is not a human architectural achievement; it is a heavenly pattern realized on earth. The Chronicler is making a sweeping theological claim about the temple's cosmic status.

intro: Chapter 29 is the grand doxology of 1 Chronicles. David's prayer — one of the most theologically profound prayers in the Old Testament — moves from praise to anthropology to gratitude to petition. The death notice that follows is among the most dignified in all of Scripture: 'full of days, riches, and honour.' The Chronicler's David dies as he lived — offering freely, rejoicing greatly.

notes.original: va'yismachu ha'am al hitnadevam ki v'lev shalem hitnadvu laYHWH — and the people rejoiced over their willing offerings, for with a whole heart they offered freely to the LORD
notes.rendering: the people rejoice because they have given willingly, for with a whole heart they offer freely to the LORD
notes.why: The phrase lev shalem — whole heart — is the Chronicler's phrase for authentic worship. It appears in David's charge to Solomon (28:9) and now describes the entire assembly. The joy of the assembly (simchah) is not emotional manipulation but the natural response of hearts aligned with their Creator. Generosity produces joy; joy produces more generosity. The theological cycle is complete.

notes.original: ki mimmekha ha'kol u'miyyadekha natanu lakh — for all things come from you and from your hand we give to you
notes.rendering: all things come from you, and of your own have we given you
notes.why: This is perhaps the most quoted verse in the entire book at Christian offering ceremonies. The theological logic is precise: Israel's giving is not a contribution to God from their own resources; it is the return of what was always God's. The word natanu (give) is used for both God's giving and Israel's giving — the same verb, reversed. Stewardship theology in one sentence.

notes.original: va'yamot b'seyvah tovah sava yamim osher v'chavod — and he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour
notes.rendering: he dies in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour
notes.why: The Chronicler's death notice for David is the most complete and dignified in the Bible. Three things are full: days (yamim), riches (osher), and honour (kavod). Notably, the Chronicler omits the deathbed scheming of 1 Kings 1–2 — the court intrigues, Adonijah's revolt, David's instructions to Solomon to settle old scores. The Chronicler's David dies in glory. This is not naivety; it is theological selectivity. The Chronicler's David is a type, not merely a biography.

intro: The opening of 1 Corinthians is calibrated with surgical precision: the community’s problem (division, status-seeking, wisdom-competition) is named by verse 11, and Paul’s theological counter-move — the word of the cross — is launched in verse 18. The rest of the chapter unfolds the logic: the cross is not a failure of power but the redefinition of what power means. The three-part OT quotation, the three rhetorical questions (‘where is the wise person?’), and the three-part catalogue of divine election (foolish, weak, low/despised) build toward the knockout line of v.28: God chose ta mē onta — things that are not.

notes.original: logos tou staurou / mōria / dynamis — the word of the cross / folly / power
notes.rendering: the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God
notes.why: Logos tou staurou — the word of/about the cross — is a phrase Paul coins here; it appears nowhere before this letter. The cross was not a symbol but an execution method for the lowest social classes: slaves and criminals. That the gospel consists in the announcement of a crucified person was, in Corinthian terms, absurd. Mōria (folly, stupidity — from mōros, the root of English ‘moron’) is the word Paul applies to what the perishing hear. Dynamis theou (power of God) is what the being-saved hear in the same word. The contrast is absolute, and it is unresolvable from within the framework of conventional wisdom.

notes.original: skandalon / mōria / dynamis theou kai sophia theou — stumbling block / folly / power and wisdom of God
notes.rendering: a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles, but to those who are called… Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God
notes.why: Skandalon (stumbling block — literally the trigger-stick of a trap) is the Jewish reaction: the cross is theologically impossible because cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (Deuteronomy 21:23). Mōria is the Greek reaction: a crucified saviour makes no sense within any Greek philosophical or religious framework. The called (klētois — same root as ‘called to be an apostle’ in v.1 and ‘called to be holy’ in v.2) see a third thing in the same cross: not a scandal or an absurdity but the power and wisdom of God simultaneously. The inversion is Paul’s central claim.

notes.original: ta mōra tou kosmou / ta asthene / ta agenē / ta mē onta — the foolish things / weak things / low things / things that are not
notes.rendering: God chose what is foolish… weak… low and despised… things that are not — to bring to nothing the things that are
notes.why: The rhetoric builds through three synonymous pairs (foolish/wise, weak/strong, low+despised / things that are) to the most radical formulation: ta mē onta — things that are not, non-beings, the ontologically invisible. Hina katargēsē ta onta — so that he might nullify the things that are, the things with status and existence and measurable weight. Katargeō (to nullify, to render inoperative, to bring to nothing) is one of Paul’s signature verbs: it appears 25 times in his letters. God’s chosen instruments are not merely humble — they are the things that do not register in the cultural ledger at all.

intro: Chapter 2 is Paul’s most sustained reflection on epistemology: how do you know something that is beyond the reach of ordinary knowing? The answer is pneumatic — through the Spirit, which alone searches the depths of God. The chapter moves from Paul’s own deliberately weak manner of preaching (the deliberate irony: the preacher of the word of the cross arrives looking like a very poor demonstration of wisdom) to the hidden wisdom prepared before the ages, and closes with the most startling claim: we have the mind of Christ.

notes.original: Iēsoun Christon kai touton estaurōmenon — Jesus Christ and him crucified (perfect passive participle)
notes.rendering: Jesus Christ — and him crucified
notes.why: Estaurōmenon is a perfect passive participle: the crucified one, the one who has been and remains crucified. The perfect tense in Greek denotes a past action with continuing effects. Paul is not deciding to know only about the historical event of the crucifixion but about the permanently crucified Lord — the one whose identity is inseparable from that cross, even now. The participle carries the weight of the resurrection: he is risen, yes, but he is risen as the crucified one. The decision Paul describes (ekrina — I judged, I decided) was a deliberate rhetorical and theological choice, not ignorance.

notes.original: ho ophthalmos ouk eiden kai ous ouk ēkousen — what eye has not seen nor ear heard
notes.rendering: what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor human heart conceived
notes.why: The quotation is composite and disputed: it does not appear verbatim anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, though it draws on Isaiah 64:4 (no ear has heard, no eye has seen any God besides you) and possibly 65:17. Paul may be citing a text no longer extant, or rendering Isaiah freely. The three faculties — eye, ear, heart (= mind/imagination) — exhaustively represent human cognitive capacity. What God has prepared exceeds all of them. The point is not mystical obscurantism but the inadequacy of unaided human wisdom to receive the gospel: revelation, not investigation, is the epistemological mode.

notes.original: psychikos anthrōpos — the soulish/natural person
notes.rendering: the natural person
notes.why: Psychikos (from psychē — soul, life, the animating principle) is the person living at the level of natural human existence, without the Spirit’s penetration. The word is difficult: ‘natural’ is the standard rendering but misses the contrast with pneumatikos (Spirit-person). ‘Soulish’ is more accurate but archaic. The anthropology here is not Greek trichotomy (spirit/soul/body as three separate substances) but a contrast between two modes of existence: the person animated by natural human life (psychikos) and the person animated by the divine Spirit (pneumatikos). Psychikos recurs in 15:44–46 for the ‘natural body’ that will be raised as a ‘spiritual body.’

intro: Chapter 3 applies the theology of chapters 1–2 to the specific problem of teacher-allegiances. If the word of the cross redefines wisdom, then those who carry it cannot be status figures to gather factions around. The farmer-watering image of vv.6–9 leads to the more pointed building image of vv.10–17, which then pivots on a question Paul deploys repeatedly in this letter: ‘Do you not know?’ The closing verses (21–23) reverse the logic of the Corinthian boasting: they were claiming to own the teachers; Paul tells them the teachers own nothing — but they (the community) own everything, because they belong to Christ.

notes.original: theou geōrgion, theou oikodomē este — God’s field, God’s building you are
notes.rendering: You are God’s field — God’s building
notes.why: Two metaphors in rapid succession, both preceded by the genitive theou (of God / God’s). Geōrgion (field, cultivated land — from geōrgos, farmer, from gē, earth + ergon, work) picks up the planting/watering imagery of vv.6–8. Oikodomē (building, construction — from oikos, house + domeō, to build) launches the construction metaphor that will dominate vv.10–17. The juxtaposition is deliberate: two entirely different images for the same community, both insisting on divine ownership. The Corinthians are not Paul’s or Apollos’s field or building; they are God’s.

notes.original: themelion — foundation
notes.rendering: no other foundation can anyone lay than what is already laid — which is Jesus Christ
notes.why: Themelion (foundation, from tithenai, to lay/place) is used here in both literal and metaphorical registers: Paul the skilled master builder (architekton — v.10, the word that gives English ‘architect’) has laid a foundation that is not a principle or a body of teaching but a person. The gar (for) that introduces v.11 makes it explanatory: the reason each builder must take care is that the foundation is fixed and irreplaceable. Anyone building incompatibly with Jesus Christ is not adding to the building but working against the structure. The image anticipates the temple language of vv.16–17.

notes.original: naos theou / phtheirei — temple of God / destroys
notes.rendering: Do you not know that you are God’s temple… If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person
notes.why: Naos (inner sanctuary — distinct from hieron, the outer courts and precincts) is the holy of holies, the inner dwelling-place of the divine presence. Paul does not say the Corinthians are like a temple; he says they are the naos. The Spirit’s indwelling of the community is as specific and as serious as the Shekinah presence in the Temple. Phtheirei…phtherei: the verb is the same in both clauses, the tenses reversed — a deliberate verbal echo that produces symmetry: destroy / will destroy. The stakes of the division are not merely relational but eschatological.

intro: Chapter 4 deploys one of Paul’s most sustained ironic performances. The Corinthians are playing the role of the triumphant: already full, already rich, already reigning. Paul and the other apostles are playing the role of the condemned, on display at the end of the parade. The inversion is deliberate: the cross-shaped life of the apostle embodies the theology of the cross that Paul has been expounding since 1:18. The chapter closes not with argument but with the emotional register of a father — the most intimate relational category in Paul’s self-description.

notes.original: hyperetai Christou / oikonomoi mystēriōn theou — under-rowers of Christ / stewards of the mysteries of God
notes.rendering: servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God
notes.why: Hyperetēs (servant, assistant — literally an under-rower, from hypo, under + eressō, to row) is a lower-status term than doulos (slave): the galley-rower who does not set course but pulls in the direction the captain directs. It is a deliberate downgrade from the teacher-patron role the Corinthians have been assigning to their favorites. Oikonomos (steward, household manager — from oikos, house + nemō, to manage) is accountable to a master, not independently authoritative. Together the two words define the apostle as derivative, accountable, and directionally controlled by Another.

notes.original: theatron egenēthēmen — we have become a theater-spectacle
notes.rendering: we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to people
notes.why: Theatron — spectacle, theater-show — is the gladiatorial or triumphal arena image: the apostles are the defeated prisoners paraded last in the triumph (epithanatious — condemned to death, literally those destined for death). The image inverts Roman triumphal procession: the victorious general first, the defeated captives last. Paul places the apostles at the end, not the beginning, of the parade. The spectators are cosmic: kosmos (world), angeloi (angels), anthrōpoi (people). The apostolic life is a public display of cruciform existence before the entire created order.

notes.original: peripsēma / perikatharmata — refuse / offscouring
notes.rendering: the scum of the world, the refuse of all things
notes.why: Two nearly synonymous words piled together for rhetorical force. Perikatharmata (offscouring, refuse — from kathaírō, to cleanse) referred to the ritual filth that was scraped off during a purification, or — in some ancient cities — to the outcast person sacrificed to cleanse the city in time of disaster. Peripsēma (rubbish, scrapings — from psaō, to rub) similarly means the waste scraped off something clean. Paul applies both words to the apostles without qualification. This is the rhetorical climax of the irony launched in v.8: the Corinthians reign; the apostles are the city’s ritual garbage.

intro: Chapter 5 is the first of three disciplinary cases Paul addresses. The offense — a man living with his father’s wife (the most natural reading is his stepmother, not his biological mother) — is flagrant enough that even Gentile communities would object. The Corinthian response is not grief but arrogance — possibly pride at their progressive open-mindedness. Paul’s response is sharp and urgent: act now, because the leaven metaphor shows what is at stake for the whole community.

notes.original: paradounai ton toiouton tō Satana eis olethron tēs sarkos — hand such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh
notes.rendering: hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved
notes.why: This verse is among the most debated in Paul. Paradounai (to hand over, to deliver — the same verb used for Jesus being betrayed / handed over) implies formal community action: the assembled church performs this handing-over. The meaning of ‘destruction of the flesh’ (olethros tēs sarkos) is disputed: does it mean physical death, physical suffering that leads to repentance, or simply the destruction of the fleshly way of life? The goal — hina to pneuma sōthē — so that the spirit might be saved — is restorative, not purely punitive. Expulsion from the community (removal from the protective sphere of Christ) is simultaneously an act of judgment and a hope for salvation.

notes.original: to pascha hēmōn etythē Christos — our Passover has been sacrificed — Christ
notes.rendering: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed
notes.why: The word order in Greek is significant: to pascha hēmōn etythē — our Passover has been sacrificed — and then Christos as the identifier. Pascha (Passover — from the Hebrew pesach) refers to both the festival and the Passover lamb; the verb etythē (was sacrificed, was slaughtered — from thyō, to sacrifice) is used of sacrificial animals. Paul does not develop this comparison at length; he states it as established fact. The implication for the metaphor: the old leaven must be purged because Passover has already happened. The community is not working toward purity; they are living in the aftermath of the sacrifice.

notes.original: tous esō / tous exō — those inside / those outside
notes.rendering: those inside the church whom you are to judge… God judges those outside
notes.why: The inside/outside distinction (esō/exō — the same words used for the inner and outer courts of the Temple) defines the community’s sphere of jurisdiction. Paul is not indifferent to the world outside — his entire missionary enterprise is directed outward — but judgment in the sense of moral accountability and communal discipline belongs within the church. The final quotation (‘drive out the wicked person’) is from Deuteronomy 17:7 and related passages, where the formula closes instructions for purging covenant-breaking from Israel. Paul applies the same covenant-community logic to the church.

intro: Chapter 6 addresses two separate problems — litigation and sexual immorality — that are united by the same underlying Corinthian theology: an inflated sense of spiritual freedom that treats the body as ethically irrelevant. Paul’s counter-claim is the resurrection: the body that will be raised is the body that matters now. The three-part ‘Do you not know?’ questions (vv.2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19) build to the theological climax of v.19–20 — the body as temple, the person as purchased property of God.

notes.original: apelousasthe / hēgiasthēte / edikaiōthēte — you were washed / you were sanctified / you were justified
notes.rendering: you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified
notes.why: Three aorist passives in sequence, all past tense — describing completed actions done to the Corinthians, not achievements of their own. The order is notable: washed (baptism imagery) then sanctified (set apart) then justified (declared righteous) — the reverse of the ordo salutis as later Protestant theology would arrange it. Paul is not giving a logical sequence but a liturgical accumulation. En tō onomati (in the name) and en tō pneumati (by the Spirit / in the Spirit) frame all three: these are the twin agents and modes of the transformation. The ‘and such were some of you’ (kai tauta tines ēte) is not condemnation but radical past-tense: the list of v.9–10 describes former identity, not present status.

notes.original: panta moi exestin — all things are permitted/lawful for me
notes.rendering: all things are permitted for me — but not all things are beneficial
notes.why: The repeated phrase panta moi exestin is almost certainly a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes and then qualifies. The Corinthians have drawn a conclusion Paul’s own gospel of freedom might seem to support: if grace abounds, and the body is passing away, then bodily actions have no moral weight. Paul’s qualification is twofold: not everything that is permitted is sympheron (beneficial, advantageous — a word from deliberative rhetoric asking what serves the common interest) and the person who claims freedom from all constraint may find themselves controlled by something new. Ouk egō exousiasthēsomai — I will not be mastered by anything — turns the freedom argument on itself: the libertine is not more free than the disciplined person but less.

notes.original: naos tou hagiou pneumatos / ēgorasthēte timēs — temple of the Holy Spirit / bought with a price
notes.rendering: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… you were bought with a price — glorify God in your body
notes.why: The temple imagery reappears from 3:16, but now it is individual: each body (sōma — the concrete physical person, not the spiritual soul) is a naos (inner sanctuary) of the Holy Spirit. The ēgorasthēte timēs — you were bought with a price — is commercial/redemption language: agorazō (to purchase, to buy in the marketplace — from agora, marketplace) plus timē (price, honor, value). The body belongs to God not by creation only but by purchase — the cross is the price. The command that follows is therefore not ethical advice but a statement of ownership: glorify God in the body that is his.

intro: Chapter 7 is Paul’s longest treatment of marriage, celibacy, and the social arrangements of the called life. It is organized by a series of cases: the married, the unmarried, the mixed-faith marriages, the question of circumcision (as a paradigm for all status-at-calling questions), and the betrothed. The governing logic is eschatological: the time is short (v.29), the present world’s form is passing away (v.31), and the question ‘how to please the Lord’ now sets the horizon for every domestic arrangement.

notes.original: charisma ek theou — gift from God
notes.rendering: each has their own gift from God — one of one kind, one of another
notes.why: Charisma (gift, grace-gift — from charis, grace) is the same word used for the spiritual gifts of chapters 12–14. Paul’s application of it here to both marriage and celibacy is significant: neither state is superior in an absolute sense; each is a specific gift of God’s grace for a specific person. The indefinite pronouns — hos men houtōs, hos de houtōs (one this way, one that way) — deliberately avoid prescribing one charism as universally better.
