This cuts against both the ascetics who were demanding celibacy of everyone and against those who read Paul’s freedom as license for any sexual behavior.

notes.original: hekastō hōs emerisen ho kyrios, hekastos hōs keklētai ho theos — as the Lord has allotted / as God has called
notes.rendering: the life that the Lord has assigned — that God has called them to
notes.why: The principle of remaining in one’s calling (klēsis — the called-condition, the state in which one was summoned) is the theological hinge of vv.17–24. Merizomai (to allot, to distribute — from meros, part, share) suggests that the specific social location of one’s calling is not incidental but part of the divine distribution. This does not mean the status quo is sacred — v.21 explicitly says ‘if you can gain freedom, use it’ — but that the gospel does not require social revolution as a precondition for faithful life.

notes.original: paragon to schēma tou kosmou toutou — the present form of this world is passing away
notes.rendering: the present form of this world is passing away
notes.why: Schēma (form, outward shape, the visible configuration of something — from schēmatizō, to form, to fashion) is the word Paul uses for the external arrangement of the world as it currently presents itself. It is not the world’s substance (ousia) that is passing but its shape, its present configuration. Parago (to pass by, to be in the act of passing — present tense) describes an ongoing movement: the world is right now in the process of its form dissolving. This eschatological pressure shapes everything Paul says about social arrangements: they are provisional, not because they are unimportant, but because everything is being reconfigured.

intro: Chapter 8 opens the idol-food section (chapters 8–10) with the epistemological key: the Corinthians’ problem is not that their theology is wrong (idols are nothing; there is one God) but that they are applying correct knowledge in a way that injures people for whom Christ died. The chapter’s architecture is deliberate: it opens and closes with the contrast between knowledge and love (vv.1–3 / v.13), and the center (vv.4–6) contains the most compressed monotheistic formula in Paul.

notes.original: gnōsis physioī, agapē oikodomei — knowledge puffs up, love builds up
notes.rendering: knowledge puffs up, but love builds up
notes.why: Physioo (to puff up, to inflate — from physa, bellows, air) is Paul’s word for Corinthian arrogance; it appears six times in this letter and nowhere else in Paul’s letters. Oikodomeō (to build up — from oikos, house + demeō, to build) is Paul’s standard word for what the community needs: edification, construction. The contrast is architectural: knowledge inflates (makes something look bigger without substance); love builds (adds real structure). The same contrast drives the entire gifts discussion in chapters 12–14: tongues (impressive, spectacular) vs. prophecy (comprehensible, building up the church).

notes.original: heis theos ho patēr… kai heis kyrios Iēsous Christos — one God the Father… and one Lord Jesus Christ
notes.rendering: one God, the Father, from whom are all things… and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things
notes.why: This is often identified as an early christological formula, possibly pre-Pauline, that Paul cites and applies to the idol-food question. It takes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 (‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one’) and distributes it between God and Christ: God (the Father) is the source (ex hou — from whom); Christ (the Lord) is the agent (di’ hou — through whom). Both prepositions appear twice — for creation and for the community’s existence: all things came through Christ; we exist through Christ. The Shema is not replaced but reread through a binitarian lens.

notes.original: apollytai ho asthenōn… di’ hon Christos apethanen — the weak one is destroyed… for whom Christ died
notes.rendering: this weak person — for whom Christ died — is destroyed
notes.why: The phrase di’ hon Christos apethanen (for whom Christ died — or on account of whom Christ died) is the theological weight-bearing element of Paul’s argument. The idol-knowledgeable Corinthian may be acting within the bounds of their own correct theology. But the person they damage by their exercise of freedom is someone for whom the crucifixion happened. Apollytai (is being destroyed, is perishing — present passive, the ongoing process of destruction) is the same verb used in 1:18 for those who are perishing. To destroy the one for whom Christ died is to enact the opposite of the cross.

intro: Chapter 9 is Paul’s personal demonstration of the principle established in chapter 8: he has apostolic rights — and he surrenders them for the sake of others. The chapter functions as a worked example, Paul himself as the case study. The argument moves through multiple layers of warrant (common practice, animal husbandry, Mosaic Law, temple precedent, the Lord’s own command) before arriving at the compulsion that makes all his talk of rights irrelevant: woe to me if I do not preach (v.16).

notes.original: anankē gar moi epikeitai — compulsion lies upon me / is laid upon me
notes.rendering: compulsion lies upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel
notes.why: Anankē (compulsion, necessity — from the verb anankaiō, to constrain) is used throughout Greek literature for the irresistible force that overrides individual will: fate, cosmic necessity, divine constraint. Paul borrows the term but reframes it: the compulsion is not cosmic fate but the divine commission, the woe (ouai — the prophetic cry of lament) that would attend his failure to preach. Epikeitai (lies upon, is laid upon — from epikeimi, to lie upon / press upon) makes the compulsion physical, felt as a weight. The paradox of freedom (v.1) and compulsion (v.16) is the paradox of Paul’s vocation: freely enslaved to a commission he did not choose.

notes.original: eleutheros… edoulōsa emauton — free… I enslaved myself
notes.rendering: though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all
notes.why: Eleutheros (free — the key Corinthian value word) is claimed and then immediately surrendered: Paul is free from all (pasīn) and has enslaved himself (edoulōsa — aorist of douloō, to enslave, to make a slave) to all. The self-enslavement is voluntary and strategic: hina tous pleionas kerdēsō (so that I might win more). Kerdainō (to gain, to win — commercial and athletic language for acquisition) frames the missionary enterprise as an economy of gain in which Paul consistently spends himself. The five groups that follow (Jews, Law-observers, outside-Law, weak, all people) are not compromises but contextual embodiments of the same self-giving logic.

notes.original: hypōpiazō… adokimos — I strike under the eye / I discipline; disqualified
notes.rendering: I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest… I myself should be disqualified
notes.why: Hypōpiazō (literally to strike under the eye, to give a black eye — from hypo, under + ōps, eye) is vivid athletic imagery: the boxer who hits himself to stay sharp. Paul applies it to his treatment of his own body. Adokimos (disqualified, not standing the test — from a-privative + dokimazō, to test, to approve) is the word for metal that fails the assay, or an athlete who is ruled ineligible. The concern is not about losing salvation but about the specific humiliation of the herald who preaches one thing and embodies another. The one who announces the race must also run it.

intro: Chapter 10 closes the idol-food section (begun in chapter 8) with two very different kinds of argument. The first (vv.1–13) is a typological reading of the Exodus generation: they had the same spiritual resources (cloud, sea, food, drink, the Rock) that the Corinthians have, and they fell. The second (vv.14–22) argues from the logic of table-participation: sharing a table creates solidarity with the one at whose table you eat — a logic that makes idol-temple dining incompatible with the Lord’s table regardless of one’s theology about idols.

notes.original: hē petra de ēn ho Christos — and the Rock was Christ
notes.rendering: that Rock was Christ
notes.why: The identification of the wilderness rock with Christ is one of Paul’s most striking typological moves. The Targum traditions identified the rock of Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 as following Israel through the wilderness — Paul knows this tradition and makes an identification the Targums do not: the following rock was Christ. The verb is ēn (was, past tense of eimi) — not ‘represented’ or ‘symbolized’ but simply was. This does not necessarily mean Paul is making a pre-existence claim in isolation, but the verse has always been read in that direction, and fits with his other uses of kyrios (Lord) as a title that encompasses Christ’s cosmic role.

notes.original: koinōnia tou haimatos / tou sōmatos — sharing/participation in the blood / body
notes.rendering: a sharing in the blood of Christ… a sharing in the body of Christ
notes.why: Koinōnia (sharing, fellowship, participation — from koinos, common) is the most important word in vv.16–20. It describes more than symbolic association: koinōnia in the ancient world was the concrete solidarity created by shared participation in a table. To share a cup is to share in what the cup represents; the participants become bound to one another and to the host. Paul extends this logic: drinking the cup of blessing creates koinōnia with Christ’s blood; eating the idol-temple meat creates koinōnia with demons. The theological conclusion follows: these tables are mutually exclusive.

notes.original: typikōs — typologically / as examples
notes.rendering: these things happened to them as examples
notes.why: Typikōs (as types, exemplarily — from typos, type, pattern, impression made by a blow) describes the hermeneutical method Paul applies to the Exodus narratives. The events were real historical events that also function as typoi — advance impressions of later realities. The Corinthians stand ‘at the ends of the ages’ (ta telē tōn aiōnōn katantēkamen — the ends of the ages have arrived at us) — meaning that the Exodus types are now meeting their antitypes in the experience of the church. This is not allegory (which substitutes a spiritual meaning for the literal) but typology: the literal event is real and forward-pointing simultaneously.

intro: Chapter 11 addresses two assembly practices. The head-covering discussion (vv.2–16) is one of the most contested passages in Paul, involving gender, honor culture, and the meaning of kephalē (head). The Lord’s Supper passage (vv.17–34) is the earliest account of the institution of the Eucharist in the New Testament — earlier than the Gospels, and embedded in a sharp pastoral crisis: the Corinthians have turned the community meal into a display of the social stratifications that the Lord’s table is supposed to abolish.

notes.original: kephalē — head
notes.rendering: the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God
notes.why: Kephalē (head — the anatomical head, but also source/origin or authority in figurative use) is the key term in vv.3–16, and its meaning is hotly debated. Two main readings: (1) head as authority/rank (the traditional reading), producing a hierarchy of God–Christ–husband–wife; (2) head as source/origin (a minority scholarly reading), reading the relationships in terms of origin rather than command. Either reading faces difficulties. The passage is further complicated by the head-covering practice itself, which is embedded in first-century Mediterranean honor culture: an uncovered head could signal social status, mourning, or sexual availability depending on context.

notes.original: paredidon — was betraying / handed over
notes.rendering: on the night when he was betrayed
notes.why: Paradidomi (to hand over, to betray, to transmit — the same verb throughout the passion narratives and in Paul’s transmission language of v.23a: ‘I received… I handed on’) is deliberately doubled here. Paul uses it both for the betrayal of Jesus (by Judas, or by human sinfulness generally — the passive ‘was handed over’ may carry divine passive overtones, as in Romans 8:32 ‘God did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all’) and for the liturgical handing-on of tradition. The night of betrayal is the night the tradition was instituted: the surrender and the gift are simultaneous.

notes.original: anamnēsin / diathēkē — remembrance / covenant
notes.rendering: Do this in remembrance of me… the new covenant in my blood
notes.why: Anamnēsis (remembrance, memorial — from anamimnēskō, to call again to mind) is not merely cognitive recall but the liturgical making-present of a past event. In the LXX, anamnēsis is used for the Passover memorial, in which the Exodus is not merely remembered but re-enacted and re-inhabited. The Lord’s Supper is the Passover of the new covenant. Diathēkē (covenant — the word translating Hebrew berith in the LXX) with the adjective kainē (new) echoes Jeremiah 31:31–34 (the new covenant written on hearts). The cup is the new covenant ‘in my blood’ — en tō emō haimati — identifying the blood of the cross as the covenant-sealing sacrifice.

intro: Chapter 12 is the first of Paul’s three great chapters on the assembly (12: body / gifts; 13: love; 14: tongues and prophecy). The body metaphor dominates, and Paul uses it to make two complementary moves: against those who feel inferior because they lack spectacular gifts (vv.15–16), and against those who feel they have no need of others (v.21). The theological grounding of the body image is Trinitarian: the one Spirit, one Lord, one God of vv.4–6 distributes gifts that are diverse precisely because the community is meant to be a differentiated unity.

notes.original: charismata / diakoniai / energēmata — gifts / ministries / activities
notes.rendering: varieties of gifts… varieties of service… varieties of activities
notes.why: Three distinct Greek words for what the Spirit distributes: charismata (grace-gifts — from charis, grace), diakoniai (ministries, services — from diakoneo, to serve, to wait on tables; the root of ‘deacon’), energēmata (workings, activities — from energeō, to work in, to be active; the root of English ‘energy’). The three-fold distribution of terms mirrors the three-fold divine source: Spirit, Lord, God. The variety of terminology signals that spiritual gifts are not one thing but three things: graces received, services rendered, and powers at work — all from the same undivided divine source.

notes.original: phanerōsis tou pneumatos pros to sympheron — manifestation of the Spirit for the common good
notes.rendering: the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good
notes.why: Phanerōsis (manifestation, making-visible — from phaneroō, to make manifest) is the umbrella term for all the gifts: each is a making-visible of the Spirit’s presence and action. Pros to sympheron (for the common good, toward what is advantageous for all — from symphero, to bring together, to be profitable) establishes the purpose-criterion for every gift. A gift that does not contribute to the common good is not functioning as a spiritual gift, regardless of how spectacular it appears. This criterion drives Paul’s evaluation of tongues vs. prophecy in chapter 14.

notes.original: eite paschei hen melos / eite doxazetai hen melos — if one member suffers / if one member is honored
notes.rendering: if one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together
notes.why: The verb sympascho (to suffer together — a compound of syn, with + pascho, to suffer) appears only here and in Romans 8:17 in Paul. The reciprocal suffering and rejoicing is the ecclesial application of the body metaphor: the unity of the body is not organizational but affective, participatory, physiological. The Corinthian status-competition (some members feeling inferior, others feeling independent) is a failure of this body-solidarity. Paul’s word here is not a command but a description of what the body is — and therefore what the community should be experiencing.

intro: Chapter 13 is not a detour from the argument about spiritual gifts: it is the argument’s theological center. Paul has been evaluating gifts by whether they build up the community (chapters 12, 14); chapter 13 names the mode of all genuine building-up: agapē. The chapter is structured as a triptych: vv.1–3 (gifts without love), vv.4–7 (the character of love), vv.8–13 (the permanence of love). The argument is both rhetorical and eschatological: love outlasts the gifts because it belongs to the age to come, while gifts belong to the partial knowledge of the present age.

notes.original: agapē — love (not erōs / philia / storgē)
notes.rendering: but have not love, I am nothing
notes.why: Agapē (the word Paul uses throughout, and the word that appears in the LXX for the covenant-love of God) is not one Greek word for love among equals. The four Greek words for love — erōs (passionate/romantic), philia (friendship/affection), storgē (family love), agapē (committed, self-giving love often associated with covenant) — overlap but are not synonymous. Paul’s choice of agapē is not arbitrary: it is the word the LXX uses for YHWH’s covenant love (hesed) for Israel, and the word Jesus uses in the commandments (‘love your neighbor as yourself’). The chapter is not defining a sentiment but a covenantal disposition.

notes.original: makrothymei / chrēsteuetai… ou physioūtai — is long-tempered / is useful-kind… is not puffed up
notes.rendering: love is patient, love is kind… it is not arrogant
notes.why: The fifteen verbs and adjectives of vv.4–7 are not abstract qualities: they are specific counterpoints to the Corinthian community’s documented behavior. Makrothymia (long-temperedness, long-suffering before anger — the opposite of the hot-temperedness that produces quarrels) targets 1:11 and 3:3. Chrēsteuomai (to be useful, to be kind — from chrēstos, useful, employed) appears only here in the NT. Ou physioutai (is not puffed up — physioo, the word used six times for Corinthian arrogance) is a direct hit: the entire catalogue describes the community they are not being. The chapter is less a hymn than a mirror.

notes.original: blepomen arti di’ esoptrou en ainigmati / tote de prosōpon pros prosōpon — we see now through a mirror in a riddle / then face to face
notes.rendering: now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face
notes.why: Di’ esoptrou (through a mirror — esoptron from eidon, to see) is a reference to bronze mirrors, which gave an indirect, often distorted reflection rather than direct sight. En ainigmati (in a riddle, in an enigma — ainigma from ainissomai, to speak obscurely) adds the note of indirection: not just unclear sight but indirect communication. The contrast with prosōpon pros prosōpon (face to face — the direct, unveiled encounter) echoes Moses’ face-to-face relation with YHWH in Exodus 33:11 and Numbers 12:8. The fullness of knowing is eschatological: then I shall know fully (tote de epignōsomai — the compound epi- adding the note of thorough, direct knowledge), even as I have already been fully known by God.

intro: Chapter 14 applies the love-criterion of chapter 13 to the specific gifts the Corinthians most prize: tongues and prophecy. The criterion is oikodomē — building up. The chapter’s structure is a careful comparison: tongues builds up the individual, prophecy builds up the assembly; in an assembly, building up the community takes priority. The command for women to be silent (vv.34–35) is one of the most contested passages in Paul, difficult to reconcile with 11:5 where women praying and prophesying in the assembly is assumed. Many scholars consider vv.34–35 a later interpolation; the NA28 text retains them without brackets.

notes.original: oikodomēn kai paraklēsin kai paramythian — building up and encouragement and consolation
notes.rendering: upbuilding and encouragement and consolation
notes.why: Three nouns define the purpose of prophecy: oikodomē (building-up — the structural/constructive metaphor that runs through chapters 8–14), paraklēsis (encouragement, exhortation, coming-alongside — the same root as paraklētos, the Advocate/Helper; from para, alongside + kaleō, to call), paramythia (consolation, comfort in grief or distress — from para, alongside + mythos, speech, story). The three form a spectrum from structural to relational to emotional: prophecy addresses the whole person in community.

notes.original: dia tou noos mou — with/through my mind
notes.rendering: I would rather speak five words with my mind than ten thousand in a tongue
notes.why: Nous (mind, faculty of understanding — Paul’s word for the rational-comprehending dimension of human personhood) is the criterion here. The assembly’s intelligence must be engaged if the community is to be built up. The number contrast — five (pente) vs. ten thousand (myrioi) — is deliberately extreme: five comprehensible words outweigh ten thousand unintelligible ones for the purpose of building up. The word myrion (ten thousand) is the root of English ‘myriad’; in Greek idiom it could mean simply ‘an uncountably large number.’

notes.original: sigatōsan en tais ekklēsiais — let them be silent in the assemblies
notes.rendering: the women should keep silent in the churches
notes.why: These verses are textually and interpretively difficult. Textually: some manuscripts (including Western texts) place vv.34–35 after v.40, suggesting possible marginal gloss origin. Interpretively: chapter 11 assumes women prophesy and pray in the assembly (11:5) without censure. Proposed resolutions: (1) interpolation (later addition by a scribe harmonizing with 1 Timothy 2:12); (2) Paul silencing a specific disruptive practice of women interrogating prophets mid-assembly, not silencing women’s speech generally; (3) a Corinthian slogan Paul quotes and then refutes in v.36. The translation renders the NA28 text as received. Readers should weigh the contextual tension with 11:5 carefully.

intro: Chapter 15 is the longest and densest argument in the letter — and the most carefully constructed. It opens with the earliest surviving creedal formula in the New Testament (vv.3–5), moves through a reductio ad absurdum of resurrection denial (vv.12–19), and arrives at the most sustained biblical argument for bodily transformation in Paul’s letters (vv.35–58). The closing verses move from argument to doxology: death is swallowed up in victory, and the labor of the faithful is not in vain.

notes.original: paredōka… ho kai parelabon — I delivered… what I also received
notes.rendering: I delivered to you… what I also received
notes.why: The formula paradidōmi… paralambanō (to hand on… to receive) is the technical language of tradition transmission in both Jewish (qibbel… masar in the Mishnah) and Hellenistic contexts. Paul places himself in a chain: he received the tradition from others (the Jerusalem apostles, presumably; cf. Galatians 1:18–2:10) and delivers it to the Corinthians unchanged. The content — died / was buried / was raised / appeared — is organized as four verbs in the aorist tense, each followed by an amplifying clause. The formula is widely thought to predate Paul, possibly traceable to the Jerusalem community within a few years of the crucifixion.

notes.original: aparchē tōn kekoimēmenōn — firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep
notes.rendering: the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep
notes.why: Aparchē (firstfruits — the first portion of the harvest offered to God, which consecrates and guarantees the rest of the harvest: Leviticus 23, Numbers 28) is Paul’s key word for Christ’s resurrection in relation to the general resurrection. The firstfruits are not separate from the harvest but the first installment of it — the pledge that the rest will follow. Christ’s resurrection is therefore not a unique anomaly but the beginning of an eschatological sequence. Kekoimēmenōn (those who have fallen asleep — perfect passive participle of koimaō, to sleep) is the euphemism for the dead that Paul consistently uses, and that became the standard Christian term (cemetery — koimētērion — sleeping-place).

notes.original: sōma psychikon / sōma pneumatikon — soulish body / spiritual body
notes.rendering: it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body
notes.why: The psychikon / pneumatikon contrast (natural/soulish body vs. spiritual body) returns the anthropological distinction of 2:14 to the question of resurrection. Psychikon sōma is not a body made of soul, nor is pneumatikon sōma a body made of spirit: both are bodies (sōma), but animated by different principles. The resurrection body is animated by the divine Spirit rather than by the natural human life-principle (psychē). This is continuity-with-transformation, not replacement: the same body, radically changed in its animating power. The Adam/Christ typology of vv.45–49 elaborates: two Adams, two modes of bodily existence, two orders of humanity.

intro: Chapter 16 descends from the heights of the resurrection argument to the practical ground of money, travel plans, and personal commendations. The collection for Jerusalem (described more fully in 2 Corinthians 8–9 and Romans 15:25–27) is Paul’s great ecumenical project: a financial expression of Gentile-church solidarity with the mother-church in Jerusalem. The chapter closes with two of the most resonant lines in the letter: the anathema and prayer of v.22, which preserves the earliest Aramaic liturgical phrase in the New Testament.

notes.original: thyra… megalē kai energēs — a door… great and effective
notes.rendering: a wide and effective door has opened to me
notes.why: The door metaphor for missionary opportunity appears in Paul (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3) and Acts (14:27). Megalē (great, large) and energēs (effective, active, at work — from energeō, the same root as energēmata in 12:6; the word that gives English ‘energy’) describe both the scale and the vitality of the opportunity. The immediate addition — ‘and there are many adversaries’ (antikeimenos polloi) — is not a qualification but an intensification: the door is open precisely in the place of greatest resistance. Paul’s view of mission does not expect open doors to be obstacle-free.

notes.original: grēgoreite / stēkete en tē pistei — be watchful / stand firm in the faith
notes.rendering: be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong
notes.why: The four imperatives in rapid succession form a compressed exhortation: grēgoreō (to be awake, to be watchful — the word used in the Gethsemane narrative), stēkō (to stand firm, to hold one’s ground — a military term), andrizō (to act like a man, to be courageous — from anēr, man; in context it means be courageous without gender-specific implication, though the word carries those resonances in its original context), krataioo (to be made strong, to be strengthened — from kratos, strength). The four verbs build from alertness through stability through courage to strength: the full posture of the person who has received the gospel of the cross.

notes.original: anathema / Marana tha — let him be accursed / Our Lord, come!
notes.rendering: let him be accursed. Marana tha — Our Lord, come!
notes.why: Two extraordinary items in one verse. Anathema (accursed, devoted to destruction — the Greek rendering of Hebrew cherem, the irrevocable devotion of something to divine judgment) is Paul’s strongest condemnation. And then immediately: Marana tha — an Aramaic phrase preserved untranslated in a Greek letter, which tells us it was already a liturgical formula the Greek-speaking community knew and used. It divides as Maran atha (Our Lord, come!) or Marana tha (Our Lord has come). The liturgical prayer-direction is toward the future: the community prays at the table for the Lord’s arrival, the parousia it is waiting for. Marana tha appears also in the Didache 10:6, as a eucharistic prayer.

intro: First John opens without a sender, a recipient, or a conventional salutation — instead it opens with a fourfold sensory testimony: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. The prologue (vv. 1–4) echoes the opening of the Fourth Gospel (In the beginning was the Word) but shifts the register: from cosmic proclamation to bodily witness. The emphasis on hands that touched is anti-docetic from the first sentence. The second half of the chapter (vv. 5–10) states the letter’s foundational theology — God is light — and immediately draws its ethical consequence through a series of three conditional clauses, each structured as “if we say… we lie.”

notes.original: ho ēn ap’ archēs — what was from the beginning
notes.rendering: What was from the beginning — what we have heard, what we have seen with our own eyes, what we looked upon and our hands have touched
notes.why: Ho ēn ap’ archēs — what was from the beginning (the neuter relative pronoun ho, not the masculine who; John refers to the event and reality of the Word of life before specifying it as person). The echo of John 1:1 (en archē ēn ho logos — in the beginning was the Word) is deliberate. But where the Gospel opens cosmically, the letter opens empirically: heard, seen, examined (etheasāmetha — the verb of careful, deliberate looking, used for gazing at something significant), touched. Epselāphēsan — our hands touched (psēlaphāō — to handle, to feel, to grope after; used in Luke 24:39 for the risen Jesus inviting the disciples to touch him). The incarnation cannot be spiritualized past the evidence of hands.

notes.original: ho theos phōs estin — God is light
notes.rendering: God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all
notes.why: Phōs — light (one of the great Johannine metaphors, appearing throughout the Gospel and letters). The declaration is absolute and symmetrical: God is light; in him is no darkness at all — the negation is doubled in Greek (skotia en autō ouk estin oudemia — darkness in him is not, not any). This is not a metaphor for divine knowledge or moral purity alone; it is an ontological claim about the character of God that generates the ethical demands that follow. If God is light, then to claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness is self-contradiction. The light/darkness binary structures the entire chapter.

notes.original: pistos estin kai dikaios — he is faithful and just
notes.rendering: he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness
notes.why: Pistos — faithful, trustworthy (from pistos — the one who keeps promises; covenantal reliability). Dikaios — just, righteous (the one who acts in accordance with right, who renders what is owed). Both attributes together: God forgives not despite his justice but through it. The forgiveness is not a moral lapse on God’s part but an expression of his covenant faithfulness and his righteous response to the confession. The word aphēi — he will forgive (from aphiemi — to release, to send away; the same verb used throughout the Gospels for the forgiveness of sins). The confession releases what the sin has bound.

intro: First John 2 introduces three of the letter’s key terms: paraklētos (advocate, 2:1), hilasmos (atoning sacrifice, 2:2), and chrisma (anointing, 2:20, 27). The chapter also contains the letter’s most explicit social diagnosis: the opponents have left the community (“they went out from us”, 2:19). Their departure is not merely sociological but theological evidence — it reveals that they were never truly embedded in the communal life of the body. The do-not-love-the-world passage (vv. 15–17) is not world-denial but a sharp diagnosis of misdirected desire.

notes.original: paraklēton echomen — we have an advocate; hilasmos — atoning sacrifice / propitiation
notes.rendering: we have an advocate with the Father — Jesus Christ the righteous. He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins
notes.why: Paraklēton — advocate, one called alongside to help (para — alongside; kaleō — to call; the term used in John 14–16 for the Holy Spirit as Paraclete). Here the advocate is not the Spirit but Christ himself — the one who stands with the Father on behalf of the sinning believer. Hilasmos — atoning sacrifice, propitiation, expiation (from hilaskōmai — to appease, to make favorable, to cover; the word used in the LXX for the mercy seat, the kappōret). The word carries both the removal of sin (expiation) and the turning of wrath (propitiation); separating them too cleanly loses the full resonance. The same word appears in 4:10.

notes.original: hē epithymia tēs sarkos kai hē epithymia tōn ophthalmōn kai hē alazoneia tou biou — desires of the flesh, desires of the eyes, pride in possessions
notes.rendering: the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride in possessions
notes.why: Alazoneia — boasting, pretension, arrogance (from alāzōn — a braggart, one who claims more than he has; the word appears in Proverbs and the Wisdom of Solomon for the self-exalting fool). Tou biou — of life, of possessions, of the material basis of existence (bios — life as lived, livelihood, property; distinct from zoē — life as vitality or eternal life). The three-part taxonomy is not an exhaustive system but a diagnosis: unchecked appetite (flesh), unchecked craving through perception (eyes), unchecked pride in what one has acquired (possessions). All three are “from the world” — they draw their value from a frame of reference that is passing away.

notes.original: to chrisma — the anointing
notes.rendering: the anointing you received from him abides in you
notes.why: Chrisma — anointing, the smeared substance (from chriō — to anoint; the same root as Christos — the Anointed One). The wordplay is intentional: those who have received the Christ have received the chrisma — an anointing that instructs them and abides in them. The antichrists (antichristoi) have gone out; the chrisma remains. John does not specify whether the anointing is the Spirit, baptism, or the word — the ambiguity may be deliberate, encompassing all three. The claim “you have no need for anyone to teach you” is not anti-intellectual but polemical: the community does not need the teaching of those who have departed.

intro: First John 3 opens with an exclamation that functions as a pivot point for the whole letter: see what kind of love the Father has given — an outburst of wonder before a theological assertion. The chapter then moves through the logic of divine parentage: children of God have God’s character, and the test of that character is practical love. The Cain passage (v.12) is the letter’s darkest intertextual moment: the opposite of the love-command is not mere indifference but murder.

notes.original: potapēn agapēn — what sort of love / what manner of love
notes.rendering: See what kind of love the Father has given to us
notes.why: Potapēn — what sort of, what manner of, how extraordinary (from what country? — originally the exclamation of someone seeing something so foreign it seems to come from another world entirely). The word is used in the Synoptics when the disciples marvel at the stones of the temple (Mark 13:1) or at the calming of the storm (Matthew 8:27). It is a word of astonishment at the unexpected and overwhelming. The love the Father has given is so alien to normal categories that the writer can only point at it and exclaim. Dedōken — has given (the perfect tense: he gave and it remains given; the love is not a past event but a present condition).

notes.original: sperma autou en autō menei — God’s seed abides in him
notes.rendering: No one born of God makes a practice of sinning, for God’s seed abides in him
notes.why: Sperma — seed (the biological and agricultural word; in context it is the divine generative principle implanted in the one born of God). The image is of organic regeneration: as a plant grown from seed carries the nature of the plant that produced it, so the one born of God carries the divine nature that generated the new birth. The verse has always troubled careful readers because it appears to claim sinlessness for believers — which ch. 1:8-10 flatly denies. The resolution lies in the present tense of the infinitives: hamartanein — to keep on sinning, to make a practice of sinning. The new birth does not produce sinless perfection; it makes continuous, habitual, unrepentant sin incompatible with the nature implanted.

notes.original: en toutō egnōkamen tēn agapēn — by this we have known love
notes.rendering: By this we know love — that he laid down his life for us
notes.why: Egnōkamen — we have come to know, we have learned by experience (the perfect of ginōskō — to know by acquaintance and experience; the knowledge remains). The sentence is structurally radical: love is not defined by an emotion or an attribute but by an event. We do not begin with a concept of love and then find it exemplified in Christ; we begin with the event — he laid down his life — and derive our understanding of what love is from that. Ekeinos tēn psychēn autou ethēken hyper hēmōn — that one laid down his soul for us (psychēn — soul, life, self; the same phrase used in John 10:11-15 for the good shepherd). The definition of love is not an abstraction. It is a cross.

intro: First John 4 contains the letter’s theological summit: twice it states, without qualification or analogy, ho theos agapē estin — God is love (vv. 8, 16). This is not a predicate applied to God from the outside (“God is loving”) but an identification of God’s being with love itself. The chapter moves from the christological test (confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, v.2) through the theological declaration (God is love, vv. 8, 16) to the ethical consequence (whoever loves God must love his brother, v.21). The three are inseparable: the test, the declaration, and the demand are one movement.

notes.original: pân pneuma ho homologei Iēsoun Christon en sarki elthēkota — every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh
notes.rendering: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God
notes.why: En sarki elthēkota — having come in the flesh (the perfect participle: he came and remains come; the incarnation is not a past event that has been superseded but a permanent state of the Son of God). This is the letter’s christological test, aimed precisely at the proto-Gnostic teachers who separated the divine Christ from the human Jesus. The confession required is not merely “Jesus is divine” but “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” — the union of the divine and the fully human in one person. Any spirit that cannot make this confession is not from God, regardless of its spiritual claims.

notes.original: ho theos agapē estin — God is love
notes.rendering: Anyone who does not love does not know God, because God is love
notes.why: Ho theos agapē estin: four words in Greek, no article on agapē, making this an identification rather than a mere characterization. The author does not say God is loving (an attribute applied from outside) or God has love (a possession) or God shows love (an action) — but God is love. The being of God and the being of love are identified. The implications are as vast as the statement is short. The statement appears again in v.16 after the incarnation argument of vv. 9–10, suggesting that we do not know what love is until we know what God did in Christ; and we do not know what God is until we see what love did on the cross.

notes.original: hē teleia agapē exō bállei ton phobon — perfect love casts out fear
notes.rendering: but perfect love casts out fear
notes.why: Ekballei — casts out, throws out, expels (from ekballō — to throw out with force; the same word used for casting out demons in the Gospels). Perfect love does not merely reduce fear or coexist with it; it drives it out. Telēia — perfect, complete, brought to its goal (from telos — end, goal, completion; the same root as the love that has been brought to its goal in v.12 and v.17). The fear in view is not healthy reverence for God but the cringing terror of a slave who expects punishment (kolasis — punishment, chastisement). Love, when it has fully formed in a person, does not leave room for this terror because the lover knows the character of the one who is loved.

intro: First John 5 gathers up the letter’s three threads — christology, ethics, and assurance — into a final movement. The closing section (vv. 13–21) is structured around the word oidamen — we know — which appears four times (vv. 15, 18, 19, 20), each time anchoring a certainty. The letter that opened with empirical testimony (“our hands touched”) closes with epistemological confidence: we know. The final verse — “little children, guard yourselves from idols” — is one of the most abrupt endings in the New Testament. No blessing. No farewell. Just one more urgent command.

notes.original: hē nikē hē nikēsasa ton kosmon — the victory that has overcome the world
notes.rendering: And this is the victory that has overcome the world — our faith
notes.why: Nikē — victory (the word that gives us the name Nike, the Greek goddess of victory). Nikēsasa — the aorist participle: the victory that overcame, that won the decisive battle. The perfect tense of nikaō appears throughout Revelation (the one who overcomes). Here the victory is not future or ongoing but already won — the aorist points to the completed event of Christ’s death and resurrection as the moment of conquest. Our faith is the participation in a victory already secured, not the effort by which we secure it. The world is overcome not by striving but by believing in the one who overcame it.

notes.original: ho elthōn di’ hydatos kai haimatos — the one who came through water and blood
notes.rendering: This is he who came by water and blood — Jesus Christ — not by the water only but by the water and the blood
notes.why: Di’ hydatos kai haimatos — through water and blood. The referents are disputed: baptism and the cross? The birth waters and the crucifixion blood? The water and blood that flowed from the side of Christ at the spear-thrust (John 19:34)? The most likely reading, given the polemical context, is the two defining events of Jesus’ public career: his baptism (when the divine Spirit descended and the voice declared him Son of God) and his crucifixion (when he died bodily). The opponents may have accepted the water — the divine Christ arriving at the baptism — while denying the blood — the divine Christ truly dying on the cross. John insists: not water only but water and blood.

notes.original: oidamen de hoti ho huios tou theou hēkei — we know that the Son of God has come
notes.rendering: And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know him who is true
notes.why: Oidamen — we know (oida — to know as settled fact, as established certainty; distinct from ginōskō — to know by growing experience). The four oidamen of this closing section (vv. 15, 18, 19, 20) are the letter’s final gift to a community that has been destabilized by the departure of confident teachers. John does not leave them with uncertainty: we know. The letter that began with the empirical certainty of eyewitness testimony ends with the theological certainty of the indwelling Son. Houtos estin ho alēthinos theos kai zoē aiōnios — he is the true God and eternal life: the most compressed summary of the letter’s entire argument.

intro: The opening chapter of 1 Kings establishes three interlocking crises: the king's failing body, an unsealed succession, and a premature power grab. The Hebrew narrator is a master of dramatic irony — Adonijah's feast is in full swing when the very thing it was meant to forestall is being accomplished at Gihon. Two key words run through the chapter: mitnasse (lifting oneself up) and yad (hand) — whose hand is on the king?

notes.original: v'ha-melech lo yeda'ah — and the king did not know her
notes.rendering: the king does not know her
notes.why: Yada — to know in the fullest sense (Genesis 4:1; Adam knew Eve). The narrator places this fact with clinical precision: the very thing that would mark full vitality is absent. David can no longer "know." The scene is not prurient; it is a royal health report with grave implications for succession. The virgin-king motif (warmth without knowledge) signals the end of an era before the narrative voice says so directly.

notes.original: mitnasse le'mor ani emloch — lifting himself up saying, "I will be king"
notes.rendering: lifts himself up and says, 'I will be king'
notes.why: Mitnasse (from nasa — to lift, to carry, to exalt) in the reflexive Hitpael: to elevate oneself, to set oneself above. The same root describes Absalom's self-promotion (2 Sam 15:1 — Absalom also got chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him). Adonijah repeats his brother's gesture almost word for word. The narrative is not subtle: this is Absalom's play, now attempted by his younger brother. David had not rebuked Absalom either (2 Sam 13:21); the same parental indulgence is noted here (v.6).

notes.original: shemen min ha'ohel — oil from the tent
notes.rendering: takes the horn of oil from the tent
notes.why: Ha'ohel — the tent, almost certainly the tent shrine David erected for the ark (2 Sam 6:17). The anointing oil is drawn from the sanctuary — this is not a military promotion but a sacred act. The horn (qeren) of oil echoes the horn used to anoint Saul (1 Sam 10:1) and David (1 Sam 16:13). Three anointing strands converge on Solomon: the priest (Zadok), the prophet (Nathan), and the military commander (Benaiah with the royal guard). It is the fullest anointing in Israel's history up to this point.

intro: Chapter 2 is a cold masterpiece of political theology. David's deathbed instructions blend covenant piety (keep the Law of Moses) with hardheaded statecraft (settle old scores). Solomon executes each commission with surgical efficiency. The narrator never condemns him; the reader is left to reckon with what it costs to establish a kingdom.

notes.original: v'shamarta et mishmeret YHWH Elohecha — and guard the charge of YHWH your God
notes.rendering: keep the charge of YHWH your God
notes.why: Shamarta (shamar — to guard, to keep, to watch over) carries the sense of a soldier at his post. The charge David gives Solomon is Deuteronomic in its structure: statutes (chuqot), commandments (mitzvot), ordinances (mishpatim), and testimonies ('edot) — the full taxonomy of covenantal obligation from Deuteronomy 17:14–20, the law of the king. Solomon's wisdom will be tested not only by the dream at Gibeon but by whether he keeps this charge.

notes.original: demei milchamah b'shalom — blood of war in peacetime
notes.rendering: he put that war-blood on the belt at his waist and the sandals on his feet
notes.why: The Hebrew is vivid: dam milchamah (blood of war) spilled b'shalom (in peace, in the time of peace). Joab killed Abner (2 Sam 3:27) and Amasa (2 Sam 20:10) through treacherous peaceable approaches — embrace and a sword. The blood-stained belt and sandals are a powerful physical image: Joab wears his guilt on his body. David died unable to punish him; he charges Solomon with the reckoning.

notes.original: v'hamamlachah nechonah b'yad Shlomo — the kingdom was established in Solomon's hand
notes.rendering: the kingdom is now firmly in Solomon's hand
notes.why: Nechonah (from kun — to be firm, established, set in place; the same root as in Hannah's prayer: 'my heart is established in YHWH') — the kingdom is not just stable but founded, rooted. The verb closes an iron frame: David's charge in v.12 promised the throne would be established (tikkon — same root); now it is. The four executions and one exile of chapter 2 are narrated without moral editorializing; the kingdom's stability is the only verdict offered.

intro: Chapter 3 is built around two divine gifts: the dream at Gibeon, where Solomon asks for a lev shome'a (a hearing heart), and the courtroom scene, where that gift is immediately displayed. The chapter also plants a tension that will crack open the book's second half — Solomon loves YHWH, and he sacrifices at the high places. Both things are true from verse three.

notes.original: lev shome'a — a listening heart
notes.rendering: a listening heart — a heart that hears
notes.why: Lev shome'a is often translated "understanding" or "discerning" heart, but the literal force is a hearing heart — one that listens. Shome'a (from shama — to hear, to obey, the same root as the Shema: Hear, O Israel) carries the full weight of attentive responsiveness, not mere intellectual capacity. Solomon does not ask for intelligence; he asks to be able to hear the people, hear the cases, hear what justice requires. The request is relational and judicial, not academic. God gives him chochmah (wisdom) and binah (understanding) in return — but what Solomon asked for was the capacity to listen.

notes.original: nichmerú rachaméha — her compassion burned for him
notes.rendering: her compassion blazes for her son
notes.why: Nichmerú (from chamar — to be hot, to burn, to ferment; used of compassion boiling up) and rachamim — compassion, tender mercy (from rechem — womb). The word for the deepest human compassion is rooted in the word for womb: the mother's feelings for her child are literally uterine. The narrator uses the biological word for the most decisive moment of the case — and Solomon reads it as evidence. The woman who would rather give up her son than see him killed is the one whose body made him.

notes.original: chochmat Elohim b'kirbo — the wisdom of God within him
notes.rendering: the wisdom of God is in him to execute justice
notes.why: Chochmat Elohim — not human cleverness or royal cunning, but divine wisdom resident in a person. La'asot mishpat — to do, to execute, to make justice (mishpat — right judgment, the ordering of claims). The people see that what happened in that courtroom was not a trick but a revelation: the king's wisdom comes from somewhere beyond him. This is the theological verdict the chapter has been building toward since verse 9.

intro: Chapter 4 is an administrative inventory — and a deliberately dazzling one. The list of officials and governors is not bureaucratic filler; it is evidence. The kingdom David dreamed and died for is now a functioning state: food secured, borders extended, peace on every side. The chapter closes by pivoting from logistical to cosmic: the same king who feeds his court with oxen and barley feeds the world with proverbs and songs.

notes.original: Yehudah v'Yisrael rabbim — Judah and Israel numerous
notes.rendering: Judah and Israel are as numerous as the sand by the sea
notes.why: Rabbim kakol asher al sephath hayam — numerous as all that is on the shore of the sea. The phrase echoes the Abrahamic promise (Genesis 22:17 — your offspring shall be as the sand on the seashore). The narrator is making a claim: the Solomonic golden age is the fulfillment of the patriarchal covenant. The people eat and drink and are glad (sameach) — a word of festive joy, the same used for the joy of harvest and the joy of worship. This is the covenant's promised result, on full display.

notes.original: ish tachat gaphno v'tachat te'enato — each man under his vine and under his fig tree
notes.rendering: every man under his own vine and under his own fig tree
notes.why: This phrase — each man under his vine and under his fig tree — becomes the Bible's image of secure peaceable prosperity (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10; John 1:48). In a subsistence agricultural economy, the vine and the fig tree are the long-term crops, planted with confidence in tomorrow. To sit under your own vine means: you own the land, the enemy is not coming, and you planted in faith. The narrator places it "from Dan to Beersheba" — the full north-south extent of the land.

notes.original: chochmah u'vinah harbeh me'od — wisdom and understanding very much
notes.rendering: God gives Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond all measure
notes.why: Rochav lev — breadth of heart/mind (rochav — width, expanse; lev — heart, seat of thought and will). The image is spatial: wisdom as a vast interior landscape. The sand on the seashore returns from v.20 — the people's number and Solomon's wisdom are both described with the same hyperbole. What the kingdom holds in bodies, its king holds in mind. The description that follows (trees, beasts, birds, fish) is proto-encyclopedic: Solomonic wisdom is not only judicial but natural-philosophical, a knowledge of the created order that runs from the cedar of Lebanon to the hyssop in the wall.

intro: Chapter 5 is the diplomacy and logistics of the Temple project. Two kings, two resources, one treaty. The narrator holds the theological and the practical in deliberate tension: YHWH gives wisdom, and Solomon uses it to negotiate labor rates and timber rafts. The use of forced labor — the mas — is noted without comment here; its consequences will surface in chapter 12.

notes.original: ein satan v'ein pega ra — no adversary and no evil occurrence
notes.rendering: no adversary, no misfortune
notes.why: Satan here is not a supernatural being but a legal/military term: a satan is an adversary, an opponent, one who brings a charge or mounts resistance (as in Numbers 22:22, where the angel stands as a satan in Balaam's path). Pega ra — evil occurrence, mishap, bad chance. Solomon's reign of peace is described in double negative: nothing opposes, nothing goes wrong. The contrast with David's warfare-surrounded reign (v.3) is the justification for why this king, not that one, builds the house.

notes.original: v'amar — as he said
notes.rendering: as YHWH said to my father David
notes.why: Solomon quotes the dynastic oracle of 2 Samuel 7:13 — your son shall build a house for my name. The Temple is not Solomon's idea; it is the fulfillment of a divine word spoken to his father. This citation serves a double function: it authorizes the project theologically, and it positions Solomon as the executor of an inherited promise rather than an entrepreneur of religion. The house is YHWH's idea, delivered through a prophet, remembered by a king.

notes.original: vaya'al ha-melech Shlomo mas — King Solomon raises a levy of forced labor
notes.rendering: King Solomon conscripts forced labor from all Israel
notes.why: Mas — corvée, forced labor, compulsory service (the same word used in Exodus 1:11 for the labor Egypt imposed on Israel: they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with forced labor). The narrator uses the Exodus word without comment. The irony is precise: the people YHWH freed from Egyptian corvée are now conscripted into royal corvée for YHWH's house. Thirty thousand men, rotating through Lebanon. The number and the word together are a seed of judgment that chapter 12 will harvest.

intro: Chapter 6 is an architectural poem. The measurements, the materials, the carvings — all of it serves a single purpose: to establish that YHWH's dwelling is the most beautiful, most painstaking, most costly structure Israel has ever made. But the chapter's theological center is not the dimensions; it is the tiny eight-verse oracle buried in verses 11–13, where YHWH interrupts the building report with a conditional: if. The house is not magic. It is a pledge contingent on obedience.

notes.original: v'ha-bayit b'hibbanoto — the house while being built
notes.rendering: no hammer, axe, or any iron tool is heard in the house while it is being built
notes.why: The silence of iron is theologically weighted. Iron tools were associated with warfare and with the violence of the nations (Joshua 8:31 — an altar of unhewn stones, over which no iron has been lifted). The Temple stones are dressed at the quarry and brought to the site already finished — so that the house of peace is built without the sound of weapons. The narrative detail is a liturgical statement: the space where YHWH dwells is shaped by what is done before it arrives, not by force at the site.

notes.original: im telekh b'chuqotai — if you walk in my statutes
notes.rendering: if you walk in my statutes... then I will fulfill my word
notes.why: The particle im — if. In the middle of seven years of construction, the word of YHWH interrupts with a conditional. The house does not guarantee the divine presence; the divine presence follows obedience. This is the chapter's irreducible theological claim: the building is not the covenant. The covenant is the covenant. A house of gold cannot contain what disobedience will drive away. The oracle is brief and easily skipped over — the narrator places it there precisely so the reader cannot say, at the end of the book, that they were not warned.

notes.original: sheva shanim — seven years
notes.rendering: he spends seven years building it
notes.why: Sheva shanim — seven years. The number is not incidental. Seven is the number of completeness, of Sabbath, of the created week. The Temple built in seven years stands as a new creation: the world made in seven days has now produced a dwelling for its Maker within it. The narrator places this number at the chapter's close, then immediately (in chapter 7) pivots to note that Solomon spent thirteen years building his own house. The juxtaposition is deliberate; every ancient reader would have noticed the arithmetic.

intro: Chapter 7 catalogues the material reality of the Solomonic project. The thirteen years for the palace against the seven for the Temple is a number the narrator simply places before the reader without comment — the arithmetic does the work. The craftsman Hiram of Tyre, the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the Molten Sea: these are the furniture of Israel's imagination of sacred space.

notes.original: shloshim esreh shanah — thirteen years
notes.rendering: it takes him thirteen years to complete it
notes.why: The juxtaposition with 6:38 (seven years for the Temple) is the chapter's first and most consequential fact. The narrator offers no judgment — none is needed. The king who asked for a listening heart has spent nearly twice as long building his own house as YHWH's. The number is not an accusation but an invitation to arithmetic that every reader will perform. What a man builds longest is what he values most.

notes.original: male chochmah u'tevunah u'da'at — full of wisdom, understanding, and skill
notes.rendering: full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for every work in bronze
notes.why: The three terms — chochmah (wisdom), tevunah (understanding, discernment), and da'at (knowledge, intimate knowing) — are the same triad used to describe the craftsman Bezalel in Exodus 31:3, whom God fills with his Spirit to build the Tabernacle. The Hiram who builds the Temple furnishings is a new Bezalel: artisan-wisdom as divine gift, not merely technical competence. The narrator signals continuity between the Tabernacle and the Temple through shared vocabulary.

notes.original: Yachin... Boaz — Jachin... Boaz
notes.rendering: he calls its name Jachin... he calls its name Boaz
notes.why: Yachin — he will establish (from kun — to be firm, the same root as nechonah in 2:46). Boaz — in him is strength (or: by strength). The two named pillars frame the entrance to the Temple: every worshipper passes between "He will establish" and "In him is strength" to approach the presence of YHWH. The names are perhaps throne-names, perhaps ritual declarations. Whatever their origin, their placement is theological: you enter YHWH's house through his promises.

intro: Chapter 8 is the theological summit of 1 Kings and one of the great prayers of the Hebrew Bible. The cloud fills the house and the priests cannot stand — and then Solomon asks the central question of the chapter: will God indeed dwell on the earth? His prayer is structured as a series of seven intercessions, each anchored in the phrase "hear in heaven your dwelling place." The Temple is not where God lives; it is where prayers are aimed and heard.

notes.original: kavod YHWH male et beit YHWH — the glory of YHWH fills the house of YHWH
notes.rendering: the glory of YHWH fills the house of YHWH
notes.why: Kavod — glory, weight, substance (from kaved — to be heavy). The kavod YHWH is the visible, substantial divine presence — the same pillar of cloud that led Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21) and filled the Tabernacle at its completion (Exodus 40:34–35). The echo is exact and deliberate: Moses could not enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had settled and the glory of YHWH filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). The Temple dedication reproduces the Tabernacle dedication; the narrator is saying: this is the same presence, in a permanent house.

notes.original: ha'shamayim u'shmei ha'shamayim lo yechalkelucha — heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you
notes.rendering: heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house
notes.why: Shmei ha'shamayim — heaven of heavens, the superlative (the farthest, the highest, the uttermost heaven). The question — will God dwell on earth? — is the most honest theological question in the chapter. Solomon builds the most magnificent house of his age and immediately acknowledges it cannot hold what it is built for. This is not false modesty; it is the correct theology. The Temple is the address where prayers go, not the box that contains the divine. The prayer that follows is accordingly addressed to heaven, not to the building.

notes.original: lo nafal davar echad mikol devaro ha'tov — not one word has fallen of all his good word
notes.rendering: not one word has failed of all his good promise
notes.why: Lo nafal davar — not a word has fallen (nafal — to fall; the same verb used of the walls of Jericho: the wall fell down flat). The inversion is precise: Jericho's walls fell so that Israel could enter the land; YHWH's words have not fallen so that Israel could remain. Every promise made to Abraham and Moses and David stands. The word lo nafal davar becomes the theological thesis of the entire Deuteronomistic History: YHWH's word does not fail. It is the book of Joshua's closing statement (Joshua 21:45; 23:14) repeated here at the moment of the kingdom's greatest glory.

intro: Chapter 9 is the hinge of 1 Kings. The second divine appearance repeats and sharpens the conditional of chapter 6: now the threat is made explicit. The house can be cast from YHWH's sight just as surely as it was consecrated. The administrative notes that follow — the Cabul cities, the building projects, the labor levy — are read differently after the oracle: prosperity and construction are not proofs of covenant faithfulness but the material in which disobedience will become visible.

notes.original: v'karat et Yisrael me'al pnei ha'adamah — I will cut off Israel from upon the face of the ground
notes.rendering: I will cut off Israel from the land I have given them
notes.why: Karat — to cut off, to sever (the same root as the covenant-making formula karat berit — to cut a covenant, where an animal was cut in two and the parties walked between the halves). The covenant that was cut can also cut. The verb is surgical and final. The house I have consecrated I will cast from my sight — shalach me'al panai, to hurl away from before my face. The same divine eyes that will be on the house forever (v.3) can also hurl it from sight. The oracle is the theological engine of the entire second half of the Deuteronomistic History.

notes.original: v'ha-bayit ha-zeh yihyeh elyonot — this house shall become a heap of ruins
notes.rendering: this house will become a heap of ruins
notes.why: Elyonot is rendered "heap of ruins" here, though the word is difficult — some read "exalted" or "notorious." The context and the parallel with "proverb and byword" (v.7) favors the negative sense: what was lifted up as the most glorious house in Israel will become a sign of desolation. The passersby who hiss and ask "why?" are the voice of future history speaking in advance. The narrator is writing after 586 BCE and knows exactly what those passersby will say; this oracle is written by someone who watched it happen.

notes.original: Eretz Kavul — land of Cabul
notes.rendering: they are called the land of Cabul to this day
notes.why: Kavul — meaning uncertain; ancient tradition reads it as "like nothing" or "good for nothing" (possibly from kevel — fetter, or simply as a placename). Hiram's displeasure at the twenty Galilean cities he receives in payment for his cedar and gold is notable. The king who built the most magnificent house in the ancient world is paying his international ally with real estate the ally considers worthless. The detail is not flattering and the narrator preserves it without comment.

intro: Chapter 10 is the golden peak — literally. Gold appears in almost every verse. The queen of Sheba arrives with spices and gold and leaves breathless. Six hundred sixty-six talents arrive annually. Shields of gold line the palace walls. Silver becomes as common as stone. But the attentive reader of Deuteronomy 17 has been counting: the law of the king forbids the multiplication of horses, gold, and foreign wives. Chapter 10 documents the first two transgressions in exhaustive, glittering detail.

notes.original: v'lo hayah bah od ru'ach — there was no longer breath in her
notes.rendering: there is no more breath in her
notes.why: Lo hayah bah od ru'ach — the breath/spirit left her (ru'ach — spirit, breath, wind; the same word as the spirit of God hovering over the waters in Genesis 1:2). The queen of Sheba is so overwhelmed by what she sees — the food, the servants, the offerings — that her ru'ach is knocked out of her. It is the Bible's most extravagant compliment: Solomon's household takes a queen's breath away. And it is precisely this excess — the food, the servants, the gold — that Deuteronomy 17 identifies as the king's characteristic temptation.

notes.original: la'asot mishpat u'tzedaqah — to execute justice and righteousness
notes.rendering: he has made you king to execute justice and righteousness
notes.why: Mishpat u'tzedaqah — justice and righteousness, the paired covenant terms. The queen of Sheba attributes Solomon's kingship not to his splendor but to YHWH's love for Israel and the mandate of justice. It is the most theologically precise statement in the chapter, and it is placed in the mouth of a foreign queen who has come from the ends of the earth. She sees more clearly than the narrative's own catalog of gold will allow. The same pair — mishpat u'tzedaqah — will be what Amos demands and what Solomon's successors abandon.

notes.original: vayeesof Shlomo rechev u'parashim — Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen
notes.rendering: Solomon also gathers chariots and horsemen — fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen
notes.why: Deuteronomy 17:16 forbids the king from multiplying horses (lo yarbeh lo susim) and from returning the people to Egypt to multiply horses. Chapter 10 closes with Solomon importing horses from Egypt and Kue, amassing fourteen hundred chariots, and making silver as common as stone. These are the three violations Deuteronomy's law of the king anticipates: horses multiplied, return to Egypt for horses, silver and gold multiplied. The narrator lists them without editorial comment, because the reader who knows Deuteronomy 17 already knows the verdict.

intro: Chapter 11 is the catastrophe the book has been preparing since chapter 3's opening verse (Solomon loves YHWH... yet he sacrificed at the high places). Three things destroy the wisest man in the world: his wives, his old age, and his heart. The narrator uses the phrase "not wholly true to YHWH" as the diagnostic — and the Hebrew word it translates is shalom: his heart was not at peace with YHWH, not complete, not whole.

notes.original: lo hayah levavo shalem im YHWH — his heart was not whole/at peace with YHWH
notes.rendering: his heart is not wholly true to YHWH his God
notes.why: Shalem — whole, complete, at peace (the root of shalom). The word David's heart was — shalem with YHWH (1 Kings 8:61, where Solomon charged Israel to have a wholly devoted heart) — is now the word Solomon's heart is not. The irony is precise: the son who prayed for a lev shome'a (a hearing heart) and built the house for YHWH's name ends with a heart that is not shalem. The high places for Chemosh and Milcom are the symptom; the divided heart is the diagnosis.

notes.original: qaroah ekra et hamamlachah me'alecha — I will surely tear the kingdom from you
notes.rendering: I will surely tear the kingdom from you
notes.why: Qaroah ekra — the infinitive absolute (qaroah) before the verb (ekra) in Hebrew signals absolute certainty: I will surely, certainly, definitely tear. The verb is qarar — to tear, to rend (the same verb used for the tearing of garments in mourning; Ahijah will enact this literally with his new garment in v.30). The tearing of the kingdom from Solomon mirrors the tearing of the kingdom from Saul (1 Samuel 15:28 — YHWH has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today). The Solomonic era ends with the same verdict as the Saulide era.

notes.original: nir l'David avdi — a lamp for my servant David
notes.rendering: that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem
notes.why: Nir — lamp, light, a wick or flame (also used of a cleared and cultivated field — a lamp is something that must be tended to keep burning). YHWH preserves one tribe for David's line not as a reward for Solomon but as a promise to David. The lamp is the dynastic flame: as long as one tribe remains in Jerusalem under a Davidic king, the lamp has not gone out. The image will recur at every Davidic king's death — he leaves a lamp in Jerusalem. It is extinguished in 2 Kings 25.

intro: Chapter 12 is the catastrophe made concrete. The kingdom that David unified and Solomon gilded tears apart in a single assembly at Shechem. The narrator's verdict is distributed: Rehoboam is a fool who takes the worst advice available; Jeroboam is a politician who substitutes religion for YHWH rather than risk losing the people's allegiance. Both men earn the history that follows.

notes.original: qotni avah mimothnei avi — my little finger is thicker than my father's waist
notes.rendering: my little finger is thicker than my father's waist
notes.why: The young men's counsel is not merely arrogant — it is anatomically absurd, and deliberately so. Qotni — my little finger (sometimes translated little member, with a cruder anatomical implication). The image of Rehoboam's little finger outmassing Solomon's entire waist/loins is the political bravado of a man who has never governed anything. The old men counseled servanthood; the young men counseled dominance theater. Rehoboam chooses the theater. The result is that he loses eighty percent of his kingdom within the week.

notes.original: hineh elohecha Yisrael asher he'elu otcha me'eretz Mitzrayim — behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from Egypt
notes.rendering: behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt
notes.why: The phrase is verbatim from Exodus 32:4 — Aaron's words at the golden calf at Sinai. The narrator is not subtle: Jeroboam's calves are a deliberate repetition of Israel's foundational apostasy. What Aaron did under pressure at Sinai, Jeroboam does as state policy in Bethel and Dan. The new northern kingdom is founded on the paradigmatic sin. Every subsequent reference to Jeroboam will carry the formula "the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat" — the calves are the sin that defines all the kings who follow him.

notes.original: asher badah me'libbo — which he devised from his own heart
notes.rendering: in the month that he devised from his own heart
notes.why: Badah — to invent, to fabricate, to make up (used only here and in 1 Kings 13:33 in this sense). Me'libbo — from his own heart. The phrase is the narrator's final and most damning verdict on Jeroboam's religious innovation: the eighth-month festival, the calves, the non-Levitical priests — all of it comes not from YHWH but from Jeroboam's own heart. The contrast with Solomon's prayer (where the heart is aimed toward heaven) is complete. Jeroboam's heart aims at himself and calls it worship.

intro: Chapter 13 is one of the most unsettling stories in the Hebrew Bible: a true prophet obeys YHWH, is deceived by a false one, disobeys, and is killed by a lion — while the false prophet who lied to him grieves at the graveside and proclaims his word true. The story refuses to be domesticated. The word of YHWH is kept, even when the human channel of that word breaks.

notes.original: Yoshiyahu shemo — Josiah is his name
notes.rendering: a son shall be born to the house of David — Josiah by name
notes.why: The prophecy names Josiah approximately three hundred years before his birth (2 Kings 23:15–16 records its literal fulfillment — Josiah exhumes and burns bones on the very altar at Bethel). Named prophecy of this specificity is rare in the Hebrew Bible. The narrator is either recording an extraordinary predictive oracle or writing with full knowledge of the outcome. Either way, the narrative stakes are enormous: Bethel's altar is already condemned before it is a year old.

notes.original: kichesh lo — he lied to him
notes.rendering: but he lied to him
notes.why: Kichesh — he lied, he deceived, he denied (from kachash — to deceive, to disown; the same root as in Proverbs 30:9 — lest I deny you and say "Who is YHWH?"). The narrator's aside is blunt and without further explanation: the old prophet's claim to have received an angelic word is a lie. Why he lies — jealousy? Loneliness? Curiosity? — the text does not say. What the text does say is that the man of God believed a human voice over the word he had directly received from YHWH. The lesson is harsh: a second voice claiming divine authority is not automatically true, even from a fellow prophet.

notes.original: wayimtza'ehu ha'ari baderekh — the lion met him on the road
notes.rendering: a lion meets him on the road and kills him
notes.why: The lion is YHWH's agent — but with a peculiarity: it kills the man of God and then stands there, neither eating the body nor mauling the donkey. This is a sign within a judgment: the lion is not hungry, not wild, but purposeful. The exact obedience of an animal to a divine commission stands in contrast to the inexact obedience of the man of God to a divine command. The donkey and the lion stand together beside the body — the scene is eerie, almost sculptural — until the old prophet arrives to witness what his lie has wrought.

intro: Chapter 14 delivers two royal judgments in parallel: Jeroboam's house is condemned through the mouth of the prophet he once consulted for good news; Rehoboam's Jerusalem loses Solomon's gold shields within five years of their making — replaced by bronze. Both kings receive what they have sown. The chapter's deepest irony is that the one person found pleasing to YHWH in all the house of Jeroboam is the sick child who never lives to sin.

notes.original: vatashlicheni acharei gavecha — you have cast me behind your back
notes.rendering: casting me behind your back
notes.why: Acharei gavecha — behind your back (gav — back, spine; the same word for the broad back of a hill or a ridge). To cast YHWH behind one's back is to set him in the place of things unseen and unregarded — the opposite of walking before YHWH, which the text repeatedly commends. The phrase is Ezekiel's as well (Ezekiel 23:35) and carries the full force of studied inattention: Jeroboam has not merely neglected YHWH but has deliberately turned away, placing him where he cannot be seen.

notes.original: ki nimtza vo davar tov el YHWH — because something good toward YHWH was found in him
notes.rendering: in him there is found something pleasing to YHWH
notes.why: The child Abijah dies — and is the only member of Jeroboam's family given an honorable burial. The reason: davar tov — something good, something well-disposed toward YHWH, was found in him. The text does not explain what this something was. The dying child is more righteous than his father the king, his mother the disguised spy, or any of the officials who will eat and die by dogs in the streets. The smallest and most helpless person in Jeroboam's house is the only one YHWH regards with favor. The narrator notes it without sentimentality.

notes.original: vayikach et kol — he took everything
notes.rendering: he takes away everything... all the shields of gold that Solomon had made
notes.why: The shields of gold — two hundred large shields and three hundred smaller ones, documented in lavish detail in 10:16–17 — are gone. Within five years of Solomon's death, his trophy room is bare. Rehoboam replaces them with bronze: the same shape, the same function, a fraction of the value. The degradation is deliberate and visible every time a shield is carried to the Temple. Bronze pretending to be gold is the book's image for a kingdom pretending to be what it was. It will keep happening.

intro: Chapter 15 is structured as a triptych: Abijam (bad, forgiven for David's sake), Asa (good — the best king Judah will see for generations), and Nadab (bad, assassinated, his dynasty erased in a single night). The chapter establishes the double standard that will govern the whole of Kings: every Israelite king is measured against Jeroboam's calves; every Judean king is measured against David's heart.

notes.original: raq b'davar Uriyah ha'Chitti — except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite
notes.rendering: except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite
notes.why: The narrator's verdict on David is nearly perfect — and then this. Raq — only, except, but. The exception clause in the most glowing royal commendation in Kings is a single name: Uriah the Hittite. No elaboration, no softening. Every reader knows what the matter of Uriah entailed (2 Samuel 11): adultery, deception, arranged battlefield murder. The single name does the work of a judgment, placed here to prevent any reader from idealizing the standard by which all subsequent kings are measured.

notes.original: vayesar et ma'achah immo mig'vurah — he removed Maacah his mother from the position of queen mother
notes.rendering: he removes Maacah his mother from being queen mother
notes.why: The gevirah — the queen mother — is a formal institutional role in the Judean court, listed in royal introductions throughout Kings (notably absent in northern Israel). She holds a seat at court, arguably the most powerful woman in the kingdom. Asa removes his own mother from this office because of her Asherah cult. The act is politically costly and personally unprecedented. The narrator notes it as evidence of Asa's wholehearted commitment: when covenant faithfulness conflicts with family loyalty, Asa chooses the covenant.

notes.original: lo hish'ir kol neshama l'Yerovam — he left no breath to Jeroboam
notes.rendering: he leaves to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathes
notes.why: Lo hish'ir kol neshama — not a soul, not a breath left (neshama — breath, the word from Genesis 2:7 — YHWH breathed into his nostrils the breath of life). Baasha's purge of Jeroboam's line is complete and immediate. The narrator twice attributes it to the word of YHWH spoken through Ahijah (v.29; cf. 14:10–11) — the violence is presented as prophetic fulfillment, not merely political murder. This pattern — dynasty rises, sins, is destroyed by the next dynasty which then sins and is destroyed in turn — becomes the rhythm of the northern kingdom.
