intro: Chapter 6 contains the letter’s second great hardship catalogue (peristasis), following the first in 4:8–9. The literary form is Stoic in origin but Paul fills it with theological content: the catalogue does not demonstrate Paul’s inner invulnerability (as Stoic usage would) but the way divine power operates through material reversal. The ‘do not be mismatched’ section (vv.14–18) interrupts the flow with a dense OT catena — woven from Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and 2 Samuel — calling the community to the separateness that befits the temple of the living God.

notes.original: kairos euprosdektos / hemera soterias — acceptable/favorable time / day of salvation
notes.rendering: now is the favorable time; now is the day of salvation
notes.why: The quotation is from Isaiah 49:8 (LXX), part of the Servant Songs. Euprosdektos (favorable, acceptable, well-received — from eu, well + prosdechomai, to receive, to accept) carries both the sense of a welcome moment and an officially recognized time — the ‘right time’ in a formal sense. Paul’s application is urgent: the Isaiah promise of divine hearing in the day of salvation is not historical past or future hope but the present moment of the gospel proclamation. The doubled ‘behold’ (idou / idou) is a Hebrew attention-marker, signaling that something of vital importance follows.

notes.original: peristasis / en hypomonē pollei — hardship catalogue / in great endurance
notes.rendering: by great endurance — in afflictions, hardships, calamities…
notes.why: The peristasis (hardship catalogue — from peri-stasis, a standing-around, a state of siege) is a recognized Hellenistic literary genre used by philosophers to demonstrate their resilience and virtue under pressure. Paul has three such catalogues in 2 Corinthians (4:8–9; 6:4–10; 11:23–29) and others in Romans and 1 Corinthians. What is distinctive in Paul’s use is the theological frame: the catalogue does not prove Stoic self-sufficiency but apostolic weakness through which divine power operates. The three groups in vv.4–5 (nine negatives: afflictions, hardships, calamities; beatings, imprisonments, riots; labors, sleepless nights, hunger) are followed by six positives in vv.6–7 and then seven antitheses in vv.8–10.

notes.original: heterozygountes / metoche / koinonia / symphonesis / synkatathesis — mismatched-yoked / partnership / fellowship / accord / agreement
notes.rendering: do not be mismatched with unbelievers… what partnership… fellowship… accord… agreement
notes.why: Heterozygeo (to be unequally yoked — from heteros, different + zygos, yoke; Leviticus 19:19 LXX forbids yoking different animals together) opens a sequence of five nouns for different kinds of relationship: metoche (partnership, sharing in), koinonia (fellowship, communal participation), symphonesis (accord, harmony, agreement of sound), synkatathesis (agreement, common approval). The cascade of relationship-words emphasizes the incompatibility of temple and idols at every level — practical, communal, verbal, and dispositional. The OT catena that follows (vv.16–18) grounds the call not in moral preference but in covenant identity: you are the temple of the living God.

intro: Chapter 7 is the emotional resolution of the crisis narrated from chapter 1. The painful visit, the severe letter, the anguished waiting in Macedonia, the relief at Titus’s arrival — all of it lands in v.4’s extraordinary compression: ‘I am filled with comfort; I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction.’ The distinction between kata theon lypē (godly grief) and tou kosmou lypē (worldly grief) in vv.9–10 is one of the letter’s most pastorally precise observations.

notes.original: ho parakalon tous tapeinous / tē parousiai Titou — the one who comforts the downcast / by the arrival of Titus
notes.rendering: God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus
notes.why: Tapeinous (the downcast, the low-lying ones — from tapeinos, low, humble; the same root as tapeinophrosyne, humility) describes Paul’s state in Macedonia without Titus: physically exhausted, fearful within. The comfort comes through a person — parousia (presence, arrival — the same word used for Christ’s coming; here used for Titus’s physical arrival) is deliberately concrete. Paul’s theology of comfort is consistently embodied: God comforts through people who show up. The tripling of paraklesis in vv.6–7 (comforted… comfort… comforted) echoes the opening of chapter 1 and closes the frame.

notes.original: kata theon lype / tou kosmou lype / ametameletos / metanoia — godly grief / worldly grief / without regret / repentance
notes.rendering: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death
notes.why: Two kinds of grief, distinguished by their object and their outcome. Kata theon lypē (grief according to God — grief that takes its measure from God, that registers offenses in relation to God) produces metanoia (repentance, literally a change of mind, the full turning of the inner person — from meta, change + nous, mind). Tou kosmou lypē (grief of the world — grief that takes its measure from worldly loss: reputation, status, advantage) produces only death. The key distinction word is ametameletos (without regret — from a-metamelomenos, not-regreted; the cognate metameleia, regret, is a remorse that changes nothing). Godly grief leads to metanoia that one does not then regret; worldly grief cycles into itself.

notes.original: spoudē / apologia / aganaktesis / phobos / epipothesis / zelos / ekdikesis — seven fruits of godly grief
notes.rendering: what earnestness… eagerness to clear yourselves… indignation… fear… longing… zeal… readiness to see justice done
notes.why: Seven nouns in asyndeton (without connecting conjunctions) cascade as evidence of genuine repentance. Spoudē (earnestness, diligence, haste); apologia (defense, answer, the clearing of oneself — root of ‘apology’ in its original sense); aganaktesis (indignation, moral outrage — from aganakteo, to feel strongly against); phobos (fear, appropriate reverence and alarm); epipothesis (longing, yearning — from epi-potheo, to desire earnestly); zelos (zeal, passionate commitment); ekdikesis (readiness to see justice done, vindication — from ek-dikē, out-of-justice). Paul’s pastoral genius is in reading the Corinthians’ repentance through the catalogue of its fruits rather than its abstract sincerity.

intro: Chapters 8–9 form Paul’s most extended treatment of the Jerusalem collection — the financial gift from the Gentile churches to the mother-church that Paul describes in Romans 15 as his supreme pastoral project, the embodied proof of Gentile solidarity with Jewish believers. Chapter 8 opens with the Macedonian churches as the model (they gave out of extreme poverty and beyond their means) and builds to the theological foundation in v.9: the poverty of Christ as the pattern and ground of Christian generosity.

notes.original: perisseia tes charas / kata bathous ptocheia / plousios hapotes — overflow of joy / deep poverty / wealth of generosity
notes.rendering: their overflow of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity
notes.why: The economic paradox is deliberate: kata bathous ptocheia (poverty according to depth, rock-bottom destitution) combined with perisseuo (overflowed, abounded — present tense: a continuing overflow) produces plousios haplotēs (wealthy simplicity, generous liberality — haplotēs meaning single-mindedness, undivided giving, the same word Paul uses in Romans 12:8 for the one who gives ‘with singleness’). The Macedonian churches (Philippi, Thessalonica, Beroea) are in Paul’s account the anti-type of the Corinthians: prosperous Corinth holds back; impoverished Macedonia overflows. Paul does not moralize; he simply presents the paradox as evidence of grace at work.

notes.original: plousios on eptocheusen / hina humeis to ekeinou ptocheia ploutesete — though rich he became poor / so that by his poverty you might be rich
notes.rendering: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich
notes.why: The verse is the theological center of the collection argument. The structure is: (1) prior state — plousios on (being rich, present participle: Christ’s eternal richness); (2) action — eptocheusen (became poor, aorist: a completed historical act, the incarnation and crucifixion); (3) purpose and result — hina humeis ploutesete (so that you might become rich). Ptochos (poor — the absolute poor, the destitute, the beggar — distinct from penes, the working poor who have barely enough) is the strongest Greek word for economic deprivation. Paul applies it to Christ’s condition without softening. The gift of the collection is to be understood within this prior and ultimate gift.

notes.original: isotes — equality, fairness
notes.rendering: that there may be fairness
notes.why: Isotēs (equality, fairness, the condition of equal measure — from isos, equal) appears twice in vv.13–14, framing Paul’s principle for the collection. It is not charity but economic mutuality: at present the Corinthians’ surplus supplies the Jerusalem church’s deficit; the formula is explicitly reversible (their abundance may supply your need). The model is the manna of Exodus 16 (v.15: whoever gathered much had nothing left over) — where divine provision leveled the daily intake. Paul’s vision of the collection is not redistribution but covenant mutuality: the gifts of different communities balance each other over time.

intro: Chapter 9 continues the collection appeal with a different emphasis: not the model of Macedonia (chapter 8) but the theology of sowing and harvest. The chapter moves from practical logistics (getting the gift ready before Paul arrives) to eschatological generosity: God who multiplies seed will multiply the harvest of righteousness. The closing verse — one word in Greek, anekdiēgētos — is one of the most compressed doxologies in the NT.

notes.original: hilaron doten agapa ho theos — God loves a cheerful giver
notes.rendering: God loves a cheerful giver
notes.why: Hilaros (cheerful, bright, glad — the root of English ‘hilarious’ in its original sense: radiant, exuberantly bright) is stronger than merely willing or ungrudging. The cheerful giver is the one who gives from a state of genuine joy, not stoic duty. The verse conflates Proverbs 22:8 (LXX) with the general principle of Deuteronomy 15:10 (give without your heart being grieved). Ananke (compulsion — the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 9:16 for the divine necessity laid on him to preach) appears here for the compulsion the giver must not feel: giving done under constraint is the opposite of the gospel’s logic.

notes.original: epichoregon / plethynai / auxesai — the one who supplies / to multiply / to increase
notes.rendering: he who supplies seed to the sower… will supply and multiply your seed… and increase the harvest
notes.why: Three verbs in sequence: epichoregeo (to supply lavishly, to provide generously — from choros, a dancing chorus, originally the patron who funded it; the word carries connotations of generous public provision), plethyno (to multiply, to cause to increase — same root as plethys, a multitude), auxano (to cause to grow — the agricultural growth verb Paul used in 1 Corinthians 3:6–7 for God giving growth to what Paul planted). The verse applies Isaiah 55:10 (rain and snow make the earth productive) to the collection: the gift given becomes the seed that God multiplies, and the harvest is not merely financial but dikaiōsynē (righteousness, right-relatedness — the moral order of the community in right relationship with God and one another).

notes.original: anekdiēgētos — inexpressible, beyond description
notes.rendering: thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift
notes.why: Anekdiēgētos (inexpressible, indescribable — from a-privative + ek-diēgeomai, to narrate fully, to describe completely; the word appears only here in the NT) closes the two-chapter collection appeal with a one-word doxology. After 39 verses of careful argument about the mechanics and theology of financial giving, Paul arrives at the gift that underlies all giving: the charis (grace, gift — the same word used throughout for the collection itself) of Christ in 8:9, who became poor so that we might become rich. That gift is anekdiēgētos — beyond the reach of full narration. The collection is an echo of a gift that cannot be fully told.

intro: Chapter 10 opens the sharp turn of the letter. After nine chapters of pastoral reconciliation and collection appeal, Paul’s tone becomes combative, ironic, and at times barely controlled. The polemic is directed at unnamed opponents who have questioned his courage, his presence, and his speaking ability. Paul’s response is to reframe the entire competition: the warfare he is waging is not one for personal honor but for the obedience of human thought to Christ — and his weapons are not rhetorical impressiveness but divine power.

notes.original: ta hopla tēs strateias / logismous / pan hypsōma / pan noēma — the weapons of warfare / arguments / every high thing / every thought
notes.rendering: the weapons of our warfare… we destroy arguments and every proud obstacle… take every thought captive
notes.why: The military metaphor runs through vv.3–6 with precision: strateia (campaign, military expedition — from strateuo, to serve as a soldier), hopla (weapons, instruments of war), kathairesis (pulling down, demolition — used of destroying fortifications), logismoi (arguments, calculations, reasonings — the intellectual constructions that constitute the ‘strongholds’), hypsōma (high thing, lofty obstacle — possibly a siege tower or rampart), noēma (thought, mental concept — from nous, mind; the same word used in 2:11 for Satan’s ‘schemes’). Paul’s warfare is cognitive: the target is the proud intellectual structures that resist the knowledge of God.

notes.original: ta de epistolai men… hē parousia tou somatos asthenēs — the letters are weighty… the bodily presence is weak
notes.rendering: his letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech of no account
notes.why: The charge against Paul is quoted verbatim (it is what they say — phēsin, he/someone says, introducing a known position). The contrast is between Paul’s impressive letters and his disappointing in-person manner: asthenes (weak, lacking strength — the word Paul will make his theological banner in 12:9–10) applied to his soma (body, physical presence) and logos (speech, word — the technical term for rhetorical delivery). The opponents are applying the criteria of the professional rhetor: impressive physical presence, powerful delivery. Paul is failing these criteria. His response is not to deny the weakness but to relocate where power actually lives.

notes.original: ho de kauchomenos en kyriō kauchasthō — let the one who boasts boast in the Lord
notes.rendering: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord
notes.why: The quotation from Jeremiah 9:24 (LXX: en touto kauchasthō ho kauchoōmenos, synienai kai ginōskein eme) — also cited in 1 Corinthians 1:31 — is Paul’s recurring answer to the competition of honor and status. In its Jeremiah context, the boast-worthy thing is knowing YHWH: his steadfast love, justice, and righteousness. Paul’s citation turns the credentials competition on its head: the one who commends himself is not approved; the one the Lord commends is. The standard of evaluation has shifted from audience to source.

intro: Chapter 11 contains Paul’s most elaborate and self-conscious rhetorical performance: the ‘fool’s speech’ (aphrosynē — foolishness, the speech a fool would make) in which Paul mimics the competitors’ boasting and then systematically empties it. The move is ironic at every level: he boasts as a fool to demonstrate that the genre of boasting itself is foolish; and when the catalogue of his credentials arrives (vv.23–29), it turns out to be a catalogue of suffering, not achievement. The Damascus basket at the end is the punchline: this is what Paul’s apostolic career looks like from the outside.

notes.original: tōn hyperlian apostolōn — the super-apostles
notes.rendering: these ‘super-apostles’
notes.why: Hyperlian apostoloi (super-apostles, arch-apostles — from hyperlian, exceedingly, to the highest degree; an adverb Paul uses only twice, both times in this letter: 11:5 and 12:11) is almost certainly Paul’s sarcastic coinage for his opponents. Whether these are the Jerusalem apostles (Peter, James, John) viewed through Corinthian elevation, or itinerant Jewish-Christian missionaries from outside who claimed apostolic authority, is disputed. The irony is that Paul, who considers himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9), compares himself favorably to those his opponents regard as supreme. The scare-quotes in the translation signal the sarcasm.

notes.original: peristasis catalogue — the apostolic hardship list
notes.rendering: with far greater labors, far more imprisonments… five times the forty minus one… three times beaten with rods
notes.why: The third great peristasis catalogue of the letter (following 4:8–9 and 6:4–10) is also the most detailed and the most personal. Unlike the others, which are general (afflictions, hardships), this one has specifics: the number of beatings (five), the form (the Jewish synagogue punishment of forty lashes minus one, from Deuteronomy 25:3 — Roman law permitted forty but Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine to avoid accidentally exceeding the limit), the number of shipwrecks (three, before the shipwreck of Acts 27), the night and day in the deep. None of these events appears in Acts, reminding us how much of Paul’s biography is unknown. The catalogue ends not with triumph but with the basket: ignominious escape through a hole in a wall.

notes.original: hē merimna pasōn tōn ekklēsiōn — the anxiety for all the churches
notes.rendering: the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches
notes.why: After cataloguing physical danger, Paul adds what may be the heaviest weight: episystasis (the pressure that bears down, the daily gathering-together of concern — from epi-systasis, a pressing-together, a mass converging on one point) combined with merimna (anxiety, care, the worried attention that divides the mind — the same word Jesus uses in Matthew 6 for the anxious worry that cannot add a cubit to one’s height). The apostle who told the Philippians ‘be anxious for nothing’ (Philippians 4:6) is himself daily anxious for all the churches. The combination of katalogos and merimna is the complete picture of apostolic cost: the body’s suffering and the mind’s unrest.

intro: Chapter 12 contains the letter’s most personal disclosure: the vision that Paul will not quite claim as his own (speaking of himself in the third person) and the thorn that prevents him from becoming conceited about it. The divine answer to Paul’s three-fold prayer — arkei soi hē charis mou — is the theological center not only of this chapter but of the entire letter’s theology of weakness. The chapter then pivots to a final defense of apostolic conduct and closes with the anxious list of what Paul fears he will find when he arrives.

notes.original: skolops tē sarki / angelos Satana — a thorn/stake in the flesh / a messenger of Satan
notes.rendering: a thorn was given me in the flesh — a messenger of Satan to harass me
notes.why: Skolops (thorn, splinter, stake — from a root meaning pointed object; the word can describe anything from a small splinter to a large pointed stake used in fortifications) is the most discussed word in the letter. Its referent has generated centuries of speculation: eye disease (Galatians 4:15), epilepsy, malaria, a speech impediment, persecution, or a persistent spiritual oppression. Paul gives no diagnosis. The phrase angelos Satana (messenger of Satan) may refer to the same thing (the thorn seen from its divine and its Satanic angles simultaneously: given by God for Paul’s formation, sent by Satan for his harm) or to a separate reality. What is certain is the divine passive: edothē moi (was given to me) — the thorn is part of the divine economy, not an interruption of it.

notes.original: arkei soi hē charis mou / hē dynamis en astheneia teleitai — my grace is sufficient for you / power is made perfect in weakness
notes.rendering: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness
notes.why: Arkei (is sufficient, is enough — from arkeō, to ward off, to be adequate, to suffice) is the answer to three petitions (v.8: three times I pleaded). The sufficiency is present tense: is sufficient now, as it is, with the thorn still in place. Teleitai (is made perfect, is brought to completion — from teleioō, to complete, to bring to its telos/goal) is also present: not ‘will be perfected’ but is being perfected, in the ongoing experience of weakness. The paradox is the letter’s thesis: the clay jar’s cracking is not the failure of the divine plan but its execution. Astheneia (weakness, lack of strength — from a-sthenos, without-strength) is revalued entirely: it is the condition in which divine power is most fully operative.

notes.original: hēdista dapanēsō kai ekdapanēthēsomai — I will most gladly spend and be spent
notes.rendering: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls
notes.why: The two verbs make a wordplay: dapanaō (to spend, to expend, to use up — commercial language for disbursing funds) and ek-dapanaō (to spend completely, to exhaust, to be wholly used up — the same root intensified by ek, completely out). Paul will spend his resources and then be spent himself — the apostle as the jar that empties itself entirely. The paradox of v.15b is equally stark: ei perissoteros hymas agapō, hēsson agapōmai — if I love you more, am I loved less? The question is genuinely pained. The parents-for-children image of v.14 and the spending image of v.15 together portrait apostolic love as structurally self-consuming.

intro: The final chapter moves from warning (examine yourselves) to the paradox at the heart of Paul’s apostolic theology (he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God — so also we) to the five imperatives of v.11 and then the letter’s closing gift: the Trinitarian benediction of v.13, the most fully Trinitarian formula in Paul’s letters and one of the earliest in Christian literature.

notes.original: estaurōthē ex astheneias / zē ek dynameōs theou — was crucified from weakness / lives from the power of God
notes.rendering: he was crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but… we will live with him by the power of God
notes.why: The verse is the clearest statement of the letter’s governing paradox. Ex astheneias (out of weakness, from weakness — the weakness being the condition from which the crucifixion proceeded: Christ did not die triumphantly but vulnerably, handed over, stripped, executed). Ek dynameōs theou (from the power of God — the resurrection’s source). The application to Paul is immediate and parallel: the same weakness-pattern, the same divine power. The apostle’s weakness is not a problem to be overcome before the ministry can begin but the very mode through which the crucified-and-risen Christ operates.

notes.original: katartisis — restoration, mending, completion
notes.rendering: your restoration is what we pray for
notes.why: Katartisis (restoration, mending, fitting-together — from katartizō, to mend, to fit out, to restore to proper condition; used in Mark 1:19 for mending nets; in Hebrews 13:21 for God equipping the believer) is Paul’s prayer-word for what he wants to see in Corinth: not simply behavioral improvement but the community’s structural restoration to wholeness. The same root appears in v.11 (katartizesthe — aim for restoration, be mended) as the first of the five final imperatives. The letter that began with the God of all comfort ends with the prayer for the community’s mending: comfort and katartisis are its two governing desires.

notes.original: charis / agapē / koinōnia — grace / love / fellowship
notes.rendering: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all
notes.why: The three-part benediction assigns a different quality to each person of the Trinity: grace (charis — unearned gift, the characteristic mode of Christ’s action toward humanity) to the Lord Jesus Christ; love (agapē — covenant love, the essential character of God in 1 John 4:8) to God the Father; fellowship or participation (koinōnia — shared life, mutual participation, the community-creating bond) to the Holy Spirit. The formula is not yet the developed Trinitarian theology of Nicaea, but it is the earliest triadic benediction in the NT and shapes all subsequent Trinitarian liturgical language. The order — Christ, Father, Spirit — follows the experiential sequence of Paul’s own theology: the believer encounters Christ, and through Christ comes to know the Father and participate in the Spirit.

intro: Second John is the shortest letter in the New Testament. It covers a single sheet of papyrus — literally: the Elder mentions that he has 'much to write' but chooses papyrus and ink (v.12) for the present and reserves the rest for face-to-face conversation. The letter is a compressed version of 1 John's concerns: truth, love, the commandment, and the threat of those who deny the Incarnation. Its two great mysteries — the identity of the Elder and the identity of the Elect Lady — remain genuinely open.

notes.original: ho presbyteros — eklektē kyria kai tois teknois autes
notes.rendering: the Elder — to the Elect Lady and her children
notes.why: Ho presbyteros — the Elder, the old man, the presbyter. The author does not name himself but uses a title of authority and seniority that would have been immediately recognisable to the recipients. The same title opens 3 John. Ancient tradition identifies the Elder with John the apostle; modern scholarship is divided — some argue for a disciple of the Apostle John, a 'John the Elder' mentioned by Papias. Eklektē kyria — Elect Lady. Kyria is the feminine of kyrios (Lord) — a woman of standing, a lady, a mistress of a household. Whether this is a literal person (a prominent woman in a house church) or a personification of the church as the Elect Lady (the church as the bride of Christ) has been debated since antiquity. The greeting of 'her children' in v.1 and 'the children of your Elect Sister' in v.13 support the church-personification reading — sister churches sending greetings.

notes.original: dia ten aletheian ten menousan en hemin — truth that abides
notes.rendering: the truth that abides in us
notes.why: Ten menousan — abiding, remaining, dwelling (from menō — the great Johannine abiding word, the vine and branches of John 15). The truth does not merely exist as information; it abides as a living presence in the community. The Johannine theology of truth is personal — truth is not a body of correct propositions but the Spirit of truth (John 14:17, 16:13), the one who guides into all truth and who, like the Father and the Son, dwells in the believer. Truth that abides is truth that has taken up residence, that will be with us for ever (eis ton aiōna — into the age). The greeting is already a theology.

notes.original: hoi me homologountes Iesoun Christon erchomenon en sarki — the Incarnation denied
notes.rendering: those who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh
notes.why: Erchomenon — coming, present participle. The phrasing is slightly different from 1 John 4:2 (Iesoun Christon en sarki elelythota — having come in the flesh, perfect participle). Here the present participle erchomenon suggests the ongoing, continuing significance of the Incarnation rather than merely the historical fact of it. To deny the Incarnation is not merely to get a doctrine wrong — it is to deny the person in whom truth abides (v.2) and through whom grace, mercy, and peace come (v.3). The antichrist (ho antichristos — the one against the anointed) is not primarily a future cosmic figure but the present denial of the flesh-taking Word.

notes.original: pas ho proagōn kai me menōn en te didache tou Christou — going ahead, not abiding
notes.rendering: everyone who goes ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ
notes.why: Ho proagōn — the one going ahead, going forward, progressing beyond. The word is ironic: those who consider themselves to be advancing, making theological progress, moving beyond the basic teaching of Christ — these are the ones who have lost God. The Johannine tradition's warning against theological novelty is not obscurantism; it is the recognition that the Incarnation (the teaching of Christ) is the ground of everything, and what seems like progress beyond it is actually departure from it. Whoever abides (menōn) in the teaching has both the Father and the Son: the menō word again — abiding in the teaching is the condition of having the persons.

notes.original: dia chartou kai melanos — paper and ink; stoma pros stoma — mouth to mouth
notes.rendering: paper and ink… talk face to face
notes.why: Chartou kai melanos — papyrus and ink. The specific materials of first-century letter-writing: the papyrus sheet and the reed-cut pen dipped in carbon-based ink. The Elder is aware that a letter is a limited medium — it can carry words but not presence, information but not the joy of full communication. Stoma pros stoma — mouth to mouth, literally (rendered 'face to face' in the translation). The phrase is the same as Numbers 12:8 (LXX: stoma kata stoma lalesō auto — I will speak with him mouth to mouth), where it describes YHWH's uniquely direct relationship with Moses. The Elder uses it for the intimacy he hopes to share with the community in person. The letter is a placeholder for presence.

intro: Third John is the most personal letter in the New Testament — a private pastoral communication to a named individual about a specific church conflict. It is also the only NT letter that does not mention Jesus by name (though 'the Name' in v.7 almost certainly refers to him). Three characters define the letter's world: Gaius (recipient, commended for hospitality), Diotrephes (absentee problem, a man who likes to be first), and Demetrius (commended, perhaps the letter-carrier).

notes.original: peri pantōn euchomai se euodousthai kai hygiainein — body and soul together
notes.rendering: I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health — as it goes well with your soul
notes.why: The health-wish at the opening of 3 John is the most physically specific greeting in the NT — euodousthai (to prosper, to have a good journey, to succeed) and hygiainein (to be in good health, to be sound in body — from which our word 'hygiene') placed alongside the state of the soul (psyche). The Elder does not spiritualise — he genuinely prays for Gaius's physical health in correspondence with his spiritual flourishing. The two are not opposed or ranked; they are prayed for together. The soul going well is the measure: may your body be as well as your soul is. This is one of the only places in the NT where physical wellbeing is explicitly included in apostolic prayer.

notes.original: meizotera toutōn ouk echō charan — no greater joy
notes.rendering: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth
notes.why: Meizotera toutōn ouk echō charan — greater than these things I do not have joy. The phrase is John's superlative of pastoral satisfaction: this is the ceiling of his joy, the thing above which nothing rises. The language of children (tekna — children, a term of deep affection used by John throughout his letters and Gospel) walking in truth (peripatountas — walking, the Hebrew idiom for living, halakha, the way one conducts one's life) is both intimate and ethical: truth is not what you believe in the abstract but how you walk day by day. The Elder's greatest joy is people living truthfully.

notes.original: hyper tou onomatos exēlthon — for the sake of the Name
notes.rendering: they have gone out for the sake of the Name
notes.why: Tou onomatos — the Name, without further specification. In Jewish usage, 'the Name' (ha-Shem) is the reverential substitute for the divine name YHWH. In early Christian usage it refers to Jesus — 'the Name above every name' (Philippians 2:9), the name into which disciples are baptised (Matthew 28:19), the name by which miracles are performed (Acts 3:6, 4:12). The travelling missionaries in 3 John have 'gone out' (exēlthon — same verb as the Johannine Jesus going out from the Father) 'for the sake of the Name' — a compressed description of mission as total dedication to the person behind the name. They take 'nothing from the Gentiles' — they do not rely on the support of non-believers, maintaining the integrity of the mission by depending only on the community of faith.

notes.original: ho philoprōteuōn autōn Diotrephes — the one who loves to be first
notes.rendering: Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first
notes.why: Ho philoprōteuōn — the one who loves to be first, who is fond of pre-eminence, who philos (loves) being prōtos (first). The compound word appears only here in the NT — and it is a devastating portrait in a single word. Diotrephes is not accused of heresy or immorality but of love of primacy — the desire to be first that Jesus in Matthew 20:26–27 said must be inverted in the kingdom: 'whoever would be great among you must be your servant.' The Elder does not rage; he names. He will bring it up when he comes. Diotrephes is the practical counterpart to the theological opponent of 2 John: where the deceiver denies the truth, Diotrephes perverts the community by installing himself at its centre.

notes.original: aspasai tous philous kat' onoma — greet the friends each by name
notes.rendering: greet the friends, each by name
notes.why: Kat' onoma — by name, according to name, name by name. The closing instruction is one of the most human details in any NT letter: not 'greet the congregation' or 'greet all the saints' but greet each friend individually, by their own name. The Good Shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3: kat' onoma kalei ta idia probata). The Elder's pastoral practice enacts the Shepherd's: every person in the community is known, named, and specifically greeted. Three John is the most personal letter in the canon — and it closes on the most personal gesture: a name, and another name, and another.

outro: Note on 2 John and 3 John as companion letters: The two letters share an author (the Elder), a closing formula (I had much to write but prefer face to face), and a concern for truth-in-walking. But they address opposite problems. Second John warns against too much hospitality — do not receive into your house those who bring false teaching. Third John commends hospitality toward travelling missionaries and rebukes Diotrephes for withholding it. Together they map the pastoral challenge of the early church: discernment about who receives welcome and who does not, without sliding into either naive openness or defensive closure. The Elder is navigating the tension between the commandment to love (2 John 5–6) and the command to guard the truth (2 John 10–11) — and his instrument in both cases is the same: walk in truth, and let truth determine the walking.

intro: Chapter 1 opens 2 Kings with a question that answers itself: is there no God in Israel? Ahaziah, son of Ahab and Jezebel, turns to Baal-zebub — the Philistine god of Ekron — to learn whether he will recover from a fall through a lattice. The contrast with his father's dynasty is complete: Ahab at least argued with Elijah; Ahaziah simply sends messengers to the wrong address. Elijah intercepts them before they arrive. Two captains of fifty die by fire from heaven; the third captain kneels and lives.

notes.original: Ba'al-zevuv — Baal-zebub, lord of the flies
notes.rendering: Baal-zebub the god of Ekron
notes.why: Ba'al-zevuv — lord of the flies (ba'al — lord/master; zevuv — fly). The name is almost certainly a polemical Hebrew distortion of Ba'al-zevul — lord of the high place or lord of the exalted house (the form preserved in the New Testament as Beelzebul). To rename the god "lord of flies" is a scribal insult: the deity of the Philistine city of Ekron reduced from a name of power to a name of filth. Ahaziah goes to a fly-god for medical information. The contempt is structural.

notes.original: ba'al se'ar v'ezor or — a man of hair with a leather belt
notes.rendering: he wore a garment of hair, with a belt of leather around his waist
notes.why: The garment of hair (se'ar — hair; possibly a rough camel-hair mantle) and the leather belt are Elijah's identifying marks — his prophet's uniform. The king identifies him from the description alone: it is Elijah the Tishbite. The same description will attach to John the Baptist in Matthew 3:4 — camel's hair, leather belt — the New Testament deliberately clothing the forerunner of Jesus in the garments of the forerunner of Elijah's ministry. The prophet's distinctive dress is a consistent visual signature across centuries.

notes.original: vayikra al birkav — he fell on his knees
notes.rendering: the third captain falls on his knees before Elijah and entreats him
notes.why: The third captain's kneeling is the chapter's moral pivot. The first two captains gave orders; this one petitions. He acknowledges what has happened (fire consumed my predecessors), names his own vulnerability (let my life be precious in your sight), and asks rather than commands. The angel immediately tells Elijah to go with him: do not be afraid of him. Humility is the condition of survival in this chapter. The king who does not kneel before YHWH — but kneels before Baal-zebub by proxy — dies in his bed.

intro: Chapter 2 is the hinge of the Elijah-Elisha cycle — the transfer of prophetic authority through a whirlwind, a cloak, and a question asked by fire. The chapter moves in three stations: Gilgal, Bethel, Jericho — the reverse of Joshua's conquest route, as though the land is being spiritually re-entered. Elisha refuses to leave three times, witnesses the departure, tears his clothes, picks up the fallen cloak, and parts the Jordan. The succession is complete. The sons of the prophets recognize it before the search party confirms the absence.

notes.original: pi sh'nayim b'ruchacha — double portion of your spirit
notes.rendering: let a double portion of your spirit be upon me
notes.why: Pi sh'nayim — mouth of two, a double mouth (the portion of the firstborn son in Deuteronomy 21:17 — he shall acknowledge the firstborn... by giving him a double portion of all he has). Elisha asks for the inheritance of a firstborn: not twice Elijah's power in some abstract sense, but the recognized heir's share of the prophetic estate. Elijah's response — you have asked a hard thing — is not a rebuke but an acknowledgment: this is not mine to give; it depends on what you see. The cloak falling from the whirlwind will answer the question.

notes.original: merkavat esh v'sussei esh — chariot of fire and horses of fire
notes.rendering: a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate the two of them
notes.why: The chariot of fire is not Elijah's transport vehicle — the text says it separates the two of them, and then Elijah goes up by the whirlwind. The chariot and horses are divine military escort: the heavenly army made briefly visible (the same vision Elisha will later pray for his servant to see in 6:17). Elijah did not ride into heaven on a chariot; he was taken up by a whirlwind while the heavenly cavalry stood between him and Elisha. Elisha's cry — the chariots of Israel and its horsemen! — is a declaration that Elijah himself was worth more than any earthly army.

notes.original: avi avi rechev Yisrael u'farashav — my father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen
notes.rendering: my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!
notes.why: The exclamation will be repeated by Joash at Elisha's deathbed in 13:14 — the identical phrase, spoken by a king rather than a prophet. It becomes the formula for lamenting the loss of a prophet: to lose such a man is to lose the military defense of the nation. The prophet, not the army, is Israel's true protection — because the prophet carries the word of YHWH, and that word is more powerful than chariots. Elisha tears his clothes: the formal gesture of mourning, the same one Reuben performs when he finds Joseph gone from the pit (Genesis 37:29).

intro: Chapter 3 is the strangest military narrative in 2 Kings: an alliance of three kings is saved from thirst by a dry streambed filling with water overnight; they mistake it for blood and charge into ambush; they win the campaign decisively — and then the king of Moab sacrifices his son on the wall and great wrath falls on Israel and they retreat. The chapter refuses to explain the ending. The narrator records it and moves on.

notes.original: asher yatsaq mayim al yedei Eliyahu — who poured water on the hands of Elijah
notes.rendering: Elisha the son of Shaphat — who poured water on the hands of Elijah
notes.why: To pour water on the hands is the gesture of a personal servant assisting at washing — intimate, subordinate, domestic. The servant's description of Elisha is not "the great prophet" or "the miracle-worker" but the man who washed Elijah's hands. The highest credential in prophetic Israel is that you served the man before you. Jehoshaphat immediately recognizes the authority: the word of YHWH is with him.

notes.original: v'hayah k'nagen ham'nagen — when the musician plays
notes.rendering: the hand of YHWH comes upon him" as the music plays
notes.why: Music as a medium for prophetic inspiration appears here and in 1 Samuel 10:5–6, where the band of prophets with instruments precede Saul's first experience of the Spirit. The verb yaganah — to play a stringed instrument — suggests a lyre or harp. The hand of YHWH (yad YHWH) is the standard formula for prophetic ecstasy or compulsion (Ezekiel uses it repeatedly: Ezekiel 1:3; 3:14; 8:1). Elisha needs music to enter the state of reception; the word is then given through the instrument as through a tuned vessel.

notes.original: vayehi qetzef gadol al Yisrael — great wrath came upon Israel
notes.rendering: great wrath comes against Israel — they withdraw
notes.why: Qetzef — wrath, fury, burning anger (the same word for YHWH's wrath elsewhere in Kings). Whose wrath this is, the text does not say. The ancient reader would have understood: the sacrifice of the Moabite king's son generates a terrible divine or cosmic response — either the Moabite god Chemosh is propitiated, or the act is so horrifying that it disrupts the Israelite forces morally and spiritually. The narrator leaves the explanation absent. They won everything and then lost the campaign because of something that cannot be named.

intro: Chapter 4 is the miracle chapter — four signs in a single narrative sweep, each displaying Elisha's prophetic power over poverty, barrenness, death, and famine. The chapter echoes 1 Kings 17 at every point: the widow and the oil mirrors the widow of Zarephath and the flour jar; the dead child raised mirrors the widow's son. Elisha is performing Elijah's miracles — which is to say, he received what he asked for.

notes.original: vayya'amod ha-shemen — the oil stopped
notes.rendering: and the oil stops
notes.why: The oil flows as long as there are empty vessels to receive it. When the last vessel is full and there are none left, the oil stops. The miracle is precisely calibrated to need: as many vessels as she borrowed, that much oil. The Shunammite's extravagance in borrowing ("not too few" was Elisha's instruction) directly determines her profit. The spiritual logic is exact: the woman who makes the most space receives the most filling. This is not magic but a parable about receptivity.

notes.original: lo chodesh v'lo shabbat — it is neither new moon nor Sabbath
notes.rendering: it is neither new moon nor Sabbath — she says: all is well
notes.why: The husband's question reveals the ordinary rhythm of prophetic consultation: people visited the man of God on new moons and Sabbaths. His question is practical, not suspicious — this is the wrong day. The woman's answer — shalom, all is well — is the most controlled lie of grief in the Hebrew Bible. Her son is dead upstairs on the prophet's bed and she is saddling a donkey. She says shalom to her husband, shalom to Gehazi's inquiry. She will not say anything other than shalom until she reaches the man of God's feet, where she breaks.

notes.original: vayighar al hayelad — he stretched himself upon the child
notes.rendering: he goes up and lies on the child, mouth on his mouth, eyes on his eyes, hands on his hands
notes.why: The gesture echoes Elijah's restoration of the widow's son in 1 Kings 17:21 (vayitmoded — he measured/stretched himself). Both prophets perform a full-body imposition: the prophet's warmth transferred to the dead child. The result here is more gradual: the flesh warms, then Elisha paces the room, then seven sneezes, then the child opens his eyes. Seven — the number of completion. The measured, seven-fold return of breath is a second creation, deliberate and unhurried.

intro: Chapter 5 is the book's most expansive theological story: an enemy commander, a captive Israelite girl, a letter misread by a king, a prophet who sends a servant instead of appearing himself, a cure in seven dips in the wrong river, and a confession of monotheism from a Syrian. The chapter ends with grace given freely and greed punished with the disease that grace just cured.

notes.original: v'YHWH natan teshu'ah l'Aram b'yado — YHWH had given victory to Syria by his hand
notes.rendering: by him YHWH had given victory to Syria
notes.why: The opening sentence is theologically audacious: YHWH has given military victory to a foreign army through a pagan commander. The divine name is not in Syria's vocabulary; Naaman does not know YHWH. Yet YHWH uses him. This is Amos's universalism (9:7 — did I not bring the Syrians from Kir?) applied to a specific man. The great Syrian general is YHWH's instrument without knowing it. The chapter then asks: what happens when such a man encounters the God who has been using him?

notes.original: avi avi — my father, my father
notes.rendering: my father, if the prophet had commanded you to do some great thing
notes.why: The servants' address to Naaman — avi, my father — is the same form of address Elisha will use to Elijah at the whirlwind (2:12) and Joash will use to Elisha at his deathbed (13:14). It is the term of deep affection and reverence. The servants' argument is the most logical in the chapter: you would have done a great thing; do the small thing. Naaman's rage at the ordinary instruction is the human response to grace that feels too simple. He nearly misses his healing because the cure was beneath his dignity.

notes.original: adamat eretz — soil of the land
notes.rendering: two mule-loads of earth
notes.why: Naaman asks for two mule-loads of Israelite soil because in the ancient Near Eastern understanding, a god is localized — properly worshipped on his own ground. To take the earth of Israel to Damascus is to carry a piece of YHWH's territory home. It is a theologically naive but completely sincere gesture: the new convert making the best accommodation he knows how. Elisha's response — go in peace — is neither corrective nor condescending. The man who has just confessed "there is no God in all the earth but in Israel" is sent home in peace.

intro: Chapter 6 moves from the intimate (a borrowed axehead retrieved from the Jordan) to the cosmic (an invisible army of fire on a hillside) to the horrifying (a mother who has eaten her son during a siege). The chapter displays Elisha's ministry in its full range: small kindnesses, strategic military intelligence, miraculous protection, and presence in the middle of the worst catastrophe a city can suffer.

notes.original: v'hu shu'ul — it was borrowed
notes.rendering: alas, my master — it was borrowed
notes.why: The crisis is economic before it is physical: the axehead cannot simply be replaced because it was not owned. In the subsistence economy of the prophetic communities, borrowed tools were not recoverable. Elisha's response treats the small need as seriously as the large ones. He does not inquire why the man was careless; he asks where it fell. The miracle of the floating iron is not theologically weightier than the healing of Naaman — it is simply smaller. The same power that opens blind eyes retrieves a borrowed tool from a river.

notes.original: rabbim asher ittanu me'asher itam — those with us are more than those with them
notes.rendering: those who are with us are more than those who are with them
notes.why: The invisible army on the mountain around Dothan is the counterpart to Elijah's "I alone am left" in 1 Kings 19. Elijah thought he was the last prophet; YHWH told him there were seven thousand. Elisha's servant sees only Syrians; Elisha sees the fire-chariot escort that accompanied Elijah's departure now standing guard around himself. The opened eyes of the servant are what the entire Elisha cycle has been training its readers toward: to see that the world contains more divine presence than the visible world reveals.

notes.original: ten et binech v'nochlennu — give your son that we may eat him
notes.rendering: give your son that we may eat him today
notes.why: The cannibal mothers appear in Deuteronomy 28:53–57 as the ultimate curse of siege warfare — the covenant's most devastating threat made literal. The king tears his clothes; he is wearing sackcloth under his royal garments. He has been mourning in secret. His rage turns on Elisha rather than on the siege or on his own policy. The horror of the text is its restraint: the narrator reports what the woman says without commentary. Deuteronomy said this would happen if the covenant was broken. Here it is.

intro: Chapter 7 resolves the siege of Samaria through the most unexpected agents in the book: four lepers sitting at the city gate who decide they might as well die trying. YHWH creates a sound of phantom armies; the Syrians flee without a battle; the lepers discover the abandoned camp and then — after a moment of self-serving silence — remember their obligation to tell the city. The captain who doubted the word of YHWH dies underfoot on the day the prophecy is fulfilled.

notes.original: arubbot ba'shamayim — windows in heaven
notes.rendering: if YHWH himself should make windows in heaven
notes.why: The captain's sarcastic hypothetical — windows in heaven, rain of flour — recalls Genesis 7:11 where the windows of heaven opened for the flood. He uses the language of divine miracle to mock the oracle. Elisha's answer is not argument: you will see it but not eat of it. The prophecy contains its own embedded judgment on the one who disbelieves it. The fulfillment is precise: the captain sees the flour sold at the gate; he dies there under the crowd's feet without eating.

notes.original: yom b'sorot hu — this is a day of good news
notes.rendering: this day is a day of good news
notes.why: B'sorot — good news, glad tidings (from basar — to bring news, to announce; the root of the NT Greek evangelion — gospel). The lepers realize they are sitting on a discovery that could save a city and are keeping it to themselves. The self-correction is moral: "we are not doing right." The word b'sorot here — good news kept silent while others starve — becomes an ironic counterpoint to every prophetic announcement of salvation in the book. Good news is only good if it is shared.

notes.original: vayirmesuh ha'am basha'ar vayamot — the people trampled him in the gate and he died
notes.rendering: the people trampled him in the gate and he dies
notes.why: The narrator repeats the prophecy's fulfillment verbatim twice (vv.17 and 20) — the same structure used to confirm that Elijah's oracle about Ahab's blood was fulfilled at the pool of Samaria (1 Kings 22:38). The double telling is the narrator's signature for prophetic fulfillment too significant to be mentioned once. The word of YHWH does not fail, even in its judgments.

intro: Chapter 8 is held together by the theme of YHWH's foreknowledge and its human cost. Elisha weeps because he knows what Hazael will do; Hazael murders his master and becomes exactly what Elisha saw. The Shunammite returns from seven years of exile to find a king who has just been told her story. Both moments — the tear-filled prophecy and the providential timing — show a God who sees the whole picture before any of the actors do.

notes.original: vayya'amad et panav — he fixed his gaze
notes.rendering: he fixes his gaze and stares at him until he is ashamed — and the man of God weeps
notes.why: The stare is prophetic and merciless. Elisha sees Hazael and sees through him to the massacres of 10:32–33 — ripped-open pregnant women, dashed children, burning fortresses. The weeping is not pity for Hazael but grief for Israel. Elisha knows two things simultaneously: what Hazael will do, and that YHWH has told him Hazael will be king. The combination of divine commission and human horror produces tears. This is prophecy as moral burden: to know the future without the power to prevent it.

notes.original: mah avdecha ha-kelev — what is your servant who is but a dog
notes.rendering: what is your servant who is but a dog that he should do this great thing?
notes.why: Hazael's self-deprecation — I am just a dog — is the standard courtly response to being given a royal commission that exceeds one's station. But the word dog, placed against the list of atrocities Elisha has just named (burning, killing, dashing, ripping), produces a sinister double meaning: the man who calls himself a dog is the man who will tear open pregnant women. Hazael's humility is the form of ambition that does not know itself yet. By tomorrow he will be king.

notes.original: lema'an David avdo — for the sake of David his servant
notes.rendering: YHWH is not willing to destroy Judah — for the sake of David his servant
notes.why: The lamp of David (nir — 1 Kings 11:36; 15:4) reappears here as the theological reason Judah survives a king who walks in the way of the house of Ahab and has married an Omrid princess. The southern kingdom's survival is not earned by Jehoram; it is gifted because of a promise made to a man who has been dead for a generation. Grace outlasting the merit of its recipients is the structure of the Davidic covenant in Kings.

intro: Chapter 9 is the execution chapter — three deaths in rapid sequence (Joram, Ahaziah, Jezebel) and an anointing that sets them all in motion. The prophet's student pours oil and runs; within hours the dynasty of Ahab is finished. The narrator's care for geographic detail — the property of Naboth the Jezreelite — makes the fulfillment precise and deliberate.

notes.original: ha-meshugga — the mad fellow
notes.rendering: why did this mad fellow come to you?
notes.why: Meshugga — mad, frenzied, mentally disturbed (from shaga — to be mad, to rave; the same root as the word for prophetic ecstasy in 1 Samuel 21:14 and Hosea 9:7 — the prophet is a fool, the man of the spirit is mad). The commanders' dismissal of the prophet as a madman is the standard cultural reaction to prophetic behavior in ancient Israel. Jehu's evasion — "you know the fellow and his talk" — is both protective and telling. They press him. What the prophet said changes everything.

notes.original: ki k'mishpat Yehu ben Nimshi — for he drives like Jehu
notes.rendering: the driving is like the driving of Jehu — for he drives furiously
notes.why: The idiom has lasted three thousand years: "driving like Jehu" still means reckless speed. Yehu ben Nimshi yehu bashshig'aon — he drives in frenzy/madness. The same root as meshugga (v.11): the prophet is called mad; the commander drives like a madman. The book is playing with words: madness is the medium through which YHWH executes judgment on the house of Ahab. The watchman recognizes Jehu's chariot dust before his face.

notes.original: Zimri — she calls him Zimri
notes.rendering: is it peace, you Zimri, murderer of your master?
notes.why: Jezebel's last words are a taunt and a prophecy she does not intend. She calls Jehu "Zimri" — the man who killed his master and reigned seven days before burning the palace down on himself (1 Kings 16:18). She means: you are a usurper and you will die like one. She is right that Jehu is a murderer. She cannot see that Jehu will reign twenty-eight years and found a dynasty. But she faces her death with paint on her eyes and a contemptuous witticism. Whatever else she is, she is not afraid.

intro: Chapter 10 completes the Jehu purge. Seventy heads in baskets at the city gate; forty-two Judean princes killed at a watering hole; the Baal temple filled by deception and emptied by swords. Jehu destroys Baal worship in Israel completely and receives a four-generation promise on his dynasty. And then the narrator adds the quiet qualification that ends the chapter: but he did not turn from the calves of Jeroboam. Even the most zealous reformer in Israel's history is assessed by the standard of the covenant, and found incomplete.

notes.original: lo yippol me'artzah midvar YHWH — nothing shall fall to the ground of the word of YHWH
notes.rendering: there shall fall to the earth nothing of the word of YHWH
notes.why: Lo yippol — shall not fall (the same verb as lo nafal davar in Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:56; Joshua 21:45). Jehu himself proclaims the theological principle as he stands over seventy heads: this is what the word of YHWH does. He is both the agent of fulfillment and its herald. The irony is that the man announcing the reliability of YHWH's word against Ahab will himself be the subject of an unfulfilled potential — he could have walked fully in YHWH's ways, but did not.

notes.original: r'eh b'kin'ati la'YHWH — see my zeal for YHWH
notes.rendering: come with me and see my zeal for YHWH
notes.why: Kin'ah — zeal, jealousy, burning passion (the same word for YHWH's jealousy in Exodus 20:5 — I YHWH your God am a jealous God; and for Phinehas's zeal in Numbers 25:11 — he was zealous with my zeal). Jehu invites a witness to his zeal. Elijah claimed the same thing at Horeb: I have been very zealous for YHWH (1 Kings 19:10, 14). But Elijah's zeal was exhausted by grief; Jehu's zeal is performed for an audience and aimed at political consolidation. The same word, different hearts.

notes.original: lo sar Yehu me'chatot Yerovam — Jehu did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam
notes.rendering: Jehu does not turn aside from the sins of Jeroboam
notes.why: The calves of Bethel and Dan serve Jehu's political purposes as well as they served Jeroboam's: they prevent the people from going to Jerusalem to worship, which would reorient loyalties toward Judah and the Davidic line. Jehu destroys the Baal system because it was Jezebel's import and a political liability. He preserves Jeroboam's calves because they are politically useful. The reform is real but incomplete — genuine zeal for YHWH entangled with dynastic self-interest. The Deuteronomistic narrator will not allow the ambiguity to go unrecorded.

intro: Chapter 11 is the one moment in Kings when the Davidic line comes within a single child of extinction. Athaliah — daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, widow of Jehoram of Judah, mother of Ahaziah — kills all the royal children she can find and reigns for six years. One child is hidden in the Temple by a priest's wife. The lamp of David, pledged to burn forever, nearly goes out. It is kept by a woman with enough courage to steal a baby in the night.

notes.original: vatignov Yehosheva — Jehosheba steals him away
notes.rendering: Jehosheba steals him away from among the king's sons being put to death
notes.why: Vatignov — she steals (ganav — to steal, the word of Jacob stealing the blessing, of Joseph's brothers claiming he was stolen). The verb is precise: Jehosheba steals the child from death the way a thief takes what does not belong to the thief. In this case the theft is righteous. She is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 22:11 as the wife of Jehoiada the priest — the same man who will produce Joash at the Temple seven years later. The couple together preserve the Davidic line: she hides the child; he crowns him.

notes.original: va'yitnu alav et ha-nezer v'et ha-edut — they put on him the crown and the testimony
notes.rendering: he puts the crown on him and gives him the testimony
notes.why: Ha-edut — the testimony, the covenant document (from edut — witness, testimony; the same word for the two tablets of the law placed in the ark, called the ark of the testimony). The king receives both the crown and the covenant text: his authority is from YHWH and bounded by the covenant. The anointing that follows (vayimshchu oto) places Joash in the succession of Davidic kings anointed with oil. He is seven years old, standing at the pillar, surrounded by armed men, receiving a document he cannot yet fully read.

notes.original: va'tiqra Atalya b'gadeha vatomar — Athaliah cries "Treason! Treason!"
notes.rendering: Athaliah tears her clothes and cries: Treason! Treason!
notes.why: Qesher — conspiracy, treason (the same word Elijah uses at Horeb when he says the people have broken the covenant: 1 Kings 19:10). Athaliah's cry is technically accurate: this is a conspiracy. It is also without legal standing: she came to power by murdering the royal family. The narrator records her cry without pity. She sees the seven-year-old king standing at the pillar — the place where the covenant was renewed, where the people pledged to YHWH — and her kingdom ends in that moment.

intro: Chapter 12 is about money: how to fund temple repair, why the first system fails for twenty-three years, and how the chest-and-accounting system works instead. The practicality of the chapter is refreshing — good institutional design, honest workers, no skimming. Then the chapter ends with Joash paying off Hazael with temple gold, and being assassinated by his own servants.

notes.original: kol yamav asher horahu Yehoyada ha-kohen — all his days that Jehoiada instructed him
notes.rendering: Jehoash does what is right... because Jehoiada the priest instructs him
notes.why: The qualification is embedded in the commendation: Joash is good as long as his mentor lives. The phrase all his days, which usually signals unconditional goodness, is immediately conditioned by the subordinate clause. In 2 Chronicles 24:17–18, Joash turns to idolatry after Jehoiada dies and has Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned to death. Kings does not narrate this, but the assassination at the end of the chapter (by his own servants, with no named cause in Kings) gains context from the Chronicler's fuller account.

notes.original: vayiqach Yehoyada ha-kohen aron echad — Jehoiada the priest takes a chest
notes.rendering: Jehoiada the priest takes a chest and bores a hole in the lid
notes.why: The chest-with-a-hole is institutional innovation under prophetic guidance: transparent, accountable, simple. The previous system (each priest collects from his donors) failed because the money never reached the repairs. The new system bypasses the priests for collection and goes directly to building workers. The narrator notes twice that the workers deal honestly (v.15 — they deal faithfully) — the unusual emphasis suggests that honesty in financial stewardship is itself worth naming as a theological achievement.

notes.original: vayishlach Yeho'ash l'Chazael — Joash sends it to Hazael
notes.rendering: Joash takes all the sacred gifts... and sends these to Hazael — and Hazael turns away from Jerusalem
notes.why: The irony is structural: Joash has just spent his reign funding the repair of the Temple treasury — and now he empties it to buy off the Syrian king. The gold that was gathered by the people and used by honest workers to restore YHWH's house is handed to a foreign king to prevent a siege. The Temple is repaired and immediately depleted. The book of Kings is full of this rhythm: restore, deplete, restore, deplete — until there is nothing left.

intro: Chapter 13 contains the death of Elisha — and then the strangest miracle of his career, performed after his death. The chapter also contains the arrow-striking scene, where a king's half-hearted obedience determines the scope of a military victory. Elisha's anger at three arrows rather than five is the most human moment of his prophetic career.

notes.original: avi avi rechev Yisrael u'farashav — my father, my father, the chariots of Israel
notes.rendering: my father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!
notes.why: The dying Elisha hears from the king of Israel the same words Elisha himself said at the whirlwind of Elijah (2:12). The circle is complete: what Elisha said of Elijah, a king now says of Elisha. The prophet was worth more than an army then; the prophet is worth more than an army now. Joash weeps because he knows that when Elisha dies, Israel loses its strategic advantage — the man who could read enemy battle plans from his bedroom (6:12) will no longer be available.

notes.original: hayita makkeh chamesh o shesh pe'amim — you should have struck five or six times
notes.rendering: you should have struck five or six times — then you would have made an end of Syria
notes.why: The arrow-striking scene is the most theologically demanding piece of prophetic instruction in the Elisha cycle. The king does not know why he is striking the ground; the prophet gives no explanation. He strikes three times — a reasonable number — and stops. Elisha's anger is not at disobedience but at inadequacy: the king could not sustain the symbolic act beyond the minimum. Three victories, not total victory. The prophet's anger reveals that symbolic actions in the prophetic world are not arbitrary gestures but causal: the ground-strikes determine the campaign's scope.

notes.original: vayigga ba'atzmot Elisha vayechi — he touches the bones of Elisha and revives
notes.rendering: as soon as the man touches the bones of Elisha, he revives and stands on his feet
notes.why: The corpse of Elisha resurrects a stranger. No prayer, no stretching, no word — just contact with the bones. The miracle is the most economical in the book: three clauses. It is also theologically the most unexpected: Elisha was the prophet who raised the dead through deliberate, agonizing prayer and bodily contact (4:34–35). After his death, his bones do what his living body did, without effort or intention. The power does not belong to the prophet but passes through him — even his remains are a channel.

intro: Chapter 14 is a tale of two hubrises: Amaziah of Judah defeats Edom and immediately challenges Israel to a fight he loses badly; Jeroboam II of Israel reaches the greatest territorial extent in the north's history — and the credit is given to a prophet named Jonah son of Amittai. The chapter plants a seed: that same Jonah will appear in his own book, fleeing in the opposite direction of his commission.

notes.original: lo yumathu avot al banim — fathers shall not be put to death for children
notes.rendering: fathers shall not be put to death because of their children
notes.why: Amaziah cites the law of Deuteronomy 24:16 when he spares the sons of his father's murderers. It is one of the rare explicit citations of the written Torah in Kings — "what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses" — and it functions as a positive character marker. The king who quotes the covenant text and follows it is doing something the narrator regards as praiseworthy, even if his subsequent challenge of Israel is foolish.

notes.original: choach ba-Lebanon shalach el ha-erez — a thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar
notes.rendering: a thistle on Lebanon sent to a cedar on Lebanon
notes.why: Jehoash's fable is one of the few extended literary parables in Kings. The thistle asks the cedar's daughter in marriage — and is trampled by a passing beast. The application is graciously indirect: Amaziah, inflated by his Edomite victory, is the thistle; Israel is the cedar. The wild beast need not be named. Jehoash gives Amaziah a genuine chance to stand down without humiliation. Amaziah does not take it. The thistle goes to war and is trampled.

notes.original: Yonah ben Amittai — Jonah the son of Amittai
notes.rendering: according to the word of YHWH... which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai
notes.why: The cameo appearance of Jonah son of Amittai — the prophet who will name his own book — places the great territorial expansion of Jeroboam II within the framework of prophetic word. Jeroboam is evil; YHWH does not permit Israel to be blotted out; Jonah prophesies a restoration of borders; it happens. The same prophet who will flee YHWH's commission to Nineveh has here already delivered a word to the most powerful king in Israel's northern history. He is not a minor prophet in the historical record — only in the canonical arrangement.

intro: Chapter 15 is the chapter of the assassins. In Israel, five kings reign in the span of forty-one years — four of them by murder. Jehu's dynasty ends with Zechariah's one-month successor; the next four kings kill their way to the throne and are killed in turn. Tiglath-pileser of Assyria appears for the first time, receiving tribute and carrying off populations. The chapter is the sound of a kingdom in freefall.

notes.original: zeh dvar YHWH asher dibber el Yehu — this was the promise of YHWH to Jehu
notes.rendering: this was the promise of YHWH that he gave to Jehu: your sons to the fourth generation
notes.why: The narrator pauses the rapid succession of assassinations to note a theological fact: Zechariah's death ends the Jehu dynasty at the promised fourth generation (10:30). Every king from Jehu to Zechariah is counted; the divine promise is measured and fulfilled exactly. The chaos of assassination is not random — it is the limit of a specific grace. YHWH keeps his word to the precise boundary he set.

notes.original: Pul melech Ashur ba al ha'aretz — Pul king of Assyria came against the land
notes.rendering: Pul the king of Assyria came against the land — Menahem gives him a thousand talents
notes.why: Tiglath-pileser III is known by two names in the Hebrew text: Pul (his Babylonian throne-name) and Tiglath-pileser. His appearance here — receiving tribute from Menahem — is the opening of the Assyrian chapter that will not close until Samaria falls in chapter 17. Menahem pays to survive: fifty shekels per wealthy man, a thousand talents total. The arithmetic of imperial subjugation has begun. Every subsequent political choice in Israel and Judah will be made in Assyria's shadow.

notes.original: vayigel Tiglat-Pileser — Tiglath-pileser carries them captive
notes.rendering: he carries the people captive to Assyria
notes.why: The first deportations. Galilee, Gilead, Naphtali — the northern territories are stripped of population and repopulated with Assyrian subjects. The practice is systematic and deliberate: remove a conquered people from their land, replace them with foreigners, prevent the formation of a resistance identity rooted in ancestral territory. The chapter notes it in one verse. Chapter 17 will explain the theological meaning. Isaiah and Hosea are preaching during these years; the silence of both in Kings makes the chapter feel like a report without a interpreter.

intro: Chapter 16 is the Ahaz chapter — the worst king Judah has seen since the Omrid intermarriage. He burns his son as an offering, calls himself Tiglath-pileser's servant and son, strips the Temple treasury to pay for Assyrian intervention, and then redesigns the Temple's altar to match a pagan model he saw in Damascus. He pays for his rescue by reordering the house of YHWH to honor his rescuer's gods.

notes.original: vaya'aver et beno ba'esh — he burns his son as an offering
notes.rendering: he even burns his son as an offering
notes.why: Child sacrifice — the burning of a son (va'aver ba'esh — to pass through fire, the standard Hebrew formula for this practice) — appears here for the first time in the Davidic line. It will reappear with Manasseh (21:6). The practice is specifically cited as the reason YHWH drove out the Canaanites before Israel (v.3). Ahaz now does what justified the Canaanites' displacement. The reversal is complete: the nation that was given the land because others defiled it is now doing the same.

notes.original: avdecha u'vincha ani — I am your servant and your son
notes.rendering: I am your servant and your son — come up and rescue me
notes.why: Eved — servant; ben — son. Ahaz offers Tiglath-pileser the language of covenantal fealty. In the ancient Near East, "I am your son" is treaty-language — the vassal calls himself son of the suzerain. Ahaz uses the language of covenant (servant, son) to the king of Assyria that should belong to YHWH alone. He empties the Temple to make the offer financially credible. The narrator records his words without comment; the theological verdict is in the vocabulary.

notes.original: vayar Achaz et ha-mizbeach — Ahaz sees the altar at Damascus
notes.rendering: he sees the altar that is at Damascus — he sends a model of it to Uriah the priest
notes.why: Ahaz is not importing Assyrian religion per se — Tiglath-pileser's Damascene altar is Syrian. But the gesture is politically and spiritually identical: the new center of power gets a new altar. The bronze altar that Solomon made — with the Molten Sea, the twelve oxen, the careful craftsmanship of Hiram son of the widow — is pushed to the side. Ahaz will use it "for inquiry" — a residual, marginal function. YHWH's altar demoted to the status of a private oracle while the new model takes the liturgical center stage.

intro: Chapter 17 is the most important theological chapter in 2 Kings — the moment where the narrator stops being a chronicler and becomes a theologian. Six verses report the fall of Samaria; seventeen verses explain why. The explanation is the Deuteronomistic History's most extended theological argument: Israel sinned, YHWH warned them through prophets, they did not listen, and so YHWH removed them from the land. The argument is not triumphalist — Judah's parallel sin is noted explicitly (v.19). The chapter reads its own future.

notes.original: vayya'ed YHWH b'Yisrael u'vi'Yehudah b'yad kol nevi'aw — YHWH warned Israel and Judah by every prophet
notes.rendering: YHWH warned Israel and Judah by every prophet and every seer: turn from your evil ways
notes.why: The great thesis: prophecy is not prediction but warning. The prophets from Elijah through Isaiah are here summarized in a single sentence — every prophet, every seer, the same message: shuvu — turn, return, repent. The same word from Elisha's prayer at Carmel (18:37 — you have turned their hearts back). YHWH's method was consistent and persistent. The failure is not divine; it is human.

notes.original: vayelku acharei ha-hevel vayehbalu — they went after empty things and became empty
notes.rendering: they went after false idols and became false
notes.why: The Hebrew wordplay is exact: hevel — emptiness, breath, vapor (the word Ecclesiastes uses for vanity). The verb vayelku — they went, they walked after. And then: vayehbalu — they became hevel. You become what you worship. The nation that followed empty things became empty. The same logic structures Psalm 115: those who make idols become like them. Israel's exile is not only punishment; it is the logical consequence of a people that has made itself into the thing it worshipped — nothing.

notes.original: ad hayom ha-zeh — until this day
notes.rendering: so Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria until this day
notes.why: Ad hayom ha-zeh — until this day. The narrator writes from within the exile or just after it. The phrase is not rhetorical; it is a historical marker. The exiled northern Israelites — the ten tribes — did not return. When the narrator says "until this day" he means: they are still there. The phrase appears throughout Kings to confirm that certain things remain true in the narrator's own time. This one is the most haunting: the exile is not a past event but a present condition.

intro: Chapter 18 introduces Hezekiah — the king of whom it is said there was none like him before or after — and immediately tests that commendation against the most formidable military machine the ancient Near East has produced. The Rabshakeh's speech is the masterpiece of imperial rhetoric in the Hebrew Bible: it correctly identifies every weakness in Jerusalem's position, inverts every theological argument it can reach, and addresses the people directly over the heads of their king and priests.

notes.original: Nechushtan — he called it Nehushtan
notes.rendering: he breaks in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made — it was called Nehushtan
notes.why: The bronze serpent (Numbers 21:8–9), made by Moses as a means of healing in the wilderness, has become an object of worship in Jerusalem. Hezekiah breaks it and gives it a dismissive name: Nechushtan — a mere thing of bronze (nachash — serpent; nechoshet — bronze; the name collapses both meanings into contempt). The thing Moses made as a channel of YHWH's healing became an idol. Hezekiah's reform begins with demolishing a sacred object from Moses — a remarkable act of theological courage. Not even the prophet's artifact escapes scrutiny.

notes.original: mishen ha-qaneh ha-ratzutz hazeh — this broken reed staff
notes.rendering: Egypt, that broken reed of a staff — it will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it
notes.why: The Rabshakeh's metaphor is shrewd and accurate: Egypt is unreliable (the Israelites discovered this at the Exodus; Judah will discover it again). The image of the broken reed — strong enough to look like a staff, fragile enough to splinter and wound the hand that grips it — is picked up by Isaiah (36:6) and Ezekiel (29:6–7). The Rabshakeh is not wrong about Egypt. His error is applying the same logic to YHWH.

notes.original: velo anu oto davar — the people answer him not a word
notes.rendering: the people are silent and answer him not a word — for the king's command was: do not answer him
notes.why: The silence of the people on the wall is one of the most powerful moments in Kings. The Rabshakeh speaks in Hebrew specifically to bypass the king's men and reach the people directly. They say nothing. The king has told them not to answer — and they obey. The discipline of that silence, under a speech designed to break it, is its own form of trust. They do not argue with the Rabshakeh; they do not negotiate. They tear their clothes and bring the words to Hezekiah.

intro: Chapter 19 is the answer to the Rabshakeh's speech. Hezekiah takes the letter into the Temple and spreads it before YHWH — a gesture at once practical and profound: the king who cannot answer the empire in military terms puts the empire's words before the one who can. Isaiah's oracle follows, and then the night of 185,000 dead bodies. The chapter asks only one question: is YHWH the living God, or is he like the gods the Assyrians have already destroyed?

notes.original: vayiphres Yechizqiyahu al penei YHWH — Hezekiah spreads it before YHWH
notes.rendering: Hezekiah goes up to the house of YHWH and spreads it before YHWH
notes.why: The gesture of spreading the letter before YHWH is unique in the Hebrew Bible.
