notes.original: olethron aiōnion apo prosōpou tou kyriou — eternal destruction away from the presence
notes.rendering: eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord and from the glory of his might
notes.why: Olethron aiōnion — eternal/age-long destruction. The phrase is one of the primary texts in the debate about the nature of final judgment. Apo prosōpou tou kyriou — away from the face/presence of the Lord. The destruction is defined spatially as separation from the divine presence — not cessation of existence but exclusion from relationship. The two phrases in apposition (destruction / away from the presence) have been read as: (1) the destruction consists of separation from the presence (the absence of God is the punishment); (2) those destroyed are driven away from the presence (they are excluded from the divine glory at the parousia). Either way, the text defines the ultimate negative reality as being apart from the presence of the Lord — the opposite of what 1 Thessalonians 4:17 promises: we will be with the Lord for ever.

intro: Second Thessalonians 2 is the most densely apocalyptic passage in the Pauline letters — and one of the most debated in the entire New Testament. The 'man of lawlessness,' the 'restrainer,' and the 'mystery of lawlessness already at work' have generated more interpretive speculation than almost any other passage in Paul. The Fireside Gospel translates the text faithfully and lays out the interpretive options in the notes without pretending to resolve what Paul himself leaves mysterious.

notes.original: tēs parousias tou kyriou hēmōn… kai hēmōn episynagōgēs ep' auton
notes.rendering: the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to him
notes.why: Two technical eschatological terms: parousia (coming, presence, arrival — the word used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city) and episynagōgē (the gathering together, the assembling — from epi + synagōgē, the assembly). The parousia of Jesus is his royal arrival; the episynagōgē is the gathering of his people to him at that arrival (echoing Matthew 24:31: he will send his angels and they will gather his chosen from the four winds). Someone has been teaching the Thessalonians that this has already happened — that they have somehow missed it, or that it is a purely spiritual event already complete. Paul's correction: two things must happen first, and neither has happened yet.

notes.original: ho anthrōpos tēs anomias… ho huios tēs apōleias — man of lawlessness, son of destruction
notes.rendering: the man of lawlessness… the son of destruction
notes.why: Two Semitic idiom phrases in Greek dress: ho anthrōpos tēs anomias (the man characterised by lawlessness, the lawlessness-person) and ho huios tēs apōleias (the son of destruction — the same phrase used for Judas in John 17:12). Both are Hebrew/Aramaic idiom constructions of the form 'son/man of X' — meaning one who belongs to X, one defined by X. The figure exalts himself in the Temple of God and proclaims himself to be God — the pattern of the Danielic abomination (Daniel 11:36) and the Roman emperor cult, both in the background. The identity of the man of lawlessness has been read as: a historical figure (Nero, Caligula, Antiochus Epiphanes), a future eschatological figure (the Antichrist of later tradition), or a symbolic description of the pattern of self-deifying opposition to God that appears throughout history.

notes.original: to katechon… ho katechōn — the restrainer (neuter then masculine)
notes.rendering: what is now restraining him… he who now restrains it
notes.why: To katechon (v.6, neuter — the restraining thing/force) and ho katechōn (v.7, masculine — the one who restrains/the restrainer) are the most debated entities in 2 Thessalonians. Paul says the Thessalonians know what it is — but he does not tell us, presumably because they already know from his oral teaching. Proposals across history include: the Roman empire and emperor (which restrains the breakdown of order), the preaching of the gospel (which must reach all nations before the end), Michael the archangel (from Daniel), God or the Holy Spirit, and Paul himself as the apostle to the Gentiles. The shift from neuter to masculine may indicate a force and its personal representative. The restrainer is a genuine mystery — and the honest interpreter acknowledges it.

notes.original: tō pneumati tou stomatos autou — the breath of his mouth
notes.rendering: the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth
notes.why: Tō pneumati tou stomatos autou — the Spirit/breath of his mouth. The phrase draws directly on Isaiah 11:4: 'he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.' The messianic king of Isaiah's vision destroys the wicked not by military force but by the word of his mouth — the same creative word that spoke the world into being (Psalm 33:6: by the word of YHWH the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host). Jesus' parousia is not a military campaign but a word-event: the appearance of the one who is the truth is the destruction of the one who is the embodiment of the lie. The lawless one is brought to nothing (katargēsei — rendered powerless, nullified) by the epiphany of Christ's coming.

notes.original: pempsei autois ho theos energeian planēs — God sends a working of delusion
notes.rendering: God sends them a strong delusion
notes.why: Energeian planēs — a working of error, an activity of delusion (energeia — activity, working, energy; planē — wandering, error, deception — the root of our word 'planet,' the wandering stars). God sending delusion is the hardening pattern from Exodus (YHWH hardening Pharaoh's heart) and Isaiah 6 (the seeing-but-not-seeing commission). Those who refused to love the truth (v.10) and took pleasure in unrighteousness are given over to the full consequences of their choice. The theological question — how can God send delusion? — is best answered through the passive-active distinction: God's 'sending' here is his confirming of the direction already chosen. He does not deceive the innocent; he confirms the self-deception of those who have already chosen the lie.

intro: Second Thessalonians 3 pivots from the eschatological intensity of chapter 2 to the very practical: prayer, imitation, and work. The shift is characteristic of Paul — the most elevated theology in the letter is immediately followed by the most concrete instruction. The problem of idleness is almost certainly connected to the eschatological confusion of chapter 2: if the Day of the Lord has arrived or is imminent, why work?

notes.original: eis tēn agapēn tou theou kai eis tēn hypomonēn tou Christou
notes.rendering: to the love of God and to the steadfastness of Christ
notes.why: Two genitives that can be read two ways each. Tēn agapēn tou theou — the love of God (God's love for us, or our love for God?). Tēn hypomonēn tou Christou — the steadfastness of Christ (Christ's own endurance, or endurance directed toward Christ?). Both objective and subjective readings are possible in both cases. The Fireside Gospel renders both as objective genitives: God's love (which the Lord directs hearts toward) and Christ's steadfastness (which is the pattern and ground of the community's endurance). Christ's hypomonē — his patient endurance under suffering — is the source from which the Thessalonians' hypomonē under persecution flows. They endure because he endured; they love because he loved.

notes.original: ei tis ou thelei ergazesthai mēde esthietō
notes.rendering: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat
notes.why: One of the most quoted verses in 2 Thessalonians — and one of the most misapplied. The context is specific: some in the Thessalonian community have stopped working, probably because they believe the end is near (or has arrived) and ordinary life is therefore irrelevant. Paul does not address poverty, disability, or structural unemployment; he addresses deliberate idleness in people who are capable of working but have chosen not to. The command (mēde esthietō — let him not eat) is not about withholding food from the destitute but about removing the social enablement of a particular kind of theological escapism. The principle has been misused to justify cutting food assistance to the poor; the text does not support that use. It supports the community holding capable members to the mutual obligation of contributing to common life.

notes.original: mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous — not busy, but busybodies
notes.rendering: not busy at work, but busybodies
notes.why: Paul's only wordplay in the letter: mēden ergazomenous (doing nothing, not working — from ergazomai, to work) and periergazomenous (being busybodies, meddling — from peri + ergazomai, working around/beyond what is one's own business). The play on the same root (erg- — work) is deliberate: they are not ergazomenoi but periergazomenoi. They are not working but they are very busy — in everyone else's business. The paradox of the idle busybody is universal in communities awaiting dramatic change: having stepped back from ordinary productive life, they fill the resulting vacuum with interference in other people's lives. Paul's remedy is not rebuke but redirection: do your own work quietly.

notes.original: ho aspasmos tē emē cheiri Paulou — the greeting in my own hand
notes.rendering: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand
notes.why: As in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11, Colossians 4:18, and Philemon 19, Paul takes the pen from his secretary to write the final greeting personally. The autograph serves as authentication: this is how I write — the handwriting itself is the proof of the letter's genuineness. The detail matters because 2:2 warned against letters 'seeming to be from us' that had been causing confusion. The personal handwriting at the close is Paul's answer to the forgery problem: you know my hand; if a letter lacks it, treat it with suspicion.

outro: Note on 2 Thessalonians as a whole: The letter addresses a community under three pressures simultaneously — external persecution, internal theological confusion, and communal dysfunction. Paul's response moves through three corresponding registers: vindication (the righteous judge will act, chapter 1), clarification (the Day has not come, and here are the signs that must precede it, chapter 2), and community ordering (stand firm, hold to tradition, work quietly, do not grow weary, chapter 3). The letter's most memorable sentence — 'if anyone will not work, let him not eat' — is not a social policy but a community discipline, grounded in Paul's own example of working night and day rather than claiming the rights his apostleship entitled him to. The eschatological urgency of chapter 2 does not diminish the importance of ordinary work; it makes it more necessary. Life in the present age, however short, is to be lived with full engagement, not in paralysed waiting.

intro: Second Timothy opens with unusual warmth even by Pauline standards — the letter is saturated with personal affection. Timothy's tears, his grandmother's faith, Paul's longing to see him. And then immediately the charge: fan into flame, do not be ashamed, guard the deposit. The letter is simultaneously a farewell and a commission.

notes.original: ou gar edōken hēmin ho theos pneuma deilias — not a spirit of fear
notes.rendering: God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control
notes.why: Deilias — cowardice, timidity, fearfulness (from deilos — fearful, cowardly). The word is strong — not merely nervousness but the failure of nerve that leads to desertion or denial. Paul uses it in the context of Timothy's ministry: do not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul's imprisonment (v.8). The three positive qualities that replace fear — dynamis (power, capacity), agapē (love), and sōphronismos (self-control, sound-mindedness, the same sōphrōn root from Titus) — describe the minister's complete character. Power for the work, love for the people, self-control of the inner life. The spirit of fear is the spirit that makes a young minister hedge, qualify, avoid the costly thing. The spirit of power-love-self-control is what Paul is asking Timothy to inhabit.

notes.original: oida gar hō pepisteuika — I know whom I have believed
notes.rendering: I know whom I have believed
notes.why: Hō — whom (personal, not 'what I have believed' as a creed but who — a person). Pepisteuika — I have believed and continue to believe (perfect tense, completed action with ongoing effect). Paul's confidence in the face of suffering and likely death is not confidence in his own endurance or his own theology — it is confidence in a person. He knows whom. The deposit (parathēkē — what has been entrusted, a legal term for something placed in another's safekeeping) that Paul is confident will be guarded until that day may refer to what has been entrusted to Paul (the gospel) or to what Paul has entrusted to Christ (his life). Both readings are coherent. The ambiguity may be intentional: Paul's gospel and Paul's life are both safe in the same hands.

intro: Second Timothy 2 gives Timothy three images for his ministry — soldier, athlete, farmer — all sharing the same quality: they endure discipline for a goal beyond the present moment. The chapter pivots on verse 9: 'the word of God is not bound' — Paul in chains, but the gospel unchained.

notes.original: all' ho logos tou theou ou dedetai — but the word of God is not bound
notes.rendering: the word of God is not bound
notes.why: Dedetai — has been bound, is bound (from deō — to bind, to chain; the same word used for Paul's chains, desmios, a prisoner). Paul is bound (dedemenon hōs kakourgon — chained like a criminal, v.9a) but the word of God is not bound (ho logos tou theou ou dedetai). The contrast is precise and defiant: the person can be imprisoned; the gospel cannot. This is Paul's theology of mission under suffering — the constraint on the messenger is not a constraint on the message. The word has its own freedom, its own momentum. Paul will repeat the thought in Philippians 1:12 (the things that have happened to me have actually served to advance the gospel). Imprisonment is not defeat; it is a different venue.

notes.original: ei apistoumen, ekeinos pistos menei — if we are faithless, he remains faithful
notes.rendering: if we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself
notes.why: The trustworthy saying climaxes in a paradox: human faithlessness cannot produce divine faithlessness, because God's faithfulness is rooted in his own identity, not in our performance. Ou dynatai gar heauton arnēsasthai — he cannot deny himself. This is not a comfortable word for the careless; it is a stabilising word for the struggling. The faithfulness of God is not contingent on the faithfulness of the believer. It flows from who God is — and God cannot be other than himself. The saying also provides the motivation for endurance: if faithlessness does not produce divine faithlessness, then endurance through faithlessness toward faithfulness is always possible.

intro: Second Timothy 3 contrasts the trajectory of difficult times (from bad to worse) with the stability of continued formation in Scripture. The famous passage on Scripture's usefulness (3:16–17) is given its note — the word theopneustos (God-breathed) is unique in the NT and one of the most theologically significant coinages in the canon.

notes.original: pasa graphē theopneustos — all Scripture is God-breathed
notes.rendering: all Scripture is breathed out by God
notes.why: Theopneustos — God-breathed (from theos — God + pneō — to breathe, to blow). The word appears only here in the NT — a Pauline coinage or very rare term. The image is of Scripture as something breathed out from God, exhaled — like speech from a speaker's mouth. The Septuagint uses the same root (emphysaō — to breathe into) for YHWH breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7). Scripture is not merely inspired in the modern sense (stimulated, encouraged) but breathed out — it is divine breath in textual form. The four profitable uses (didaskalia/teaching, elegmos/reproof, epanorthōsis/correction, paideia/training in righteousness) cover the full range of what formation requires: instruction in what is true, identification of what is wrong, setting back on course, and the long work of shaping a life.

notes.original: hina artios ē ho tou theou anthrōpos — complete, equipped
notes.rendering: so that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work
notes.why: Artios — complete, fully fitted, capable of meeting any situation (from the same root as the NT artiōs — exactly, precisely; the word suggests perfect fit, nothing missing). Exērtismenos — thoroughly equipped, fully outfitted (perfect passive participle — the equipping has been completed and the state of equipping persists). The goal of Scripture's usefulness is not theological sophistication but practical completeness: the person of God who has been formed by Scripture is capable of every good work. The verse grounds the whole of Timothy's ministry in the formation that has already happened — 'from childhood' (v.15) — and declares it sufficient for what lies ahead.

intro: Second Timothy 4 is Paul's last words to the church in letter form. The solemn charge (vv.1–5) is followed by the most personal farewell in the Pauline corpus — the drink offering, the fight, the race, the faith kept. Then the immediate mundane reality: Demas left, bring my cloak, I need the books, it's getting cold.

notes.original: egō gar ēdē spendoumai — I am already being poured out as a drink offering
notes.rendering: I am already being poured out as a drink offering
notes.why: Spendoumai — I am being poured out as a libation, as a drink offering (from spendō — to pour out a libation). The drink offering (nesech in Hebrew, sponde in Greek) was poured out at the base of the altar as the final act of a sacrifice — it accompanied the burnt offering and completed it. Paul uses the image in Philippians 4:17 as well. Here in 2 Timothy it is his self-description at the moment of death: his life is the drink offering being poured out in completion of the ministry-sacrifice. The present tense (spendoumai — I am being poured) suggests the process is already underway — not future, not hypothetical. The hour of departure (analuseos — an untying, a loosing of moorings, as a ship leaves harbour) has come.

notes.original: ton kalon agōna ēgōnismai — I have fought the good fight
notes.rendering: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith
notes.why: Three perfect tenses — completed actions with present consequences. Ton kalon agōna ēgōnismai (the good fight I have fought — the athletic/military contest of ministry); ton dromon teteleka (the race I have completed — the running of the course); tēn pistin tetērēka (the faith I have kept — guarded, held to, maintained). These are not boasts of achievement but attestations of faithfulness: the fight was fought as it should be fought, the race was run to its end, the trust was not betrayed. The three images together cover the whole of Paul's life in ministry — the contest (suffering), the course (perseverance), the keeping (faithfulness). And they are spoken from prison, near death, having been deserted by most of his companions. This is what the good fight looks like at its end.

notes.original: ton phelonen… kai ta biblia malista tas membranas — bring the cloak and the books
notes.rendering: bring the cloak… also the books, and above all the parchments
notes.why: The most unexpectedly human verse in the letter — and one of the most human in all of Paul. After the solemn charge and the magnificent farewell, Paul remembers: he is cold (bring the cloak — phelones, a heavy travelling cloak), he wants to read (bring the books — ta biblia, probably scrolls), and above all (malista — especially, most of all) the parchments (tas membranas — vellum notebooks, perhaps his personal copy of Hebrew Scripture or notes for writing). The mundane detail is not incidental. Paul in prison, facing death, still wants his books. Still studying. Still working. The man who has kept the faith is keeping it by continuing to think. The parchments matter most.

outro: Note on 2 Timothy as a whole: The letter is structured as a farewell with a forward lean. Paul is finishing; Timothy is continuing. Everything Paul says about his own ending is said in the service of Timothy's beginning: guard the deposit, be unashamed, fan the flame, preach the word, endure. The personal details at the end — Demas deserted, Luke stayed, bring the cloak, it's winter coming — are not afterthoughts but the texture of the actual life Paul is describing. The great fight of faith is fought in specific places, by specific people, with specific books and specific coats. The crown of righteousness laid up for Paul is also laid up for all who have loved the appearing — which includes Timothy, and every reader who comes after him.

intro: Acts opens as the second volume of a two-volume work addressed to Theophilus, carrying Luke’s Gospel narrative forward. The key word of the prologue is ‘began’ — a signal that this account records not what Jesus did but what he continues to do through the Spirit. The ascension (vv. 9–11) and the upper-room waiting (vv. 12–14) bracket the community’s first act of discernment: the last use of lot-casting in the New Testament.

notes.original: ērxato poieīn kai didāskein — began to do and to teach
notes.rendering: everything Jesus began to do and to teach
notes.why: Ērxato — began (aorist of archō — to begin, to be first). The verb is not incidental. If Acts is a sequel, what the Gospel records is what Jesus began; Acts is its continuation — what he continues to do through the Spirit and the community. The address to Theophilus ties this volume directly to Luke 1:3, forming a single literary and theological unit.

notes.original: heōs eschatou tēs gēs — to the end of the earth
notes.rendering: to the ends of the earth
notes.why: This single phrase is the structural outline of the entire book: Jerusalem (ch. 1–7), Judea and Samaria (ch. 8–12), the ends of the earth (ch. 13–28). It echoes Isaiah 49:6 — ‘that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth’ — marking the apostolic mission as the fulfilment of Israel’s servant calling. The geographic programme is simultaneously a theological one: the expansion of the witness is the expansion of the kingdom.

notes.original: edōkan klērous autoīs — they gave / cast lots for them
notes.rendering: They cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias
notes.why: This is the last occurrence of lot-casting in the New Testament. From Pentecost onward the community discerns by the Spirit’s direct guidance, not by chance. The detail quietly marks a threshold: the book opens with an old-covenant practice and closes with the Spirit directing the mission outward. The Twelve are reconstituted before Pentecost — the restoration of Israel’s twelve-tribe symbol precedes the Spirit’s outpouring.

intro: Acts 2 is the pivot of the book — the Pentecost event that launches the community into its mission. Peter’s sermon is the theological centrepiece: it reads the crucifixion and resurrection through Israel’s scriptures and declares that the Jesus who was killed is now both Lord and Messiah. The chapter closes with a community portrait — teaching, koinōnia, breaking of bread, prayer, generosity — that has defined the church’s self-understanding ever since.

notes.original: pnoēs baiaīas — of a violent wind/breath; glōssai — tongues / languages
notes.rendering: a sound like the rush of a violent wind”; “tongues of fire
notes.why: Pnoē — breath, wind (same root as pneuma — spirit). The sound is not the wind itself but like it — a comparison, not a meteorological event. Glōssai — the same word for the anatomical tongue and a human language. The fire ‘divides’ (diamerizomenai) and rests individually: the Spirit is simultaneously corporate (filling the house) and personal (resting on each one).

notes.original: lusas tas ōdīnas tou thanātou — loosing the birth-pangs of death
notes.rendering: loosing the birth-pangs of death
notes.why: Ōīdīn — birth-pang, labour pain. The image is startling: death itself has birth-pangs that God loosens. Some scholars see a Hebrew idiom behind this (chebelē māwet — the ropes of death, Ps 18:5), rendered as ōdīnas in the LXX. Either way, the resurrection is not a gentle resuscitation but the violent breaking of death’s grip. The word ‘impossible’ (ouk ēn dunaton) is equally stark: it was metaphysically inconceivable that death could retain him.

notes.original: tē koinōnia — the fellowship / the shared life
notes.rendering: the fellowship
notes.why: Koinōnia — fellowship, sharing, participation (from koinos — common). The word carries the sense of having things in common, not merely warm feeling. It sits alongside teaching, bread-breaking, and prayer as one of the four structural pillars of community life. Verses 44–45 define koinōnia in practice: shared property distributed according to need. This is not incidental generosity but the structural expression of belonging entirely to one another.

intro: Acts 3 pairs a miracle with its interpretation. The healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate becomes the occasion for Peter’s second major address, in which the sign is re-read as evidence of the resurrection’s power. The sermon’s closing appeal (vv. 19–21) is the most eschatologically rich passage in the early chapters — times of refreshing, the restoration of all things, the return of the appointed Messiah.

notes.original: argýrion kai chrýson ouk hypārchei moi — silver and gold I do not have
notes.rendering: Silver and gold I have none — but what I do have I give you
notes.why: The contrast is precise and deliberate: what the man expects (alms — eleemosūnē) and what he receives (healing in the name of Jesus) define the economy of the resurrection. The formula is memorable: I have no x, but what I have I give. The name (onoma) of Jesus is not an incantation; it is the agent of power — a claim Peter will make explicit before the council in 4:12.

notes.original: archēgōn tēs zōēs — author / pioneer / originator of life
notes.rendering: You killed the Author of life
notes.why: Archēgos — one who leads the way, a founder, a pioneer (from archē — beginning, and agō — to lead). The word appears four times in the NT: Acts 3:15; 5:31 (‘Prince and Saviour’); Hebrews 2:10 (‘pioneer of salvation’); 12:2 (‘pioneer and perfecter of faith’). The irony here is devastating: the one who is the very source and pioneer of life is the one you killed. The resurrection is the divine reversal of that verdict.

notes.original: kairoi anapsyxēs — times of refreshing / of cool breath
notes.rendering: times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord
notes.why: Anapsyxis — a cooling, a refreshing, relief through fresh air (from anapsyō — to cool, to revive). The word is rare in the NT (only here) and evocative: the presence of the Lord is experienced as cool air in a scorching place. It pairs with apokatastāseōs (v. 21) — the restoration of all things — suggesting that the present refreshing anticipated in repentance is a foretaste of the full cosmic restoration at the Messiah’s return.

intro: Acts 4 moves from miracle to confrontation: the healed man becomes the occasion for the first arrest and first defence before the Jerusalem authorities. The chapter pivots around Peter’s declaration in 4:12 — the most absolute claim in the book so far — and closes with the community’s prayer and a second community portrait, now defined by shared possessions and apostolic boldness under pressure.

notes.original: ouk estin en allō oudeni hē sōtēria — there is in no other the salvation
notes.rendering: There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among people by which we must be saved
notes.why: The claim is unqualified and universal: sōtēria (salvation — deliverance, wholeness, rescue) exists in no other. The allusion to Psalm 118:22 in verse 11 (‘the stone the builders rejected’) places this declaration in Israel’s scriptures: the rejected stone is now the only cornerstone. The audience is the Jerusalem council — the builders of the metaphor are the builders before whom Peter speaks.

notes.original: agrāmmatoi kai idiōtai — unlettered and ordinary men
notes.rendering: ordinary, unschooled men
notes.why: Agrāmmatos — one without formal scribal or rhetorical training. Idiōtēs — a private person, one without professional standing (the source of the English ‘idiot’, though the Greek simply means ‘layperson’ or ‘commoner’). The council’s astonishment is that these unaccredited men speak with such authority. The recognition that follows — ‘they had been with Jesus’ — is the answer: their formation is not institutional but personal.

notes.original: kardia kai psychē mia — heart and soul one
notes.rendering: one in heart and soul
notes.why: The phrase echoes the Shema’s command to love God with all one’s heart and soul (Deut 6:5), here applied to the community’s internal unity. Kardia (heart — the seat of will and understanding) and psychē (soul — the whole person, the life) together describe a unity of purpose and being. The shared-possession practice that follows is not the cause of this unity but its expression: the inner oneness manifests as economic solidarity.

intro: Acts 5 moves on two tracks: the internal discipline of the community (Ananias and Sapphira) and the external pressure of the authorities (the second arrest). Together they define the community’s double vulnerability — to corruption from within and hostility from without. Gamaliel’s speech is among the most rhetorically effective passages in Acts: the council is persuaded by a Pharisee to release the very men they want to kill.

notes.original: epseusatō to pneuma to hagion — to lie to the Holy Spirit
notes.rendering: you have not lied to men but to God
notes.why: The equivalence Peter draws between lying to the Holy Spirit (v. 3) and lying to God (v. 4) is one of the most direct statements of the Spirit’s divine status in the NT. Ananias’s sin is not stinginess but deception — he pretends to give everything while keeping something back. The community portrait of 4:32–37 is directly violated: the death that follows is the judgment of a community whose integrity depends on truthfulness about possessions.

notes.original: peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois — it is necessary to obey God rather than men
notes.rendering: We must obey God rather than men
notes.why: The formula is absolute and programmatic: it echoes Socrates’ famous reply to the Athenian court (Plato, Apology 29d) and establishes a principle the community will apply throughout Acts. The verb dei — it is necessary, it must be — is the language of divine compulsion, the same word used in 1:16 (‘the Scripture had to be fulfilled’). The apostles are not being defiant; they are being obedient to a higher authority.

notes.original: katexiōthēsan — were counted worthy / honoured
notes.rendering: rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name
notes.why: The paradox is striking: katexiōthēsan (were counted worthy / honoured) for atimasthēnai (to be dishonoured / shamed). The beatitude tradition stands behind this — blessed are those persecuted for righteousness (Matt 5:10–12). Suffering for the name is reframed as a privilege. The word ‘name’ (onoma) without further qualification has by this point in Acts become a technical term: the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.

intro: Acts 6 introduces the figure of Stephen, the first martyr, whose story will run through chapter 7. The chapter also records the first internal administrative crisis of the community: the neglect of the Hellenistic widows. The solution — the appointment of the Seven — is significant not merely as an organisational fix but as a model of shared leadership and Spirit-discernment.

notes.original: Hellēnistōn pros Hebraious — Hellenists against Hebrews
notes.rendering: the Hellenistic Jews among them raise a complaint against the Hebraic Jews
notes.why: Hellēnistēs — a Greek-speaking Jew of the diaspora, one who has absorbed the language and culture of the Hellenistic world. Hebraios — a Hebrew-speaking Jew, likely Aramaic-speaking, rooted in the Palestinian tradition. This is the first recorded cultural tension within the Jerusalem community: the fracture runs not between Jew and Gentile but between two kinds of Jews. The neglect of widows — those most economically vulnerable — is the presenting symptom.

notes.original: martyroumenōs — testified about / of good reputation
notes.rendering: seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom
notes.why: The criteria are three: good testimony (martyroumenōs — witnessed to, vouched for), fullness of the Spirit, and wisdom (sophia — practical discernment). The last two are paired throughout Acts and the wisdom tradition: the Spirit’s gift and the mind’s discipline belong together. All seven names are Greek, suggesting the Seven are chosen from the aggrieved Hellenist community — an elegant structural solution to the complaint.

notes.original: hōsei prosōpon angelou — like the face of an angel
notes.rendering: his face is like the face of an angel
notes.why: The detail is anticipatory and ambiguous: it could signal divine favour (Moses’ face shone after his encounter with God, Ex 34:29–35) or, in the eyes of the council, something uncanny and threatening. Stephen’s face anticipates the content of his speech: he will speak as one who has seen, as Moses did, the heavenly reality behind the earthly forms. The comparison sets up the climax of 7:55–56, where Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.

intro: Stephen’s speech is the longest in Acts and the most radical in its argument. He retells Israel’s history to show a single pattern: God’s deliverers are consistently rejected by the people, and God consistently works outside the expected structures. The speech reaches its climax in the accusation of 7:51–53 and the vision of 7:55–56. Stephen dies praying the same prayer Jesus prayed from the cross: ‘Do not hold this sin against them.’

notes.original: touto’n ho theōs archonta kai lutrōtēn apēstalken — this one God sent as ruler and redeemer
notes.rendering: this man God sends as both ruler and redeemer
notes.why: The rejected-and-sent pattern is the spine of Stephen’s argument. Moses was rejected by his people (‘who made you a ruler?’) and sent by God as ruler and lutrōtēs — redeemer, liberator, one who ransoms (from lytrō — to ransom). The word is rare but resonant: it points forward to the Messiah whom the same pattern will claim. The audience has already been told in 3:15 and 4:10 that the Jesus they rejected is the one God raised. Stephen is making the same argument from a longer arc of history.

notes.original: all’ ouch ho hypsistos en cheiropoiqētois katoikei — the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands
notes.rendering: the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands
notes.why: Cheiropoiqētos — made by human hands (cheir — hand; poieō — to make). The word recurs in the context of idols (Lev 26:1 LXX; Isaiah 2:18) and carries a polemical charge: to call the temple ‘made by hands’ is to put it in the category of idolatry. This is the charge latent in the false witnesses’ accusation (6:13–14). Stephen is not rejecting the temple but insisting that no building can contain the God who made heaven and earth.

notes.original: horais tōn ouranōn dianoigomenous — he sees the heavens opened
notes.rendering: I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God
notes.why: The vision inverts Daniel 7:13–14: there the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days; here he stands at his right hand. The posture — standing rather than seated — may suggest readiness to receive the martyr, or it may be the posture of witness (a legal term: one who stands to give testimony). Stephen dies as a witness — martys — in both senses of the word that will come to define the community.

intro: Acts 8 is the fulfilment of Acts 1:8’s second movement: Judea and Samaria. The scattering caused by Stephen’s martyrdom becomes the vehicle of expansion — the persecution that was meant to silence the word instead scatters it. Philip’s encounter with the Ethiopian eunuch is one of the most quietly radical scenes in Acts: a sexually marginalised foreign official, reading Isaiah on his chariot, becomes the first recorded Gentile convert.

notes.original: hoi men oun diasparēntes diēlthon euangelizomenoi ton logon — those scattered went about preaching the word
notes.rendering: Now those who are scattered go about preaching the word
notes.why: Diasparēntes — scattered (from diaspairō — to scatter, the same root as diaspora). The scattering intended to silence the word instead multiplies it. The pattern is Lukan and theological: what appears to be defeat turns out to be advance. The word euangelizomenoi (preaching the good news) — the root of ‘evangelism’ and ‘gospel’ — is a participle of ongoing action: they go about continually announcing.

notes.original: Aithiops eunouchos dynastes Kandākēs — an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official of Candace
notes.rendering: an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians
notes.why: The description is precise and loaded. Ethiopian — from the ends of the earth (the geographic edge of the known world for ancient writers). Eunouchos — a castrated male, excluded from the assembly of Israel (Deut 23:1). Court official (dynastes) — a person of power and status. Isaiah 56:3–87 promises that the eunuch who keeps God’s covenant will receive ‘a name better than sons and daughters’ — the very passage the man may have been searching for as he read Isaiah.

notes.original: arxamenos apo tēs graphēs tautēs euēngelisatō autō ton Iēsoun — beginning from this scripture he preached to him Jesus
notes.rendering: beginning with this Scripture he tells him the good news about Jesus
notes.why: The formula is programmatic: Philip begins from the text — Isaiah 53:7–8 — and moves to Jesus. This is the pattern of early Christian interpretation: the scriptures of Israel are the starting point and Jesus is the destination. The Ethiopian’s question — ‘about whom does the prophet say this?’ — is the question that opens the entire interpretive project. Philip’s answer is the whole Gospel in miniature.

intro: Acts 9 contains three of the most significant scenes in the book: the conversion of Saul, the healing of Aeneas, and the raising of Tabitha. Together they demonstrate the reach of the resurrection’s power: the enemy is transformed, the paralysed are restored, and the dead are raised. The conversion of Saul is told three times in Acts (here, 22:1–21, 26:1–23) — a narrative emphasis that signals its theological importance.

notes.original: Saoul, Saoul, ti me diōkeis — Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?
notes.rendering: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” — “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting
notes.why: The double address (Saoul, Saoul) echoes the divine calls of Moses (Ex 3:4) and Samuel (1 Sam 3:10) — a marker of solemn summons. The question and its answer establish the foundational Lukan theology of the body of Christ: to persecute the community is to persecute Jesus himself. The risen Lord identifies completely with those who bear his name. Saul’s persecution was directed at followers; the voice tells him he has been attacking the Lord.

notes.original: skeuos eklogēs estin moi houtos — this one is a chosen vessel / instrument for me
notes.rendering: he is a chosen instrument of mine
notes.why: Skeuos — a vessel, a container, a utensil (from skēnē — tent; the word Paul himself will use in 2 Cor 4:7 — ‘we have this treasure in jars of clay’). Eklogē — election, selection (from eklego — to choose out). The mission is threefold and deliberately ordered: Gentiles first, then kings, then the children of Israel. The one who persecuted the church now carries the name to the world.

notes.original: hē ekklesia … eichēn eirēnēn — the church had peace
notes.rendering: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria has peace
notes.why: This is one of several summary verses in Acts — editorial pauses in which Luke steps back to describe the community’s state. Eirēnē — peace, wholeness, the Hebrew shalom: not merely the absence of persecution but the positive flourishing of the community. The three regions named — Judea, Galilee, Samaria — recall the geographic programme of 1:8. The community is now established across the territory Jesus himself walked.

intro: Acts 10 is the theological watershed of the book. The conversion of Cornelius’s household is told at length — in fact retold in chapter 11 and invoked again at the Jerusalem Council in chapter 15 — because it answers the decisive question: does the gospel cross the boundary between Jew and Gentile? The answer is the Holy Spirit’s own: the Spirit falls before baptism, undeniable and uncontainable.

notes.original: ha ho theōs ekathārisen su mē koinou — what God has cleansed, do not call common
notes.rendering: What God has made clean, do not call common
notes.why: Koinos — common, shared, unclean in the ritual sense (as opposed to hāgios — holy, set apart). The vision is about far more than food: its application is immediate in the arrival of Cornelius’s men (v. 19) and explicit in Peter’s own interpretation (v. 28 — ‘God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean’). The sheet of animals is an enacted parable: the boundary between clean and unclean has been redrawn by the God who made all things.

notes.original: ouk estin prosōpolqēmptēs ho theōs — God is not a receiver of faces / a respecter of persons
notes.rendering: Truly I understand that God shows no partiality
notes.why: Prosōpolqēmptia — partiality, literally ‘receiving of faces’ (prosōpon — face; lambanō — to receive/take). The idiom comes from the Hebrew nasa’ panim (to lift up the face — to show favour). God does not ‘lift the face’ of the powerful or the privileged. This is the most explicit statement of divine impartiality in Acts and the theological foundation of Gentile inclusion: no ethnic or national status can make one more or less acceptable to God.

notes.original: epepesen to pneuma to hagion epi pantas tous akouontas ton logon — the Holy Spirit fell upon all those hearing the word
notes.rendering: the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the word
notes.why: The Spirit falls during the sermon — before the water. This sequence is the opposite of Samaria (8:15–17, where the Spirit comes after baptism via apostolic hands) and signals divine sovereignty: the Spirit will not wait for the institution to catch up. The Gentile Pentecost — tongues and praise, exactly as at Acts 2 — is the argument Peter will use at the Jerusalem Council (15:8): God gave them the same gift as us; who am I to stand in God’s way?

intro: Acts 11 records two consequences of the Cornelius episode: the Jerusalem community’s initial resistance and eventual acceptance (vv. 1–18), and the emergence of the Antioch community as the second great centre of the mission (vv. 19–30). Antioch is where Gentiles first receive the word in significant numbers, where Barnabas and Saul find their joint vocation, and where the disciples first receive the name that will define them.

notes.original: tis ēmēn dynāmenos kōlyai ton theon — who was I, able to prevent God?
notes.rendering: who was I that I could stand in God’s way?
notes.why: The rhetorical question is the argument’s pivot. Peter does not say ‘I decided to include Gentiles’; he says ‘God already acted — what could I do?” The theology is passive and doxological: the community’s role is not to decide who is in but to recognise what God has already done. The Jerusalem community’s silence (v. 18) is not agreement in principle but submission to fact: the Spirit has moved.

notes.original: hoi men … oudēsī Ioudāiois … hoi de … Hellenas — some … only to Jews … but others … to Greeks
notes.rendering: speaking the word to no one except Jews” / “speak to the Greeks also
notes.why: The contrast is Luke’s editorial observation: some scattered believers continue the Jewish-only mission; unnamed men from Cyprus and Cyrene cross the boundary without authorisation, without a vision, without an apostolic commission. They simply speak to Greeks. The hand of the Lord is with them (v. 21). The expansion of the mission is not always directed from the centre; it breaks out at the margins first.

notes.original: christiānous prōtos en Antiocheia — Christians first in Antioch
notes.rendering: in Antioch the disciples are first called Christians
notes.why: Christianos — a follower of Christ, formed on the Latin pattern used for members of a household or political faction (Herodians, Caesareans). The name may have been given by outsiders — a label that stuck and was eventually embraced. It marks the moment the movement is visible enough and distinct enough to be named from the outside. Antioch thus produces two things that define later Christianity: the Gentile church and the name by which it will be known.

intro: Acts 12 is a chapter of sharp contrasts: James is killed without deliverance; Peter is delivered without explanation. The difference is not faith or merit but the sovereign freedom of God. The chapter closes with the briefest and most striking of Luke’s summary verses — ‘the word of God grows and multiplies’ — placed immediately after Herod’s gruesome death. The persecutor is consumed; the word advances.

notes.original: proseuchē de ēn ektenōs ginomenē hypo tēs ekklesias pros ton theon peri autou — but earnest prayer was being made to God by the church for him
notes.rendering: earnest prayer for him is being made to God by the church
notes.why: Ektenōs — earnestly, intensely, stretched out (from ekteino — to stretch, to extend). The same word is used in Luke 22:44 of Jesus praying ‘more earnestly’ in Gethsemane. The imperfect tense (ginomenē) indicates continuous, ongoing prayer: the church is praying without ceasing while Peter sleeps. The irony of verse 15 — the praying community refuses to believe their prayer is answered — is tender rather than condemnatory.

notes.original: epataisen auton angelos kyriou anth’ hōn ouk ēnekōn tēn doxan tō theō — an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give glory to God
notes.rendering: immediately an angel of the Lord strikes him down, because he does not give God the glory
notes.why: The contrast with Peter’s deliverance is structural. Peter is struck to be woken (v. 7); Herod is struck to die (v. 23). Peter deflects honour (v. 26 of ch. 10: ‘stand up; I too am a man’); Herod accepts divine acclamation. The charge — he did not give God the glory — is the defining sin of the powerful in Luke–Acts: the appropriation of honour that belongs to God alone.

notes.original: ho de logos tou theou ēuxanen kai eplqthēneto — but the word of God grew and multiplied
notes.rendering: But the word of God grows and multiplies
notes.why: This is the fourth of Luke’s growth summaries (cf. 2:47; 6:7; 9:31) and perhaps the most compressed. Two verbs: auxanō — to grow, to increase in size; plqthūnomai — to multiply, to become many. The juxtaposition with Herod’s death is pointed: the king who sought to contain the word is eaten by worms; the word itself grows. Luke’s summaries are theological arguments, not just statistics.

intro: Acts 13 marks the opening of the great Gentile mission. Paul’s synagogue sermon at Pisidian Antioch is his longest speech in Acts and follows the same pattern as Peter’s Pentecost sermon: Israel’s history leads to Jesus, the resurrection fulfils the scriptures, and forgiveness is announced. The pivotal turn of verse 46 — ‘we are turning to the Gentiles’ — will be repeated twice more (18:6; 28:28), marking the narrative’s stages.

notes.original: eipēn to pneuma to hagion — the Holy Spirit said
notes.rendering: the Holy Spirit says, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul’
notes.why: The commission for the first missionary journey comes from the Spirit, not from any human authority, and is received during worship and fasting. Aphorisate — set apart (from aphorizō — to separate, to designate). Paul uses the same word of himself in Romans 1:1 (‘set apart for the gospel of God’) — perhaps a retrospective echo of this moment. The phrase ‘for the work to which I have called them’ implies a prior call; the commissioning here is the public recognition of it.

notes.original: di’ toutou aphēsis hamartiōn kai apo pantōn hōn ouk ēdynqēthe … dikaiothēnai — through this one forgiveness of sins and from all things you were not able to be justified
notes.rendering: through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed … everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses
notes.why: This is the most explicitly Pauline theology in Acts, and one of Luke’s clearest bridges to the letters. Dikaioo — to justify, to acquit, to declare righteous (the same word at the heart of Romans and Galatians). The law cannot justify; faith in the raised Jesus does. The parallel with Peter’s 3:19 (‘repent and turn back that your sins may be wiped away’) shows the same gospel in different vocabularies.

notes.original: hosoi ēsan tetagmenoi eis zōēn aiŋnion — as many as were appointed/ordered for eternal life
notes.rendering: as many as are appointed to eternal life believe
notes.why: Tassō — to appoint, to order, to arrange (used of military deployment, official assignment). The verse is one of the most contested in Acts on questions of divine election: does tetagmenoi mean God appointed them, or they disposed themselves? The perfect passive participle most naturally implies prior divine action. Luke does not resolve the tension between divine appointment and human response; he presents both as true within the same narrative.

intro: Acts 14 moves between two modes of response to the gospel: murderous rejection (Iconium, Lystra’s stoning) and misguided veneration (Lystra’s attempt to sacrifice to the apostles as gods). The Lystra episode is remarkable: it is the first sermon in Acts addressed to a purely pagan, non-Jewish audience, and it appeals not to Israel’s scriptures but to the witness of creation itself.

notes.original: kai hēmeis homoiopatheis esmen hymin anthrōpoi — we too are of like passions with you, human beings
notes.rendering: We also are men, of like nature with you
notes.why: Homoiopatheis — of like feelings/sufferings (homoios — like; pathos — feeling, passion, experience). The word insists on the apostles’ full humanity: they are not divine emissaries in human form but ordinary people through whom an extraordinary God acts. The contrast is with the living God (theon zōnta) who made all things: the Creator is distinguished from his creatures, even his most conspicuous instruments.

notes.original: ouk amartyron heauton aphēken — he did not leave himself without witness
notes.rendering: yet he did not leave himself without witness
notes.why: Amartyros — without witness (a— negative; martys — witness). The argument is from natural theology: rain, fruitful seasons, food, gladness are all divine testimony inscribed in creation for those who have never heard the scriptures. This is the first appearance in Acts of what will be developed more fully in Paul’s Areopagus speech (17:24–28): God’s self-revelation in creation precedes and underlies the specific revelation in Christ.

notes.original: di’ pollōn thlipseōn dei hēmas eiselthein eis tēn basileian tou theou — through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter the kingdom of God
notes.rendering: through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary (divine compulsion, not mere probability). Thlipsis — tribulation, pressure, distress (from thlibō — to press, to crush). This is the theology Paul will repeat in his letters (Rom 8:17; 2 Cor 4:17) and that Jesus announces in the Beatitudes. The missionaries say this to communities they have just built: they are not promising safety but preparing the disciples for the cost of faithfulness.

intro: Acts 15 is the structural centre of the book. The Jerusalem Council resolves the question that the Cornelius episode raised: what are the terms of Gentile inclusion? The answer — faith and grace, not circumcision — is unanimous, grounded in the Spirit’s own testimony and anchored in scripture. The chapter ends with a jarring note: the apostolic partnership of Paul and Barnabas fractures over John Mark. Luke does not soften it.

notes.original: kardiognōstēs — the one who knows hearts; katharīsas tē pistei — having cleansed by faith
notes.rendering: God, who knows the heart, bore witness … having cleansed their hearts by faith
notes.why: Kardiognōstēs — knower of hearts (kardia — heart; ginōskō — to know): a title for God used only here and in 1:24. Peter’s argument is from divine testimony: God, who sees what no human sees, gave the same Spirit to the uncircumcised Cornelius household. The cleansing is katharīsas tē pistei — by faith, not by circumcision. The verb is aorist — a completed act: they are already clean.

notes.original: tithēntes zugon epi ton trachqlon tōn mathētōn — placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples
notes.rendering: why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples?
notes.why: Zugos — yoke (an implement of binding, submission, or servitude). Peter’s language is blunt: requiring circumcision of Gentiles is not zeal for the law but a test of God (peirazete ton theon — the same phrase used of Israel’s wilderness failures). The addition ‘that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear’ is a remarkable concession from a devout Jew: the law itself has been humanly unbearable.

notes.original: edoxen gar tō pneumati tō hagiō kai hēmin — for it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
notes.rendering: it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us
notes.why: The formula is unprecedented: a council letter that names the Holy Spirit as co-author. Dokeo — to seem, to appear, to be judged. The same word governs the council’s own verdict (v. 22: edoxen — it seemed good). The Spirit’s judgement and the community’s judgement are placed in parallel — a theology of conciliar discernment that grounds human decision in divine guidance without removing human responsibility.

intro: Acts 16 brings the gospel into Europe for the first time. Three conversion accounts anchor the chapter: Lydia (a wealthy merchant, converted at prayer), the slave girl (delivered from exploitation), and the jailer (a Roman official, converted in crisis). Together they illustrate the gospel’s reach across the social spectrum. The ‘we’ passages begin here (v. 10), inserting the narrator into the action.

notes.original: anqr horamai Makedones — a vision … a Macedonian man; sunebibasan hoti — concluding that
notes.rendering: a man of Macedonia … Come over and help us” / “concluding that God has called us
notes.why: The ‘we’ of verse 10 marks the sudden first-person shift that has fascinated readers since antiquity: the narrator joins the party at Troas. Sunebibasan — concluding, inferring (from sumbibazō — to bring together, to infer). The community reasons from the vision to a conclusion. The gospel’s European expansion is not a dramatic revelation but a piece of communal discernment: they look at what they know and conclude God is calling.

notes.original: hēs ho kyrios diēnoixen tēn kardian — whose heart the Lord opened
notes.rendering: The Lord opens her heart to pay attention to what Paul says
notes.why: Dianoīgō — to open fully, to open wide (from dia — through; anoigō — to open). The word is used of the disciples on the Emmaus road (‘he opened the scriptures to us’, Luke 24:45). Lydia is already a worshipper of God (seboomenē ton theon — a God-fearer); the Lord opens what is already oriented toward him. Faith is not created from nothing but from the prior grace of attentiveness.

notes.original: ti me dei poiein hina sōthō — what must I do that I may be saved?
notes.rendering: Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” — “Believe in the Lord Jesus
notes.why: The jailer’s question and Paul’s answer form the most compressed gospel exchange in Acts. Pisteuon — believe, trust (pistis — faith, trust, reliance). The answer is not a list of requirements but a single act of trust directed at a specific person: the Lord Jesus. The household baptism that follows the same night, after they have heard the word (v. 32), enacts the promise ‘you and your household’.

intro: Acts 17 contains Paul’s most philosophically sophisticated speech — the Areopagus address. Addressed to Athenian philosophers rather than synagogue audiences, it argues from creation, natural theology, and Greek poetry to the resurrection. It is the fullest example in Acts of the gospel engaging pagan intellectual culture on its own terms.

notes.original: hoi tēn oikoumenēn anastatōsantes — those who have turned the inhabited world upside down
notes.rendering: These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also
notes.why: Anastatō — to unsettle, to overturn, to stir up (from anistēmi — to stand up, to raise; the same root as anastasis — resurrection). The charge against Paul and Silas is the best unintentional testimony in Acts: the accusers are describing exactly what the resurrection gospel does. Oikoumenē — the inhabited world, the civilised order. The charge is sedition; the truth behind it is transformation.

notes.original: en autō gar zōmen kai kinoumētha kai esmen — for in him we live and move and exist
notes.rendering: In him we live and move and have our being
notes.why: Paul quotes two Greek poets: the first line is attributed to Epimenides of Crete (c. 600 BCE); the second to Aratus of Cilicia (c. 315–240 BCE), in his Phaenomena. The strategy is significant: Paul does not invent a connection between Greek thought and Jewish-Christian theology but finds threads already present in the culture and pulls them toward the God of Israel and the resurrection. The poets spoke better than they knew.

notes.original: tous chronous tēs agnoias huperidōn — having overlooked the times of ignorance
notes.rendering: The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent
notes.why: Hypehorāo — to overlook, to pass over without punishing (from hyper — over; horaō — to see). The theological argument is: what was previously left without clear verdict is now brought to a head. The resurrection is not just a datum but a verdict: it constitutes the assurance (pistin — faith-ground, proof) that the Judge is real and the day is coming. The call to repent is universal — pantas pantachou — all people everywhere.

intro: Acts 18 covers Paul’s eighteen-month stay in Corinth — his longest anywhere in Acts — and the brief but significant episode of Apollos. Two details stand out: the Lord’s night vision assuring Paul of protection (vv. 9–10), which sustains the long Corinthian ministry, and the mentoring of the gifted Apollos by Priscilla and Aquila (vv. 26–28), one of the most understated scenes of discipleship in the book.

notes.original: skqnopoioi — tentmakers
notes.rendering: by trade they are tentmakers
notes.why: Skēnopoios — one who makes tents or leather goods (skēnē — tent; poieō — to make). Paul’s practice of working with his hands while preaching is a consistent feature of his self-presentation in the letters (1 Cor 4:12; 1 Thess 2:9; 2 Thess 3:8). In the ancient world, a philosopher who worked with his hands was unusual and sometimes scorned; Paul’s manual labour is a deliberate statement about the non-mercenary nature of his apostleship.

notes.original: lalēi … ou sioqēsēis — speak … do not be silent; laos polys — many people
notes.rendering: Do not be afraid … for I have many in this city who are my people
notes.why: The night vision comes at a moment of vulnerability: Paul has just been driven from the synagogue (v. 6) and is living next door to it (v. 7). The command not to be silent echoes the prophetic calls of Jeremiah and Isaiah. Laos polys — many people (laos — the people, used in the LXX as the technical term for Israel). In Corinth, the Lord already has a people who are not yet gathered: the mission is to find them.

notes.original: akribēs autoīs exethēnto tēn tou theou hodon — they explained to him the way of God more accurately
notes.rendering: they take him aside and explain to him the way of God more accurately
notes.why: Akribēs — accurate, precise, exact (the word Luke uses in 1:3 of his own careful investigation). Apollos already knows the way of the Lord and teaches accurately about Jesus, but his understanding is incomplete — bounded by John’s baptism rather than the full Pentecost reality. The correction is offered privately and hospitably: Priscilla’s name appears first in v. 26, suggesting she may be the primary teacher in this mentoring pair.

intro: Acts 19 is the climax of Paul’s Ephesian ministry and the longest account of his work in any single city. The chapter moves from the incomplete disciples of John (vv. 1–7) through two years of teaching (vv. 8–10) and extraordinary signs (vv. 11–20) to the Artemis riot (vv. 23–41). The riot’s cause is economic: the gospel is bad for the idol trade. Luke’s irony is sharp — the city’s defence of the goddess is really a defence of its markets.

notes.original: tēn hodon — the Way
notes.rendering: speaking evil of the Way
notes.why: Hodos — road, way, path (used throughout Acts as a technical name for the Jesus movement: 9:2; 18:25–26; 19:23; 22:4; 24:14, 22). The name is almost certainly self-chosen and theologically rich: Jesus himself said ‘I am the way’ (John 14:6). The movement is not a set of doctrines but a path to walk — a way of life as much as a set of beliefs. The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall available in the midday heat when the teacher was absent.

notes.original: Iēsoun ginōskō kai ton Paulon epistramai, humeis de tines este — Jesus I know and Paul I recognise, but who are you?
notes.rendering: Jesus I know, and Paul I recognise, but who are you?
notes.why: The evil spirit’s reply is one of the wryest lines in Acts. Ginōskō — to know (relational knowledge); epistamai — to recognise, to be acquainted with (a weaker term). The distinction may be deliberate: Jesus the spirit knows deeply; Paul it merely recognises. The sons of Sceva are neither. The episode makes a precise theological point: the name of Jesus is not a magical formula transferable to any user, but operates through personal relationship and divine authority.

notes.original: ou monon Ephesou alla schēdon pasēs tēs Asias — not only of Ephesus but of almost all Asia
notes.rendering: not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia
notes.why: Demetrius’s speech is the most accurate assessment of Paul’s impact in Acts — and it comes from an opponent. The two-year teaching programme in the hall of Tyrannus (v. 10) has resulted in the evangelisation of the whole province. The Pauline letters corroborate this: the churches of Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis (Col 1:2; 4:13) were likely founded during this period by Paul’s co-workers.

intro: Acts 20 contains Paul’s only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders — the Miletus farewell to the Ephesian elders. It is the most personal address in the book: a pastor reviewing his own ministry, warning of dangers ahead, and commending the community to God and the word. The speech echoes the Pastoral Epistles in tone and vocabulary, and ends in a scene of communal grief that is among the most emotionally direct in all of Luke–Acts.

notes.original: all’ oudenos logon poioumai tēn psychēn timian emautō — but I do not count my life of any account as precious to myself
notes.rendering: I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself
notes.why: The Greek is compressed: logon poioumai — I make account (logon — account, reckoning; poieo — to make). Timian emautō — precious to myself. The renunciation is total: life itself is not worth more than the completion of the ministry. The word dromos — course, race — picks up the athletic metaphor Paul uses in his letters (1 Cor 9:24; 2 Tim 4:7). The same verb for ‘finish’ (teleioō) is used of Jesus completing his work in Luke 13:32.

notes.original: tēn ekklesian tou theou hēn periepoiēsato dia tou haimatos tou idiou — the church of God which he obtained through his own blood
notes.rendering: the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood
notes.why: Peripoieō — to make one’s own, to acquire, to preserve (from peri — around; poieō — to make). The phrase ‘his own blood’ (tou haimatos tou idiou — the blood of his own) is one of the strongest statements in Acts about the divine significance of the crucifixion. Some read ‘his own Son’s blood’ (taking idios as ‘own’ rather than a possessive); either reading grounds the pastoral charge in the cost of redemption.

notes.original: makarion estin mallon didonai ē lambanein — it is more blessed to give than to receive
notes.rendering: It is more blessed to give than to receive
notes.why: This is the only saying of Jesus in Acts not found in the Gospels — an agraphon, an unwritten saying preserved through oral tradition and cited here as the theological warrant for Paul’s self-supporting work. Makarios — blessed, happy, favoured (the same word as in the Beatitudes). The saying is introduced as a remembered word of the Lord Jesus himself — a reminder that the Jesus tradition was larger than the four Gospels and lived in the community’s memory.

intro: Acts 21 is the turning point of the book’s second half: Paul’s arrival in Jerusalem mirrors Jesus’s in the Gospel, complete with prophetic warnings, a city in uproar, and arrest. The ‘we’ narrative reaches Jerusalem and then falls silent. From here Paul will be in Roman custody until the book’s end. His decision to go despite the Spirit’s warnings (vv. 4, 11) is not defiance but the same willingness Jesus showed on the road to Jerusalem.

notes.original: oitines tō Paulon elegon … mē epibainein eis Hierosolyma — who through the Spirit told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem
notes.rendering: through the Spirit they tell Paul not to go on to Jerusalem
notes.why: The Spirit’s warnings here (and through Agabus in v. 11) are not prohibitions but prophetic declarations of what will happen — which the community then interprets as commands to stay. Paul does not disobey the Spirit; he interprets the warnings differently, as Jesus interpreted the cross — as the path through, not away. Luke does not adjudicate between the two interpretations, leaving the reader with the ambiguity intact.

notes.original: hetoimais echō ou monon dethēnai alla kai apothanein — I am ready not only to be bound but also to die
notes.rendering: I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus
notes.why: The echo of Jesus in Luke 9:51 (‘he set his face to go to Jerusalem’) and 13:33 (‘it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem’) is deliberate. Paul’s Jerusalem journey is the Lukan parallel to the Passion narrative. The phrase ‘breaking my heart’ (synthryptontes mou tēn kardian) is vivid: you are crushing my heart. Paul’s resolve is not coldness but the costlier form of love.

notes.original: aite ho laos boon — the crowd of people was crying out
notes.rendering: the mob of the people follows, crying out, ‘Away with him!’
notes.why: Aire — take away, lift up, remove (the same word in Luke 23:18 at Jesus’ trial: ‘Away with this man, release to us Barabbas’). The verbal echo is structural: Paul before the crowd in Jerusalem parallels Jesus before the crowd. Luke is showing the reader that the pattern of rejection and custody is not unique to Paul but follows the path of the one whose name he carries.

intro: Acts 22 is the second of Paul’s three conversion accounts and the most personally inflected — delivered in Aramaic, from the temple steps, to the Jerusalem crowd that has just tried to kill him. The speech is an act of identification: Paul presents himself as one of them, formed in their tradition, zealous as they are, before recounting the encounter that reoriented everything. It fails, as Jesus predicted it would (v. 18).

notes.original: bebaideumēs para tous podas Gamaliel — educated at the feet of Gamaliel
notes.rendering: educated at the feet of Gamaliel
notes.why: Para tous podas — at the feet of (a rabbinic idiom for discipleship; students sat at the feet of the teacher). Gamaliel was the leading Pharisaic scholar of the first century, grandson of Hillel and the one who argued for restraint toward the apostles in 5:34–39. Paul claims the best credentials available: born a diaspora Jew, raised in Jerusalem, trained by the finest teacher of the age, zealous to the point of violence. His encounter with the risen Jesus is thus not the conversion of a pagan but the reorientation of a devout insider.

notes.original: baptisai kai apolousai tas hamartias sou epikalesamenos to onoma autou — be baptized and wash away your sins calling on his name
notes.rendering: Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name
notes.why: The verb apolousai — wash away (from apolouomai — to wash off, to cleanse completely) is used only here and in 1 Corinthians 6:11 in the NT. The combination of baptism and calling on the name echoes the programmatic statement of 2:21 (everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved) and 2:38 (be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins). The conversion account is a compressed gospel in miniature.

notes.original: egō pollou kephalaou tēn politeian tautēn ektqsāmēn — I acquired this citizenship for a large sum
notes.rendering: I bought this citizenship for a large sum” — “But I am a citizen by birth
notes.why: The Roman citizenship is a narrative device Luke uses three times (16:37–39; 22:25–29; 25:10–12) to move Paul through the Roman legal system toward Rome. The tribune bought his citizenship — possibly under Claudius when citizenship was commercially available. Paul’s birth citizenship (likely from Tarsus, a civitas libera) outranks it. The detail establishes Paul’s legal standing and complicates the Roman authorities’ attempts to dispose of him informally.

intro: Acts 23 moves Paul from the Jerusalem Sanhedrin to Roman custody in Caesarea. The chapter contains the most important divine word of the entire final section (v. 11 — ‘you must testify also in Rome’) and one of its most human details (Paul’s nephew overhears the assassination plot). The Lord’s promise of v. 11 functions as the theological guarantee that Paul will reach Rome regardless of what his enemies plan.

notes.original: peri elpidos kai anastaseōs nekrōn egō krinoma — concerning hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged
notes.rendering: It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial
notes.why: The tactical brilliance of the statement is obvious: Paul divides the council by appealing to the Pharisee–Sadducee fault line. But the theological content is also genuine: the resurrection of Jesus is indeed the fulcrum of Paul’s entire mission. Elpis — hope: not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in what God has already done. The hope of the resurrection was Israel’s hope before it was Paul’s; he insists he is on trial for believing what every Pharisee believes.

notes.original: tharsei — take courage
notes.rendering: Take courage, for as you have testified … in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome
notes.why: Tharsei — take courage, be of good cheer (from tharsoō — to be bold, to have confidence; Jesus uses the same word at key moments in the Gospels: Matt 9:2, 22; Mark 10:49; John 16:33). The Lord’s appearance at this precise moment — after the Sanhedrin fiasco — is the narrative’s hinge. Paul’s arrival in Rome is no longer a mission plan but a divine appointment. The dei — must — of verse 11 is the language of divine necessity used throughout Luke–Acts.

notes.original: ho hyios tēs adelphqs Paulou — the son of Paul’s sister
notes.rendering: the son of Paul’s sister hears of their ambush
notes.why: The single reference to Paul’s family in Acts — and it is a family member who saves his life. The nephew is unnamed, his age unclear (the Greek could support ‘young man’ or simply ‘the boy’). Luke’s narrative never tells us how the nephew learned of the plot. The detail is reported with the matter-of-fact texture of eyewitness recollection — a person remembered precisely because he was there and it mattered.

intro: Acts 24 is a formal legal hearing in which Paul defends the Way as the authentic continuation of Israel’s hope. The contrast between Tertullus’s flattery and Paul’s direct speech is pointed. Felix’s alarm at Paul’s words about righteousness and judgement (v. 25) is one of the most telling moments in the trial narratives: the gospel reaches the governor, and he refuses it for two years while hoping for a bribe.

notes.original: tēn hairesis tōn Nazōraiōn — the sect of the Nazarenes
notes.rendering: a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes
notes.why: Hairesis — sect, school, party (from haireo — to choose; the source of the English ‘heresy’, though in the first century it simply meant a distinct group with shared beliefs, like the Pharisees or Sadducees). Tertullus uses the charge structure of Roman law: sedition (stirring up riots), religious desecration (profaning the temple), and sectarian leadership. Paul will counter each charge precisely. The label ‘Nazarenes’ is the earliest external name for the Jesus movement in Acts.

notes.original: kata tēn hodon hēn legousin hairesin — according to the Way, which they call a sect
notes.rendering: according to the Way, which they call a sect
notes.why: Paul accepts the name ‘the Way’ but rejects the term ‘sect’ — or rather, he redefines it as the authentic continuation of Israel’s hope. His defence is that he believes everything in the Law and the Prophets — he is not a schismatic but a fulfilment. The resurrection of both just and unjust (v. 15) grounds his claim in a hope shared with the Pharisees. Felix’s knowledge of ‘the Way’ (v. 22) suggests the movement is well known enough to have reached Roman administrative circles.

notes.original: peri dikaiosynqs kai enkrateias kai tou krimatos tou mellontos — concerning righteousness and self-control and the coming judgement
notes.rendering: as he reasons about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgement, Felix is alarmed
notes.why: The three topics are precisely calibrated to Felix’s situation: righteousness (dikaiosynē — right conduct, justice) speaks to a governor infamous for corruption; enkrateia (self-control, continence) to his adulterous marriage to Drusilla (who had left her husband for him); and the coming judgement to his ultimate accountability. Felix’s alarm (emphobos — filled with fear) is the gospel doing exactly what it is supposed to do. His delay is the text’s tragic note.

intro: Acts 25 turns on two pivots: Paul’s appeal to Caesar (vv. 10–12), which locks in his trajectory to Rome, and Festus’s summary of the case to Agrippa (vv. 18–19), which provides the most concise Roman view of the entire dispute. Festus’s bafflement is revealing: he can find no legal charge, only a theological argument about a dead man whom Paul claims is alive.

notes.original: Kaisara epikaloumai — I appeal to Caesar
notes.rendering: I appeal to Caesar
notes.why: Epikaleō — to call upon, to appeal to (from epi — upon; kaleō — to call). The appeal to Caesar (provocatio ad Caesarem) was a formal Roman legal procedure available to Roman citizens threatened with irregular provincial jurisdiction. It transferred the case to Rome and placed the defendant under imperial protection in transit. Luke presents the appeal as Paul’s own decision — not a panic response but a deliberate move toward the city he has been told he must reach (23:11).

notes.original: peri tinos Iēsou tethnēkotos hon ephesken ho Paulos zēn — about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul claimed to be alive
notes.rendering: a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive
notes.why: Festus’s summary is the most economical statement of the gospel’s central claim in Acts, and it comes from an unbeliever. Tethnēkotos — who had died (perfect participle — a completed and permanent state). Zēn — to be alive (present infinitive — ongoing life). The contrast between the perfect and present tenses is exact: the death is a historical fact; the life is a present claim. Festus’s confusion (‘at a loss’, v. 20) is the honest response of Roman empiricism to a resurrection.

notes.original: peri hou asphalēs ti graphai tō kyriō ouk echō — concerning whom I have nothing definite to write to my lord
notes.rendering: I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him
notes.why: The irony is complete: Paul has been in Roman custody for two years (24:27), has appeared before three governors, and not one of them has found a charge worth writing down. Luke’s forensic narrative is building to an implicit verdict — the same verdict Pilate gave before three hearings of Jesus (‘I find no fault in him’). The prisoner is innocent; the system cannot say so; and so it sends him to the emperor.

intro: Acts 26 contains the fullest and most theologically developed of the three conversion accounts. Speaking before a king who knows the prophets, Paul places his experience within Israel’s entire story and declares the resurrection of the Messiah as its fulfilment. Agrippa’s near-persuasion (v. 28) and the final verdict (v. 31 — this man is innocent) close the forensic sequence. The prisoner is innocent; the empire cannot release him; and Rome awaits.

notes.original: sklqron soi pros kentra laktizein — hard for you to kick against the goads
notes.rendering: It is hard for you to kick against the goads
notes.why: The proverb appears only in this account of the conversion (not in ch. 9 or 22). Kentron — goad, spike (an ox-goad used to direct stubborn animals). The image is of an animal kicking against the spike that prods it — only injuring itself. The Greek proverb was well known (Euripides, Pindar, Aeschylus). Its presence in the Hebrew-language speech to Paul (v. 14) may be Luke’s literary choice. Either way it suggests that Paul’s persecution was itself a form of resistance to a divine call already at work in him.

notes.original: tou epistrepsai apo skotous eis phōs — to turn them from darkness to light
notes.rendering: to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God
notes.why: The commission is the most comprehensive statement of the Gentile mission in Acts. Four movements: darkness to light (illumination), power of Satan to God (liberation), forgiveness of sins (justification), a place among the sanctified (incorporation). The language echoes Isaiah’s servant songs (42:6–7; 49:6) and frames Paul’s ministry as the fulfilment of Israel’s calling to be a light to the nations — the same text cited in 13:47.

notes.original: en oligo me peitheis Christianon poiēsai — in a little you persuade me to make a Christian
notes.rendering: In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?
