The New Testament will use the same structure: liberation (redemption through Christ) precedes belonging (adoption as children of God) precedes inheritance (the promised new creation).

Note on the genealogy of Exodus 6:14–27 and its placement: The genealogy interrupts the narrative at an apparently awkward moment — between Moses’ commission (6:13) and its renewal (6:28–30). Its purpose is to anchor Moses and Aaron firmly in the covenant family of Israel before the plagues begin: they are Levites, descendants of Levi through Kohath through Amram, the same family as Abraham’s covenant. The genealogy also plants seeds for later narrative: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu will die offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10); Eleazar and Phinehas will lead the priesthood forward. The genealogy is not interruption but grounding: before the signs and wonders begin, the narrator makes sure the reader knows exactly who Moses and Aaron are and where they come from.

intro: Exodus 7 opens the plague sequence with the formal commissioning statement (YHWH has made Moses like God to Pharaoh) and the first two signs: the staff-serpent and the blood of the Nile. The chapter establishes the narrative pattern that will govern all ten plagues, and the first plague strikes at the most sacred resource in Egypt.

notes.original: r’eh n’tatticha Elohim l’Phar’oh
notes.rendering: I have made you like God to Pharaoh
notes.why: YHWH does not say Moses is God but that he is k’Elohim — like God, as God, in the position of God — to Pharaoh. In the ancient Near Eastern view, the king was a mediator between the divine and human realms; Pharaoh himself was considered divine. YHWH now appoints Moses as the divine figure in this encounter, with Aaron as his prophet (navi). The reversal is deliberate: the man Pharaoh dismissed as a shepherd from the wilderness stands before him as the representative of the only God who matters. The language of prophet and spokesperson mirrors the relationship between God and the human messenger throughout the prophetic literature.

notes.original: v’harb’iti et-ototai v’et-moft’ai
notes.rendering: though I multiply my signs and wonders
notes.why: Otot (signs) and moftim (wonders, portents) are the two standard Hebrew terms for the Exodus plagues throughout Deuteronomy and the Psalms (e.g. Deuteronomy 4:34; Psalm 78:43; 105:27). Signs (otot) point to a meaning beyond themselves — they signify who YHWH is. Wonders (moftim) are events that produce awe and astonishment. Together they describe acts that both communicate and overwhelm. The plagues are not random catastrophes; they are a sustained theological argument addressed to Pharaoh, to Egypt, to Israel, and to all nations: this is who YHWH is.

notes.original: v’yad’u Mitzrayim ki ani YHWH
notes.rendering: the Egyptians shall know that I am YHWH
notes.why: The knowledge formula — ‘they shall know that I am YHWH’ — is the theological purpose statement of the plague narrative. It appears throughout chapters 7–14 with both Egypt and Israel as the subject: Egypt will know (7:5; 14:4, 18), Pharaoh will know (7:17; 8:10, 22; 9:14), the Israelites will know (6:7; 10:2), and all the earth will know (9:14). Pharaoh asked: ‘who is YHWH?’ (5:2). The plagues are the answer, addressed systematically to the most powerful empire in the world.

notes.original: vayivla mateh Aharon et-matotan
notes.rendering: Aaron’s staff swallows up their staffs
notes.why: Bala means to swallow, to devour, to engulf. The magicians can replicate the sign — their staffs also become serpents. But Aaron’s staff swallows theirs. The sign itself interprets the contest: one power swallows all the others. The magicians’ ability to replicate the sign is not dismissed; it is acknowledged and then exceeded. This pattern — magicians can do this but not that — will structure the plague narrative through the third plague, after which the magicians declare: ‘This is the finger of God’ (8:19).

notes.original: b’zot teida ki ani YHWH
notes.rendering: By this you shall know that I am YHWH
notes.why: The knowledge formula directed specifically at Pharaoh. Each plague contains an announcement of its purpose: not merely to punish but to make known. The Nile turning to blood is not ecological catastrophe for its own sake; it is a word addressed to Pharaoh: you will know who YHWH is. The Nile was the lifeblood of Egypt, the source of its agricultural abundance, and the object of religious veneration (the Nile god Hapi was among the most important in the Egyptian pantheon). Striking the Nile is striking Egypt’s source of life and its object of worship simultaneously.

notes.original: v’lo shat libbo gam l’zot
notes.rendering: he does not take even this to heart
notes.why: Lo shat libbo — he does not set his heart to this, he pays no attention even to this. The phrase ‘set the heart’ (sum lev / shet lev) means to pay attention, to take seriously, to be moved by. Pharaoh’s failure is not ignorance but inattention: he turns and goes into his house. The plague has happened; the fish are dead; the Nile stinks; all Egypt is digging for water. And Pharaoh turns his back. The hardening of the heart is not always a dramatic supernatural act; sometimes it is simply a man choosing not to look at what is in front of him.

outro: Note on the plague narrative structure: Each plague follows a consistent pattern, though with variations that signal different levels of intensity. Most plagues include: (1) a divine commission to Moses and/or Aaron; (2) a warning to Pharaoh (some plagues have no warning: 1, 5, 6, 9, 10); (3) the execution of the plague; (4) Pharaoh’s response (hardening, negotiation, or capitulation); (5) the removal of the plague (for most plagues). The repetition is not narrative laziness; it is the steady drumbeat of escalating divine pressure on an increasingly stubborn opponent. Each cycle demonstrates the same theological reality — YHWH is sovereign, Pharaoh is not — with increasing intensity.

intro: Exodus 8 contains plagues two through four — frogs, gnats, and flies. Three decisive moments mark the chapter’s theological movement: the magicians fail for the first time (gnats), the magicians declare ‘this is the finger of God,’ and Goshen is set apart from Egypt for the first time, drawing a visible line between YHWH’s people and the rest.

notes.original: hitpa’er alai l’matai e’tar lecha
notes.rendering: This honour is yours — tell me when
notes.why: Hitpa’er alai is one of the most unusual phrases in the plague narrative: ‘glorify yourself over me,’ ‘have the distinction over me,’ or as rendered here, ‘this honour is yours.’ Moses is offering Pharaoh the extraordinary privilege of naming the time for the removal of the frogs. It is simultaneously an act of generosity and a demonstration of confidence: Moses can set any time Pharaoh names because YHWH will keep it exactly. Pharaoh says: tomorrow. The frogs could be gone today, immediately, right now — but Pharaoh says tomorrow. Commentators have long puzzled over this: why not say ‘now’? Perhaps Pharaoh was testing whether the removal would actually happen. He would spend one more night with the frogs to see if Moses was bluffing.

notes.original: vayachbed libbo… kira’at harevachah
notes.rendering: he hardens his heart… when he sees that there is a respite
notes.why: Chazaq — he makes his heart heavy, he hardens. The respite (revachah — relief, space to breathe, breathing room) is what undoes the negotiation. When the pressure is on, Pharaoh negotiates. When the pressure lifts, he hardens. The cycle is the anatomy of a particular kind of resistance: not the resistance of someone who doesn’t believe, but the resistance of someone who believes but refuses to let the belief change them. Pharaoh knows what is happening. He asks Moses to pray to YHWH. He just doesn’t follow through when the crisis passes.

notes.original: etzba Elohim hi
notes.rendering: This is the finger of God
notes.why: The magicians’ declaration is the turning point of the contest between YHWH’s representatives and Egypt’s. They have replicated the blood and the frogs; they cannot replicate the gnats. Their recognition — ‘this is the finger of God’ — is the most remarkable acknowledgment in the plague narrative: Egypt’s own magicians concede that what is happening is divine. Etzba Elohim (finger of God) appears one other time in the Exodus: the tablets of stone at Sinai are written with the finger of God (31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10). The same divine finger that writes the law drives the plague. Jesus uses the same phrase in Luke 11:20 (‘if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons’), connecting his ministry to the Exodus.

notes.original: v’hifleti… et-eretz Goshen… l’vilti heyot sham arov
notes.rendering: I will set apart the land of Goshen… no swarms of flies shall be there
notes.why: Hifleti comes from palah (to separate, to distinguish, to make wonderful) — the same root as pele (wonder, miracle). YHWH will make a distinction, a marvel of separation, between his people and Egypt. From the fourth plague onward, the plagues fall only on Egypt and not on Goshen. The separation is the theological escalation of the plague narrative: YHWH is not merely showing power; YHWH is showing that his power is specifically exercised on behalf of his people and against their oppressors. The distinction between Goshen and Egypt is the visible, geographical proof that these events are not random disasters but targeted divine acts.

notes.original: al yosef Phar’oh hatel’l l’vilti shalach et-ha’am
notes.rendering: let not Pharaoh cheat again
notes.why: Moses names Pharaoh’s pattern explicitly: do not act deceitfully again by not letting the people go. Hatel from talal — to deceive, to mock, to deal falsely. Moses has watched Pharaoh negotiate and renege through the frogs. He names the pattern before it repeats. The naming does not stop it — Pharaoh hardens his heart again in v.32 — but it establishes that the cycle of promise-and-reneging is recognized, named, and will be answered.

intro: Exodus 9 contains three plagues in escalating intensity: livestock, boils, and hail. The hail plague is the most dramatic so far and contains the most theologically significant speech of the plague sequence — YHWH’s declaration that Pharaoh has been raised up for a purpose, and that purpose is the proclamation of the divine name throughout the earth.

notes.original: vayishla Phar’oh v’hineh lo met… vayichbed lev Phar’oh
notes.rendering: Pharaoh sends… not one is dead… the heart of Pharaoh is hardened
notes.why: The sequence is devastating in its compression. Pharaoh is skeptical enough to check: he sends someone to verify whether the Israelite livestock have actually been spared. They have. Every single animal of Israel is alive; every Egyptian animal is dead. The evidence is total and unambiguous. And Pharaoh hardens his heart. This is the most explicit example in the plague narrative of hardening as a chosen response to clear evidence. He sees the proof; he refuses to let it move him. The hardening is not confusion or ignorance; it is decision in the face of evidence.

notes.original: vay’chazzeq YHWH et-lev Phar’oh
notes.rendering: YHWH hardens the heart of Pharaoh
notes.why: The sixth plague marks the first explicit statement that YHWH (not Pharaoh himself) hardens the heart. In the earlier plagues, Pharaoh hardens his own heart (7:22; 8:15, 19, 32; 9:7). Now YHWH hardens it. Scholars debate whether this represents a theological shift (YHWH taking over a process Pharaoh started) or simply two descriptions of the same reality (Pharaoh chooses; YHWH works through and beyond that choice). Paul’s use of this passage in Romans 9:17–18 focuses on the divine sovereignty: God hardens whom he wills. The biblical tension — Pharaoh chooses, YHWH acts — is maintained throughout without resolution.

notes.original: uv’avur zot he’emadticha… l’ma’an sapp’r sh’mi b’chol ha’aretz
notes.rendering: But for this purpose I have raised you up… so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth
notes.why: He’emadticha — I have caused you to stand, I have raised you up, I have set you in place. The declaration is stunning in its scope: YHWH has placed Pharaoh in his position of power precisely so that the confrontation of the Exodus could happen and YHWH’s name could be proclaimed throughout the whole earth. The hardened heart of Pharaoh is not a failure of divine communication; it is an instrument of divine revelation. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17 as a demonstration of divine sovereignty over human history. The proclamation of YHWH’s name ‘in all the earth’ is what the plagues are ultimately for.

notes.original: hayare’ et-d’var YHWH… asher lo sam libbo el-d’var YHWH
notes.rendering: whoever fears the word of YHWH… whoever does not take the word of YHWH to heart
notes.why: The hail plague introduces a division within Egypt itself: those among Pharaoh’s servants who fear the word of YHWH bring their livestock to safety; those who do not leave them in the field. The plague is not indiscriminate; it falls on those who have not heeded the warning. The fear of YHWH (yir’at YHWH — the same quality that drove the midwives of Exodus 1 to defy Pharaoh) is now visible even among Egyptians. The plagues are creating a new moral geography: the dividing line is no longer between Israelite and Egyptian but between those who heed YHWH’s word and those who do not.

notes.original: chatati hapa’am… YHWH hatzaddiq
notes.rendering: I have sinned this time… YHWH is in the right
notes.why: Pharaoh’s confession is the most explicit in the plague narrative. Chatati (I have sinned) — the same root as chatat, sin, the crouching creature at Cain’s door. YHWH hatzaddiq — YHWH is righteous, YHWH is in the right. And: ani v’ammi har’sha’im — I and my people are wicked, in the wrong. The confession sounds complete. But Moses’ response (v.30) identifies what is missing: ‘I know that you do not yet fear YHWH God.’ The words are right; the fear is absent. Pharaoh can say the right things about YHWH without actually fearing him. The confession is real but not transforming.

notes.original: ki l’YHWH ha’aretz
notes.rendering: the earth is YHWH’s
notes.why: Moses’ declaration to Pharaoh as he goes out to pray for the removal of the hail: the earth is YHWH’s. This is the theological summary of the hail plague and, by extension, of the entire plague sequence. Egypt is not Pharaoh’s; the Nile is not Hapi’s; the land is not under the authority of Egyptian gods or Egyptian kings. The earth belongs to YHWH. The Psalmist will quote this confession in Psalm 24:1 (‘The earth is YHWH’s and everything in it’). Moses says it to Pharaoh in the middle of a plague, as a statement of the reality that the plagues are demonstrating.

outro: Note on the theological purpose of the plague narrative: The plagues are commonly understood as punishment, and they are. But the text consistently frames them as something more specific: revelation. The repeated purpose statement — ‘that you/they may know that I am YHWH’ — identifies the plagues as a sustained act of divine self-disclosure. YHWH is making himself known to Egypt, to Israel, and through both of them to all nations. The method is not theological argument or prophetic preaching but enacted power: events that cannot be explained by any framework except the sovereignty of YHWH. The proclamation of YHWH’s name ‘in all the earth’ (9:16) is achieved not through Israel’s witness but through Pharaoh’s resistance — the very hardness of Pharaoh’s heart becomes the instrument by which YHWH’s power is most fully displayed.

Note on the magicians and their progressive defeat: The magicians of Egypt are significant not because they are villains but because they are the measure of the contest. Through the first two plagues (blood, frogs) they replicate YHWH’s signs. At the third plague (gnats) they fail for the first time and declare ‘this is the finger of God.’ At the sixth plague (boils) they cannot even appear before Moses — they are themselves afflicted. By the seventh plague (hail) they are never mentioned again. Their progressive incapacitation maps the progressive demonstration of YHWH’s sovereignty over everything Egypt’s wisdom and power can produce. What begins as a contest ends as a concession, plague by plague.

intro: Exodus 10 introduces a new theological purpose for the plagues: not only that Egypt and Pharaoh may know YHWH, but that Israel will tell the story to their children and grandchildren across every generation (10:2). The plague narrative is being written into the memory of a people before it is finished. And the chapter ends with the final rupture: Pharaoh dismisses Moses with a death threat, and Moses accepts the finality.

notes.original: ul’ma’an t’sapper b’oznei vincha uven-bincha
notes.rendering: that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson
notes.why: The intergenerational transmission of the Exodus memory is introduced here, before the Exodus has happened, as one of its explicit purposes. YHWH is not only acting for Israel in Egypt; he is creating a story that will be told across generations. The same language of transmission — telling to sons, to grandsons — will structure the Passover Haggadah’s four questions: ‘Why is this night different?’ The liturgical obligation to retell the Exodus is built into the Exodus itself. The event and its annual retelling are both part of YHWH’s purpose.

notes.original: ad matai me’anta l’hikanea mippanai
notes.rendering: How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?
notes.why: Hikanea — to humble oneself, to be brought low, to submit. The question ‘how long?’ (ad matai) is a lament form found throughout the Psalms (Psalm 6:3; 13:1–2; 35:17; 79:5; 80:4; 89:46; 90:13). YHWH uses the lament form to address Pharaoh — as if the Creator is genuinely aggrieved by the stubbornness, as if Pharaoh’s refusal to humble himself is something that costs YHWH something. The question has an answer embedded in it: you will humble yourself; the only question is when.

notes.original: hal’teda ki avedat Mitzrayim
notes.rendering: Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?
notes.why: Pharaoh’s own servants make the theological declaration the narrative has been building toward: Egypt is ruined (avad Mitzrayim — Egypt has perished, Egypt is destroyed). The word avad — to perish, to be lost, to be destroyed — is the same word used for the perishing of the wicked throughout the Psalms and Proverbs. The servants see what Pharaoh refuses to see: the contest is over. The only question is how much more damage Pharaoh’s hardness will cause before he finally concedes. Their intervention produces the partial negotiation of v.8–11 — but Moses will not accept partial liberation.

notes.original: choshech asher yimmashesh
notes.rendering: darkness to be felt
notes.why: Choshech asher yimmashesh — darkness that can be felt, darkness that gropes, palpable darkness. The verb mashash means to feel about, to grope in the dark, to search by touch. The darkness of the ninth plague is not merely the absence of light but a physical presence — thick, tangible, suffocating. Three days of it. The Egyptians cannot see each other; no one rises from their place. Meanwhile: all the people of Israel had light where they lived (orot haya l’vnei Yisra’el b’moshvotam). The separation of light and darkness in the ninth plague echoes the first act of creation (Genesis 1:3–4): YHWH separates light from darkness; here YHWH separates Israel’s light from Egypt’s darkness.

notes.original: l’ch me’alay… b’yom r’ot’cha fanai tamut… ken dibbarta
notes.rendering: Get away from me… you shall die… As you say
notes.why: The final exchange between Moses and Pharaoh before the tenth plague is a formal severing. Pharaoh’s threat — on the day you see my face you shall die — is met by Moses’ calm acceptance: as you say, I will not see your face again. The confrontation that began at the burning bush has reached its terminus. Moses will not return to Pharaoh again until the night of the tenth plague, when Pharaoh summons him (12:31). The prophecy that Moses will not see Pharaoh’s face — said by Pharaoh as a threat — turns out to be exactly true, but in the opposite direction from what Pharaoh intended: it is Pharaoh who will be broken, not Moses.

intro: Exodus 11 is a brief chapter — only ten verses — but it carries enormous weight. It is the announcement of the tenth plague, delivered in the same moment that Moses breaks off negotiations with Pharaoh in hot anger. The chapter is both ending and beginning: the ending of the plague negotiations, the beginning of the final act.

notes.original: shalach yish’lach etchem mizzeh k’lah garshe’sh y’garesh etchem mizzeh
notes.rendering: he will let you go… he will surely drive you out
notes.why: The double verb is emphatic: shalach yish’lach (sending he will send) and garosh y’garosh (driving he will drive out). Pharaoh will not merely permit Israel to leave; he will expel them, push them out, desperate for them to be gone. The same verb garash (to drive out, to expel) was used of Adam and Eve being driven out of the garden (Genesis 3:24). The expulsion from Egypt reverses the expulsion from Eden: Israel is driven out into a wilderness that will become the site of the covenant, moving toward the land of promise rather than away from the land of blessing.

notes.original: hagadol m’od b’eretz Mitzrayim
notes.rendering: the man Moses is very great in the land of Egypt
notes.why: The narrator’s aside about Moses’ stature is unexpected and significant. The man who began by saying ‘I am not a man of words’ (4:10), who described himself as having uncircumcised lips (6:12), has become gadol me’od — very great — in the sight of Pharaoh’s servants and all the people. Pharaoh’s question ‘who is YHWH?’ (5:2) has been answered in part by watching what YHWH does through his representative. The servant’s greatness reflects the master’s.

notes.original: mikol b’chor b’eretz Mitzrayim yamut
notes.rendering: every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die
notes.why: The scope of the tenth plague is total and symmetrical. From the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the slave girl at the handmill — the range spans from the highest to the lowest in Egyptian society, including the livestock. The announcement echoes the earlier declaration of 4:22–23: Israel is my firstborn; you refused to let him go; your firstborn will die. The tenth plague is the fulfillment of the covenant warning given before the first plague began.

notes.original: ul’chol b’nei Yisra’el lo yecheratz kelev l’shono
notes.rendering: not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel
notes.why: Yecheratz — shall sharpen, shall whet — used of a dog sharpening its tongue against someone, i.e., growling or barking. The image is precise and slightly comic in its contrast: in Egypt every firstborn from the palace to the mill will die and a great cry will go up from every house; but among Israel not even a dog will bark. The distinction between Egypt and Israel will be so complete that even the ambient sounds will be different: screaming in Egypt, silence in Goshen. The contrast between the great cry of Egypt and the silence of Israel is the completion of the separation that began with the flies.

notes.original: vayetzeh me’et Phar’oh b’chori-af
notes.rendering: he goes out from Pharaoh in hot anger
notes.why: Chori-af — the burning of anger, hot wrath. Moses leaves Pharaoh’s presence in anger. This is the only place in the plague narrative where Moses’ own emotional state is described. He has delivered the announcement of the final plague and listened to Pharaoh’s dismissal; he has watched nine plagues cycle through announcement, execution, negotiation, and reneging; he has heard Pharaoh say ‘go, you shall die.’ He goes out angry. The anger is not inappropriate; it is the anger of a man of God who has watched sustained injustice and sustained refusal to respond to overwhelming evidence. Moses is human throughout the Exodus, and the anger at the end of chapter 11 is the most human moment yet.

outro: Note on the structure of the ten plagues: The ten plagues are conventionally grouped in three sets of three plus one. The first three (blood, frogs, gnats) are performed by Aaron’s staff without prior warning to Pharaoh for the last one. The second set of three (flies, livestock, boils) introduces the distinction between Goshen and Egypt from the first plague of the set. The third set of three (hail, locusts, darkness) escalates in cosmic scale. The tenth plague (death of the firstborn) stands alone as the culmination, announced before the Passover instructions are given. The structure is deliberate: each group of three pushes the demonstration of YHWH’s sovereignty into a new domain — water, living creatures, the land itself, animals, human bodies, light, agricultural fertility, and finally life itself.

intro: Exodus 12 is the most liturgically dense chapter in the Book of Exodus. Before the tenth plague falls, before Israel leaves Egypt, YHWH interrupts the narrative to establish the Passover as a permanent annual feast. The event and its ritual re-enactment are given equal space — the narrative insists that what happens this night must be repeated every year, forever, in every generation. The structure of the chapter enacts its own theology: the instruction comes before the event, because the meaning of the event is established before it occurs.

notes.original: hachodesh hazeh lachem rosh chadashim
notes.rendering: This month shall be for you the beginning of months
notes.why: The first commandment given to Israel as a people is a commandment about time: this month is now the first month. The Exodus resets the calendar. Israel’s year will now begin from the month of the Passover — not from the agricultural new year or the Babylonian cosmological new year but from the month of liberation. The reorientation of time is the first act of covenant formation: before the lamb is selected, before the blood is applied, YHWH remakes Israel’s relationship with time itself. Every year thereafter begins with the memory of this night.

notes.original: v’achaltem oto b’chipazon Pesach hu laYHWH
notes.rendering: You shall eat it in haste. It is YHWH’s Passover.
notes.why: Chipazon means haste, urgency, the speed of someone who cannot wait. The posture of eating — belted, sandalled, staff in hand, eating in haste — enacts the urgency of departure. The meal is eaten as if already leaving. The word Pesach (Passover) appears here for the first time in the text, immediately after the instruction about haste. Pesach comes from pasach — to pass over, to skip over, to spare. YHWH’s passing over (pesach) of the marked houses is the act from which the feast takes its name. It is YHWH’s Passover — not Israel’s; YHWH’s act of protection defines the feast that will remember it.

notes.original: uv’chol elohei Mitzrayim e’eseh sh’fatim
notes.rendering: on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments
notes.why: The ten plagues are implicitly addressed to the gods of Egypt throughout the plague narrative; here it is made explicit. Each plague targeted a domain over which an Egyptian deity claimed sovereignty: the Nile (Hapi), the frog (Heqet), the sun (Ra), the livestock (Hathor and Apis), and so on. The tenth plague — the death of the firstborn, including the firstborn of Pharaoh who was himself considered divine — is the judgment on the divine status of Pharaoh himself. YHWH does not merely overpower Egypt; YHWH demonstrates the nullity of Egypt’s entire divine order. The Exodus is a theological polemic in the form of a historical event.

notes.original: ur’iti et-hadam ufasachti aleichem
notes.rendering: when I see the blood, I will pass over you
notes.why: The blood is a sign — lachem l’ot (for you, a sign). The blood does not protect by its own power; it is a sign that YHWH recognises. YHWH sees the blood and passes over. The act of applying the blood to the doorposts is an act of faith — trusting that the sign YHWH has appointed will be honoured. The hyssop used to apply the blood (v.22) is the same plant used in purification rites (Leviticus 14:4, 6, 51; Numbers 19:6, 18; Psalm 51:7). The blood that protects is associated from the beginning with purification and cleansing.

notes.original: mah ha’avodah hazot lachem… zevach Pesach hu laYHWH
notes.rendering: What do you mean by this service?”… ‘It is the sacrifice of YHWH’s Passover’
notes.why: The question-and-answer format of the child asking and the parent explaining is built into the Passover rite before the first Passover has even occurred. The intergenerational transmission mentioned in 10:2 is now given its liturgical form: the child’s question, the parent’s answer, the story retold. This catechetical structure — question, answer, explanation of the rite — is the prototype of the Passover Haggadah, which has structured Jewish observance of Passover for at least two thousand years. The feast exists, in part, to generate the question.

notes.original: v’gam erev rav alah ittam
notes.rendering: A mixed multitude also goes up with them
notes.why: Erev rav — a mixed multitude, a great mixture. The Exodus is not exclusively ethnic. A large and diverse group leaves Egypt with Israel. The identity of this erev rav is not specified; they may be other Semitic peoples who had been enslaved alongside Israel, or Egyptians who had come to fear YHWH (as some of Pharaoh’s servants did in 9:20), or people of various national origins. The Passover regulations of vv.43–49 address their inclusion: the foreigner who is circumcised may participate; the law is one for native and sojourner alike. The Exodus creates a mixed community from its first night.

notes.original: leil shimmurim hu laYHWH
notes.rendering: a night of watching kept to YHWH
notes.why: Leil shimmurim — a night of vigils, a night of watching. The root shamar (to watch, to keep, to guard) is used twice: YHWH watched over Israel that night; Israel watches in every subsequent generation to commemorate it. The night is kept (shamar) just as the Passover statute is kept (shamar, vv.24–25). The same verb of covenant-keeping describes YHWH’s protection and Israel’s memorial. The night that YHWH guarded is the night Israel guards in memory across all generations.

outro: Note on the Passover as re-enacted history: Exodus 12 establishes a pattern that runs through all subsequent Jewish and Christian liturgy: the present worshipper participates in the past event. The Passover is not merely a commemoration of what happened in Egypt; it is a re-enactment in which each generation eats the lamb as if they themselves are about to leave Egypt. The Mishnah (Pesachim 10:5) makes this explicit: ‘In every generation a person is obligated to see himself as if he personally left Egypt.’ The meal is structured to produce identification with the original participants, not merely memory of them. This pattern — enacted participation in a constitutive historical event — is the liturgical logic of the Eucharist as well (do this in remembrance of me, Luke 22:19), which Jesus institutes explicitly in the context of a Passover meal.

Note on the 430 years (12:40–41): The 430 years of Israel’s sojourn in Egypt (counting from Jacob’s descent) is stated with unusual precision: ‘on that very day’ (b’etzem hayom hazeh) all the hosts of YHWH went out. The same phrase ‘on that very day’ was used of the flood (Genesis 7:13) and of Abraham’s circumcision (Genesis 17:23). It marks an event of absolute, divinely appointed precision: the Exodus happens on exactly the day it was determined to happen, to the day. Paul uses the 430 years in Galatians 3:17 to argue that the law, given 430 years after Abraham’s covenant, cannot annul the promise made to Abraham. The precision of the number is the precision of the covenant.

intro: Exodus 13 is the chapter of transitions: from Egypt to the wilderness, from the Passover night to the ongoing life of the people, from the event to its memorialization in the body. The firstborn consecration connects the tenth plague to the life of Israel going forward. And the chapter ends with the most tangible expression of the divine presence in the entire Exodus: a pillar of cloud by day, a pillar of fire by night, that does not depart.

notes.original: qadesh-li chol-bechor
notes.rendering: Consecrate to me all the firstborn
notes.why: Qadash means to be holy, to be set apart for YHWH’s use. The consecration of the firstborn is the living extension of the tenth plague into Israel’s ongoing life: because YHWH spared Israel’s firstborn when Egypt’s died, every firstborn of Israel belongs to YHWH. The principle is not punitive but relational — the firstborn is the sign that the rest of the family is alive. To consecrate the firstborn is to acknowledge that all of life is a gift from the one who preserved it. The redemption price for firstborn sons (v.13) institutionalizes this acknowledgment as a recurring act rather than a one-time event.

notes.original: v’higgadta l’vincha bayom hahu
notes.rendering: You shall tell your son on that day
notes.why: Higgadta — you shall tell, you shall narrate, you shall make plain. The root nagad (to tell, to declare) is the word from which Haggadah derives: the telling of the Passover story. The command to tell the son on that day — the day of the feast, in the context of the unleavened bread, with the smell and taste of the rite in the air — is the template for all liturgical catechesis. The body does something; the child asks; the parent tells. Embodied practice creates the question; the story provides the answer.

notes.original: l’ot al-yadcha ul’zikaron bein einecha
notes.rendering: as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes
notes.why: The Exodus is to be worn on the body: a sign (ot) on the hand, a memorial (zikaron) between the eyes. Later Jewish interpretation understood this as the command to wear tefillin — the small leather boxes containing Torah passages bound to the hand and forehead during morning prayer. Whether the original command was intended literally or metaphorically, its force is the same: the memory of the Exodus is not merely in the mind; it is inscribed on the body, carried through life, visible in every act of the hand and every direction of the gaze.

notes.original: pen yinachem ha’am bir’otam milchamah v’shavu Mitzraimah
notes.rendering: Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt
notes.why: YHWH’s reason for the indirect route is pastoral: the people are not ready for the direct confrontation with the Philistines that the coastal road would bring. The wilderness route is longer, harder, and less obvious — but it is the route the people can survive spiritually, not only physically. God’s guidance takes into account not only the destination but the capacity of those being guided. The longer way is the way that preserves the people for the covenant they are about to receive.

notes.original: et-atzmot Yosef immo
notes.rendering: Moses takes the bones of Joseph with him
notes.why: Joseph’s dying words (Genesis 50:25) are being fulfilled: paqod yifqod Elohim — God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here. Moses carries the bones. The Exodus is not only the deliverance of the living; it is the completion of a promise made to the dead. Joseph’s bones travel through the wilderness, through the conquest, and are finally buried at Shechem (Joshua 24:32) — in the field Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor. The covenant that began with Abraham’s purchase of a burial cave reaches its completion when Joseph’s bones rest in the land.

notes.original: amud anan… amud esh… lo yamish
notes.rendering: pillar of cloud… pillar of fire… does not depart
notes.why: The pillars of cloud and fire are the most visible manifestation of the divine presence in the wilderness narratives. YHWH goes before them — not behind, not beside, but before, leading the way. The pillar does not depart (lo yamish — it does not remove itself, it does not leave its post). The divine presence is continuous, day and night, cloud and fire. The two forms serve the two necessities: shade and guidance by day, warmth and light by night. Both are YHWH. The pillar is not a symbol of YHWH’s presence; it is YHWH’s presence in the form that the wilderness journey requires.

outro: Note on the bones of Joseph as the thread connecting Genesis to Exodus: Moses carrying Joseph’s bones is one of the most quietly significant actions in the entire Exodus narrative. It takes a single verse (13:19) and has no dramatic weight in the immediate story — the bones travel in a container, presumably on a cart or a person’s back, unnamed and unremarked through the plagues, the crossing, the wilderness, the conquest. But those bones are the physical continuity between the promise made to Abraham in Genesis and the possession of the land that Joshua will complete. Joseph’s last act was to make Israel swear an oath; Moses’ act of picking up the bones at the Exodus is the oath’s beginning of fulfillment. The bones of the man who said ‘God will surely visit you’ travel through the visitation as evidence that the promise was always going to be kept.

intro: Exodus 14 is the crossing of the sea — the single most defining event in the Hebrew Bible’s understanding of salvation. The Exodus from Egypt is cited more than any other event in the Old Testament as the paradigm of divine deliverance. And at its centre is a moment of total impossibility: the sea ahead, the army behind, and the people crying out. YHWH’s answer is not to remove the obstacle but to walk Israel through it.

notes.original: v’nichbadti b’Phar’oh
notes.rendering: I will get glory over Pharaoh
notes.why: Nichbadti — I will be glorified, I will be honoured, I will get weight — from kavod (glory, weight, honour). The word kavod appears three times in chapters 14–15 as YHWH’s stated purpose: glory over Pharaoh (14:4, 17, 18). The crossing of the sea is not only a rescue; it is a revelation. YHWH’s glory — his weight, his reality, his character — is displayed by what happens to Pharaoh’s army. The Egyptians will know that YHWH is YHWH when the waters come back. The knowledge formula from the plague narrative reaches its climax here.

notes.original: uv’nei Yisra’el yotz’im b’yad ramah
notes.rendering: while the people of Israel are going out boldly
notes.why: B’yad ramah — with a raised hand, with a high hand, boldly, defiantly. The phrase describes the posture of people who leave without shame, without hiding, without the crouched urgency of fugitives. They walk out with their heads up, their arms raised, openly. The high hand is the opposite of the broken spirit of Exodus 6:9. Whatever was crushed in them by the slavery has been lifted by the Passover night. They leave with dignity.

notes.original: hityatzvu ur’u et-y’shu’at YHWH… YHWH yilachem lachem v’atem tacharishun
notes.rendering: Stand firm and see the salvation of YHWH… YHWH will fight for you, and you have only to be silent
notes.why: Moses’ words to the panicking people are among the most memorable in the Exodus: hityatzvu — take your stand, station yourselves, hold your ground. See (ur’u) the salvation YHWH will work today. The Egyptians you see today you will never see again. YHWH will fight for you. And you: be silent (tacharishun — from charash, to be still, to hold one’s peace). The silence is not passivity; it is the active posture of someone who has stopped trying to solve the problem themselves and is making space for YHWH to act. The salvation of YHWH is worked in the space Israel makes by standing still.

notes.original: mah-titz’aq elai dabber el-b’nei Yisra’el v’yisa’u
notes.rendering: Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward
notes.why: YHWH’s response to Moses’ prayer is startling: stop praying, start moving. The time for standing still has passed. Moses has told the people to stand still (v.13); YHWH tells Moses to tell them to move (v.15). The tension is not contradiction but sequence: stand still enough to trust, then move in the direction of the impossible. The sea is ahead. Go forward. The obedience of forward movement is itself the act of faith that opens the way.

notes.original: vayehi he’anan v’hachoshech vayaer et-halaylah
notes.rendering: there is the cloud and the darkness. And it lights up the night
notes.why: The pillar that was cloud by day and fire by night now serves a dual function simultaneously: it is darkness to the Egyptians (blocking their advance and their sight) and light to Israel (illuminating their crossing). The same pillar; two experiences. The divine presence that guides Israel is the divine presence that confounds Egypt. YHWH’s protection of Israel is YHWH’s opposition to those who threaten Israel — the same action experienced differently from either side of it.

notes.original: vayiru ha’am et-YHWH vaya’aminu b’YHWH uv’Moshe avdo
notes.rendering: the people fear YHWH, and they believe in YHWH and in his servant Moses
notes.why: The chapter ends with two verbs: yir’ah (fear) and emunah (belief, trust, faithfulness). The people who cried out in panic at the sight of Pharaoh’s chariots now fear YHWH. The people who said ‘it would have been better to serve the Egyptians’ now believe in YHWH. The sequence is important: they see the great hand YHWH used (v.31), then they fear, then they believe. Faith comes through seeing what YHWH does. The Song of the Sea that follows is the expression of that faith in full voice.

outro: Note on the crossing of the sea and its place in the biblical imagination: The crossing of the sea is the pivotal event of the entire Hebrew Bible. It is cited more than any other single act of God as the paradigm of divine salvation: the Psalms return to it again and again (Psalm 66:6; 77:16–20; 78:13; 106:9; 114:3, 5; 136:13–15), the prophets invoke it as the model for future redemption (Isaiah 43:2, 16–17; 51:10; 63:11–13; Ezekiel 20:33–38), and the New Testament reads the crossing as a type of baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). What happens at the sea is not merely a historical rescue; it establishes the grammar through which Israel will speak of salvation for the rest of its existence: YHWH makes a way through the impossible.

intro: Exodus 15 contains the Song of the Sea — Shirat HaYam — which is among the oldest extended poems in the Hebrew Bible and possibly in world literature. Its archaic vocabulary, its distinctive poetic structures, and its theological compression have made it one of the most studied texts in biblical scholarship. The chapter closes with the first post-Exodus complaint and the first direct divine self-identification as healer.

notes.original: ashirah l’YHWH ki ga’oh ga’ah
notes.rendering: I will sing to YHWH, for he has triumphed gloriously
notes.why: Ga’oh ga’ah is an emphatic infinitive absolute: he has triumphed triumphing, he has been gloriously exalted, he has risen high. The root ga’ah means to rise up, to be exalted, to be high — often used of the swelling of the sea (Psalm 46:3; Job 38:11). There is a deliberate irony: the word for YHWH’s triumph is the word for the sea’s swelling. The sea that was Israel’s enemy is now the medium of YHWH’s glory. The opening line is the thesis of the entire poem: YHWH is exalted; the horse and rider are in the sea.

notes.original: ozi v’zimrat Yah vayehi li lishu’ah
notes.rendering: YHWH is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation
notes.why: The word zimrat can mean song or strength — it is a crux of the text. Some read it as ‘my strength and my might’; others as ‘my strength and my song’ (the reading followed here and in most English versions). The phrase is quoted verbatim in Isaiah 12:2 and Psalm 118:14 — two of the most important salvation contexts in the Hebrew Bible. Yah is the short form of YHWH — appearing here for the first time in the Bible in its short form. The verse is the most compact expression of the theology of the Exodus: YHWH is the source of strength, the content of song, and the act of salvation all at once.

notes.original: YHWH ish milchamah YHWH sh’mo
notes.rendering: YHWH is a man of war; YHWH is his name
notes.why: Ish milchamah — a man of war, a warrior. The description of YHWH as a divine warrior is one of the most ancient theological categories in the Hebrew Bible and one of the most uncomfortable for modern readers. The Song of the Sea does not soften it: YHWH is the one who fights, who casts Pharaoh’s army into the sea, who shatters the enemy with his right hand. The warrior imagery is not primitive theology to be transcended; it is the theology of the oppressed who have been liberated by force when no other liberation was possible. Isaiah 42:13 and Isaiah 59:17 use the same warrior language for the eschatological redemption.

notes.original: b’ruach appecha n’ermu mayim
notes.rendering: At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up
notes.why: The blast of YHWH’s nostrils — the breath of divine anger, the wind-that-is-wrath — is the force that piled up the waters. The same word ruach (breath, wind, spirit) that hovered over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and drove back the sea at the crossing (14:21) appears here as the nostrils’ blast that makes the waters stand in a heap. Creation and Exodus share the same divine breath. The waters that covered the face of the deep in Genesis 1 stand in a wall at YHWH’s command in Exodus 15. The God of the crossing is the God of the creation.

notes.original: mi-chamocha ba’elim YHWH
notes.rendering: Who is like you, O YHWH, among the gods?
notes.why: Mi-chamocha — who is like you? The question is the theological heart of the poem and one of the most important rhetorical questions in the Hebrew Bible. It is not an assertion that other gods do not exist but that none of them compares to YHWH. Majestic in holiness (nedar baqodesh), awesome in glorious deeds (nora t’hillot), doing wonders (oseh fele). The three descriptors mark YHWH’s incomparability in three registers: character (holiness), history (glorious deeds), and act (wonders). The question will echo through the Psalms (Psalm 35:10; 71:19; 89:6, 8) and the prophets as the irreducible confession of Israel’s monotheism.

notes.original: nachita v’chasd’cha am-zu ga’alta
notes.rendering: You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed
notes.why: Chesed appears in the Song of the Sea: the steadfast love that was the framework of the Genesis covenant (Abraham’s servant praying for hesed in chapter 24, Joseph receiving hesed in prison in chapter 39) is now the mode of the Exodus guidance. YHWH does not lead Israel by power alone; he leads them in steadfast love. The redeemed people are the people of chesed — led by it, sustained by it. The poem moves here from the triumph at the sea (vv.1–12) to the future guidance toward the promised land (vv.13–17), suggesting that the chesed that brought them through the sea is the same chesed that will bring them into the land.

notes.original: Miryam han’vi’ah… vatiqach Miryam… vatasha r lah hem
notes.rendering: Miriam the prophetess… takes a tambourine… and Miriam sings to them
notes.why: Miriam is called han’vi’ah — the prophetess — making her one of the earliest named prophets in the Hebrew Bible. She takes a tof (tambourine, hand drum) and leads the women in dance and song. Her song is the opening couplet of Moses’ song — the thesis line — which she sings with the women as a response or refrain. The scene is the earliest description of communal worship in Israel: women, music, dance, and the words of the song that the men have already sung. Miriam’s tambourine and the women’s dancing are the community’s response to salvation. The Exodus ends in liturgy.

notes.original: YHWH rop’echa
notes.rendering: I am YHWH your healer
notes.why: YHWH Rop’echa — YHWH your healer. The divine name-formula ‘I am YHWH’ that drove the plague narrative (I am YHWH who strikes Egypt) is now applied to healing: I am YHWH who heals you. The same YHWH who executed judgment on Egypt will now heal Israel in the wilderness. The healing is conditional in the immediate context (if you listen, if you obey), but the name itself is unconditional: this is who YHWH is — not only warrior and liberator but healer. The wilderness will test that name at every complaint and crisis in the chapters ahead.

outro: Note on the Song of the Sea as the oldest text in the Hebrew Bible: Shirat HaYam (Exodus 15:1–18) is among the oldest extended literary compositions in the Hebrew Bible. Its archaic orthography, its distinctive grammatical forms, and its linguistic features suggest composition in a very early period of Israelite history — possibly among the earliest written Hebrew poetry we possess. The Song of Deborah (Judges 5) is its closest parallel in age and character. Both are victory poems celebrating a moment when YHWH intervened in battle to save Israel. The antiquity of the Song of the Sea means that the theology it expresses — YHWH as incomparable divine warrior, YHWH as the one who redeems and leads in steadfast love, YHWH as the one who will establish his people on his holy mountain — is not late theological reflection on earlier events but contemporary testimony from within living memory of the Exodus itself.

Note on Marah and the pattern of wilderness testing (15:22–27): The transition from the Song of the Sea to the bitter water at Marah in three days is the sharpest emotional pivot in the Exodus narrative. The people who were singing ‘Who is like you among the gods?’ are now grumbling ‘What shall we drink?’ The pivot is not presented as a failure but as the beginning of a pattern: the wilderness is the place of testing (YHWH tests them, v.25), and testing produces the conditions for learning what it means to trust YHWH beyond the moment of salvation. The song is real; the thirst is real; both are part of the journey. Elim — twelve springs and seventy palm trees — waits on the other side of the bitter water. The wilderness’ harshness and its abundance are both gifts of the same Guide.

intro: Exodus 16 is the manna chapter — and it is primarily a chapter about trust. The manna is not only food; it is a daily test of whether Israel will trust YHWH one day at a time, or try to secure themselves against tomorrow. Embedded in the manna’s provision is the first explicit teaching about the Sabbath in the Exodus narrative.

notes.original: lu-mutnu b’yad YHWH b’eretz Mitzrayim… al-sir hab’sar
notes.rendering: Would that we had died by the hand of YHWH in Egypt… the meat pots
notes.why: The first grumbling in the wilderness is a wish for death in Egypt as preferable to life in the wilderness. Sir hab’sar — the pots of meat. The people’s memory of Egypt has already been romanticised: the bread to the full and the meat pots erase the slavery, the taskmasters, the mortar and the brick. Nostalgia for the house of slavery is one of the most consistent patterns of the wilderness narrative — it will recur at Marah (15:24), at Rephidim (17:3), at Sinai (32), at Taberah (Numbers 11:1), at the graves of craving (Numbers 11:4–6). The complaint is real (they are hungry), and the solution to it will be real (YHWH will feed them); but the framing — better to have died slaves with full stomachs — is the voice of people who have not yet learned what freedom costs.

notes.original: l’chem min-hashamayim… l’ma’an anas’sennu hayeilech b’torati im-lo
notes.rendering: bread from heaven… that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not
notes.why: L’chem min-hashamayim — bread from the heavens. The manna is explicitly described as bread from heaven, not bread produced by the earth. Its origin is above; it comes down as gift, not as harvest. And the giving is explicitly a test (nasah — the same verb used for YHWH testing Abraham in Genesis 22:1 and Israel at Marah in 15:25): will they gather only what they need for one day, or will they try to secure themselves against tomorrow? The manna tests the fundamental question of the wilderness: can Israel live by trust in YHWH’s daily provision, or will they always reach for more?

notes.original: man hu… man
notes.rendering: What is it?… manna
notes.why: Man hu — what is it? The people’s question on seeing the manna becomes its name. Manna is the question, preserved as a word: what is it? The food that sustains Israel through forty years of wilderness is named for the incomprehension of the people who first encountered it. Deuteronomy 8:3 will give the theological gloss: ‘he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of YHWH.’ Jesus quotes this in Matthew 4:4 during his own wilderness testing.

notes.original: hamarbeh lo he’edif v’hamam’it lo hech’sir
notes.rendering: whoever gathered much has nothing left over, and whoever gathered little has no lack
notes.why: The equalising principle of the manna is remarkable: regardless of how much or how little each person gathered, when measured out everyone had exactly what they needed. The manna refuses to be hoarded and refuses to leave anyone short. Paul quotes this verse in 2 Corinthians 8:15 as the principle of Christian generosity: ‘As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”’ The manna’s arithmetic is the arithmetic of the kingdom of God: sufficiency for all, excess for none, scarcity for none.

notes.original: Shabbat shabbaton qodesh l’YHWH machar
notes.rendering: Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to YHWH
notes.why: Shabbat shabbaton — a Sabbath of deep rest, a Sabbath of Sabbaths, a complete and solemn rest. The superlative form intensifies the ordinary: this is not merely a day off but a day of holy completeness. The Sabbath’s first explicit teaching in the Exodus comes not from the Ten Commandments (chapter 20) but from the manna: the manna does not fall on the seventh day, so you must not go out to gather it. The Sabbath is taught by the food itself — by the absence of provision on one day and the doubled provision on the day before. Creation rests from giving; Israel rests from gathering.

notes.original: vayoch’lu ven’ei-Yisra’el et-haman arba’im shanah
notes.rendering: The people of Israel eat the manna forty years
notes.why: The manna lasts exactly forty years — until the day after they eat the produce of the land of Canaan (Joshua 5:12). It begins on the fifteenth day of the second month (v.1) and ends when the land can feed them. The provision is precisely calibrated to the need: not one day more, not one day less. Forty years of daily bread from heaven. The number forty in the Hebrew Bible marks a complete period of testing and formation (Moses on the mountain 40 days, Israel in the wilderness 40 years, Elijah’s journey 40 days, Jesus’ testing 40 days). The manna is the daily sacrament of the forty years’ formation.

outro: Note on the manna as a theology of daily dependence: Exodus 16 establishes the manna as a theological discipline before it is a physical provision. The rules governing it — gather only what you need for today, gather double on the sixth day, do not go out on the seventh day — are designed to train Israel in the practice of daily trust. The manna that spoils overnight if hoarded makes accumulation impossible. The manna that does not fall on the Sabbath makes rest necessary. The manna that appears each morning makes gratitude renewable. It is a forty-year curriculum in the posture of a creature before the Creator: open-handed, one-day-at-a-time, trusting that tomorrow’s bread will also come. The Lord’s Prayer — ‘give us today our daily bread’ (Matthew 6:11) — is the manna prayer given to every generation.

intro: Exodus 17 contains two episodes that test Israel from two different directions: thirst tests their trust in YHWH’s provision, and Amalek tests their capacity to defend what YHWH has given. Both are answered, but in strikingly different ways — one through Moses alone striking a rock, one through Moses’ arms held up by two men.

notes.original: yariv… y’nassun… Massah um’rivah
notes.rendering: quarrel… test… Massah and Meribah
notes.why: Riv means to quarrel, to contend, to bring a legal dispute. The people’s complaint against Moses takes the form of a legal accusation. Nassah means to test, to put to the proof — the same verb used of YHWH testing Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and testing Israel with the manna (Exodus 16:4). But here it is Israel testing YHWH: the question they ask — ‘Is YHWH among us or not?’ — is the forbidden test, demanding evidence of divine presence before they will trust. The place names preserve both charges: Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarrelling). The Psalms return to these place names repeatedly as the paradigmatic moments of wilderness faithlessness (Psalm 95:8–9; 106:32).

notes.original: hineni omed l’fanecha sham al-hatzur b’Chorev
notes.rendering: Look — I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb
notes.why: YHWH will stand on the rock before Moses strikes it. The sequence is extraordinary: YHWH places himself on the rock, then Moses strikes the rock, then water flows. The rabbinic tradition was deeply troubled by the implied image and developed the tradition of the travelling rock (1 Corinthians 10:4 follows this: ‘they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ’). Paul’s reading of the rock as Christ is the most significant New Testament interpretation of this passage. YHWH standing on the rock before Moses strikes it is the image that drives the typological reading.

notes.original: vayehi ka’asher yarim Mosheh yado v’gavar Yisra’el
notes.rendering: Whenever Moses holds up his hand, Israel prevails
notes.why: The raised hands of Moses are the most discussed detail of the Amalek battle. The causal connection between Moses’ raised hands and Israel’s military success is stated without explanation: when the hands go up, Israel prevails; when they come down, Amalek prevails. The raised staff (the staff that struck the Nile, that parted the sea) is in Moses’ hands — the staff’s power concentrated in the posture of intercession. Later Jewish tradition read the raised hands as prayer; Christian tradition has read them as a prefiguring of the cross (Justin Martyr; Tertullian). Whatever its precise theological mechanism, the text is clear that the battle is not won by military superiority alone.

notes.original: vayehyu yadav emunah ad-bo hashemesh
notes.rendering: So his hands are steady until the going down of the sun
notes.why: Emunah — faithful, steady, firm — from the same root as amen and as the hesed-and-emet (steadfast love and faithfulness) that runs through the covenant vocabulary. Moses’ hands are emunah — not merely physically supported but faithful, unwavering, sustained in the posture of intercession. The word for the steadiness of Moses’ hands is the word for covenant faithfulness. The battle is won by emunah: Aaron and Hur holding up the arms of the intercessor until the sun goes down.

notes.original: YHWH Nissi
notes.rendering: YHWH-Nissi
notes.why: Nissi means my banner, my standard, my ensign — from nes (banner, pole, sign raised on a height). Moses builds an altar and names it YHWH is my banner. The altar-name is a declaration: the victory over Amalek belongs not to Joshua’s sword or Moses’ raised hands but to YHWH who is the battle-standard of Israel. The same word nes will be used in Isaiah 11:10, 12 for the sign that will be raised to gather the nations at the end of days. YHWH Nissi is the name that claims the battle for its true commander.

outro: Note on the question ‘Is YHWH among us or not?’ (17:7): The question the Israelites ask at Meribah is the most theologically pointed question in the wilderness narrative. After all they have seen — the plagues, the crossing, the pillar of cloud and fire, the manna every morning — they ask: is YHWH among us or not? The question exposes the logic of wilderness faithlessness: each act of divine provision is sufficient for the moment it addresses, but it does not seem to build cumulative trust. The next crisis feels like the first crisis. This is not presented as exceptional wickedness but as the consistent pattern of human beings under pressure: we ask the present-tense question without the past-tense evidence landing as we think it should. The Psalms that return to Massah and Meribah (Psalm 95) use them as warnings to future generations: do not harden your hearts as they did. The warning is necessary because the tendency is universal.

intro: Exodus 18 is the most practically focused chapter in the Exodus narrative, and also one of the most theologically interesting. The priest of Midian — a foreigner — arrives at the camp of Israel, hears the story of the Exodus, declares YHWH greater than all gods, offers sacrifices, and then gives Moses the best piece of organisational advice in the Torah. Wisdom comes from outside the covenant community.

notes.original: Yitro kohen Midyan choten Mosheh
notes.rendering: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses’ father-in-law
notes.why: Jethro is introduced with two titles: kohen Midyan (priest of Midian) and choten Mosheh (father-in-law of Moses). The priest title is significant: he is not a layman from outside Israel’s tradition but a religious leader in his own right, serving a god or gods of Midian. His worship of YHWH in v.12 — bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices to God — raises the question of whether he was already a worshipper of YHWH (some scholars connect Midianite religion to early YHWH worship — the Kenite hypothesis) or whether he converts upon hearing of the Exodus. The text is ambiguous, and that ambiguity is productive.

notes.original: vayichad Yitro… attah yadati ki gadol YHWH
notes.rendering: Jethro rejoices… Now I know that YHWH is greater than all gods
notes.why: Vayichad — he rejoices, he is glad. Then: attah yadati — now I know. The same ‘now I know’ structure as the knowledge formula of the plague narrative — and the same recognition that YHWH is incomparable (‘who is like you among the gods?’ 15:11). But here it is a Midianite priest who makes the confession, not a plague-struck Egyptian. The outsider who hears the story of the Exodus reaches the theological conclusion that the plagues were designed to produce. Jethro’s confession is the first Gentile response to the Exodus. It anticipates Rahab (Joshua 2:10–11), Ruth, and the nations who will ultimately acknowledge YHWH.

notes.original: ki v’davar asher zadu aleihem
notes.rendering: because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people
notes.why: Jethro’s theological observation is precise: YHWH’s superiority was demonstrated specifically in the reversal of Egyptian arrogance. Zadu — they acted presumptuously, they dealt arrogantly. The Egyptians who tried to destroy Israel by the Nile, who built the store cities on their backs, who pursued them to the sea — their arrogance was the occasion for the display of YHWH’s greatness. The pattern is the one Paul will articulate in Romans: God chose what is weak to shame the strong, what is low and despised to bring to nothing the things that are.

notes.original: lo tov hadavar asher attah oseh… naval tibbal… ki-chaved mimm’cha hadavar
notes.rendering: What you are doing is not good… you will certainly wear out… the thing is too heavy for you
notes.why: Jethro’s assessment is frank and structural: not a personal criticism of Moses’ commitment but an observation about system design. Naval tibbal — you will wear yourself out, you will wither and fall. Chaved — heavy, too much. The word kavod (glory, weight) in its negative application: the burden is too weighty for one person. The same word for YHWH’s glory is the word for the burden that is crushing Moses. Jethro’s counsel is the counsel of a man who has watched leaders before: you cannot carry everyone’s cases to God alone. Share the weight.

notes.original: anshei chayil yir’ei Elohim anshei emet son‧ei vatza
notes.rendering: men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe
notes.why: Jethro’s four criteria for delegated judges: capable (anshei chayil — men of strength, of substance), God-fearing (yir’ei Elohim — the quality of the midwives in Exodus 1, of Joseph in Genesis 39), truthful/trustworthy (anshei emet — men of emunah, faithfulness), and those who hate unjust gain (son’ei vatza — hating the cut, despising the bribe). Four qualities in ascending order of difficulty: competence is easiest to assess; hatred of financial corruption is hardest to maintain. The criteria are not primarily intellectual or administrative but moral and theological. The judge must fear God before they judge between people.

notes.original: vayishma Mosheh l’qol chotno
notes.rendering: Moses listens to the voice of his father-in-law
notes.why: The same verb shama (to hear, to listen, to obey) that YHWH has been pleading for from Israel throughout the Exodus. Moses, the mediator between God and Israel, demonstrates toward his Midianite father-in-law the quality of listening that he cannot get the people to demonstrate toward YHWH. He simply listens. The most powerful man in the Israelite camp receives counsel from a foreigner and acts on it without debate or defensiveness. The wisdom to listen is the beginning of the wisdom to lead.

outro: Note on Jethro as the voice of wisdom from outside: Exodus 18 is the only chapter in the Pentateuch where the primary source of wisdom is a foreigner. Jethro is not an Israelite; he has no part in the covenant; he worships a god whose identity is not specified before this chapter. And he gives Moses the organizational insight that will shape Israelite jurisprudence for the wilderness period and beyond. The Deuteronomy version of the same episode (Deuteronomy 1:9–18) has Moses take the initiative rather than Jethro — a difference that has generated much scholarly discussion. But in Exodus, the wisdom comes from outside: the priest of Midian sees what the mediator of the covenant cannot see because he is too close to it. This is one of the Hebrew Bible’s most striking acknowledgments that truth and wisdom are not Israel’s exclusive possession. They can arrive on the lips of a foreigner at the foot of the mountain, before the law is given.

Note on the placement of Exodus 18 before Sinai: Jethro’s visit is placed in chapter 18, immediately before the Sinai theophany of chapters 19–20. The juxtaposition is deliberate: the people arrive at the mountain of God (18:5), the judicial system is established (18:13–27), and then YHWH speaks from the mountain (19:1ff). The order suggests that the covenant people need not only the law that comes from above but the practical wisdom about how to live together that comes from lateral human counsel. Moses receives instruction from two directions at Sinai: from YHWH above, and from Jethro beside him. Both are given without embarrassment or ranking. The law requires wisdom for its implementation; wisdom requires the law for its grounding.

intro: Exodus 19 is the approach to Sinai — the preparation for the most concentrated divine speech in the entire Torah. Everything in the chapter is threshold: the consecration, the limits set around the mountain, the three days of waiting, the growing trumpet blast. YHWH is about to speak the Ten Words directly to the people, and the chapter’s every detail communicates the weight of that event.

notes.original: v’essa etchem al-kanfei n’sharim va’avi etchem eilai
notes.rendering: I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself
notes.why: Kanfei n’sharim — wings of eagles. The image is one of the most beautiful in the Exodus: YHWH did not merely lead Israel out of Egypt but carried them, the way an eagle lifts its young on its own wings. Deuteronomy 32:11–12 develops the image: as an eagle stirs up its nest, hovers over its young, spreads its wings, catches them and carries them on its pinions — so YHWH alone led Israel. The direction of the carrying is the key phrase: va’avi etchem eilai — and I brought you to myself. The Exodus is not primarily an escape from Egypt; it is a journey toward YHWH. The destination was always YHWH himself, not merely the land.

notes.original: s’gulah… mamlecht kohanim v’goy qadosh
notes.rendering: treasured possession… kingdom of priests and a holy nation
notes.why: S’gulah means personal treasure, cherished possession, the property that is kept close rather than traded. The word is used in Ecclesiastes 2:8 for the particular treasures of a king. YHWH calls Israel his s’gulah among all the peoples — not because the other peoples do not belong to him (kol ha’aretz li — all the earth is mine) but because Israel has a particular closeness. Mamlecht kohanim — a kingdom of priests, a priestly kingdom. Every Israelite is, in some sense, what Aaron will be in particular: one who stands between the people and the holy, who has access to the divine presence. Goy qadosh — a holy nation: set apart, different, belonging to YHWH. These three phrases (s’gulah, mamlecht kohanim, goy qadosh) are the covenant vocation of Israel in its most compressed form.

notes.original: kol asher dibber YHWH na’aseh
notes.rendering: All that YHWH has spoken we will do
notes.why: The people’s response before hearing the law is their greatest moment of covenant commitment — and its brevity and totality are both its glory and its problem. Na’aseh — we will do. Not ‘we will try’, not ‘we will do most of it’, not ‘we will do it if it seems reasonable’: all that YHWH has spoken, we will do. The commitment is made before the specific demands are known. This is covenant in its covenant form: unconditional, prior, total. The Talmud records a tradition that Israel said na’aseh before nishma (we will do before we will hear), and that the angels marvelled at this: they said ‘we will do’ before they heard what was required. Golden calf notwithstanding, the na’aseh of chapter 19 is the most complete covenant affirmation in Exodus.

notes.original: q’lot uv’raqim v’anan kaveid… v’qol shofar chazaq m’od
notes.rendering: thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud… a very loud trumpet blast
notes.why: Q’lot (thunders, voices) uv’raqim (lightnings, flashes). The phenomena of the Sinai theophany — thunder, lightning, dense cloud, fire, smoke, earthquake, and trumpet blast — are the language of the Divine Warrior arriving for battle (see Psalm 18:7–15; Habakkuk 3:3–15). The theophany vocabulary is not merely meteorological; it is the literary register of YHWH’s presence in its full weight and terror. Hebrews 12:18–21 cites the Sinai phenomena as the fearful approach to the old covenant, contrasted with the joyful approach to the new: ‘you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest…’

notes.original: Mosheh y’dabber v’ha’Elohim ya’an’nenu b’qol
notes.rendering: Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder
notes.why: The exchange between Moses and God at the mountain is described in terms of speech and thunder — dialogue conducted in the register of storm. God answers Moses in qol (voice, sound, thunder) — the same word used for the thunders of the theophany. The boundary between YHWH’s voice and the storm’s thunder is deliberately blurred. This is the literary form of divine speech at Sinai: the thunder is the voice, and the voice has the weight of thunder. The Sinai theophany is the most dramatic expression in the Hebrew Bible of the truth that divine speech is not merely information but power.

outro: Note on the structure of Exodus 19 as threshold: The entire chapter is a preparation for what cannot yet be spoken. YHWH announces the covenant vocation (vv.3–6), the people affirm it (v.8), the preparation is commanded (vv.10–13), the signs increase (vv.16–19), and still the chapter ends with Moses going back down to tell the people, rather than with the law being given. Chapter 19 is pure anticipation: the mountain on fire, the trumpet growing louder, the people trembling at the foot, Moses going up and down like an intermediary at a divine court. The law has not yet been given, but everything in the chapter makes the reader feel the weight of what is coming. The preparation is the theology: what YHWH is about to say has such mass that it requires three days of consecration and a trembling nation at the mountain’s base before the first word is spoken.

intro: Exodus 20 contains the Decalogue — the Ten Words (aseret had’varim — literally ‘ten words’ or ‘ten things,’ not ‘ten commandments,’ though that is their function). They are the most influential piece of legislation in Western history and the theological centre of the Sinai covenant. Every word has been weighed for millennia.

notes.original: vay’dabber Elohim et kol-had’varim ha’elleh
notes.rendering: And God speaks all these words
notes.why: Had’varim ha’elleh — these words. The Ten Commandments are called aseret had’varim (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 4:13; 10:4) — ten words, ten things, ten utterances. Not aseret hamitzvot (ten commandments) in the Hebrew text — that is a later interpretive tradition. They are first and foremost words, utterances, speech-acts of the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. The word d’var (word, thing, matter) is the building block of all divine speech in the Hebrew Bible. YHWH’s words at Sinai are not primarily laws to be obeyed but words to be received — the speech of the God of the Exodus directed at the people he has just redeemed.

notes.original: anochi YHWH Elohecha asher hotzeitich m’eretz Mitzrayim
notes.rendering: I am YHWH your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt
notes.why: The prologue to the Decalogue is not a commandment but an identity declaration: I am YHWH your God, who brought you out. The commandments that follow are grounded in a prior act of redemption. YHWH does not say ‘obey these laws and I will bring you out of Egypt’; he says ‘I have already brought you out; now here is how to live as people who belong to me.’ The order is irreversible: grace precedes law; redemption precedes obligation; the indicative grounds the imperative. The prologue is the most important verse in the Decalogue for understanding what the Decalogue is.

notes.original: lo yihyeh l’cha Elohim acherim al-panai
notes.rendering: You shall have no other gods before me
notes.why: Al-panai — before my face, in my presence, against my face, beside me. The phrase is richer than ‘before me’ in the sense of priority alone: it means in my presence, in the space where I am, alongside me. The first word does not deny the existence of other gods in the ancient world; it declares that none of them may occupy the space where YHWH is, the relationship where YHWH is known. The First Word is not philosophical monotheism but relational exclusivity: in your life, in your worship, in your allegiance, there is no room for another. This is the jealousy of love (v.5: qanna, a jealous God), not merely the exclusivity of power.

notes.original: El qanna… oseh chesed la’alafim
notes.rendering: a jealous God… showing steadfast love to thousands
notes.why: Qanna means jealous, zealous — passionate in the demand for exclusive loyalty, unwilling to share devotion with another. The word describes the emotional register of YHWH’s response to idolatry: it is not merely a legal violation but a personal betrayal. The punishment described — visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation of those who hate him — must be read alongside the mercy: chesed to thousands (la’alafim) of those who love him and keep his commandments. The asymmetry is deliberate: three or four generations of consequence; thousands of generations of steadfast love. The jealousy and the chesed are both expressions of the same passionate commitment.

notes.original: lo tissa et-shem YHWH Elohecha lashav
notes.rendering: You shall not take the name of YHWH your God in vain
notes.why: Nasa means to lift, to carry, to take up. The name is not merely spoken but carried, borne, taken up. Shav means emptiness, worthlessness, vanity — the same word as in Ecclesiastes (hebel, vanity). The Third Word prohibits carrying YHWH’s name as if it were an empty thing — using it without weight, without seriousness, without the reality it points to. The prohibition is broader than avoiding blasphemy; it covers every use of the divine name in empty oath, false claim, magical formula, or casual speech. To take up the name of YHWH is to bear a weight. The word lashav is the warning that the name must not be carried as if it were weightless.

notes.original: zachor et-yom hashabbat l’qad’sho
notes.rendering: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy
notes.why: Zachor — remember. Not merely observe or keep but remember. The Sabbath is an act of memory: remember what YHWH did in the six days of creation, and rest as YHWH rested. The Deuteronomy version of the same commandment uses shamor (guard, keep) instead of zachor (remember) — the two versions have generated centuries of rabbinic reflection on the Sabbath’s dual character: it is both a memory (zachor) and a practice (shamor). The Exodus version grounds the Sabbath in creation (v.11); the Deuteronomy version grounds it in the Exodus (Deuteronomy 5:15: you were slaves in Egypt). The Sabbath is simultaneously the rhythm of the cosmos and the rhythm of the liberated.

notes.original: lo tirtzach… lo tin’af… lo tignov… lo ta’aneh… lo tachmod
notes.rendering: You shall not murder… commit adultery… steal… bear false witness… covet
notes.why: The five short words (the Sixth through Tenth) are among the most terse legislation in world history. Lo tirtzach — you shall not murder (ratzach is specifically wrongful killing: murder, not all killing). Lo tin’af — you shall not commit adultery (na’af is specifically the violation of the marriage bond). Lo tignov — you shall not steal. Lo ta’aneh ed shaqer b’rei’echa — you shall not answer (in court, as a witness) as a false witness against your neighbour. Lo tachmod — you shall not covet (chamad is desire, appetite, the inner wanting that precedes the act). The Tenth Word alone regulates an interior state, not an outward act. Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount follows the same logic: from acts to the desires that produce them.

outro: Note on the Decalogue’s structure and the numbering traditions: Different religious traditions number the Ten Words differently. The Jewish tradition counts ‘I am YHWH your God’ (v.2) as the First Word. The Protestant tradition combines ‘you shall have no other gods’ and the image prohibition into one commandment and splits the covetousness prohibition into two to maintain ten. The Catholic and Lutheran traditions count the prologue as the First Commandment, combine the other gods and image prohibitions, and split covetousness. The Fireside Bible presents the text in its Hebrew sequence without privileging any numbering tradition, using the prologue and the words as the text presents them.
