The positioning of the Sabbath command immediately before the Tabernacle building instructions — as in chapters 31–32 — makes the same theological point: the building of the holy space does not override the holy time. The Sabbath is the frame within which all sacred construction occurs.

notes.original: kol asher nsa'o libo… kol nadiv lev… n'davah laYHWH
notes.rendering: everyone whose heart stirs them… all who are generous of heart… a freewill offering to YHWH
notes.why: The chapter returns obsessively to the language of the willing heart. Nda'vo libo (his heart stirred him), nadiv lev (generous of heart), n'davah (freewill offering, from the same root): the vocabulary of voluntary giving pervades the passage. The contrast with the golden calf episode is deliberate and devastating. In chapter 32 the people stripped their gold earrings at Aaron's request to make an idol. Here they bring the same kinds of gold objects — brooches, earrings, signet rings, armlets (v.22 matches precisely) — as a freewill offering for the Tabernacle. The same gold, the same gestures, the same people: but now the direction is reversed. What was plundered for idolatry is freely given for the dwelling of YHWH. The t'shuvah — the turning — is enacted not in a speech but in a gift.

notes.original: v'chol-ishah chachmat-lev b'yadeyha tavu… v'chol-hanashim asher nasa liban otanah b'chochmah
notes.rendering: every skilled woman spins with her own hands… all the women whose hearts stir them to use their skill
notes.why: The women of Israel appear here as active participants in the construction of the Tabernacle — not spectators but craftspeople. The language given to the women mirrors the language given to Bezalel: chachmat-lev (skill of heart, wisdom of heart) is the phrase used for the craftsmen throughout. The women spin the linen and the goats' hair; the women's work is the fabric of the Tabernacle itself — its curtains, its veil, its hanging screens. The text names both the motivated skill (chachmah — wisdom) and the moved will (nasa liban — their heart stirring them). The Tabernacle is built by the whole people, men and women, leaders and craftspeople, spinners and goldsmiths, each contributing what they have and what they know.

notes.original: ul'horot natan b'libo hu v'Oholiav
notes.rendering: he has given him — and Oholiab — the ability to teach
notes.why: This detail, added to the restatement of Bezalel and Oholiab's commission, is quietly significant. The Spirit-given skills are not only for personal excellence; they are for transmission. L'horot — to teach, to show, to direct (from the same root as Torah). The craftsmen who have been filled with skill are commissioned not only to build but to instruct others. The Tabernacle is not built by two inspired individuals working alone; it is built by a community of craftspeople whom Bezalel and Oholiab have taught. The Spirit's gift is not hoarded but spread. In this detail the Tabernacle project becomes a model of what the community called to build the holy space looks like: diverse in skill, unified in purpose, taught by those who have been filled.

intro: Exodus 36 opens the execution of the Tabernacle blueprint in earnest. The chapter begins with the most extraordinary moment in the entire building narrative (vv.1–7) before moving into the first of the construction reports — the curtains and frames that directly mirror the instructions of chapter 26. The repetition is the point: what YHWH commanded is what Israel builds, word for word, cubit for cubit.

notes.original: v'heim hevi'u eilav od n'davah baboqer baboqer… vayikal'u ha'am mehavi
notes.rendering: they keep bringing freewill offerings every morning… the people are restrained from bringing
notes.why: The over-giving of Israel is one of the most remarkable moments in the Pentateuch and one of the least commented upon. The people bring so much — gold, silver, bronze, linen, skins, oil, spices — that Moses has to issue a proclamation to make them stop. Vayikal'u ha'am mehavi — the people were held back, restrained, kept from bringing. The verb kala means to hold in, to contain, to shut up. Israel has to be shut up from generosity. The contrast with the golden calf is now complete: there the people gave their gold when asked; here they give without being asked, and then they give more, and then more still, until Moses stops them. The same community, the same gold. What changed? The direction of the giving — and the fact that this time it is entirely willing. The Tabernacle is built on the excess of a people who could not stop giving.

notes.original: vaya'asu kol-chacham-lev b'osei ham'lachah et-hamishkan
notes.rendering: all the skilled craftsmen among the workers make the Tabernacle
notes.why: Chacham-lev — skilled of heart, wise of heart. The phrase appears throughout the execution chapters (35:10, 25, 35; 36:1, 2, 4, 8) and is the execution counterpart to the command chapters' repeated 'every skilled craftsman.' The skill is always located in the heart, not merely the hands: chochmah in the Hebrew tradition is not technical competence alone but wisdom — the integrated intelligence of understanding what something is for and how to make it rightly. The craftsmen who build the Tabernacle are filled with this heart-skill. The Tabernacle is not merely constructed; it is understood.

notes.original: (mirror of chapter 26)
notes.rendering: The execution mirrors the blueprint exactly
notes.why: Chapters 36–39 are the most formally repetitive section of Exodus — and, arguably, of the entire Pentateuch. The execution reports repeat the blueprint instructions almost verbatim, with the verbs shifted from imperative ('you shall make') to perfect ('he made'). This near-verbatim repetition has puzzled and frustrated modern readers who expect narrative economy. But in the ancient world, the exact repetition of a divine command in its execution was a theological statement: Israel did exactly what YHWH commanded, precisely as commanded, nothing added and nothing omitted. The repetition is obedience rendered visible in prose. What God said became what Israel did, word for word. In a narrative that has just described the golden calf — Israel's catastrophic invention of an unauthorised substitute — the meticulous fidelity of the execution chapters is the counter-narrative. This is what faithfulness looks like: it looks like doing exactly what you were told.

outro: Note on Exodus 34–36 as the recovery arc: These three chapters enact the return from the catastrophe of chapters 32–33. The movement is precise: the covenant is renewed (chapter 34) — the tablets written, the name proclaimed, Moses' face made radiant. The Sabbath is restated (35:1–3) — the sign of the covenant is back in place before the building begins. The people bring their offerings (35:4–29) — and bring them with the same willing hearts that gave gold for the calf, now redirected. The craftsmen receive the commission (35:30–36:7) — filled with the Spirit, equipped to teach. And the building begins. The recovery is not narrated as a spiritual experience; it is narrated as activity. Israel recovers not by feeling better about the golden calf but by doing the thing they failed to do: giving their gold for YHWH's dwelling instead of YHWH's replacement. The Tabernacle, built from the over-abundance of a people who could not stop giving, is the material form of the covenant's renewal.

Note on the chiasm's A' movement and the theology of execution: A striking feature of the A' movement (chapters 35–40) is that it replaces YHWH's first-person speech with third-person narration. In chapters 25–31 YHWH speaks: 'You shall make... you shall overlay... you shall place.' In chapters 35–40 the narrator reports: 'He made... he overlaid... he placed.' The divine imperative becomes human indicative. The blueprint becomes a building. This grammatical shift is the formal expression of what the entire section is about: the movement from divine command to human obedience, from the mountain to the camp, from the word of YHWH to the work of Israel's hands. The chiasm's two halves are grammatically as well as thematically mirror images of each other.

intro: Exodus 37 is the most interior chapter of the execution section — it covers the four objects of the Holy Place and the Most Holy: the Ark, the Table, the Lampstand, and the Incense Altar. These are the objects closest to YHWH's presence, the furnishings that Bezalel himself is named as making. The chapter is brief and precise, a craftsman's record rather than a theologian's meditation — but a few details reward close attention.

notes.original: vaya'as Betzal'el et-ha'aron
notes.rendering: Bezalel makes the ark
notes.why: Bezalel is named explicitly as the maker of the Ark — the innermost and most sacred object in the Tabernacle. In the blueprint chapters (25–31), the commands are given to Moses and addressed in the second person plural: 'they shall make.' Here, in the execution, the verbs shift to the third person singular: Bezalel made, he overlaid, he cast. The personal attribution of the Ark's construction to Bezalel is the execution chapters' way of honouring the Spirit-filled craftsman: the man filled with ruach Elohim (31:3) is the one who makes YHWH's throne. The Ark is not mass-produced by anonymous workers; it is made by a named human being acting under divine inspiration. Craftsmanship and holiness are not in tension here; they are the same thing.

notes.original: vaya'as et-shemen hamishchah qodesh v'et-q'toret hasamim tahor
notes.rendering: he also makes the holy anointing oil and the pure fragrant incense
notes.why: Verse 29 is easy to pass over — a single line at the end of the chapter — but it is quietly remarkable. Bezalel the goldsmith and woodworker also makes the anointing oil and the incense: he is a perfumer as well as a metalsmith. The verse confirms the breadth of the Spirit's gift: Bezalel's filling with skill (31:3–5: chochmah, t'vunah, da'at, kol-m'lachah) covers every kind of craft, including the blending of sacred scent. The holy anointing oil and the incense are not incidental accessories; they are the olfactory dimension of the Tabernacle's holiness — the smell of the sacred. Bezalel makes the gold throne of YHWH and the fragrance that fills his house. He makes the weight and the atmosphere of the holy.

intro: Exodus 38 moves from the innermost objects outward to the altar and court — the threshold spaces of the Tabernacle. It contains two of the most unusual passages in the execution section: the enigmatic note about the women's mirrors (v.8) and the detailed inventory of materials (vv.21–31) — the only financial audit in the Pentateuch.

notes.original: bimar'ot hatzov'ot asher tzav'u petach ohel mo'ed
notes.rendering: from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting
notes.why: This is one of the most mysterious verses in Exodus. The basin — the object whose dimensions were left unspecified in the blueprint (30:17–21) — is made from the bronze mirrors of women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting. The mirrors are polished bronze discs, the standard mirror of the ancient world. Three questions arise and none is fully answered by the text: who are these women, what is their service, and why do they give their mirrors? The women (nshim hatzov'ot) appear nowhere else in the Pentateuch; the word tzova (serve, assemble) has a military connotation in some contexts — assembled troops — but here describes a group of women stationed at the tent entrance. Their giving of mirrors — personal objects of self-regard, vessels of the visible self — for the basin that purifies the priests before they enter may carry symbolic weight: they give what shows the human face so that those who approach YHWH may be washed. The detail is preserved without interpretation, as if its full meaning is known to those who need to know it.

notes.original: elleh f'qudei hamishkan… al-pi Itamar ben-Aharon hakohen
notes.rendering: these are the records of the Tabernacle… under the direction of Ithamar
notes.why: The inventory of materials is unique in the Pentateuch — a detailed accounting of every ounce of gold, silver, and bronze contributed and used. The record is kept by the Levites under Ithamar's supervision: an audit trail for the sacred construction. The numbers are staggering: 29 talents of gold (roughly a ton), 100 talents of silver (roughly three and a half tons), 70 talents of bronze. And the census number — 603,550 men over twenty — is confirmed here by the arithmetic of the half-shekel: 603,550 half-shekels = 301,775 shekels = exactly 100 talents and 1,775 shekels. The text has done the mathematics, and it checks out. The Tabernacle is built on counted, weighed, audited material. Sacred construction requires sacred accounting. The God who commanded exact measurements for every plank and curtain also requires exact records of every shekel.

intro: Exodus 39 is the completion chapter for the priestly garments, and it builds to one of the most deliberately resonant moments in the book: Moses surveying the finished work and blessing the people. The formula 'just as YHWH commanded Moses' (ka'asher tzivah YHWH et-Mosheh) runs through the chapter like a refrain — it occurs seven times in the garment descriptions alone, and twice more in the summary (vv.42–43). By the time Moses blesses the people, the reader has heard the phrase of perfect obedience so many times that it has become the chapter's heartbeat.

notes.original: vayeraq'u et-pachei hazahav viqatzatz p'tilim
notes.rendering: they hammer out sheets of gold and cut them into threads
notes.why: The technique described — hammering gold into sheets and then cutting it into fine threads to weave into fabric — is well-attested in ancient Near Eastern goldwork and has been confirmed archaeologically. Gold thread woven into textile requires extraordinary skill and patience: the threads must be fine enough to behave like fibre while retaining gold's lustre and weight. The ephod is not merely decorated with gold; it is woven from it. The fabric is the gold and the gold is the fabric. This is the kind of detail that validates the execution narrative's claim to preserve authentic memory of the craft traditions it describes.

notes.original: ka'asher tzivah YHWH et-Mosheh ken asu… vayvarech otam Mosheh
notes.rendering: just as YHWH commanded Moses, so they did… and Moses blessed them
notes.why: The completion formula — ka'asher tzivah YHWH et-Mosheh ken asu — is the grammatical spine of the execution chapters, occurring eighteen times across chapters 39–40. Its repetition is not careless; it is cumulative. Each use adds another layer to the claim that Israel's execution of the Tabernacle was exact, complete, and faithful. After the golden calf — Israel's great act of unauthorised worship — the execution chapters demonstrate with relentless specificity that Israel can and does do what YHWH commands, exactly as commanded. The Moses blessing in verse 43 is the payoff: it echoes Genesis 1, where God surveys each day's work and sees that it is good, and Genesis 2:3, where God blesses the seventh day. Moses seeing the finished work and blessing the people is the human counterpart to the divine rest at creation's end. The Tabernacle project is presented as a new creation — and Moses' blessing is its sabbath.

intro: Exodus 40 is the final chapter of the book — the assembly of the Tabernacle and the descent of the glory. The chapter is structured in three movements: YHWH's command to assemble (vv.1–15), Moses' meticulous execution of that command (vv.16–33), and the arrival of the divine presence (vv.34–38). The last five verses are the climax not only of Exodus but of the entire Torah's opening movement — the answer to the question posed by the Exodus itself: can YHWH and Israel dwell together? The answer comes in a cloud and a fire.

notes.original: b'yom ha'echad lachodesh har'ishon bash'nah hash'nit huqam hamishkan
notes.rendering: on the first day of the first month of the second year the Tabernacle is erected
notes.why: The date is precisely one year after the Exodus began. In 12:2 YHWH told Moses: 'This month shall be for you the beginning of months — the first month of the year.' The Passover was the fourteenth of that month; the Tabernacle goes up on the first. Israel left Egypt in the first month of the first year; the Tabernacle stands in the first month of the second year. The year between is the year of Sinai: covenant received, covenant shattered, covenant renewed, Tabernacle planned, Tabernacle built. The calendar precision matters: YHWH's dwelling among his people is dated, located, historical. It begins on a specific day, in a specific year, in a specific place in the wilderness. The Incarnation — in the New Testament's telling — will perform the same move: the Word dwelt (eskenosen, 'tabernacled') among us, on a specific day, in a specific place.

notes.original: vay'chal Mosheh et-ham'lachah
notes.rendering: and Moses finishes the work
notes.why: Vay'chal — and he finished, he completed. The verb is kala, to finish, to complete, to bring to an end. It is the same verb used in Genesis 2:2: vay'chal Elohim bayom hash'vi'i m'lachto — 'God finished on the seventh day his work.' The echo is unmistakable and deliberate. When God finished creation, he rested and blessed the seventh day. When Moses finishes the Tabernacle, he blesses the people (39:43). The Tabernacle is the new creation — the ordering of material reality around the presence of YHWH — and its completion is described in the language of Genesis. Moses' vay'chal positions the Tabernacle project as the culmination of the creation project: the world was made to house the divine presence, and now, at last, the house is ready.

notes.original: vay'chasse he'anan et-ohel mo'ed uch'vod YHWH male et-hamishkan
notes.rendering: the cloud covers the tent of meeting, and the glory of YHWH fills the Tabernacle
notes.why: The two verbs are the chapter's climax: kasa (covered, overwhelmed) and male (filled, was full). The cloud that covered Sinai (24:15–16) now covers the tent of meeting. The glory that burned on the mountain now fills the dwelling in the camp. YHWH has moved from the mountain to the middle of Israel. The Tabernacle theology of 25:8 — 'let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst' — is here fulfilled. V'shachanti b'tocham is now a present-tense fact: YHWH is dwelling among them. The cloud and fire of the Exodus guidance (13:21–22 — pillar of cloud by day, pillar of fire by night) are now located not outside the camp leading the way but at the centre of the camp, over the Tabernacle. YHWH has come home.

notes.original: v'lo yachol Mosheh lavo el-ohel mo'ed ki shachan alav he'anan
notes.rendering: Moses cannot enter the tent of meeting — because the cloud has settled on it
notes.why: The detail that Moses himself cannot enter is one of the most theologically charged lines in the book. Moses — who spoke with YHWH face to face as a friend (33:11), who stood in the cleft of the rock while the glory passed, who spent eighty days on the mountain in YHWH's presence — cannot enter the tent because the glory is too full. The presence that Moses spent the entire second half of Exodus negotiating for has now arrived in such abundance that the negotiator himself is excluded. The fullness of the answer exceeds the capacity of the one who asked. This detail will be replicated at the dedication of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:11: 'the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud'). The glory that fills YHWH's house is beyond the management of those who built it.

notes.original: b'hei'alot he'anan… v'esh tih'yeh layla bo l'einei chol-beit Yisrael b'chol mas'eihem
notes.rendering: whenever the cloud lifts… fire in it by night — in the sight of all the house of Israel, throughout all their journeys
notes.why: The book ends not with arrival but with movement. The cloud lifts; Israel sets out. The cloud settles; Israel stops. The Tabernacle, for all its elaborate construction and sacred weight, is a portable dwelling — built to travel, built for the wilderness, built for a people who are always in motion toward a destination they have not yet reached. The final phrase — b'chol mas'eihem, throughout all their journeys — is the last word of Exodus. The book that began with Israel enslaved in Egypt ends with Israel moving through the wilderness under the cloud and fire of YHWH's presence. The destination is not yet visible. But the presence is real, the direction is forward, and the cloud leads the way.

outro: Note on the ending of Exodus and its theological achievement: The book of Exodus begins with a people enslaved, nameless, crushed under Egypt's weight. It ends with a cloud of divine presence filling a portable dwelling at the centre of their camp. Between those two images — the slave pits of Egypt and the glory-filled Tabernacle — is everything: the burning bush, the ten plagues, the Passover, the crossing of the sea, the manna and quail, Sinai, the Decalogue, the Covenant Code, the blood of the covenant, the meal on the mountain, the blueprint, the golden calf, the intercession, the cleft of the rock, the thirteen attributes, the second tablets, Moses' radiant face, the willing offerings, the craftsmen filled with the Spirit, the meticulous building. Every thread of this immense narrative converges on the last five verses. The cloud covers the tent. The glory fills the Tabernacle. The God who said 'let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst' now dwells in their midst. The Exodus is complete — not because Israel has arrived in the land, but because Israel has arrived at this: YHWH among them, cloud by day, fire by night, throughout all their journeys.

Note on Exodus 40 and the New Testament: The closing verses of Exodus cast a long shadow across the New Testament. John 1:14 — 'the Word became flesh and dwelt (eskenosen — tabernacled) among us, and we saw his glory' — is the most direct echo: the Incarnation is narrated in Tabernacle language. The glory (doxa) that fills the Tabernacle in Exodus 40 is the glory John's community sees in the face of Jesus. The cloud and fire of divine presence become the Spirit descending at the Transfiguration and at Pentecost. And the detail that Moses could not enter because the glory was too full — resolved in the New Testament by a high priest who entered the Most Holy Place not with animal blood but with his own (Hebrews 9:12) — suggests that the Tabernacle's story is not closed at Exodus 40 but opened: the glory has arrived, and the question of how human beings can stand in its presence is still being answered.

intro: Ezekiel 1 is the merkavah — the chariot-throne vision. It is the most described, most debated, most carefully restricted passage in ancient Judaism: certain rabbis ruled it could only be taught to a scholar one-on-one. The vision deliberately resists clarity — the language piles up likenesses upon likenesses ('the likeness of,' 'like,' 'as it were'), guarding the Holy from any final grasp. It is not careless obscurity; it is theological grammar.

notes.original: biš'nat ha-šəlōšîm — in the thirtieth year
notes.rendering: in the thirtieth year
notes.why: The thirtieth year is most likely Ezekiel's own age — the year a Levitical priest would enter full service. He is by the Chebar canal instead of the Jerusalem altar. The irony is structural.

notes.original: marʾôṯ ʾĕlōhîm — visions of God
notes.rendering: visions of God
notes.why: marʾôṯ = visions (plural); ʾĕlōhîm used here as an intensifier (divine visions, extraordinary visions). The word marʾeh ('appearance') recurs throughout the chapter as the text insists on mediation between viewer and Reality.

notes.original: ḥašmal — gleaming metal
notes.rendering: something like gleaming metal
notes.why: ḥašmal is a hapax in this sense; ancient translators puzzled over it. LXX: ēlektron (amber/electrum). Rashi: a kind of supernatural fire. Modern: possibly electrum (gold-silver alloy). The word carries an aura of danger — something unnameable at the center of the fire.

notes.original: pənê ʾaryēh / pənê šôr / pənê nešer
notes.rendering: lion / ox / eagle faces
notes.why: The four faces recur in Revelation 4:7 as the four living creatures around the throne. Early Christian exegesis mapped them onto the four evangelists. In Ezekiel the faces represent the pinnacle of wild, domestic, aerial, and human creation — the whole creaturely world before the throne.

notes.original: ʿôp̄an bəṯôḵ ʿôp̄an — a wheel within a wheel
notes.rendering: one wheel inside another
notes.why: The mechanical image suggests omni-directional movement requiring no turning — YHWH's mobility is total, unimpeded by orientation. The wheels moving with the creatures (vv. 19–21) means divine action is carried through creaturely agency without the creatures directing it.

notes.original: marʾēh haqqešeṯ — the appearance of the rainbow
notes.rendering: like the appearance of the rainbow
notes.why: The rainbow in Genesis 9 is God's covenant sign after the flood — mercy after judgment. Its appearance here, surrounding the glory, is probably not accidental: even in the vision of overwhelming divine power, the mercy-sign frames it. Ezekiel falls on his face.

intro: Chapter 2 is the call narrative. Its structure mirrors the great prophetic calls — Isaiah 6, Jeremiah 1 — but with a distinctive feature: the prophet is told before he starts that no one will listen, and he is commissioned anyway. 'Whether they hear or refuse' is the refrain. The scroll written on both sides — lamentations, mourning, woe — is what he will eat.

notes.original: ben-ʾādām — son of man
notes.rendering: son of man
notes.why: ben-ʾādām = son of a human being; the phrase appears 93 times in Ezekiel — the most of any book. It simultaneously addresses Ezekiel's humanity and marks the distance between the human and the divine voice addressing him. Daniel and (later) the New Testament will develop it in new directions.

notes.original: gôy ha-môrədîm — nation of rebels
notes.rendering: nation of rebels
notes.why: môrədîm = active participle: those who are in the act of rebelling. The rebellion is continuous, not merely historical. 'They and their fathers' spans generations — this is not a recent failure but a constitutive one.

notes.original: qimməšônîm ûsəlônîm — briers and thorns
notes.rendering: briers and thorns
notes.why: Both words are rare; qimmāšôn appears only here and in Hosea 9:6. The image is of the prophet sitting in hostile terrain — like clearing brushland — and the 'scorpions' beneath may be literal or figurative for enemies. The triple 'do not fear' marks how formidable the commission is.

notes.original: qînîm wə-hegeh wā-hî — lamentations, mourning, woe
notes.rendering: lamentations and mourning and woe
notes.why: Three words for grief, escalating in weight. The scroll is pre-written — the prophet does not compose his message, he receives it. Written on front and back: not a short message. There is much grief to announce.

intro: Chapter 3 brings together the scroll-eating (sweetness despite the content of grief), the watchman commission, and the binding/muteness that will mark Ezekiel's ministry. The prophet who must speak is rendered mute — he will only speak when YHWH opens his mouth. This is perhaps the most theologically precise description of prophetic inspiration in the Bible.

notes.original: mātôq kəḏḇaš — sweet as honey
notes.rendering: sweet as honey
notes.why: The same image appears in Ps 19:10 and Rev 10:9–10 (where the scroll is sweet in the mouth but bitter in the stomach). Ezekiel gives no such qualification — the word of YHWH is simply sweet, even if its content is lamentation. The prophet's relationship to the word transcends its message.

notes.original: ḥizzəqê-mēṣaḥ ûqəšēh-lēḇ — hard forehead, stubborn heart
notes.rendering: hard forehead and stubborn heart
notes.why: mēṣaḥ = forehead (the place of visible expression; a hard forehead is a shameless face); lēḇ = heart (the seat of will and decision). The diagnosis is complete: no shame and no yielding. YHWH responds by making Ezekiel's forehead harder still — diamond against flint.

notes.original: Tel-abib / šāmem — overwhelmed
notes.rendering: overwhelmed among them for seven days
notes.why: Tel-abib (tel = mound, abib = grain-ear; possibly 'mound of the flood' in Akkadian: til abubi) was an exile settlement. šāmem = stupefied, stunned, overwhelmed; the same root as šammāh (desolation) used of the land throughout the book. The prophet is desolated before he preaches desolation.

notes.original: ṣôpeh nəṯattîḵā — watchman I have made you
notes.rendering: I have made you a watchman
notes.why: ṣāpāh = to watch, to scan the horizon (from a high place). The watchman's job is not to compose news but to relay what is coming. His responsibility is the warning; the response is the hearer's. This reframes prophetic accountability with precision: guilt attaches to silence, not to unbelief.

notes.original: lǝšônkā ʾadbîq — your tongue I will stick
notes.rendering: I will make your tongue stick
notes.why: Total muteness — not selective silence but the prophet's voice completely under divine control. The mouth that ate the scroll sweet will not speak until given permission. The contrast with the talkativeness of later false prophets (ch. 13) is pointed.

intro: Ezekiel 4 is the first of the enacted prophecies — Ezekiel uses his own body as a scroll. He draws Jerusalem on a clay brick, lays siege to it in miniature, then lies on his side for over a year bearing the years of Israel's and Judah's sin. The siege bread rations prefigure the actual famine during the 586 siege. The prophet's body precedes historical reality.

notes.original: l'ḇēnāh — clay tablet
notes.rendering: clay tablet
notes.why: liḇnāh = brick, tile; the medium of Babylonian city-mapping. Ezekiel uses the conquerors' material to depict the conquered city — a quietly devastating irony.

notes.original: šəlōš-mēʾôṯ ûtəšîʿîm — 390 days
notes.rendering: 390 days
notes.why: The chronological reckoning is debated; 390 years approximately reaches back to the division of the kingdom (930 BCE). The forty days for Judah may point to the forty years of wilderness wandering. The numbers are symbolic-historical, not merely arithmetical.

notes.original: gəlĕlê ha-ʾāḏām — human dung
notes.rendering: human dung
notes.why: The use of human waste for fuel — the most extreme defilement for a priest — images the total collapse of the covenant order. Ezekiel's protest (v. 14) is the only instance in the book where he pushes back on a command, and YHWH immediately accommodates him: cow dung instead.

notes.original: lōʾ nitméʾtî — I have never defiled myself
notes.rendering: I have never defiled myself
notes.why: The priestly protest of a priest whose entire identity is bound to purity distinctions. Ezekiel's objection is honored — the one place in the book where prophetic duty and priestly identity negotiate. Paul cites a similar issue in 1 Cor 8, though in a very different key.

intro: The razor-and-hair sign is followed by the most explicit statement of Jerusalem's unique culpability in the entire book: she was set at the center of the nations as a light, and she became darker than those around her. The punishment is correspondingly superlative: what I will do to you, I have never done before and will never do again.

notes.original: tahar ha-gallaabim -- barber razor
notes.rendering: barber razor
notes.why: A priest shaving his own head is defilement (Lev 21:5); the command enacts the very thing the law forbids. Ezekiel body is undone by the signs he must perform.

notes.original: bəṯôḵ haggôyim — center of the nations
notes.rendering: center of the nations
notes.why: Jerusalem as omphalos — the navel of the earth. The cosmological privilege heightens the guilt: given the center, she scattered. Medieval maps (mappa mundi) literally placed Jerusalem at the center; this verse is part of the theological cartography.

notes.original: hămōnəkem — turbulent / more than the nations
notes.rendering: more turbulent than the nations
notes.why: hāmôn = noise, tumult, multitude; here a moral turbulence. The argument is rhetorical: even the nations follow some moral order; Israel has not followed hers. Paul makes a related point in Romans 2.

notes.original: bəqinʾāṯî — in my jealousy
notes.rendering: in my jealousy
notes.why: qinʾāh = zeal, jealousy — the word used of YHWH throughout the covenant texts. It is not petty jealousy but the jealousy of covenant betrayal: the passion of a spouse who has been unfaithful to. Ezekiel will develop the marriage metaphor fully in chapters 16 and 23.

intro: Chapter 6 turns the oracular address to the mountains themselves — the high places where Israel worships at outdoor shrines. The judgments are spatial: the landscape of idolatry becomes the landscape of desolation. But within the judgment comes the first note of remnant and remembrance — a small but decisive opening.

notes.original: hārê yiśrāʾēl — mountains of Israel
notes.rendering: mountains of Israel
notes.why: The mountains are addressed as legal parties; the land itself participates in the covenant and the judgment. This is not animism but covenant theology: the land YHWH gave can be rendered desolate by its inhabitants' unfaithfulness (Lev 18:28).

notes.original: nišbartî — I have been broken
notes.rendering: I have been broken
notes.why: nišbar = passive of šābar — broken, shattered. YHWH describes himself as broken over Israel's idolatry. The image is staggering: the covenant God experiences something like grief or injury in the rupture. This is one of the most intimate divine self-disclosures in the prophets.

notes.original: lāzōnîm — lustful
notes.rendering: lustful heart / eyes that go lusting
notes.why: The same sexual vocabulary used throughout Ezekiel for idolatry: adultery, prostitution, lust. Israel's relationship with YHWH is cast as a marriage; going after other gods is sexual betrayal. Chapters 16 and 23 will extend this metaphor to its fullest — and most disturbing — expression.

notes.original: middeḇar diḇlāṯāh — from wilderness to Riblah
notes.rendering: from wilderness to Riblah
notes.why: Riblah (in Syria) marked the northern extreme of the land; the wilderness the southern. The desolation is total — from one end of the promised land to the other. Riblah is also where Nebuchadnezzar executed Zedekiah's sons and blinded the king (2 Kings 25:6–7) — a grim double reference.

intro: Chapter 7 is one long tolling of doom — a drumbeat of 'end,' 'coming,' 'day.' The Hebrew is deliberately breathless and repetitive, piling up synonyms for disaster the way a collapsing structure piles up debris. The most devastating line is v. 26: prophet, priest, and elder all fail simultaneously — the three institutions of covenant mediation go dark at once.

notes.original: ha-qetz ba — the end is coming
notes.rendering: the end has come
notes.why: The same wordplay as Amos 8:2 (qayitz/qetz). The end (qetz) has awakened (heqitz) against you (v. 6) — YHWH uses the sound of the word as part of the announcement. Ezekiel inherits Amos's rhetoric.

notes.original: hatzpira ba — your doom / the crown
notes.rendering: your doom has come
notes.why: Tzpira is rare: possibly 'doom' (so most translators) or 'crown/wreath' (LXX: heos). If crown, the image is ironic: your coronation day is your execution day.

notes.original: zehavam l'niddah — their gold becomes unclean
notes.rendering: their gold becomes unclean
notes.why: Niddah = the ritual impurity of menstruation — the most complete defilement image in Torah. Wealth that was their idol is now utterly defiling. The very thing they trusted becomes what separates them from God.

notes.original: hazon m'navi — vision from the prophet
notes.rendering: they will seek a vision from the prophet
notes.why: Triple institutional collapse: prophet (vision), priest (torah/law), elder (counsel). These are the three channels of divine guidance in Israel. All three go silent on the day of disaster. Compare Micah 3:11 — when all three are corrupted, the silence is their judgment.

intro: Chapter 8 is a guided tour of desecration. Ezekiel is transported to Jerusalem in a vision and shown, chamber by chamber, what is happening inside the temple complex: an idol in the north gate, secret rites in the dark, women weeping for the Babylonian fertility god Tammuz, men worshipping the sun with their backs to the Holy Place. Each revelation ends with 'you will see greater abominations still.'

notes.original: semel haqin'ah — image of jealousy
notes.rendering: image of jealousy
notes.why: Semel = image, statue; qin'ah = jealousy (the covenant word for YHWH's passionate exclusivity). The statue provokes YHWH's covenant jealousy by its very presence at the temple gate. Some scholars identify it with the Asherah pole Manasseh installed (2 Kings 21:7).

notes.original: shiv'im ish — seventy elders
notes.rendering: seventy elders
notes.why: Seventy is the number of the Sanhedrin and echoes the seventy elders who ate and drank before YHWH at Sinai (Exod 24:9–11). The same number who stood in the presence of God at Sinai now stand burning incense to idols in the dark. The corruption is total, from the top.

notes.original: mevakot et ha-Tammuz — weeping for Tammuz
notes.rendering: weeping for Tammuz
notes.why: Tammuz (Dumuzi in Sumerian) was a Babylonian vegetation deity who died each year and was mourned in summer rites. The women weeping for him are practicing fertility cult worship inside the temple precincts — the Babylonian captors' religion has penetrated the house of the God who sent Babylon against them.

notes.original: mishtachavitim qedmah la-shemesh — worshipping toward the east
notes.rendering: worshipping the sun toward the east
notes.why: Their backs to the Holy of Holies, faces east toward the rising sun — the posture of sun worship is the inversion of temple worship. The deliberate turning of the back is the physical enactment of apostasy. The detail is anatomical and damning.

notes.original: shalchu et ha-zmorat — they put the branch to their nose
notes.rendering: they put the branch to their nose
notes.why: One of the most obscure phrases in Ezekiel. The 'branch' (zmoret) may refer to a ritual object in sun worship; some translate as 'stench' (reading z'morotam). Either way, the image is of wanton provocation right under YHWH's nose, in his own house.

intro: Chapter 9 is one of the most theologically charged passages in the prophets: the slaughter of Jerusalem begins at the temple itself, with the elders (cf. chapter 8's seventy), but the man in linen first marks those who grieve over the city's sin. The mark on the forehead anticipates Revelation 7 and 14. The criterion of survival is not ethnic identity but moral sensitivity to sin.

notes.original: ish lavush ha-badim — man clothed in linen
notes.rendering: man clothed in linen
notes.why: Linen (bad) is the priestly garment (Lev 16:4). The recording angel wears the high priest's clothing — he is the one who marks the innocent, as the priest marks what is holy. He appears again in chapters 10 and Daniel 10, 12.

notes.original: tav — the mark
notes.rendering: put a mark on the foreheads
notes.why: Tav is the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet; in the ancient script (paleo-Hebrew) it was written as an X or a cross. The mark (tav) that saves is the final letter — a detail the early church found irresistible. Origen, Tertullian, and Jerome all note it. The mark identifies those who groan over sin — grief is the saving sign.

notes.original: ha-ne'enachim v'ha-ne'enaqim — those who sigh and groan
notes.rendering: who sigh and groan over all the abominations
notes.why: Two different words for grief: ne'enach (to sigh, to moan) and ne'enaq (to cry out, to groan under weight). Both are physical, bodily expressions of anguish. Moral grief — not moral performance — is the criterion. This is astonishing: what preserves them is that they feel what YHWH feels.

notes.original: u-mimikdashi tachelu — begin at my sanctuary
notes.rendering: begin at my sanctuary
notes.why: Judgment begins at the house of God — a principle Peter will cite directly in 1 Pet 4:17. The elders who were burning incense to idols in chapter 8 are the first to fall. Greater privilege, greater accountability: the most theologically central statement of the chapter.

intro: Chapter 10 is the beginning of the glory's departure — one of the most momentous movements in the entire Bible. The divine presence, which had filled the temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10–11), now begins to withdraw. It moves to the threshold, then to the east gate (v. 19), and will eventually leave the city entirely (11:23). The chapter deliberately echoes chapter 1: Ezekiel confirms these are the same creatures he saw at Chebar.

notes.original: gachalei esh — burning coals
notes.rendering: burning coals
notes.why: The coals scattered over the city prefigure the actual burning of Jerusalem (586 BCE). The fire comes from between the cherubim — from the very presence of God. Judgment is not an absence of God but an act of God. Compare Isaiah 6:6–7 where a coal from the altar purifies the prophet's lips.

notes.original: vayarom kevod YHWH — the glory rose
notes.rendering: the glory of YHWH rises
notes.why: The beginning of the departure. YHWH's kavod (glory, weight, presence) had been enthroned between the cherubim in the Holy of Holies since Solomon's dedication. Its rising from the cherub is the beginning of the end of the first temple. This movement will take three stages: cherub to threshold (10:4), threshold to east gate (10:19), east gate to the mountain east of the city (11:23).

notes.original: ha-galgal — the whirling wheels
notes.rendering: the whirling wheels
notes.why: Galgal = wheel, whirl, rolling thing. The word is onomatopoeic in Hebrew. In later Jewish mysticism (merkavah tradition) these wheels become the ofanim — a class of angels. The sound of the wheels is like the voice of God Almighty (v. 5) — the mobility of the divine presence is deafening.

notes.original: penei ha-keruv — face of a cherub
notes.rendering: the face of a cherub
notes.why: In chapter 1 the first face was an ox face; here it is a cherub face. This may be a textual variant or a deliberate theological revision: the ox-face of creaturely vulnerability is here named as the cherub-face of divine attendant. Ezekiel's later reference (1:10) clarifies the ox reading; the discrepancy may be intentional.

intro: Chapter 11 contains both the final departure of the glory and the first great promise of the new heart — the passage that Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 will develop into the new covenant. The departure of the glory (v. 23) to the Mount of Olives is the theological nadir of the book: YHWH has left his house. The promise of the new heart is offered in the same breath.

notes.original: hi ha-sir v'anachnu ha-basar — the city is the pot, we are the meat
notes.rendering: the city is the pot, and we are the meat
notes.why: The princes boast: we are protected inside Jerusalem like meat in a cooking pot. Ezekiel inverts the metaphor: the slain in the streets are the meat; the princes will be extracted from the pot and judged outside it. The image they chose as comfort becomes their condemnation.

notes.original: Pelatyah ben-Benayah vayyamot — Pelatiah died
notes.rendering: Pelatiah the son of Benaiah dies
notes.why: A named figure in the vision dies during the vision — one of the strangest moments in the book. Is this a real-time death five hundred miles away? A vision of a death to come? Either way, Ezekiel reacts with the same intercession as chapter 9. The prophet cannot help but plead for the people he is sent to condemn.

notes.original: mikdash me'at — a sanctuary for a while / a little sanctuary
notes.rendering: I have been a sanctuary to them for a while
notes.why: Me'at = a little, a small amount, a while. YHWH himself becomes the temple for the exiles who have no temple — the radical claim that divine presence does not require the building. The synagogue as institution may root partly in this verse. Rabbinic tradition reads it as: wherever Israel is exiled, the Shekhinah goes with them.

notes.original: lev echad — one heart / lev basar — heart of flesh
notes.rendering: one heart / heart of flesh
notes.why: The new heart promise: one (echad) heart — undivided, not pulled in multiple directions by multiple loyalties. And flesh (basar) instead of stone (even) — not harder but softer; not invulnerable but feelable. The heart that can be wounded is the heart that can love. Ezekiel 36:26 will repeat this promise in expanded form.

notes.original: vayamod al ha-har asher miqqedem la'ir — stands on the mountain east of the city
notes.rendering: stands on the mountain east of the city
notes.why: The Mount of Olives — the same mountain from which, according to Zechariah 14:4, YHWH will return. The glory pauses on the mount before departing entirely. The return route is thus already implied in the departure.

intro: Chapter 12 contains two enacted signs and a direct confrontation with the popular proverb that prophecy never comes true. The baggage-of-exile sign enacts the coming deportation; the hole in the wall specifically predicts Zedekiah's escape attempt (2 Kings 25:4–7 — he flees by night through a breach, is caught, and is blinded before being taken to Babylon: he went to Babylon but did not see it). The final section attacks prophetic cynicism head-on.

notes.original: keli golah — exile's baggage
notes.rendering: exile's baggage
notes.why: Keli = vessel, implement, baggage; golah = exile (from galah, to uncover, to go into exile). The exile's bundle is the sign. Everything Ezekiel carries becomes a visual sermon: the audience is watching whether they understand it or not.

notes.original: ot natattika — I have made you a sign
notes.rendering: I have made you a sign
notes.why: The prophet's body is the sign (ot). Ot is the same word as the mark/tav in chapter 9 and the rainbow-sign of Genesis 9. Ezekiel's whole life becomes a semiotic act: eating, lying down, shaving, packing — all of it is divine communication.

notes.original: lo yireh otah — he shall not see it
notes.rendering: he shall not see it
notes.why: A precise prediction: Zedekiah will go to Babylon but not see it — because Nebuchadnezzar blinds him at Riblah before the deportation (2 Kings 25:7). The word of YHWH fulfills itself in a detail so specific it reads as either remarkable prophecy or post-event narration. The text itself takes the former position.

notes.original: kol chazon l'navi — every vision comes to nothing
notes.rendering: every vision comes to nothing
notes.why: A popular proverb of prophetic skepticism — the ancient equivalent of 'preachers have been saying the end is near for centuries.' YHWH's response is not to extend the timeline but to shorten it: the days are near, not far. The problem with 'the end is always delayed' is that one day it isn't.

intro: Chapter 13 is Ezekiel’s most sustained attack on false prophecy. The central image is devastating: the false prophets are like builders who whitewash a flimsy wall — cosmetic work that makes structural rot look sound. When the storm comes, wall and plasterers fall together. The section on prophetesses (vv. 17–23) addresses women practicing a form of binding magic — a rare direct oracle against female religious practitioners.

notes.original: ke-shu'alim ba-choravot — like jackals among ruins
notes.rendering: like jackals among ruins
notes.why: Jackals (shu'alim) inhabit desolate places; these prophets do not build but scavenge. They exploit collapse rather than preventing it. The image positions them as creatures of the disaster they help cause.

notes.original: lo alitem ba-perazot — you have not gone up into the breaches
notes.rendering: you have not gone up into the breaches
notes.why: The breach (peretz) in a city wall is where defenders must stand. The prophet’s job is to stand in the gap between the people and judgment — to intercede, to repair, to hold. The false prophets abandon the wall and plaster it from a safe distance.

notes.original: shalom v’ein shalom — peace when there is no peace
notes.rendering: peace when there is no peace
notes.why: Shalom = wholeness, completeness, right-orderedness. The false prophets announce it when the social and spiritual fabric is shredded. Jeremiah faces the identical charge (Jer 6:14; 8:11): the two prophets are parallel witnesses to the same institutional failure.

notes.original: kesatot — magic bands
notes.rendering: magic bands
notes.why: Kesatot is a hapax — its meaning is uncertain. LXX: proskephalaia (pillows/cushions). The most likely reading is binding amulets worn on the wrist, used in a form of soul-hunting magic. The prophetesses profit from both killing (cursing) and preserving (blessing) souls — for barley and bread.

intro: Chapter 14 introduces the doctrine of idols in the heart — inner religious allegiance that makes even sincere-looking consultation of the prophet useless — and then pushes individual accountability to its limit: even the three most righteous men in tradition (Noah, Daniel, Job) could not save anyone but themselves when a land’s sin reaches saturation. Corporate solidarity does not override personal accountability.

notes.original: gillulim b’lib’bam — idols in their hearts
notes.rendering: idols into their hearts
notes.why: Gillulim is Ezekiel’s characteristic contempt-word for idols (used 39 times in the book), likely derived from galal (dung-pellets). The idols are not merely in shrines but interiorized — the problem has moved inside. This is Ezekiel’s most psychologically penetrating diagnosis.

notes.original: pittîthi et ha-navi — I have deceived that prophet
notes.rendering: I, YHWH, have deceived that prophet
notes.why: One of the most disturbing verses in the prophets: YHWH permits or causes false prophets to be deceived when they serve a people who consult with idols in their hearts. Compare 1 Kings 22:20–22 (the lying spirit in the prophets’ mouths). The hardening of Pharaoh’s heart operates by similar logic.

notes.original: No’ach Dani’el v’Iyov — Noah, Daniel, and Job
notes.rendering: Noah, Daniel, and Job
notes.why: The three are not the obvious triad. Daniel here is almost certainly not the book’s protagonist (who would be a contemporary of Ezekiel, not yet legendary) but the ancient Ugaritic figure Danel, a righteous judge known from Canaanite literature. All three survived catastrophic judgment by personal righteousness alone.

notes.original: arba’ shefatai ha-ra’im — my four disastrous acts
notes.rendering: my four disastrous acts of judgment
notes.why: Sword, famine, beasts, pestilence — the tetrad of covenant curse (Lev 26; Deut 32). They appear as YHWH’s four weapons throughout Ezekiel (5:17; 14:21; 33:27). The fourfold redundancy enacts completeness: no angle of escape.

intro: Chapter 15 is the shortest in the book — eight verses, one image, one point. The vine (Israel’s traditional self-image, from Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5) is shown to be worthless as timber: it produces fruit or it produces nothing. Charred at both ends, it is fit only for burning. The allegory’s brevity is its force.

notes.original: etz ha-gefen — the wood of the vine
notes.rendering: the wood of the vine
notes.why: The vine (gefen) is Israel’s proudest self-image: Ps 80:8–11 (you brought a vine out of Egypt), Isa 5:1–7 (the vineyard song), John 15:1 (I am the true vine). Ezekiel takes this cherished symbol and asks: what is vine wood actually good for? Nothing. It cannot even make a peg.

notes.original: lim’lacha — useful for anything
notes.rendering: useful for anything
notes.why: The repeated question (vv. 3, 4, 5) builds the case by logic: if the vine is worthless whole, it is more worthless charred. The argument moves from general to particular — and the particular is Jerusalem, now burned at both ends by the first deportation and awaiting final destruction.

intro: Chapter 16 is the longest in Ezekiel and the most disturbing in the entire Bible. It is a sustained metaphor of marriage betrayal: YHWH as husband, Jerusalem as wife rescued from abandonment as an infant. The explicit sexual imagery is unrelenting and has occasioned enormous interpretive debate across centuries. But the chapter ends where no one expects: with the unconditional promise of an everlasting covenant — not because Jerusalem deserves it, but because YHWH remembers.

notes.original: b’yom huledet otach — on the day you were born
notes.rendering: on the day you were born
notes.why: The birth scene itemizes the care a newborn should receive and did not: cord uncut, no water-washing, no salt-rubbing, no swaddling. Abandonment at birth was practiced in the ancient world; the infant girl is cast into an open field. YHWH’s act of saying ‘Live!’ twice (v. 6) is pure gratuitous grace with no precondition.

notes.original: ufʾros kanaph — I spread the corner of my garment
notes.rendering: I spread the corner of my garment over you
notes.why: The gesture of covering with the garment’s corner (kanaph) is the marriage proposal gesture — Ruth uses it to propose to Boaz (Ruth 3:9). The same word. YHWH’s proposal to Jerusalem is an echo of Boaz’s kinsman-redeemer role. The covenant is framed as marriage from the beginning.

notes.original: gaʾavon... shʾbat hashqet vʾshalom — pride, excess of food, prosperous ease
notes.rendering: pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease
notes.why: Ezekiel’s definition of Sodom’s sin — notably absent: sexual immorality (the traditional reading). The Sodom of Ezekiel 16 is condemned for comfortable indifference to the poor. This verse reframes the entire Sodom tradition and is cited widely in social ethics discussions.

notes.original: vʾzkharti ani et bʾiriti — yet I will remember my covenant
notes.rendering: yet I will remember my covenant
notes.why: The turn of the chapter. After the most extended indictment in the Bible, YHWH does not say: therefore I am done with you. He says: I will remember. The covenant is not contingent on Israel’s faithfulness but on YHWH’s memory. This is the theological axis on which the whole terrible chapter turns.

notes.original: bʾkhaphʾri lach — when I atone for you
notes.rendering: when I atone for you for all that you have done
notes.why: Kipper — to atone, to cover, to ransom. YHWH himself will perform the atonement for all that Jerusalem has done. The shame that silences (you will never open your mouth again) is not the silence of condemnation but the silence of one who has been forgiven more than they can speak. Paul’s argument in Romans 11 operates in a similar register.

intro: Chapter 17 is a mashal — a riddle-allegory — followed by its own interpretation. The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar, the cedar-top is Jehoiachin, the planted vine is Zedekiah. The second eagle is Pharaoh, and Zedekiah’s treacherous turn toward Egypt is the vine bending toward the second eagle. But the chapter does not end with Zedekiah’s judgment: it ends with YHWH planting his own tender twig on the mountain of Israel — the messianic shoot.

notes.original: nesher gadol — great eagle
notes.rendering: a great eagle
notes.why: The eagle (nesher) is the royal image of Babylon throughout the ancient Near East. The cedar of Lebanon is the traditional symbol of Judean royalty. The allegory maps the political situation precisely: Babylon takes the crown prince (Jehoiachin) to Babylon (a city of merchants) and plants a vassal king (Zedekiah) in Jerusalem.

notes.original: lishmorot et bʾirito — by keeping his covenant
notes.rendering: by keeping his covenant it might stand
notes.why: Zedekiah’s oath to Nebuchadnezzar is treated by Ezekiel as binding before YHWH — not merely a political arrangement but a covenantal obligation. When Zedekiah breaks it, he is not just committing treason; he is covenant-breaking in a theological sense. YHWH is the guarantor of oaths.

notes.original: anokhi eqqach — I myself will take
notes.rendering: I myself will take
notes.why: The emphatic ani (I) signals a divine act in contrast to Nebuchadnezzar’s taking (v. 3). What the empire seized, YHWH will plant — a tender twig from the same cedar. The messianic reading is irresistible: the Davidic sprig planted by God himself on the mountain of Israel. Compare Isa 11:1 (a shoot from the stump of Jesse).

notes.original: kol tzipor kol kanaf — every kind of bird
notes.rendering: every kind of bird
notes.why: The great tree sheltering birds of every kind echoes Daniel 4 and the Parable of the Mustard Seed (Matt 13:31–32). The image is of universal shelter under the restored Davidic kingdom — the nations finding refuge in Israel’s restoration.

intro: Chapter 18 is the Magna Carta of individual accountability in the Hebrew Bible. It directly attacks the popular proverb of inherited guilt (‘the fathers ate sour grapes’) and replaces it with a radical assertion: every soul answers to God for its own conduct — not its parents’. The chapter ends with one of the most urgent invitations in the prophets: turn, and live.

notes.original: avot yochlu voser — the fathers ate sour grapes
notes.rendering: the fathers have eaten sour grapes
notes.why: The proverb is also cited in Jeremiah 31:29–30, where the new covenant specifically abolishes it. The exiles use it as a fatalistic excuse: we are suffering for what our ancestors did. Ezekiel’s counter is structural: three generations, each judged on their own account.

notes.original: hanefesh hachotet hi tamut — the soul who sins shall die
notes.rendering: the soul who sins shall die
notes.why: Nefesh = the living self, the whole person (not merely the spiritual component). The statement is repeated in v. 20 as a theological axiom. Each person’s account is individual before God. This does not negate corporate solidarity (Ezekiel is acutely aware of communal sin) but it does resist fatalistic paralysis.

notes.original: hachafetz achpatz bʾmot harasha — have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?
notes.rendering: have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked?
notes.why: The rhetorical question expects the answer: no. YHWH does not delight in judgment — he delights in the turning (shuv) of the wicked. This verse has been foundational in Christian and Jewish theology of repentance: divine judgment is the last resort, not the first desire.

notes.original: asu lachem lev chadash vʾruach chadasha — make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit
notes.rendering: make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit
notes.why: In chapter 11:19 and 36:26, YHWH promises to give the new heart. Here he commands Israel to make it. The tension is intentional: repentance is both divine gift and human act. The paradox is never resolved in Ezekiel — it is held as the full truth of what transformation requires.

notes.original: shuvu vʾchiyu — turn and live
notes.rendering: turn, and live
notes.why: Shuv — the great prophetic word for repentance: to turn around, to return. It is physical, directional, total. The entire chapter builds to these two words. The invitation is unconditional: any soul, any time, the door is open.

intro: Chapter 19 is a qinah — a formal funeral dirge, sung in the limping 3+2 meter of Hebrew lament. It is the only complete poem in the first half of the book. The two cubs represent Jehoahaz (taken to Egypt by Pharaoh Necho, 2 Kings 23:33–34) and Jehoiachin or Zedekiah (taken to Babylon). The vine section repeats the vine imagery of chapters 15 and 17, but now as elegy: once towering, now burning.

notes.original: qinah — lament / dirge
notes.rendering: raise up a lament
notes.why: Qinah is both the genre name and the meter: lines of 3+2 stresses, the long line followed by a short one, enacting a kind of limping grief. Amos used it over living Israel (Amos 5:2); Ezekiel uses it over the princes. The form itself is the message: these are already dead.

notes.original: beshachat nitkad — caught in their pit
notes.rendering: caught in their pit
notes.why: Shachat = pit, trap (also used for the grave/Sheol). The lion who hunted men is himself hunted — the hunter becomes prey. Jehoahaz was taken to Egypt in 609 BCE and died there. His capture is described with the same vocabulary as animal trapping.

notes.original: ruach ha-qadim hovisha piryah — east wind dried up its fruit
notes.rendering: the east wind dried up its fruit
notes.why: The east wind (qadim) is the sirocco, the hot desert wind from the Arabian plateau that scorches vegetation. Throughout Ezekiel it is the image of Babylonian conquest. The vine that once promised scepters is now fuel. Chapter 15’s logic returns: vine wood is good for nothing but fire.

notes.original: vʾthi qinah hi — it has become a lamentation
notes.rendering: this is a lamentation, and it has become a lamentation
notes.why: The closing line is unusual: the prophet notes that the qinah is itself now a qinah — the lament has become reality. The word-sign and the historical event have merged. What was sung in anticipation is now sung in fulfillment.

intro: Chapter 20 is the most comprehensive historical review in Ezekiel — a three-generation account of rebellion in Egypt, in the wilderness (first generation), and in the wilderness again (second generation), plus the entry into Canaan. At every point YHWH restrains judgment for the sake of his own name. The chapter’s theological centre is the name-logic: God’s faithfulness is grounded not in Israel’s merit but in YHWH’s own reputation among the nations.

notes.original: lemaʾan shʾmi — for the sake of my name
notes.rendering: I acted for the sake of my name
notes.why: The phrase repeats three times (vv. 9, 14, 22) — once for each generation. YHWH’s restraint is not sentimentality but reputation: if he destroyed Israel in Egypt or the wilderness, the nations would conclude his promise was empty. His faithfulness is a theological necessity, not merely an emotional one. Paul develops this in Romans 3:25–26.

notes.original: et Shabbetotai natati lahem — my Sabbaths I gave them
notes.rendering: I gave them my Sabbaths, as a sign
notes.why: The Sabbath as covenant sign (ot) echoes Exodus 31:13–17. In Ezekiel’s theology, Sabbath-breaking is not merely liturgical failure but covenant betrayal — the visible weekly sign of who owns Israel’s time. It becomes a marker of apostasy throughout the book.

notes.original: gam ani natati lahem chuqqim lo tovim — I gave them statutes that were not good
notes.rendering: I gave them statutes that were not good
notes.why: One of the most disturbing verses in the book. YHWH says he gave Israel bad laws — permitting or even ordaining their moral degradation as judgment. This likely refers to the laws permitting child sacrifice being ‘given’ in the sense of not being prevented: divine abandonment to the logic of their own idolatry. Compare Romans 1:24–28 (God gave them up).

notes.original: bʾmassort ha-bʾrit — into the bond of the covenant
notes.rendering: into the bond of the covenant
notes.why: Massoret = bond, binding, obligation. The image of passing under the rod is the shepherd counting sheep — each one assessed, the rebels separated. The new exodus will involve a new wilderness winnowing before the land is entered. The covenant is re-established, not abandoned.

intro: Chapter 21 is the sword poem — the most kinetically violent chapter in Ezekiel. The sword is sharpened, polished, drawn, and wielded; YHWH himself claps his hands as it falls. The crossroads scene (vv. 18–22) is remarkable: Nebuchadnezzar at the fork in the road, shaking arrows and reading livers to decide whether to go to Jerusalem or Rabbah. The point: even pagan divination is YHWH’s instrument.

notes.original: hikhrati mimech tzaddiq vʾrashah — cut off righteous and wicked
notes.rendering: cut off both righteous and wicked
notes.why: The sword does not discriminate — war never does. This is not a reversal of chapter 18’s individual accountability but its complement: historical catastrophe is not a precise instrument. The righteous die in the fall of cities. Ezekiel does not paper over this.

notes.original: bʾqilqal chitzim — he shakes the arrows
notes.rendering: he shakes the arrows
notes.why: Belomancy — divination by arrows. The arrows are marked with place-names and shaken; the one that falls out first indicates where to attack. Nebuchadnezzar also reads sheep-livers (hepatoscopy) and consults household gods (teraphim). Three forms of divination — all pointing to Jerusalem. YHWH uses the whole pagan toolkit.

notes.original: hasir ha-mitznefet vʾharem ha-atarah — remove the turban, take off the crown
notes.rendering: remove the turban and take off the crown
notes.why: The priestly turban (mitznefet) and royal crown (atarah) are both stripped — the two institutions of Israelite leadership abolished together. The upheaval formula (exalt the low, bring low the exalted) appears also in the Magnificat (Luke 1:52) and is a recurring motif of divine reversal.

notes.original: ad bo asher lo ha-mishpat — until he comes whose right it is
notes.rendering: until he comes whose right it is
notes.why: A messianic formula — the same structure as Genesis 49:10 (the scepter shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh comes). The ruin is complete but not permanent: it holds until the rightful claimant arrives. The crown is not abolished; it is held in trust.

intro: Chapter 22 delivers three separate indictments: the city catalogued crime by crime, the furnace image (Israel as dross, Jerusalem as the smelting pot), and the four-station failure — prophets, priests, princes, people — each institution corrupt in sequence. The chapter ends with one of the most poignant verses in the book: YHWH searching for one intercessor, finding none.

notes.original: sigim hayu li — they have become dross to me
notes.rendering: the house of Israel has become dross
notes.why: Sigim = dross, the worthless residue left after smelting. Israel was supposed to be silver; instead the smelting process reveals only slag. The furnace image inverts the purification metaphor: usually the furnace refines; here it reveals there is nothing left to refine.

notes.original: vʾlo hivʾdilu bein ha-qodesh lʾkhol — no distinction between holy and common
notes.rendering: made no distinction between the holy and the common
notes.why: The priest’s foundational task is havdalah — distinction-making: holy/common, clean/unclean, permitted/forbidden. When the priests collapse the categories, the entire social and moral structure loses its grammar. Ezekiel the priest-prophet feels this failure with particular sharpness.

notes.original: vaʾavaqqesh mehem ish gozer gader — I sought for a man to build a wall
notes.rendering: I sought for a man who should build up the wall
notes.why: The image recalls 13:5 (false prophets not going up into the breaches). Now YHWH himself searches for an intercessor — an Abraham, a Moses — and finds none. The contrast with Moses in Ps 106:23 (he stood in the breach) is exact and devastating. The gap has no one in it.

intro: Chapter 23 is the companion to chapter 16, the most explicit of the two sisters allegories. Oholah (Samaria, the northern kingdom) and Oholibah (Jerusalem, the southern) are both condemned for political alliances with great powers framed as sexual betrayal of YHWH. The chapter is deliberately and shockingly graphic; its function is not titillation but horror — the same horror YHWH expresses at Israel’s apostasy.

notes.original: Oholah / Oholibah — her tent / my tent is in her
notes.rendering: Oholah" and "Oholibah
notes.why: Oholah = ‘her own tent’ — Samaria’s illegitimate sanctuaries (Bethel, Dan). Oholibah = ‘my tent is in her’ — Jerusalem, where the temple stood. Oholibah’s guilt is greater because YHWH’s presence was actually in her city. Greater gift, greater accountability: the logic of chapter 5 in two names.

notes.original: vʾtiqqa nephshah mehem — she turned from them in disgust
notes.rendering: she turned from them in disgust
notes.why: Naphsha tiqqa = her soul revolted from them. The verb tiqqeʹ means to be loathsome, to feel revulsion. Oholibah tires of her Babylonian lovers after using them — and then YHWH says: as she turned from them in disgust, so I turned from her in disgust (v. 18). The mirroring is exact and terrible.

notes.original: bʾderekh achotekh halakht — you have gone the way of your sister
notes.rendering: you have gone the way of your sister
notes.why: The cup of Samaria passes to Jerusalem. The cup (kos) imagery — drinking the cup of judgment — appears throughout the prophets (Isa 51:17, Jer 25:15–17) and reaches its NT resonance in Gethsemane (Matt 26:39). The cup Jerusalem drinks is her sister’s cup.

notes.original: uʾnegativʾtem chet gilluleikhem — bear the penalty for your sinful idolatry
notes.rendering: bear the penalty for your sinful idolatry
notes.why: The closing formula of the chapter: the women bear what they did. No proxy, no transfer. The accountability of chapter 18 applies at the corporate level too. And then: you shall know that I am YHWH. Even in the most extreme judgment, the purpose is recognition — not destruction for its own sake.

intro: Chapter 24 marks the pivot of the book. On the day the siege of Jerusalem begins, YHWH kills Ezekiel’s wife — and commands him not to mourn. His silent grief is the enacted sign of what Israel will feel when the temple falls: a grief too large for ritual, too total for tears. The chapter ends with the promise that when the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives, Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened. The long silence is almost over.

notes.original: kʾtov et shem ha-yom — write down the name of this day
notes.rendering: write down the name of this day
notes.why: The date — 10th Tevet, year 9 of Jehoiachin’s exile (January 588 BCE) — is the beginning of the siege of Jerusalem. It is still observed as a fast day in Judaism. The precision of Ezekiel’s dating system throughout the book (fifteen dated oracles) is part of his priestly character: records matter, history is specific.

notes.original: al tzachach sela samah — on the bare rock she put it
notes.rendering: she put it on the bare rock
notes.why: Blood uncovered — left visible instead of being absorbed into the earth (Lev 17:13, which requires covering blood with dust) — cries out for vengeance. The blood of Abel cried from the ground (Gen 4:10). Jerusalem’s blood is exposed on rock: it cannot sink in, it cannot be silenced, it must be answered.

notes.original: machmat einekha — the delight of your eyes
notes.rendering: the delight of your eyes
notes.why: The phrase is used twice: for Ezekiel’s wife (v. 16) and for the temple (v. 21). Wife and temple are parallel objects of grief — both taken on the same day (or signifying the same loss). Ezekiel’s domestic life is made a microcosm of national catastrophe. His personal grief is the nation’s grief, and he must not perform it.

notes.original: tippatach picha — your mouth will be opened
notes.rendering: your mouth will be opened
notes.why: The muteness of 3:26 is lifted at last — but only when the news arrives. Ezekiel has been unable to speak freely since his commission; when Jerusalem falls, he will speak again. The opening of his mouth is the end of the first movement of the book and the beginning of the second: from judgment to hope.

intro: Chapter 25 opens the oracles against the nations (chapters 25–32), turning the prophetic eye outward from Israel to her neighbours. Four oracles in quick succession: Ammon (gleeful at Jerusalem’s fall), Moab (dismissive: Judah is just another nation), Edom (vengeful), and Philistia (malicious ancient enmity). Each ends with the recognition formula: then they will know that I am YHWH.

notes.original: yaʾan amrekh ‘achʾ — because you said ‘Aha!’
notes.rendering: because you said ‘Aha!’
notes.why: The exclamation of malicious satisfaction at another’s ruin. Ach (or heach) is the sound of gloating — a wordless cry of delight at a rival’s collapse. Ammon’s sin is not military aggression but the joy of the spectator. Schadenfreude is judged.

notes.original: kʾkhol haggoyim beit Yehudah — like all the other nations
notes.rendering: the house of Judah is like all the other nations
notes.why: Moab’s theology: Judah has no special status; its God is one among many. This is the dismissal of YHWH’s covenant particularity. The response — judgment — is itself the demonstration that Judah is not like all the nations, because YHWH is not like all the gods.

notes.original: bʾhinaqem naqam — acting revengefully
notes.rendering: acted revengefully
notes.why: Edom’s sin is old and deep — the fraternal enmity of Esau and Jacob extended to national history. The book of Obadiah is devoted entirely to Edom’s conduct at the fall of Jerusalem. Here the charge is the same: exploiting the catastrophe of a brother.

notes.original: Kerethim — Cherethites
notes.rendering: Cherethites
notes.why: The Cherethites are a Philistine sub-group, likely Cretan in origin (keret = Crete in some readings). They are associated with the Philistines throughout Samuel and Kings. David’s personal guard included Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Sam 8:18) — irony that the king’s bodyguard came from the ancestral enemy.

intro: Chapter 26 opens the longest sustained oracle in the book — three full chapters (26–28) against the great Phoenician trading city of Tyre, the commercial superpower of the ancient Mediterranean. Tyre’s sin is commercial opportunism at Jerusalem’s expense: the gate of the peoples is broken, she says — now trade will flow through me instead. Greed that gloats over ruin is judged.

notes.original: shaʾar haʾammim — the gate of the peoples
notes.rendering: the gate of the peoples
notes.why: Jerusalem sat astride major trade routes; Tyre’s gloating is economic as much as military. With Jerusalem destroyed, Tyre expects the caravan trade to reroute through her. She is not an enemy of principle but of profit. Ezekiel’s judgment: commercial predation on human catastrophe is a sin.

notes.original: sikhsakhti atzamah — I will scrape her soil from her
notes.rendering: I will scrape her soil from her
notes.why: The image of the bare rock (tzur) is a wordplay on Tyre’s name (Tzor = rock, fortress). Tyre the rock-city will be scraped back to bare rock — the name becomes the judgment. The fulfilled image is remarkable: Alexander the Great in 332 BCE built a causeway to the island using the rubble of the mainland city, scraping it into the sea.

notes.original: vʾhehshavti harmon shirotayikh — I will stop the music of your songs
notes.rendering: I will stop the music of your songs
notes.why: The silencing of music marks total desolation — the same phrase appears in the oracles against Babylon (Isa 14:11) and echoes in Revelation 18:22 (the voice of harpists and musicians will be heard no more in you). Music is the sign of civic vitality; its absence is the sound of death.

notes.original: eretz tachtiot — the world below
notes.rendering: the world below
notes.why: The descent to the pit (bor) and the world below (tachtiot) uses the imagery of Sheol — the underworld. Tyre will join the company of dead cities, ancient ruins. The phrase ‘ruins from of old’ suggests a collective of destroyed civilisations. Babylon will receive the same sentence in chapter 32.

intro: Chapter 27 is the great trading inventory — the most detailed catalogue of ancient Mediterranean commerce in the Bible. Ezekiel constructs Tyre as a magnificent ship whose cargo list is the known trading world, then sinks her with the east wind. The chapter is simultaneously an economic document (scholars use it to reconstruct ancient trade routes) and a theological statement: commercial empire, however magnificent, is mortal.

notes.original: ani kʾlilat yofi — I am perfect in beauty
notes.rendering: I am perfect in beauty
notes.why: Kʾlilat yofi = completeness of beauty, perfection of beauty. The same phrase will be used of the prince of Tyre in chapter 28 (you were the seal of perfection) and ironically of Jerusalem in Lamentations 2:15 (is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty?). Beauty and pride are intertwined; both precede the fall.

notes.original: nefesh adam — human beings
notes.rendering: human beings
notes.why: Nefesh adam = human souls. Tyre traded in human slaves — listed matter-of-factly alongside bronze vessels. Ezekiel does not editorialize; the horror is in the plain listing. Amos 1:9 condemns Tyre for the same slave trade. The NT will echo the slave-trading list in Revelation 18:13 (bodies and souls of men).

notes.original: ruach ha-qadim — the east wind
notes.rendering: the east wind has wrecked you
notes.why: The east wind (qadim, the sirocco) is Ezekiel’s standard image for Babylon (as in 17:10, 19:12). The magnificent ship is sunk not by a military fleet but by a wind — YHWH’s instrument. The sudden transition from inventory to shipwreck (v. 25 to v. 26) is one of Ezekiel’s great rhetorical effects.

notes.original: ballahot hayit — you have come to a dreadful end
notes.rendering: you have come to a dreadful end
notes.why: Ballahah = horror, terror, sudden calamity (from bahal, to terrify). The word is used throughout Ezekiel for the shock of divine judgment. The merchants who profited from Tyre now hiss over her ruin — the same marketplace logic that celebrated her success abandons her in collapse.

intro: Chapter 28 contains two of the most theologically charged passages in the oracles against the nations: the oracle against the prince of Tyre (human ruler who claims divinity) and the lament for the king of Tyre (a mythopoetic figure who echoes Eden, cherubim, and primordial perfection before the fall). The second oracle has generated centuries of debate about its relation to the Satan tradition.

notes.original: el ani — I am a god
notes.rendering: I am a god
notes.why: The Tyrian king’s claim to divinity is the theological heart of the oracle. He sits in the seat of the gods (moshav elohim) in the heart of the sea. The response: you are a man (adam), not a god. The boundary between creature and Creator, when deliberately crossed by pride, draws the sharpest judgment in Ezekiel.

notes.original: chacham attah mi-Daniel — wiser than Daniel
notes.rendering: wiser than Daniel
notes.why: The same Daniel referenced in 14:14 — almost certainly the ancient Ugaritic Danel, proverbially wise, not the book’s contemporary figure (who would be Ezekiel’s peer, not yet legendary). The sarcasm is pointed: you think yourself wiser than the wisest of the ancients; even so, you are still a man.

notes.original: bʾEden gan ha-Elohim hayita — you were in Eden, the garden of God
notes.rendering: you were in Eden, the garden of God
notes.why: The oracle moves into mythological register: the king of Tyre is addressed as a primordial being who walked among the stones of fire on the mountain of God. This is not biography but typology — the pattern of Eden, perfection, pride, and fall. Whether it reflects a lost Phoenician creation myth or is Ezekiel’s own construction is debated.

notes.original: kerub mimshach ha-sokek — anointed guardian cherub
notes.rendering: anointed guardian cherub
notes.why: The cherub who guards Eden (Gen 3:24) is here addressed directly — or rather, the king is identified with that guardian figure.
