The uncleanness he confesses is not general sinfulness but the specific impurity of one whose mouth has been used for ordinary speech and is now confronted with the source of all speech. S'fatayim — lips (dual form; both lips, the whole speaking apparatus). The progression from I to my people is significant: he does not distinguish himself from the community he has spent five chapters indicting. He is among them, not above them. The coal from the altar (v.7) cleanses the precise instrument that must be made holy.

notes.original: zera qodesh matzavtah — the holy seed is its stump
notes.rendering: The holy seed is its stump
notes.why: The final phrase of the commission is the most compressed theological statement in the chapter. The nation will be felled — cut down to a stump — but the stump is not dead. Matzeveth — a standing pillar, a stump, something upright that remains. Zera qodesh — holy seed: the remnant that survives judgment is not merely a biological remainder but a seed with generative potential. The image pulls together the judgment of the whole chapter (burning, desolation, removal) and refuses to let it be the last word. From the stump of a felled tree, the Branch of 4:2 will grow.

intro: Chapter 7 is one of the most debated passages in the Hebrew Bible, and the Immanuel sign at its centre has generated more interpretive controversy than almost any other verse. The immediate political context is the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734 BCE — two kings are marching on Jerusalem. Isaiah's word to the panicking Ahaz is: be quiet, stand firm. Ahaz refuses the offered sign; YHWH gives one anyway.

notes.original: im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu — if you do not believe, you will not be established
notes.rendering: If you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all
notes.why: The Hebrew wordplay is untranslatable but essential: ta'aminu (you believe, from aman — to be firm, to trust) and te'amenu (you will be established, also from aman). The same root does both work: faith and stability are not two things but one. The word amen — used liturgically in every tradition — comes from this root. Isaiah is telling Ahaz that political stability and theological trust are the same act: the king who will not believe will not endure. The pun encodes the theology.

notes.original: ha'almah harah v'yoledet ben — the young woman is pregnant and giving birth to a son
notes.rendering: the young woman is pregnant and is about to give birth to a son, and she will call his name Immanuel
notes.why: Ha'almah — the young woman (with the definite article, suggesting a specific woman known to Isaiah and Ahaz). Almah means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not specify virginity (that is betulah). The sign has an immediate fulfilment — the child serves as a timeline marker for the fall of the two threatening kings (v.16). Matthew 1:23 quotes the LXX translation, which renders almah as parthenos (virgin), reading the text as a second, deeper fulfilment in the birth of Jesus. Both readings are in the tradition; neither cancels the other. Immanuel — El with us, God with us — is the theological load the name carries regardless of which child bears it.

notes.original: b'ta'ar hash'kirah — with a razor that is hired
notes.rendering: the Sovereign will shave with a razor hired beyond the River — with the king of Assyria
notes.why: The image is mordantly precise: Assyria is a razor that YHWH hires — a tool, not an independent agent. Ta'ar — razor, the blade of a barber. Sh'kirah — hired, leased. The shaving of head, beard, and body hair was the ultimate humiliation in the ancient Near East — it stripped a man of dignity and marked him as conquered. The metaphor says that the very instrument of Judah's shame is in YHWH's hand, employed for purposes that go beyond Assyrian ambition. The sovereign who whistled for the fly and the bee now employs the empire.

intro: Chapter 8 continues the Immanuel cluster with a second sign-child whose name — Maher-shalal-hash-baz, the longest name in the Hebrew Bible — encodes a different message: swift is the spoil, speedy is the plunder. The chapter then turns inward: Isaiah withdraws from public life, binds up his testimony among disciples, and waits. The community of those who trust YHWH in the dark becomes itself a sign.

notes.original: maher shalal chash baz — swift is the spoil, speedy is the plunder
notes.rendering: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
notes.why: The name is a four-word sentence and the longest personal name in the Hebrew Bible. Maher — swift, hurrying; shalal — spoil, plunder (what an army takes); chash — hastening, speeding; baz — prey, booty. The name is the oracle: before this child speaks, Damascus and Samaria will be looted. The public inscription of the name before witnesses (v.2) makes the prophecy a legal document — dated, witnessed, irrefutable. If the child is born and the event occurs, the prophet has spoken truth. Isaiah stakes his reputation on the timeline.

notes.original: mey hashiloach haloch'im l'at — the waters of Shiloah that flow gently
notes.rendering: the waters of Shiloah that flow gently
notes.why: Shiloah (later Siloam) was Jerusalem's modest water supply — a slow, quiet channel from the Gihon spring. The people have rejected its quiet flow in favour of the dramatic politics of Rezin and Pekah. The contrast Isaiah sets up is between the unhurried provision of YHWH (the gentle waters) and the spectacular flood of Assyria (the River — the Euphrates — in full fury, vv.7–8). To despise the slow, steady gift of God is to invite the overwhelming torrent that replaces it. The gentle waters of Shiloah will later be the pool where Jesus heals a blind man (John 9) — the echo is not accidental in the tradition.

notes.original: v'hayah l'miqdash ul'even negeph — he will be a sanctuary and a stone of stumbling
notes.rendering: He will become a sanctuary — but also a stone one strikes against, a rock one stumbles over
notes.why: The same YHWH who is sanctuary (miqdash — the holy place of protection) is also even negeph (stone of striking — the rock the foot catches on) and tzur michshol (rock of stumbling). The difference is not in the rock but in the approach. Paul quotes this passage in Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8 applies it to Christ: the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence. The verse articulates a permanent paradox in the theology of the holy: the presence that saves and the presence that judges are the same presence, encountered differently depending on one's orientation.

intro: Chapter 9 opens with the greatest reversal in the first half of Isaiah: out of the darkness of chapter 8's closing verses, a great light. The throne-oracle at the chapter's centre (vv. 1–7) is among the most celebrated passages in the Hebrew Bible — four throne names, a birth announcement, and the promise of endless peace. The chapter then returns to the refrain that has driven the judgment oracles: his hand is still stretched out.

notes.original: ha'am hahol'chim b'choshech ra'u or gadol — the people walking in darkness have seen a great light
notes.rendering: The people walking in darkness have seen a great light. On those living in the land of the shadow of death — a light has dawned
notes.why: The perfect tense (ra'u — they have seen) makes the future certain by describing it as already accomplished — the prophetic perfect, a signature of Isaiah's visionary style. Tzalmavet — shadow of death (tzal — shadow + mavet — death): the compound word appears in Psalm 23 ('the valley of the shadow of death'). The light that dawns (naga — to shine, to touch, to reach) is not a general illumination but a specific arrival. Matthew 4:15–16 quotes this verse to describe Jesus's ministry in Galilee — Isaiah's geography becomes Matthew's map.

notes.original: pele' yo'etz el gibbor avi'ad sar shalom — Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace
notes.rendering: His name will be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace
notes.why: The four throne names are a compound royal title, each pair forming a unit. Pele' yo'etz — wonder of a counsellor, one whose counsel is beyond human (pele' — wonder, the miraculous; the same word used for YHWH's wonders in Exodus). El gibbor — mighty God or divine warrior (el — God, gibbor — warrior champion; not merely 'godly' but carrying the divine name el). Avi'ad — father of eternity, everlasting father (ad — perpetuity, forever). Sar shalom — prince of peace (shalom — wholeness, completeness, the flourishing of all). The names accumulate: the child who is born is also, in some sense, the God who acts.

notes.original: livenim nafalu v'gazit nivneh — the bricks have fallen but we will build with dressed stone
notes.rendering: The bricks have fallen, but we will build with dressed stone. The sycamores have been cut down, but we will put cedars in their place
notes.why: The boast is the response to partial judgment — not repentance but defiant upgrading. We will rebuild bigger and better. Gazit — hewn stone, dressed ashlar (more expensive and durable than mud brick). The cedars of Lebanon replace the common sycamore-fig. The arrogance is structural: they interpret disaster as a building challenge rather than a moral summons. The refrain that closes each section of the judgment oracle (his hand is still stretched out) is YHWH's response to this boast: you have not understood what is happening to you.

intro: Chapter 10 resolves the theological problem that Assyria creates: if YHWH uses a foreign empire as his instrument of judgment, what happens to Assyrian accountability? Isaiah's answer is exact — YHWH uses the axe, but the axe that boasts of its own power will be broken. The empire that served as YHWH's rod will itself be judged for its arrogance.

notes.original: hoy Ashur shevet appi — woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger
notes.rendering: Woe to Assyria — the rod of my anger and the staff in whose hand is my fury
notes.why: Shevet — rod, staff, sceptre (the same word used for a ruler's sceptre and a shepherd's crook). YHWH names Assyria his instrument of punishment — then immediately (v.7) acknowledges that Assyria has no idea it is an instrument: it intends its own agenda, not YHWH's. The theological precision is remarkable: divine sovereignty and human agency are both fully operative simultaneously. Assyria is genuinely guilty of its ambitions; YHWH is genuinely sovereign over the outcome. Neither cancels the other.

notes.original: hayit'pa'er hagar'zen al hachot'ev bo — shall the axe boast over the one who hews with it
notes.rendering: Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it?
notes.why: The image of the boasting tool is one of Isaiah's finest satirical moments. Garzen — axe; mesor — saw. The absurdity is complete: the axe did not choose to swing, the saw did not choose to cut. Assyria's claim that 'by the strength of my hand I have done it' (v.13) is the claim of a tool that thinks it wielded the carpenter. The same logic underlies Isaiah's later satire on idol-makers in chapter 44: the human who carves the god and then worships it has confused the agent with the instrument.

notes.original: she'ar yashuv — a remnant will return
notes.rendering: A remnant will return — the remnant of Jacob — to the mighty God
notes.why: She'ar yashuv is the name of Isaiah's first son (7:3) — the child who stood beside him at the conduit when he met Ahaz. The name Isaiah chose before the crisis embeds the remnant theology in a person: the boy is a walking oracle. Yashuv — will return (shub — to turn, to return, the great word of prophetic repentance and also of literal homecoming). The remnant that returns turns back to el gibbor — the Mighty God — the same title given to the child of 9:6. The threads knit together: the shoot from Jesse, the child born to us, the remnant that returns are converging images.

intro: Chapter 11 is the apex of Isaiah's messianic vision in the first movement of the book. It answers chapter 10's felled forest with a shoot from a stump — the Davidic dynasty appears to be cut down, but life remains in the root. The Spirit-endowed king brings justice, then the created order itself is healed. The chapter closes with the image of a second exodus — the scattered returning home along a highway.

notes.original: v'yatza choter migeza Yishai v'netzer misharashav yifreh — a shoot from the stump of Jesse, a branch from his roots
notes.rendering: A shoot will come up from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots will bear fruit
notes.why: Choter — a twig, a shoot (from a root meaning to cut). Netzer — a branch, a sprout (from natzer — to preserve; netzer carries the sense of something kept alive through cutting back). The choice of Jesse rather than David is deliberate: the dynasty is traced to its pre-royal root, before the corruption of kingship set in. The stump (geza — the cut trunk) picks up the imagery of chapter 10:34 where Lebanon falls — the forest of empire is cut down, and from the apparently dead stump of the Davidic line, life springs. Netzer becomes a messianic title: Jesus of Nazareth may carry an echo of this word (Matthew 2:23).

notes.original: ruach YHWH — the Spirit of YHWH in sixfold form
notes.rendering: The Spirit of YHWH will rest on him — the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of YHWH
notes.why: Six attributes of the Spirit are named in three pairs: wisdom (chokhmah) / understanding (binah); counsel (etzah) / strength (gevurah); knowledge (da'at) / fear of YHWH (yir'at YHWH). The pairs are not random: wisdom and understanding govern perception; counsel and strength govern action; knowledge and fear govern relationship with God. The LXX adds a seventh attribute (piety/eusebeia), producing the seven gifts of the Spirit in Christian tradition. The verb nuach — to rest, to settle, to alight — is the same word used of Noah's ark settling on the mountain (Genesis 8:4). The Spirit comes to rest and stays.

notes.original: ki mal'ah ha'aretz de'ah et YHWH kamayim layam m'kasim — for the earth will be full of the knowledge of YHWH as the waters cover the sea
notes.rendering: the earth will be full of the knowledge of YHWH as the waters cover the sea
notes.why: Da'ah — knowledge (from yada — to know with full intimacy; the covenantal knowing of 3:2 in Amos). The simile is absolute: as completely as water fills the sea basin — with no gaps, no dry patches, no exceptions — so the knowledge of YHWH will fill the earth. Habakkuk 2:14 repeats the image almost verbatim. The verse is the theological destination of the whole passage: the shoot, the Spirit, the justice, the healed creation — they all serve this end. The world YHWH made will finally know him as the sea knows water.

intro: Chapter 12 is the shortest chapter in this section of Isaiah — a single hymn of six verses that functions as the doxological close to the first great movement of the book (chapters 1–12). After ten chapters of woe and judgment and conditional promise, the book pauses for song. The structure echoes the Song of the Sea in Exodus 15: deliverance accomplished, God's name proclaimed, joy that cannot be contained.

notes.original: YHWH Elohim ozi v'zimrati — YHWH God is my strength and my song
notes.rendering: YHWH God is my strength and my song — and he has become my salvation
notes.why: The line is almost word for word from Exodus 15:2 — the Song of the Sea sung by Moses and Israel after crossing the Red Sea. Oz — strength, might. Zimrat — song (but also, by a closely related root, protection, defence). The verse encodes a second exodus: what the people sang on the far side of the sea, they will sing again on the far side of judgment and exile. YHWH has become (vayehi — the same narrative past tense of Exodus) my salvation. The use of the Exodus diction is not quotation but typological identification: this future deliverance is a new Exodus.

notes.original: ush'avtem mayim b'sason mima'ayney hayeshu'ah — you will draw water with joy from the wells of salvation
notes.rendering: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation
notes.why: Ma'ayaney hayeshu'ah — wells of salvation (ma'ayan — a spring, a source; yeshu'ah — salvation, the word from which the name Yeshua / Jesus derives). The image picks up the water of Shiloah from 8:6 — the gentle flow that was rejected. Now the people will draw joyfully from the springs of the very thing they despised. B'sason — with gladness, with exultation (sason — the kind of joy that breaks into noise). Jesus quotes this passage at the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:37–38), standing up and crying out as the water-drawing ceremony reached its climax: 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.'

notes.original: gadol b'qirb'cha q'dosh Yisrael — great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel
notes.rendering: great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel
notes.why: Q'dosh Yisrael — the Holy One of Israel: this is Isaiah's signature name for God, appearing twenty-five times in the book and almost nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. It combines the absolute otherness of the throne-room vision (holy, holy, holy) with the relational specificity of covenant: the Holy One who is ours, who dwells among us. B'qirb'cha — in your midst, in your interior, inside you (qerev — the inner parts, the inward being). The chapter that began with YHWH's anger (v.1) ends with the Holy One dwelling inside the people. The whole arc of chapters 1–12 — indictment, judgment, sign, remnant, messianic shoot, second exodus — arrives here.

intro: Chapter 13 opens the second great section of the book — the Oracles Against the Nations (chapters 13–23). The placement of Babylon at the head of this collection is significant: in Isaiah's own eighth-century context, Assyria was the dominant power, not Babylon. The Babylon oracle looks forward, past the Assyrian crisis, to a judgment that lies beyond Isaiah's own lifetime. It is the most cosmic of the oracles — the stars go dark, the earth shakes, humanity becomes rarer than gold.

notes.original: massa Bavel — the oracle concerning Babylon
notes.rendering: The oracle concerning Babylon
notes.why: Massa — oracle, burden, pronouncement (from nasa — to lift up, to carry). The word means both the lifting of the voice to deliver a message and the weight of the message delivered — a burden in both senses. It becomes the technical heading for the foreign nation oracles. The oracles against Babylon in chapters 13–14 and 21 are among the most fully developed in the Hebrew prophetic canon — matched only by Jeremiah 50–51. The placement here signals that Babylon is not merely one enemy among others but the archetypal empire, the successor to Assyria as the book's symbolic antagonist.

notes.original: v'shavati al tevel ra'ah — I will punish the world for its evil
notes.rendering: I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity
notes.why: Tevel — the inhabited world, the whole earth in its human occupancy (from yaval — to bring forth; the productive, populated earth as distinct from eretz, the land). The scope of the oracle shifts here from Babylon specifically to the world in general: YHWH's action against Babylon is simultaneously a judgment on the principle of arrogant empire wherever it operates. The Day of YHWH in these verses (vv. 9–13) exceeds any single nation — it is a cosmic reckoning. The darkening of the stars, the shaking of the heavens, the rarity of human life: this is the language of de-creation.

notes.original: u'Vavel tz'vi mamlachot... v'lo teshev lanetzach — Babylon, glory of kingdoms... will never be inhabited
notes.rendering: Babylon — the glory of kingdoms, the splendour and pride of the Chaldeans — will be like Sodom and Gomorrah... She will never be inhabited or lived in from generation to generation
notes.why: Tz'vi mamlachot — the beauty of kingdoms, the ornament of empire (tz'vi — gazelle, beauty, glory; the same word used of the Land of Israel as the tz'vi of all lands). The comparison to Sodom and Gomorrah removes Babylon from history into eschatology: not merely conquered but abolished. Lo teshev lanetzach — never inhabited, into perpetuity (netzach — to the victor, to the ever-continuing). The wild animal catalogue of vv.21–22 (ostriches, jackals, hyenas) is the anti-creation: where human civilization built its greatest monuments, only creatures of desolation remain.

intro: Chapter 14 contains one of the most dramatically realized passages in the Hebrew Bible: the taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon, which reaches its climax in the descent of the 'Day Star' — a passage that later tradition has read as the fall of Satan. The chapter then pivots quickly to shorter oracles against Assyria and Philistia, establishing the pattern of the oracle collection.

notes.original: mashal — taunt, parable, proverb
notes.rendering: you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon
notes.why: Mashal — a saying, a proverb, a taunt-song (from mashal — to be like, to compare; a mashal draws a comparison that illuminates by analogy). The mashal in its taunt form is a public shaming utterance — it was sung over the defeated as they were led through the streets. Amos uses no mashal; Isaiah uses several. The irony of this particular mashal is its literary grandeur: the mockery of the tyrant is composed in the most elevated poetic register, which makes the fall more complete. The king who claimed to ascend to heaven is mocked in language worthy of heaven.

notes.original: heylel ben shachar — Day Star, son of the dawn
notes.rendering: How you have fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of the dawn!
notes.why: Heylel — the shining one, the brilliant one (from halal — to shine; related to hallelujah). Ben shachar — son of the dawn. The image is the morning star (Venus) at its most brilliant — the last bright point before the sun rises, which then disappears in the daylight. The king who claimed to ascend above the stars is compared to the star that cannot hold its position at sunrise. The Latin Vulgate translated heylel as Lucifer (the light-bearer), and the passage became in Christian tradition the account of Satan's fall (Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:9). In its original context it is a political taunt; in the wider tradition it carries cosmic weight.

notes.original: ki YHWH tzvaot ya'atz — for YHWH of hosts has purposed
notes.rendering: For YHWH of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?
notes.why: Ya'atz — has purposed, has counselled, has decided (from ya'atz — to counsel, to advise; the same root as yo'etz in the throne-name Wonderful Counsellor, 9:6). The rhetorical questions — who will annul? who will turn back? — expect the answer: no one. The hand stretched out against the nations (v.26) is the same hand that was stretched out in judgment against Israel throughout chapters 5 and 9–10, now turned outward. YHWH's purposes are not hostage to any empire's survival.

intro: The oracle against Moab (chapters 15–16) is remarkable for its tone. Unlike the stark condemnation of Babylon, this oracle is saturated with grief — Isaiah himself weeps for Moab (15:5, 16:9, 11). The nation east of the Dead Sea is an ancient enemy and a kinsman people (descended from Lot). The oracle mourns what it announces. It is one of the few places in prophetic literature where the prophet explicitly laments the judgment he is delivering.

notes.original: massa Moav — the oracle concerning Moab
notes.rendering: The oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone
notes.why: The doubling of the opening — Ar laid waste / Kir laid waste, each in a single night — creates a drumbeat of catastrophe. The two cities function as a merismus for the whole of Moab: north and south, this and that. Dumah — is undone, is silenced (dumam — to be still, to be destroyed; also the name for a region of silence, which the LXX connects to death). The night setting (layelah — in the night) gives the destruction the quality of sudden ambush: by morning the country that was a nation is ruins.

notes.original: libi l'Moav yiz'aq — my heart cries out for Moab
notes.rendering: My heart cries out for Moab
notes.why: The intrusion of prophetic lament in the middle of an oracle of judgment is one of the most human moments in Isaiah. Libi — my heart (lev — the seat of emotion and will). Yiz'aq — cries out (za'aq — the cry of distress, the same word used for the cry of the poor who cannot get justice in 5:7). The prophet who announced the oracle now grieves it. This is not contradiction but the double consciousness of prophetic vocation: to know what is coming and to sorrow over it simultaneously. Jeremiah will make this the defining posture of his entire ministry.

notes.original: ki mey Dimon male'u dam — for the waters of Dimon are full of blood
notes.rendering: For the waters of Dimon are full of blood
notes.why: Dimon is likely Dibon (a major Moabite city), with a deliberate shift in spelling to echo dam — blood. The wordplay (Dimon / dam) makes the geography embody the catastrophe: the name of the place becomes the name of its fate. This kind of sound-play between place names and their prophetic meaning runs through the oracle collection — Moab, Edom, and the Philistine cities are all named in ways that resonate with their announced destruction. Isaiah inherited this technique from Amos (the qayitz/qetz play of Amos 8) and deploys it throughout.

intro: Chapter 16 completes the Moab oracle and is among the most emotionally complex passages in the prophetic literature. The prophet weeps openly over the vineyards and harvests of a foreign nation he has been sent to condemn. The oracle embeds within itself a messianic promise (v.5) before returning to grief — as if to say that what Moab might have sheltered toward, had it humbled itself, is the very throne it will not see.

notes.original: v'hukin b'chesed kisse — a throne established in steadfast love
notes.rendering: then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness, in the tent of David, one who judges and seeks justice
notes.why: Chesed — steadfast love, covenant loyalty (the great covenantal word of the Hebrew Bible, untranslatable in a single English term). Emet — faithfulness, truth, reliability. The throne of David characterised by these two qualities is the antithesis of Moab's pride (v.6). The passage interrupts the lament to offer a glimpse of what authentic kingship looks like — and by implication, what Moab is fleeing toward when it seeks refuge at Zion. The one 'swift to do righteousness' (memahair tzedek) is the messianic counterpart to the judge who is slow to act in 1:23.

notes.original: al ken evkeh bivki Yazer — therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer
notes.rendering: Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah. I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh
notes.why: The prophet's tears appear explicitly three times in this oracle (15:5, 16:9, 16:11). This is not conventional mourning formula — it is personal lament for a foreign nation. Evkeh — I weep (first person singular, emphatic). The agricultural imagery is precise: Sibmah was famous for its vines; Heshbon and Elealeh were associated with abundant harvests. Isaiah mourns the silencing of the harvest shout (heydad — the joyful cry of grape-treaders at the vintage), the cessation of the thing that made these places themselves. To destroy a people's harvest is to destroy what makes them who they are.

notes.original: bishloshah shanim kiSHnot sachir — in three years, like the years of a hired worker
notes.rendering: In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt
notes.why: Sachir — a hired worker, a day labourer (one who counts his days exactly, working no more and no less than contracted). The simile is about precision and finality: three years, counted exactly, no extension. The glory of Moab (kevod Moav) that has been catalogued across two chapters — its pride, its vineyards, its cities, its religious high places — will be dishonoured (niqlah — made light of, despised) within that exact term. The oracle that began in grief ends in a date.

intro: The oracle against Damascus is also an oracle against Ephraim — the northern kingdom of Israel that allied with Aram against Judah in the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. Both Damascus and Samaria will be brought low together, since they conspired together. The oracle closes with a remarkable nocturnal image: the vast army of nations that threatens, gone by morning like a bad dream.

notes.original: ke'olelet zeitim — as when an olive tree is beaten
notes.rendering: Yet gleaning will remain, as when an olive tree is beaten — two or three berries in the top of the highest bough
notes.why: Olelet — gleaning (the olive harvest practice of beating the branches to dislodge fruit; what remains on the topmost branches after the harvest is left for the poor, per Leviticus 19:10 and Deuteronomy 24:20). The remnant theology that has run through chapters 6–11 is here rendered in agricultural terms: the judgment is a thorough beating, but something remains at the very top where the beater cannot reach. Two or three berries — the number is precise in its smallness. The remnant is real but barely.

notes.original: ki shachacht Elohei yish'ech — for you have forgotten the God of your salvation
notes.rendering: For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge
notes.why: Shachacht — you have forgotten (shachach — to forget, to neglect through inattention rather than deliberate rejection). The indictment is not idolatry in the dramatic sense but forgetfulness — the slow drift from what should be central. Tzur — Rock (one of YHWH's oldest titles; Deuteronomy 32:4 — the Rock, his work is perfect). The pleasant plants of the foreign vine (verse 10b) are the substitutes that fill the space where memory of God should be: beautiful, cultivated, producing nothing that lasts. The harvest flees away (v.11) because the cultivator has cultivated everything except the relationship that makes the land fruitful.

notes.original: l'et erev v'hineh v'liphney voker einenu — at evening and behold, before morning they are gone
notes.rendering: At evening — behold, sudden terror! Before morning — they are gone!
notes.why: The compression is extraordinary: a whole military campaign, a whole existential crisis, resolved between evening and morning. Hineh — behold (the particle of sudden appearance, of something that bursts into view). The pattern recalls the annihilation of Sennacherib's army in chapter 37 — 185,000 dead in a night. But here the oracle speaks proverbially of all such threats: the nations that roar like the sea are as temporary as the night. Goral — lot, portion (the shares allotted by destiny or by divine decree). Those who loot will receive as their lot exactly what they were dealing out.

intro: Chapter 18 is one of the shorter and stranger oracles — addressed to Cush (ancient Ethiopia, roughly modern Sudan), the great southern power that in Isaiah's time dominated Egypt. The oracle opens with the urgency of ambassadors and closes with those same distant peoples bringing gifts to Zion. Between those two moments, YHWH watches silently from heaven while events unfold below him.

notes.original: eretz tziltzal k'nafayim — land of whirring wings
notes.rendering: Woe to the land of whirring wings that lies beyond the rivers of Cush
notes.why: Tziltzal k'nafayim — the whirring or buzzing of wings (tziltzal — a buzzing, a whirring sound; k'nafayim — of wings). The phrase is disputed: it may refer to the insects abundant in sub-Saharan Africa, or to the fleet of papyrus boats whose oars churn the water, or to a poetic description of the country itself as alive with motion and energy. The oracle's opening is designed to evoke distance, strangeness, and exotic power — a nation so remote and impressive that its ambassadors arrive by boat on the Nile, which was itself a marvel to Near Eastern observers who rarely saw the sea.

notes.original: v'ashqitah v'abitah b'michoni — I will quietly look on from my dwelling
notes.rendering: I will quietly look on from my dwelling — like shimmering heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest
notes.why: The divine inaction is itself the oracle's theological centre. YHWH does not intervene loudly — he watches, silently, like the haze of summer heat (chom or — the shimmering of sunshine on a hot day) or the morning dew cloud. The images are of patient, ambient presence rather than dramatic action. The pruning that follows (v.5) happens at the exact moment of harvest readiness — not before, not after. YHWH's silence is not absence but timing. This is the quietest image of divine sovereignty in the oracle collection.

notes.original: yuval shay l'YHWH tzvaot — gifts will be brought to YHWH of hosts
notes.rendering: At that time gifts will be brought to YHWH of hosts from a people tall and smooth... to Mount Zion
notes.why: The oracle that began with ambassadors leaving Cush ends with Cush itself coming to Zion — not as a conquered nation but as a gift-bearer. Shai — a gift, a tribute brought voluntarily (not the forced tribute of conquest). The repetition of the description of Cush (tall and smooth, feared near and far, mighty and conquering, rivers dividing the land) from verse 2 to verse 7 creates a formal envelope: the same impressive nation that sent messengers out ends by bringing something in. The oracle's movement is from human urgency to divine patience to eschatological pilgrimage — the same pattern as the mountain vision of chapter 2.

intro: Chapter 19 is theologically the most radical of the nation oracles. After the familiar structure of judgment against Egypt, the chapter turns and delivers something unprecedented in the Hebrew prophets: Egypt and Assyria — the two superpowers that have oppressed Israel — are called 'my people' and 'the work of my hands' by YHWH. The covenant titles reserved for Israel are extended to her greatest enemies.

notes.original: hineh YHWH rochev al av kal — YHWH riding on a swift cloud
notes.rendering: YHWH is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt
notes.why: The theophany image — God riding the storm cloud — is drawn from the Canaanite tradition where Baal was the 'rider of the clouds' (rkb 'rpt in the Ugaritic texts). Isaiah applies the title to YHWH, asserting that the storm deity the nations fear is not Baal but YHWH. The cloud is av — thick cloud, dark storm cloud (not the pillar-cloud of the wilderness). YHWH comes to Egypt not as a visitor but as a conqueror entering enemy territory in his war-chariot. The idols of Egypt tremble at his arrival because they know who he is.

notes.original: v'naga YHWH et Mitzrayim nagof v'rafo — YHWH will strike Egypt, striking and healing
notes.rendering: YHWH will strike Egypt, striking and healing — they will return to YHWH, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them
notes.why: The double infinitive nagof v'rafo — striking and healing — is the pattern of YHWH's action throughout the prophets: judgment is never the final word. The verb rafo — to heal — is the same root as Raphael and carries the full weight of restoration (Hosea 6:1 uses the identical pair: he has torn, and he will heal). Egypt will cry to YHWH (v.20) and YHWH will send a deliverer — the same pattern as the book of Judges, now extended to a foreign nation. The implication is that Egypt, having been judged, can enter the same cycle of cry-and-deliverance as Israel.

notes.original: Mitzrayim ami v'Ashur ma'aseh yadai v'Yisrael nachalati — Egypt my people and Assyria the work of my hands and Israel my inheritance
notes.rendering: Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance
notes.why: The three covenant titles are carefully distributed. Ami — my people: the title of the Sinai covenant (Exodus 6:7). Ma'aseh yadai — the work of my hands: the title of the creation relationship (Isaiah 29:23; 60:21). Nachalati — my inheritance: the title of the election (Deuteronomy 4:20). Egypt receives the relational title; Assyria receives the creative title; Israel retains the elective title — but all three are now inside the orbit of divine blessing. This is the most universalist statement in Isaiah's first movement and one of the most universalist in the entire Hebrew Bible.

intro: Chapter 20 is one of the most striking biographical passages in the prophets. Isaiah walks naked and barefoot through Jerusalem for three years as a living oracle — his body is the message. The chapter is brief but unforgettable: a dated historical event (Sargon's capture of Ashdod, 711 BCE), a command that tests the limits of prophetic obedience, and a sharp political warning against relying on Egypt.

notes.original: haloch arom u'yachef — walking naked and barefoot
notes.rendering: walking naked and barefoot... as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush
notes.why: Arom — naked, stripped (not necessarily fully unclothed but divested of the outer garment, in the minimal clothing of a prisoner or a poverty-stricken person). Yachef — barefoot (the sandal is a basic marker of dignity and status in the ancient Near East; to remove the sandal is to relinquish standing). The sign-act (ot u'mofet — sign and portent; the paired words of the Exodus plagues) lasts three years — not three days or three hours. Isaiah's body bore this message for three years while the political debates about the Egyptian alliance continued around him. The prophet is not separate from his oracle; he is its embodiment.

notes.original: u'vachat miBabel tibrach — they will be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope
notes.rendering: they will be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and Egypt their boast
notes.why: Miqveh — hope, expectation (from qavah — to wait, to hope). The nations that have placed their confidence in Egypt and Cush will find that confidence evacuated. The coastland peoples (probably referring to Philistia and the Judean court that was tempted by the Egyptian alliance) will watch the very powers they relied on led away in chains. The political argument Isaiah has been making in prose (chapters 30–31 will develop it fully) is here made bodily: Egypt cannot save you because Egypt cannot save itself. Trust in YHWH, not in the chariots of Egypt (31:1).

intro: Chapter 21 contains one of the most viscerally dramatic passages in the oracle collection — the fall of Babylon announced through a watchman's report, with the prophet himself sick with anguish at what he is hearing. The brief oracles against Dumah and Arabia that follow are among the most enigmatic in the book, the Dumah oracle particularly so: it is a riddle that does not fully resolve.

notes.original: mil'u motnai chalchalah — my loins are filled with anguish
notes.rendering: my loins are filled with anguish. Pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labour
notes.why: The physical description of prophetic experience is exceptional in its detail. Chalchalah — writhing, trembling (from chul — to writhe, to be in labour). The prophet's body participates in the vision: he cannot hear, cannot see, staggers (v.4). Na'avah levavi — my heart has gone astray, staggers (na'av — to stray, to wander in confusion). The oracle he receives destroys his composure not because Babylon's fall is bad news but because the weight of divine revelation, even of good news, is overwhelming. Jeremiah 4:19 uses identical language for the same visceral experience of prophetic reception.

notes.original: naflah naflah Bavel — fallen, fallen is Babylon
notes.rendering: Fallen, fallen is Babylon! And all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground
notes.why: The double fall — naflah naflah — is the emphatic announcement, the prophetic perfect treating the future as accomplished. The watchman who has stood through the whole night (v.8) finally sees the riders and hears the word. Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 quote this exact formula: 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great' — the echo runs from Isaiah through the Psalms to the apocalyptic tradition, where Babylon becomes the cipher for every oppressive empire. The shattering of her gods' images is the verification: the idols of Egypt trembled (19:1); Babylon's are broken. YHWH who rode the cloud to Egypt has now dealt with the empire to the east.

notes.original: Shomer mah milailah — Watchman, what of the night?
notes.rendering: Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?" The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night
notes.why: The Dumah oracle (Dumah means silence, stillness — possibly Edom, whose name sounds similar) is deliberately cryptic. The question is desperate: how long is it until morning? The answer refuses to be a timetable: morning is coming and so is another night. The watchman's reply is not evasive but honest about the shape of history — relief comes, then darkness returns, then relief again. If you want to know, come back and ask again. The oracle denies false comfort without denying hope. It is the most compressed expression in Isaiah of the ambiguity that pervades prophetic time.

intro: Chapter 22 is the oracle against Jerusalem itself — the Valley of Vision, the city where YHWH dwells. It is the most personally anguished of all the oracles: Isaiah weeps and asks not to be comforted (v.4). The second half of the chapter delivers a remarkably specific oracle against a named court official, and introduces an image — the key of the house of David — that the New Testament will attach to Christ.

notes.original: achol v'shato ki machar namut — let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die
notes.rendering: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die
notes.why: The phrase — one of the most famous in the Hebrew Bible — is the response of Jerusalem's population to the approach of the Assyrian army. Rather than weeping and mourning as YHWH called for (v.12), they throw a party. The logic is fatalistic hedonism: if destruction is coming, nothing matters. Paul quotes this exact phrase in 1 Corinthians 15:32 to describe the logic of those who deny resurrection. Isaiah's indictment is that the feast is not a response to despair but a refusal to look at the One who could save — they saw the weapons (v.8) and counted the houses (v.10) but did not look to him who planned it long ago (v.11).

notes.original: u'netati mafteach beyt David al shichmo — I will place the key of the house of David on his shoulder
notes.rendering: I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He will open and none will shut, and he will shut and none will open
notes.why: The key of the house of David is the symbol of the royal steward's authority — the one who controls access to the king. Mafteach — key (from patach — to open). The imagery of opening and shutting with no reversal possible signals absolute delegated authority. Revelation 3:7 applies this verse directly to Christ: 'The words of the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens.' The oracle against a corrupt official becomes, in the tradition, the investiture of the messianic doorkeeper.

notes.original: yimot yated ha't'qu'ah bamaqom ne'eman — the peg fastened in a secure place will give way
notes.rendering: the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way. It will be cut down and fall
notes.why: The oracle against Eliakim (vv. 20–25) has an unexpected reversal: the man installed as the secure peg will himself give way under the weight of the family network that accumulates on him (v.24). The image of v.23 (peg in a secure place) is undone by v.25. Human appointment, however confident, is provisional. Only YHWH's own fastening holds permanently. The oracle uses Eliakim to demonstrate that even the best replacement for a corrupt official carries within him the seeds of the same institutional failure — unless the Lord builds the house.

intro: Chapter 23 closes the oracle collection with an elegy for Tyre — the great Phoenician trading city whose commercial empire spanned the Mediterranean. Unlike Babylon's permanent abolition or Moab's grief, Tyre's judgment comes with a timeline (seventy years) and an unexpected ending: her trade, once profane, will become holy and will provision those who dwell before YHWH. Even commercial empire has a redemptive destination in Isaiah's vision.

notes.original: mi ya'atz zot al Tzor — who has purposed this against Tyre?
notes.rendering: Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes? YHWH of hosts has purposed it — to defile the pride of all glory
notes.why: The rhetorical question and its immediate answer is a favourite Isaianic move (cf. 10:8–11). Tyre is ha'ateret – the crown-bestower, the city so commercially dominant that it made kings of merchants. Bizz'on — to dishonour, to treat as contemptible (bizayon). The theological point: it is not Babylon or Assyria who brings Tyre down but YHWH, acting to humble the principle of commercial pride itself. Tyre did not make war; she made money. But the pride of commerce and the pride of empire are the same pride viewed from different angles.

notes.original: k'shirat hazonah — like the song of the prostitute
notes.rendering: it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute: 'Take a harp — go about the city, O forgotten prostitute!'
notes.why: The comparison of Tyre to a prostitute who uses music to recover her clientele is mordant social satire — not a moral condemnation of sexuality but a commercial metaphor. Tyre 'sold herself' to every nation for profit; after seventy years of obscurity she will start trading again, playing her commercial music to be remembered. The surprising reversal of v.18 — her wages becoming holy — is the oracle's theological punch: the same commercial energy that served pride will be redirected to provision the community of YHWH. Commerce is not condemned; its direction is what matters.

notes.original: yihyeh sach'rah v'ethnanah qodesh l'YHWH — her merchandise and wages will be holy to YHWH
notes.rendering: Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to YHWH... her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before YHWH
notes.why: Qodesh l'YHWH — holy to YHWH: the phrase inscribed on the high priest's turban (Exodus 28:36) and on the bells of the horses in Zechariah 14:20. The most commercial of all cities ends up with its trade consecrated. Lo ye'aser v'lo yechasan — not stored or hoarded: the accumulation that was Tyre's defining characteristic is reversed. The profit flows outward, to those who dwell before YHWH (yoshvey lifney YHWH — those who sit in YHWH's presence, the priestly community). This is the oracle collection's final word: even Tyre's economy belongs to YHWH's future.

intro: Chapter 24 opens the 'Isaiah Apocalypse' — chapters 24–27, a section distinct in character from the surrounding oracle collection. The scope expands from individual nations to the whole earth, from historical judgment to cosmic dissolution. The earth is not merely punished; it is undone. And yet from within the undoing, a remnant sings.

notes.original: k'am k'cohen — as with the people, so with the priest
notes.rendering: as with the people, so with the priest; as with the servant, so with his master
notes.why: The sixfold levelling — six pairs of social opposites, all equalized in judgment — is Isaiah's most explicit statement that divine reckoning recognizes no privilege of status. Priest and peasant, master and servant, creditor and debtor: every hierarchy that structures ordinary life is collapsed in the day of YHWH. The list is structurally parallel to the social inventory of chapter 3 (where leadership is stripped away) but wider: here it is not just leadership that fails but every social distinction. The earth returns to an undifferentiated state of accountability.

notes.original: ki avru torot chalfu choq heferoo brit olam — they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant
notes.rendering: they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant
notes.why: Brit olam — the everlasting covenant: in Genesis 9:16 this is the covenant with all flesh (Noah's rainbow covenant); in Isaiah it refers to the foundational moral order binding all creation, not merely Israel. The earth is defiled (chonefah — made profane, ritually polluted) because its inhabitants have broken the covenant that predates Sinai — the covenant with all humanity that establishes the basic conditions of creaturely life. This universalises the judgment: it is not Israel's failure of the Mosaic covenant but humanity's failure of the most ancient compact.

notes.original: v'chapher halvanah u'voshah hachammah ki malach YHWH tzvaot — the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for YHWH of hosts reigns
notes.rendering: Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed — for YHWH of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem
notes.why: Chafer — to be confounded, to blush with shame (the same word used in 1:29 of those ashamed of their sacred oaks). The moon and sun, worshipped throughout the ancient Near East as deities, are not destroyed but embarrassed — made irrelevant by the one whose radiance outshines them. The image returns to 13:10 (the cosmic darkness over Babylon) but transforms it: there the lights went out as judgment; here they are dimmed by glory, not by wrath. YHWH reigns — malach, the perfect of accomplished fact — in the place where the whole earth once streamed (chapter 2). The circle closes.

intro: Chapter 25 is the lyrical heart of the Isaiah Apocalypse — a hymn of praise followed by the most sweeping eschatological vision in the Hebrew prophets: the feast on the mountain for all peoples, the swallowing of death, the wiping of every tear. It is the passage that Revelation 21:4 draws from directly, and it has shaped the church's understanding of the resurrection hope more than almost any other text outside the Psalms.

notes.original: mishteh shmanim mishteh shmarim — a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine
notes.rendering: a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine — of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined
notes.why: The feast imagery draws on the covenant meal tradition: the elders of Israel ate and drank before God on Sinai (Exodus 24:11). But this feast is l'chol ha'amim — for all peoples, the universal guest list that chapter 2 implied but did not spell out. Shmanim — rich foods, fatted things (from shemen — oil, fat; the word for the best cuts, the choicest portions). Shmarim m'zuqqaqim — well-aged wines carefully filtered and refined (shmarim — the lees, the sediment; m'zuqqaqim — clarified, strained clear). The feast is not rough abundance but refined abundance — the best of everything, prepared with care, for everyone.

notes.original: v'bil'ah hamavet lanetzach — he will swallow up death forever
notes.rendering: He will swallow up death forever. The Sovereign YHWH will wipe away tears from all faces
notes.why: Bila — to swallow, to engulf (the same verb used of the sea swallowing, of the earth swallowing Korah). Death is here personified as the great swallower — the power that consumes all human life — and YHWH reverses the direction: he swallows the swallower. Lanetzach — forever, to the victor (netzach — perpetuity, also the word for the choirmaster in the Psalms). Macha YHWH dim'ah — YHWH will wipe away the tear (dim'ah — a tear, the individual drop). Paul quotes v.8 in 1 Corinthians 15:54 as the resurrection text; Revelation 21:4 draws directly on the wiping of tears. These two phrases — death swallowed, tears wiped — become the grammar of Christian eschatology.

notes.original: hineh Eloheinu zeh qivvinu lo — look, this is our God — we have waited for him
notes.rendering: Look — this is our God! We have waited for him, that he might save us. This is YHWH — we have waited for him
notes.why: Qivvinu — we have waited (qavah — to wait, to hope, to strain toward; the same root as the rope metaphor of hope stretched taut). The declaration hineh Eloheinu zeh — look, this is our God — is the cry of recognition, the moment when what was waited for arrives and is identified. The repetition (we have waited for him / we have waited for him) captures the breathlessness of arrival after long expectation. The whole apocalypse has been building to this point of seeing: the mountain, the feast, the veil removed, death gone, tears wiped — and then, at last, the face.

intro: Chapter 26 is the sustained song of the faithful community inside the apocalypse — those who wait while the earth is judged. It moves from confidence (the strong city, the everlasting rock) through lament (we gave birth only to wind) to the most explicit statement of bodily resurrection in the pre-exilic prophets: your dead will live, their bodies will rise.

notes.original: yetzer samuch titzor shalom shalom — the mind stayed on you, you keep in perfect peace
notes.rendering: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you — because he trusts in you
notes.why: Shalom shalom — peace peace: the doubled word is the Hebrew superlative of completeness. The mind that is stayed (samuch — leaning, supported, propped up against) on YHWH receives not partial peace but total peace, the shalom that is wholeness, flourishing, and undivided wellbeing. Yetzer — the inclination, the formed imagination (from yatzar — to form; the same root as the potter of 64:8). The formed imagination that has YHWH as its support-point is the one that receives this double peace. The verse has become one of the most-quoted in the entire book.

notes.original: haraynu chul k'yaldnu ruach — we were pregnant, we writhed, we gave birth only to wind
notes.rendering: We were pregnant — we writhed — but we gave birth only to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth
notes.why: The metaphor of labour without birth is one of Isaiah's most devastating images of human futility — the maximum effort that produces nothing. Ruach — wind, breath, spirit (the word is deliberately ambiguous: they gave birth to breath, to nothing, to emptiness). The community confesses that all its own striving for salvation — political alliances, military preparations, religious observance — has produced no yesha (deliverance, the noun of salvation) for the earth. The confession prepares for the resurrection promise of v.19: what human effort cannot produce, YHWH will accomplish directly.

notes.original: yich'yu metecha n'velatecha yekumun — your dead will live, their bodies will rise
notes.rendering: Your dead will live — their bodies will rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!
notes.why: This is one of only two unambiguous statements of bodily resurrection in the Hebrew Bible (the other is Daniel 12:2). Metecha — your dead (YHWH's dead, those who belong to him). N'velatecha yekumun — their bodies (or corpses) will rise (qum — to arise, to stand up). Shochney afar — those who dwell in the dust (the dwelling-place of the dead; dust is the common grave of Genesis 3:19). The dew image is striking: tal oroth — dew of lights, luminous dew (the morning dew that makes things grow, now bringing resurrection growth). The earth gives birth (tapil) to what the community could not: the new life that labour alone cannot produce.

intro: Chapter 27 closes the Isaiah Apocalypse and brings together its governing images in a final resolution: the dragon slain, the vineyard restored and tended with care, Jacob taking root and filling the world with fruit, and the great trumpet calling the scattered home to Jerusalem. The vineyard of chapter 5 — neglected, given over to briars — is here tended by YHWH himself, every moment, night and day.

notes.original: Livyatan nachash bariyach... Livyatan nachash aqalaton — Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent
notes.rendering: YHWH will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent — Leviathan the twisting serpent — and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea
notes.why: Leviathan appears in the Ugaritic texts (Lotan, the seven-headed sea serpent) as the chaos monster defeated by Baal. Isaiah takes the mythological combat narrative and historicises it: YHWH's hard and great and strong sword (cherev haqashah v'hagedolah v'hachazaqah — three adjectives accumulating like blows) dispatches the ancient chaos beast. Bariyach — fleeing, fugitive (the serpent that always escapes). Aqalaton — twisting, coiling (the serpent that cannot be straightened). The dragon in the sea (tannin basayam) is the Egyptian chaos-serpent of Ezekiel 29:3. All the forces of chaos are named and dispatched in a single verse.

notes.original: ani YHWH nots'rah — I, YHWH, am its keeper
notes.rendering: I, YHWH, am its keeper. Every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day
notes.why: The contrast with chapter 5 is exact and deliberate. In 5:6 YHWH abandoned the vineyard: I will command the clouds not to rain on it. Here he waters it every moment (lirgaim eshqenah — at each moment I will water it). In 5:5 he removed the hedge. Here he stands guard night and day. The same YHWH who stripped the vineyard of its protection now provides total protection. The difference is not in the vineyard (Israel has not suddenly become worthy) but in the state of relationship — the future tense of grace, not the present tense of deserving.

notes.original: v'tqa shofar gadol — a great trumpet will be blown
notes.rendering: a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship YHWH on the holy mountain at Jerusalem
notes.why: Shofar gadol — the great ram's horn trumpet, the instrument of the Jubilee (Leviticus 25:9) and of the Day of Atonement. The gathering of the lost (ha'ovdim — the perished, the strayed ones, those who are gone) from Assyria and the driven-out (hanídu'chim) from Egypt mirrors the two great directions of exile — east and west — and reverses both. The holy mountain at Jerusalem (b'har haqodesh biYrushalayim) is where the nations streamed in chapter 2 and where the feast was set in chapter 25. The Apocalypse ends where the book began: all roads lead to the mountain.

intro: Chapter 28 opens the second great woe-collection of the book (chapters 28–33) with a double target: drunken Ephraim (already fallen) and drunken Jerusalem (about to fall). The chapter's theological centre is the cornerstone oracle and the magnificent parable of the farmer — an argument from agricultural wisdom that YHWH's judgments, like a farmer's methods, are calibrated to purpose.

notes.original: tzav latzav tzav latzav qav laqav qav laqav — precept upon precept, line upon line
notes.rendering: precept upon precept, precept upon precept — line upon line, line upon line — here a little, there a little
notes.why: The mocking syllables (tzav, qav — possibly baby-talk or the incoherent babble of the drunk, or the contemptuous mimicry of a student imitating the prophet's teaching) have been read in multiple ways. The most likely reading: the Jerusalem leaders are mocking Isaiah's repeated simple warnings as childish repetition — 'is this all he has to say?' The irony of v.13 is that the very words they mock will become the form of their judgment: YHWH will speak to them in a foreign language (v.11) that sounds equally incomprehensible. The scoffers will become the stumbling.

notes.original: hineni yissad b'Tzion even — look, I am laying in Zion a stone
notes.rendering: Look — I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation. Whoever believes will not be in haste
notes.why: Even bochan — a tested stone (bochan — tested, assayed, proved reliable; the word used for testing precious metals). Pnat yiqrat — a precious cornerstone (pnat — corner, the load-bearing angle stone; yiqrat — of value, precious). Musar — a sure foundation (from yasad — to found, to establish). The one who believes (ha'ame'in) will not be in haste — lo yachish — will not flee in panic when the scourge comes through (v.18). Peter quotes this verse in 1 Peter 2:6 and Paul in Romans 9:33, both applying it to Christ as the tested stone. The foundation that outlasts the covenant with death.

notes.original: nifla etzah higdil tushiyyah — wonderful in counsel, excellent in wisdom
notes.rendering: he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom
notes.why: Nifla etzah — wonderful in counsel (nifla — wonderful, miraculous, the same root as pele in the throne-name Wonderful Counsellor of 9:6; etzah — counsel, plan). Higdil tushiyyah — he has made great wisdom (tushiyyah — practical wisdom, sound understanding, the wisdom that produces effective results; from yasha — to save, with a connotation of wisdom that delivers). The parable of the farmer is Isaiah's argument from analogy: just as the farmer uses different tools for different grains — not crushing the delicate dill with a cart wheel — so YHWH calibrates his judgments. The destruction that seems random is precise. The counsel behind it is wonderful.

intro: Chapter 29 turns the oracle against Ariel — a poetic name for Jerusalem, possibly meaning 'lion of God' or 'hearth of God' — and produces one of the book's great theological confrontations: the potter and the clay. The chapter moves from the sealed book of incomprehension (vv.11–12) through the indictment of lip-service religion (v.13) to the reversal where the deaf hear and the blind see.

notes.original: b'fiv uvisafatav kibduni v'libboh richaq mimeni — with their mouth and lips they honour me but their heart is far from me
notes.rendering: this people draw near with their mouth and honour me with their lips while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men
notes.why: The indictment is precise: the problem is not the absence of religion but its disconnection from the interior. Kibbeduni — they honour me (kibbud — the honour due to parents, to God; it is being performed correctly). Libbam rachaq mimeni — their heart is far from me (rachaq — to be distant, to withdraw). The fear of God (yir'atam oti) has become a mitzvat anashim m'lummadah — a commandment learned by rote from people, a human tradition rehearsed without conviction. Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 15:8–9 and Mark 7:6–7 against the Pharisees' tradition: the ancient indictment of Temple religion becomes the indictment of scribal tradition.

notes.original: hafoch'chem — you turn things upside down
notes.rendering: You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay?
notes.why: Hafoch'chem — your overturning (from hafach — to turn, to overturn, to transform; the same verb used of the overturning of Sodom in Genesis 19:25). The image of the potter and clay first appears here in Isaiah and will be fully developed in 64:8. Jeremiah 18 makes it the controlling metaphor of his temple sermon. Paul draws on it in Romans 9:20–21. The theological force: the creature that questions its creator has confused the roles so completely that it cannot even perceive the absurdity of what it is doing. The clay telling the potter he has no understanding is the epistemological crisis of chapter 5 (calling evil good) pressed to its logical extreme.

notes.original: shamu vayom hahu hachrashim divrei sefer — in that day the deaf will hear the words of a book
notes.rendering: In that day the deaf will hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind will see
notes.why: The reversal of vv.11–12 (where neither the literate nor the illiterate could read the sealed book) is now complete: those who were deaf will hear. Cherashim — the deaf (those whose ears are blocked). The blind will see from afelah u'choshech — from gloom and darkness (the vocabulary of 9:1–2, the great light in the land of deep darkness). Jesus quotes this cluster of reversals in his answer to John the Baptist's question (Matthew 11:5): the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear. Isaiah's catalogue of eschatological signs becomes the index by which Jesus identifies himself.

intro: Chapter 30 is Isaiah's fullest argument against the Egyptian alliance — the policy of relying on Pharaoh's cavalry rather than YHWH's word. But the chapter's theological centre is not the indictment; it is the verse of astonishing grace at v.18 and the quiet word behind the ear at v.21. The chapter that contains some of Isaiah's most scorching political critique also contains some of his most intimate pastoral promises.

notes.original: b'shuvah v'nachat tivvashe'un b'hashqet uvivtacha tihyeh gevuratechem — in returning and rest you will be saved, in quietness and trust will be your strength
notes.rendering: In returning and rest you will be saved — in quietness and trust will be your strength
notes.why: Four words of counter-political wisdom: shuvah (returning — the great repentance word, turning back to YHWH), nachat (rest — the settling of anxiety, the stillness of one who has stopped running), hashqet (quietness — the silence of one who is not agitating), and bitachon (trust — the confident resting of weight on something reliable, from batach — to lean on). The four form a programme: return, rest, be quiet, trust. The political leaders want horses and speed; YHWH offers the opposite of every military value. The refusal — lo avitem — but you were not willing — is one of the most heartbreaking phrases in Isaiah.

notes.original: v'lachen yechakkeh YHWH lachannchem — therefore YHWH waits to be gracious to you
notes.rendering: Therefore YHWH waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you
notes.why: The lachen — therefore — that opens v.18 is unexpected: the preceding verses have catalogued rebellion, refusal, and rout. The logical connective of judgment becomes the logical connective of grace. Yechakkeh — he waits (chakah — to wait in expectation, to be on the lookout; the same word used of the watchman in 21:8). YHWH is waiting for the moment when he can be gracious. He is not withholding grace out of reluctance but out of the timing required by justice. The same word used of those who wait for YHWH (v.18b: ashrei kol chokei lo — blessed are all who wait for him) is the word used of YHWH waiting for them. Both are waiting.

notes.original: v'oznecha tishma'nah davar me'acharecha — your ears will hear a word behind you
notes.rendering: your ears will hear a word behind you saying, 'This is the way — walk in it,' when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left
notes.why: The image is of the shepherd's voice heard from behind the flock — the guide who calls direction without the sheep needing to see the path ahead. Me'acharecha — from behind you (not from ahead, where the destination is uncertain, but from behind, where the authoritative word follows and redirects). Zeh haderech l'chu bo — this is the way, walk in it: the imperative of direction. The dual condition (when you turn right / when you turn left) covers every possible deviation. The pastoral intimacy of this promise — a personal word for each turning — stands in sharp contrast to the grand political machinery the chapter has been dismantling.

intro: Chapter 31 is the compressed theological core of the Egyptian alliance argument — nine verses that state the issue, the counter-argument, and the resolution with great precision. The contrast between flesh and spirit, between horses and YHWH's hovering presence, reaches its climax in v.8: Assyria will fall not to any human sword but to a sword of no mortal hand. The military argument dissolves into theological statement.

notes.original: Mitzrayim adam v'lo El v'suseihem basar v'lo ruach — Egypt is human and not God, their horses are flesh and not spirit
notes.rendering: The Egyptians are human, and not God. Their horses are flesh, and not spirit
notes.why: The contrast adam/El and basar/ruach is one of Isaiah's sharpest theological formulations. Adam — the human being, the creature of the earth (from adamah — ground). El — God, the divine. Basar — flesh, the mortal, creaturely substance. Ruach — spirit, the animating breath of YHWH. The political argument against the Egyptian alliance is theological: Egypt is in the category of the creaturely, and all creaturely things stumble when YHWH stretches out his hand. To trust in flesh is to trust in something that shares the condition of mortality. The argument does not denigrate Egypt — it simply places it correctly in the order of being.

notes.original: k'tzipporim ofot — like birds hovering overhead
notes.rendering: Like birds hovering overhead, so YHWH of hosts will protect Jerusalem
notes.why: The two animal images in vv.4–5 work together: YHWH as lion (who cannot be driven off by shepherds' shouting) and YHWH as hovering bird (who shields the nest with spread wings). The bird image draws on the eagle-wings of Exodus 19:4 and Deuteronomy 32:11 — the exodus protection renewed over Jerusalem. Tzipporim ofot — birds in flight, birds hovering (af — to fly; the participle gives the sense of sustained, circling hovering rather than a single pass). Ganen v'hitzil v'pasoch v'himlit — he will protect and deliver, he will pass over and rescue: four verbs of salvation, the last (pasoch) carrying the unmistakeable echo of the Passover (pesach — to pass over, to spare).

notes.original: v'nafal Ashur b'cherev lo ish — the Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man
notes.rendering: The Assyrian will fall by a sword, but not of man. A sword, but not of mortals, will devour him
notes.why: Lo ish — not of a man; lo adam — not of mortals: the double negation removes human agency from the Assyrian defeat entirely. This is the theological point toward which the whole Egyptian alliance argument has been moving: you do not need Egyptian horses because the battle will not be decided by human weapons. The historical fulfilment is Sennacherib's defeat in 37:36 — 185,000 troops struck down in a night by the angel of YHWH, with no Israelite sword drawn. The no-human-sword of the oracle becomes the no-human-sword of the event.

intro: Chapter 32 moves between three registers: the vision of the righteous king whose officials become shelters (vv.1–8), the warning to complacent women that echoes chapter 3 (vv.9–14), and the promise of the Spirit poured from on high that transforms wilderness into fruitful field and produces the fruit of righteousness as peace. The chapter makes explicit what has been implicit throughout: it is the Spirit, not political engineering, that produces the shalom Isaiah has been describing.

notes.original: v'hayah ish k'machaveh ruach — each will be like a hiding place from the wind
notes.rendering: Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land
notes.why: The four images of shelter — hiding place from wind, cover from storm, streams in desert, rock-shade in exhausted land — describe what a just official does for the vulnerable. The righteous leader is not primarily a decision-maker or a strategist but a shelter: something people can stand behind and survive. The images draw on wilderness and desert survival: in a land where shade and water are the difference between life and death, the just ruler provides what the landscape itself withholds. The messianic king of chapter 11 judged with equity; this king's officials embody that equity as practical refuge.

notes.original: ad yiqqareh aleinu ruach mimmarom — until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high
notes.rendering: until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field
notes.why: Yiqqareh — will be poured out (from arah — to pour, to empty out; used of water poured from a vessel). The outpouring of the Spirit from on high (mimmarom — from the height, from the heavenly realm) is what converts the wilderness to fruitful field. The same movement — wilderness to fertility — appears in 35:1–2 and 40–55 repeatedly. What human effort and political alliance cannot accomplish, the Spirit effects directly. Joel 2:28–29 develops this outpouring image; Peter identifies its fulfilment at Pentecost (Acts 2:17). Isaiah's is the root text.

notes.original: v'hayah ma'aseh hatzedaqah shalom — the effect of righteousness will be peace
notes.rendering: And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever
notes.why: Ma'aseh — the effect, the work, the product (from asah — to make, to do). Tzedaqah produces shalom as a tree produces fruit: the relationship is organic, not mechanical. Righteousness is not rewarded with peace from outside; it generates peace from within. The second clause: u'vadut hatzedaqah hashqet uvetach ad olam — the service/product of righteousness is quietness and trust forever. The three words — shalom, hashqet (quietness), vetach (trust/security) — are the same three denied to the sea-churned wicked in 57:20–21. Those who have righteousness have what the wicked cannot find.

intro: Chapter 33 closes the great woe-collection (chapters 28–33) and functions as its doxological resolution — a liturgical composition in which the community cries for help (v.2), YHWH arises (v.10), sinners tremble (v.14), the righteous are described (v.15–16), and the vision opens onto the king in his beauty and the city of peace (vv.17–24). It is the hinge between the Assyrian crisis material and the historical narrative of chapters 36–39.

notes.original: emunat ittecha chosen yeshu'ot — the faithfulness of your times, the abundance of salvations
notes.rendering: He will be the stability of your times — abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge. The fear of YHWH is Zion's treasure
notes.why: Emunat ittecha — faithfulness of your times (emunah — reliability, the steadiness of what can be trusted; the same root as amen). The phrase addresses the anxiety of living in a time of political chaos: the times themselves are made stable by YHWH's faithfulness. Chosen yeshu'ot — wealth of salvations, abundance of deliverances (chosen — stored wealth, treasury; yeshu'ot — plural of salvation, multiple acts of rescue). The fear of YHWH — yir'at YHWH — is named as Zion's treasure (otsar — the treasury, the storehouse). Not military strength, not Egyptian cavalry: the reverential knowledge of YHWH is what makes the city rich.

notes.original: mi yagur lanu esh ochelah — who among us can dwell with the consuming fire?
notes.rendering: Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?" He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly
notes.why: The question in v.14 echoes Psalm 15 and 24 — the entrance liturgy asking who may ascend the mountain of YHWH. The answer (v.15) is moral, not ritual: the one who walks righteously (holech tzedaqot), speaks uprightly (dover mesharim), rejects oppressive profit, refuses bribes (me'afen kapav — waves away his palms, shaking them free of bribery), stops his ears from blood-hearing and shuts his eyes from evil-seeing. The five negative acts of rejection mirror the consuming fire: the person who can dwell with YHWH's holiness is the person who has already been burning away what is false.

notes.original: ki YHWH shofteinu YHWH mechoqeqeinu YHWH malkeinu — YHWH is our judge, YHWH is our lawgiver, YHWH is our king
notes.rendering: For YHWH is our judge. YHWH is our lawgiver. YHWH is our king. He will save us
notes.why: The triple naming of YHWH in three governmental roles — shofet (judge), mechoqeq (lawgiver, engraver of statutes), and melech (king) — is a deliberate replacement of the three human institutions that have failed: the corrupt judges of chapter 1, the legislators of unjust statutes in chapter 10, the kings who made covenants with death in chapter 28. YHWH assumes all three offices simultaneously. The climactic fourth clause — hu yoshi'enu — he will save us — is the simplest statement of the whole book's message: not the Egyptian horseman, not the Assyrian deliverer, not the clever counsellor, but YHWH himself.

intro: Chapter 34 is the dark twin of chapter 35 — judgment and restoration set side by side as the anti-creation and the new creation. Edom (Israel's ancient brother-enemy, descended from Esau) receives the most thoroughgoing desolation oracle in the book: not merely conquest but a return to primordial chaos, the measuring line of tohu and bohu stretched over it. The wild animals that inherit the land are not random; they are named with care, as if the new occupants are being registered.

notes.original: v'naqlu kol tzva hashamayim v'niggalu kassefer hashamayim — all the host of heaven will rot, the skies will be rolled up like a scroll
notes.rendering: All the host of heaven will rot away — the skies will be rolled up like a scroll
notes.why: Niggalu kassefer — rolled up like a scroll (from galal — to roll; sefer — scroll, book). The image of the sky as a scroll being rolled closed appears here for the first time in the prophets and echoes through apocalyptic literature: Revelation 6:14 quotes it directly. The stars that nations worshipped as gods (the host of heaven — tzeva hashamayim) melt away (namaqqu — to putrefy, to dissolve). The cosmic framework of Edom's religious world — the astral deities — collapses with it. This is the opposite of creation: in Genesis the heavens were spread out; here they are rolled up.

notes.original: v'natah aleha qav tohu v'avney vohu — he will stretch over it the measuring line of chaos and the plumb line of emptiness
notes.rendering: He will stretch over it the measuring line of chaos and the plumb line of emptiness
notes.why: Tohu va'vohu — chaos and emptiness: the exact phrase from Genesis 1:2, the condition of the earth before creation ('without form and void'). The builder's measuring line (qav) and plumb line (avney — stones) are the tools of construction; here they are applied not to build but to measure out and confirm desolation. YHWH un-creates Edom. The land is returned to its pre-creation state. The theological point: the same divine ordering that made the cosmos can unmake what has stood in permanent hostility to his purposes.

notes.original: dirshu missefer YHWH u'qra'u — seek and read from the scroll of YHWH
notes.rendering: Seek and read from the scroll of YHWH: not one of these will be missing — none will lack her mate
notes.why: The command to consult 'the scroll of YHWH' is unique in the prophets — it appears to refer to the prophetic record itself, the written oracle the reader holds. Lo ne'edrah echad — not one will be missing (ne'edrah — to be absent, lacking). The wild animals inhabiting the desolated Edom are not there by accident: YHWH has cast the lot for each one and portioned out the land with a measuring line (v.17). Even the ecology of judgment is purposeful and recorded. The scroll guarantees it: what YHWH has spoken will be exactly fulfilled, creature by creature.

intro: Chapter 35 is one of the supreme lyric achievements of the Hebrew Bible — a ten-verse poem of pure restoration that stands as the counterpart to chapter 34's desolation.
