Where 34 measured out chaos, 35 measures out abundance. Where 34 ended with wild creatures inhabiting ruin, 35 ends with the ransomed of YHWH walking the highway home. The two chapters function as the theological brackets around the historical narrative that follows.

notes.original: yasus midbar v'tziyah v'tagel aravah v'tifrah kachavatzelet — the wilderness will be glad, the desert will rejoice and blossom like a crocus
notes.rendering: The wilderness and the dry land will be glad — the desert will rejoice and blossom like a crocus
notes.why: Yasus — will be glad, will exult (the verb of intense joy, used of bridegrooms and warriors celebrating victory). The subject is midbar — the wilderness itself. The desert does not merely receive water; it actively rejoices. Kachavatzelet — like a crocus (chavatzelet — a bulb flower, possibly the narcissus or asphodel; a flower that springs suddenly from apparently dead ground). The image sets the tone: what was dead is not merely healed but transformed into an agent of joy. The wilderness has its own voice and its own song before any human arrives.

notes.original: derech haqodesh yiqqarei lah — it will be called the Way of Holiness
notes.rendering: a highway will be there, and it will be called the Way of Holiness. The unclean will not pass over it
notes.why: Derech haqodesh — the Way of Holiness (the sacred road). The highway (mesillah — a raised, built road, a causeway; the same word used in 11:16 for the highway from Assyria) runs through the transformed wilderness. Its defining characteristic is that it is for the redeemed, not for the unclean (tame — ritually impure) or the fool (evil — the morally simple who strays). But the astonishing clause — v'ilu evilim lo yit'u — even if fools travel it, they will not go astray — suggests that the road is so clear and the guidance so certain that even those who would normally get lost cannot miss it. The way is safer than the travellers.

notes.original: u'feduyei YHWH yeshuvun u'va'u Tzion b'rinnah — the ransomed of YHWH will return and come to Zion with singing
notes.rendering: the ransomed of YHWH will return and come to Zion with singing. Everlasting joy will be upon their heads
notes.why: Peduyei YHWH — the ransomed of YHWH (from padah — to ransom, to redeem by payment; a commercial-legal term for purchasing freedom). This verse is repeated almost word for word in 51:11, the second great movement of the book — the comfort oracles. The repetition is not accidental: chapter 35 is the destination that all of chapter 40–55 is journeying toward. Simchat olam — everlasting joy (simchah — rejoicing; olam — forever). Al rosham — upon their heads (the heads that wore sackcloth in chapter 3, that are bald in chapters 15 and 22). Sorrow and sighing flee: the same two words (yagon v'anahah) appear in 51:11. The ransomed carry joy where they carried mourning.

intro: Chapter 36 begins the historical narrative that occupies chapters 36–39 — largely parallel to 2 Kings 18–20. The Rabshakeh's speech is one of the great pieces of political rhetoric in the ancient world: psychologically shrewd, theologically audacious, delivered in the language of Judah within earshot of the defenders on the wall. It is the test case for everything Isaiah has been saying about trust and fear for thirty-five chapters.

notes.original: mish'enet haqaneh hara'utz hazeh — this broken reed of a staff
notes.rendering: that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt
notes.why: Qaneh ratzutz — a crushed, broken reed (qaneh — a reed stalk; ratzutz — shattered, crushed). The image is Isaiah's own from chapter 30: the Egyptians are human, not God. The Rabshakeh deploys it with precision — he has read, or at least absorbed, the same political analysis as the prophet. The irony is exquisite: the Assyrian field commander makes the same argument against Egypt that Isaiah has been making for twenty years. He is right about Egypt. He is catastrophically wrong about YHWH. The same analysis that correctly identifies Egyptian weakness misidentifies YHWH as another failed national deity.

notes.original: YHWH amar elai aleh el ha'aretz hazzot v'hashchitah — YHWH said to me: go up against this land and destroy it
notes.rendering: is it without YHWH that I have come up against this land to destroy it? YHWH said to me, Go up against this land and destroy it
notes.why: The Rabshakeh's most theologically daring claim — that YHWH himself commissioned the Assyrian campaign against Judah — is not entirely wrong (cf. 10:5–6, where YHWH sends Assyria as his rod of anger). But the Rabshakeh does not know this through prophetic revelation; he is using it as a psychological weapon. The question is whether the population on the wall can distinguish between YHWH using Assyria as a tool and YHWH being subordinate to Assyrian power. The entire speech is designed to collapse that distinction.

notes.original: v'hecherishu v'lo anu oto davar — they were silent and answered him not a word
notes.rendering: But they were silent and said not a word — for the king's command was, 'Do not answer him'
notes.why: The silence of Hezekiah's officials in the face of the Rabshakeh's speech is the political enactment of Isaiah 30:15 — in quietness and trust will be your strength. They do not argue, do not counter-claim, do not engage the rhetoric. The king had commanded silence, and silence is what they give. The theological wisdom: to engage the Rabshakeh's speech on its own terms is already to concede his framework. The torn garments they bring to Hezekiah (v.22) are the response — not words but grief, and then prayer (chapter 37). The silence is not weakness; it is the refusal to play the game.

intro: Chapter 37 is the resolution of the Assyrian crisis — the moment every oracle from chapter 1 onward has been building toward. Hezekiah's prayer is a masterpiece of covenantal theology: he acknowledges Sennacherib's victories, concedes that the other nations' gods failed because they were wood and stone, and makes the case that YHWH's honour is at stake. The 185,000 dead in the Assyrian camp is the book's great vindication of Isaiah's forty years of counter-political preaching.

notes.original: YHWH tzvaot Elohei Yisrael yoshev hak'ruvim — YHWH of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim
notes.rendering: O YHWH of hosts, God of Israel, who is enthroned above the cherubim — you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth
notes.why: Yoshev hak'ruvim — enthroned above the cherubim: the title of the ark's presence, the innermost sanctuary of the temple (1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2). Hezekiah spreads the letter before YHWH (v.14) — he treats the correspondence physically, as something YHWH himself needs to read, in the posture of one laying a case before a sovereign. The prayer's theological structure is exact: YHWH is named as the God of Israel's covenant history (YHWH of hosts), of Israel's sanctuary (enthroned above the cherubim), and of all the earth (you alone are the God of all kingdoms). The scope moves from particular to universal, arriving at the monotheistic claim that dismantles the Rabshakeh's argument.

notes.original: halo shamata — have you not heard? I determined it long ago
notes.rendering: Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass
notes.why: The question put to Sennacherib — have you not heard? — is the same question put to Israel at the opening of Deutero-Isaiah (40:21, 28). The theological point: Sennacherib's campaigns, which he attributes entirely to his own prowess, were planned by YHWH before Sennacherib was born. Mi'yamim qedem — from days of old (qedem — the ancient past, the primordial time of divine counsel). The boast of vv.24–25 (I felled the cedars, I dried up the rivers) is answered: you were the instrument. The plan was mine. This is the theological answer to the Rabshakeh's speech of chapter 36 — YHWH does not merely react; he has been directing the whole drama.

notes.original: vayetzei malach YHWH vayach b'machaneh Ashur — the angel of YHWH goes out and strikes in the camp of the Assyrians
notes.rendering: the angel of YHWH goes out and strikes 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning — look, these were all dead bodies
notes.why: The event is narrated in three clauses with almost clinical brevity. No dramatic description of the dying, no battle account — simply: went out, struck, morning, dead bodies. Malach YHWH — the messenger/angel of YHWH (the same figure who struck the firstborn in Egypt, who appeared to Gideon and Elijah). The number 185,000 is either historical or a round number expressing totality: the entire army rendered inoperable. The oracle of 31:8 — the Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man — is fulfilled. The sword that killed 185,000 left no human wielder. Isaiah's forty years of preaching against military alliance comes down to this: YHWH did what no Egyptian cavalry could have done.

intro: Chapter 38 recounts Hezekiah's illness, his prayer, and the psalm of thanksgiving he composes after his recovery. The psalm — sometimes called the 'Writing of Hezekiah' — is one of the most personal documents in the Hebrew Bible: a king's interior account of facing death, being spared, and making sense of the reprieve. It sits alongside Psalms 22 and 88 as a meditation on the silence of God in extremity.

notes.original: zachar na et asher hithalach'ti l'fanecha be'emet uvlev shalem — remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart
notes.rendering: remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight
notes.why: The prayer is not a bargain but a testimony — Hezekiah presents his life as evidence. Emet — faithfulness, truth (the same root as amen; the lived reliability of covenant obedience). Lev shalem — a whole heart (shalem — complete, undivided; the root of shalom and also of Jerusalem's second syllable). The weeping (yivk'eh bechi gadol — he wept with great weeping) is not performance but grief: a king at the height of his power and purpose, told the door is closing. YHWH's response — I have seen your tears — makes the tears themselves part of the evidence.

notes.original: v'atta chashaqta nafshi mishachat beli — in love you delivered my life from the pit of destruction
notes.rendering: it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness. But in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction. For you have cast all my sins behind your back
notes.why: Chashaqta — you loved (from chashaq — to be attached to, to cleave to with desire; the word used in Deuteronomy 7:7 for YHWH's attachment to Israel). The pit of destruction (shachat beli — the pit of corruption, the grave that causes decomposition) is where Hezekiah nearly went. The casting of sins behind YHWH's back — hashlichta acharei gevecha kol chata'ai — is a vivid physical image: YHWH takes the sins and throws them where he himself cannot see them. The motif connects to Micah 7:19 (he will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea) and anticipates the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31:34 (I will remember their sins no more).

notes.original: lo she'ol tod'cha mavet yihalel'cha... chai chai hu yod'cha — Sheol does not thank you... the living, the living, they thank you
notes.rendering: For Sheol does not thank you — death does not praise you... The living — the living — they thank you, as I do this day
notes.why: The psalm makes a theological argument from liturgy: the dead cannot praise. Therefore survival is itself a vocation — to praise is the reason for being kept alive. Chai chai — the living, the living: the doubled form is emphatic (as in qadosh qadosh qadosh of chapter 6, or naflah naflah of chapter 21). The father who teaches the children your faithfulness (emet'cha) is the transmission mechanism: each generation kept alive becomes the carrier of the knowledge of YHWH to the next. Hezekiah's individual recovery becomes a picture of the whole mission of the living — to keep the praise going forward.

intro: Chapter 39 is the book's great pivot. Eight verses that close one era and open another: the Assyrian crisis is behind; Babylon is now on the horizon. Hezekiah's inexplicable pride — showing the Babylonian envoys everything — is the seed of the exile that chapters 40–55 will address. The chapter ends with Hezekiah's chilling response, one of the most uncomfortable conclusions to a narrative in the Hebrew Bible.

notes.original: v'yismach alehem Chizkiyahu — Hezekiah welcomes them
notes.rendering: Hezekiah welcomes them and shows them his treasure house — the silver, the gold, the spices, the fine oil, his whole armoury
notes.why: Yismach — he rejoiced, was glad (from samach — to rejoice). The same verb used for the joy of the ransomed in 35:10. Hezekiah's delight at the Babylonian delegation is the delight of a man who has just survived death and a siege: he is alive, his city stands, and distant Babylon is sending congratulations. The showing of everything (kol asher nimtza b'otzrotav — all that was found in his treasuries) is the act of a man giddy with survival, not calculating the political cost. It is the opposite of the quiet trust Isaiah has preached: not trusting in YHWH's protection but displaying the very wealth that will attract Babylon's appetite.

notes.original: hineh yamim ba'im v'nissa kol asher b'veitcha — look, days are coming when everything in your house will be carried to Babylon
notes.rendering: Look — days are coming when everything in your house... will be carried to Babylon. Nothing will be left... And some of your own sons will be taken away and will become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon
notes.why: The oracle is specific in its reversal: the treasure house Hezekiah showed them is the treasure house that will be emptied. The sons he will father will end up as court eunuchs — the most permanent form of subjugation, cutting off the dynastic line itself. Sarisei — eunuchs (saros — a castrated court official; the term used for the highest-ranking palace administrators in the ancient Near East). The Babylonian exile is announced in two verses. Everything chapters 40–55 will address — the deportation, the long captivity, the yearning for home — is seeded here in Hezekiah's treasure room.

notes.original: tov d'var YHWH asher dibbart — the word of YHWH that you have spoken is good
notes.rendering: The word of YHWH that you have spoken is good." For he thinks, "There will be peace and security in my days.
notes.why: Hezekiah's response has appalled readers for millennia. Tov — good: not good in the sense of welcome or deserved, but good in the sense of acceptable to me, because it will not happen on my watch. Ki yihyeh shalom v'emet b'yamai — for there will be peace and truth in my days. The final word — b'yamai, in my days — is the most damning possible response to a prophecy of his children's captivity. The king who wept bitterly at his own death sentence accepts his children's slavery with equanimity. It is not heroic acceptance but self-absorption. The book of Isaiah now turns its face toward those children and their descendants in Babylon — and chapter 40 begins.

intro: Chapter 40 is one of the supreme openings in world literature. After the eight bleak verses of chapter 39 — the treasure shown, the oracle of exile, the king's chilling indifference — the voice breaks through: Comfort, comfort my people. The chapter moves from the herald's cry in the wilderness through the incomparability of God to the great promise of renewed strength for those who wait. Everything that follows in chapters 40–55 is an unfolding of this chapter's themes.

notes.original: nacham nacham ami — comfort, comfort my people
notes.rendering: Comfort, comfort my people," says your God. "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned
notes.why: Nacham nacham — the doubled imperative of comfort (nacham — to comfort, to console, to breathe deeply in response to grief; the word of the midwife, the mourner's friend). The doubling is urgency: comfort her now, comfort her thoroughly. Al lev — speak to the heart (literally: speak upon the heart; the idiom of intimate persuasion, used of a man speaking tenderly to a woman he loves in Genesis 34:3 and Ruth 2:13). Tzeva'ah — her warfare, her hard service (the word for military campaign or forced labour). The exile is over. The debt is paid. Not merely acquitted but overpaid — kiflayim, double — more than enough has been received.

notes.original: u'devar Eloheinu yaqum l'olam — but the word of our God will stand forever
notes.rendering: The grass withers, the flower fades — but the word of our God will stand forever
notes.why: The contrast is between kol basar (all flesh — the universal mortal category) and devar Elohenu (the word of our God). Grass and flower wither because the ruach YHWH — the breath/wind of YHWH — blows on them: the same divine breath that gives life also reveals the fragility of everything creaturely. But the word stands (yaqum — rises, stands upright, endures). Peter quotes this verse in 1 Peter 1:24–25, applying it to the gospel. The word that will stand forever is the word now being proclaimed in the good news. The ancient comfort oracle becomes the foundation of apostolic preaching.

notes.original: v'qovei YHWH yachalifu koach — those who wait for YHWH shall renew their strength
notes.rendering: they who wait for YHWH shall renew their strength. They shall mount up with wings like eagles. They shall run and not be weary. They shall walk and not faint
notes.why: Qovei YHWH — those who wait for YHWH (qavah — to wait with taut expectation, the same rope-of-hope root as chapter 25:9 and 33:2). Yachalifu koach — they shall exchange strength (chalaf — to change, to pass through, to renew; the word used of changing clothes). The three images ascend: mounting up with wings (flight, transcendence), running (sustained effort), walking (the ordinary faithful pace). The order is counter-intuitive: flight first, then running, then walking. The climactic achievement of the redeemed life is not the spectacular but the sustainable — to walk day after day and not faint. This is the life that the comfort oracles are preparing for.

intro: Chapter 41 opens the great courtroom scenes of Deutero-Isaiah — YHWH summons the nations and their gods to a trial of prediction and proof. The chapter's central oracle (vv.8–13) — the 'fear not' address to Israel as YHWH's servant — is among the most tender passages in the book. It is bracketed by the challenge to the idol-makers who cannot predict anything: YHWH alone has the track record of announced-and-fulfilled history.

notes.original: ani YHWH rishon v'et acharonim ani hu — I, YHWH, the first and with the last, I am he
notes.rendering: I, YHWH — the first and with the last. I am he
notes.why: Rishon — the first (the one who was before all else). Et acharonim — with the last ones (those who come at the end of time; YHWH is not merely first but present with all who come after). Ani hu — I am he: the divine self-identification formula that runs through Deutero-Isaiah (43:10, 43:13, 46:4, 48:12) and culminates in the 'I am' sayings of John's Gospel. The formula declares identity across time: the one who stirred up Cyrus is the same one who spoke at Sinai and the same one who will be present at the end. History is not random; it has a single directing will.

notes.original: al tira ki imm'cha ani — do not fear, for I am with you
notes.rendering: do not fear, for I am with you. Do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you — yes, I will help you. I will uphold you with my righteous right hand
notes.why: Al tira — do not fear (the most-repeated divine command in all of Scripture; it appears here in its fullest Deutero-Isaianic form). Ki imm'cha ani — for I am with you (the formula of divine accompaniment: the covenant presence that makes fear irrational). The four verbs of divine action that follow accumulate like a hand tightening its grip: imatzticha (I will strengthen you), af azarticha (yes, I will help you — the af intensifies: indeed, surely), temachticha (I will uphold you, support you from beneath). Ymin tzidqi — my righteous right hand: the right hand is the hand of power and covenant-keeping; tzidqi — my righteousness, my rightness. YHWH upholds with his character, not merely his strength.

notes.original: go'alcha q'dosh Yisrael — your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel
notes.rendering: Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel
notes.why: Go'el — redeemer (from ga'al — to redeem by right of kinship; the go'el is the nearest relative who buys back the enslaved family member, who marries the widow to preserve the family line, who avenges the murdered kinsman). YHWH takes on the role of Israel's nearest relative — the one with the legal obligation and the family right to redeem. The pairing of Go'el with Q'dosh Yisrael — Redeemer with Holy One of Israel — is characteristic of Deutero-Isaiah: the Holy One who is absolutely other becomes the Kinsman who is absolutely near. The two attributes that seem most in tension — transcendent holiness and intimate family obligation — are united in YHWH's self-presentation to the exiles.

intro: Chapter 42 introduces the Servant of YHWH — the figure who will dominate chapters 42–53 in four distinct songs (42:1–4, 49:1–6, 50:4–9, 52:13–53:12). The Servant is at once Israel's ideal and Israel's replacement: the nation that failed to be the light it was called to be is confronted with one who will accomplish what Israel could not. The chapter then turns to indict Israel itself as a blind and deaf servant — the painful irony of a servant who cannot see or hear.

notes.original: hen avdi etmach bo, b'chiri ratzatah nafshi — look at my servant whom I uphold, my chosen one in whom my soul delights
notes.rendering: Look at my servant, whom I uphold — my chosen one in whom my soul delights. I have put my Spirit upon him
notes.why: Hen — look! (the particle of presentation, of showing something: here, attend to this person). Avdi — my servant (eved — slave, servant, worshipper; the most intimate and most lowly title YHWH gives). Etmach bo — whom I uphold (tamach — to grasp, to hold firmly; the word of one steadying another who might fall). Ratzatah nafshi — my soul delights (ratzah — to be pleased, to take pleasure in; nafshi — my soul, my whole self). Matthew 3:17 and 12:18 quote this verse at Jesus's baptism and in identification of Jesus's healing ministry. The three gifts named — the servant's identity (my chosen), YHWH's delight, and the Spirit — are all present at the Jordan River.

notes.original: qaneh ratzutz lo yishbor u'fishtah chehah lo y'chab'enah — a bruised reed he will not break, a faintly burning wick he will not quench
notes.rendering: A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench. He will faithfully bring forth justice
notes.why: Qaneh ratzutz — a bruised reed (ratzutz — crushed, the same adjective used for the Egyptian reed-staff of 36:6; here applied to the fragile, the barely-alive). Pishtah chehah — a dimly burning wick (pishtah — flax, the material of wicks; chehah — faint, guttering, nearly extinguished). The Servant's justice is not the justice of the powerful crushing the weak: he handles what is almost broken with the care that keeps it alive. The contrast with the Rabshakeh's method (volume, intimidation, public shaming) is total. Matthew quotes this in 12:20 as the principle of Jesus's healing ministry — the exact opposite of the triumphalism the crowds expected of the Messiah.

notes.original: v'ettencha livrit am l'or goyim — I will give you as a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations
notes.rendering: I will give you as a covenant for the people, as a light for the nations — to open the eyes that are blind
notes.why: Livrit am — as a covenant for the people (the Servant does not merely carry the covenant; he embodies it, he is the covenant). L'or goyim — as a light for the nations: the mission of 2:2–4 (nations streaming to the mountain) is now concentrated in a single person. The three infinitives that follow — to open eyes, to bring out prisoners, to release those in darkness — describe what a covenant-in-person does: not a legal document but a liberating presence. Simeon quotes this verse in Luke 2:32 at the presentation of the infant Jesus: a light for revelation to the Gentiles. The Servant who is the covenant becomes the light who fulfils the mountain vision.

intro: Chapter 43 moves between the most intimate language in the book — I have called you by name, you are mine, you are precious and I love you — and the most radical announcement: the former things are to be forgotten. The new exodus will surpass the old exodus so completely that memory of the Red Sea crossing should be eclipsed. The chapter also contains the most compressed and absolute statement of sole divinity in the Bible: before me no god was formed, nor will there be any after me.

notes.original: lo tira ki g'altich qara'ti v'shimcha li atah — do not fear, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by name — you are mine
notes.rendering: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by name — you are mine
notes.why: G'altich — I have redeemed you (ga'al — the kinsman-redeemer verb; YHWH acting as the nearest relative who buys back the enslaved). Qara'ti v'shimcha — I have called you by name (the naming that establishes personal relationship, the intimacy of knowing someone's individual name rather than their category). Li atah — you are mine (not: you belong to my category, my people, my nation — but the more intimate possessive: mine, personally). The three declarations — redeemed, named, owned — form a complete account of what YHWH has done. The fear that exile produces is met with a relationship that predates the exile and cannot be cancelled by it.

notes.original: hineni oseh chadashah — look, I am doing a new thing
notes.rendering: Look — I am doing a new thing. Now it springs forth — do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert
notes.why: Chadashah — a new thing (from chadash — new, fresh; the same root as the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and the new creation of Isaiah 65). Titzmacha — now it springs forth (tzamach — to sprout, to grow; the verb of the Branch of chapter 4:2 and the shoot from Jesse in 11:1). The new thing is being planted even as the prophet speaks. The wilderness-way and desert-rivers of vv.19–20 reverse the exodus direction: in the first exodus YHWH made a path through the sea; in the new exodus he makes a path through the desert. The geography of return is different from the geography of escape — but the maker of ways is the same.

notes.original: anochi anochi hu mocheh f'sha'echa — I — I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake
notes.rendering: I — I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins
notes.why: Anochi anochi hu — I, I am he: the doubled pronoun is emphatic to the point of exclusivity. Mocheh — blots out (machah — to wipe away, to obliterate, as one wipes a tablet clean). L'ma'ani — for my own sake: YHWH's motivation for forgiveness is not Israel's merit or repentance but YHWH's own character and purposes. This is theologically radical: the forgiveness is not earned, not deserved, not conditional on adequate prior repentance. It flows from YHWH's identity. The parallel with 8:12 — I will remember their sins no more — is exact; the new covenant promise and the comfort oracle share the same verb: lo ezkor.

intro: Chapter 44 contains Deutero-Isaiah's most extended and biting satire on idol-making — the careful carpenter who roasts his dinner on one half of the log and worships his god carved from the other. The chapter closes with the first naming of Cyrus: the Persian king who will be YHWH's shepherd to rebuild Jerusalem. The naming of a ruler by name over a century before his birth is one of the most discussed features of the book.

notes.original: ki etzon mayim al tzameh v'nozlim al yababah etoch ruchi al zar'echa — I will pour water on the thirsty and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit on your offspring
notes.rendering: For I will pour water on the thirsty land and streams on the dry ground. I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring and my blessing on your descendants
notes.why: The double outpouring — water on the land, Spirit on the people — is a single act: the physical and spiritual restoration are simultaneous and inseparable. Etoch ruchi — I will pour my Spirit (natzal — to pour out, to shed; ruach — Spirit). The image of the Spirit poured like rain echoes 32:15 and anticipates Joel 2:28 (I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh), which Peter quotes at Pentecost. The willows by flowing streams (v.4) that spring up among the grass are the image of the restored community: rooted in the Spirit's water, growing visibly, multiplying beyond the original family ('this one' and 'another' and yet 'another' in v.5).

notes.original: ro'eh efer — he feeds on ashes
notes.rendering: He feeds on ashes. A deluded heart has led him astray
notes.why: Ro'eh efer — the one who shepherds ashes, who pastures on ash. The satirical culmination of the idol-maker passage: the man who thought he was making a god has been feeding himself on nothing. The word ro'eh — shepherd — is the same word used of Cyrus in v.28 (he is my shepherd). The man who feeds on ash-gods is contrasted with the man YHWH designates as his shepherd for the nations. Libbah huttal — his heart has been turned aside, led astray (tua — to be diverted, to wander). The idol does not merely fail to deliver; it actively misleads the heart that manufactured it.

notes.original: ha'omer l'Koresh ro'i — who says of Cyrus, he is my shepherd
notes.rendering: who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he will fulfil all my purpose,' saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid'
notes.why: The naming of Cyrus (Koresh — the Persian form of the name) is unprecedented in prophetic literature: a foreign ruler named by name and commissioned before his birth (Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BCE; this text is dated by most scholars to the exile, making the naming prospective). Ro'i — my shepherd (the same title YHWH claims for himself in 40:11, now given to a Gentile king). Kol cheftzi yashlem — he will complete all my pleasure, fulfil my purpose. The idol-maker of vv.9–20 could not deliver; Cyrus, YHWH's designated shepherd, will. The irony is complete: YHWH uses a pagan conqueror to accomplish what Israel's religion could not.

intro: Chapter 45 reaches the theological apex of the Cyrus oracles and contains the most sweeping monotheistic declaration in the Hebrew Bible — every knee will bow, every tongue swear allegiance. Cyrus is called YHWH's anointed (mashiach) — the same word as messiah — applied here to a Gentile, which is theologically shocking. Paul quotes verse 23 in Romans 14:11 and Philippians 2:10–11 as the eschatological destination of all creation.

notes.original: l'Koresh meshicho — to Cyrus, his anointed
notes.rendering: Thus says YHWH to his anointed — to Cyrus
notes.why: Meshicho — his anointed (mashiach — the anointed one; messiah). The word is applied throughout the Hebrew Bible to kings of Israel (Saul, David), to the high priest, and once to the patriarchs as YHWH's anointed (Psalm 105:15). Here, for the only time in the Bible, it is applied to a Gentile ruler. The theological audacity is deliberate: YHWH's purposes cannot be contained within Israel's political structures. He raises up and anoints whom he will — including a Persian king who does not know him (v.4). This is the Cyrus cylinder's historical figure transformed into a theological statement about divine sovereignty over all kingdoms.

notes.original: yotzer or uvore choshech — I form light and create darkness
notes.rendering: I form light and create darkness — I make well-being and create calamity. I am YHWH, who does all these things
notes.why: The verse is a theological statement aimed at Persian Zoroastrianism, which posited two equal divine powers — Ahura Mazda (light/good) and Ahriman (darkness/evil). YHWH claims both: I am the maker of both or and choshech, shalom and ra (well-being and calamity). The monotheism of Deutero-Isaiah is absolute: there is no second divine power that manages darkness while YHWH manages light. The theological consequence is uncomfortable but honest — YHWH is responsible for both dimensions of reality. The ancient morning prayer (Yotzer Or) of Jewish liturgy takes its name from this verse, reciting it daily as a declaration of monotheism against all dualist alternatives.

notes.original: panu elai v'hivvashe'u kol afsei aretz — turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth
notes.rendering: Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth — for I am God, and there is no other. By myself I have sworn — from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that will not return: 'To me every knee will bow, every tongue will swear allegiance'
notes.why: The invitation panu elai — turn to me — is universal: kol afsei aretz, all the ends of the earth, not merely Israel. The sworn oath (bi nishba'ti — by myself I have sworn; since YHWH has no one greater to swear by, 6:13) makes the universal homage irrevocable. Tichra kol berech — every knee will bow (kara — to bend the knee in submission or worship). Tishava kol lashon — every tongue will swear (shava — to take an oath of allegiance). Paul quotes this in Romans 14:11 for the final accountability of all humanity and in Philippians 2:10–11 as the consequence of Christ's exaltation. The exile community's promise of universal YHWH-recognition becomes the New Testament's picture of cosmic Christological lordship.

intro: Chapter 46 opens with a scene of deliberate comedy: Bel and Nebo — the great gods of Babylon, whose cult statues were paraded through the city at the New Year festival — are pictured being loaded onto ox-carts as refugees, carried away by their worshippers who are themselves being carried away into exile. The contrast with YHWH who carries Israel from the womb to old age is the theological spine of the chapter.

notes.original: kara Bel qores Nevo — Bel bows down, Nebo stoops
notes.rendering: Bel bows down. Nebo stoops. Their idols are on beasts and livestock... They themselves go into captivity
notes.why: Bel (from Akkadian Bel — Lord) is the title of Marduk, the chief deity of Babylon; Nebo (Nabu) is his son, the god of writing and wisdom. Both were carried in solemn procession during the Babylonian New Year (Akitu) festival — the moment of cosmic renewal when the gods decreed the year's fate. Isaiah inverts the scene: instead of gods processing in triumph, they slump (kara — to bow, to collapse) and stoop (qores — to crouch, to bend under weight). The gods who were supposed to carry the city's destiny are being carted off as baggage. The irony is exact: objects meant to be borne in worship are being borne in defeat.

notes.original: va'ani asiti va'ani essa va'ani esbol va'amalet — I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save
notes.rendering: Even to your old age I am he, and to grey hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear. I will carry and will save
notes.why: The contrast with Bel and Nebo is total and deliberate. The idol-gods must be carried by their worshippers (nasa — lifted, carried; the same verb). YHWH carries his people (the same verb). The direction of carrying is opposite: idol-worshippers exhaust themselves carrying dead weight; YHWH carries those who cannot carry themselves. Asiti — I have made (the one who made Israel carries what he made). V'amalet — and I will save (from malat — to escape, to deliver; the rescue of one in danger). Four verbs of divine carrying: made, will bear, will carry, will save. The lifecycle framing (before birth to grey hairs) makes the carrying permanent and unconditional.

notes.original: maggid mereshit acharit — declaring the end from the beginning
notes.rendering: declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose'
notes.why: Maggid mereshit acharit — the one who announces from the beginning the end (rishit — beginning, origin; acharit — end, outcome; the same word used for the latter days in eschatology). The argument of Deutero-Isaiah's trial scenes returns: the test of deity is the capacity to predict and fulfil. Only YHWH has the track record of announced-and-accomplished history that constitutes genuine prediction. Atzati taqum — my counsel shall stand (atzah — counsel, purpose; qum — to stand, to be established). The bird of prey from the east (v.11) is Cyrus again — called like a trained raptor from a falconer's fist, swift and precise.

intro: Chapter 47 is a funeral dirge sung over a city not yet fallen — a taunt-song that strips Babylon of its pretensions one by one. The chapter's structure mirrors that of the taunt over the king of Babylon in chapter 14: height, then humiliation. The specific charge against Babylon is cruelty in the exercise of power given to it by YHWH himself — the instrument exceeded its brief.

notes.original: qatzafti al ami chilalti nachalati — I was angry with my people, I profaned my heritage
notes.rendering: I was angry with my people. I profaned my heritage. I gave them into your hand. But you showed them no mercy. On the aged you made your yoke very heavy
notes.why: The divine self-disclosure here is striking: YHWH acknowledges that he handed Israel to Babylon as punishment — then holds Babylon accountable for exceeding the terms of the assignment. Lo samti alehem rachamim — you did not set compassion on them. The aged (zaqen) were made to bear the heaviest yoke: this is the specific charge, the cruelty that went beyond judicial punishment into sadism. The instrument of divine discipline became an agent of independent cruelty. The theology is consistent with chapter 10 (the Assyrian rod that overreached): YHWH uses imperial power as a tool, then judges the tool for its excesses.

notes.original: ani v'efsi od — I am, and there is no one besides me
notes.rendering: who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me. I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children'
notes.why: Ani v'efsi od — I am, and there is nothing besides me: the precise phrase YHWH uses of himself in 45:5 and 45:6 is here placed in the mouth of Babylon. The empire has committed the ultimate blasphemy — claiming divine self-sufficiency. The I-am formula that belongs to YHWH alone (45:22; 43:10–11) is usurped by the city-state that thought its commercial and military dominance made it invulnerable. The widow-and-childless-mother imagery picks up from Lamentations: the city that thought itself eternally mistress will wear the mourning-dress of the most socially vulnerable position in the ancient world.

notes.original: hovrei shamayim ha'osherim bakochavim — those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars
notes.rendering: those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what will come upon you... Look — they are like stubble. The fire consumes them
notes.why: Babylon was the ancient world's great centre of astronomical observation and astrological prediction — hovrei shamayim (dividers of the heavens, those who section the sky into zones for reading) and chozim bakochavim (star-gazers) were the empire's equivalent of strategic intelligence analysts. They could not predict the coming of Cyrus. They cannot save the city their predictions were meant to protect. The fire that consumes them is not the coal of chapter 6 (which purified Isaiah's lips) and not the fire of the altar (which was life-giving): this is the fire of judgment that produces no warmth and no light for anyone.

intro: Chapter 48 closes the first great movement of Deutero-Isaiah (chapters 40–48) and functions as its uncomfortable coda: the exiles who are about to be liberated are not idealized. They swear by YHWH's name but not in truth. They are obstinate, with an iron sinew for a neck. YHWH's grace to them is explicitly not because of their merit but for his own name's sake. The chapter ends with the exodus-call — Go out from Babylon — and the jarring final note: there is no peace for the wicked.

notes.original: hineh tzaraftich v'lo v'chasef b'chor oni b'charatich — I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction
notes.rendering: Look — I have refined you, but not as silver. I have tried you in the furnace of affliction
notes.why: Tzaraftich — I have refined you (tzaraf — to smelt, to refine metal; the word of the refiner's fire that tests and purifies). Lo v'chasef — but not as silver: the exile has been a furnace (kur oni — furnace of affliction; kur — the smelting furnace, the most intense heat a metallurgist applies), but YHWH has not been refining Israel as pure silver is refined — the process cannot produce the yield a silversmith expects. Israel has come through the furnace changed but not purified in the way one might hope. The image is honest about the limits of what suffering accomplishes on its own, apart from divine grace.

notes.original: v'attah Adonai YHWH shalchani v'rucho — and now the Sovereign YHWH has sent me, and his Spirit
notes.rendering: And now the Sovereign YHWH has sent me, and his Spirit
notes.why: This half-verse is one of the most theologically significant in the chapter — a sudden first-person intrusion that breaks the divine speech: a speaker says 'the Sovereign YHWH has sent me.' Who is speaking? The possibilities are: the prophet himself (identifying his mission), the Servant figure of chapters 42 and 49 (whose commission is precisely to be sent), or a prefiguring of the trinitarian mission formula that Jesus picks up in John 20:21. The verse is deliberately ambiguous in its context. What is clear is the dual sending: YHWH sends the speaker and his Spirit together — the mission and the empowerment are inseparable.

notes.original: lu hiqshavta l'mitzvotai vayehi cha'nahar shlomecha — oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river
notes.rendering: Oh that you had listened to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea
notes.why: Lu — oh that (the particle of unfulfilled wish, the counterfactual sigh). The verse is YHWH mourning the path not taken: what Israel's shalom and righteousness could have been, expressed in two of the most beautiful similes in the book. Ka'nahar shlomecha — your peace like a river (the deep, wide, powerful flow of a perennial stream — not a seasonal wadi but the Jordan or the Euphrates at full flow). Tzidqatcha k'galei hayam — your righteousness like the waves of the sea (the endless, rolling succession of waves, each one coming from behind the last). The exile was not YHWH's preference; it was the consequence of the path Israel chose. The wish-lament is genuine grief.

intro: Chapter 49 opens the second half of Deutero-Isaiah (chapters 49–55) with the Second Servant Song — and immediately introduces a tension that will run through the remaining songs: the Servant who is called Israel cannot simply be Israel, because the Servant's mission is to restore Israel. The chapter's other great passage is YHWH's answer to Zion's despair — the nursing-mother image and the engraved palms — perhaps the most tender passage in the entire book.

notes.original: vayasem pi k'cherev chaddah — he made my mouth like a sharp sword
notes.rendering: He made my mouth like a sharp sword. In the shadow of his hand he hid me. He made me a polished arrow. In his quiver he concealed me
notes.why: The two weapon images — sword and arrow — describe the Servant's instrument (the mouth, the word) and the paradox of his hiddenness. Cherev chaddah — a sharp sword (sharp implies precision and penetration, not brutality). Chetz barur — a polished arrow (barur — selected, purified, the best arrow in the quiver). But both are concealed: b'tzel yado histarani (in the shadow of his hand he hid me), b'ashpato hechbiyaniy (in his quiver he concealed me). The Servant is prepared and powerful but not yet deployed. The hiddenness is not abandonment but preservation — held in reserve for the moment of greatest need.

notes.original: n'tatich l'or goyim lihyot yeshu'ati ad q'tzeh ha'aretz — I will make you a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth
notes.rendering: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth
notes.why: The commission of 42:6 (light for the nations) is here reformulated with an explicit scope: ad q'tzeh ha'aretz — to the end of the earth. Paul and Barnabas quote this verse in Acts 13:47 to justify their turn to the Gentiles after rejection by the Jewish community in Pisidian Antioch: 'I have set you to be a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.' The Servant's mission exceeds the restoration of Israel (which is called 'too light a thing') — it encompasses the salvation of the whole earth. The narrowest commission (restore Israel) is embedded within the widest possible one.

notes.original: hativ'chach ishah et ulah... hen al kapayim chakoticha — can a woman forget her nursing child? Look, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands
notes.rendering: Can a woman forget her nursing child?... Even these may forget — yet I will not forget you. Look — I have engraved you on the palms of my hands
notes.why: The nursing-mother image is YHWH's most intimate self-comparison in the book. Ulah — her nursing child (from ul — to suckle; the infant at the breast who depends entirely on the mother's body for survival). The question expects the answer 'impossible' — but YHWH goes one further: even if the impossible happened, I would not forget. Chakoticha — I have engraved you (chakak — to cut, to inscribe, to carve permanently; the word for inscribed law). The palms of the hands are the most visible, most constantly-in-use surface of the body. Zion's name is cut into YHWH's working hands — present at every act, every moment.

intro: The Third Servant Song (vv.4–9) is the most explicitly biographical of the four: the Servant describes his daily discipline of listening, his willingness to receive violence without flinching, and his unshakeable confidence in YHWH's vindication. The legal language of vindication — who will contend, who will declare guilty — anticipates the courtroom of chapter 53. The Servant's face set like flint becomes a controlling image for the Gospel accounts of Jesus's journey toward Jerusalem.

notes.original: lashon limmudim — the tongue of those who are taught
notes.rendering: The Sovereign YHWH has given me the tongue of those who are taught — that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary
notes.why: Lashon limmudim — the tongue of disciples (limmud — a taught one, a student; the same root as the talmid of later tradition). The Servant is not self-taught — he has a tongue that has been formed by listening, not by brilliance. The purpose of this discipled tongue is pastoral rather than prophetic: la'ut et ye'ef davar — to sustain/know how to help the weary with a word (ye'ef — the exhausted, the worn out; davar — a word, the right word). The Servant's primary gift is not proclamation to the masses but the capacity to say the right thing to the person at the end of their strength. This is the ministry described in Matthew 11:28–30.

notes.original: gabi natati l'makkim u'l'hochim et l'chayai — I gave my back to those who strike and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard
notes.rendering: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard. I did not hide my face from disgrace and spitting
notes.why: The three acts of violence are specific and escalating: striking the back (punishment), pulling the beard (the ultimate humiliation in ancient Near Eastern culture — the beard was a man's honour, to tear it was to strip his dignity), spitting in the face (the gesture of absolute contempt, used in Numbers 12:14 and Deuteronomy 25:9 as a judicial shaming act). Natati — I gave (the verb is active and voluntary, not passive: the Servant presents himself for the violence). The passion narrative in all four gospels mirrors these three acts in sequence. Isaiah's Servant does not merely predict suffering — he enacts the theology of non-retaliation.

notes.original: v'panai samti k'challamish — I have set my face like a flint
notes.rendering: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame
notes.why: Challamish — flint (the hardest common stone of the Levant, used for cutting tools; its hardness is proverbial). The face set like flint is the face that will not turn aside, will not be read, will not betray fear to those who are trying to humiliate it. Luke 9:51 uses the identical idiom of Jesus — he set his face to go to Jerusalem — at the moment he begins his final journey. The combination of physical resolve and theological certainty (I know I will not be put to shame) is the Servant's answer to the violence of v.6: not stoicism but confidence in YHWH's vindication that makes the suffering bearable.

intro: Chapter 51 is a chapter of triple summons: listen (vv.1–3), listen (vv.4–6), listen (vv.7–8), then awake (vv.9–11), then rouse yourself (v.17). The community calls for YHWH's arm to awaken (vv.9–11) and YHWH in turn calls Zion to awaken and rise (v.17). The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drained is now transferred to her tormentors — the direction of divine judgment reverses.

notes.original: habitu el Avraham avichem v'el Sarah techol'lechem — look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you
notes.rendering: Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you — for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him
notes.why: Echad — one: Abraham was singular when YHWH called him, a single person with a barren wife (Sarah's barrenness is implied in the Sarah reference). From that single called one, a people multiplied. The argument is from precedent to present: you are few and in exile — but so was Abraham. The rock from which Israel was hewn is a single man's faith. The quarry from which they were dug is the womb of one woman who laughed at the promise. If YHWH could do it then from nothing, he can do it now from exile. The demographic despair of the exiles is answered by the demographic miracle of the patriarchs.

notes.original: uri uri livshi oz zero'a YHWH — awake, awake, put on strength O arm of YHWH
notes.rendering: Awake, awake! Put on strength, O arm of YHWH. Awake, as in days of old... Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea?
notes.why: Uri uri — awake, awake (the doubled imperative of urgent summons; the same call that will be redirected to Zion in 52:1). Zero'a YHWH — the arm of YHWH (the executive power of divine action, the raised arm of combat). Rahab — the mythological sea-monster (not the woman of Jericho) representing the chaos of the primordial waters and, typologically, Egypt. The prayer calls for the cosmic victory of creation (Rahab and the dragon) and the historical victory of the exodus (the dried sea, the path for the redeemed) to be reenacted now. The same arm that defeated chaos-at-creation and Egypt-at-the-sea is the arm the exiles are asking to move for Babylon.

notes.original: hineh laqachti miyad'chi et kos hatar'elah — look, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering
notes.rendering: I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering. The bowl of my wrath you will drink no more. And I will put it into the hand of your tormentors
notes.why: Kos hatar'elah — the cup of staggering (tar'elah — reeling, dizziness, the vertigo of the drunk; but here the intoxication is divine judgment). The cup of wrath image (cf. Jeremiah 25:15–28, Lamentations 4:21, Psalm 75:8) is one of the Hebrew Bible's most powerful metaphors for judgment: to drink the cup is to absorb the full force of divine anger until you stagger. YHWH now takes the cup from Jerusalem's lips and hands it to her tormentors — the exacting justice of history reversed. The tormentors who forced Jerusalem to the ground (v.23) will themselves drink what they dispensed. Revelation 14:10 and 16:19 draw on this cup imagery directly.

intro: Chapter 52 opens with the mirror-image of chapter 51's summons: YHWH was called to awaken his arm; now Zion is called to awaken and dress. The herald passage (vv.7–10) is the joyful announcement that precedes the Fourth Servant Song — the most theologically weighty passage in the book — which begins at 52:13 and runs through 53:12.

notes.original: mah na'vu al heharim raglei m'vasser — how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the herald
notes.rendering: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news — who publishes peace, who brings good news of happiness, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, 'Your God reigns!'
notes.why: Na'vu — beautiful, lovely (from naveh — the loveliness of rightness in place). The feet are beautiful not for their own sake but because of where they have been going and what news they carry. M'vasser — the herald, the one who brings good news (basar — to bring news; this is the verbal root of the Greek euangelion — gospel). The five things the herald publishes: shalom (peace), tov (good things), yeshu'ah (salvation), and the royal proclamation malach Elohayich — your God reigns. Paul quotes this verse in Romans 10:15 as the basis for the sending of the gospel messenger. The mountains are the same mountains from which the signal was raised throughout the book.

notes.original: hineh yaskil avdi... mishchat me'ish mar'ehu — my servant will act wisely... his appearance was marred beyond human semblance
notes.rendering: Look — my servant will act wisely. He will be high and lifted up and exalted greatly. As many were astonished at you — his appearance was so marred beyond human semblance
notes.why: Yaskil — will prosper, will act wisely, will have insight (sakal — to be prudent, to succeed, to bring to a right outcome; the word of the wise administrator). The threefold exaltation — yarum v'nissa v'gavah m'od — echoes the throne-room vision of 6:1 where YHWH sat ram v'nissa (high and lifted up). The Servant will share in the divine exaltation. But the route to it goes through mishchat — disfigurement (from shachat — to ruin, to corrupt, to spoil; the pit-word). The juxtaposition of marred appearance and supreme exaltation in adjacent verses is the book's central paradox made visible.

intro: Isaiah 53 is the most quoted chapter of the Hebrew Bible in the New Testament and the most debated passage in all of Jewish-Christian dialogue. Its identity has been contested for two millennia: is the Servant Israel, a prophet, the ideal Israel, or a messianic figure? The text does not resolve the question — it holds all possibilities in tension while describing a suffering and vindication that has never been adequately explained by any single identification. The notes below address the three most theologically significant phrases.

notes.original: achen cholayenu hu nasa v'mach'oveinu s'valam... v'hu m'cholal mipsha'einu — surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows... he was pierced for our transgressions
notes.rendering: Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows... he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities
notes.why: The substitution language is exact and accumulating. Nasa — lifted up, bore (the word of the scapegoat in Leviticus 16:22 who bears the sins of the people into the wilderness). S'valam — carried them (saval — to bear as a burden, to carry a heavy load). M'cholal — pierced, wounded (chalal — to pierce through; but also chalal — to begin, to profane; the word carries overtones of being made common, made nothing). Medukka — crushed, shattered (dakka — to crush to powder). The prepositions — mipsha'einu (for our transgressions), me'avonoteinu (for our iniquities) — are substitutionary: the consequences meant for us fell on him. Matthew 8:17 applies v.4 to Jesus's healings; 1 Peter 2:24 applies v.5 to the cross.

notes.original: v'YHWH chafetz dak'o he'cheli — yet it was the will of YHWH to crush him
notes.rendering: Yet it was the will of YHWH to crush him. He has put him to grief. When his soul makes an offering for guilt, he will see his offspring
notes.why: Chafetz dak'o — it pleased YHWH to crush him (chafetz — to desire, to take pleasure in; dak'o — his crushing, from dakah — to crush). The most theologically difficult line in the chapter: YHWH deliberately wills the Servant's crushing. It is not explained, justified, or ameliorated. The following clause adds: asham — a guilt offering, the specific sacrificial term (Leviticus 5–6) for the offering that makes restitution and atones. The Servant's soul (nefesh) becomes an asham — a guilt offering. After this, he sees his offspring (zera — seed, descendants) and his days are prolonged: death is reversed, the crushed one lives. The movement from crushing to offspring to prolonged days is the structural grammar of resurrection.

notes.original: v'hu chet rabbim nasa uvlaposh'im yafgia — he bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors
notes.rendering: yet he bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors
notes.why: The final verse closes the song with its most concentrated statement of the Servant's twofold work. Nasa chet rabbim — he bore the sin of the many (nasa again — the carrying-verb of v.4; chet — sin in its most basic form, the missing of the mark; rabbim — the many, not all universally but the large representative group). V'laposh'im yafgia — and for the transgressors he makes intercession (paga — to meet, to encounter, to intervene; in its intercessory sense, to approach on behalf of another; the same verb used in 59:16 where YHWH himself interposes). The Servant is both the sin-bearer and the intercessor. Luke 22:37 cites this verse directly — Jesus quotes it of himself at the Last Supper.

intro: Chapter 54 is the song that follows the Fourth Servant Song as naturally as resurrection follows crucifixion. The barren, abandoned, widowed woman is Zion — and her song is triggered by what the Servant accomplished in chapter 53. The chapter reaches its theological climax in the covenant-of-peace oracle (vv.9–10), where YHWH swears by the Noahic covenant that his love will not depart even if the mountains move.

notes.original: ranni aqarah lo yaladah — sing, O barren one who did not bear
notes.rendering: Sing, O barren one, who did not bear — break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not been in labour! For the children of the desolate one will be more than the children of her who is married
notes.why: Aqarah — barren (the word of Sarah in Genesis 11:30, of Rebekah in Genesis 25:21, of Samson's mother in Judges 13:2). The barren-woman-who-sings is one of the great recurring figures of the Hebrew Bible: Hannah, Elizabeth, and here Zion-as-barren-exile. Shomemah — the desolate one (the city in ruins, the woman whose husband has left). Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 4:27 as an allegory of the Jerusalem above — the mother of the free, which corresponds to the barren Sarah rather than the enslaved Hagar. The point: the community that seems least capable of producing offspring will produce the most.

notes.original: b'rega qaton azavtich uv'rachamim g'dolim aqabtzeich — for a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great compassion I will gather you
notes.rendering: For a brief moment I deserted you, but with great compassion I will gather you. In overflowing anger for a moment I hid my face from you — but with everlasting love I will have compassion on you
notes.why: The two contrasts are temporal and qualitative: rega qaton (a brief moment) vs. rachamim g'dolim (great compassion); shetzef qetzef (overflowing anger — shetzef from shatzaf, to flood over; qetzef from qatzaf, wrath) vs. chesed olam (everlasting love — chesed, the covenant-loyalty word; olam, forever). YHWH acknowledges the abandonment — does not deny the exile was real. But the proportions are inverted: the anger was brief and overflowing; the love is everlasting. The exile is a moment in a love story whose timescale is eternity.

notes.original: v'chesed'i meittach lo yamush u'vrit shlomi lo tamut — my steadfast love will not depart and my covenant of peace will not be removed
notes.rendering: the mountains may depart and the hills be removed — but my steadfast love will not depart from you, and my covenant of peace will not be removed
notes.why: Brit shlomi — my covenant of peace (brit — the binding agreement, the sworn commitment; shalom — the wholeness, wellbeing, and full flourishing of the relationship). The comparison is to the Noahic covenant (v.9) — the one covenant in the Hebrew Bible explicitly sworn to all flesh with a natural guarantee (the rainbow). YHWH places his commitment to Zion in the same category as the covenant that keeps the waters from flooding the earth: a cosmic oath. The mountains — the most stable things in the ancient imagination — may move before this love does. Numbers 23:19 is the theological ground: God is not a man that he should lie; lo yamush — it will not budge.

intro: Chapter 55 is the great closing invitation of Deutero-Isaiah — the passage that gathers up all of chapters 40–54 and issues an open summons to the thirsty, the hungry, and the wayward. It is a marketplace cry transformed into theology: come without money, buy without price. The chapter closes Deutero-Isaiah with the promise of the word that does not return empty — the guarantee that all of chapters 40–55 will accomplish what it was sent to do.

notes.original: hoy kol tzameh l'chu lamayim — ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters
notes.rendering: Ho! Everyone who thirsts — come to the waters. And he who has no money — come, buy and eat!
notes.why: Hoy — the exclamation of the marketplace crier, the vendor calling out his wares (the same word as the prophetic woe, but here stripped of judgment and used as invitation). Kol tzameh — everyone who thirsts (universal scope: kol, all; tzame, the parched throat). The commercial terms — buy, sell, money — are all present but inverted: come without money (b'lo chesef), buy without price (b'lo mechir). The wine and milk are the luxuries of abundance given freely. John 7:37–38 echoes this verse: Jesus stands up at the feast and cries out — if anyone thirsts, let him come to me. The marketplace cry becomes the Christological invitation.

notes.original: ki lo mach'sh'votai mach'sh'voteichem — for my thoughts are not your thoughts
notes.rendering: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, declares YHWH. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways
notes.why: The saying is widely quoted as a counsel against theological presumption — but in context it is an argument for the extravagance of YHWH's forgiveness. The preceding verses (vv.6–7) call the wicked to return and promise that YHWH will abundantly pardon. The human objection to such lavish forgiveness — 'that cannot be right, that is too much' — is answered by the verse: your category of 'too much' does not apply to me. YHWH's mercy exceeds human categories of proportion just as the heavens exceed the earth in height. The verse is not about inscrutability but about the surplus of grace.

notes.original: lo yashuv elai reiqam ki im asah et asher chafatzti — it will not return to me empty, but it will accomplish what I purpose
notes.rendering: so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth. It will not return to me empty, but it will accomplish that which I purpose and will succeed in the thing for which I sent it
notes.why: Reiqam — empty, void (the word of the empty jar, the hollow vessel, the space that contains nothing). The word of YHWH has the character of effective action rather than mere communication: it goes out and it does. Asah et asher chafatzti — it will do what I desired (asah — to do, to make, to accomplish; chafatz — to take pleasure in, to desire; the same verb used of YHWH's will to crush the Servant in 53:10). The rain-and-snow analogy is ecological: water does not return to the sky without having watered the earth first. Similarly the word of YHWH does not return to YHWH without having accomplished its mission. This is the guarantee seal on all of chapters 40–55.

intro: Chapter 56 opens the final section of the book (Trito-Isaiah, chapters 56–66) with a startling expansion of the covenant community. The two groups most excluded by Deuteronomy 23 — eunuchs (23:1) and foreigners (23:3) — are explicitly welcomed into YHWH's house. The chapter closes with a sharp indictment of the leadership who are blind watchmen and dumb dogs — precisely the opposite of what chapter 52:8 promised.

notes.original: v'al yomar ben hanechar hanilva el YHWH — let not the foreigner who has joined himself to YHWH say...
notes.rendering: Let not the foreigner who has joined himself to YHWH say, 'YHWH will surely separate me from his people.' And let not the eunuch say, 'Look — I am a dry tree'
notes.why: Ben hanechar — a son of the foreigner (the term for the resident alien, the non-Israelite who has attached to the community). Saris — eunuch (those castrated either in infancy for court service or by injury; excluded from the assembly of YHWH in Deuteronomy 23:1). The eunuch's self-description — etz yavesh, a dry tree — captures the despair of one who cannot produce offspring and therefore has no future in a community where lineage is everything. YHWH's response inverts the dry-tree image: I will give you yad vashem (a monument and a name — the Hebrew phrase that gives the Holocaust memorial its name) better than sons and daughters. Memory and presence replace biological legacy.

notes.original: ki veiti beyt tefillah yiqqare l'chol ha'ammim — my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples
notes.rendering: For my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples
notes.why: L'chol ha'ammim — for all peoples: the universal guest list that chapter 2 announced in the mountain vision is here given a specific architectural form. The temple is the gathering point. Jesus quotes this verse in all three Synoptic Gospels (Matthew 21:13, Mark 11:17, Luke 19:46) when he drives out those who have turned the house of prayer into a den of robbers. The reversal is pointed: Isaiah's expansion of temple access to foreigners and eunuchs is being realized even as the temple authorities are shrinking it for profit. The verse that was a promise becomes an indictment.

notes.original: tzofav ivreem kullam — Israel's watchmen are blind
notes.rendering: Israel's watchmen are blind. They are all without knowledge. They are all silent dogs — they cannot bark
notes.why: Tzofav — his watchmen (tzafah — to look out, to watch; the professional prophetic guardians of the community). Ivreem — blind (the same blindness indicted in 42:18–20, where Israel was called a blind servant). Kalbim ilmim — silent dogs (ilem — mute, unable to speak; the watchdog that cannot bark is worse than useless — it gives the sense of security while providing none). The catalogue of leadership failure — blind, ignorant, silent, sleeping, greedy, self-directed — is the exact opposite of the Servant of chapters 42 and 50, who listened morning by morning, spoke the discipled word, and set his face like flint. The community's shepherds are anti-Servants.

intro: Chapter 57 contains one of the most theologically powerful paradoxes in the book: the God who inhabits eternity and the high holy place also dwells with the person of contrite and lowly spirit. The indictment of idolatry that fills the first half is answered not by judgment alone but by healing — I will heal him, I will lead him, peace to the far and to the near.

notes.original: ki koh amar ram v'nissa shochen ad v'qadosh sh'mo — for thus says the high and lifted up one who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy
notes.rendering: For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: I dwell in the high and holy place — and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit
notes.why: Ram v'nissa — high and lifted up: the exact description of YHWH in the throne-room vision of 6:1 (ram v'nissa) is now self-applied with the addition of shochen ad — dwelling eternity (shochen — the one who dwells, who settles in a place; ad — perpetuity, the endless duration). Q'dosh sh'mo — Holy is his name: chapter 6's triple-holy collapsed to a single name. The double dwelling — in the high holy place AND with the contrite (daka — crushed, lowly; from dakah — the same root as the Servant's crushing in 53:5) — is the chapter's theological summit. The God who is absolutely transcendent is simultaneously the God of absolute nearness to the broken.

notes.original: shalom shalom larochok v'laqarov — peace, peace to the far and to the near
notes.rendering: Peace, peace, to the far and to the near," says YHWH, "and I will heal him
notes.why: Shalom shalom — peace, peace: the doubled superlative of 26:3 (perfect peace for the stayed mind) now extended in both directions — larachok (to the far one, the distant, the exile) and laqarov (to the near one, the present, those who have remained). No one is excluded from the doubling: the peace is for those far away in Babylon and for those who stayed in the land. V'rephatiu — and I will heal him: the healing word that appeared in 53:5 (by his wounds we are healed) reappears here as YHWH's direct promise. The Servant who was wounded accomplishes the healing that YHWH here personally applies.

intro: Chapter 58 is the great manifesto on true religion in Trito-Isaiah — the passage that defines authentic worship not by its ritual forms but by its social consequences. It asks the same question as Amos 5 (what does YHWH actually want?) and gives the same answer (justice, not ceremony), but in a more pastoral and less confrontational register: here the people are genuinely confused about why their fasting isn't working.

notes.original: halo zeh tzom evcharehu — is not this the fast that I choose?
notes.rendering: Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke? Is it not to share your bread with the hungry?
notes.why: The fast YHWH chooses is defined entirely by what it does to other people. Fatteach — to loosen (the bonds of wickedness; rishah — wickedness, the binding up of people in unjust systems). L'chofshi y'shallach r'tzutzim — to send free the oppressed (chofshi — freedom, the state of the released slave; r'tzutzim — the crushed ones, from ratzatz — to crush; the same word used of the bruised reed in 42:3). The accumulation of verbs of release — loosen, undo, let go free, break — builds the picture of a religion that liberates rather than one that performs. Jesus reads from chapter 61 in the Nazareth synagogue, but this chapter's programme of liberation is equally present in Luke 4:18.

notes.original: az yibbaqa kashachar orech — then your light will break forth like the dawn
notes.rendering: Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will spring up speedily
notes.why: Yibbaqa — will break forth, will crack open (baqa — to split, to burst through, as water breaks through a dam or light through clouds). Kashachar — like the dawn (the first light, before sunrise, when the sky cracks open at the horizon). The light of Zion that chapter 60 will celebrate in full is here made conditional on the social practice of chapter 58. The sequence is causal, not coincidental: justice → light, social healing → the glory of YHWH as rear guard. The return from exile is not merely geographical; it requires a community whose practices match its worship.

notes.original: u'vanu mimm'cha chorv'ot olam — your ancient ruins will be rebuilt
notes.rendering: Your ancient ruins will be rebuilt. You will raise up the foundations of many generations. You will be called the repairer of the breach, the restorer of streets to dwell in
notes.why: Chorvot olam — ruins of ages (charv — ruin, the desolate remains of something once inhabited; olam — of eternity, of long ages). Three titles accumulate for the community that practises true fasting: boneh chorv'ot (builder of ruins), meqomem y'sodot (one who raises up foundations), gozer perets (repairer of the breach). Perets — a breach in a wall (the same word used in Amos 4:3 where Israel goes out through the breaches in the wall under judgment). The community that was judged by the breach now repairs it. Each title implies the reversal of a specific catastrophe: ruins rebuilt, foundations raised, walls repaired, streets resettled.

intro: Chapter 59 is the great communal confession that precedes the glory of chapter 60 — one of the most searching self-indictments in Scripture, moving from description (vv.3–8) through corporate confession (vv.9–15) to the moment when YHWH himself puts on armour because no human intercessor can be found (vv.16–17). Paul quotes v.7–8 in Romans 3:15–17 as part of his universal indictment of humanity.

notes.original: ki im avonoteichem hayu mavdilim beinichem l'vein Eloheichem — your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God
notes.rendering: your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear
notes.why: Mavdilim — making a separation (badal — to divide, to separate; the word of the creation separation in Genesis 1, of the priestly division between clean and unclean in Leviticus). Sin re-enacts the uncreation of relationship: the separation that sin creates between humanity and God is a reversal of the creation intimacy. Histu panim — hidden his face (the hiding of the divine face is the deepest possible image of abandonment in the psalms: Psalm 13:1, 27:9, 88:14). The answer to the community's complaint that YHWH's hand is too short (v.1) is: his arm is long enough; the distance is on your side.

notes.original: vayar ki ein ish vayishtomem ki ein mafgia — he saw there was no man and was appalled that there was no one to intercede
notes.rendering: He saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no one to intercede. Then his own arm brought him salvation
notes.why: Vayishtomem — was appalled, was horrified (shamem — to be devastated, to stare in shock; the same root as the devastation of the land). The verse is a meditation on intercessory vacancy: the community's moral collapse has left no one capable of the mediating role that Abraham, Moses, and the Servant were called to. So YHWH acts himself. Zero'o lam yoshia — his own arm brought him salvation (zero'a — arm; the arm of YHWH called to awaken in 51:9 is now awakened without being summoned). The armour of v.17 (righteousness as breastplate, salvation as helmet, vengeance as garment, zeal as cloak) is echoed in Paul's armour of God in Ephesians 6:14–17.

notes.original: u'va l'Tzion go'el — a Redeemer will come to Zion
notes.rendering: And a Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression... my Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, will not depart from your mouth... from this time forth and forevermore
notes.why: Go'el — Redeemer (the kinsman-redeemer of chapter 41, 43, 44, 49, 54; now arriving at Zion). The Redeemer comes l'shavei fesha b'Ya'aqov — to those who turn from transgression in Jacob (shav — who turn, from shub — the great repentance word). Paul quotes v.20 in Romans 11:26 as the eschatological promise of Israel's restoration: 'the Deliverer will come from Zion.' The Spirit-and-word covenant of v.21 is the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 in condensed form: the word internalized and transmitted through generations, neither departing nor being forgotten. The covenant is not of stone tablets but of Spirit-inscribed mouths.

intro: Chapter 60 is the great dawn chapter of Trito-Isaiah — the vision of Zion as a light-city to which all nations stream with their wealth, their camels, their gold and frankincense, their ships and their kings. It answers the darkness of chapters 58–59 with the most lavish vision of restored glory in the book. The chapter's closing image — YHWH himself as the everlasting light, replacing sun and moon — is the image Revelation 21:23–24 draws on for the new Jerusalem.

notes.original: qumi ori ki va orech — arise, shine, for your light has come
notes.rendering: Arise, shine — for your light has come, and the glory of YHWH has risen upon you
notes.why: Qumi ori — arise, shine (two imperatives addressed to Zion, personified as a woman waking from sleep in the dark). Ki va orech — for your light has come (the perfect tense: arrived, present, already here). The light is YHWH's glory (k'vod YHWH — the specific term of the Sinai theophany, the tabernacle's filling, the temple's dedication). The structure is: arise because the light is already there, not: become the light. Zion does not generate the light; she reflects it. The distinction matters: the community's task is to wake up and orient toward the glory that has risen over it — not to produce that glory by its own effort.

notes.original: kulam miSheva yavo'u — all those from Sheba will come, they will bring gold and frankincense
notes.rendering: All those from Sheba will come. They will bring gold and frankincense, and will proclaim the praise of YHWH
notes.why: The verse is the direct source of the Magi tradition in Matthew 2:11 — the gifts of gold and frankincense (and by extension myrrh from 60:17's precious materials) brought by those who come from the east to the one born to be king. Sheba — the ancient kingdom of southern Arabia (the Queen of Sheba of 1 Kings 10), the origin of the incense trade route. The camels of Midian and Ephah (the northern Arabian tribes) add to the picture of the whole caravan route from the east converging on Zion. Isaiah's eschatological vision becomes Matthew's historical geography.

notes.original: v'hayah lach YHWH l'or olam — YHWH will be your everlasting light
notes.rendering: The sun will no more be your light by day... but YHWH will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory. Your sun will no more go down... for YHWH will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning will be ended
notes.why: The sun and moon — the two great lights of Genesis 1:16, created on the fourth day to govern day and night — are superseded. Not destroyed but rendered redundant. Lo yavo od shim'shech — your sun will no more go down (the sun that went down at noon over the land in Amos 8:9 as judgment, reversed: the light that fails no more). Revelation 21:23 quotes this directly: the city has no need of sun or moon because the glory of God illuminates it and its lamp is the Lamb. The new creation's light is not natural but personal — YHWH himself as the light source, available without cessation.
