intro: Chapter 61 is the passage Jesus reads in the Nazareth synagogue at the opening of his public ministry (Luke 4:18–19) — the most explicit moment of Servant-identification in the Gospels. The Anointed One brings good news to the poor, binds up the brokenhearted, proclaims liberty, and announces the year of YHWH's favour. The chapter's final note is the sprouting of righteousness — the organic, unstoppable growth of what YHWH has planted.

notes.original: ruach Adonai YHWH alai ya'an mashach YHWH oti — the Spirit of the Sovereign YHWH is upon me, because YHWH has anointed me
notes.rendering: The Spirit of the Sovereign YHWH is upon me, because YHWH has anointed me to bring good news to the poor
notes.why: Mashach — anointed (the verbal form of mashiach — messiah). The Anointed One of 45:1 (Cyrus) is here replaced by a speaker who announces his own anointing by the Spirit — bringing together the Spirit-endowment of 42:1, the mouth-of-a-sword of 49:2, and the commission of 50:4. Lev'sser anavim — to bring good news to the afflicted/poor (b'sser — the herald's good news; anavim — the humble, the meek, those crushed low; the word of Psalm 34:2 and the Beatitudes' 'poor in spirit'). Jesus reads these verses, closes the scroll, sits down, and says: 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing' (Luke 4:21).

notes.original: liqqro shnat ratzon l'YHWH — to proclaim the year of YHWH's favour
notes.rendering: to proclaim the year of YHWH's favour and the day of vengeance of our God
notes.why: Shnat ratzon — year of favour, year of acceptance (ratzon — the pleasure, the goodwill, the favoured moment; the word of 56:7 for the acceptable offering). The 'year' is the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25) — the fiftieth year when debts are cancelled, slaves freed, and land returned. The Anointed proclaims not merely a liturgical calendar event but its eschatological fulfilment. The day of vengeance (yom naqam) follows — but notably Jesus stops reading after 'year of YHWH's favour' and before 'day of vengeance' in Luke 4:19. The truncation is itself interpretive: the first coming fulfils the favour; the vengeance awaits its proper time.

notes.original: pe'er tachat efer shemen sason tachat evel — beautiful headdress instead of ashes, oil of gladness instead of mourning
notes.rendering: to give them a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a faint spirit
notes.why: The three exchanges are reversals of mourning practice. Pe'er — a headdress, a turban, a crown of honour (pe'er from pa'ar — to beautify, to glorify); tachat efer — instead of ashes (the ashes of mourning poured on the head). Shemen sason — oil of gladness (the anointing oil of festivity, used at weddings and celebrations); tachat evel — instead of mourning (evel — the formal mourning state). Ma'ateh t'hillah — garment of praise; tachat ruach kehah — instead of a faint spirit (kehah — dim, flagging, the guttering flame of 42:3). Each exchange names what the anointed mission actually does: it replaces the marks of grief with the markers of celebration.

intro: Chapter 62 is a sustained meditation on the new names that Zion will receive — the renaming that signals transformation of identity. The prophet declares that he will not be silent until Jerusalem's righteousness burns like a torch. Four old names are replaced by four new ones, each reversing a condition of exile: forsaken becomes my-delight-is-in-her, desolate becomes married.

notes.original: v'qore lach shem chadash asher pi YHWH yiqv'enu — you will be called by a new name that the mouth of YHWH will give
notes.rendering: you will be called by a new name that the mouth of YHWH will give
notes.why: Shem chadash — a new name (shem — the name that encodes identity, as Jacob became Israel, Abram became Abraham; chadash — new, fresh, the word of the new thing of 43:19 and the new covenant of Jeremiah). The giving of a new name by the mouth of YHWH is an act of re-creation: the city that was defined by its desolation receives an identity that corresponds to its new reality. Revelation 2:17 and 3:12 promise a new name to the one who overcomes — the Zion-new-name promise extended to the individual believer in the eschatological community.

notes.original: lo ye'amer l'cha od azuvah v'l'artzech lo ye'amer od sh'mamah — you will no more be called Forsaken and your land no more called Desolate
notes.rendering: You will no more be called Forsaken, and your land will no more be called Desolate — but you will be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married
notes.why: The four names are in Hebrew: Azuvah (Forsaken, from azav — to abandon, to leave behind), Sh'mamah (Desolate, the devastation-word of 34:11 and Lamentations), Cheftzi-vah (My Delight Is in Her, from chafetz — to take pleasure in; the same verb as YHWH's delight in crushing the Servant in 53:10, now redirected to delight in Zion), and B'ulah (Married, from ba'al — to marry, to be in covenant relationship as husband). The name-pair swap encodes the theology: abandonment and desolation are replaced by delight and covenant intimacy. The land itself is married — the relationship includes the territory, not just the people.

notes.original: u'mesos chatan al kalah yasis alayich Elohayich — as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you
notes.rendering: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so will your God rejoice over you
notes.why: Yasis alayich — will rejoice over you (sus — to leap for joy, to exult; the same verb Zion was called to perform in 35:1 and 65:18). The initiative of joy is reversed: it is not only Zion who rejoices in YHWH (61:10) but YHWH who rejoices in Zion. The bridegroom-rejoicing is the divine pleasure of Zephaniah 3:17 (he will rejoice over you with gladness, he will exult over you with loud singing). The marriage metaphor that has run through the prophets — from Hosea's unfaithful wife through Ezekiel's abandoned bride — reaches its eschatological resolution: the wedding is consummated, the joy is mutual.

intro: Chapter 63 opens with the most jarring theophany in the book — a blood-soaked Divine Warrior returning from Edom, alone, having trampled the nations — before pivoting into the most extended communal lament prayer in Isaiah. The chapter swings between divine triumph and human desolation, ending with the community's desperate self-description: we are like those over whom you have never ruled.

notes.original: mi zeh ba me'Edom chamutze v'gadim miBotzrah — who is this coming from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah?
notes.rendering: Who is this coming from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah — he who is splendid in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength? 'It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save'
notes.why: The dialogue structure is unusual: an unnamed questioner asks, YHWH answers. Edom — Israel's ancient brother-enemy, symbol of ultimate hostility since Esau/Jacob — is the location of the divine judgment. Chamutze v'gadim — crimsoned of garments (chamutz — dyed red, reddened; not the red of the warrior's costume but the red of treading the wine vat, where grape juice stains the treader's clothing). The wine-press image runs through the prophets (Joel 3:13, Lamentations 1:15) and into Revelation 14:19–20 and 19:15. The warrior comes alone (v.3 — badad dorakhti — I trod alone), which echoes the Servant of 53 who also suffered alone.

notes.original: b'chol tzaratam lo tzar — in all their affliction he was afflicted
notes.rendering: In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them. In his love and in his pity he redeemed them
notes.why: Lo tzar — he was afflicted/troubled with them (the text is disputed; some manuscripts read lo as 'not' — he was not afflicted; others as the personal pronoun 'to him' — to him it was distress). The Masoretic pointing supports 'to him' or 'with them': YHWH's own inner parts are moved by Israel's suffering, as v.15 suggests (where compassion is described as the stirring of his inner parts). Malach panav — the angel of his presence (the unique phrase: not a representative angel but the one who bears YHWH's own face, his personal emissary, the figure of the exodus). He carried them: nasa — the word of the Servant who bears the sin, and of YHWH who carries Israel from womb to old age in 46:3–4.

notes.original: ki attah avinu — for you are our Father
notes.rendering: For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, O YHWH, are our Father — our Redeemer from of old is your name
notes.why: The appeal to divine fatherhood over against the patriarchal lineage is remarkable: even if Abraham and Jacob (Israel) have no claim on us, you are still our Father. Avinu — our Father: not the Father of Israel's founding narrative but the Father of direct relationship, the one who created and formed and chose regardless of historical connection. Go'aleinu meolam — our Redeemer from of old: the go'el relationship (kinsman-redeemer) predates the patriarchs; it is YHWH's character from the ancient time, not a recently contracted obligation. The prayer strips away every secondary claim and goes to the foundational one: you made us. You are our Father.

intro: Chapter 64 is the climax of the communal lament that began in chapter 63 — the most desperate prayer in the book, in which the community confesses its uncleanness, acknowledges that YHWH has hidden his face, and nonetheless addresses him as Father and Potter. The prayer ends not with a resolution but with the open wound of the question: will you keep silent?

notes.original: umei'olam lo sham'u lo he'ezinu ayin lo ra'atah — from of old no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen
notes.rendering: From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear — no eye has seen a God besides you who acts for those who wait for him
notes.why: Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 2:9 as the foundation for his teaching about the mystery of God's wisdom: 'What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him.' The Isaianic context is the incomparability of YHWH's historical actions on behalf of those who wait (qavah — the same hope-verb of 40:31). Paul applies it to the cross — the thing no one anticipated, the wisdom hidden in mystery — as the fulfilment of Isaiah's 'no eye has seen.' The unprecedented becomes the hermeneutical key to the gospel.

notes.original: k'veged iddim kol tzidqoteinu — all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment
notes.rendering: all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away
notes.why: Beged iddim — a menstrual cloth, a garment rendered ritually impure (iddim — the plural of niddah, the term for menstrual impurity in Leviticus 15). The verse is a statement about the contamination of even righteous acts when performed by a community that has abandoned the relationship they were meant to express. The image does not say righteousness is worthless — it says these righteous acts, performed in this relational context of abandonment, carry the stain of impurity. The falling leaf (navel — dried, withered; the word of 40:7–8, where the grass withers) and the wind (avon — iniquity, but also the wind that blows the chaff away) make the image of dissolution complete.

notes.original: v'attah YHWH avinu anachnu hachomer v'attah yotz'renu — but now O YHWH you are our Father, we are the clay and you are our potter
notes.rendering: But now, O YHWH, you are our Father. We are the clay, and you are our potter. We are all the work of your hand
notes.why: V'attah — but now: the turning-word that pivots from confession to appeal (the same v'attah that structures many psalms of lament). Hachomer v'attah yotz'renu — the clay and you are our potter (chomer — clay, the material of pottery and the material from which Adam was formed in Genesis 2; yotzer — potter, from yatzar — to form, the word of both the creator and the anxiety-prone imagination of 26:3). The potter-clay image of 29:16 (which indicted those who reversed the roles) is here reclaimed by the community: we are clay, you are potter, we cannot remake ourselves. The confession is simultaneously the petition: the one who formed us can reform us.

intro: Chapter 65 contains YHWH's answer to the lament of chapters 63–64 — and it is simultaneously judgment and new creation. The answer to 'will you keep silent?' is not silence but the most expansive vision of restoration in the book: new heavens, new earth, a Jerusalem of joy, long life, secure labour, and the wolf grazing with the lamb. Revelation 21 draws directly on this chapter for its vision of the new Jerusalem.

notes.original: nidrashhti l'lo sha'alu nimtzeti l'lo viqshuni — I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me
notes.rendering: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me. I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name
notes.why: The opening verse is YHWH's counter to the community's complaint that he is absent. Not: I was absent — but: I was present and you were not looking. Nidrashhti — I allowed myself to be sought (from darash — to seek; the Niphal passive/reflexive suggests YHWH is the one making himself available, not merely being discovered by accident). Hineni hineni — here I am, here I am: the doubled response of availability (hineni — the word Abraham said to God on Moriah, that Moses said at the burning bush, that Isaiah said in the throne-room). Paul quotes v.1–2 in Romans 10:20–21 as describing the Gentiles who found YHWH without seeking and Israel who resisted YHWH's outstretched hands.

notes.original: ki hineni bore shamayim chadashim v'aretz chadashah — for look, I create new heavens and a new earth
notes.rendering: For look — I create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered or come into mind
notes.why: Bore — creating (bara — the creation verb of Genesis 1:1, used exclusively of divine creative action). Shamayim chadashim v'aretz chadashah — new heavens and a new earth: the word chadash (new, fresh) signals not replacement but transformation — a new quality of existence, not destruction of the old order but its renovation. Lo tizakernahh v'lo ta'alenu al lev — they will not be remembered or come upon the heart (al lev — literally upon the heart, into the consciousness; the former troubles will not even be a memory). Revelation 21:1 opens with this verse; 2 Peter 3:13 quotes it as the Christian's hope. The book that began with Israel's rebellion against YHWH ends with a creation that cannot contain grief.

notes.original: v'hayah terem yiqra'u va'ani e'eneh — before they call I will answer
notes.rendering: Before they call I will answer — while they are yet speaking I will hear. The wolf and the lamb will graze together
notes.why: Terem yiqra'u — before they call (terem — before, preceding; the anticipatory grace that does not wait for the request but moves before it). The response-before-request reverses the entire structure of the lament psalms, where the community cries and waits for an answer. In the new creation, the prayer is anticipated: YHWH hears before the words are formed. The wolf-and-lamb image returns from 11:6–7 to close the chapter — the same vision of the healed creation that the messianic Shoot from Jesse inaugurated. What chapter 11 promised of the king's reign is here the permanent ecology of the new earth. The book returns to its own beginning.

intro: Chapter 66 is the last chapter of Isaiah and one of the most compressed in the book — it covers the rejection of false worship, the sudden birth of a nation, the mother-comfort of Zion, the judgment of the nations, the calling of Gentile priests and Levites, and the final vision of universal worship on the new Sabbath. It ends, jarringly, with a verse about the worm and the fire that the tradition found too disturbing to leave as the book's last word — synagogue practice repeats v.23 after v.24.

notes.original: v'el zeh abit el ani un'keh ruach u'chared al d'vari — but this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word
notes.rendering: But this is the one to whom I will look — he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word
notes.why: The question of v.1 (what house can you build me? where can I rest?) is answered not with a temple description but with a person-description. Ani — humble, poor, afflicted (the same anavim of 61:1). N'keh ruach — contrite in spirit (nakah — struck, smitten; ruach — spirit). Chared al d'vari — trembling at my word (charad — to tremble, to be shaken by awe). The three qualities are all forms of receptivity: poverty of self-assertion, brokenness of spirit, responsive trembling before the word. The temple YHWH inhabits is not built of cedar and stone but of this human disposition. Stephen quotes v.1–2 in Acts 7:49–50 as the basis for Israel's history of misplaced temple trust.

notes.original: k'ish asher immo t'nachamenu ken anochi anachomchem — as one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you
notes.rendering: As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you — you will be comforted in Jerusalem
notes.why: The verse echoes and fulfils the promise of 40:1 (comfort, comfort my people) and the nursing-mother image of 49:15 (can a woman forget her nursing child?). K'ish asher immo — like a man whose mother (the grown child, not the infant, returning to the mother's comfort). The comfort is located: in Jerusalem (b'Yerushalayim t'unachamu — the city whose name contains shalom). The book that opened with Jerusalem as an unfaithful city (1:21 — how the faithful city has become a whore) ends with Jerusalem as the mother whose comfort is YHWH's own comfort. The whole arc of the book is in this verse.

notes.original: kol basar l'hishtachavot l'fanai — all flesh will come to worship before me
notes.rendering: From new moon to new moon, and from Sabbath to Sabbath, all flesh will come to worship before me," declares YHWH
notes.why: The liturgical calendar of the new creation: mide'i chodesh b'chodsho — from new moon to new moon (the monthly cycle of time); umide'i shabbat b'shabbato — from Sabbath to Sabbath (the weekly cycle). Kol basar — all flesh: the universal congregation of 40:5 (all flesh will see it together), now gathered not just to see but to worship (l'hishtachavot — to bow down, to prostrate oneself). The book that began with YHWH summons heaven and earth as witnesses against Israel (1:2) ends with all flesh as YHWH's worshippers. The witnesses become the congregation. The indictment becomes the invitation. Here ends the Book of Isaiah.

intro: James 1 establishes the letter’s two great axes: the vertical (the God who gives wisdom and good gifts without reproach or change) and the horizontal (the community that must hear, speak, and act accordingly). The chapter moves with characteristic Jamesian speed — no long arguments, only compressed aphorisms that land like hammer strikes. Verse 17 may quote or echo a Greek poem; its rhythm in Greek is distinctly musical. The double-minded man of verse 8 may be James’s own coinage.

notes.original: Iakōbos doulos theou — Iakōbos, servant of God
notes.rendering: Yakov — a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ
notes.why: Iakōbos is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew Yaʿaqov — Jacob, the patriarch. The name arrived in English as James through a chain of phonological transformation so complete it erased the original: Yaʿaqov → Iakōbos → Latin Jacobus → Late Latin Jacomus → Old French Gemmes → James. This rendering uses Yakov to restore the writer to his actual name and his actual tradition. He does not call himself bishop, elder, or brother of the Lord — only doulos, slave or servant. The restraint is striking given his status in Jerusalem. His authority rests not on his family connection to Jesus but on his relationship to the God whom Jesus revealed.

notes.original: anēr dipsychos — a double-minded man
notes.rendering: He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways
notes.why: Dipsychos — double-souled (dis — twice; psychē — soul, self, inner life). This compound may be James’s own formation; it does not appear in earlier Greek literature. The image is of a person with two centers of gravity — pulled simultaneously toward God and the world, committed to neither, anchored to nothing. Akatastatos — unstable, restless (a — not; kathistemi — to set in place, to establish). The double-souled person is not fixed anywhere. The word reappears in 4:8 where James commands the double-minded to purify their hearts. The diagnosis in chapter 1 becomes the imperative in chapter 4.

notes.original: pasa dosis agathē kai pan dōrēma teleion anōthen estin — every good gift and every perfect gift is from above
notes.rendering: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights
notes.why: The verse has a marked rhythmic quality in Greek that suggests it may cite or echo a poetic source. Dosis — a giving, an act of generosity; dōrēma — a gift, a bestowed thing (the distinction may be between the act and the object, or the two may be in parallel). Apatōr aposkiasma — no variation or shadow due to change: the Father of lights — the one who made the stars and governs the celestial lights whose shadows shift and whose phases change — is himself without shadow or turning. The constancy of the giver guarantees the goodness of the gifts. Against any suspicion that God tempts (v.13), James sets the character of the Father: all that comes down from him is good.

intro: James 2 is the letter’s most contested chapter. The faith-and-works argument of vv. 14–26 has been read as a direct contradiction of Paul (Romans 3–4; Galatians 2–3) and as a complement to him. The tension largely dissolves when one notes that James and Paul use the word “faith” differently: for Paul, faith is personal trust in Christ; for James, “faith” in the argument is the bare intellectual assent that even demons possess. The chapter also contains one of the New Testament’s sharpest social critiques: the assembly that gives the best seat to wealth and puts the poor on the floor has not merely been rude — it has reconstructed the world’s values inside the church.

notes.original: mē en prosōpolēmpsiais echete tēn pistin — do not hold the faith with face-receivings
notes.rendering: do not hold the faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while showing favoritism
notes.why: Prosōpolēmpsia — partiality, favoritism (prosōpon — face; lambanō — to receive, to take). The word translates the Hebrew nasa panim — to lift the face of someone, to show them special regard based on status or appearance. In the LXX it describes the judicial corruption of giving favorable verdicts to the powerful (Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:19). The Leviticus Holiness Code commands against it (19:15): you shall not be partial to the poor nor defer to the great. James applies the same principle to seating arrangements in the assembly. The gospel cannot be held in one hand while the social hierarchies the gospel dismantles are held in the other.

notes.original: kai ta daimonia pisteuousin kai phrissosin — even the demons believe and shudder
notes.rendering: Even the demons believe that, and they shudder!
notes.why: Phrissosin — shudder, bristle with terror (phrisso — to stand on end, of hair rising in fear; a physical word for visceral dread). The argument is devastating in its economy: if bare monotheistic confession (“God is one” — the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4) were sufficient for salvation, demons would be saved — for they believe it, and their belief produces the appropriate emotional response. The problem is not the content of what they believe but that it produces no transformation of life. James’s argument is not against faith but against a faith that stops at intellectual assent and goes no further.

notes.original: philos theou eklēthē — he was called friend of God
notes.rendering: and he was called a friend of God
notes.why: Philos theou — friend of God: an OT honorific for Abraham found in 2 Chronicles 20:7 (Abraham your friend forever) and Isaiah 41:8 (Abraham my friend; the Hebrew is ohavi — my lover, the one who loves me). The Greek philos carries the full weight of friendship: loyalty, mutual knowledge, intimacy. The title is not merely warm; it is relational and covenantal. Abraham’s justification by faith (Genesis 15:6, which Paul also cites) and his works (the offering of Isaac, Genesis 22) are not in tension for James: the works are the completion and demonstration of the faith, not its substitute. A friend of God does what friends do — they act on what they know of the one they love.

intro: James 3 contains the New Testament’s most extended meditation on speech, and one of its most cosmologically charged images. The tongue passage (vv. 1–12) escalates from the practical (bits in horses, rudders on ships) to the terrifying: the tongue is a world of unrighteousness, set on fire by Gehenna. The wisdom section (vv. 13–18) offers the positive counterpart — a sevenfold description of wisdom from above that reads almost as a portrait of the character of God.

notes.original: hē glōssa pyr — the tongue is a fire; trochos tēs genesēos — the wheel of existence / the course of life
notes.rendering: And the tongue is a fire — a world of unrighteousness
notes.why: Kosmos tēs adikias — a world of unrighteousness: not merely an instrument of wrong but a microcosm of it, a compressed universe of everything that is against right order. Trochos tēs genesēos — the wheel of existence (trochos — wheel; genēsis — origin, existence, the course of created life). The phrase is unusual enough that some scholars find Orphic or Buddhist resonance in it; more likely it is a vivid Greek expression for the whole sweep of mortal life. The tongue, set on fire by Gehenna (the smoldering rubbish valley outside Jerusalem, byword for final destruction), sets the entire course of human existence ablaze. The image is not rhetorical excess; James means it as a precise diagnosis.

notes.original: hē de anōthen sophia — the wisdom from above
notes.rendering: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere
notes.why: The seven qualities form a deliberate list — the only such list in James, carefully ordered. Hagnē — pure, chaste (the root of hagios — holy; the wisdom of God shares the character of God). Eirenikē — peaceable (from eirēnē — peace; wisdom from above produces what it is: it is peace and makes peace). Epieikēs — gentle, equitable, fair (a word with strong legal connotations: the willingness to yield one’s strict legal rights for the sake of fairness). Eupeithēs — open to reason, persuadable, compliant (eu — well; peithō — to persuade). Adiakri-tos — impartial, without partiality (the same root as the favoritism condemned in 2:4). Anypokritos — without hypocrisy, sincere (a — not; hypokrinō — to play a role, to act a part). The wisdom from above has no gap between performance and reality.

notes.original: karpos de dikaiosynēs en eirēnēi speiretai — a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace
notes.rendering: And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace
notes.why: The image is agricultural and paradoxical: a harvest is sown, not reaped. The fruit of righteousness grows from a seed of peace planted by peacemakers. The verse functions as a hinge between the two halves of the chapter: the tongue that curses and the tongue that blesses; the wisdom that is earthly-unspiritual-demonic and the wisdom that is pure-peaceable-sincere. The peacemakers who plant peace will harvest justice — a quiet answer to the quarrels and conflicts that open chapter 4.

intro: James 4 returns to the double-minded man of 1:8 and names his condition: friendship with the world and enmity with God. The opening question — where do wars and fights among you come from? — answers itself with characteristic Jamesian directness: from the pleasures (hēdonai — the root of hedonism) at war within. The chapter’s second half turns to two forms of presumption: judging the neighbor and planning tomorrow without reference to the will of God.

notes.original: moichalides — adulterous people / adulteresses
notes.rendering: Adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?
notes.why: Moichalides — adulteresses (the feminine plural). James borrows the prophetic tradition’s marriage metaphor for the covenant: Israel is YHWH’s bride (Hosea, Jeremiah, Ezekiel), and unfaithfulness to God is adultery. The feminine form does not address women specifically; it addresses the community as the collective bride who has gone after another lover. The starkness is deliberate: the divided loyalty that appeared as double-mindedness in 1:8 is now named as adultery. Philia — friendship (from philos — friend, the word used for Abraham the friend of God in 2:23): to be a friend of the world is to love what God’s enemy loves. The categories are not negotiable.

notes.original: ho theos hyperēphanois antitassetai — God arrays himself against the proud
notes.rendering: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble
notes.why: Antitassetai — opposes, arrays himself against, sets himself in battle formation against (anti — against; tassō — to arrange, to draw up in military order; a word from the world of armies and tactical deployment). James cites Proverbs 3:34 in the LXX form, which differs slightly from the Hebrew. The image is alarming: when a person is proud, God takes up a position against that person as one army faces another. Hyperēphanois — the proud (hyperēphanos — one who shows himself above others; hyper — above; phainomai — to appear, to show oneself). The word connotes contempt — the person who makes himself visible by stepping over others.

notes.original: atmēs gar este — you are a mist / vapor
notes.rendering: You are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes
notes.why: Atmēs — steam, vapor, mist (the root of the English word atmosphere). The image of human life as vapor appears throughout the Hebrew wisdom tradition: Qohelet’s hebel hebel — vapor of vapors, everything is vapor — uses the same metaphor. The comparison is not nihilistic but calibrating: the presumption of the merchant who plans next year’s trade route without reference to God rests on a foundational error about his own nature. He is vapor. His plans are vapor’s plans. The antidote is not despair but the phrase “if the Lord wills” — not a pious formula but an accurate description of the conditions under which vapor is permitted to act.

intro: James 5 opens with a prophetic thunderclap against the rich — the closest thing in the New Testament to Amos 6 — and closes with a vision of a praying community that heals, confesses, and retrieves those who have wandered. The contrast is total: the rich hoard and the laborers cry; the community of faith prays and restores. The letter ends without a formal farewell, mid-sentence almost, as if the community were the ongoing argument Yakov refuses to conclude.

notes.original: Kyrios Sabaōth — Lord of Hosts / Lord of Armies
notes.rendering: the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts
notes.why: Kyrios Sabaōth — Lord of Hosts (Sabaōth is a transliteration of the Hebrew tsevaʻot — armies, hosts). This is the only use of the title in the New Testament outside of Romans 9:29 (which cites Isaiah). The title is the great OT name for YHWH as the commander of heavenly armies — the one who marshals all the powers of heaven. James deploys it here in the context of defrauded laborers: the God who hears their cries is not the mild Father of personal piety but the Lord of armies. The choice of title is not decorative; it is a warning. The defrauded cry, and the one who hears is the one who commands every power in heaven and earth.

notes.original: deēsis dikaiou energoumenē — the prayer of a righteous person working / energizing
notes.rendering: The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it works
notes.why: Energoumenē — working, energizing, being effective (from energeō — to be at work; the root of the English word energy). The participle may be passive (prayer that is energized by God) or middle (prayer that actively works, that is itself an effective force). Either reading intensifies the claim: prayer is not passive speech into a void but an active power. Ischuei — has power, is strong (ischys — strength, might). The prayer of the righteous is strong and working. The example of Elijah (vv. 17–18) makes the claim concrete: a human being, with a human nature like ours (homoiopathēs — of like passions, subject to the same emotions), prayed and altered the weather of an entire region.

notes.original: kalypsei plēthos hamartiōn — will cover a multitude of sins
notes.rendering: whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins
notes.why: Kalypsei plēthos hamartiōn — will cover a multitude of sins: an allusion to Proverbs 10:12 (love covers all offenses) and possibly Psalm 32:1 (blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered). The covering is not concealment but atonement — the sin addressed and no longer counted. The letter closes without a benediction, without a farewell, without the conventional courtesy of epistolary endings. The final image is of one person going after another who has wandered, retrieving them from death. Yakov ends where he began: with action. Not the faith that nods at truth from a comfortable seat, but the faith that gets up and goes.

intro: Jeremiah 1 is the most intimate of the prophetic call narratives. It sets the two poles that define the whole book: the divine word that will not fail (v.12 — I am watching over my word) and the prophet's terror of that calling. The double vision — almond branch and boiling pot — moves from reassurance to threat, establishing the register of everything that follows.

notes.original: b'terem etzorcha b'veten y'da'ticha — before I formed you in the womb I knew you
notes.rendering: before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out from the womb I set you apart
notes.why: Yada'ticha — I knew you (yada — to know with the full weight of covenantal intimacy; see Amos 3:2). The divine knowing precedes the human existence. Etzorcha — I formed you (yatzar — to form, to fashion as a potter forms clay; the same verb in Genesis 2:7 when YHWH forms the adam from dust). Jeremiah's call is not an appointment but a creation: he was shaped for this before he was born. The phrase anticipates the whole theology of Jeremiah's person — the prophet who did not choose but could not refuse.

notes.original: shaqed — almond tree; shoqed — watching
notes.rendering: I see a branch of an almond tree... I am watching over my word
notes.why: The wordplay is the vision's entire point. Shaqed (almond) sounds like shoqed (watching, keeping vigil — from shaqad, to be wakeful, to watch). The almond is the first tree to blossom in Israel after winter — it wakens while everything else still sleeps. YHWH names the connection: as the almond watches for spring, I watch over my word to perform it. Hebrew puns are not ornamental; they are the structure of the revelation. This one gives the whole book its nerve: YHWH is awake and his word will not sleep.

notes.original: ir mivtzar ul'amud barzel ul'chomotei n'choshet — a fortified city and an iron pillar and bronze walls
notes.rendering: I have made you today a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls
notes.why: Three images of impregnability stacked together. Ir mivtzar — a fortified city (mivtzar — a fortress, a stronghold; used of cities that withstand siege). Amud barzel — an iron pillar (the vertical, load-bearing image). Chomotei n'choshet — walls of bronze (the horizontal perimeter image). The prophet who trembles at speaking is made architecturally indestructible. The physical images answer the psychological terror: you will not break because you have been made of material that does not break. Against the whole land — king, official, priest, and people — Jeremiah stands alone and unmovable. The book will test this claim for forty years.

intro: Jeremiah 2 is the great covenant lawsuit — the rib pattern from Israel's legal tradition, where YHWH takes his own people to court. The charges are not political but relational: Israel has abandoned the one who loved her first. The chapter's most devastating images are domestic and erotic — bride, wilderness, wild donkey — making the betrayal visceral rather than merely theological.

notes.original: chesed n'urayich — the loyalty of your youth
notes.rendering: I remember the loyalty of your youth, your love as a bride
notes.why: Chesed — lovingkindness, covenant loyalty, steadfast love (the great Old Testament covenant word; it reappears throughout Jeremiah, Hosea, and the Psalms). N'urayich — of your youth (ne'urim — the early years, the first season of life). YHWH recalls Israel's wilderness period not as the years of grumbling and apostasy (Numbers) but as a honeymoon — the days when she still followed. This idealised memory is rhetorical: the contrast with present faithlessness is made sharper by remembering the time when faithfulness existed. Hosea uses the same move (Hosea 2:15 — she will sing there as in the days of her youth).

notes.original: b'orot shavurim asher lo yachilu hamayim — broken cisterns that cannot hold water
notes.rendering: they have forsaken me, the spring of living water, and hewed out cisterns for themselves — broken cisterns that cannot hold water
notes.why: Maym chayyim — living water (spring water, flowing water, water that is alive because it moves; the opposite of stagnant cistern water). YHWH is characterised as a living spring — the source of water that is always new. Israel has exchanged this for bor — a cistern, a hewn-out hole in bedrock for storing rainwater. And not just any cistern: bor shavoir — a cracked cistern, one that leaks. The image is both practical (anyone who has survived a dry summer on broken cisterns knows the terror of this) and theological: idols are cracked cisterns. They hold nothing.

notes.original: s'riqah — choice vine
notes.rendering: I planted you as a choice vine — entirely from the best seed. How then have you turned degenerate before me?
notes.why: Soreka — choice vine, the best variety (used in Genesis 49:11 for the finest grapevine; the word implies quality breeding, the best cultivar). YHWH planted Israel from the finest stock. The degeneration — how you have turned to the shoots of a wild vine (gefen nokriyyah — foreign vine, alien vine, a vine that has gone wild) — is therefore not just apostasy but a botanical catastrophe: the best vine producing wild, useless growth. The image anticipates the vineyard parable traditions (Isaiah 5; Mark 12), where YHWH's investment in Israel is measured and found fruitless.

intro: Jeremiah 3 deploys two of the Hebrew prophets' most characteristic moves: the legal category of divorce applied to covenant (v.1, drawing on Deuteronomy 24) and the comparison between the northern kingdom (Israel, exiled in 722) and the southern (Judah, still standing). Judah watched the north destroyed and learned nothing. The chapter ends with one of the most tender invitations in the whole prophetic literature.

notes.original: pol shamoa tashov eilav — would you actually return to him?
notes.rendering: If a man divorces his wife... will he return to her? Would not that land be greatly defiled? But you have played the whore with many lovers — and would you return to me?
notes.why: The legal allusion is to Deuteronomy 24:1–4, which prohibits a man from taking back a wife who has remarried — such a thing defiles the land (chanuph tachanuph ha'aretz — the land would be utterly defiled). YHWH presses the legal impossibility to its limit: by any human legal standard, the relationship is over, done, legally unrepeatable. And then the invitation comes anyway: would you return to me? The question is not rhetorical. The answer YHWH is looking for is yes. The whole chapter turns on this: the law says no, but YHWH says come back.

notes.original: shuvi meshuvah Yisrael — return, faithless Israel
notes.rendering: Return, faithless Israel — declares YHWH. I will not look on you in anger, for I am faithful
notes.why: Shuvi — return (shuv — the great prophetic word for repentance and return; it means both 'turn back' and 'return home'). Meshuvah — faithlessness, apostasy (also from shuv, but in the sense of turning away rather than turning back). YHWH calls the faithless one (meshuvah) to return (shuv): the same root, inverted. The name of the disease is the prescription. The one who has been turning away is called to turn back. The divine reason for the invitation is striking: ki chasid ani — for I am faithful (chasid — one who practices chesed, the covenant loyalty of v.3:2; YHWH's faithfulness is the ground of Israel's possible faithfulness).

notes.original: eich asitcha v'banim — how gladly would I treat you as a son
notes.rendering: How gladly would I treat you as a son, and give you a delightful land... And I thought you would call me My Father
notes.why: The grammar here reveals the ache: v'amarti — and I said to myself, I thought (the reflexive use of amar — to say, here meaning an interior deliberation, a hope cherished privately). YHWH imagines what fatherhood would feel like with this people. The hoped-for word is Avi — my Father. The word is not a title but a name for intimacy, the word a small child uses. The irony is that Judah does use this word (v.4 — have you not just now called to me 'My Father'?) — but only in crisis, only as a manipulation. YHWH wanted the word freely given; instead it comes as a bargaining chip. The chapter ends with Israel finally confessing genuinely what it had been saying cynically.

intro: Jeremiah 4 contains the most terrifying passage in the book — the uncreation vision of vv.23–26, where the prophet sees Genesis run backward: the earth returns to tohu wavohu, the void before the beginning. The chapter also introduces the formal personhood of the prophet's interior anguish, a voice that will recur throughout.

notes.original: niru lachem nir — break up your fallow ground
notes.rendering: Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns
notes.why: Nir — fallow ground, unploughed land left to rest (or land that has gone to waste through neglect). The agricultural command functions as a spiritual metaphor: before you can sow anything that will grow, the hardened surface of uncultivated ground must be broken. The parallel prohibition — do not sow among thorns — makes the same point negatively. The thorns are the competing loyalties, the false gods, the habits of infidelity. Sowing among them produces nothing. Hosea uses the same agricultural metaphor (Hosea 10:12 — sow righteousness for yourselves; break up your fallow ground). The image anticipates the parable of the sower.

notes.original: tohu wavohu — formless and void
notes.rendering: I look at the earth — and behold, it is formless and void
notes.why: The phrase is drawn directly from Genesis 1:2 — the condition of the earth before creation (v'ha'aretz hayetah tohu wavohu — and the earth was formless and void). Jeremiah sees creation in reverse: the light extinguished, the mountains returning to chaos, the birds fled, the cities in ruins. It is as though YHWH is withdrawing the act of creation itself from a people who have refused to live as creation. The phrase occurs only twice in the entire Hebrew Bible — Genesis 1:2 and here. Jeremiah's audience would have heard the allusion instantly. The thing YHWH made out of chaos is being returned to chaos.

notes.original: me'ai me'ai — my anguish, my anguish
notes.rendering: My anguish, my anguish! I writhe in pain — oh the walls of my heart!
notes.why: Me'ai — my bowels, my gut, my inner parts (the Hebrew seat of emotion — what we would call the heart or stomach; the place where grief is felt physically). The doubling is an intensifier of distress. Cholov libbi — the walls of my heart (cholov — walls, partitions; not the heart itself but the chambers around it). This is the first of Jeremiah's 'confessions' — the outbursts of personal anguish that punctuate the book and are unlike anything else in the prophets. The prophet cannot separate himself from the catastrophe he announces. He is not a reporter of judgment; he is its first casualty.

intro: Jeremiah 5 stages a searching test — one honest person would be enough to save Jerusalem — and finds none. The chapter then moves to describe the occupying army with deliberate vagueness (a nation from afar, a nation whose language you do not know) and closes with its most devastating observation: the false prophets, corrupt priests, and people who prefer lies are not a failure of the system. They are the system, working exactly as its participants intend.

notes.original: im timtz'u ish... oseh mishpat m'vaqesh emunah — if you find a man doing justice, seeking truth
notes.rendering: If you find a person — if there is anyone who does justice, who seeks truth — then I will pardon her
notes.why: The premise echoes Abraham's negotiation over Sodom (Genesis 18:23–32) — where ten righteous people would have been enough. Here the threshold is lower: one. Mishpat — justice (right judgment, righteous conduct in the courts and marketplace). Emunah — truth, faithfulness (from aman — to be firm, reliable, trustworthy; the root of 'amen'). The juxtaposition is characteristic of prophetic ethics: justice is the external practice; faithfulness is its interior disposition. The search returns empty not because no one performs religious duties but because no one is reliably just.

notes.original: hagvul olam v'lo ya'avor — a perpetual barrier it cannot pass
notes.rendering: I placed the sand as the boundary of the sea — a perpetual barrier it cannot pass
notes.why: Chol — sand (the individual grain, the stuff of beaches and deserts). YHWH has bounded the sea with sand — which seems absurd, since a single wave carries more force than any sandbar. The point is the divine word behind the boundary: the sea obeys. The raging ocean that terrifies every coastal people holds itself back because YHWH has set the limit. The contrast with Israel is complete: the waves obey but the people do not. The sea, which is chaos itself, demonstrates more faithfulness than YHWH's covenant people.

notes.original: v'kohanim yirdu al y'deihem — the priests rule by their own authority
notes.rendering: the prophets prophesy falsely, and the priests rule by their own authority, and my people love it this way
notes.why: Yirdu — they rule, they exercise power (from radah — to rule, to have dominion; the same verb in Genesis 1:28 — have dominion over the fish of the sea). Al y'deihem — by their own hands, on their own authority, through their own agency (y'deihem — their hands; the phrase means without divine mandate, self-authorised). The catastrophic closing observation: v'ami ahev ken — my people love it this way. The false system is not imposed from outside; it is chosen from inside. The people who want comfort get prophets who provide it and priests who enforce it. The whole system is a conspiracy of mutual satisfaction — with no one left to tell the truth.

intro: Jeremiah 6 opens and closes with metalworking images — the grape-harvest turned military sweep (v.9) and the smelting furnace that cannot purify the ore (vv.29–30). The chapter's pivot is the invitation to the ancient paths (v.16) — the one moment of genuine offer — answered immediately with 'we will not walk in it.' The rejected silver image at the close gives the chapter its final verdict.

notes.original: shalom shalom v'ein shalom — peace, peace, when there is no peace
notes.rendering: They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace
notes.why: Qal — lightly, superficially (the healing is skin-deep, a bandage over a fracture). Shalom shalom — the doubled word is an intensifier; the false prophets are insisting on comprehensive wellbeing, total safety. V'ein shalom — and there is no peace (shalom — completeness, wholeness, the state of things being right; not merely absence of conflict but the positive presence of flourishing). The line will recur in Jeremiah 8:11 with identical wording. It became the defining characterisation of false prophecy: the prophets who told people what they wanted to hear, who plastered over cracks, who prescribed comfort for a patient who needed surgery.

notes.original: shalu l'nitivot olam — ask for the ancient paths
notes.rendering: Stand at the crossroads and look; ask for the ancient paths — where the good way is — and walk in it and find rest for your souls
notes.why: Nitivot olam — ancient paths, eternal paths (nativ — a path, a track worn by repeated walking; olam — ancient, eternal, from the distant past). The image is of a traveller at a crossroads consulting older, established routes rather than cutting a new path through untested ground. U'mtz'u margoah l'nafshchem — and find rest for your souls (margoah — rest, repose, the settling of the self; nefesh — soul, life-breath, the whole animated person). The promise attached to the ancient paths is not victory or prosperity but rest — the deepest gift to a people worn out by its own restlessness. Jesus echoes this precisely: come to me, all who are weary, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28–29 — even quoting the same word, anapausis in Greek, for margoah).

notes.original: me'as kesef kar'u lahem — rejected silver they are called
notes.rendering: The bellows blow fiercely; the lead is consumed by the fire. In vain the refining goes on, for the wicked are not removed. Rejected silver they are called, for YHWH has rejected them
notes.why: The smelting image: lead was added to silver ore in the furnace; when heated, the lead would draw impurities to the surface (as slag), leaving pure silver behind. If the process fails — if the slag will not separate — the ore is declared nimas (rejected, worthless, fit only to be thrown away). Nirpu — they are rejected (from maas — to reject, to despise; the same word used when YHWH rejects Saul in 1 Samuel 15:26). The people have gone through every form of purifying discipline YHWH has applied — famine, drought, military defeat, prophetic warning — and the impurities remain. The furnace has failed not because the process is wrong but because the material will not yield.

intro: Jeremiah 7 is the Temple Sermon — the most dangerous speech in the book. Standing at the gate of the very temple the people treat as a magical talisman, Jeremiah announces that YHWH destroyed Shiloh and will destroy Jerusalem. The logic of the sermon drives a wedge between the building and the God: the house is not YHWH; the house cannot save those who defile it.

notes.original: heikal YHWH heikal YHWH heikal YHWH hemah — the temple of YHWH, the temple of YHWH, the temple of YHWH
notes.rendering: Do not trust in these deceptive words: 'This is the temple of YHWH, the temple of YHWH, the temple of YHWH'
notes.why: The triple repetition mimics a liturgical chant or a magical formula — the kind of incantation that guarantees protection through repetition. The people have turned the temple's identity into a protective charm. Divrei hashaqer — deceptive words (sheqer — falsehood, deception, the lie; the opposite of emunah — faithfulness). Jeremiah's accusation is that the slogan itself is the idolatry: treating the divine name as a formula rather than a person. The argument recurs in Jesus's 'den of robbers' quotation (Matthew 21:13), which is itself a quotation of Jeremiah 7:11.

notes.original: me'arat perizim — a den of robbers
notes.rendering: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes?
notes.why: Me'arat — cave, den (me'arah — a cave used as a lair or hiding place). Perizim — robbers, violent men (from paratz — to break, to burst through). The image is of criminals who commit crimes in the countryside and then retreat to a safe hideout where they cannot be touched. The temple has become the hideout: sin out there, come in here for sanctuary. Jesus quotes this verse at the cleansing of the temple (Mark 11:17), combining it with Isaiah 56:7 (a house of prayer for all nations). The pairing is deliberate: what the temple was supposed to be (a house of prayer) versus what it has become (a robbers' cave).

notes.original: asher lo tziviti v'lo altah al libi — which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind
notes.rendering: to burn their sons and daughters in the fire — which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind
notes.why: V'lo altah al libi — and it did not come up upon my heart (lev — heart, the seat of thought and will; altah — it arose, it came up; the idiom means it never occurred to me, I never considered it). The force of the phrase is emphatic repudiation: child sacrifice is not a version of worship that YHWH finds offensive but somehow accepts. It is something he never imagined, never commanded, never contemplated. The Valley of Hinnom — gehinnom in later Hebrew — becomes the word for hell precisely because of what happened here: the place where children were burned becomes the word for the place of fiery destruction.

intro: Jeremiah 8 contains three of the book's most haunting images: the migrating birds that know their seasons while Israel does not know YHWH (v.7), the failed harvest that ends in the despairing cry 'the summer is ended and we are not saved' (v.20), and the question that closes the chapter — is there no balm in Gilead? — which has become one of the most resonant lines in all of religious literature.

notes.original: chasidah v'torim v'sis va'agur — the stork and the turtledove, swallow and crane
notes.rendering: Even the stork in the heavens knows her times; and the turtledove, swallow, and crane keep the time of their coming. But my people know not the rules of YHWH
notes.why: Four migratory birds named, each known for instinctive return at the appointed season. Chasidah — the stork (from chesed — lovingkindness; the bird named for its supposed loyalty to its young). Mo'adah — her appointed time (mo'ed — the appointed time, the fixed festival, the meeting time; the same word for the sanctuary of meeting and the religious calendar). The birds know their mo'ed; Israel does not know mishpat YHWH — the ordinance, the way, the settled pattern of YHWH. The comparison is devastating: creatures with no Torah observe a natural law more faithfully than the people who have Torah.

notes.original: avar qatzir kalah qayitz v'anachnu lo noshanu — the harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved
notes.rendering: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved
notes.why: The agricultural calendar used as an image of spiritual desperation. Qatzir — the grain harvest (spring). Qayitz — summer fruit (figs, late harvest). When both have passed without salvation arriving, the people face the long dry winter with nothing stored. Lo noshanu — we have not been saved (yasha — to save, to deliver, to create space; the root of Yeshua — Jesus). The cry is not petulant but desperate: we waited through every opportunity and salvation did not come. The sentence has three beats in Hebrew — past-ended-not-saved — and they fall like the tolling of a bell.

notes.original: ha'tzori ein b'Gil'ad — is there no balm in Gilead?
notes.rendering: Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?
notes.why: Tzori — balm (the resinous gum from the balsam tree, used medicinally across the ancient Near East; Gilead east of the Jordan was famous for its medicinal trees). The question is rhetorical: there is balm in Gilead; Gilead is precisely the place famous for healing. So the failure of healing is not a deficiency of medicine but a deficiency of will — or a wound too deep for any available medicine. The three questions build: the remedy exists, the healer exists, yet health has not come. The African American spiritual 'There Is a Balm in Gilead' reverses the rhetorical force of the question into an affirmation of divine healing — answering Jeremiah's despairing question with confident faith.

intro: Jeremiah 9 opens with the wish for inexhaustible tears — the poet-prophet at his most naked — and closes with the most theologically precise summary in the book: the only legitimate boast is knowing YHWH. Between these poles the chapter maps a society so saturated with deceit that neighbour cannot trust neighbour. The weeping is not sentimental; it is the appropriate response to the collapse of the human community.

notes.original: mi yitten roshi mayim — oh that my head were waters
notes.rendering: Oh that my head were waters, and my eyes a spring of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people
notes.why: Mi yitten — who will give (the idiom for a wish that cannot be fulfilled by the speaker's own will; literally 'who will provide?'). The image of the head becoming water and the eyes a spring (meqor dim'ah — a source of tears, a spring of weeping) is one of the most personal statements in the prophetic literature. The prophet does not wish to speak more powerfully or to be heeded. He wishes to weep. This is the register Jeremiah inhabits throughout the book: not triumphant announcement but grief-saturated witness. The tradition that calls him the Weeping Prophet begins here.

notes.original: vayidrekhu et l'shonam qasht'am shaqer — they bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood
notes.rendering: They bend their tongue like a bow; falsehood and not truth has grown strong in the land
notes.why: Qeshet — a bow (the weapon that projects an arrow at a distance). The tongue bent like a bow fires falsehood (shaqer) as its arrow. V'lo emet gavaru ba'aretz — and truth has not prevailed/grown strong in the land (gavar — to be strong, to be mighty, to overcome; emet — truth, faithfulness, the solid reliable thing). The inversion is complete: in the land where truth should be the strongest thing, falsehood has the power. The following verses map the consequences of this inversion: if the tongue is a weapon, then every social relationship is a battlefield — brother against brother, neighbour against neighbour (v.4).

notes.original: ki im b'zot yit'halel hamit'halel — but let him who boasts boast in this
notes.rendering: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom... but let him who boasts boast in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am YHWH who practices steadfast love, justice, and righteousness
notes.why: The triad rejected: chochmah (wisdom — the intellectual virtue), gevurah (might — military and physical power), osher (riches — economic power). The triad affirmed: chesed (steadfast love, covenant faithfulness), mishpat (justice, right judgment in the courts), tzedaqah (righteousness, right relationship). The knowledge that YHWH practices these things — and that he delights in them — is the only legitimate ground of human boasting. Paul quotes this passage in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17 ('Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord') as the basis for his theology of the cross: human wisdom, power, and status are exactly what the cross exposes as insufficient.

intro: Jeremiah 10 is the book's great doxology — a sustained contrast between the living God and the manufactured idol. The satire of idol-making (vv.3–5) draws on a tradition shared with Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115, but Jeremiah's version has a particular sharpness: the idol cannot move, cannot speak, and has to be carried. The chapter closes with one of the most profound petitions in the whole book: correct me, but in justice, not in anger.

notes.original: k'tomer miqshah hem — they are like scarecrows in a cucumber field
notes.rendering: They are like scarecrows in a cucumber field — they cannot speak; they have to be carried, for they cannot walk
notes.why: Tomer — a palm trunk, a post, a scarecrow frame (the word suggests an upright figure set in a garden to frighten birds). Miqshah — a cucumber field (the summer gourd garden, a common sight in the Levant). The image is deliberately comic: the idol is functionally identical to the stake driven into a vegetable patch to scare crows. It stands upright only because it is propped up. It requires transport because it cannot walk. The comparison dismantles the terror that idolatry depends on: you have been afraid of something that cannot frighten a bird.

notes.original: YHWH Elohim emet hu Elohim chayyim u'melech olam — YHWH is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King
notes.rendering: But YHWH is the true God; he is the living God and the everlasting King. At his wrath the earth quakes
notes.why: Emet — true, faithful, the real thing (from aman — to be firm, solid, reliable; the opposite of the idols' hevel — vapour, vanity, breath). Elohim chayyim — the living God (chayyim — living, alive; the God who has the quality of life in himself, as opposed to the idols in whom ein ruach — there is no breath/spirit, v.14). The contrast is total: they are dead objects; he is the living King whose anger shakes the earth. The confession u'melech olam — and King of eternity/forever — sets his reign against the temporary glitter of the nations' manufactured gods.

notes.original: lo v'adam darko — the way of man is not in himself
notes.rendering: I know, O YHWH, that the way of man is not in himself — it is not in man who walks to direct his steps
notes.why: Darko — his way (derek — the road, the path, the direction of travel; also the way of life, the established pattern of conduct). Lo b'adam — not in man (the humility is absolute: the creature does not choose its own path; the human being cannot be the final judge of its own direction). The prayer that follows — correct me, but in justice, not in anger — is one of the most intimate moments in the book. Jeremiah does not ask to escape correction; he asks only that it be administered with the measure of justice rather than the full weight of wrath. It is the prayer of someone who knows they need discipline but fears annihilation.

intro: Jeremiah 11 opens the covenant lawsuit that structures much of the first half of the book and closes with the first of the assassination attempts against Jeremiah — this one by his own townsmen from Anathoth. The image of himself as a gentle lamb led to slaughter (v.19) is one of the most striking in the prophetic literature, later applied in the New Testament to the Servant of Isaiah and to Jesus.

notes.original: zayit ra'anan y'feh pri to'ar — a green olive tree, beautiful in fruit and form
notes.rendering: YHWH once called you a green olive tree, beautiful in fruit and form
notes.why: Ra'anan — fresh, green, flourishing (the adjective of thriving growth; used of trees in full leaf, of people in full health). The olive tree was the most valued tree in the ancient Levant — long-lived, productive, its oil essential for food, light, and worship. To be called a green olive tree was a title of honour and beauty. The image is Hosea's again (Hosea 14:6 — his splendour shall be like the olive tree); here Jeremiah invokes it only to watch it burn. The past tense — YHWH once called you — marks the rupture. The name no longer fits.

notes.original: k'seh aluf yuval livzoach — like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter
notes.rendering: But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me that they devised schemes
notes.why: Seh aluf — a tame lamb, a pet lamb (aluf — familiar, tame, the animal that follows without resistance). Yuval livzoach — led to slaughter (zabach — to slaughter, to sacrifice; the same word for ritual sacrifice at the altar). The image captures Jeremiah's complete unsuspecting innocence: he did not know they were plotting against him. The verse is applied to the Suffering Servant in Isaiah 53:7 (like a lamb led to the slaughter he did not open his mouth) and thence to Jesus throughout the New Testament. Jeremiah's personal experience of innocent suffering becomes the template for the theology of vicarious affliction.

notes.original: bochen k'layot valev — who tests the kidneys and the heart
notes.rendering: O YHWH of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind
notes.why: K'layot — kidneys (the Hebrew seat of deepest emotion and motivation; what we call the gut or the soul; the k'layot are the inmost parts, the parts even the person cannot fully examine). Lev — heart (the seat of thought and will). YHWH tests both — the rational deliberation (lev) and the pre-rational impulse (k'layot). The appeal to YHWH as the one who sees what no human court can see is Jeremiah's ground for petition: I cannot prove my innocence before men, but you know the whole interior. The forensic image recurs throughout the Psalms (Psalm 7:9; 26:2) and Paul uses the same logic in 1 Corinthians 4:3–5.

intro: Jeremiah 12 is the first of the great 'confessions' — the raw theodicy dialogues between prophet and God that are unlike anything else in the prophetic literature. The question 'why do the wicked prosper?' is as old as Job, but here it is addressed directly to YHWH as a legal brief. YHWH's answer is bracing rather than comforting: if the footsoldiers have worn you out, what will you do against the cavalry?

notes.original: tzaddiq atah YHWH ki arib eilecha — you are righteous, O YHWH, when I bring a case before you
notes.rendering: You are righteous, O YHWH, when I bring a case before you. Yet I would speak with you about justice: why does the way of the wicked prosper?
notes.why: Arib eilecha — I bring a legal case against you, I argue my suit with you (riv — a legal dispute, a lawsuit, a formal complaint; the same word as in the covenant lawsuit of chapter 2). Jeremiah opens by conceding the verdict before the case begins: you are righteous. This is not flattery but legal precision — he acknowledges YHWH's judicial authority even as he lodges the complaint. The combination of submission and challenge is the mark of genuine prayer as opposed to either servile flattery or raw protest. The question that follows — why do the wicked prosper? — is the question of every generation that has tried to believe in divine justice.

notes.original: qarov atah b'fihem v'rachok miki'l'votam — you are near in their mouths yet far from their kidneys
notes.rendering: You are near in their mouths yet far from their kidneys
notes.why: The spatial metaphor maps onto the anatomy of hypocrisy. Pi — mouth (the organ of speech, the place where names are pronounced, where oaths are made). K'layot — kidneys (the deepest interior, the seat of genuine feeling and motivation; see note on 11:20). YHWH is close on their lips — they speak his name, perform the rituals, make the offerings — but far from their inmost being. The description is the precise anatomy of religious performance without interior reality. It is the same diagnosis as Isaiah 29:13 (this people honour me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me) and Jesus's application of Isaiah in Mark 7:6.

notes.original: im et hareglaim ratztah vayilukha — if you have raced with men on foot and they have wearied you
notes.rendering: If you have raced with men on foot and they have wearied you — how will you compete with horses? And if in a safe land you are so trusting, what will you do in the thicket of the Jordan?
notes.why: YHWH's answer to the complaint about suffering is not a defence but a challenge. The logic is escalation: Jeremiah is worn out by ordinary treachery (men on foot). The trials ahead will be like cavalry. The g'on haYarden — the pride/thicket of the Jordan — refers to the dense tangled jungle that grew along the Jordan riverbank, the habitat of lions (Jeremiah 49:19; 50:44). If the open country is dangerous, what happens in the undergrowth? The answer to 'why is this happening?' is: this is nothing yet. What YHWH offers is not explanation but preparation — and not the preparation of comfort but of toughening.

intro: Jeremiah 13 deploys two of the book's most vivid enacted signs — the buried loincloth and the smashed wine jugs — to dramatise theological truths that words alone cannot carry. The loincloth sign is the more remarkable: the intimacy of the garment makes the ruination visceral. A people who were meant to cling to YHWH like linen to skin have instead rotted in the ground.

notes.original: davaq — to cling
notes.rendering: For as the loincloth clings to the waist of a man, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me
notes.why: Davaq — to cling, to adhere, to stick fast (the same word in Genesis 2:24 — a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife; and Ruth 1:14 — Ruth clung to Naomi). The loincloth image is shocking precisely because of its intimacy: the garment that touches skin directly, that holds the body's warmth, that is most personally identified with the person wearing it. That is how close YHWH intended Israel to be. The contrast with the buried, rotted loincloth — useful for nothing — gives the whole parable its force. The intimacy of the design makes the ruin of it all the more devastating.

notes.original: ha'yachapoch Kushi oro — can the Ethiopian change his skin?
notes.rendering: Can the Ethiopian change his skin or the leopard his spots? Then also you can do good who are accustomed to do evil
notes.why: The two examples establish natural impossibility: skin colour and leopard spots are fixed at birth; they are not chosen and cannot be changed by effort. The application is theological and diagnostic rather than racial: those who are habituated (limmudei — trained, accustomed; from lamad — to learn, to train; the same root as talmid, disciple) to doing evil cannot simply choose to do good. The inability is not original nature but acquired character — the terrifying conclusion that the habit of sin becomes the person's second nature, as unchangeable as what was there from birth. This is not fatalism but a clinical account of moral deformation.

notes.original: b'mistariym tivkeh nafshi — my soul will weep in secret
notes.rendering: But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride
notes.why: B'mistariym — in secret places, in hiding (seter — a hiding place, a secret shelter). The prophet who must stand in the gate and pronounce judgment weeps privately where no one can see. The word pride (ge'avah — exaltation, arrogance, but also the pride that goes before a fall) is what the weeping is over: not merely Israel's sin but its fatal dignity — the pride that will not stoop to return. The image of the prophet weeping alone, hidden, for the people he is judging is one of the most psychologically precise portraits in the whole book. Jeremiah is not detached from his message. His proclamation costs him everything.

intro: Jeremiah 14 is structured as a liturgy of drought — description, lament, divine refusal, prophetic weeping, final plea. The three-fold refusal to accept intercession (vv.10, 11–12, 14–15) is the most sustained 'no' in the book so far. The chapter's theological tension is between the prayers the prophet cannot stop making and the command he has received not to make them.

notes.original: miqveh Yisrael moshi'o b'et tzarah — O Hope of Israel, its Saviour in time of trouble
notes.rendering: O Hope of Israel, its Saviour in time of trouble, why should you be like a stranger in the land, like a traveller who turns aside to tarry for a night?
notes.why: Miqveh — hope, the thing waited for (from qavah — to wait, to hope; miqveh is the object of waiting, the hoped-for thing). The title 'Hope of Israel' inverts the accusation of chapter 2 (they have forsaken me, the spring of living water) into a desperate petition: you are the very thing we are waiting for. The image that follows makes the theological crisis vivid: YHWH feels like a ger (stranger, sojourner, temporary resident) and an orach (a traveller passing through for a single night). The people who were once strangers in Egypt now feel as though YHWH is a stranger among them — passing through, uncommitted, almost gone.

notes.original: sheqer hem niv'im — they are prophesying lies
notes.rendering: The prophets are prophesying lies in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them
notes.why: Shav' — emptiness, vanity, nothingness (v.14 — chezyon shav — a vision of emptiness/falsehood); sheqer — lie, deception; qesem — divination (forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10). The three synonyms stack up: what the false prophets offer is simultaneously empty, deceptive, and illegitimate in its methods. The decisive phrase is lo shalachtiym — I did not send them. In Jeremiah's theology, the criterion of authentic prophecy is not the content of the message (though false content is symptomatic) but the sending: true prophets are those sent by YHWH. The false prophets speak from their own interior (tartut libbam — the delusion of their own heart).

notes.original: ha'yesh b'havlei hagoyim m'gashmim — are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain?
notes.rendering: Are there any among the false gods of the nations that can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, O YHWH our God?
notes.why: The drought becomes the argument for monotheism. The Baals were fertility gods — their whole domain was rain, harvest, agricultural abundance. If they cannot produce rain in a drought, what good are they? The question is rhetorical but also polemical: Baal worship was precisely an appeal for rain (1 Kings 18 — the Carmel contest between Elijah and the Baal prophets turns on who can bring fire and rain). Jeremiah reduces the entire competing religious system to its functional claim and finds it empty. The chapter that began with cracked earth ends with this: the only one who can open the heavens is the God they have been running from.

intro: Jeremiah 15 contains the most scalding of the confessions — the accusation that YHWH has been to him like a deceptive brook (v.18), an image of stunning audacity. To call God unreliable, to accuse the spring of living water of running dry, is the most dangerous thing Jeremiah has yet said. YHWH's response does not defend himself but challenges Jeremiah to return to his calling.

notes.original: nimtz'u d'varecha va'ochlam — your words were found, and I ate them
notes.rendering: Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart
notes.why: Va'ochlam — and I ate them (the image of eating the divine word; consuming it as food). The image recurs in Ezekiel 3:1–3 (the scroll eaten that tastes like honey) and Revelation 10:10 (the little scroll). For Jeremiah, the word of YHWH was not received as information to be analysed but as nourishment to be consumed — taken into the body, becoming part of the person. Sason u'simchat l'vavi — joy and delight of my heart (sason — exuberant joy; simchah — gladness, deep pleasure). The cruel irony the confession traces: the word that was once joy has become the source of unceasing pain (v.18). The same word that fed him is now destroying him.

notes.original: hayoh tih'yeh li k'akzav mayim lo ne'emanu — will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
notes.rendering: Will you be to me like a deceitful brook, like waters that fail?
notes.why: Akzav — a deceptive thing, a lie (from kazav — to lie, to deceive). The akzav nachal — the deceptive stream — is the wadi that looks full in winter but runs dry in summer when you need it most (see the broken cisterns of 2:13 — Jeremiah returns to water imagery for theological betrayal). Ne'emanu — that cannot be relied upon (from aman — faithfulness, reliability; the root of emet and amen). The accusation is that YHWH, who called himself the spring of living water, has behaved like the seasonal wadi — present in good times, absent when the need is greatest. This is the most daring line in all of Jeremiah's confessions. YHWH does not rebuke the question but uses it as a call to return.

notes.original: im tashov va'ashivecha — if you return, I will restore you
notes.rendering: If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before me
notes.why: The symmetry of the Hebrew is precise: im tashov — if you return (shuv); va'ashivecha — I will return you, I will restore you (the same root, causative form). Return is answered by return. The condition is not performance of duty but the prior act of the prophet's own turning — YHWH will not carry Jeremiah through without Jeremiah's own consent to the task. V'amadta l'fanai — and you shall stand before me (amad l'fanei — to stand in the presence of, the posture of the servant before the master, the prophet before YHWH). The prophet who wished he had never been born is called back to his station.

intro: Jeremiah 16 contains one of the book's most unusual divine commands: the prophet is forbidden to marry. The celibacy is not ascetic choice but enacted prophecy — a living sign that the normal human future (children, continuity, family) has been suspended for this generation. The chapter moves from this darkest personal cost to a surprising universalist horizon: nations from the ends of the earth will come and confess their inherited lies.

notes.original: lo tiqach l'cha ishah — you shall not take a wife
notes.rendering: You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place
notes.why: The prohibition is without precedent in the prophetic literature. Marriage, children, and family continuity were the fundamental goods of Israelite life — the sign of blessing, the means of covenant inheritance. To forbid them is to embody the interruption of the future. The reason YHWH gives (vv.3–4) is explicit: children born here will die terrible deaths unlamented. Jeremiah's childlessness is not a private deprivation but a public theology: this land has no future to offer its children. The prophet's body is the text.

notes.original: asafti et shlomi me'et ha'am hazeh — I have taken away my peace from this people
notes.rendering: Do not enter the house of mourning, for I have taken away my peace from this people — my steadfast love and mercy
notes.why: Shalom — peace, wholeness, flourishing (the comprehensive wellbeing that YHWH's presence brings). Chesed v'rachamim — steadfast love and mercy (chesed — covenant loyalty; rachamim — the plural of rechem — womb; the word for womb-love, the love of a mother for the child of her body). YHWH names precisely what he is withdrawing: not just protection but the interior quality of the relationship — the tenderness, the intimacy. To be told not to mourn because divine compassion has been withdrawn is to be left in a grief beyond mourning.

notes.original: YHWH uzi um'uzzi uma'nusi b'yom tzarah — O YHWH, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble
notes.rendering: O YHWH, my strength and my stronghold, my refuge in the day of trouble, to you shall the nations come from the ends of the earth
