notes.why: Uzi — my strength (oz — strength, power, might; as in Psalm 46). U'ma'uzi — my fortress (ma'oz — a place of refuge, a stronghold). U'manuzi — my refuge (manos — a place of flight, a shelter to flee to). Three near-synonyms of protection stacked together — the prophet who has been denied family and comfort finds his entire security in YHWH alone. The nations' confession that follows (they have inherited nothing but lies, hebel — vapour, nothingness) is the universalist reversal of everything: the idols that Israel was seduced by are acknowledged as empty by the very nations that worshipped them.

intro: Jeremiah 17 moves through a remarkable sequence: engraved sin, the two trees of Psalm 1 rewritten, the famous diagnosis of the deceitful heart, a prayer for healing, and a Sabbath discourse that seems oddly placed but makes theological sense — the Sabbath is the discipline of not grasping, the regular practice of trusting YHWH to sustain what human striving would destroy.

notes.original: chatot Yehudah k'tuvah b'et barzel — the sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron
notes.rendering: The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart
notes.why: Et barzel — a pen of iron (an iron stylus, used to incise letters into stone or metal). Tziporen shamir — a point of diamond or flint (shamir — emery, the hardest cutting material known in antiquity; used to cut stone and engrave metal). The sin is not written in ink that can be washed away. It is cut into the stone of the heart. Luach libam — the tablet of their heart: the image deliberately inverts the promise of 31:33, where YHWH will write his law on their hearts. Here the people have written their own sin on the same surface. The tablet of the heart that was supposed to bear Torah bears idolatry instead.

notes.original: aqov halev mikol va'anush hu — the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick
notes.rendering: The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick — who can understand it?
notes.why: Aqov — deceitful, crooked, treacherous (from aqav — to take by the heel, to trip up; the same root as Jacob's name, the heel-grasper, the supplanter). The heart that deceives others also deceives itself — it is aqov, it trips even the one who owns it. Anush — desperately sick, incurable (from anash — to be sick, to be weak, to be beyond cure; used of incurable wounds in 15:18 and 30:12). Mi yeda'enu — who can know it? (the rhetorical question implies: no human being can fully diagnose their own heart). The answer comes immediately in v.10: I, YHWH, search the heart. The one who cannot be deceived by the deceiving heart is YHWH alone.

notes.original: baruch hagever asher yivtach b'YHWH — blessed is the man who trusts in YHWH
notes.rendering: Blessed is the man who trusts in YHWH... He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream
notes.why: The tree-by-water image recapitulates Psalm 1:3 with added detail: the roots extended toward the stream (yishalach shorashav al yuval — it sends its roots toward the river channel). The tree does not fear drought because its roots reach water that the surface drought cannot touch. The theological mechanics are explicit: trust in YHWH is the root system that reaches the deep water when the surface dries up. The contrast with the shrub in the desert (v.6 — arar ba'aravah, a juniper in the dry wilderness — seeing no good, dwelling in parched salt land) maps the two destinies of trust and distrust onto the Palestinian landscape itself.

intro: Jeremiah 18 gives the book its most famous image: the potter working the clay. But the sign at the potter's house is more theologically nuanced than its popular use suggests — it is not simply an image of divine sovereignty but of divine responsiveness. The potter can remake a ruined vessel; YHWH can relent from announced judgment if the people turn. The freedom is mutual. The chapter closes with another assassination plot and Jeremiah's most unnerving imprecation.

notes.original: nishchat hak'li asher hu oseh — the vessel he is making is spoiled
notes.rendering: And the vessel he is making of clay is spoiled in the potter's hand, and he reworks it into another vessel
notes.why: Nishchat — it is ruined, it is spoiled (shachat — to destroy, to corrupt, to ruin; the same word used when creation is corrupted in Genesis 6:12 and when Sodom is destroyed). The clay that was meant to become one thing becomes ruined in the process. But the potter's response is not to discard the clay — he reworks it (yashov vaya'asehu k'li acher — he turns and makes it into another vessel). The theological import is not fatalism (the potter shapes whatever he wants) but possibility: ruined clay is not wasted clay. The judgment of vv.7–10 applies the principle both ways: announced disaster can be averted by turning; announced good can be withdrawn by apostasy.

notes.original: ha'ya'azov mitzur sadai sheleg Levanon — does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags?
notes.rendering: Does the snow of Lebanon leave the crags of Sirion? Do the mountain waters run dry, the cold flowing streams?
notes.why: The two questions establish natural constancy: the snow on Lebanon's peaks is permanent (Lebanon's name may itself derive from lavan — white, from its snow). The mountain streams fed by snowmelt run with cold dependability. These things do not change. Then the indictment: but my people have forgotten me. Israel has done what snow and stone cannot do — abandoned its natural character. The images deliberately reverse 8:7 (the migrating birds that know their seasons). Creation, from the smallest migrating bird to the permanent snowfields, is more faithful to its nature than the covenant people.

notes.original: ha'yushalem tachat tovah ra'ah — is evil a repayment for good?
notes.rendering: Is evil a repayment for good? Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them
notes.why: The imprecation that follows (vv.21–23) is the most violent prayer in the confessions — Jeremiah calling down famine, sword, death, and childlessness on his enemies. The theological problem it poses is real: this is not abstract vengeance but specific personal rage from a man of prayer, a man who interceded for the same people he now curses. The shock is intentional. Jeremiah is not presented as a saint who has transcended human bitterness. He is a human being destroyed by a calling he did not choose, praying the only prayers he can manage. The tradition does not edit out the rage.

intro: Jeremiah 19 is the climax of the enacted sign sequence. The potter's wheel of chapter 18 showed clay that could be remade; the broken flask of chapter 19 shows pottery that cannot. The vessel is fired and hardened — beyond reworking. The location is deliberately chosen: the Valley of Hinnom where children were burned. The sign is performed where the sin was committed.

notes.original: asher lo yukal l'hirapeh od — so that it can never be mended
notes.rendering: So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended
notes.why: Lo yukal l'hirapeh — it cannot be healed, it cannot be repaired (rapah — to heal, to mend; the same root as rofeh — physician). The contrast with the wheel in chapter 18 is exact: the soft clay can be reworked; the fired pot cannot. The clay of chapter 18 represented a people still in process — capable of being reshaped. By chapter 19 the firing has been completed. The hardened pot is the image of a judgment that has passed the point of reversal. This is not theological fatalism but chronological urgency: there was a window for change; it has closed.

notes.original: titzalnah shte oznav — the ears of everyone who hears will tingle
notes.rendering: I am bringing such disaster upon this place that the ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle
notes.why: Titzalnah — they will tingle, they will ring (tzalal — to tinkle, to ring like a bell or a struck instrument; the same word in 1 Samuel 3:11 and 2 Kings 21:12 for the singular shock of terrible news). The ears as the primary organ of reception: the news will be so shocking that it will physically affect the hearing apparatus — a ringing in the ears, a kind of sonic vertigo. The formula appears three times in the Hebrew Bible for the three worst national disasters (the fall of Shiloh, the fall of Jerusalem under Manasseh, and here). The tingling ear is the physiological response to civilisational catastrophe.

notes.original: sha'ar hacharsuith — the Potsherd Gate
notes.rendering: go out to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the entry of the Potsherd Gate
notes.why: Sha'ar — gate (the city gate, the point of entry and exit, also the place of judgment and commerce). Hacharsuith — of the potsherds (cheres — pottery, broken pottery, shards; the gate where broken pottery was discarded). The sign is performed at the gate named for broken things, in the valley where children were killed. Every element of the staging is deliberate: the location enacts the meaning before the flask is raised. Jeremiah walks to the place of breakage carrying the object of breakage, and breaks it there. The Hebrew prophets understood that location is theology.

intro: Jeremiah 20 contains the darkest passage in the whole book — the final confession, which moves in a single chapter from accusation (you deceived me), through defiant praise (sing to YHWH!), to a death-wish so extreme it curses the day of his own birth. The whiplash is not incoherence but the most honest portrait of faith under extremity in the entire prophetic literature.

notes.original: piteetani YHWH va'eepat — O YHWH, you have deceived me, and I was deceived
notes.rendering: O YHWH, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed
notes.why: Piteetani — you deceived me, you seduced me (patah — to entice, to seduce, to open up; the word used in Exodus 22:16 for a man who seduces a virgin; in Proverbs for the temptation of the adulteress). Jeremiah accuses YHWH of seduction: you enticed me into this calling with promises I trusted, and now I am destroyed by it. Va'techazeq mineni vattukal — you were stronger than I and you prevailed (chazaq — to be strong, to overpower; yakal — to be able, to prevail). The prophet was overpowered. The charge is devastating. It is also, within the tradition, the most honest thing ever said about the prophetic calling.

notes.original: k'esh bo'eret atzur b'atzmotai — like a burning fire shut up in my bones
notes.rendering: There is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary of holding it in, and I cannot
notes.why: Esh bo'eret — burning fire (bo'er — to burn, to blaze, to consume). Atzur b'atzmotai — shut up in my bones (atzar — to restrain, to hold back; atzamot — bones, the skeletal structure, the deepest physical interior). The word of YHWH that Jeremiah tried to suppress becomes like fire contained in the bones themselves — not the soft tissue of emotion but the hard structure of the body. The containment is impossible. V'nilfeti lo uchal — I am worn out holding it in and I cannot. The prophet who most wanted to stop prophesying discovers that the word will come out regardless. He is not the master of his own message.

notes.original: arur hayom asher yulladti vo — cursed be the day on which I was born
notes.rendering: Cursed be the day on which I was born! The day when my mother bore me — let it not be blessed!
notes.why: The death-wish that closes the chapter is unparalleled in its extremity. Unlike Job (3:3 — let the day perish on which I was born), Jeremiah does not curse the day itself but the messenger who announced his birth. The distinction is pointed: he is not wishing for cosmic un-creation but for the particular chain of events that led to his specific existence and his specific calling. V.18 reduces the complaint to its simplest form: why did I come out of the womb to see toil and sorrow and spend my days in shame? The book that began with YHWH's tenderness (before I formed you I knew you) ends this chapter with the prophet wishing he had never been formed. The confession is not resolved. The chapter simply stops.

intro: Jeremiah 21 marks a structural pivot in the book: the prophetic oracles give way to the historical narrative of Jerusalem's siege. The theological shock of the chapter is that YHWH will fight against Jerusalem rather than for it — the divine warrior tradition turned against its own people. The 'way of life and the way of death' (v.8) deliberately echoes the Deuteronomic language of covenant choice, but the choice now available is catastrophically reduced.

notes.original: nilchamti ani itchem b'yad n'tuyah — I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand
notes.rendering: I myself will fight against you with outstretched hand and strong arm, in anger and in fury and in great wrath
notes.why: The divine warrior image is inverted. Yad n'tuyah u'zero'a chazaqah — outstretched hand and strong arm — is the standard formula for YHWH's saving action in the Exodus (Deuteronomy 4:34; 5:15; 26:8). Israel was brought out of Egypt by the outstretched hand. Now the same arm is directed against them. The formula the people had turned into liturgical comfort (YHWH who saves with a mighty arm) is redeployed as judgment. Three words for divine anger are stacked: af (anger), chemah (fury, heat), qetzef (wrath, indignation). The triple stack signals that this is not a corrective blow but a consuming one.

notes.original: hineni noten lifneichem et derech hachayyim v'et derech hammavet — I set before you the way of life and the way of death
notes.rendering: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death
notes.why: The echo of Deuteronomy 30:15 (see, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil) is exact and devastating. In Deuteronomy the choice is between obedience and disobedience — a genuine moral binary with time to decide. Here the choice has collapsed to a single tactical option: surrender to Babylon and live, or stay and die. The rich moral framework of the Deuteronomic covenant has narrowed to an evacuation instruction. The language of covenant choice survives, but what it points to is no longer virtue but bare survival. This is what the long refusal to choose has produced.

notes.original: dinu laboqer mishpat — execute justice in the morning
notes.rendering: Execute justice in the morning, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed
notes.why: Laboqer — in the morning (boqer — the early morning, the first light; the time when the city gates open and the day's business begins, including the sitting of courts for judgment). The command is not merely timely but urgent: first thing, before anything else. The morning is when the day's character is set. The specific command — deliver the one robbed from the hand of the oppressor — identifies whose justice matters: not the powerful (who can access courts whenever they want) but the robbed, the extorted, the person who has already lost. It is identical to Amos 5:15 (establish justice in the gate) and anticipates what the failure to do this will cost.

intro: Jeremiah 22 is a gallery of royal portraits, each darker than the last: the ideal king who does justice (vv.3–5), Shallum who died in exile unmourned, Jehoiakim who built his palace on unpaid labour, and Coniah — the signet ring torn from YHWH's hand and cast away. The chapter's theological centre is v.16: to judge the cause of the poor is to know YHWH. Knowing God is not mystical experience but enacted justice.

notes.original: dan din ani v'evyon — he judged the cause of the poor and needy
notes.rendering: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well. Is not this to know me? declares YHWH
notes.why: Dan din — he judged the judgment, he executed justice (the cognate accusative intensifies: truly judging, actively executing the verdict). Ani v'evyon — the poor and the needy (ani — the afflicted, the lowly, one crushed by circumstance; evyon — the destitute, the one who craves because he has nothing; see Amos 2:6 — the same pair). Ha'lo hi da'at oti — is not this knowing me? (da'at — knowledge, but in the full covenantal sense of intimate acquaintance; yada — to know as a husband knows a wife, as a shepherd knows the flock). The equation is radical: to know YHWH is not to have correct doctrine or religious experience. It is to do justice for the poorest.

notes.original: chatam al yad y'mini — the signet ring on my right hand
notes.rendering: Even if Coniah were the signet ring on my right hand, yet I would tear you off
notes.why: Chatam — a signet ring (the seal used to authenticate documents, pressed into wax or clay; the most personal and powerful object a king or official owned; to lose it was to lose authority and identity). Al yad y'mini — on my right hand (the dominant hand, the hand of power, the hand closest to the king's body). The image concedes everything: Coniah is as close to YHWH as the signet on his right hand — the most intimate and authoritative position imaginable. And even so, ki im — even so. The intimacy of position does not exempt from judgment. The signet is torn off (natosh — to pull out, to uproot; the same verb used for uprooting nations in 1:10). The Davidic dynasty has reached its limit.

notes.original: eretz eretz eretz — O land, land, land
notes.rendering: O land, land, land, hear the word of YHWH!
notes.why: The triple address — eretz eretz eretz — is unique in the Hebrew Bible. The land itself is summoned as witness and recipient of the word. In Hebrew rhetoric, doubling intensifies (holy, holy, holy in Isaiah 6:3; the tripling is even more extreme). The land that was promised, that was given, that was defiled, that mourned (4:28; 12:4) is now called to hear its own fate. The rhetorical move bypasses the people entirely: YHWH speaks over their heads to the ground they stand on. The land will outlast them and will hear what they refused to.

intro: Jeremiah 23 is the book's most sustained attack on false prophecy, structured around a single diagnostic criterion: have you stood in the council of YHWH (v.18)? The chapter also contains the messianic promise of the Righteous Branch — the one future king who will finally embody what the failed shepherds of vv.1–2 refused to be. The wordplay on 'burden' that closes the chapter is a piece of sustained irony that defies easy translation.

notes.original: Tsemach tzaddiq — a righteous Branch; YHWH tzidqenu — YHWH is our righteousness
notes.rendering: I will raise up for David a righteous Branch... and this is the name by which he will be called: 'YHWH is our righteousness'
notes.why: Tsemach — a sprout, a branch, a shoot (the word for new growth from a stump or root; used in Isaiah 4:2 and Zechariah 3:8; 6:12 for the messianic figure). Tzaddiq — righteous (the one who embodies right relationship, whose governance produces equity). The name — YHWH tzidqenu — is a deliberate reversal of the last king's name: Zedekiah means 'YHWH is my righteousness' or 'YHWH is righteous.' The coming king's name will be the same claim made true rather than merely claimed. What Zedekiah's name asserted but his reign denied, the Branch will make real.

notes.original: mi amad b'sod YHWH — who among them has stood in the council of YHWH
notes.rendering: For who among them has stood in the council of YHWH to see and to hear his word?
notes.why: Sod — secret council, inner circle, the gathering where deliberation happens (the same word in Amos 3:7 — YHWH does nothing without revealing his sod to his servants the prophets). The sod YHWH is the divine assembly, the heavenly court where decisions are made and decrees issued. The true prophet is one who has been admitted to that council, who has overheard the deliberation. The false prophets run without being sent (v.21) because they have not stood in the council; they have not waited to hear. Their messages are their own inventions dressed in divine authority. The criterion of true prophecy is not eloquence or popularity but access — and access comes only through being called.

notes.original: ha'lo choh d'vari k'esh — is not my word like fire, and like a hammer that breaks the rock
notes.rendering: Is not my word like fire — declares YHWH — and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?
notes.why: Two images of irresistible force: esh — fire, which consumes and cannot be stopped once it takes hold; and patish — a hammer (the heavy forging hammer, not a carpenter's tool), which breaks rock. The contrast with the dream-prophecies of v.28 (straw versus wheat) is completed by these images: straw is flammable in a different sense — it ignites quickly and burns to nothing; wheat is substantial, nourishing. The hammer on rock produces fragments that reveal the interior of what seemed solid. The divine word does not accommodate itself to its hearers; it breaks what refuses to yield.

intro: Jeremiah 24 delivers the book's most theologically surprising reversal: those already in exile — the ones who seem to have been punished — are the good figs. Those who remain in the land and feel secure — who regard the exiles as the rejected ones — are the bad figs, inedible and useless. The vision dismantles the instinctive equation of presence with blessing and absence with curse.

notes.original: t'einim tovot me'od k'bikkurot — very good figs, like first-ripe figs
notes.rendering: One basket had very good figs, like first-ripe figs, but the other basket had very bad figs, so bad that they could not be eaten
notes.why: Bikkurot — first-ripe figs (bikkurim — the firstfruits, the first produce of the harvest; the word carries the sense of prime quality, the best of the season's yield). The bikkurah fig was a delicacy — the first sweet fruit of early summer, before the main harvest, prized precisely because it came first. The contrast with the bad figs is absolute: lo ye'achelu me'roa — they cannot be eaten because of their badness. The two baskets before the temple are a sorting device. The surprise is which community gets which basket.

notes.original: v'natati lahem lev lada'at oti — I will give them a heart to know me
notes.rendering: I will give them a heart to know me, that I am YHWH, and they shall be my people and I will be their God
notes.why: Lev lada'at oti — a heart to know me (lev — heart, the seat of will and understanding; lada'at — to know, in the full covenantal sense). This is the first appearance in Jeremiah of the promise that will be fully articulated in 31:33–34 — the new covenant where the law is written on hearts and all will know YHWH. The gift is a heart capable of knowing. The problem diagnosed throughout the book (17:9 — the deceitful heart; 5:23 — the stubborn rebellious heart) is addressed not by human effort but by divine gift: I will give. The covenant formula — my people, my God — echoes Exodus 6:7 and frames the return as a second exodus.

notes.original: k'te'einim hatovot ha'eleh — like these good figs
notes.rendering: Like these good figs, so I will regard as good the exiles from Judah, whom I have sent away from this place
notes.why: The theological inversion is total. The exiles who were taken to Babylon were widely regarded — including by those who remained — as the cursed ones, the rejected, the people YHWH had abandoned. The ones who stayed in Jerusalem felt vindicated: they were still in the land, still near the temple, still (apparently) in YHWH's favour. The vision reverses this completely. The exile is not abandonment but the vehicle of preservation and future. The phrase asher shilachti — whom I have sent away (shalach — to send, the same word used of the sending of prophets and the sending of Israel into the wilderness) — is deliberate: the exile was not accidental. YHWH sent them. The going away is the path to the return.

intro: Jeremiah 25 is the book's great chronological and geographical pivot. The twenty-three years of Jeremiah's ministry are summarised, a number is put on the exile (seventy years), and the cup of wrath is passed around every nation on the map. The chapter functions as a kind of intermission: the first major collection of oracles ends here, and the book's second half — more biographical, more historical — is about to begin.

notes.original: Nevukhadnetzar melech Bavel avdi — Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant
notes.rendering: I will send for Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, my servant
notes.why: Avdi — my servant (eved — servant, worker, one who acts on behalf of another). The title given to Nebuchadnezzar is the same given to Moses, David, and the prophets. It is not a term of honour for Babylon but a statement of divine sovereignty: even the pagan king who will destroy Jerusalem is an instrument in YHWH's hand, executing a commission he does not know he has received. The theology is consistent with Isaiah's use of Cyrus as YHWH's anointed (Isaiah 45:1). YHWH does not endorse Babylon's character; he deploys Babylon's power. The distinction matters.

notes.original: shiv'im shanah — seventy years
notes.rendering: These nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years
notes.why: Shiv'im — seventy (a round number in Hebrew for a complete generation, a full period; seven is the number of completeness; seventy is completeness intensified). The number became enormously significant in later tradition: Daniel 9 recalculates it as seventy weeks of years; Zechariah 1:12 asks how long until the seventy years are complete; the rabbis debated its precise reckoning. Jeremiah himself does not explain the arithmetic — he simply announces the duration. The practical effect is to put a horizon on the exile: not permanent, not forever, but a defined and endurable span with a promised end.

notes.original: kos hayyayin hachema — the cup of the wine of wrath
notes.rendering: Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it
notes.why: Kos — cup (the drinking vessel, but also in prophetic literature the vessel of divine judgment; see Psalm 75:8 — in YHWH's hand there is a cup). Yayin hachema — the wine of wrath (chema — heat, fury, poison; the word can mean both burning anger and venom). The image of the cup of wrath passed from nation to nation becomes a dominant image in prophetic eschatology (Isaiah 51:17, 22; Ezekiel 23:31–34; Revelation 14:10; 16:19). Jeremiah's version is distinctive: the prophet himself is commanded to hand the cup around. He is the waiter at the banquet of judgment.

intro: Jeremiah 26 is the book's great trial scene — a formal legal proceeding in the temple court with Jeremiah's life at stake. The chapter is the narrative counterpart to the Temple Sermon of chapter 7: we saw what he said, now we see what it cost. The elders who cite Micah's precedent are making a sophisticated legal argument about prophetic freedom. Uriah's fate in the chapter's closing verses shows what happens when that argument fails.

notes.original: hineni v'yedchem — behold, I am in your hands
notes.rendering: As for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me as seems good and right to you
notes.why: The formal surrender to the court — hineni v'yedchem, I am placed in your hands — is the most vulnerable moment in the narrative. Jeremiah makes no defense of his own person, only of the message: I am not asking you to spare me; I am telling you that killing me will not silence the word. The posture echoes the suffering servant of Isaiah 53:7 (he opened not his mouth) and anticipates Jesus before Pilate. The defence that follows is theological rather than personal: not I am innocent but you will incur blood-guilt if you act against YHWH's messenger. The man is expendable; the accountability is not.

notes.original: Micha HaMorashti nibbah — Micah of Moresheth prophesied
notes.rendering: Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and said: Zion shall be ploughed as a field
notes.why: The elders' precedent-citation is remarkable legal reasoning: a century earlier, Micah said the same thing Jeremiah is saying (the quote is from Micah 3:12 — Zion shall be ploughed as a field). Hezekiah did not execute Micah but repented — and YHWH relented. The argument is: if executing Micah would have been wrong, and Jeremiah is saying the same thing, executing Jeremiah is equally wrong. It is the most precise example of prophetic case law in the Hebrew Bible. The precedent saves Jeremiah's life. What saved Uriah was only the presence of a well-placed friend (v.24 — the hand of Ahikam was with Jeremiah).

notes.original: ulai yishm'u v'yashuvu — it may be they will listen and every one turn
notes.rendering: It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster
notes.why: Ulai — perhaps, it may be (the word of uncertain hope; used in Genesis 16:2 — perhaps through her I will be built; in Numbers 22:6 — perhaps I can defeat them). YHWH sends the prophet with an ulai — not a guarantee but a possibility. The disaster is not predetermined; it can be averted. The command not to hold back a word (v.2 — al tigra davar) is paired with this conditional: full proclamation paired with genuine possibility of response. This is the theological structure of the whole prophetic enterprise: not the announcement of fate but the creation of a crisis in which choice is still possible. YHWH is still hoping.

intro: Jeremiah 27 is an enacted sign of the most politically charged kind: Jeremiah walks through Jerusalem and the courts of foreign envoys wearing a wooden yoke on his neck, proclaiming that submission to Babylon is the will of YHWH. The message is identical for every nation in the region. The theological nerve of the chapter is the claim that even Babylon's empire is on divine loan — given for a season, to be called in at the appointed time.

notes.original: moserot u'moto — straps and yoke-bars
notes.rendering: Make yourself straps and yoke-bars, and put them on your neck
notes.why: Moser — a strap, a bond, a restraint (from asar — to bind; the word for the restraint used on a draught animal). Mot — a yoke-bar (the crosspiece of the yoke that goes across the back of the neck of the animal pulling the load). The prophet wears the full apparatus of agricultural servitude in public. The sign is not symbolic decoration but full enacted embodiment: Jeremiah becomes the animal under Babylon's yoke, demonstrating what the nations must accept. The yoke will reappear in chapter 28 when the false prophet Hananiah breaks it off Jeremiah's neck — and Jeremiah prophesies that the wooden yoke will be replaced with one of iron.

notes.original: anochi asiti et ha'aretz b'kochi hagadol — it is I who by my great power have made the earth
notes.rendering: It is I who by my great power and my outstretched arm have made the earth, with the men and animals that are on the earth, and I give it to whoever seems right to me
notes.why: The theological ground for the political command: YHWH made the earth and therefore disposes of it as he sees fit. La'asher yashar b'einai — to whoever seems right in my eyes (the divine prerogative of disposal; yashar — straight, right, fitting; the one who made it determines who holds it and for how long). The logic is uncomfortable but coherent: if YHWH is creator, then no earthly empire holds its territory by inherent right, only by divine permission. Babylon's dominion is on loan. The gift to Nebuchadnezzar has a duration (v.7 — until the time of his own land comes). All empires are temporary; the creator is not.

notes.original: yifg'u na b'YHWH tzvaot — let them intercede with YHWH of hosts
notes.rendering: If they are prophets, and if the word of YHWH is with them, then let them intercede with YHWH of hosts, that the vessels may not go to Babylon
notes.why: The challenge is devastating in its simplicity: if the prophets who promise the temple vessels will return are genuine prophets, let them prove it by interceding for the vessels still in Jerusalem to remain. This is the test of the true prophet: not eloquent proclamation but effective intercession. Paga b' — to intercede (literally to meet, to encounter; the prophet who stands in the council of YHWH and therefore has access to intercede). Jeremiah himself has been told not to intercede for the people (14:11) — the irony is that the false prophets who have no access to YHWH are the ones offering hope, while the true prophet who had access has had it withdrawn. The chapter does not resolve this.

intro: Jeremiah 28 is the book's sharpest single confrontation between true and false prophecy — not abstract but physical. Hananiah breaks the yoke off Jeremiah's neck and walks away. Jeremiah's initial response is startling: Amen. May it be so. The true prophet does not oppose the hopeful message out of perversity; he wishes it were true. The criterion he offers (v.9) is the only one available in the moment: time will tell.

notes.original: amen ken ya'aseh YHWH — amen, may YHWH do so
notes.rendering: Amen! May YHWH do so; may YHWH make the words you have prophesied come true
notes.why: The response is theologically courageous and humanly honest. Jeremiah does not immediately denounce Hananiah as a liar — he says amen. The word (amen — truly, so be it; from aman — firmness, reliability) is the language of agreement and desire. Jeremiah means it: he would rather his own message of judgment be false and Hananiah's message of restoration be true. The prophet of doom does not enjoy doom. What follows — the criterion of verification (v.9) — is not a denunciation but a challenge: let us wait and see whose word holds. The death of Hananiah two months later (v.17) is the verification.

notes.original: navi asher yinnave l'shalom — the prophet who prophesies peace
notes.rendering: As for the prophet who prophesies peace, when the word of that prophet comes to pass, then it will be known that YHWH has truly sent the prophet
notes.why: The criterion of true prophecy in Deuteronomy 18:22 (if the thing does not come to pass, YHWH has not spoken) is here applied specifically to prophets of shalom. The implication is that the default prophetic tradition ran toward judgment rather than peace: the accumulated witness of the earlier prophets (v.8) is war, famine, and pestilence. A prophet of shalom bears the heavier burden of proof precisely because his message is so desirable. The test is chronological — time is the judge. In the meantime, Jeremiah cannot prove Hananiah is lying; he can only state the criterion. The two months between the confrontation and Hananiah's death are the most theologically tense interval in the book.

notes.original: motot etz shavarta va'asita tachat'ehem motot barzel — you have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron
notes.rendering: You have broken wooden bars, but you have made in their place bars of iron
notes.why: The reversal is exact. The wooden yoke of chapter 27 was the symbol of Babylon's dominion — submit to it and live. Hananiah broke the wood, announcing freedom. YHWH's response: the wood you broke is replaced with iron. The escalation from wood to iron is not merely material — it is the intensification of the judgment that premature hope prevented. False prophecy does not liberate; it hardens the situation it tries to dissolve. The people who were offered a wooden yoke but encouraged to refuse it now face iron. Every act of false comfort that prevents repentance makes the eventual reckoning worse.

intro: Jeremiah 29 contains the most pastorally radical command in the book: build houses, plant gardens, seek the welfare of Babylon, pray for it. The exiles are told not to wait in spiritual suspension for rescue but to live fully in the place of their captivity. The plans for welfare (v.11) — perhaps the most-quoted verse in all of Jeremiah — must be read in this context: the future is real, but it runs through the present.

notes.original: dirshu et shalom ha'ir asher higlaiti etchem shamah — seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile
notes.rendering: Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to YHWH on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare
notes.why: Dirshu et shalom — seek the shalom (shalom — welfare, completeness, flourishing; the comprehensive wellbeing of the whole community). The command to pray for Babylon is without precedent: Israel is told to intercede for the empire that destroyed Jerusalem. V'hitpalelu ba'avdah — and pray on its behalf (ba'avdah — for it, on its behalf; the preposition of intercession). Ki bishlamah yih'yeh lachem shalom — for in its shalom you will have shalom. The exiles' wellbeing is bound up with the city's wellbeing. This is not collaboration with evil but the recognition that genuine community flourishing is indivisible. Paul echoes it: pray for kings and all who are in authority (1 Timothy 2:2).

notes.original: ki anochi yodea et hamachshavot — for I know the plans I have for you
notes.rendering: For I know the plans I have for you — declares YHWH — plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope
notes.why: Machshavot — plans, thoughts, designs (from chashav — to think, to reckon, to devise; the same root as the craftsman's skilled designing in Exodus 31:4). The plans are already complete in YHWH's mind; the exile does not catch him by surprise. L'shalom v'lo l'ra'ah — for welfare and not for evil (shalom — flourishing; ra'ah — disaster, evil, harm; the two poles of the covenant choice). Tiqvah — hope (from qavah — to wait, to expect; tiqvah is the thing waited for, the cord of expectation, literally a thread or cord — the same word as Rahab's scarlet cord in Joshua 2:18). The hope is not wishful thinking but a future with substantive content, already held in YHWH's intention.

notes.original: bnu batim v'shevu... qechu nashim — build houses and live in them; take wives
notes.rendering: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters
notes.why: The commands are the full vocabulary of permanence and investment: building, planting, marrying, having children. Everything the exiles might withhold — waiting for the return that any day now might come — YHWH commands them to give. The pastoral insight is precise: a community that lives in suspension, refusing to invest in the present because it is only temporary, will be spiritually and practically hollowed out. Seventy years is not temporary in human terms — it is three generations. Three generations of children who do not know the land, the language, the skills of ordinary life. YHWH tells them: live. The future will come; in the meantime, live.

intro: Jeremiah 30 opens the Book of Consolation (chapters 30–33) — the luminous centre of the book, a collection of restoration promises embedded in the darkest period of Jeremiah's ministry. The structural move is extraordinary: at the lowest point of the nation's history, the prophet is commanded to write a book of hope. Chapter 30 moves from the anguish of Jacob's trouble to the astonishing reversal: the wound that was incurable, YHWH will heal.

notes.original: et tzarah hi l'Yaakov umimmenah yivashea — it is a time of distress for Jacob, yet he shall be saved out of it
notes.rendering: Alas! That day is so great there is none like it; it is a time of distress for Jacob. Yet he shall be saved out of it
notes.why: Et tzarah — a time of distress, a time of anguish (tzarah — narrowness, constriction, the tight place; the word for distress throughout the psalms of lament). The phrase et tzarah l'Yaakov — the time of Jacob's trouble — became a significant eschatological term in later Jewish and Christian interpretation, applied to the final tribulation before redemption. Umimmenah yivashea — yet out of it he shall be saved (yasha — to deliver, to create space; the Hebrew root of Yeshua). The grammar is important: not from it, as if the trouble could be bypassed, but out of it — through the distress, not around it. Salvation comes through the narrow place.

notes.original: ki arucah a'aleh lach umimakotayich erphaech — for I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal
notes.rendering: For I will restore health to you, and your wounds I will heal — declares YHWH
notes.why: Arucah — healing, restoration of health (the word for the new flesh that grows over a wound, the restored tissue; from arac — to be long, to extend; arucah is the lengthening of life, the growing over of the wound). The theological reversal from v.12 is complete: your hurt is incurable (v.12) becomes I will heal your wounds (v.17). What human medicine cannot do, YHWH will do. The reason given is almost defiant: because they called you an outcast, for whom no one cares. YHWH heals precisely because the world has written Zion off. The abandoned is the one YHWH comes for.

notes.original: v'hiqravtihu v'nigash elai — I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me
notes.rendering: Their prince shall be one of themselves; their ruler shall come out from their midst; I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me
notes.why: The coming ruler is described by intimacy of access. Nigash — he shall approach (nagash — to draw near, to come close; used of the priest approaching the altar, of the prophet approaching YHWH). Mi hu zeh arav et libbo lagshet elai — who would dare of himself to approach me? The question implies the extraordinary nature of the access: normally, no one dares draw near to YHWH uninvited. The coming prince draws near because YHWH himself draws him. The image is of a ruler whose authority is grounded not in human appointment but in direct divine intimacy — the priestly and royal functions merged in one figure who has unrestricted access to the divine presence.

intro: Jeremiah 31 is the theological summit of the book and one of the most important chapters in the entire Hebrew Bible. It contains the promise of the new covenant (vv.31-34), the weeping Rachel whose children will return (v.15), and the declaration of everlasting love (v.3). The new covenant passage is the most extensively quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament letter to the Hebrews. It is the horizon toward which the whole book has been pointing.

notes.original: ahavat olam ahavtich — I have loved you with an everlasting love
notes.rendering: I have loved you with an everlasting love; therefore I have continued my faithfulness to you
notes.why: Ahavat olam — love of eternity, everlasting love (olam — eternity, the vast stretch of time in both directions; the love that has no beginning or end). Al ken m'shachtich chesed — therefore I have drawn you with faithfulness (mashach — to draw, to pull, to extend; the image of drawing water from a well, or drawing someone toward oneself with a cord). The love is the ground; the drawing is the action. YHWH's love for Israel is not responsive to Israel's faithfulness — it precedes it and persists through its absence. The declaration comes after all the adultery charges of the earlier chapters: through all of that, the love was everlasting. It was never not there.

notes.original: qol b'Ramah nishma Rachel m'vaka — a voice is heard in Ramah, Rachel weeping
notes.rendering: A voice is heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping. Rachel is weeping for her children; she refuses to be comforted, because they are no more
notes.why: Rachel — the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, the ancestral mother of the northern tribes. Ramah was on the road north, the staging point where exiles gathered before deportation. Rachel's tomb was near Bethlehem. The image: the mother of the nation weeping at the roadside as her children are marched past into exile. Me'anah l'hinachem — she refuses to be comforted (nacham — to be comforted, to relent; the same word used when YHWH relents and when the prophet is consoled; she will accept none of it). The promise that answers her refusal (v.16 — there is hope for your future) comes not as an argument but as a divine declaration. Matthew quotes this verse for the slaughter of the children in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18), hearing in it the same voice of maternal grief.

notes.original: brit chadashah... v'natati et torati b'qirbam — a new covenant... I will put my law within them
notes.rendering: Behold, the days are coming when I will make a new covenant... I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts... For I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more
notes.why: Brit chadashah — new covenant (brit — covenant, the binding agreement between YHWH and Israel; chadashah — new, fresh, not previously existing). The newness is not the replacement of Torah but its relocation: from stone tablets to the human heart (lev — heart, the seat of will and understanding). The three great promises: (1) interior law — not external command but inscribed desire; (2) universal knowledge — all shall know me, from least to greatest, without instruction; (3) complete forgiveness — I will remember their sin no more (lo ezkur od — I will not remember any more; the divine forgetting that is the condition of the relationship's renewal). The letter to the Hebrews quotes this passage twice (Hebrews 8:8–12; 10:16–17), treating it as the scriptural basis for the entire new covenant inaugurated by Jesus.

intro: Jeremiah 32 is the most audacious act in the book: a man in prison, in a city under siege, whose own prophecy is that the city will fall — buys a field. The deed is signed, witnessed, sealed, and stored in a clay jar for the long term. It is an enacted prophecy of return: the most concrete possible statement that the future is real and will be inhabited.

notes.original: va'eshqol et hakeseph shiva asar sheqel kesef — I weighed out seventeen shekels of silver
notes.rendering: I weigh out the money to him — seventeen shekels of silver
notes.why: The specificity is the point. Not a vision, not a parable — seventeen shekels, weighed on scales, witnessed, documented. The transaction is recorded with the legal precision of a conveyancer's notebook. In the middle of a siege, when property values are functionally zero, Jeremiah pays market price and follows every step of the legal process: signing, sealing, witnessing, storing in a sealed vessel. The absurdity of the purchase is the theology of the purchase. To buy land you cannot use, in a city about to fall, following all the normal legal forms, is to act as though the future is as real as the present.

notes.original: lo yipaleh mimcha kol davar — nothing is too hard for you
notes.rendering: Ah, Lord YHWH! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power. Nothing is too hard for you
notes.why: Lo yipaleh — nothing is too wonderful, too difficult, too extraordinary (pala — to be wonderful, to be beyond ordinary capacity; used of miraculous acts throughout the exodus narrative). The prayer begins by grounding the absurd purchase in YHWH's character as creator: the one who made heaven and earth by outstretched arm can certainly restore a land to its exiled people. The question YHWH echoes back in v.27 — is anything too hard for me? — is not rhetorical doubt but rhetorical confirmation. The prophet's prayer and YHWH's response share the same word, forming a liturgical loop: Jeremiah asserts it, YHWH returns it as a question whose answer is already known.

notes.original: v'samti yiratiy b'libam — I will put the fear of me in their hearts
notes.rendering: I will rejoice in doing them good, and I will plant them in this land in faithfulness, with all my heart and all my soul
notes.why: B'chol libbi uv'chol nafshi — with all my heart and all my soul (the full Shema language of Deuteronomy 6:5 — you shall love YHWH your God with all your heart and all your soul and all your strength). The command given to Israel is here claimed by YHWH himself: the wholehearted devotion the covenant demands of the people is matched by YHWH's own wholehearted commitment to their good. YHWH will plant them v'emet — in faithfulness (the root emet — truth, reliability, the solid thing). The God who demands whole-hearted love gives it.

intro: Jeremiah 33 is the companion chapter to 31, completing the Book of Consolation with three great promises: the voice of the bridegroom restored (v.11), the Righteous Branch enthroned (v.15–16), and the covenant as permanent as the day-night cycle (vv.20–26). The prisoner in the court of the guard hears YHWH promise that the silence of desolation will give way to the voices of a wedding feast.

notes.original: qr'a elai v'e'eneh lach — call to me and I will answer you
notes.rendering: Call to me and I will answer you, and will tell you great and hidden things that you have not known
notes.why: B'tzurot — hidden things, inaccessible things (batsar — to cut off, to make inaccessible; a fortified city is mivtzar — a place cut off and defended; b'tzurot are things similarly enclosed, beyond reach). The promise: not merely that YHWH will answer but that the answer will include things beyond the prophet's horizon — things not accessible by observation or deduction. The verse comes in the darkest biographical moment: Jeremiah is imprisoned, the city is besieged, the worst has almost arrived. And yet the promise is of enlarged knowledge, widened revelation. The cell is the place where the hidden things are disclosed.

notes.original: qol sason v'qol simcha qol chatan v'qol kallah — the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride
notes.rendering: There shall be heard again the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride
notes.why: The exact formula used three times in judgment passages (7:34; 16:9; 25:10) to describe what YHWH will silence when desolation comes — the sounds of wedding and celebration. Here the same formula appears with the word od — again, once more. What was silenced will be un-silenced. The wedding voices that were the signal of normal human life, of the future being born, of generations continuing — these are the specific sounds that mark restoration. Revelation 19:7 uses wedding imagery for the eschatological restoration; John heard Jeremiah's silence and its reversal.

notes.original: im tapheru et briti hayom — if you can break my covenant with the day
notes.rendering: If you can break my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night, so that day and night will not come at their appointed time, then also my covenant with David my servant may be broken
notes.why: The argument is from natural regularity to covenant reliability. The day-night cycle is YHWH's covenant with creation (b'riti — my covenant, the same word as the Sinai covenant and the new covenant). Its unbroken regularity is the pledge of covenant faithfulness. The Davidic and Levitical covenants are as reliable as the sun. This is a remarkable theological move: the constancy of the natural order is not merely background — it is itself a covenant sign, a standing reminder of divine faithfulness. Every sunrise is a covenant renewal.

intro: Jeremiah 34 narrates one of the most theologically precise episodes in the book: a covenant of slave-release, made in good faith during the siege, broken the moment the Babylonian army temporarily withdrew. The breach is not just a social failure but a covenant violation that triggers YHWH's most bitter irony — proclaiming liberty to the sword, famine, and pestilence.

notes.original: hin'ni qore lachem deror — behold, I proclaim to you liberty
notes.rendering: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty, every one to his brother. Behold, I proclaim to you liberty — to the sword, to pestilence, and to famine
notes.why: Deror — liberty, release (the Jubilee word from Leviticus 25:10 — proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants; the inscription on the Liberty Bell). The people proclaimed deror to their slaves and then revoked it. YHWH's response is a savage irony: I now proclaim deror to you — the liberty of being released to destruction. The rhetorical reversal is complete: the same legal formula used for the slave-release becomes the instrument of judgment. You freed your slaves and took them back; I will free you into the hands of your enemies. The word for liberation becomes the vocabulary of catastrophe.

notes.original: ha'egel asher karat u'vayit'halchu bein b'tarav — the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts
notes.rendering: I will make them like the calf that they cut in two and passed between its parts
notes.why: The covenant-cutting ceremony: an animal was bisected and the parties to the covenant walked between the halves, enacting the self-curse — may what happened to this animal happen to me if I break this covenant (see Genesis 15:17, where only YHWH passes between the pieces, taking the oath upon himself). Those who made the covenant of slave-release and broke it have now incurred the self-curse they enacted. The bodies of the transgressing officials shall be like the covenant-calf: split, left for birds and beasts. The covenant's own ritual becomes the grammar of their punishment.

notes.original: vatashavu va'ta'asu et hayashar b'einai — you recently repented and did what was right in my eyes
notes.rendering: You recently repented and did what was right in my eyes by proclaiming liberty, each to his neighbour
notes.why: The most painful element of the chapter: the people actually did the right thing. They repented, made a genuine covenant, freed their slaves. The brief moment of faithfulness is acknowledged by YHWH before the apostasy is condemned. This makes the reversal worse than if they had never obeyed at all. The sin is not ignorance but knowing repentance followed by calculated revocation — freeing the slaves when Babylon's army was at the gates, reclaiming them when the army withdrew. The text implies the slave-release was tactical rather than genuine, a bargaining chip with YHWH. YHWH does not accept it as such.

intro: Jeremiah 35 uses the Rechabites as a living parable: a clan that has kept its founder's commands for generations without fail — while Israel has ignored YHWH's commands for the same period. The comparison is lethal. The Rechabites obey a human patriarch; Israel cannot obey the living God. The chapter closes with the only unconditional blessing in the whole book: the Rechabites will never lack a man to stand before YHWH.

notes.original: ki tzivanu Yonadav ben Rechav avinu — for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us
notes.rendering: We will drink no wine, for Jonadab the son of Rechab, our father, commanded us: you shall not drink wine... you shall live in tents all your days
notes.why: The Rechabites were a clan associated with the Kenites, desert-dwellers who had attached themselves to Israel (1 Chronicles 2:55). Jonadab their ancestor had commanded a counter-cultural discipline: no wine, no agriculture, no permanent structures — the nomadic life as covenant faithfulness. The commands are not Torah but family tradition, maintained for over two centuries. The point is not that their specific practices are normative but that their fidelity is exemplary. They kept what a human founder said. Israel cannot keep what YHWH himself commanded.

notes.original: diber aleihem hashkem v'daber v'lo sh'matem elai — I have spoken to you persistently and you have not listened
notes.rendering: I have spoken to you persistently, and you have not listened to me
notes.why: Hashkem v'daber — rising early and speaking (the idiom for persistent, urgent communication; literally to rise at dawn and go to work at it; see 7:13; 11:7; 25:3 — the same phrase repeated throughout the book). YHWH has been sending prophets urgently, from early morning, day after day. The Rechabites heard their father once and obeyed for two centuries. Israel has been hearing YHWH's servants for generations and has not listened once. The asymmetry is the indictment. The contrast is not between law and grace but between obedience and deafness — and the deaf party is the covenant people.

notes.original: lo yikaret l'Yonadav ben Rechav ish omeid l'fanai — Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me
notes.rendering: Jonadab the son of Rechab shall never lack a man to stand before me
notes.why: Lo yikaret — shall not be cut off (karat — to cut off, to eliminate; the word used for the covenant-cutting ceremony and for the ultimate covenantal punishment of being cut off from the people). The Rechabites will never be cut off; they will always have a representative before YHWH. Omeid l'fanai — standing before me (the posture of the servant, the courtier, the priest who has access to the divine presence). The blessing mirrors what was promised to the Davidic line (33:17) and the Levitical priests (33:18). Faithfulness to a human father earns the same promise as the royal and priestly covenants. The chapter is a theology of obedience in miniature.

intro: Jeremiah 36 is the book's most dramatic single chapter: the scroll dictated, read publicly, reported to officials, read again to the king — who cuts it column by column into the fire. The response of Jehoiakim is the definitive portrait of the hardened heart. He is not troubled, does not tear his garments, and reaches for a knife. YHWH's response: dictate it again, with additions.

notes.original: yiqra'enah b'ta'ar hasopher v'yashlich el ha'esh — he cuts them off with a knife and throws them into the fire
notes.rendering: As Jehudi reads three or four columns, the king cuts them off with a knife and throws them into the fire, until the entire scroll is consumed
notes.why: The scene is a precise inversion of Josiah's response to the discovered scroll in 2 Kings 22: Josiah heard the words and tore his garments (qara et b'gadav — he tore his clothes, the gesture of mourning and repentance). Jehoiakim hears the same kind of words and tears the scroll (qara — the same root). One king tears his clothes; the other tears the text. The contrast is the theology of chapter 36. Josiah's tearing produced a national reformation. Jehoiakim's tearing produces only a fire pot and a second scroll. The word cannot be burned.

notes.original: vayosef aleihem od d'varim rabim kahemah — and many similar words are added to them
notes.rendering: Jeremiah takes another scroll and gives it to Baruch, who writes on it all the words of the scroll that Jehoiakim had burned. And many similar words are added to them
notes.why: The final verse is the book's most quietly triumphant moment. The king burned the scroll. YHWH's response: write it again, longer. The attempt to silence the word by destroying its physical form produces a fuller word. This is the theology of prophetic literature as a whole: the word that is opposed, suppressed, and burned does not diminish. It grows. Many similar words are added — the Hebrew suggests expansion, amplification, the word producing more of itself under pressure. Chapter 36 is possibly the closest thing in scripture to a theology of the written word itself.

notes.original: ulai yishm'u beit Yehudah — it may be the house of Judah will hear
notes.rendering: It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the disaster that I intend to do to them, so that every one may turn from his evil way
notes.why: Ulai — perhaps (the word of uncertain hope; see 26:3). YHWH sends the scroll with an ulai — a possibility, not a certainty. Even at this late stage, in the reign of the penultimate king before the fall, the word goes out with genuine hope attached. The scroll is not a death certificate but an eleventh-hour summons. The conditional is real: if they hear and turn, I will forgive. Jehoiakim's response — the knife, the fire, the silence — closes that window. But the ulai was genuine when it opened. YHWH has not given up before the king does.

intro: Jeremiah 37 brings the biographical narrative to the siege of Jerusalem. The irony is layered: the king who refuses to heed the prophet privately summons him for secret counsel. Zedekiah knows Jeremiah has the word of YHWH — he just cannot bring himself to act on it. The private question (is there any word from YHWH?) and the unvarnished answer (you shall be delivered into the hand of Babylon) captures the whole tragic relationship between the two men.

notes.original: ha'yesh davar me'et YHWH — is there any word from YHWH?
notes.rendering: The king questions him secretly in his house and says: Is there any word from YHWH? Jeremiah says: There is. Then he says: You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon
notes.why: The secret consultation is one of the book's most human moments. Zedekiah cannot ask publicly — the political cost would be too high. He cannot not ask — the existential need is too great. So he summons the prophet in the middle of the night and asks the only question that matters: is there a word? And Jeremiah tells the truth: yes. And the word is what it has always been. The king who hoped for a different answer receives the same one. The prophet who could have softened it for self-preservation gives it straight. The courage of Jeremiah's answer — given to a king who has the power to kill him — is as remarkable as anything in the confessions.

notes.original: meh chataiti lach — what wrong have I done to you?
notes.rendering: What wrong have I done to you or your servants or this people, that you have put me in prison? Where are your prophets who prophesied: the king of Babylon will not come against you?
notes.why: The plea is also an indictment. Jeremiah has been imprisoned for prophesying what came true. The prophets who said the opposite — the comfortable ones, the ones who said Babylon would not come — where are they now? The argument is practical as much as theological: I told the truth and you imprisoned me; they told lies and you rewarded them. Now the truth has arrived. The question hangs in the air of Zedekiah's private chamber, unanswered. Zedekiah cannot defend the injustice and cannot correct it. He compromises: moving Jeremiah from the dungeon to the court of the guard, where at least there is bread.

notes.original: v'lo shama hu v'avadav v'am ha'aretz el divrei YHWH — neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listen to the words of YHWH
notes.rendering: Neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listen to the words of YHWH that he speaks through Jeremiah the prophet
notes.why: The summary indictment of Zedekiah's reign in the opening verse establishes the chapter's tragic register. Three concentric circles of non-listening: the king, his servants, and the people of the land. The failure is total and structural — not one resistant individual but the entire social hierarchy. Yet within this total deafness, Zedekiah secretly wants to hear (v.17). The contradiction is the man: he cannot obey what he cannot help wanting to know. The chapter is the portrait of a man destroyed by the gap between what he knows and what he is willing to do.

intro: Jeremiah 38 completes the portrait of Zedekiah: a man who is afraid of his officials (v.5 — the king can do nothing against you), afraid of the deserters (v.19), and ultimately unable to obey even when the cost of obedience is clear and the cost of disobedience is explicitly laid out. Ebed-melech the Ethiopian — a foreigner, a eunuch, a man of no political standing — is the one person in Jerusalem who acts with courage. His rescue of Jeremiah from the mud is one of the book's most vivid scenes.

notes.original: v'ein mayim b'bor ki im tit — there is no water in the cistern, but only mud
notes.rendering: There is no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sinks in the mud
notes.why: The cistern (bor — a pit, a hole cut in bedrock for storing water; the same word used for the pit Joseph is thrown into in Genesis 37:24) is dry — it is the end of the siege season, the water reserves depleted. What remains is tit — mud, mire (the word used in Psalm 69:2 — I sink in deep mire, there is no foothold; the lament that anticipates precisely this situation). Jeremiah is slowly sinking in a dry pit. The image is as close to burial alive as possible without death. The rescue through old rags and worn clothes — the padding Ebed-melech thinks to provide so the ropes do not cut into Jeremiah's armpits — is a masterpiece of practical compassion recorded with the precision of an eyewitness.

notes.original: ki ha'melech lo yukal davar etchem — the king can do nothing against you
notes.rendering: Behold, he is in your hands, for the king can do nothing against you
notes.why: The most pathetic sentence in the entire royal history of Judah. The king who should be the protector of the prophet, the administrator of justice, the man who sits on David's throne executing righteousness in the morning (21:12) confesses total impotence before his own officials. Zedekiah cannot save Jeremiah because he is afraid of the men who want to kill him. The structural collapse of royal authority is complete. What 22:16 said about Josiah (he judged the cause of the poor and needy — is not this knowing me?) finds its tragic negative in Zedekiah: a king who cannot do justice for one man in his own court.

notes.original: Eved-Melech ha-Kushi — Ebed-melech the Ethiopian
notes.rendering: When Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a eunuch who was in the king's house, hears that they had put Jeremiah into the cistern... he goes from the king's house and says to the king: these men have done evil
notes.why: The rescue comes from the most unlikely source: an African eunuch, a foreigner, someone with no tribal allegiance to Judah, no political stake in the outcome, no prophetic training. He hears what has happened and goes immediately to the king — not to protect himself but to report an injustice. He calls it by its name: these men have done evil. His courage is the more remarkable for its ordinariness. He does not make a speech; he simply reports a fact and requests a remedy. The contrast with the officials who threw Jeremiah in and the king who let them is total. Ebed-melech's faithfulness will be remembered and rewarded (39:15–18).

intro: Jeremiah 39 delivers what the whole book has been building toward: the breach in the wall, the Babylonian officials sitting in the middle gate, Zedekiah's flight and capture, the blinding. What Jeremiah said would happen has happened, word for word. The chapter closes with the promise to Ebed-melech — the Ethiopian who pulled the prophet from the mud will himself be pulled from the catastrophe.

notes.original: va'y'aver et einei Tzidqiyahu — he puts out the eyes of Zedekiah
notes.rendering: He puts out the eyes of Zedekiah and binds him in chains to take him to Babylon
notes.why: The fulfilment of two apparently contradictory prophecies. Jeremiah had said Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon eye to eye (32:4; 34:3) — and he does, at Riblah. Ezekiel had said he would be taken to Babylon but not see it (Ezekiel 12:13). Both are true: he sees Nebuchadnezzar face to face, then his eyes are put out, and he is taken blind to Babylon. The final image of Zedekiah — the man who could have saved himself and his city by a single act of obedience — is of a man led in chains, sightless, to a land he will never see. The last thing his eyes ever looked on was the execution of his sons.

notes.original: u'midallat ha'am asher ein lahem m'umah — some of the poor people who owned nothing
notes.rendering: Nebuzaradan leaves in the land of Judah some of the poor people who owned nothing, and gave them vineyards and fields
notes.why: The people who are left in the land are the dalat — the poorest, the propertyless (dal — thin, weak, reduced to nothing; the word for the lowest economic stratum). The Babylonians give them what they had never had: vineyards and fields. The reversal is political and economic: the prosperous elite are taken into exile; the destitute are given their land. Amos's vision of justice (let justice roll down like waters) is enacted by pagan conquerors without any of them knowing it. The land returns to those who work it.

notes.original: ki vatach bi — because you have put your trust in me
notes.rendering: For I will surely save you, and you shall not fall by the sword, but you shall have your life as a prize of war, because you have put your trust in me
notes.why: The promise to Ebed-melech is the theological conclusion of the fall narrative. He will have his life as a prize — nafsh'cha l'shalal — the same phrase used for the people who surrendered to Babylon (21:9; 38:2). The formula given to those who chose submission is given to the man who chose courage. The ground of his salvation is not his nationality, his status, or his legal standing, but batach bi — he trusted me. The Ethiopian eunuch with no stake in the outcome, who acted anyway, is the book's model of faith at the moment of catastrophe.

intro: Jeremiah 40 opens the book's final historical section: life in the ruins. The irony is exquisite — a pagan Babylonian officer summarises the theology of Jeremiah's entire ministry (vv.2–3) more accurately than any Judean king managed. Gedaliah's brief governorship represents the last chance for the remnant in the land, and his fatal trust in good faith is about to destroy it.

notes.original: YHWH dibber et hara'ah hazot al ha'maqom hazeh — YHWH pronounced this disaster against this place
notes.rendering: YHWH your God pronounced this disaster against this place. YHWH has brought it about, and has done as he said. Because you sinned against YHWH and did not obey his voice, this thing has come upon you
notes.why: The theological summary of forty years of Jeremiah's ministry is delivered by a Babylonian military officer. Nebuzaradan has no stake in Israelite theology; he is reading the situation as a pragmatic administrator. But his analysis is exact: YHWH said it; it happened; the cause was disobedience. He arrives at the same conclusion Jeremiah spent a lifetime proclaiming. The pagan sees clearly what the covenant people refused to see. The summary is not triumphalism but tragedy: the word that was rejected has been vindicated in the worst possible way.

notes.original: kol ha'aretz l'fanecha — the whole land is before you
notes.rendering: See, the whole land is before you; go wherever you think it good and right to go
notes.why: The phrase echoes YHWH's words to Abram in Genesis 13:9 (the whole land is before you). What was once a promise of inheritance is now a grant of freedom amid ruins. The land that was given is now offered to a freed prisoner by his conqueror. Jeremiah, who has been imprisoned for most of the siege, is given the land back as a gift from Babylon. He chooses to stay — with Gedaliah, among the poorest remnant, in the land. It is the choice of the field-buyer from chapter 32: to be present in the ruins, to inhabit the promise before it is visible.

notes.original: ki shaqer atah dover el Yishmael — for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael
notes.rendering: You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking falsely of Ishmael
notes.why: Gedaliah's refusal to believe the warning about Ishmael is one of scripture's great tragic misjudgments. The Hebrew makes his error explicit: he does not merely disbelieve Johanan — he accuses him of lying. The word shaqer — falsehood, the lie — has been used throughout the book for false prophecy, false comfort, false worship. Here it appears as Gedaliah's diagnosis of genuine warning. His commitment to good faith, which makes him an excellent governor, becomes his destruction. He cannot believe that someone would lie to him about assassination. The chapter ends on the knife-edge of the coming catastrophe.

intro: Jeremiah 41 is the fall of the last hope. Gedaliah's assassination at the dinner table he shared with his killer is one of the most brutal scenes in the book. The eighty mourners from the north, still bringing offerings to the ruined temple, massacred and thrown into a cistern — the cistern that King Asa had built for defence against a previous enemy now filled with bodies. Every structure of hope is being systematically destroyed.

notes.original: vayochlu lechem yachdav b'Mitzpah — as they eat bread together at Mizpah
notes.rendering: As they eat bread together there at Mizpah, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah and the ten men with him rise up and strike down Gedaliah
notes.why: The shared meal is the most sacred bond of hospitality in the ancient Near East: to eat bread together is to enter a covenant of mutual protection. Ishmael violates it completely. The betrayal at the table is the specific nature of the sin: not merely murder but the desecration of the covenant of bread. The same social horror appears in Psalm 41:9 (even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me) — language Jesus applies to Judas. The community of the remnant is destroyed from within, at a shared meal, by one of its own.

notes.original: zequnam m'gulachim u'v'gadeihem q'ruim — their beards shaved and their clothes torn
notes.rendering: Eighty men arrive from Shechem and Shiloh and Samaria, with their beards shaved and their clothes torn and their bodies gashed, bringing grain offerings and incense
notes.why: The mourning rites are the formal gestures of grief over the destroyed temple: shaved beard (the beard as the sign of dignity, its removal as self-humiliation), torn garments (q'ruim — torn; the gesture of grief that appears from Genesis 37 through the Passion narratives), gashed bodies (the self-wounding that Torah prohibits but that extreme grief could produce). These men are coming from the north — the former territory of the destroyed kingdom of Israel — to present offerings at a temple that no longer stands. Their pilgrimage of grief is stopped by a murderer who lures them with false comfort. The scene is almost unbearably poignant.

notes.original: et ha'bor hagadol asher asa ha'melech Asa — the large cistern that King Asa had made for defence
notes.rendering: The cistern into which Ishmael cast all the bodies... was the large cistern that King Asa had made for defence against Baasha king of Israel
notes.why: The historical note is devastating in its irony. Asa built the cistern as a defensive measure against a previous enemy king. Now it is filled with the bodies of slaughtered Israelite pilgrims, by an Israelite assassin, in the ruins of Israel's last hope. The structure built for protection becomes the mass grave. The note also serves as authentic documentary record: the author knows the cistern's history and names it. This is not legend but chronicle — the kind of specific, verifiable detail that marks genuine historical memory preserved in the tradition.

intro: Jeremiah 42 records a consultation that is not a genuine inquiry but a ratification-seeking exercise. The people ask beautifully — whether good or bad, we will obey — but the ten-day delay before the answer comes, and the answer itself, suggests YHWH already knows what they intend to do. The word is addressed to people who have already decided. The chapter is a tragedy of performed obedience.

notes.original: im lo k'chol hadavar asher yishlach'cha YHWH Elohecha elenu ken na'aseh — whatever YHWH sends you to us, so we will do
notes.rendering: Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of YHWH our God to whom we are sending you, that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of YHWH our God
notes.why: The oath is impeccably worded. Good or bad — tov o ra — covering every possible response. The witness is YHWH himself. The commitment is unconditional. And it is not kept. The word they swear by is the word they will reject. The tragedy is not that they ask falsely — they may be sincere in the moment. It is that their decision is already made and the oath they swear cannot hold against it. Egypt has already been decided. They are asking for confirmation, not for direction. The word good or bad is the tell: it sounds open-handed but reveals the fear — they are hoping YHWH will say good. When he says stay, they will go.

notes.original: nachamti el hara'ah asher asiti lachem — for I relent of the disaster that I did to you
notes.rendering: I relent of the disaster that I did to you
notes.why: Nichamti — I relent, I am moved to compassion (nacham — the great word of divine change of course; used when YHWH relents from punishment in Exodus 32:14, and when Jeremiah's intercessions succeeded in 7:2–6 before they were stopped). After the fall of Jerusalem, the destruction of the temple, the murder of Gedaliah — YHWH says nachamti. He is done with the disaster. The word that was withheld during the siege, the word the prophet was forbidden to pray for, now comes unbidden: I relent. If they stay, they will be built and planted. The door that seemed permanently closed opens again in the ruins.

notes.original: ki hit'tem b'nafshoteichem — for you have gone astray at the cost of your lives
notes.rendering: You have gone astray at the cost of your lives. For you sent me to YHWH your God... and I have this day told you, but you have not obeyed
notes.why: Hit'tem — you have made a fatal mistake, you have wandered to your own destruction (ta'ah — to wander, to err, to go astray; related to the word for error and for leading astray that runs through the false-prophecy passages). The verb b'nafshoteichem — against your own lives, at the cost of your souls (nefesh — soul, life, the animating self). The self-destruction is explicit: the people who asked for the word in order to know which way to go will destroy themselves by refusing the direction they were given. Jeremiah's conclusion is not angry but sorrowful: I told you everything and you have not obeyed. The pattern that defined the whole book repeats itself in the ruins.

intro: Jeremiah 43 records the last journey: the prophet who was told by YHWH to stay in the land is dragged to Egypt by the very people who asked him for YHWH's word and then rejected it. He performs one final enacted sign in the courtyard of Pharaoh's palace: stones buried in mortar, marking where Nebuchadnezzar's throne will stand. Babylon will come even to Egypt. There is no safe place.

notes.original: shaqer atah medaber — you are telling a lie
notes.rendering: Azariah the son of Hoshaiah and all the insolent men say to Jeremiah: You are telling a lie. YHWH our God did not send you
notes.why: The accusation is the exact reversal of everything Jeremiah has stood for: the man who spent forty years distinguishing true from false prophecy is now accused of being a false prophet. Lo sh'lacha YHWH — YHWH did not send you. This is the criterion Jeremiah himself used to expose Hananiah (28:15). Now it is used against him. The word shaqer — lie — has been Jeremiah's diagnosis of the false prophets throughout the book. It is now the false prophets' diagnosis of him. The inversion is total. The chapter records no defence from Jeremiah — only his obedience to yet another prophetic command, this time in Egypt.

notes.original: t'men otam b'malben asher b'pitach beit Par'oh b'Tachpanches — hide them in the mortar at the entrance to Pharaoh's house
notes.rendering: Take in your hands large stones and hide them in the mortar in the pavement that is at the entrance to Pharaoh's house, in the sight of the men of Judah
