The Scripture citation is unclear — no single OT text matches exactly, but Isaiah 58:11 (a spring whose waters do not fail), Zechariah 14:8 (living waters flowing from Jerusalem), and Ezekiel 47 (the river from the Temple) all contribute. Either way, the feast context is decisive: on each morning of Tabernacles, priests carried a golden pitcher from the Pool of Siloam to pour water at the altar — a ceremony re-enacting the wilderness water from the rock. Jesus stands on the great last day and declares himself the fulfilment of what the pitcher was pointing to.

notes.original: oudepote houtōs elalesen anthrōpos
notes.rendering: no one ever spoke like this man
notes.why: The officers sent to arrest Jesus return empty-handed and can only say: no one ever spoke like this. It is the most inadvertently theological line in chapter 7. They were sent to bring a man; they have encountered a voice unlike any they have heard, and they cannot override what they have heard with what they were told to do. The Pharisees' response (have you also been deceived?) confirms the irony: the authorities sent to enforce their judgment are undone by the same words the crowds have been puzzling over. And Nicodemus, who first came by night, speaks for the first time in public — tentatively, procedurally, but speaking.

intro: John 8 contains the most sustained confrontation in the Gospel — a chapter-long dispute in the Temple treasury that escalates from a debate about testimony (vv.12–20), through the question of origins (vv.21–30), to a full rupture over Abraham (vv.31–59), ending with the most absolute I AM in the Gospel and an attempt to stone Jesus. The chapter's movement is from 'many believe in him' (v.30) to 'they pick up stones' (v.59) — faith and murderous intent coexist in the same crowd.

notes.original: ego eimi to phos tou kosmou
notes.rendering: I AM the light of the world
notes.why: The second I AM with predicate — to phos tou kosmou, the light of the world. The Feast of Tabernacles context is essential: on each evening of the feast, four great golden menorahs were lit in the Court of Women, illuminating all Jerusalem (the Mishnah says there was not a courtyard in Jerusalem that did not reflect their light). Jesus stands in the treasury — the room adjacent to the Court of Women where those menorahs burned — and says I AM the light of the world. The lamps of Tabernacles were themselves remembrances of the pillar of fire that led Israel through the wilderness. Jesus claims to be what the pillar of fire was: the divine light that guides through the dark.

notes.original: ean gar me pisteusete hoti ego eimi… tote gnosesthe hoti ego eimi
notes.rendering: unless you believe that I AM… then you will know that I AM
notes.why: Two absolute I AM statements in rapid succession — the first a condition (unless you believe that I AM, you will die in your sins), the second a promise (when you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I AM). The Greek ego eimi here has no predicate — it is the bare divine name, the Septuagint's rendering of YHWH's self-identification in Exodus 3:14 (ego eimi ho on — I AM the one who is) and the repeated ego eimi of Isaiah 40–55. The lifting up of the Son of Man (hypsōthē, the cross/glorification word from 3:14 and 12:32) is the moment when I AM will become undeniable — even to those who do not believe now.

notes.original: he aletheia eleutherösei hymas
notes.rendering: the truth will set you free
notes.why: Aletheia — truth. In John's Gospel, truth is not primarily a philosophical category (accurate propositions) but a person: Jesus is the truth (14:6), the Spirit is the Spirit of truth (14:17, 15:26, 16:13). Eleutherosei — will free, will liberate. The freedom Jesus offers is freedom from slavery to sin (v.34: everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin), which in John's framework means freedom from the condition of being unable to abide in the Father's house. The Jews' immediate objection (we have never been enslaved) is historically inaccurate (Egypt, Babylon, Rome) and spiritually revealing: they cannot see the slavery because they cannot see the sin. The truth that liberates is first the truth that convicts.

notes.original: ekeinos anthropoktonos en ap' arches… hoti pseudes estin kai ho pater autou
notes.rendering: he was a murderer from the beginning… he is a liar and the father of lies
notes.why: Anthropoktonos — human-killer, murderer of people. The background is Genesis 3 (the serpent's deception) and the rabbinic tradition that the devil brought death into the world through the Fall. The description of the devil as having no truth in him (ouk estin aletheia en auto) is the negative image of Jesus who is the truth: where Jesus is characterised by aletheia (truth), the devil is characterised by pseudos (lie) and his complete inability to stand in truth. The devil and Jesus are the two ultimate origins in John — the one from above (God/truth/life/light), the one from below (lie/death/darkness). The confrontation of chapter 8 is the visible form of this invisible cosmic opposition.

notes.original: prin Abraam genesthai, ego eimi
notes.rendering: before Abraham was, I AM
notes.why: The climax of the chapter and the most theologically explosive sentence in the Gospel to this point. The grammar is deliberately asymmetric: prin Abraam genesthai (before Abraham came to be — aorist infinitive, a point in time, a beginning) and ego eimi (I AM — present tense, no beginning, no point of origin). Abraham became; Jesus simply is. The contrast between becoming and being is the contrast between creature and Creator. The response of those present is immediate and instinctive: they pick up stones, because they have understood exactly what has been claimed. In their reading of the Torah, this is blasphemy — a man claiming the divine name for himself. They are wrong about the conclusion but right about the claim.

outro: Note on the Pericope Adulterae (7:53–8:11): The story of the woman caught in adultery is one of the most beloved passages in the entire New Testament — and one of the most textually uncertain. The Fireside Gospel presents it in full, set apart visually from the surrounding text, with an explanatory note. This approach follows the same principle applied to Mark 16:9–20: the passage is part of the Christian tradition, it deserves to be read and honoured, and the reader deserves to know its textual status. The writing in the dust, the progressive departure of the accusers, and the final words — 'neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more' — are among the most perfectly constructed lines in any Gospel. Whatever their origin, they sound exactly like Jesus.

intro: John 9 is the most dramatically sustained chapter in the Gospel — a single narrative running from the miracle (vv.1–7) through three scenes of interrogation (by neighbours, by Pharisees, by authorities with parents) to Jesus' final encounter with the healed man and his devastating conclusion (vv.35–41). The chapter is structured as a trial in which the wrong people are in the dock: the authorities investigate the miracle and end up convicting themselves, while the man born blind, under pressure from every side, gradually sees more and more clearly — not just physically but theologically.

notes.original: tis hemarton, houtos e hoi goneis autou… all' hina phanerothe ta erga tou theou en auto
notes.rendering: who sinned… so that the works of God might be displayed in him
notes.why: The disciples' question assumes that suffering has a moral cause — either prenatal sin (debated in rabbinic thought) or parental sin (Exodus 20:5). Jesus refuses both options without denying the framework. The blindness is not punishment; it is an occasion — hina phanerōthē, so that the works of God might be revealed/displayed. The word phanerōō (to manifest, make visible) is one of John's key verbs: the works of God become visible through this man's life. The answer is not theodicy but vocation: this man's blindness is the place where God's work will be seen. Whether this is consolation or challenge depends entirely on whether the works are actually done.

notes.original: hypago nipsai eis ten kolymhbetran tou Silōam, ho hermeneuetai Apestalmenos
notes.rendering: go wash in the Pool of Siloam — which means Sent
notes.why: The Pool of Siloam (from shilloach, sent) is the reservoir at the southern end of Jerusalem fed by Hezekiah's tunnel from the Gihon spring — and it is from this pool that the water was drawn each morning during the Feast of Tabernacles. John notes the etymology: Sent. In John's Gospel, Jesus is the one sent by the Father (more than forty references to the one who sent me). The blind man is healed by mud, sent to the pool of the Sent One, and comes back seeing. The layers of the sign accumulate silently: the sent man goes to the pool named Sent, in the feast where water from that pool was poured at the altar, and sees.

notes.original: hen oida hoti typhlos on arti blepō
notes.rendering: one thing I know: I was blind — now I see
notes.why: The most perfectly calibrated sentence in the chapter. The authorities demand a theological verdict (give glory to God — a formula for confessing guilt — we know this man is a sinner). The man refuses to give what he does not have: a verdict on Jesus' moral status. What he has is testimony, not theology. Hen oida — one thing I know. Not 'one thing I believe' or 'one thing I feel' — oida, the perfect of seeing, means 'one thing I have seen and continue to know.' I was blind, I now see: two facts, both verifiable, neither requiring interpretation. The simplicity of the sentence has made it one of the most quoted in the entire Gospel. It is the epistemology of testimony: I speak of what I know.

notes.original: en hamartiais su egennethe holos kai su didaskeis hemas
notes.rendering: you were born in utter sin — and are you trying to teach us?
notes.why: The expulsion from the synagogue is the chapter's legal climax — and it is entirely ironic. The authorities who began by trying to determine who sinned (v.2: who sinned, this man or his parents?) end by declaring that the man was born in utter sin (en hamartiais su egennethe holos — in sins you were entirely born). They have completed the circle of their own logic and expelled the evidence that disproves their theology. The man who began as a beggar outside the gates has been brought inside to testify and thrown back outside — and it is in the outside, with Jesus, that he comes to full sight.

notes.original: hina hoi me blepontes blepōsin kai hoi blepontes typhloi genōntai
notes.rendering: those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind
notes.why: The chapter's theological conclusion, spoken to Pharisees who have just asked 'are we also blind?' The reversal is total and deliberate: the man born blind sees — spiritually as well as physically — while those who have always seen are revealed as blind. The irony of verse 41 is precise: if you were blind (if you acknowledged your inability to see), you would have no sin — because blindness is not guilt, it is need. But you say 'we see' (we have knowledge, we have the tradition, we have Moses): therefore your sin remains. The refusal to acknowledge blindness is the very thing that makes it permanent. The chapter that began with a question about whose sin caused blindness ends with a declaration about the sin that perpetuates it: the certainty of those who do not know they cannot see.

outro: Note on John 7–9 as the Tabernacles movement: These three chapters are set entirely in and around the Feast of Tabernacles — the festival of water and light, of harvest and wilderness memory, of booths and pilgrimage. The feast provides the symbolic register for two of Jesus' most charged declarations: rivers of living water (chapter 7, during the feast's water ceremony) and I AM the light of the world (chapter 8, in the treasury where the great menorahs burned during the feast's lamp-lighting ceremony). Chapter 9, the healing of the man born blind, is the enacted form of both declarations simultaneously: Jesus gives sight — literal light — to someone born in darkness, using mud and the water of the pool of the Sent One. The feast celebrates what happened in the wilderness; these chapters declare that the wilderness provision — water from the rock, fire to lead the way — has arrived in person. The pillar of fire that lit Israel's path through the dark has come to live among them, and those who manage the feast cannot see him.

intro: John 10 contains two I AM sayings — the gate (vv.7, 9) and the good shepherd (vv.11, 14) — followed by the most compact statement of divine unity in the Gospel (v.30: I and the Father are one). The chapter is set against two feast backgrounds: it opens during or immediately after Tabernacles (chapters 7–9) and pivots at verse 22 to Hanukkah, the Feast of Dedication — the winter festival commemorating the rededication of the Temple after the Maccabean revolt. In both feast contexts, Jesus is in the Temple or its colonnades, and in both the authorities move toward violence.

notes.original: ho poimen ho kalos ten psychen autou tithenai… ego titheemi ten psychen mou
notes.rendering: the good shepherd lays down his life… I lay down my life
notes.why: Tithemi ten psychen — to place, set down, lay down the soul/life. Psyche in Greek carries both meanings simultaneously: life (the biological fact of being alive) and soul (the inner self, the person). The laying down is voluntary and deliberate — tithemi is an active verb, not a passive one. Jesus is not a victim; he is an agent who chooses the moment and manner of his death. Verse 18 makes the point explicit three times: no one takes it from me (ouk airei ap' emou), I lay it down of my own accord (ego titheemi auten), I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up. The cross in John is never merely something done to Jesus; it is something Jesus does.

notes.original: alla probata echō ha ouk estin ek tes aules tautes… mia poimne, heis poimen
notes.rendering: other sheep that are not of this fold… one flock, one shepherd
notes.why: The other sheep are one of John's most quietly significant phrases — other sheep, not of this fold (aule — enclosure, court, fold), who will also hear his voice and be gathered. The result is mia poimne, heis poimen — one flock, one shepherd. Not many flocks and one shepherd, but one flock. The distinction matters: the flock is not defined by its origin (Jewish, Gentile, this fold, that fold) but by its unity under the one shepherd. The phrase anticipates the ingathering of Gentiles that will be narrated in the book of Acts and theorised in Paul's letters — here it is simply declared as the shepherd's intention.

notes.original: ego kai ho pater hen esmen
notes.rendering: I and the Father are one
notes.why: Hen esmen — we are one thing. The word hen is neuter — not heis (one person, masculine) but hen (one thing, one reality). The statement claims unity of nature and will and action, not personal identity: Jesus and the Father are not the same person (the whole discourse has been about the relation between the one sent and the one who sent, between the shepherd and the Father who owns the flock). They are one in the sense that everything Jesus does is what the Father does, that to see Jesus is to see the Father, that the Father's hand and Jesus' hand are the same protection (vv.28–29). The authorities understand the claim as blasphemy — a man making himself God — and they are right about the claim even if wrong about the conclusion.

notes.original: hina gnote kai ginoskete hoti en emoi ho pater kago en to patri
notes.rendering: so that you may know and keep knowing that the Father is in me and I am in the Father
notes.why: The double verb is precise: gnote (aorist — a moment of knowing, a breakthrough) and ginoskete (present — a continuing state of knowing). Jesus is asking not merely for a moment of intellectual recognition but for an ongoing, developing knowledge of the mutual indwelling of Father and Son. The phrase en emoi ho pater kago en to patri — the Father in me and I in the Father — is the mutual indwelling language that will reach its fullest expression in chapters 14–17. Here it is offered as the content of the knowledge the works are meant to produce.

intro: John 11 is the narrative and theological hinge of the entire Gospel. The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign — the one that directly precipitates the decision to kill Jesus (v.53). Everything in chapters 1–10 has been building toward it; everything in chapters 12–21 flows from it. The chapter contains the fifth I AM saying (the resurrection and the life), the shortest verse in the Bible (Jesus wept), and one of the most theologically ironic speeches in Scripture (Caiaphas' unconscious prophecy).

notes.original: haute he astheneia ouk estin pros thanaton
notes.rendering: this illness is not to death
notes.why: Ouk estin pros thanaton — not toward death, not aimed at death, not culminating in death. The statement appears to be immediately falsified: Lazarus dies. But Jesus' meaning is prospective, not descriptive of the immediate outcome. The illness does go through death — Lazarus does die — but death is not its destination. Its destination is the glory of God (hina doxasthe ho huios tou theou). The tension between the statement and the death is the theological argument of the chapter: what looks like death is not death's final word. Jesus will make this explicit in verse 25 before he has acted on it — the claim precedes the proof, and the claim is what Martha is being asked to believe.

notes.original: ego eimi he anastasis kai he zoe… pisteueis touto
notes.rendering: I AM the resurrection and the life… do you believe this?
notes.why: The fifth I AM with predicate — ego eimi he anastasis kai he zoe — and uniquely, the most comprehensive claim among the seven. Not 'I will bring the resurrection' or 'I will give life' but I AM the resurrection. The resurrection is not an event Jesus will perform; it is an identity Jesus possesses. Martha has just confessed her belief in a future resurrection (v.24: I know he will rise on the last day) — the standard Pharisaic hope. Jesus does not deny the future resurrection; he claims to be its source, available now. The question he asks — do you believe this? — is the question the entire chapter is posing to the reader. Lazarus' raising is the enacted answer, but the question is addressed to those who will not see a raising but will still need to answer it.

notes.original: enebrimesato to pneumati kai etaraxen heauton… palin embrimomenos en heauto
notes.rendering: he is deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled… deeply moved again
notes.why: Enebrimesato — the word is almost untranslatable. It comes from embrimaomai, which in other Greek contexts means to snort with anger, to be indignant, to groan with intensity. It is not the soft word for sorrow (lypeō); it is a visceral, physical response. Something in Jesus is stirred in a way that goes beyond sympathy — some interpreters read anger (at death itself, at the unbelief of the mourners, at the situation that has brought him here), some read anguish, some read a combination. Whatever the precise register, John is describing an embodied, turbulent interior response — not calm divine composure. And it happens twice (v.33 and v.38), bracketing the shortest verse.

notes.original: edakrysen ho Iesous
notes.rendering: Jesus wept
notes.why: Edakrysen — he shed tears, he wept. The verb is different from the one used for Mary and the Jews weeping (klaiō — sobbing, crying aloud). Jesus' weeping is quieter, different in character — not the public mourning of the crowd but something more interior. The verse is two words in Greek (edakrysen ho Iesous) and the shortest in the New Testament. Its weight comes from everything surrounding it: the claim to be the resurrection and the life just made, the raising about to happen, and yet — he weeps. The one who will call Lazarus out of the tomb in minutes stands at the tomb and sheds tears. The tears are not meaningless performance; they are the real response of the one who has taken on full humanity to the weight of human death and grief.

notes.original: sympherei hymin hina heis anthropos apothane hyper tou laou… kai ouch hyper tou ethnous monon
notes.rendering: it is better for one man to die for the people… and not for the nation only
notes.why: Caiaphas speaks better than he knows. His words are a cynical political calculation (one man's death is preferable to national destruction), but John tells us he speaks as high priest — prophesying, not merely strategising. Ho archiereus on tou eniautou ekeinou — being high priest that year: the office carries prophetic weight even when the occupant is acting in bad faith. What Caiaphas means as political pragmatism, John reads as theological precision: one man will indeed die for the people — not only for Israel but to gather into one (synagagē eis hen) the scattered children of God. The gathering of the one flock under the one shepherd (10:16) is now given its cost. Caiaphas has inadvertently described the atonement.

intro: John 12 is the last chapter of Jesus' public ministry in the Fourth Gospel. After verse 36 he hides himself, and chapters 13–21 are addressed entirely to the disciples or to those at the trial and crucifixion. The chapter moves from the intimacy of Mary's anointing to the public acclamation of the entry to the theological climax of the 'hour has come' discourse — the moment when the scope of the cross becomes explicit. It closes with the narrator's reflection on unbelief and Jesus' final public appeal.

notes.original: he de Mariam labousa litran myrou nardou pistikes polytimou eleipsen tous podas tou Iesou
notes.rendering: Mary takes a litre of expensive perfume — pure nard — and anoints Jesus' feet
notes.why: In John, Mary anoints Jesus' feet (not his head, as in Matthew and Mark). The gesture is one of radical humility: anointing the head is an act of honour (as with kings and priests), but anointing the feet and wiping them with her hair is self-abasement — the hair, a woman's glory (1 Corinthians 11:15), becomes the towel. The house is filled with the fragrance (he de oikia eplerothe ek tes osmes tou myrou): the scent of the perfume, the weight of the act, the coming burial it anticipates — everything fills the room. This is the scene immediately before Jesus begins his final journey to Jerusalem, and it is the only explicit act of worship directed at Jesus in the Fourth Gospel before the resurrection.

notes.original: ean me ho kokkos tou sitou pesōn eis ten gen apothane, autos monos menei
notes.rendering: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone
notes.why: The grain of wheat is John's only real parable — a single image compressed into two verses, doing the theological work that the Synoptics spread across many parables. Autos monos menei — it remains alone, it abides by itself. The word monos (alone) echoes throughout the Gospel: the Father does not leave Jesus alone (8:29, 16:32), the disciples will not be left orphans (14:18). The seed that refuses to die remains alone — isolated, unfruitful, hoarding its life. The seed that falls and dies — apothane, the same word for Jesus' death throughout — bears much fruit (karpon polun). The cross is not the tragedy that precedes the resurrection; it is the necessary condition of the abundance the resurrection produces.

notes.original: kago ean hypsōthō ek tes ges, pantas helkysō pros emauton
notes.rendering: when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself
notes.why: Hypsōthō — lifted up (the same cross/glorification verb as 3:14 and 8:28). The third and fullest use of the hypsoō word: here the scope is made explicit — pantas helkysō, I will draw all people, all humanity. Helkysō — to draw, to pull, to attract with force (the same word used for hauling nets in 21:11 and for the Father drawing people to Jesus in 6:44). The lifting up on the cross is the centripetal act of the Gospel: it draws everything toward itself. The Greeks who want to see Jesus (v.21) are the first representatives of the pantas — and their arrival triggers the announcement that the hour has come. The world has come to the door; the seed will now fall.

notes.original: tauta eipen Esaias hoti eiden ten doxan autou
notes.rendering: Isaiah says this because he saw his glory
notes.why: One of John's most startling theological claims, made in passing. When Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on his throne, high and exalted, in the Temple vision of Isaiah 6 — the vision where the Trisagion is sung and the prophet's lips are cleansed — John says he saw the glory of Christ (ten doxan autou — his glory, referring to Jesus). The pre-incarnate Word, the logos who was with God and was God in the beginning, is the divine glory Isaiah saw. John's high Christology reaches back before the Incarnation: the glory that the disciples see in 1:14 is the same glory Isaiah saw centuries earlier, now made flesh.

notes.original: nyn he psyche mou tetaraktai… alla dia touto elthon eis ten horan tauten
notes.rendering: now is my soul troubled… but for this purpose I have come to this hour
notes.why: John's equivalent of Gethsemane — compressed into two sentences. Tetaraktai — has been troubled, stirred, shaken (from tarassō — the same word for the troubled waters of the pool in chapter 5). Jesus does not suppress or deny the trouble; he names it. The question he raises — shall I ask the Father to save me from this hour? — is immediately answered by the purpose clause: but for this purpose I have come to this hour. In the Synoptics, Gethsemane is a sustained nocturnal agony. In John, the same interior struggle is acknowledged in two verses, in daylight, before the crowd — and the response is not resignation but consecration: Father, glorify your name. The voice from heaven is the answer John gives in place of the Synoptic angel of comfort.

outro: Note on John 10–12 as the turning-point movement: These three chapters are the hinge between the first half of John (the Book of Signs, chapters 1–12) and the second half (the Book of Glory, chapters 13–21). Chapter 10 concludes the Temple controversies with the claim that I and the Father are one. Chapter 11 performs the greatest sign and precipitates the decision to kill Jesus — the raising of Lazarus is simultaneously the proof of the resurrection and the cause of the crucifixion. Chapter 12 marks the end of public ministry: the hour has come, the grain of wheat will fall, and Jesus hides himself. What follows is addressed not to the crowds but to the Twelve — the Farewell Discourse, the prayer, the passion, the resurrection. The Book of Signs ends at 12:50 with Jesus' claim that the Father's commandment is eternal life. Everything he has said and done has been the Father's words; now the cross will be the Father's final word, and the resurrection the Father's Yes to it.

intro: John 13 opens the Book of Glory — chapters 13–21, entirely addressed to the disciples. Where the Book of Signs (chapters 1–12) was public, the Book of Glory is private: a supper, a foot washing, a long conversation at table, a garden, a trial, a cross, an empty tomb, a lakeside breakfast. The chapter's first verse is one of the most theologically loaded in the Gospel, and the foot washing that follows is its enacted commentary.

notes.original: agapesas autous eis telos
notes.rendering: having loved his own who are in the world, he loves them to the uttermost
notes.why: Eis telos — to the end, to the uttermost, to completion. The word telos will appear again at the cross: tetelestai, it is finished, it is completed (19:30). The love that begins this chapter finds its completion and expression in the death that ends the Book of Glory. Eis telos is simultaneously temporal (to the very end of his life) and intensive (to the fullest possible degree). John is saying both: Jesus loves them until his last breath, and he loves them with everything there is in love. The foot washing that follows is the enacted declaration of this love — the Lord taking the position of the lowest slave and washing feet.

notes.original: tithēsin ta himatia… elaben lention kai diezōsen heauton
notes.rendering: lays aside his outer garments… taking a towel, he ties it around himself
notes.why: Tithēsin ta himatia — he sets aside his garments. The verb tithēmi is the same one used for the Good Shepherd laying down his psyche (10:11, 17, 18): the shepherd lays down his life; the teacher lays aside his garments. The enacted parable is exact: the stripping of the outer clothing is a preview of the stripping at the cross, the towel a preview of the burial cloth. He takes the position of the lowest household slave — foot-washing was too menial for Jewish slaves and was assigned to Gentile slaves or women. The one through whom all things were made (1:3) wraps a towel around himself and washes feet.

notes.original: ean me nipsō se, ouk echeis meros met' emou
notes.rendering: if I do not wash you, you have no share with me
notes.why: Meros met' emou — a share with me, a portion in me. The word meros (share, portion, part) is a covenant term — what belongs to you in a relationship, what is yours by right of belonging. Peter's refusal to be washed is not humility but a refusal to receive: to reject the washing is to refuse the participation it enacts. The washing is not merely a lesson in servanthood (though it is that); it is a participation in what Jesus is about to do. Those who cannot receive his service cannot share in his life. Peter's over-correction (then wash my head and hands too!) is equally wrong: the point is not the quantity of washing but the willingness to be served by the one who is going to die for you.

notes.original: apo arti legō hymin pro tou genesthai, hina hotan genetai pisteusete hoti egō eimi
notes.rendering: I am telling you this now, before it happens, so that when it does happen you may believe that I AM
notes.why: Another absolute I AM — ego eimi without predicate — at the end of a sentence about foreknowledge. Jesus tells them of the betrayal in advance so that when it happens their faith in I AM is confirmed rather than destroyed. The betrayal, the denial, the scattering — none of it will be a surprise to him; all of it has been said. The I AM who knows the end from the beginning is not undone by the events of the passion; he has already incorporated them into his self-disclosure. Even Judas going out into the night is under the sovereignty of ego eimi.

notes.original: entolen kainen didomi hymin, hina agapate allelous
notes.rendering: a new commandment I give to you: love one another
notes.why: Entolen kainen — a new commandment. The word kainos means new in kind or quality, not merely in time (neos means chronologically recent; kainos means qualitatively new, of a new order). The love command is not new in the sense of unprecedented — Leviticus 19:18 commands love of neighbour. It is new in its standard: kathōs egapesa hymas, as I have loved you. The measure of the love is Jesus' own self-giving love, enacted in the foot washing and about to be enacted on the cross. The commandment to love one another is only as demanding as the love by which it is measured — which turns out to be infinitely demanding.

intro: John 14 is the heart of the Farewell Discourse — the most sustained address Jesus gives to his disciples in any Gospel. The chapter moves from consolation (let not your hearts be troubled, v.1) through the sixth I AM saying to three interlocking promises: the dwelling places, the Paraclete, and the peace. Each promise is given in response to a question: Thomas asks about the way (v.5), Philip asks to see the Father (v.8), Judas (not Iscariot) asks why the revelation is private (v.22).

notes.original: en te oikia tou patros mou monai pollai eisin
notes.rendering: in my Father's house are many dwelling places
notes.why: Monai — dwelling places, rooms, abiding-places, from the same root as menō (to abide, remain, dwell). The word monē appears only twice in the New Testament: here (many dwelling places) and in verse 23 (we will come and make our dwelling/monē with him). The Father's house has many places to abide — and the promise of chapter 14 is that the mutual indwelling Jesus has been describing throughout the Gospel (you in me, I in you) is the content of those places. The dwelling places Jesus goes to prepare are not rooms in a celestial real estate development; they are the condition of abiding in him who abides in the Father.

notes.original: ego eimi he hodos kai he aletheia kai he zoe
notes.rendering: I AM the way, the truth, and the life
notes.why: The sixth and most comprehensive I AM with predicate — three nouns joined under one ego eimi. Hodos — the way, the road, the path (the word early Christianity used for itself before it was called Christianity: Acts 9:2, 'those belonging to the Way'). Aletheia — truth (the word that runs through the Gospel like a spine: the Spirit of truth, the truth that sets free, full of grace and truth). Zoe — life (the word that has been at the centre since 1:4: in him was life). The three are not independent predicates but a single compound claim: the way to the Father is through the one who is the truth about the Father and the life of the Father. Thomas asked 'how can we know the way?' and the answer is: you know him already.

notes.original: allon parakleton… to pneuma tes aletheias
notes.rendering: another Advocate… the Spirit of truth
notes.why: Allon parakleton — another Advocate, another Helper, another Comforter. The word allon (another of the same kind, as opposed to heteron — another of a different kind) implies that Jesus himself is the first Paraclete. The Spirit is 'another' in the sense of continuing what Jesus has been for the disciples: presence, counsel, advocacy, comfort. Parakletos literally means one called alongside — a legal advocate, a counsellor, a witness for the defence. The four Paraclete sayings in the Farewell Discourse (14:16, 14:26, 15:26, 16:7–14) describe what the Spirit will do: dwell with them, teach them, remind them of Jesus' words, testify about Jesus, convict the world, guide into all truth, and glorify Jesus. The Spirit does not speak independently; he speaks what he hears, and what he hears is Jesus.

notes.original: ouk apheso hymas orphanous, erchomai pros hymas
notes.rendering: I will not leave you as orphans — I will come to you
notes.why: Orphanous — orphans: children bereft of a parent, those without a home or a protector. The word is the most tender in the Farewell Discourse — it names the disciples' vulnerability in the starkest terms. They are about to lose their teacher, their protector, the one who has called them his own. Jesus names the fear before addressing it: I will not leave you orphaned. The coming (erchomai pros hymas) is deliberately ambiguous — it refers to the resurrection appearances, to the coming of the Spirit (who is 'another' Jesus), and to the final coming in glory. All three are true and all three are consolation.

notes.original: eirenen aphiemi hymin, eirenen ten emen didomi hymin
notes.rendering: peace I leave with you — my peace I give to you
notes.why: Eirene — peace. The Greek word translates the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, completeness, the flourishing of every relationship, the absence of the things that fragment and destroy. Ou kathōs ho kosmos didōsin — not as the world gives. The world's peace is the temporary absence of conflict, the fragile arrangement of competing interests. The peace Jesus gives is his own (ten emen — my peace): the peace that characterises his relationship with the Father, the peace that exists in the mutual indwelling. It is given not as a commodity but as a participation: you share the peace that I have, because you share in me.

intro: John 15 contains the seventh and final I AM saying with predicate — the true vine — and the fullest expression of the menō (abiding) theology that has been building since chapter 1. The vine image draws on the deep roots of Israel's self-understanding as YHWH's vineyard (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80, Ezekiel 15, Jeremiah 2:21), but with a crucial difference: where the Old Testament vine is Israel as a whole, Jesus is the vine himself. The disciples are not the vine; they are the branches, and their fruitfulness depends entirely on their remaining in him.

notes.original: ego eimi he ampelos he alethine
notes.rendering: I AM the true vine
notes.why: The seventh and final I AM with predicate. Alethine — true, genuine, real (from aletheia — truth). The qualifier 'true' distinguishes Jesus from the vine that Israel has been — and found wanting. In Isaiah 5:1–7 Israel is YHWH's vineyard that produced wild grapes; in Psalm 80 the vine is brought out of Egypt but is now trampled; in Ezekiel 15 the vine wood is good for nothing but burning. Jesus is the alethine ampelos — the genuine vine, the vine that actually is what a vine is supposed to be, the vine that bears the fruit YHWH's vine was always meant to bear. The Father as vinedresser (georgos — farmer, grower) is not an absentee landlord but an active presence: he prunes, he removes, he tends.

notes.original: meinate en emoi kago en hymin… choris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden
notes.rendering: Abide in me, and I in you… apart from me you can do nothing
notes.why: Meinate en emoi — abide in me, remain in me, dwell in me. The great menō imperative — the theological summation of everything the word has been carrying since 1:38–39 (where do you stay? come and see, and they remained with him that day). The mutual abiding (I in you, you in me) is the vine-and-branch relationship made explicit: the branch does not merely stay near the vine; it is joined to it, draws its life from it, is organically continuous with it. The consequence of non-abiding is equally stark: choris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden — apart from me you are not able to do anything. Not 'you will find it difficult' or 'you will be less effective' — nothing. The branch cut from the vine does not produce smaller fruit; it produces no fruit and withers.

notes.original: meizona tauten agapen oudeis echei, hina tis ten psychen autou the hyper ton philon autou
notes.rendering: greater love than this no one has: that someone lay down his life for his friends
notes.why: The greatest love is defined not by its feeling but by its cost: ten psychen autou the (lay down his psyche/life) hyper ton philon (on behalf of the friends). The language is the Good Shepherd's language (10:11, 15, 17, 18: I lay down my psyche for the sheep). The disciples who were called servants (douloi) are now called friends (philoi) — a reclassification based not on their achievement but on what Jesus has shared with them: panta ha ekousa para tou patros mou egnorisa hymin — everything I heard from my Father I made known to you. A servant is not told the master's business; a friend is. The transition from servant to friend is the transition from duty to intimacy, from obedience without understanding to love with full knowledge.

notes.original: ouch hymeis me exelexasthe all' ego exelexamen hymas
notes.rendering: you did not choose me — I chose you
notes.why: Exelexamen — I chose, I selected, I elected (from eklegō — to pick out, to choose). The priority of divine choice over human initiative runs through John from the first call of the disciples (Jesus sees Simon and Andrew, Jesus finds Philip, Jesus sees Nathanael) through the foot washing (I know whom I have chosen, 13:18) to this declaration. You did not choose me: the disciples' following of Jesus began with Jesus' choice of them. The consequence is not passivity but fruitfulness: I appointed you (etheka hymas) so that you might go and bear fruit, and that your fruit might remain (meine — the abiding word again). The fruit of the chosen branch abides because it draws from the vine that abides.

notes.original: ho parakletos hon ego pempso hymin para tou patros, to pneuma tes aletheias ho para tou patros ekporeuetai
notes.rendering: the Advocate whom I will send from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who goes out from the Father
notes.why: The third Paraclete saying — and the most precise about the Spirit's origin. Two prepositional phrases together: hon ego pempso hymin para tou patros (whom I will send to you from the Father — Jesus as sender) and ho para tou patros ekporeuetai (who goes out from the Father — the Father as source). Both the Son and the Father are involved in the Spirit's sending — the verse that became the centre of the centuries-long Filioque controversy about whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son. John does not resolve this systematically; he simply says both. The Spirit is sent by Jesus and goes out from the Father, as Jesus was sent by the Father while being one with the Father.

outro: Note on John 13–15 as the intimacy movement: These three chapters are the most interior of the Gospel — the last supper table, the foot basin, the towel, the morsel of bread, the night Judas walks into. After twelve chapters of public controversy and signs, the Farewell Discourse narrows the frame to a single room, a single table, eleven men, and a voice they will not hear for much longer. The chapter sequence enacts what it describes: just as the disciples are to abide in Jesus as branches in a vine, so the reader abides in this discourse — surrounded by it, sustained by it, returning to its phrases again and again (peace, dwelling places, Advocate, love one another, abide in me). The Farewell Discourse is not information delivered once; it is a dwelling to inhabit. The vine image is John's final gift to us for understanding what the Gospel has been about from its first word: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. Now he says — abide in me, and I in you. The tent has become a vine, and we are the branches.

intro: John 16 completes the Farewell Discourse — the fourth and final Paraclete saying, the childbirth analogy for the passion and resurrection, and the closing declaration that carries the whole weight of what has been said: I have conquered the world. The chapter moves between Jesus speaking and the disciples' incomprehension, as throughout the discourse — but the incomprehension is gently noted rather than condemned. They will understand. The hour is coming.

notes.original: sympherei hymin hina ego apelthō
notes.rendering: it is to your advantage that I go away
notes.why: Sympherei — it profits, it benefits, it is advantageous (from sympherō — to bring together, to be useful). The word is jarring in context: the disciples are grief-stricken at the prospect of Jesus leaving (v.6: sorrow has filled your heart), and he tells them it is to their advantage. The logic is pneumatological: if he does not go, the Advocate will not come. The permanent, indwelling presence of the Spirit — in all disciples, everywhere, always — is greater than the localised, bodily presence of Jesus in first-century Palestine. The departure that feels like loss is the precondition of a more abundant presence. This is the most counter-intuitive claim in the Farewell Discourse.

notes.original: elenchei ton kosmon peri hamartias kai peri dikaiosynes kai peri kriseōs
notes.rendering: he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment
notes.why: Elenchei — convicts, exposes, brings to light, cross-examines (a legal term for the work of an advocate in the opposing direction: not defending but exposing). The Spirit acts as prosecuting counsel against the world's self-understanding. Three counts: sin — not moral failure in general but specifically the refusal to believe in Jesus (ou pisteuousin eis eme); righteousness — because Jesus goes to the Father and is vindicated by his return, proving that the world's judgment of him was wrong; judgment — because the ruler of this world has been judged, meaning the whole system of accusation and condemnation by which the world operates has been overturned at the cross. The Spirit's courtroom work is to make the world's self-justification untenable.

notes.original: he gyne hotan tiktte lypen echei, hoti ēlthen he hora autes
notes.rendering: when a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come
notes.why: He hora autes — her hour has come. The hour-language used throughout John for Jesus' death and glorification is here applied to the woman in labour. The analogy works at multiple levels: the sorrow of labour is real and the joy of birth is real, and the joy does not cancel the sorrow but completes it. The disciples' grief at the passion will be real; the resurrection joy will be real. And the joy will be of a different order from the grief — not merely relief that the sorrow is over, but the arrival of a new life that the sorrow was the cost of bringing forth. The woman no longer remembers the anguish (ou mnemoneuei tes thlipseōs) — not because it is suppressed but because the joy of what has been born fills the space.

notes.original: en emoi eirenen echete… ego nenikeka ton kosmon
notes.rendering: in me you have peace… I have conquered the world
notes.why: Nenikeka — I have conquered, I have overcome, perfect tense: a completed act with ongoing effects. The perfect tense is the theological key: Jesus speaks of a victory he has not yet visibly accomplished (he has not yet died or risen) as already complete. This is John's characteristic realised eschatology applied to the cross: the victory is settled in the purposes of God even before it is enacted in history. En emoi eirenen echete — in me you have peace: the preposition en (in) is the abiding-language again. Peace is not a feeling to be achieved; it is a condition of being in Jesus, who is the place of peace. The world gives tribulation (thlipsis — pressure, tribulation, the crushing weight of opposition); Jesus gives peace. Both are real; both are simultaneously true; one is deeper than the other.

intro: John 17 is the most sustained act of divine speech in the Gospel — Jesus praying to the Father, overheard by the disciples, recorded by the evangelist. It has been called the High Priestly Prayer since the sixteenth century (Melanchthon's term), because in it Jesus consecrates himself for the sacrifice, intercedes for those who belong to him, and prays for their sanctification and unity. It is set as verse in the Fireside Gospel because it is prayer — the one place in the narrative where we are inside the conversation of the Trinity.

notes.original: haute de estin he aionios zoe, hina ginoskōsin se ton monon alēthinon theon
notes.rendering: this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God
notes.why: The only definition of eternal life in the Gospel. Not a duration but a relationship; not immortality but knowledge. Ginōskōsin — they know, present active subjunctive: ongoing, developing, living knowledge. The word is not eidōsin (to know as a fact, to have information) but ginōskōsin (to know as a relationship, to come to know, to be in knowing). Eternal life is the kind of knowing you have of a person you love — not data about them but the living knowledge that grows through shared presence. This is why Jesus can say in v.3 that eternal life is knowing God and Jesus Christ, and in v.25–26 that he will continue to make God's name known so that the love in the Father will be in the disciples: the knowing and the loving are the same movement.

notes.original: pater hagie, tereson autous en to onomati sou hō dedokas moi, hina osin hen kathōs hemeis
notes.rendering: Holy Father, keep them in your name… that they may be one, even as we are one
notes.why: Pater hagie — Holy Father. The address is unique: Jesus has prayed 'Father' throughout the Gospel (11:41, 12:27, 12:28) and will address 'righteous Father' in v.25, but 'Holy Father' appears only here. The holiness of the Father is the ground of the prayer: what the disciples need is to be kept in the name of the Holy One, because the holy name is what distinguishes them from the world. The petition that they may be one (hina osin hen) uses the same neuter hen as 10:30 (I and the Father are one). The unity of the disciples is patterned on the unity of the Father and Son — not organisational uniformity but the organic oneness of mutual indwelling.

notes.original: hagiason autous en te aletheia; ho logos ho sos aletheia estin
notes.rendering: sanctify them in the truth — your word is truth
notes.why: Hagiason — sanctify, set apart, make holy (from hagios — holy). The disciples are to be consecrated the way the Temple and its vessels were consecrated: set apart for a holy purpose. En te aletheia — in the truth: sanctification happens through/in truth, not merely by resolution or ritual. Your word is truth: the ground of sanctification is the word God has spoken — and Jesus is that word (the logos who is truth, 14:6). The prayer for sanctification in v.17 is followed immediately by the statement that Jesus consecrates himself (v.19: hagiazō emauton) for their sake. The disciples' sanctification is grounded in Jesus' own consecration: he sets himself apart for the cross so that they may be set apart through the truth of what the cross reveals.

notes.original: hina pantes hen osin… hina osin teteleioumenoi eis hen
notes.rendering: that they may all be one… that they may become perfectly one
notes.why: The unity prayer is structured in two movements. First (v.21): that they may be one, as you Father are in me and I in you, that they also may be in us — unity as participation in the divine life. Second (v.23): that they may become perfectly one (teteleioumenoi eis hen — having been brought to completion into oneness) — unity as mission: so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them. The unity of the church is not an end in itself but the means by which the world recognises the love of the Father. Division in the church is not merely sad; it obscures the love that the church is meant to make visible. The prayer is both the most intimate in the Gospel and the most missionary.

notes.original: thelo hina hopou eimi ego kakeinoi osin met' emou, hina theōrōsin ten doxan ten emen
notes.rendering: Father, I want those you have given me to be with me where I am — to see my glory
notes.why: Thelo — I want, I will, I desire. Jesus prays not by petition alone but by declaration of desire. The desire is total inclusion: he wants the disciples where he is (hopou eimi ego — where I AM, with the characteristic I AM resonance) and he wants them to see his glory. The glory they are to see is the glory given before the foundation of the world (pro kataboles kosmou — before the world's foundation, the same phrase as in 1 John 1:1 and Ephesians 1:4). What began before creation ends in the disciples seeing the love that predates everything. The prayer closes on love: the love with which the Father has loved the Son from before the world began will be in the disciples, and Jesus in them. The Gospel's last word before the passion is love.

intro: John 18 is the chapter of reversals. Jesus goes forward to meet his arresters; they fall back. Peter, who said he would lay down his life, says three times "I am not." The authorities who maintain ritual purity to eat the Passover hand the Passover Lamb to Pilate. Pilate, who asks "what is truth?" is standing in front of the one who said "I am the truth." The chapter's irony is systemic and precise — the Gospel has been building to this moment of cosmic misrecognition.

notes.original: ego eimi… kai epeson chamai
notes.rendering: I AM… and they fall to the ground
notes.why: The arrest scene in John is unlike any in the Synoptics. When Jesus says ego eimi — I AM, identifying himself — the arresting party draws back and falls to the ground (epeson chamai — they fell to the earth). The falling is John's deliberate disclosure: the divine name has power that the armed soldiers cannot stand against. They come with lanterns and torches and weapons to arrest the Light of the World, and when he speaks his name they collapse. The arrest continues only because Jesus allows it (v.8: if you seek me, let these men go). The passion in John is not something that happens to Jesus; it is something Jesus does — moving forward to meet his arresters, giving himself over, protecting his disciples. Even in the garden, he is sovereign.

notes.original: to poterion ho dedoken moi ho pater, ou me piō auto
notes.rendering: the cup the Father has given me — shall I not drink it?
notes.why: John's Gethsemane is entirely absent as a scene — no prostration, no sweating blood, no 'if it is possible, let this cup pass.' Instead the cup appears only here, in a rebuke to Peter. John has already given us the equivalent of Gethsemane in 12:27 (now is my soul troubled — but for this purpose I have come to this hour). Here the cup is not something Jesus begs to avoid but something he moves toward: shall I not drink it? The rhetorical question expects the answer yes. The cup the Father has given is not forced on Jesus; he drinks it freely, as he has laid down his life freely (10:18).

notes.original: ouk eimi… ouk eimi
notes.rendering: I am not… I am not
notes.why: Peter's three denials in John are each framed around the words ouk eimi — I am not. The echo of ego eimi is devastating: while Jesus stands inside giving testimony to what he is (20–21: I have spoken openly to the world), Peter stands outside denying what he is. The contrast is the structural argument of the scene: two men, two responses to the same moment. Jesus speaks clearly; Peter denies. Jesus says I AM; Peter says I am not. The fire where Peter warms himself (v.18: anthrakia — a charcoal fire) will appear once more in the Gospel, at the lakeside restoration of chapter 21 (21:9: another charcoal fire, anthrakia). John has placed Peter's failure and Peter's restoration at the same kind of fire.

notes.original: hina me mianthōsin alla phagōsin to pascha
notes.rendering: so that they will not be defiled and may eat the Passover
notes.why: The Passover irony is John's most cutting. The chief priests will not enter the governor's headquarters (the residence of a Gentile) because they would be ritually defiled and unable to eat the Passover. They maintain scrupulous ritual purity while handing the Passover Lamb over to be killed by Gentiles. John has placed the crucifixion on the Day of Preparation — the afternoon when the Passover lambs are slaughtered in the Temple (19:14, 31). The authorities who will not risk defilement for a doorstep are the ones ensuring that the Lamb of God (1:29) dies at precisely the hour the Passover lambs are killed. The ritual purity they preserve is the frame around the deepest ritual impurity.

notes.original: ti estin aletheia
notes.rendering: what is truth?
notes.why: Three words in Greek — the most famous unanswered question in the Gospels. Pilate does not wait for an answer; he goes back out immediately to the crowd. The question hangs. But the Gospel has already answered it — in chapter 14, Jesus said ego eimi he hodos kai he aletheia kai he zoe. Truth is not a philosophical category to be debated; it is a person standing in front of Pilate. The tragedy of the scene is not that the question is unanswerable but that the answer is right there and Pilate turns his back on it. He asks 'what is truth?' in the presence of the one who said 'I AM the truth' — and leaves without waiting.

outro: Note on John 16–18 as the transition from discourse to passion: These three chapters mark the most dramatic tonal shift in the Gospel. Chapters 13–16 are entirely interior — a room, a table, a conversation. Chapter 17 is still interior but cosmic: the Son praying to the Father, encompassing all who will ever believe. Then, without transition, chapter 18: a garden, torches, soldiers, the sound of a sword, a cock crowing in the dark, a charcoal fire in a courtyard, a governor asking questions he does not stay to hear answered. The movement from 'that they may all be one' (17:21) to 'are you not also one of his disciples? I am not' (18:25) is one of the most abrupt and painful transitions in Scripture. The prayer of unity and the denial of belonging occupy the same night.

intro: John 19 is structured as a sustained royal enthronement scene — a grotesque coronation that is simultaneously ironic and true. Jesus is crowned (with thorns), robed (in purple), hailed (by soldiers who mock), presented as a king (by Pilate twice), and enthroned (on the cross). The title on the cross — in three languages, unretractable — is Pilate's inadvertent proclamation of the truth he refused to recognise when he asked 'what is truth?' The passion in John is not defeat; it is the moment the Word completes what the Word came to do.

notes.original: idou ho anthropos
notes.rendering: Look — the man!
notes.why: Idou ho anthropos — Behold the man! The Latin Ecce homo has echoed through Western culture for two millennia. But the Greek carries more than dramatic presentation. Ho anthropos — the man, the human being. Pilate presents Jesus as simply a man, pitiable and beaten, to defuse the crowd's demands. But John's Gospel has been making a different claim about this man since its first verse: the logos became flesh (sarx egeneto) — became a human being. When Pilate says 'behold the man,' he is, without knowing it, pointing to the one the Gospel has been revealing. The Ecce homo is John's Christological statement spoken by a pagan governor who does not believe it.

notes.original: ho gegrpha gegrpha
notes.rendering: what I have written, I have written
notes.why: Ho gegrapha, gegrapha — what I have written, I have written. The perfect tense used twice: it is written, and it stands written. Pilate's refusal to change the inscription is one of the Gospel's great ironies — the man who asked 'what is truth?' has inadvertently written the most theologically precise statement in the passion narrative and will not change it at the request of the religious authorities. The title JESUS THE NAZARENE, THE KING OF THE JEWS in three languages (Aramaic, Latin, Greek) is the Gospel's three-language proclamation of the truth Pilate declined to stay and hear: this is the King, and what has been written will not be unwritten.

notes.original: teteletai… paredōken to pneuma
notes.rendering: it is finished… he gives up his spirit
notes.why: Tetelestai — it is finished, it is completed, it has been brought to its telos. The word is the perfect of teleō, and its root telos is the same as in 13:1: agapesas autous eis telos — having loved them to the uttermost. The love that began the Book of Glory with eis telos finds its completion on the cross with tetelestai. The word is not a cry of defeat but of accomplishment: the work the Father gave him to do (17:4: I glorified you, having completed the work) is done. Paredōken to pneuma — he handed over the spirit. The verb paradidōmi is the passion verb throughout: Judas hands him over, Pilate hands him over to be crucified. Now Jesus hands over his spirit. But in John the word pneuma carries its full theological weight: he hands over the Spirit. The disciples gathered at the cross (19:25–27) may be the first recipients of what will be formally given in 20:22.

notes.original: kai euthys exelthen haima kai hydōr
notes.rendering: at once blood and water come out
notes.why: The blood and water from the pierced side have generated centuries of theological interpretation. In John's symbolic world: water has been the image of the Spirit (7:37–39: rivers of living water flowing from within), and blood has been the image of the Eucharist (6:53–56: unless you drink my blood). The two great sacramental gifts — baptism (water) and the Lord's Supper (blood) — flow from the pierced side of Jesus. The witness of verse 35 (he who saw it has borne witness) insists on the physical reality: this is not symbol alone but something that actually happened and was actually seen. The physical and the theological are one, as the flesh and the Word are one.

notes.original: en de en to topo hopou estaurōthe kēpos, kai en to kēpo mnēmeion kainon
notes.rendering: in the place where he is crucified there is a garden, and in the garden a new tomb
notes.why: Kēpos — garden. John alone specifies that the crucifixion and burial take place in a garden. The resurrection will also take place in a garden (20:15: Mary supposes him to be the gardener). The garden echoes Eden — where the first Adam's death began (Genesis 3) and where the last Adam's death ends and new life begins. John's Jesus, who is the light of the world and the life, is buried in a garden and will be mistaken for the gardener: the Creator tending his new creation, the second Adam completing what the first one broke.

intro: John 20 is the resurrection chapter — four scenes of encounter with the risen Jesus, each one revealing a different dimension of what resurrection means. Mary Magdalene in the garden (recognition through a name), the disciples in the locked room (peace, sending, breath), Thomas eight days later (seeing and believing), and the Gospel's own statement of purpose. The chapter moves from darkness (20:1: while it is still dark) to belief.

notes.original: to soudarion ho en epi tes kephales autou, ou meta ton othonier keimenon alla choris entetyligmenon eis hena topon
notes.rendering: the face cloth… rolled up in a place by itself
notes.why: The soudarion — face cloth, burial napkin — is described with precise detail: not lying with the linen wrappings but rolled up (entetyligmenon — wrapped together, folded) in a separate place. The detail has been interpreted variously. The most theologically significant reading: a body hastily stolen (Mary's first assumption, v.2) would not have left the grave clothes arranged; a resurrection of a different order from resuscitation (Lazarus came out still bound, v.44: lusen auton, loose him) left the cloths in their place while the body passed through them. The Beloved Disciple sees the face cloth and believes (v.8) — before seeing the risen Jesus, before understanding the Scripture. Something in the arrangement of cloth and space is sufficient.

notes.original: Mariam… me mou haptou, oupō gar anabebeka pros ton patera
notes.rendering: Mary… do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended
notes.why: The scene turns on a name and a touch. Jesus has asked twice 'whom are you seeking?' (the same question he asked the soldiers in the garden of arrest, 18:4, 7 — and the question the disciples asked in 1:38). Mary does not recognise him until he says her name: Mariam. The Aramaic form, not the Greek Mariam — the familiar, intimate address. She responds Rabbouni — not Rabbi (teacher) but the heightened, intimate form: my teacher, dear teacher. Jesus' response — me mou haptou — is often rendered 'do not touch me,' but haptō means to grip, to cling, to hold on. She has seized him and is holding on. He tells her not to cling because the ascension is coming and the relationship they have had is about to change: not less intimate but differently present, through the Spirit who will dwell in them.

notes.original: enephysesen kai legei autois, labete pneuma hagion
notes.rendering: he breathes on them and says: 'Receive the Holy Spirit'
notes.why: Enephysesen — he breathed into, he blew upon. The word is used only one other time in the Greek Bible: in Genesis 2:7, where YHWH breathes into the nostrils of the adam and he becomes a living being (enephysesen eis to prosopon autou pnoen zoes). The resurrection appearance in the locked room is a new creation scene: as God breathed life into the first human being, Jesus breathes the Holy Spirit into the new community. The Easter evening is John's Pentecost — the giving of the Spirit that the Farewell Discourse promised, now enacted in a single breath. John does not narrate a Pentecost fifty days later; the Spirit is given on the day of resurrection, in a breath.

notes.original: ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou
notes.rendering: my Lord and my God!
notes.why: Ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou — my Lord and my God. Thomas's confession is the theological climax of the Gospel — the highest human Christological statement in the entire New Testament, and the answer to the question the prologue raised (the Word was God, 1:1). The Gospel that opened with a declaration about the divine nature of the Word closes with a human disciple's recognition of that divinity in the risen flesh before him. The wounds are the proof: Thomas asked to see the marks of the nails and the spear; Jesus shows them; Thomas confesses God. The resurrection does not leave the cross behind — the risen body still bears the wounds, and it is the wounds that elicit the highest confession. My Lord and my God is addressed to the wounded, risen Christ.

notes.original: makarioi hoi me idontes kai pisteusantes
notes.rendering: blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed
notes.why: The beatitude is addressed not to the disciples in the room but to the reader. Every reader of the Gospel is among those who have not seen and yet are asked to believe. The purpose statement that follows (vv.30–31) confirms this: the Gospel is written for those who were not present — so that by reading they may believe, and by believing they may have life in Jesus' name. The Gospel is itself a form of the Beloved Disciple's witness: he saw and believed (v.8); the book he wrote is offered to those who must believe without seeing. Thomas's beatitude at the end of chapter 20 is the invitation the whole Gospel has been extending since its first word.

intro: John 21 is widely regarded as an epilogue — chapter 20 ends with what reads like a conclusion (vv.30–31), and chapter 21 opens a new scene. Whether it was added later or always intended, it is now canonical and inseparable from the Gospel's meaning. It gives us three things the Gospel could not end without: the restoration of Peter, the clarification of the Beloved Disciple's role, and a breakfast by a lake that undoes a denial by a fire.

notes.original: anthrakia… keimenēn kai opsarion epikeimenon kai arton
notes.rendering: a charcoal fire… with fish lying on it, and bread
notes.why: Anthrakia — charcoal fire. The word appears only twice in the New Testament: here, and in 18:18, where Peter warms himself at a charcoal fire in the high priest's courtyard and denies Jesus three times. John's choice of the same rare word is not accidental. The restoration of Peter takes place at the same kind of fire as the betrayal. The breakfast fire is the re-staging of the denial fire — the same warmth, the same intimacy, now used not for denial but for restoration. Peter's three confessions of love (vv.15–17) correspond to his three denials (18:17, 25, 27). The fire that witnessed his failure now witnesses his re-commissioning.

notes.original: agapas me… phileis me… panta sy oidas, sy ginōskeis hoti philō se
notes.rendering: do you love me (agapaō)… do you love me (phileō)… you know everything; you know that I love you (phileō)
notes.why: The question of whether the shift from agapaō (v.15–16) to phileō (v.17) is theologically significant has been debated for centuries. Both words mean love in Greek; John uses them sometimes interchangeably. But the pattern here is deliberate: Jesus asks twice with agapaō (the love-word of the commandment to love one another, 13:34, and of God's love in 3:16); Peter responds twice with phileō (the friendship-love, the word used for the Father's love for Jesus in 5:20). On the third question, Jesus shifts to Peter's own word, phileō — and Peter is grieved. The grief may be because the third question recalls the three denials, or because Jesus has come down to Peter's level. Either way, the third exchange ends with panta sy oidas — you know everything — which echoes 16:30 (now we know that you know all things). Peter offers what he has: not the agapē he cannot claim to have but the philia he knows he has, and trusts Jesus to know it.

notes.original: hotan de gērasēs… alloi se zōsousin kai oisousin hopou ou theleis
notes.rendering: when you are old, you will stretch out your hands — and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go
notes.why: The restoration of Peter ends not with comfort but with a cross. The one who refused to let Jesus wash his feet (13:8) and drew his sword in the garden (18:10) will stretch out his hands and be led where he does not want to go: the tradition identifies this as martyrdom by crucifixion (Eusebius records Peter crucified upside down). The command that follows — akolouthei moi, follow me — is the original call (1:43) repeated at the end of everything. The invitation is the same; the cost is now made explicit. Follow me means: as I laid down my life, you will too.

notes.original: ean auton thelō menein heōs erchomai, ti pros se
notes.rendering: if it is my will that he remain until I come — what is that to you?
notes.why: Menein — to remain, to abide. The Beloved Disciple's role in the Gospel is described with the great menō word: if it is my will that he remain (menein). The disciple whose identity is defined by his proximity to Jesus at the supper (reclining close to him, 13:23) and at the cross (standing near, 19:26) is the one Jesus speaks of remaining. But the saying is not a promise of immortality: Jesus says if it is my will, not that it is. The Gospel that opened with 'they remained with him that day' (1:39) and built its entire theology around the word menō closes with it: the Beloved Disciple's remaining is the sign and source of the Gospel itself.

notes.original: oude auton oimai ton kosmon chorein ta graphomena biblia
notes.rendering: I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written
notes.why: The Gospel closes with hyperbole — and with an 'I' that is the only first-person singular in the whole book (the narrator becomes visible for one sentence at the very end). The world could not contain the books: this is not merely a figure of speech but a theological statement. Jesus is the logos — the Word through whom all things were made (1:3). To write everything he said and did would require more books than the cosmos can hold, because the one who is being written about is larger than the cosmos. The Gospel that could not contain everything has contained what was necessary: that you may believe, and by believing have life in his name. The Word made flesh exceeds every word written about him.

outro: Note on John 19–21 as the completion of the Gospel's arc: The Gospel opens in the beginning — en arche — before creation, with the Word who was God. It closes at a lakeside breakfast, with bread and fish on a charcoal fire and a question asked three times. Between the beginning and the breakfast: a prologue, seven signs, seven I AM sayings, a foot washing, a prayer, a cross, and an empty tomb. The arc from cosmic declaration to intimate restoration is the Gospel's structural argument about what the Incarnation means: the Word who pitched his tent among us (1:14) cooks breakfast for fishermen (21:12) and asks a broken man if he loves him (21:17). The answer to the question 'who is this?' — the question raised in the storm in Mark, answered in heaven at the baptism, answered by the centurion at the cross — is answered in John by Thomas: my Lord and my God. And the answer is addressed to the wounded, risen body of the one who first said 'follow me' and now, at the end of everything, says it again.

intro: Jonah 1 is one of the most compressed and perfectly constructed chapters in the Hebrew Bible. The flight from YHWH is described in a cascade of downward movements — he goes down to Joppa, goes down into the ship, goes down into the ship's hold, is hurled down into the sea. The pagan sailors are more religiously responsive than the prophet: they pray, they spare Jonah as long as possible, they seek divine guidance, and at the end they fear YHWH greatly and make vows. The chapter is a gentle comedy at the prophet's expense.

notes.original: qum lech el-Nineveh ha-ir haggedolah
notes.rendering: Rise — go to Nineveh, that great city
notes.why: Qum lech — arise, go: the standard prophetic commission formula (compare YHWH to Abram in Genesis 12:1: lech-lecha — go). Nineveh is the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BCE. For a Hebrew prophet to be sent to preach repentance to Nineveh would be roughly equivalent to a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust being sent to preach to Berlin. The 'great city' (ha-ir haggedolah) designation appears four times in Jonah (1:2, 3:2, 3:3, 4:11) — it is what makes the commission so extraordinary. This is not a small provincial town; it is the greatest city in the world, the seat of Israel's oppressor.

notes.original: va-yaqom Yonah livroach Tarshishah mi-liphnei YHWH
notes.rendering: Jonah rises to flee to Tarshish — away from the presence of YHWH
notes.why: Mi-liphnei YHWH — from before the face of YHWH, from YHWH's presence. The phrase is repeated three times in verses 3 and 10 — Jonah's flight is defined entirely by what he is fleeing toward (Tarshish, the far western end of the known world) and what he is fleeing from (the face of YHWH). The theological irony is that Jonah has just identified himself as one who fears YHWH the God of heaven who made the sea and the dry land (v.9) — and he is trying to escape by sea from the God who made the sea. The comedy is built into the geography.

notes.original: et-YHWH Elohei ha-shamayim ani yare asher asah et-hayam v'et-hayabashah
notes.rendering: I fear YHWH, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land
notes.why: The most ironic verse in chapter 1. Jonah confesses to the terrified sailors that he fears (yare — the same root as the awe/reverence the sailors develop at the end of the chapter) YHWH, the God who made the sea. He is confessing his faith while being the direct cause of the storm that the God he confesses has sent. The sailors then respond with even more fear — not only is there a storm, but the one who caused it is fleeing from the God who made the sea they are sailing on. The confession that should be reassuring has the opposite effect.

notes.original: va-yiqre'u el-YHWH — the sailors pray to YHWH by name
notes.rendering: they cry out to YHWH
notes.why: The sailors' prayer is addressed to YHWH — the covenant name of Israel's God, not to their own gods (v.5: each cries to his own god). They have learned the name from Jonah, and they use it. The prayer is theologically precise: do not lay innocent blood on us, for you YHWH have done as it pleased you. They acknowledge YHWH's sovereignty and their own moral limits simultaneously. These Gentile sailors pray a more faithful prayer than the prophet who is asleep in the hold. The pattern echoes Matthew's Gospel: the centurion, the Magi, the Canaanite woman — Gentiles often see what the covenant people miss.

notes.original: va-yeman YHWH dag gadol — a great fish, not specified
notes.rendering: YHWH appoints a great fish
notes.why: Dag gadol — a great fish. Not a whale (the Hebrew word for whale is not used here; the LXX uses ketos — a sea monster or large sea creature), not a specific species, not a named creature. The Fireside Bible renders it exactly as the Hebrew: a great fish. The verb va-yeman (appoints, assigns, prepares) is the same verb used in chapter 4 for the qiqayon (4:6), the worm (4:7), and the scorching wind (4:8) — YHWH assigns creatures to serve his purposes throughout the book. The fish is not a punishment; it is a rescue. Without it, Jonah drowns. The belly of the fish is the place where the prayer of chapter 2 is prayed — it is the place of salvation, not destruction.

intro: Jonah 2 is a psalm embedded in a prose narrative — and a psalm with a peculiar temporal structure. Jonah is still inside the fish when he prays, yet the prayer is written in the past tense as if already delivered: 'you answered me,' 'you heard my voice,' 'you brought up my life from the pit.' The prayer looks back at the drowning as if from the safety of the shore. This is the characteristic Hebrew form of the thanksgiving psalm — prayed in confidence before the deliverance is physically complete. Jonah prays his rescue before he is rescued.

notes.original: mibeten sheol shivati — out of the belly of Sheol
notes.rendering: out of the belly of Sheol I cried for help
notes.why: The word beten (belly) appears three times in the chapter: the belly of Sheol (v.2), the belly of the fish (v.1), and implicitly in the deep pit of verse 6. The fish's belly is identified with Sheol — the realm of the dead, the underworld. The great fish is not an implausible miracle to argue about; it is a symbol of death and resurrection. Jonah has died — gone down to the place of no return — and will be brought back. The psalm is the literary form of that passage: the lament of the drowning man (vv.2–7) and the thanksgiving of the delivered man (vv.8–9) held in a single poem.

notes.original: garashti mi-neged einecha — I am driven from your sight
notes.rendering: I am driven away from your sight
notes.why: Garashti — I am driven, expelled, cast out. The word is used for the expulsion from the Garden (Genesis 3:24) and for the driving out of nations. Jonah, who fled from the face of YHWH (1:3, 10), now laments that he has been driven from YHWH's sight — and immediately expresses the confidence that contradicts the lament: yet I shall again look upon your holy Temple. The psalm holds the two realities simultaneously: I have been cut off, and I will see you again. The confidence that YHWH's Temple is accessible even from the belly of the fish is the theological heart of the prayer.

notes.original: meShamerim havlei-shav chasdham ya'azovu — those clinging to empty vanities forsake their mercy
notes.rendering: those who cling to empty idols forsake their source of mercy
notes.why: Havlei-shav — emptied vapours, breaths of nothing, vanities (havlei is the plural of hebel — the same word as Ecclesiastes' vapor/breath). The idol worshippers cling to what is insubstantial and in doing so abandon their chesed — their steadfast love, their mercy, their covenant loyalty. The Fireside Bible renders this as 'their source of mercy' because chesed here refers to YHWH's lovingkindness that could have been theirs. The verse is Jonah's theological reflection from inside the fish: those who look to false things lose the real thing. The irony is that Jonah himself has been running from the God of mercy — the rest of the book will make this explicit.

notes.original: yeshuatah la-YHWH — salvation belongs to YHWH
notes.rendering: salvation belongs to YHWH
notes.why: Yeshuatah la-YHWH — the salvation is YHWH's. The climactic declaration of the psalm. Yeshuah — salvation, deliverance — is the same root as the name Yeshua/Joshua/Jesus (YHWH saves). From the belly of the fish, Jonah confesses that salvation belongs entirely to YHWH — not to his own clever escape routes, not to the ship to Tarshish, not to the depth of sleep in the hold. The irony is that after this magnificent confession of trust in YHWH's sovereign mercy, Jonah will spend chapter 4 furious that YHWH exercises that same sovereign mercy toward Nineveh.

intro: Jonah 3 is the most compressed revival narrative in the Bible. Five words of Hebrew preaching produce the repentance of the greatest city in the world.
