The person is not yet declared unclean; they are in a holding state while the priest gathers more information. Rendered “isolate” throughout as the closest modern equivalent.

notes.original: The uniform of exclusion
notes.why: The person declared unclean must wear torn clothes (a sign of mourning and catastrophe), let their hair hang loose or disheveled (another mourning gesture — cf. Ezek 24:17), and cover their upper lip — also a mourning sign (cf. Ezek 24:22). They must call out: Unclean! Unclean! — a double warning to all who might approach. The full uniform is the dress of someone in mourning for themselves, living as if they have already died to the community. Tsaraʼat is a social death before it is anything else: the person is alive but excluded, present but unreachable.

notes.original: Outside the camp
notes.why: Dwelling outside the camp is the spatial marker of exclusion from Israel’s covenant community. The camp is organized around the Tent of Meeting at its center — proximity to the holy determines one’s place. To be outside the camp is to be outside the orbit of divine presence. The same spatial logic governs the burning of sin-offering remains (4:12, 4:21), the scapegoat (16:22), and the bodies of executed blasphemers (24:14). Outside the camp is the zone of death, impurity, and expulsion.

notes.original: Tsaraʼat in fabric
notes.why: The same diagnostic category applied to human skin is now applied to fabric and leather. This is not a metaphor — the priestly system treats mildew in cloth as genuinely analogous to disease in skin: it spreads, it must be examined, isolated, re-examined, and if persistent, burned. The logic is consistent with the priestly world-view that uncleanness is an objective property of matter, not merely a social label. A robe with spreading greenish-reddish mold is ontologically similar to a body with spreading skin disease. Both are disorders that the priest must diagnose and manage.

notes.original: ממאֶרֶת (memaʼeret)
notes.why: Persistent mildew — literally “a stubborn” or “fretting” disease, from a root meaning to eat away or to be corrosive. The word appears only in chapters 13–14. An article with memaʼeret is one where the mold has entrenched itself and cannot be washed out — it has eaten into the fibers. Such an article must be burned. The term is the fabric equivalent of the “chronic skin disease” of v. 11 — a condition that has gone past the point of possible cleansing.

notes.original: Re-entry from exile
notes.why: Chapter 14 is the mirror image of chapter 13. There the priest goes outside the camp to declare a person unclean; here he goes outside the camp to declare them clean. The priest comes to the excluded person — the person cannot yet come to the priest. This directionality matters: the re-integration begins with the priest crossing the boundary to meet the one who has been living in the zone of death. The healed person does not simply walk back in; they are brought back by a ritual that retraces and reverses the path of exclusion.

notes.original: The two-bird ritual
notes.why: One bird is slaughtered over a clay vessel of fresh water; its blood mingles with the living water. The second bird, along with cedar wood, crimson yarn, and hyssop, is dipped in the blood-water mixture and the seven-fold sprinkling performed. Then the living bird is released over the open field. The structure is identical to the two-goat ritual of chapter 16: one dies, one lives and carries the impurity away into the wilderness. In both rites, the substitute that departs alive bears what the community has laid on it. Death and release together accomplish what neither can alone.

notes.original: אֵזֹב (ʼezov, hyssop)
notes.why: Hyssop — almost certainly Origanum syriacum (Syrian oregano), not the European hyssop of later tradition. It is a small, bushy, fragrant plant whose dense branches make it an effective aspergillum for sprinkling liquids. Hyssop appears in every major purification context in the Hebrew Bible: Exodus 12:22 (the Passover blood), Numbers 19:18 (the red heifer rite), Psalm 51:7 (“purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean”), and John 19:29 (at the cross). It carries a consistent association with blood, purification, and transition across the entire biblical canon.

notes.original: עֵץ אֶרֶז (ʾets erez, cedar wood)
notes.why: Cedar wood appears alongside hyssop and crimson yarn in the purification bundles of Leviticus 14 and Numbers 19 (the red heifer). The cedar is one of the largest and most enduring trees known to the ancient Israelite; the hyssop is one of the smallest (1 Kings 4:33 contrasts them explicitly). The pairing of the highest and lowest plants may symbolize comprehensiveness — from the greatest to the least, the purification covers the whole range. Cedar’s association with strength and permanence contrasts with the decay of the diseased condition being reversed.

notes.original: The three stages of re-entry
notes.why: Re-entry into the community is staged across eight days. Day 1 (outside camp): the two-bird ritual, sprinkling, declaration of clean — but the person may only enter the camp, not their tent. Days 1–7: inside the camp but outside their tent. Day 7: full shaving — head, beard, eyebrows, every hair removed — washing, and bathing. Day 8: the full offering sequence at the Tent of Meeting. The progressive re-integration mirrors the progressive exclusion that preceded it, and the stripping of all hair on day 7 is a complete erasure of the body’s surface — a fresh start from the skin outward.

notes.original: Blood on ear, thumb, toe — again
notes.why: The identical ritual to Aaron’s ordination (8:23–24). The lobe of the right ear, the thumb of the right hand, the big toe of the right foot — the extremities of hearing, doing, and going. At ordination these are consecrated for holy service; here they are reclaimed for restored community life. The healed person does not simply re-enter — they are re-consecrated. Exclusion from the camp is a form of death to the community; return through this rite is a form of resurrection. The theological implication is striking: full restoration looks like ordination.

notes.original: Oil over blood
notes.why: The oil application in vv. 15–18 follows the blood application and covers the same three points — ear, thumb, toe — with the remainder placed on the head. The oil goes over the blood, not instead of it. The sequence matters: blood establishes atonement; oil establishes consecration. The layering of oil on blood at the extremities and on the head replicates precisely the ordination sequence of chapter 8, where anointing oil was poured on Aaron’s head after the ordination blood rite (8:12, 30).

notes.original: Graduated offering — again
notes.why: As in 5:7–13 and 12:8, the Torah provides a scaled-down but fully valid alternative for the poor. Two birds replace the two lambs; the guilt-offering lamb is retained because there is no cheaper substitute for an individual guilt offering. The same ear-thumb-toe ritual is performed with the same oil. The healed poor person and the healed wealthy person receive the same ritual outcome — clean, re-consecrated, restored. The priestly system does not create a tiered restoration. Completeness is available to everyone.

notes.original: וְאֲנִי נָתַתִּי (weʼani natatti)
notes.why: “And I put a diseased spot.” God is the explicit grammatical subject of the house disease. This is theologically startling: the mildew is not an accident of nature, not an enemy’s curse, but a divine act. The priestly world-view does not separate natural processes from divine agency — all circumstances fall within the sphere of YHWH’s governance. The law is also proleptic: given in the wilderness, it anticipates life in the land. The house laws are a promise and a warning addressed to a people who do not yet have houses.

notes.original: שְׁקַעֲרוּרֹת (shekaʼarurot)
notes.why: Depressions, cavities, hollow pits — a hapax legomenon (appearing only here) describing the specific visual sign of house mildew: not just discoloration but depressions in the plaster or stone that suggest the disease has eaten below the surface. The precise technical term signals that the priestly tradition had specific criteria for what constituted a reportable condition, not merely a subjective impression. The priest looks for color (greenish or reddish) and depth (the cavity going below surface level) — two observable, teachable criteria.

notes.original: The demolished house
notes.why: If the mildew persists after two rounds of stone replacement and replastering, the entire structure comes down — stones, timber, and all plaster. Nothing is salvaged or reused; everything goes to the unclean place outside the city. The demolition is the ultimate application of the principle that persistent uncleanness, when it cannot be expunged, must be removed entirely. The same logic governs the burning of the sin-offering carcass outside the camp (4:12) and the destruction of the contaminated clay vessel (11:33). What the uncleanness has thoroughly entered cannot be recovered; it must be eliminated.

notes.original: Two-bird ritual for a building
notes.why: The same two-bird rite performed for the healed person (vv. 4–7) is performed for the healed house (vv. 49–53), with only minor adaptations: the house is sprinkled rather than a person. The ritual logic is consistent: the living bird carries the mildew’s uncleanness away as it goes free over the open field. The house is then declared clean and atonement is made for it — a building receiving its own atonement rite. The priestly system extends moral-ritual categories to material objects in a way that is foreign to modern categories but internally coherent in its world-view.

notes.original: Moses and Aaron together
notes.why: Chapter 15 is the fourth time YHWH addresses both Moses and Aaron (cf. 11:1; 13:1; 14:33). The discharge laws, like the food laws and the disease laws, belong to the domain of communal instruction rather than priestly officiation. Both leaders are responsible for teaching these rules to Israel. The chapter covers bodily functions that touch daily domestic life — far removed from the altar — yet governed by the same holiness logic.

notes.original: זָב (zav)
notes.why: The man with a discharge. The condition described in vv. 2–15 is an abnormal, persistent, or recurrent genital discharge — distinct from normal seminal emission (vv. 16–18). The description matches what modern medicine would classify as a urethral discharge from infection (possibly gonorrhea or similar). The contamination network created by the zav is extensive: bed, seat, anything he touches, anyone who touches him, even his spittle (v. 8). Contact transmits not disease but ritual status. The seven-day post-healing period and two-bird offering mirror the structure of the skin disease laws.

notes.original: שִכְבַת זֶרַע (shichvat zaraʼ)
notes.why: Emission of semen. Crucially, this is a categorically lighter uncleanness than the abnormal discharge: it lasts only until evening with bathing, requires no offering, and does not generate a wide contamination network. Normal bodily function is not sinful but does require ritual reorientation before approaching the holy. The inclusion of the woman in v. 18 is notable — the couple together is addressed, and both bear the same uncleanness equally and symmetrically.

notes.original: נִדָּה (niddah)
notes.why: Menstrual separation — from a root meaning to be removed or set apart. The woman during her monthly period is in a state of niddah: a seven-day period of separation that transfers to anything she lies or sits on and to anyone who touches her. The niddah laws are not a statement about female inferiority or sinfulness — blood is the carrier of the same holiness-tension that governs all the discharge laws. The niddah system became a central feature of Jewish domestic life, formalized extensively in later rabbinic literature.

notes.original: The abnormal female discharge
notes.why: The woman with a chronic or irregular blood discharge is in a continuous state of niddah-like uncleanness for however long her discharge lasts. This is the condition of the woman in Mark 5:25–34 who has had a bleeding disorder for twelve years — twelve years of ritual exclusion from communal worship, from touching others without transmitting uncleanness. Her touch of Jesus’ garment, and his declaration that she is healed and her faith has saved her, is a direct engagement with this legal condition. The Leviticus context makes the narrative’s force fully visible.

notes.original: The theological rationale
notes.why: Verse 31 is the only place in chapter 15 where the purpose of all these laws is stated: to keep Israel separate from uncleanness so they do not die by defiling the dwelling of God in their midst. The logic is spatial and relational: YHWH’s presence is located at the center of the camp in the Tent of Meeting. Uncleanness radiating outward from individuals threatens to reach the divine dwelling and the result is death. The discharge laws are not about hygiene or morality — they are about managing the dangerous interface between ordinary human life and holy presence.

notes.original: After the death of Aaron’s sons
notes.why: The Day of Atonement law is anchored explicitly in the catastrophe of chapter 10. The connection is not incidental — it is the theological premise: Nadab and Abihu died because they approached the inner sanctuary without authorization. Chapter 16 provides the one legitimate, prescribed, annual approach. The entire elaborate ritual is the answer to the question chapter 10 raises: if the holy fire kills those who approach improperly, how can anyone approach at all? The answer: once a year, this way, this precisely.

notes.original: כַפֹּרֶת (kapporet)
notes.why: The atonement cover — the gold lid of the ark of the covenant, flanked by the cherubim. Traditionally rendered “mercy seat” (KJV), following Luther’s Gnadenstuhl. But kapporet is from the root kpr (to atone, to cover), and “atonement cover” is more accurate: it is the surface on which the atoning blood is sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. The cloud of divine presence (v. 2) appears over this cover — it is the locus of divine-human encounter in the innermost place. The blood that touches it each year is the concentrated symbol of all that the Day of Atonement accomplishes.

notes.original: The linen garments
notes.why: On this one day Aaron lays aside his ornate high priestly vestments — the gold ephod, the jeweled breastpiece, the multi-colored robe, the golden crown. He enters the Holy of Holies not in the full regalia of his office but in simple white linen: tunic, undergarments, sash, turban. No gold, no gems, no marks of rank. Before God in the innermost place, all human dignity is stripped away. The white linen is the garment of purity, not of status. He will change back into his regular vestments when he comes out (v. 23–24).

notes.original: עֲזָאזֵל (ʼAzazel)
notes.why: One of the most debated terms in the Hebrew Bible, with three main interpretations. (1) A supernatural entity — a demon or fallen being in the wilderness to whom the sin is dispatched (supported by the parallel structure: one goat for YHWH, one for Azazel; also by 1 Enoch’s identification of Azazel as a fallen angel). (2) A geographical term — meaning “precipice” or “rough terrain,” describing the destination rather than a recipient. (3) A portmanteau for “the goat that departs” (ez + azal), the etymology behind Tyndale’s 1530 invention of “scapegoat.” The text renders Azazel as a proper noun throughout, preserving the ambiguity the Hebrew itself preserves.

notes.original: The incense cloud
notes.why: Aaron must enter the Holy of Holies carrying burning coals and incense. He puts the incense on the fire before the LORD so that the cloud of incense covers the kapporet — and then he will not die. The cloud is protective: it veils the direct manifestation of divine glory from human sight. The same theology governs the cloud at Sinai (Exod 19:9) and the cloud filling the Temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10–11). No human being can survive unmediated encounter with YHWH’s visible glory; the incense cloud is the buffer that makes the annual blood rite possible.

notes.original: The confession over the scapegoat
notes.why: Aaron places both hands on the live goat’s head — the full double-hand semikah — and confesses over it all the iniquities, transgressions, and sins of Israel. The sins are transferred through speech and touch onto the animal, which then carries them physically away from the community into a remote wilderness. The structure is identical to the living bird of chapter 14: one animal dies (the sin offering), one lives and carries the uncleanness away. What cannot be burned on the altar is sent beyond the reach of the camp. The two complementary mechanisms — blood atonement and physical removal — address two different dimensions of sin’s problem.

notes.original: לְעַנּוֹת נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם (leʼannot nafshoteikhem)
notes.why: To afflict yourselves — literally “to humble your inner selves.” The verb ענה (ʼanah) means to humble, to suppress, to deny. The traditional understanding (fasting) is confirmed by later texts (Isa 58:3–5) where the Day of Atonement fast is implied. The phrase “sabbath of complete rest” (shabbat shabbaton, v. 31) is used only for the most solemn days — the weekly Sabbath and Yom Kippur. The Day of Atonement is the Sabbath of Sabbaths: all work ceases, all food ceases, and the focus narrows to a single act of collective humility before God.

notes.original: The annual character and the narrative close
notes.why: The Day of Atonement is explicitly annual — once a year, for all the sins of Israel. The phrase “all their sins” (kol chatotʼam) is comprehensive: not specific sins for which offerings have already been brought, but the accumulated residue of whatever has not been addressed, known or unknown. The final sentence of the chapter (“And it was done as the LORD commanded Moses”) is a narrative postscript — the first person narrator steps in to confirm compliance. It marks the close of the chapter with a characteristic formula of obedient fulfillment.

notes.original: שְׂעִירִים (seʼirīm)
notes.why: Goat-demons — literally “hairy ones” or “goat-figures.” The term appears in Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14 alongside desert spirits and suggests demonic or semi-divine beings imagined in goat form, associated with the wilderness. The command that all sacrifice be centralized at the Tent — rather than in the open field — is explicitly motivated by the need to stop Israel from offering to these beings. The verse implies that some Israelites had been doing exactly that, “prostituting themselves” after the goat-demons. The centralization of sacrifice is both a logistical and a theological anti-idolatry measure.

notes.original: Bloodguilt for slaughter outside the Tent
notes.why: The man who slaughters an animal outside the Tent without bringing it to the LORD incurs bloodguilt — the word used (dam, blood) is the same word for the blood of a murder victim. The logic is striking: to take a life (even an animal’s) without the ritual acknowledgment that life belongs to God is a form of violence. Killing and eating outside the sacred framework is treated as if the animal’s blood cries from the ground. This law is eventually modified in Deuteronomy 12:20–25 to accommodate life in the land, where distance from a central sanctuary makes full compliance impractical.

notes.original: כִּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ בַּדָּם הִוא (ki hanefesh baddam hiʼ)
notes.why: “For the life is in the blood.” This is the theological foundation of the entire blood prohibition system. Nefesh — the life-principle, the animating force, the being of the creature — resides in its blood. To eat the blood is to consume the life itself. The prohibition is therefore not merely ritual but reflects a deep theological conviction about what blood is. It applies equally to Israelite and resident alien (v. 12), and it will be restated in 17:14 with added emphasis.

notes.original: אֲנִי נְתַתִּיו (ʼani netattiv)
notes.why: “I have given it to you.” God is the subject: the blood is not something humans discovered or invented as an atoning mechanism — it is a gift given by YHWH for the specific purpose of making atonement. The atoning capacity of blood is not inherent in the substance but derives from the divine donation. The blood makes atonement “by the life it carries” (banefesh) — it is the nefesh in the blood that does the atoning work. This verse is the closest thing in the Torah to an explicit theology of blood atonement.

notes.original: Covering the blood of game
notes.why: When a wild animal or bird is killed in hunting — outside the sacrificial system, since game animals are not brought to the altar — its blood must be poured out and covered with earth. The covering is an act of acknowledgment: the life of the creature is returned to the ground from which it came, rather than consumed. The gesture recognizes that even a hunted animal’s life belongs to God. It is a minimal but real ritual of respect for the nefesh that was taken.

notes.original: אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלהֵיכֶם (ʼani YHWH ʼeloheikhem)
notes.why: “I am the LORD your God.” The opening formula of chapter 18 — and the formula that will recur throughout chapters 18–26 — grounds every ethical command in the identity of the lawgiver rather than in the logic of the commands themselves. The laws are not justified by their social benefit or their natural rationality, though both may be present. They are grounded in who YHWH is and what YHWH has done (bringing Israel out of Egypt). The “not like Egypt, not like Canaan” framing defines Israel’s identity by contrast with those who surrounded them.

notes.original: וָחַי בָהֶם (vechai bahem)
notes.why: “And shall live by them.” The statutes and ordinances are life-giving — the person who does them will live. The ambiguity is deliberate: life means both physical survival in the land and the fullness of covenant existence. Paul will quote this verse in Galatians 3:12 and Romans 10:5 to argue about the limits of Torah-keeping; Ezekiel 20:11 and Nehemiah 9:29 use the same phrase positively for the Torah’s life-giving purpose. The verse is one of the most cited in the Hebrew Bible, carrying enormous weight in later Jewish and Christian theology.

notes.original: עֶרְוַת (ervah)
notes.why: Nakedness — the legal formula throughout chapter 18. “To uncover the nakedness of” (galah ervah) is the priestly idiom for sexual access. The term ervah means exposed genitalia or shameful exposure; uncovering another person’s ervah is to transgress the boundary of their body and its associated relationships. The formula is consistent across all 13 forbidden kinship relations of vv. 6–18. In several cases the prohibition is stated obliquely — “you shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” = you shall not have sex with your father’s wife (your father’s sexual partner is his nakedness, not yours to uncover).

notes.original: זִמָּה (zimmah)
notes.why: Depravity, lewdness, wickedness. The term zimmah carries a stronger evaluative force than the general ervah formula — it signals that the act is not merely prohibited but morally repugnant. It appears in Leviticus only here and in 19:29 and 20:14. Taking a woman and her daughter (or granddaughter) is singled out as especially gross, perhaps because it treats the family unit as a pool of available sexual partners rather than as a set of relationships with their own integrity. The word zimmah marks the particular vileness of this specific violation.

notes.original: מֹלֶך (Molech)
notes.why: Molech — a deity associated with child sacrifice, attested in Phoenician, Punic, and Ammonite religious practice. The name may derive from a root meaning king (melek) with a vowel change from the Hebrew word for shame (boshet) added by later scribes as a mark of disgust. The appearance of the Molech prohibition in the middle of a list of sexual laws has puzzled interpreters: some ancient and modern scholars have proposed that “give your seed to Molech” is a sexual euphemism. The more straightforward reading remains cultic child sacrifice, placed here because the family violations of chapter 18 extend to the most extreme misuse of one’s own children.

notes.original: תּוֹעֲבָה (toʼevah)
notes.why: Abomination, detestable act. The term toʼevah in the Hebrew Bible signals something that provokes revulsion or disgust, whether ritual or moral. In Leviticus it is applied here (18:22) and to the offenses listed in 18:26–27 and 20:13. Beyond Leviticus it is used for: eating forbidden animals (11:10–13), dishonest weights (Prov 11:1), idolatry (Deut 7:25), and various ethical violations in Ezekiel and Proverbs. The term is an intensifier of the prohibition — among the forbidden acts of chapter 18, this one is specifically marked as especially repugnant. The verse states the prohibition as written; interpretive traditions both ancient and modern continue to debate its scope and application.

notes.original: וָתָקִא הָאָרֶץ (vataqeʼ haʼrets)
notes.why: And the land vomited. The verb is the same root used for human vomiting — the land is given a digestive system and the agency to use it. The Holiness Code’s theology of the land is striking: the land is not merely real estate that changes ownership, but a moral entity that can be defiled and that responds to defilement by expelling its occupants. The Canaanites were vomited out (past tense, v. 25); Israel is warned that the same will happen to them (future tense, v. 28). The land’s tolerance of defilement has a limit, and that limit applies to everyone who lives on it, regardless of covenant status.

notes.original: Conditional tenure
notes.why: Verse 28 is one of the most sobering statements in Leviticus: the land will vomit out Israel just as it vomited out the nations before them, if Israel defiles it with the same practices. The covenant gives Israel the land but not unconditional possession of it. This conditional theology of the land runs throughout the Holiness Code and will be stated explicitly in chapter 26 in the blessings and curses. It is, historically, the theological framework within which the exile is later interpreted — the land finally vomited Israel out in 586 BCE.

notes.original: קְדֹשִים תִהְיוּ (qedoshim tihyu)
notes.why: Be holy. The same command that first appeared in 11:44–45 is now spoken to the entire congregation — not just the priests, not just the leaders, but all the people together. This is the chapter’s controlling principle: holiness is the vocation of the whole community, enacted through the full range of actions that follow, from honoring parents to using honest scales. The imitatio Dei theology is explicit — Israel is to be holy because YHWH is holy, not merely in order to become holy. The divine identity both grounds and shapes the human calling.

notes.original: פֵּאָה / לֶקֶט (peʼah / leqet)
notes.why: The corner of the field (peʼah) and the gleanings (leqet) are Israel’s built-in poverty provision. Farmers are commanded to leave the edges of their fields unharvested and not to pick up what falls — these are left for the poor and the resident alien to gather for themselves. The law assumes active agency by the poor: they must come and glean, they are not passive recipients of handouts. The Book of Ruth (2:2–23) depicts this system in action — Ruth gleaning in Boaz’s fields is a direct application of this law, and Boaz’s generosity is shown by instructing his workers to let extra grain fall.

notes.original: Wages by nightfall
notes.why: The hired worker’s wages must be paid before sunset on the day of work — not held overnight. The law reflects a day-labor economy where workers had no savings and needed their wages to buy food that same evening. Withholding wages overnight is not merely a breach of contract; it is a form of exploitation with a theological name: the same word used for extortion (osheq). The law is repeated in Deuteronomy 24:14–15, where it extends to resident aliens as well. Economic justice — protecting the vulnerable from exploitation — is here located squarely within the domain of holiness.

notes.original: The deaf and the blind
notes.why: The prohibition on cursing the deaf and placing stumbling blocks before the blind is remarkable because both prohibitions protect people who cannot know they are being harmed. The deaf cannot hear the curse; the blind cannot see the obstacle. The law’s reach extends to acts the victim will never know about. The grounding clause is significant: “you shall fear your God” — not “you will be punished.” When no human enforcement is possible, the conscience before God is the operative deterrent. The law is an ethic of integrity when no one is watching.

notes.original: וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ (veʼahavta lereʼakha kamokha)
notes.why: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This is the most cited verse in Leviticus and one of the most cited in the entire Bible. Its context is essential: it comes at the end of a four-step sequence — do not hate (v.17a), rebuke honestly (v.17b), do not take vengeance or hold grudges (v.18a), then love (v.18b). The love command is the culmination of a process of working through conflict, not a replacement for it. Jesus identifies this verse alongside Deuteronomy 6:5 as the summary of the Torah and the Prophets (Matt 22:37–40; Mark 12:28–31). Paul calls it the fulfillment of the law (Rom 13:9; Gal 5:14). James calls it the royal law (Jas 2:8).

notes.original: כִלְאַיִם (kilʼayim)
notes.why: Two kinds — a mixture of categories that should remain distinct. Kilʼayim applies to animal breeding, agricultural sowing, and fabric weaving (here wool and linen; cf. Deut 22:11 for the fuller form shaʼatnez). The anti-mixing principle reflects a creation theology in which each category of thing was made according to its kind (lemineihu, Genesis 1) and is to be maintained in its kind. The laws do not declare mixing evil but rather maintain the integrity of the created order by preventing its categories from blurring. Their practical application generated extensive rabbinic discussion.

notes.original: וְאָהַבְתָּ לוֹ כָּמוֹךָ (veʼahavta lo kamokha)
notes.why: The love command extended to the foreigner — word for word the same formula as 19:18 applied now to the ger (resident alien). The same verb (ahav), the same comparative (kamokha, “as yourself”). Chapter 19 thus presents love of neighbor and love of foreigner as structurally identical commands. The motivation is memory: “for you were foreigners in Egypt.” Israel’s own experience of vulnerability in a foreign land is the ethical foundation for their treatment of foreigners in their own land. This grounding of ethics in historical memory is one of the Holiness Code’s most distinctive features.

notes.original: Honest weights
notes.why: Dishonest weights and measures — the manipulation of scales, volume measures, and length measures — are placed here in the holiness chapter because economic integrity is a form of holiness. Using false weights is not merely cheating; it is a desecration of the social fabric, a form of theft hidden behind the appearance of fair dealing. The motivation given is the Exodus: “I the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt.” The God who liberated a people from oppression does not permit them to practice economic oppression on one another. Honest commerce is covenant faithfulness.

notes.original: מוֹת יוּמָת (mot yumat)
notes.why: He shall surely be put to death — the death-penalty formula. The doubling of the verbal root (mot from mwt, to die) is a Hebrew intensive construction: “dying he shall die.” Its force is emphatic and absolute. The formula appears throughout chapters 20 and also in Exodus 21–22 for capital offenses. Chapter 20’s penalties directly correspond to chapter 18’s prohibitions: the two chapters form a diptych, the first stating what is forbidden, the second specifying the consequence. The community’s obligation to execute judgment (v. 2) is itself part of the law: turning a blind eye (v. 4) incurs divine judgment on the community.

notes.original: Cursing parents
notes.why: The death penalty for cursing a father or mother echoes the fifth commandment’s honor requirement (Exodus 20:12) but in its negative form. The connection between chapter 19’s command to “fear” parents (19:3) and chapter 20’s death penalty for cursing them forms a deliberate bracket. The family is the foundational social unit of the covenant community; undermining it from within — through active cursing rather than mere neglect — carries the most severe consequence. The phrase “their blood is on their own head” shifts moral responsibility entirely to the offender.

notes.original: Graduated penalties
notes.why: The sexual violations of chapter 18 reappear here with their penalties, but the punishments are not uniform. Death (mot yumat) applies to adultery, the most severe kinship violations, male same-sex intercourse, and bestiality. Karet (“cut off” — divine rather than human execution) applies to several others including lying with a woman during her period. Some violations result only in childlessness (vv. 20–21) — a consequence rather than a judicial execution. The graduated scale reflects the gravity of the relationship violated: the closer the bond broken, the more severe the consequence.

notes.original: אֲנִי הִבְדַּלְתִּי אֶתְכֶם (ʼani hivdalti ʼetkhem)
notes.why: “I have separated you.” The verb hivdil (to separate, to distinguish, to divide) appears here in its most theologically concentrated form. The same root runs through the entire book: God separates light from darkness (Gen 1:4), the priest distinguishes holy from common and clean from unclean (10:10; 11:47), and now YHWH states that the separation of Israel from the nations is a divine act already accomplished. The identity of Israel is not self-created but given — a being-set-apart that precedes and grounds all the holiness laws. The phrase “a land flowing with milk and honey” (eretz zavat chalav udevash) appears here as both promise and rationale for what has been required.

notes.original: Separated to be mine
notes.why: The final verse of the holiness section (before the appendix on mediums in v. 27) closes with the most personal statement of the entire chapter: “I have separated you from the peoples to be mine.” The goal of separation is not self-sufficiency or superiority but belonging — Israel is set apart for YHWH. The holiness laws are not burdens imposed on an unwilling people but the shape of a relationship. To be holy is to be the LORD’s. The trajectory of the Holiness Code that began in chapter 17 arrives here at its relational foundation.

notes.original: קְרוֹבִים (qerovim)
notes.why: Close relatives — those near enough that mourning them is permitted. The priest may defile himself by touching a corpse only for the seven named relatives: mother, father, son, daughter, brother, and virgin sister. A wife is notably absent from the explicit list — v. 4 addresses this ambiguously, and rabbinic interpretation generally allowed mourning a wife as implied. The restriction is not heartlessness; it reflects the priest’s elevated status as one who regularly handles holy things. Contact with the dead is the most severe source of uncleanness in the priestly system (cf. Numbers 19), and the priest’s holiness requires that even grief be bounded.

notes.original: שְרֵפָה (serefah)
notes.why: Burned in fire — the punishment for a priest’s daughter who profanes herself through prostitution. This is uniquely severe: the same death-by-fire reserved for the most extreme sexual violations in chapter 20 (v. 14) is applied here. The reasoning is accountability by association: a priest’s daughter bears her father’s honor, and her conduct reflects on the holiness of the priestly house. The heightened responsibility of the priestly family is a consistent theme of chapters 21–22.

notes.original: כֹּהֵן גָדוֹל (kohen gadol)
notes.why: The great priest — the high priest. His restrictions extend beyond those of the ordinary priest in three ways: he cannot dishevel his hair or tear his garments even in mourning (the standard grief gestures), he cannot defile himself even for father or mother, and he cannot leave the sanctuary at all during his service. The anointing oil on his head is the reason given in v. 12 — the oil creates a consecration so total that the normal claims of family grief cannot override it. He is, in a sense, the living embodiment of the sanctuary’s holiness.

notes.original: The blemish list
notes.why: The fourteen conditions that disqualify a priest from altar service range from blindness and lameness to skin conditions and genital injury. This is not a statement about the personal worth or spiritual standing of men with these conditions — v. 22 explicitly says a blemished priest may eat all the holy food, meaning he retains full priestly status and receives his full priestly share. The disqualification is from officiating at the altar specifically. The underlying theology mirrors the requirement for unblemished animals (22:17–25): the person who represents Israel before God in the most solemn rites is to embody the wholeness (tamim) that the offerings themselves must possess.

notes.original: מִקְדָּשַי (miqdashay)
notes.why: My sanctuaries. The plural is notable — not just the altar but the entire sanctuary complex. The rationale given for the blemish restriction is not about the priest’s merit but about the sanctuaries’ holiness: allowing a blemished man to officiate would “profane” the sacred spaces. The theology is spatial and representative — the priest at the altar stands in for the wholeness of the people before God, and that representation requires a visible completeness. The same word (chillul, to profane) governs both this law and the restrictions on a priest’s family (21:9, 15).

notes.original: קֳדָשִים (qodashim)
notes.why: Holy things — the technical term for sacred offerings and their portions. The chapter’s concern is that priests in a state of uncleanness do not eat the qodashim, which would constitute a desecration. The categories of uncleanness listed (skin disease, discharge, corpse-contact, seminal emission, swarming creature, human uncleanness) mirror the uncleanness laws of chapters 11–15. Until now, those chapters covered laypeople’s daily life; here they are applied specifically to the priests’ access to holy food. The priest has the most to gain from the qodashim and therefore the most to lose when unclean.

notes.original: זָר (zar)
notes.why: Unauthorized person — literally “foreigner” or “stranger”, but in this context meaning any non-priest. A toshav (sojourner/guest) and a sakhir (hired worker) in the priest’s household are explicitly named as unauthorized, even if they live in his home. But a purchased slave is permitted, and a daughter who returns widowed or divorced to her father’s house is permitted. The household boundary is not blood alone but legal dependency: those fully under the priest’s household authority share in the priestly food; those who are temporary workers or guests do not.

notes.original: חוּמשִיתוֹ (chamishito)
notes.why: A fifth added — the same restitution surcharge as in 5:16 (accidental trespass against sacred things). The accidental eating of holy food by an unauthorized person is treated as a trespass against God’s property, requiring both restoration of the full value and an additional twenty percent. The theological logic is consistent: sacred things belong to God, and misappropriating them — even inadvertently — requires over-payment to restore the relationship.

notes.original: Animal blemishes
notes.why: The animal blemish list (vv. 22–25) directly parallels the priestly blemish list (21:17–20): both priest and animal must be tamim (without blemish, whole). The specific defects listed for animals — blindness, injury, mutilation, skin conditions, crushed testicles — overlap closely with the priestly list. The theological consistency is deliberate: the offering system requires wholeness at every point of the transaction, from the human officiating to the animal offered. One exception is noted (v. 23): an animal with a limb too long or short may be offered as a freewill offering but not for a vow — spontaneous generosity has slightly more latitude than formal obligation.

notes.original: Mother and young on the same day
notes.why: You shall not slaughter an ox or sheep together with its young on the same day. This law — not explained by the text — has generated extensive commentary. The most common interpretation is that it reflects an ethic of care toward the bonds of the natural world: even in a system that permits animal slaughter, there is a limit to what can be taken from a family unit in a single day. The parallel law in Deuteronomy 22:6–7 (sending away a mother bird before taking eggs) reflects the same principle. The Talmud and Maimonides both connect these laws to minimizing animal suffering and respecting natural bonds.

notes.original: The closing doxology
notes.why: The chapter closes with the fullest form of the doxological formula that punctuates the Holiness Code: I am the LORD who makes you holy / who brought you out of Egypt to be your God / I am the LORD. This triple grounding — in divine identity, in divine action (the Exodus), and in covenant relationship — is the theological bedrock beneath all of chapters 17–22. Every law in these chapters is grounded not in pragmatics or social utility but in who YHWH is and what YHWH has done. The priestly holiness laws close with the same logic with which they opened.

notes.original: מוֹעֲדֵי יְהוָה (moʼadei YHWH)
notes.why: Appointed times of the LORD — not merely “festivals” but scheduled encounters. The root yʼad means to appoint, to meet at a fixed time and place. The moʼed is an appointment God keeps with Israel. The same word is used for the Tent of Meeting (ʼohel moʼed, the Tent of Appointment). The sacred calendar is a framework of recurring divine-human meetings built into the structure of the year. Each feast is an appointment Israel keeps because the LORD has set it.

notes.original: The Sabbath as the first feast
notes.why: The weekly Sabbath is listed first among the moʼadim — not as a separate category but as the foundational feast. Every other appointed time derives its character from the Sabbath principle: cessation, holy convocation, and no ordinary work. The Sabbath is the prototype of sacred time; all the annual festivals are extensions of its logic across the year. Placing Sabbath first also signals that the sacred calendar begins not with the agricultural cycle but with the rhythm of creation.

notes.original: The omer and the day after the Sabbath
notes.why: The wave-sheaf offering (the omer) is to be brought “on the day after the Sabbath.” This phrase generated one of the most significant disputes in Second Temple Judaism: does “Sabbath” mean the weekly Sabbath (so the omer falls on a Sunday, fifty days later giving Shavuot on a Sunday — the Sadducean/Karaite position) or the first festival day of Passover (so the omer’s day varies, as in the Pharisaic/rabbinic tradition)? The ambiguity in the Hebrew was real and contested. The New Testament’s Pentecost (Acts 2) falls on a Sunday, consistent with the weekly-Sabbath interpretation.

notes.original: The Feast of Weeks (Shavuot)
notes.why: Fifty days after the omer — hence the Greek name Pentecost (pentekoste, fiftieth). Unlike Passover and Sukkot, Shavuot has no explicit historical memory attached in Leviticus 23 (later tradition identifies it with the Sinai revelation). It is characterized by two notable features: the leavened bread (unique among altar offerings — the only time leaven goes up), and the immediate restatement of the gleaning law in v. 22 (identical to 19:9–10). The harvest festival is bounded by the poor: you feast, and you leave the margins for those who cannot feast.

notes.original: תְרוּעָה (teruʼah)
notes.why: A trumpet blast or a loud shout — the specific sound-type is debated. The day is called “a memorial of teruʼah” in Leviticus; Numbers 29:1 calls it “a day of teruʼah.” The rabbinic title Rosh Hashanah (New Year) does not appear here — the text locates it on the first day of the seventh month, not as a new year celebration. The combination of rest, blast, and holy convocation marks it as a solemn preparation for the Day of Atonement ten days later, rather than a celebratory new year.

notes.original: The Feast of Booths (Sukkot)
notes.why: Two requirements define Sukkot: the four species (v. 40 — the fruit of a splendid tree, palm branches, leafy boughs, and willows, identified by tradition as the etrog-citron, lulav-palm, hadas-myrtle, and aravah-willow) waved before the LORD, and dwelling in temporary booths for seven days. The booths are explicitly tied to historical memory (v. 43): they commemorate Israel’s booth-dwelling in the wilderness. Sukkot is the most joyful feast in the Torah; Deuteronomy 16:14–15 commands rejoicing explicitly. It is also the feast most fully representing the vulnerability of human life — intentionally living without permanent shelter.

notes.original: תָמִיד (tamid)
notes.why: Continually — the same word used for the perpetual altar fire (6:12–13). The lamp must never go out, the fire must never go out: perpetuity is the mark of the two central sancturary installations. The lampstand’s pure beaten oil (not simply pressed oil) and Aaron’s daily tending from evening to morning create a rhythm of human faithfulness maintaining the divine light. The menorah is lit each evening — darkness is the moment of kindling, not dawn. The seven lamps illuminate the sanctuary’s interior throughout every night.

notes.original: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים (lechem hapanim)
notes.why: The bread of the presence — literally “bread of the face” or “bread before the face”, meaning bread set before the divine presence. Twelve loaves represent the twelve tribes before God at all times — the people are permanently present at the table in the sanctuary. They are renewed every Sabbath: the old loaves are removed and eaten by the priests, replaced by fresh ones. The stale loaves are “most holy” — a week in the divine presence has not diminished their sacredness. The frankincense on the rows is the portion that actually goes up as an offering; the bread itself feeds the priests.

notes.original: The blasphemer’s identity
notes.why: The man is identified by both his parents: an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father. This detail is not incidental — the narrative uses this case to address a legal question the earlier laws had not explicitly resolved: does the blasphemy law apply to someone of mixed Israelite-Gentile heritage? The verdict in v. 16 answers clearly: foreigner and native-born alike are subject to the same law when they blaspheme the Name. The case becomes the vehicle for establishing legal equality between resident aliens and Israelites in this most serious matter.

notes.original: הַשֵּם (hashem)
notes.why: The Name. Blasphemy in this chapter is not merely insulting speech but the specific desecration of the divine name — treating the name of YHWH as common, as a curse-word, or as a tool of casual speech. The Name is the focal point of divine identity; to blaspheme it is to attack YHWH’s honor in the most direct way possible. Later Jewish tradition avoided pronouncing the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) entirely, substituting “Adonai” or simply “HaShem” (the Name) — a practice rooted partly in the severity of this law.

notes.original: Eye for eye — the lex talionis
notes.why: The lex talionis (“law of retaliation”) — fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth — is widely misunderstood as endorsing literal retributive mutilation. Its function in ancient law was the opposite: to impose a ceiling on retaliation. In societies where a minor injury might provoke a killing or a killing might provoke a blood-feud, the lex talionis established proportionality: the punishment may not exceed the injury. The principle appears in Exodus 21:23–25 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Rabbinic tradition understood it as requiring monetary compensation equivalent to the injury, not literal extraction. Jesus’ teaching in Matthew 5:38–39 addresses not the legal principle but its misuse as a personal justification for vengeance.

notes.original: On Mount Sinai
notes.why: Chapter 25 is one of only two passages in Leviticus explicitly located at Sinai (cf. 7:38; 26:46). The detail is not incidental: the Sabbath year and Jubilee laws are given the same Sinai authority as the Decalogue itself. The land laws are not pragmatic policy but covenant law received at the mountain of divine presence. The Sinai setting frames what follows as the most fundamental level of obligation — not Tent-of-Meeting instruction but the original covenant terms.

notes.original: שַבַּת לָאָרֶץ (shabbat laʼarts)
notes.why: A Sabbath for the land. The seventh year is not merely a human agricultural rest but the land’s own Sabbath to the LORD. The land is addressed as a subject that observes the covenant — it needs rest, and that rest is owed to God. Anything that grows in the seventh year without sowing belongs to the land’s own yield, not to any owner; it is available for everyone, including servants, hired workers, sojourners, and even wild animals (v. 7). The land’s Sabbath democratizes its produce.

notes.original: יוֹבֵל (yovel)
notes.why: Jubilee — from the word for a ram’s horn (yovel), the instrument blown to announce it on Yom Kippur. The Jubilee is announced on the Day of Atonement: the year of liberation begins with the nation’s annual reconciliation with God. The word is the origin of the English “jubilee” through Latin. The precise calendar math — seven times seven years = forty-nine, and the fiftieth year is the Jubilee — is itself symbolic: the Jubilee is the Sabbath of Sabbaths of years, as Yom Kippur is the Sabbath of Sabbaths of days.

notes.original: דְּרוֹר (deror)
notes.why: Liberty, release, freedom. The word deror appears in the Hebrew Bible primarily in liberation contexts: the release of slaves (Jer 34:8; Ezek 46:17), the Jubilee proclamation, and Isaiah 61:1 (“to proclaim liberty to the captives”). Leviticus 25:10 — “Proclaim liberty throughout all the land to all its inhabitants” — is the verse inscribed on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia. The founders who chose this verse understood the Jubilee as a model for political freedom. The text itself does not limit deror to freedom from political oppression; it is fundamentally economic — freedom from debt-slavery and alienation from ancestral land.

notes.original: כִּי לִי הָאָרֶץ (ki li haʼarts)
notes.why: For the land is mine. This is the theological foundation of the entire Jubilee system. Land cannot be permanently alienated because it was never permanently owned by any human in the first place. YHWH is the ultimate landlord; Israel are tenant-sojourners. The word achuzzah (ancestral holding/possession) implies custodianship rather than absolute ownership: families hold land as hereditary stewards, but reversion to its original allotment every fifty years corrects the inevitable drift of wealth concentration. The theological claim — God owns the land — has radical social implications.

notes.original: נֶשֶׁךְ / תַרְבִּית (neshekh / tarbit)
notes.why: Two words for lending at interest. Neshekh (literally “bite”) refers to interest deducted from a loan at the time it is made. Tarbit (literally “increase”) refers to interest added at repayment. Together they cover every form of profiting from lending to an impoverished neighbor. The prohibition is specific: lending at interest to a poor Israelite brother is forbidden. The Exodus motivation (v. 38) grounds the prohibition in God’s act of liberation — the God who freed Israel from exploitation does not permit them to exploit their brothers.

notes.original: עֲבוֹדַת עֶבֶד (ʼavodat ʼeved)
notes.why: The labor of a slave — the kind of slave-work an impoverished Israelite may not be compelled to do. The chapter distinguishes sharply between an Israelite who sells himself into service (treated as a hired worker until Jubilee) and permanent chattel slavery. The reason is explicit in v. 42: the Israelites are already God’s servants. No human being can own as a slave someone who belongs to YHWH. The liberation from Egypt created a people whose primary servitude is to God alone — which means no human may claim the total ownership over them that slavery implies.

notes.original: גְּאֻלָה (geʼulah)
notes.why: Redemption — the right of the kinsman-redeemer (goʼel) to buy back what a family member has sold. The geʼulah system is one of the Torah’s primary social safety nets: the extended family is the first line of protection against permanent loss of land or freedom. The goʼel (redeemer) appears throughout the Hebrew Bible — in Boaz’s role in Ruth, in the redemption of Jeremiah’s family land (Jer 32), and as a title for YHWH himself (Isa 41:14; 44:6) who acts as Israel’s ultimate kinsman-redeemer. The final verse (v. 55) closes the chapter by returning to the Exodus: God redeemed Israel from Egypt, and that prior redemption gives God the claim that no human owner may exercise permanently.

notes.original: The Jubilee’s theology as a whole
notes.why: The chapter’s logic is built on four interconnected claims: the land belongs to God (v. 23); the people of Israel are God’s servants (v. 42, 55); God brought them out of Egypt (vv. 38, 42, 55); and therefore neither land nor persons may be permanently alienated from their original covenant condition. The Jubilee is not merely economic legislation — it is an enacted theology of divine ownership, human dignity, and covenant memory. Whether the Jubilee was ever implemented in Israel’s history is disputed; no historical source records its observance. But its vision shaped Jewish, Christian, and Islamic thinking about economic justice across millennia.

notes.original: The blessings
notes.why: The blessings of obedience are stacked in four domains: agricultural (rains, harvest), military (security, victory), demographic (fruitfulness), and — most profoundly — relational: “I will walk among you and will be your God, and you shall be my people” (v.12). The climactic blessing is not abundance but divine presence. The Exodus memory returns in v.13 as the foundation: the God who broke their yoke once can ensure they never wear it again. V.11 uses the word mishkan (dwelling) for the divine presence among the people — the same word used for the tabernacle itself.

notes.original: קֶרִי (qeri)
notes.why: Contrary, hostile, stubborn. The word qeri — used seven times in chapter 26 for Israel’s posture and twice for God’s response — is one of the most debated terms in Leviticus. Its root may be qrh (to encounter casually, accidentally) suggesting treating the covenant carelessly, or it may come from a root meaning hostility. The LXX often renders it with words for “accidentally” or “casually.” Whatever its etymology, in context it means a fundamental unwillingness to engage God seriously — treating the covenant as optional, avoidable, or negotiable.

notes.original: Sevenfold escalation
notes.why: The curses escalate in four rounds, each introduced by “if in spite of this you will not listen” and each multiplied sevenfold. The sevenfold structure is not mathematical (the punishments are not literally seven times more severe) but qualitative: seven signals completeness and totality in the priestly system. Each round adds new disasters: first, disease and military defeat; then drought and wild animals; then war and pestilence; finally, the most terrible — siege cannibalism, destruction of sanctuaries, and exile. The structure is deliberately cumulative, showing a God who gives Israel repeated opportunities to turn back before the ultimate consequence.

notes.original: Siege cannibalism
notes.why: The eating of sons and daughters (v.29) is the nadir of the curse section — the most terrible image in the chapter. It is not hyperbole: 2 Kings 6:28–29 records exactly this during the Assyrian siege of Samaria, and Lamentations 2:20 and 4:10 describe it during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. The ancient reader would have recognized this as a curse that came literally true. For those who first read Leviticus in or after the exile, the entire curse section of chapter 26 would have been a description of their lived experience.

notes.original: The land’s Sabbaths in exile
notes.why: The land “enjoys its Sabbaths” during the exile because it did not receive them when Israel was living on it. This is the theological framework used by the Chronicler to interpret the Babylonian exile: “to fulfill the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah, until the land had enjoyed its Sabbaths. All the days it lay desolate it kept Sabbath, to fulfill seventy years” (2 Chr 36:21). The seventy-year exile is calculated as the missed Sabbath years catching up with the land. This is one of the clearest examples in the Hebrew Bible of a later text interpreting a historical disaster through the lens of Leviticus.

notes.original: The restoration: confession and memory
notes.why: Restoration comes through confession — the same word (hitvaddah) used in 5:5 for confession before the sin offering. The condition is not simply stopping the sin but naming it, together with “the iniquity of their ancestors.” The heart must be uncircumcised no longer — the internal condition matching the outward rite. YHWH’s response is to “remember” the covenant — a verb (zakar) that in Hebrew means active engagement, not passive recollection. The ancestors are named in reverse chronological order (Jacob → Isaac → Abraham), perhaps suggesting that the most recent failure is addressed before reaching back to the original promise.

notes.original: The unconditional limit
notes.why: Verse 44 is the most important qualification in the chapter: even at the worst — in the land of enemies, abandoned, scattered — YHWH will not destroy Israel utterly or break the covenant. The curses are real and terrible, but they have a floor. This verse is the ground of Jewish hope through every subsequent catastrophe, including the Shoah. The covenant cannot be annihilated because YHWH will not break it, regardless of human faithlessness. Paul’s argument in Romans 11 that “all Israel will be saved” rests on this same logic, explicitly citing the patriarchal covenant.

notes.original: The valuation scale
notes.why: The sliding scale by age and gender reflects the economic labor value of persons in the ancient agricultural economy: peak working-age males (20–60) are valued highest; children, the elderly, and women proportionally less. These are not statements about the intrinsic worth of persons — the valuations are for the purpose of commuting a vow with a payment, not for selling people. The provision for the poor (v.8) is significant: the priest adjusts the assessment to what is actually affordable. The vow system is not designed to bankrupt the devout.

notes.original: חֵרֶם (cherem)
notes.why: The devoted thing — the most extreme form of dedication, irrevocable and absolute. Unlike ordinary vows (which can be redeemed with a fifth added), cherem cannot be redeemed, bought back, or transferred. It passes entirely and permanently to the LORD. The word cherem appears throughout the Hebrew Bible with two related senses: sacred dedication (as here) and the ban of total destruction in holy war (Joshua 6–7). Both senses involve irreversibility and the removal of something from ordinary human use. A person under cherem cannot be ransomed (v.29) — the most absolute claim the law makes about irreversible consecration.

notes.original: The tithe
notes.why: The tithe (maʼaser, the tenth) is distinct from voluntary offerings and vows — it is automatic, already owed. Verse 30 states flatly: every tithe of the land is the LORD’s. The tithe is not a gift but an acknowledgment of divine ownership of the land’s produce (the same theology as chapter 25’s land-ownership claim). The tithe of herds and flocks (v.32) is determined by counting — every tenth animal passing under the shepherd’s staff is the LORD’s, regardless of its quality. The randomness prevents cheating: you cannot pick the worst animals as the tenth.

notes.original: The final colophon
notes.why: The book closes with the same phrase that opened chapter 25: “on Mount Sinai.” The two colophons (26:46 and 27:34) form a bracket around the closing chapters, and together with 7:38 and 25:1 they locate the entire book within the Sinai revelation. The final word of Leviticus is “Sinai” — the mountain of encounter, the source of everything the book contains. Everything from the first burnt offering to the final tithe law is Sinai law: received at the mountain, carried into the wilderness, and eventually into the land. The book ends where it began — in the presence of the God who speaks.

intro: Every rendering below diverges in some meaningful way from standard English translations, including the WEB. Each is driven by the Greek text of the NA28. A note on voice follows the tables.
I. The Prologue (1:1–4)

notes.original: epechēsan
notes.rendering: taken in hand
notes.why: Epicheireiō is a vivid verb — to put one’s hand to something, to undertake with real effort. Luke uses it to acknowledge his predecessors while signalling his own work will be more rigorous. The physical energy of the verb is worth preserving.

notes.original: peplērophorēmenōn
notes.rendering: brought to completion
notes.why: Plērophoreō means to bring to full measure, to carry out completely. These are not merely events that occurred — they are events that have run their full intended course. The word carries a sense of divine purpose fulfilled.

notes.original: hypēretai tou logou
notes.rendering: attendants of the word
notes.why: Hypēretēs literally means an under-rower — one who pulls an oar below decks. It comes to mean an active subordinate servant. These witnesses did not merely see; they devoted themselves to serving the word. “Attendant” catches the active, dedicated quality.

notes.original: parekolōuthēkoti
notes.rendering: having followed carefully
notes.why: Parakolouthē means to follow alongside, to trace a path, to investigate by tracking. It is the word of a historian doing painstaking research — following the trail wherever it leads. Luke is not an eyewitness; he is a thorough investigator.

notes.original: asphalēian
notes.rendering: the certainty
notes.why: Asphaleia means firmness — the quality of ground that will not give way. Luke’s goal is not that Theophilus would believe more emotionally but that he would stand on solid ground. This is an epistemological claim.

notes.original: steira
notes.rendering: barren
notes.why: Steira is the specific clinical word for a woman unable to conceive. It places Elizabeth in the company of Sarah, Hannah, and Rachel — barren women through whom God overturns expectation. The word marks the situation as humanly hopeless before the reversal.

notes.original: ēlachen
notes.rendering: the sacred lot falls
notes.why: Lanchanō means to obtain by lot. The incense altar was assigned by lot (the Tamid); a priest might serve once in a lifetime, or never at all. This is Zechariah’s one moment. He does not choose it. God arranges it. The explanatory phrase “as it sometimes did” is added for the modern reader who does not know the priestly system.

notes.original: dēsis
notes.rendering: petition
notes.why: Dēsis is a specific request — a petition for a particular thing. Zechariah has been praying for a child, probably for decades. The angel connects this moment directly to that precise, long-held prayer. “Petition” preserves the specificity that “prayer” blurs.

notes.original: apeithēs
notes.rendering: the disobedient
notes.why: Apeithēs literally means the unpersuaded — those who have heard and refused to be convinced. This is not simple moral failure but stubborn resistance to the call. John’s ministry targets hard hearts.

notes.original: kata ti gnōsomai touto
notes.rendering: How am I supposed to know?
notes.why: The Greek is literally “According to what shall I know this?” — a request for a sign or evidence. The fireside voice renders it as natural spoken speech: a startled old man pushing back. The meaning is identical; the register is human.

notes.original: parēstēkōs
notes.rendering: I stand
notes.why: A perfect active participle: I have taken my stand and remain standing. Gabriel’s status before God is permanent and ongoing. He is never anywhere else.

notes.original: chaire
notes.rendering: Rejoice
notes.why: Chaire is the common Greek greeting, but it derives from chairō, to rejoice. More importantly, it echoes the LXX messianic cry to Zion: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion” (Zechariah 9:9; Zephaniah 3:14). Gabriel’s opening word to Mary is the signal that the long-awaited moment has arrived. “Greetings” misses this entirely.

notes.original: kecharitomentē
notes.rendering: you who have been graced
notes.why: A perfect passive participle of charitoou — to grace, to pour grace upon. The perfect tense means: this has already happened. Mary arrives already graced. The angel does not confer the grace — he names what God has already done.

notes.original: andra ou ginōskō
notes.rendering: I haven’t known a man
notes.why: Ginōskō is the LXX word for sexual knowledge (Genesis 4:1, etc.). Mary’s question is not naive — she understands conception. The present tense describes her current state: she has not been with a man. The fireside rendering keeps the idiom but in plain English.

notes.original: episkiasei
notes.rendering: will overshadow
notes.why: Episkiazō is used in the LXX for the glory-cloud settling on the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). Luke is deliberate: Mary becomes a new tabernacle. The divine presence that filled the tent of meeting will fill her.

notes.original: to gennōmenon hagion
notes.rendering: the holy one being born
notes.why: Literally: the holy thing/one being born. The holiness is simultaneous with the birth — not a quality Jesus will acquire. The present participle “being born” keeps this immediacy.

notes.original: pân rhēma
notes.rendering: No word from God
notes.why: Rhēma is a spoken word, a specific utterance — not logos (the abstract Word). The angel says: no spoken thing from God is without power. This echoes Genesis 18:14 LXX — God’s word about Sarah’s impossible pregnancy. Mary’s faith in v.38 is a direct answer to this promise.

notes.original: megalynei
notes.rendering: make the Lord great
notes.why: Megalynō: to make great, to magnify. Mary’s praise is not passive — it actively enlarges who God is, the way a lens makes something larger and clearer. The soul does something here.

notes.original: ēgalliasen
notes.rendering: exults
notes.why: Agalliaō is one of the strongest joy words in Greek — to leap for joy, to exult bodily. It shares a root with the leaping of John in the womb (v.44). Mary’s spirit does not merely feel glad; it leaps.

notes.original: hyperephánous
notes.rendering: the arrogant
notes.why: Hyperephános: one who displays himself above others. Not simply proud in the heart, but performing superiority for an audience. God scatters them in the very schemes they’ve been hatching.

notes.original: Aorist verbs
notes.rendering: The prophetic aorists
notes.why: The Magnificat’s verbs in vv.51–53 are all aorist — grammatically past tense. He scattered. He brought down. He lifted up. He filled. He sent away. None of this has visibly happened when Mary sings. This is the prophetic aorist: what God has decreed is already accomplished in the divine economy. Mary sings the revolution as a done deal. The aorists are retained. Flattening them to present tense loses the theological punch.

notes.original: dynastas
notes.rendering: the powerful
notes.why: Dynastes: one who holds actual power over others — a potentate, a ruler. This is not a spiritualized “mighty.” The Magnificat has a concrete political and economic edge. People with real power are removed.

notes.original: epēskepsato kai epoiēsen lytrōsin
notes.rendering: visited and accomplished redemption
notes.why: Two aorists. Episkeptomai: to visit, to come to look after someone with intent to help — the word of God’s Exodus intervention. Poieō lytrōsin: to make, to accomplish, to produce redemption. Zechariah prophesies as though it has already happened — because in God’s purpose, it has.

notes.original: keras sōtērias
notes.rendering: a horn of salvation
notes.why: The horn of a ram or bull — concentrated, focused power. A deeply Psalmic image (Psalm 18:2; 132:17). Smoothing it to “a mighty savior” loses the image. The horn is worth keeping. It should sound slightly strange.

notes.original: anatolē ex hypsous
notes.rendering: the rising sun from on high
notes.why: Anatolē: rising (of the sun), the east. But in the LXX it also renders the Hebrew tsemach — the Branch, the Messianic Shoot of Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12. Luke may hold both simultaneously: the dawn breaking AND the promised Branch. “The rising sun will visit us from on high” attempts to honour both registers.

notes.original: en tais erēmois
notes.rendering: in the wilderness
notes.why: The Greek is plural: in the wildernesses, the deserted places. John does not retreat to one location — he moves through desolate country. The singular “wilderness” is retained as it reads more naturally in English, but the sense of wandering, sparse, open landscape should be felt.

intro: Luke 2 is the most familiar chapter in the Gospel, and familiarity is the translator's chief obstacle. Centuries of Christmas tradition have fixed certain images in English — the inn, the manger, the angelic choir — that the Greek does not quite support. The renderings below recover the concrete vocabulary underneath: a guest room, a feeding trough, a heavenly army. The chapter closes with the only story of Jesus' boyhood in the canonical Gospels, and its final exchange turns on a phrase whose ambiguity Luke may well have intended.

notes.original: tēn oikoumenēn
notes.rendering: the inhabited world
notes.why: Oikoumenē means the inhabited, civilised world — the Roman Empire as understood by its subjects. “All the world” (WEB) is vague. “The inhabited world” captures the imperial scope Luke intends without over-claiming.

notes.original: phatsnē
notes.rendering: feeding trough
notes.why: Phatsnē is a feeding trough or manger — the concrete, unglamorous object. “Manger” has become so churchy it no longer registers. “Feeding trough” restores the shock of the image: a newborn king in an animal’s food box.

notes.original: katalyma
notes.rendering: guest room
notes.why: This is the most significant change in the chapter. Katalyma is not the word for a commercial inn (that is pandocheion, used in the Good Samaritan, 10:34). Luke uses katalyma in 22:11 for the upper room of the Last Supper — clearly a guest room in a private house. Mary and Joseph most likely arrived in Bethlehem and found no room in a relative’s guest quarters. The child is born in the lower part of the house, where animals were kept — not in a roadside inn.

notes.original: esparganōsen
notes.rendering: swaddling bands
notes.why: Spargana are the long strips of cloth wound around a newborn to restrict movement, keep warmth, and ‘form’ the limbs. “Strips of cloth” (WEB) is accurate but generic. “Swaddling bands” is specific and traditional without being archaic — and it echoes the angel’s sign in v.12.

notes.original: stratias ouraniou
notes.rendering: heavenly army
notes.why: Stratia is an army, a military host. The “heavenly army” is not a choir of gentle angels but a vast marshalled force — which is why the shepherds were terrified. “Heavenly host” is traditional but has lost its military edge. “Heavenly army” restores it.

notes.original: eudokias (genitive)
notes.rendering: among the people of his favor
notes.why: The genitive eudokias (“of favor/goodwill”) is the better-attested reading (P75, ס, B, A). The nominative eudokia (“goodwill toward men”, KJV/WEB) entered via later manuscripts. The genitive means “people marked by God’s favor” — not humanity in general, but those on whom God’s grace rests. This is a Lukan theme: the upside-down kingdom, the lowly favored.

notes.original: symballousa
notes.rendering: turning them over and over
notes.why: Symballō means to throw things together, to compare, to consider from multiple angles. It’s an active, analytical word — Mary is not passively brooding but actively working to understand. “Turning them over and over” tries to catch this. Compare v.51: diatērei (to keep carefully, preserve) — a different verb, slightly more protective in tone.

notes.original: apolyeis (present)
notes.rendering: you are releasing
notes.why: The Greek is present tense: apolyeis — “you are releasing,” not “you dismiss” (imperatival) or “you may dismiss”. The release is happening now, in this moment, as Simeon holds the child. The present tense makes the Nunc Dimittis immediate and embodied rather than a general request.

notes.original: Phanouel
notes.rendering: Phanuel
notes.why: The Greek is Phanoúēl. The WEB renders this as “Penuel,” the Hebrew form of the name (the place where Jacob wrestled). The Greek form is Phanuel. Since we are translating from the Greek text, Phanuel is correct.

notes.original: odynōmenoi
notes.rendering: in anguish
notes.why: Odynaōmai means to be in pain, to suffer distress. It is a strong word — Luke uses it for the rich man in Hades (16:24–25). Mary is not merely “worried” or “frantic”; she is in real pain. “In anguish” recovers the emotional weight.

notes.original: en tois tou patros mou
notes.rendering: about my Father’s affairs
notes.why: This phrase is famously ambiguous. Literally: “in the [things] of my Father.” It can mean “in my Father’s house” (oikos implied), “about my Father’s business/affairs,” or “among those belonging to my Father.” “In my Father’s house” is traditional and suits the temple setting, but “about my Father’s affairs” preserves the broader ambiguity Luke may intend — the boy is not just in a building, he is already occupied with his Father’s work.

notes.original: hypotassomenos
notes.rendering: submits to them
notes.why: Hypotassō means to arrange under, to subordinate, to submit. It is a deliberate, active word — not mere compliance but chosen subordination. The Son of God, who just claimed to be about his Father’s affairs, goes home and submits to his earthly parents. The tension Luke builds here is theological, not just biographical.

notes.original: proekopten
notes.rendering: advances
notes.why: Prokoptō means to cut forward, to make progress, to advance — like clearing a path through undergrowth. It is dynamic and directional. “Grew” (WEB) is biological; “advances” is volitional. Luke’s Jesus is not just maturing passively — he is pressing forward.

outro: Note on v.24 — the offering of the poor: The Law of Moses (Leviticus 12:6–8) required a lamb for purification after childbirth. If the family could not afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons were permitted. Luke’s quiet detail here — turtledoves, not a lamb — signals that Mary and Joseph are poor. This is consistent with everything else Luke tells us about Jesus: born in a borrowed space, worshiped first by field workers, raised in Galilee rather than Jerusalem. The economic texture is intentional and theologically significant.

intro: Luke 3 moves through four distinct registers: the formal Thucydidean dating formula, John’s blunt prophetic preaching, the brief and luminous baptism scene, and the genealogy with its quiet theological climax. Each section makes its own demands on the translator.
I. The Word Comes to John (3:1–6)

notes.original: Six rulers named
notes.rendering: The dating formula
notes.why: Luke opens with six synchronised political and religious datings — an unmistakably Thucydidean move. The Greek historian dated events by magistrates and offices. Luke is claiming: this is not myth. This happened in verifiable, datable history. The syntax is allowed to stay slightly formal here because the formality is Luke’s own rhetorical purpose.

notes.original: rhēma theou
notes.rendering: a word from God
notes.why: Rhēma is a specific spoken utterance — not logos (the abstract Word). The phrasing echoes the Hebrew prophetic formula: “the word of the LORD came to...” (debar YHWH in the OT; always rhēma or logos kyriou in the LXX). Luke uses rhēma here deliberately: John stands in the prophetic succession. This is the divine commissioning of a prophet.

notes.original: metanoia
notes.rendering: repentance
notes.why: Metanoia means a change of mind — a fundamental reorientation of thought and will. Not merely remorse or regret (that would be metameleia). The baptism does not produce repentance; it marks and announces it. John baptizes those who have already turned.

notes.original: aphesis hamartiōn
notes.rendering: release of sins
notes.why: Aphesis means release, letting go, freedom — the word used for the release of a prisoner or a debt cancelled. “Forgiveness” is accurate but softer. “Release” restores the liberation image: sins are a captivity, and the baptism announces that captivity’s end. The choice between “forgiveness” and “release” is a real translation decision with theological weight; “release” is used here to honour the Jubilee resonance Luke develops throughout his gospel.

notes.original: pharángx
notes.rendering: ravine
notes.why: Pharagx is a ravine, a gorge — a steep-sided cleft in the land. The standard “valley” is too gentle. The landscape of the Isaiah quotation is dramatic and rugged. Ravines will be filled in. Mountains will be levelled. The scale of transformation is geological.

notes.original: gennēmata echidnōn
notes.rendering: offspring of vipers
notes.why: Literally: children/offspring of vipers. Echidna is specifically a viper — a venomous snake. “Brood” is traditional and not wrong; “offspring” is slightly more literal and slightly more contemptuous. John is not calling them dangerous; he is calling them what they are by nature.

notes.original: hypedeixen
notes.rendering: tipped you off
notes.why: Hypodeiknymi means to show secretly, to give a private warning, to tip someone off. It implies insider knowledge passed along quietly. John’s question is pointed: who warned you ahead of time? Who gave you the inside track? The word implies that the crowd’s repentance may be more opportunistic than genuine — they are fleeing wrath, not turning to God.

notes.original: kēitai (present tense)
notes.rendering: is lying
notes.why: The axe is not on its way. It is not being sharpened elsewhere. It is already at the root — keitai, present tense, lying there right now. The judgment is not a future threat; it is a present reality paused on the edge of action. This is one of the most urgent present-tense images in the gospels.

notes.original: chitōnas
notes.rendering: shirts
notes.why: Chitōn is the basic undergarment — a tunic worn next to the skin. The outer garment (himation) was more valuable. John is talking about something as basic as a shirt. The ethics of the kingdom begin with the most ordinary thing in your wardrobe. “Tunic” is accurate; “shirt” is plainer and more immediate for modern readers.

notes.original: diaseisete
notes.rendering: shake anyone down
