notes.why: Diaseiaō means to shake violently — it is the word for shaking a tree to get fruit to fall, applied here to soldiers extorting money by threat or intimidation. “Don’t shake anyone down” is a modern idiom that happens to be the exact Greek metaphor. It is kept.

notes.original: sykophantēsete
notes.rendering: make false accusations
notes.why: Sykophanteō means to accuse falsely in order to extort. Roman soldiers could bring false charges against civilians with near-impunity. John names both forms of military corruption precisely: violent extortion (diaseiaō) and legal extortion by false accusation (sykophanteō).

notes.heading: III. The One Who Is Coming (3:15–18)

notes.original: prosdokōntos tou laou
notes.rendering: full of expectation
notes.why: Prosdokaō means to wait for, to expect, to look for. The genitive absolute here sets the scene: the people are in a state of active, tense anticipation. Not passive curiosity but real messianic expectation. The air is charged.

notes.original: ischyroteros
notes.rendering: the one who is stronger
notes.why: Ischyroteros is the comparative of ischyros — strong, powerful. “Stronger than me” is more precise and more interesting than “mightier” (which has become a vague synonym for “more important”). John is making a specific claim about power: the one coming has more of it than he does.

notes.original: hikanos
notes.rendering: not fit
notes.why: Hikanos means sufficient, adequate, fit for the task. John says he is not sufficient — not qualified, not up to the job — even to untie a sandal strap. In rabbinic tradition, a disciple could perform many menial tasks for a rabbi, but not handle his sandals; that was a slave’s work. John places himself below the level of a slave.

notes.original: en pnēumati hagiō kai pyri
notes.rendering: in the Holy Spirit and in fire
notes.why: The “and fire” is not a separate baptism from the Spirit — it is one baptism in both. Fire in this context is ambiguous in the best way: purifying fire (refiner’s fire, Isaiah 48:10) and consuming fire (the judgment of v.17). The same Spirit-and-fire will fall on some to purify and on others to consume. Luke develops this at Pentecost (Acts 2), where tongues of fire rest on the disciples.

notes.original: ptyon / achuron / asbetos
notes.rendering: winnowing fork / chaff / unquenchable
notes.why: Three precise agricultural terms. Ptyon is a winnowing fork or shovel — used to toss threshed grain into the wind so the chaff blows away. Achuron is the chaff and straw left over — light, worthless, combustible. Asbetos means unquenchable, unable to be put out — the same word used in the LXX for God’s fire of judgment. The image is domestic and terrifying at once: a farmer clearing his floor, a fire that doesn’t go out.

notes.original: proseuchomenou
notes.rendering: while he is praying
notes.why: Only Luke mentions that Jesus is praying when heaven opens. Matthew and Mark do not. Luke’s Jesus is characteristically a man of prayer — he prays before every major event in this gospel: before calling the Twelve (6:12), before Peter’s confession (9:18), at the Transfiguration (9:29), in Gethsemane (22:41). The baptism is the first of these prayer-moments. Heaven opens while Jesus is praying.

notes.original: sōmatikō eidei
notes.rendering: in bodily form
notes.why: Only Luke adds sōmatikō eidei — in bodily form, in physical appearance. The other gospels say the Spirit descends like a dove; Luke says it descends in bodily form, like a dove. This is Luke the physician, or Luke the historian: he wants you to know this was visible, physical, real. Not metaphorical. Not a subjective impression. Something was there.

notes.original: ho agapētos
notes.rendering: the Beloved
notes.why: Agapētos can mean beloved or only — as in an only child, uniquely cherished. Both meanings are present. The voice does not say “a son” but “my Son — the Beloved.” The article and the adjective together make this particular, not generic. There is only one like this.

notes.original: eudokēsa
notes.rendering: I am well pleased
notes.why: Eudokeō means to be pleased, to take delight in, to regard with favor. The aorist here is debated: some read it as a timeless aorist (“I delight in you”); others as pointing to a specific moment (“I have set my delight on you”). Either way, the divine pleasure is directed, personal, and particular. This is not general divine approval of humanity. This is a Father speaking to his Son.

notes.original: hōs enomizeto
notes.rendering: or so it was thought
notes.why: Nomizō means to consider, to suppose, to assume according to custom. The parenthetical is Luke’s own precision: Joseph was the legal father, the publicly recognized father — but the reader of chapters 1–2 knows what actually happened. Luke is not contradicting the virgin birth; he is flagging the gap between public knowledge and theological reality.

notes.original: hōsei etōn triakonta
notes.rendering: about thirty years old
notes.why: Hōsei means approximately, roughly. Luke does not say Jesus is exactly thirty — he says about thirty. This is historiographical modesty: Luke gives the round number without claiming precision he doesn’t have.

notes.original: tou Adam, tou Theou
notes.rendering: son of Adam — son of God
notes.why: The genealogy ends here, and this is everything. Matthew’s genealogy runs from Abraham to Jesus — tracing Jewish messianic lineage. Luke’s runs from Jesus back to Adam, and then one step further: Adam, son of God. Luke’s Jesus is not merely the Jewish Messiah. He is the son of all humanity, and humanity’s origin is in God. The phrase “son of God” at the end of the genealogy forms a direct echo with the voice from heaven in v.22: “You are my Son.” The genealogy is a theological frame for the baptism. Jesus is the Son of God — and through him, what Adam lost is recovered.

outro: Note on the dating formula (3:1–2): Luke synchronises six rulers to date the beginning of John’s ministry. This is the most precise historical dating in the New Testament. “The fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar” most likely refers to AD 28–29 (depending on whether Luke counts from Tiberius’s co-regency in AD 11–12 or from Augustus’s death in AD 14). The point is not to settle the date with modern precision but to recognize what Luke is doing: he is writing the kind of history that can be checked. These are real people. This is a real time. The events he describes happened in the same world where Pontius Pilate governed and Caiaphas officiated.

Note on the two genealogies (Matthew 1 vs. Luke 3): Matthew’s genealogy descends from Abraham to Jesus and is structured in three groups of fourteen generations. Luke’s ascends from Jesus to Adam and contains seventy-seven names. The two lists diverge after David — Matthew follows the royal line through Solomon; Luke follows a different Davidic line through Nathan. Various explanations have been proposed: one is Joseph’s line, one is Mary’s; one is biological, one is legal; both reflect different genealogical traditions in circulation. Luke’s theological point is clear regardless: by tracing Jesus to Adam and then to God, he places Jesus at the head of a new humanity — not just a new Israel.

intro: Luke 4 is one of the most carefully crafted chapters in the gospel. The temptation is a verbal duel in three rounds. The Nazareth scene is the programmatic statement of Jesus’ entire ministry. The exorcism at Capernaum raises the question the rest of the gospel will answer: who is this? Each section makes distinct demands on the translator.
I. The Temptation (4:1–13)

notes.original: plērēs pneumatos hagiou
notes.rendering: full of the Holy Spirit
notes.why: Plērēs means completely full — filled to capacity. Luke has already told us Jesus was baptized and the Spirit descended on him bodily (3:22). Now he uses plērēs: the Spirit doesn’t just rest on Jesus, it fills him. This same fullness characterises the Spirit-filled people throughout Luke-Acts. The temptation happens to a man overflowing with the Spirit — not to a man running low.

notes.original: en tō pneumati
notes.rendering: the Spirit leads him
notes.why: The Spirit does not merely permit the testing — it actively leads Jesus into the wilderness. Luke’s en tō pneumati (in the Spirit) is directional. The wilderness is not an ambush; it is an appointment. Matthew uses anachthē (was led up); Mark uses ekballei (drives/throws him out). Luke’s language is the gentlest of the three, but the agency is unmistakable.

notes.original: peirazomenos
notes.rendering: tested
notes.why: Peirazō means to test, to try, to probe — the same root as the English ‘trial.’ The English ‘tempt’ implies moral seduction; ‘test’ implies a probe of what is really there. Both are present, but ‘tested’ is used here because the devil is not merely trying to seduce Jesus into sin — he is probing the nature of his identity and mission.

notes.original: epēinasen
notes.rendering: he is starving
notes.why: Peinao means to be hungry, but after forty days without food the word carries its full biological weight. Not ‘he was hungry’ (a mild inconvenience) but ‘he is starving’ — the body at its limit. The vulnerability is real. The temptation arrives at the point of genuine physical weakness.

notes.original: ei huios ei tou theou
notes.rendering: If you are the Son of God
notes.why: This is a first-class conditional in Greek — the condition is assumed to be true for the sake of the argument. The devil is not expressing doubt. He is saying: given that you are the Son of God, use that power now. The temptation is not to doubt Jesus’ identity but to misuse it — to deploy divine sonship in the service of self-provision, self-display, and self-exaltation. All three tests have this same structure.

notes.original: paradedotai
notes.rendering: it has been handed over to me
notes.why: Paradedotai is perfect passive indicative: it has been handed over and remains in my possession. The passive implies an agent — someone handed it to him. Luke does not refute the claim. The devil has been given real authority over the kingdoms of the world. This is a serious theological statement, consistent with John 12:31 (‘the ruler of this world’) and 2 Corinthians 4:4 (‘the god of this age’). Jesus does not dispute it. He refuses the offer.

notes.original: achri kairou
notes.rendering: until an opportune time
notes.why: Kairos means a ripe moment, a season — not just any time (chronos) but the right time. The devil doesn’t give up; he waits. Luke signals that the temptation is not over — only paused. The next kairos will be Gethsemane, where Luke notes that the hour of darkness arrives (22:53) and Satan enters Judas (22:3).

notes.original: tethrammenos
notes.rendering: where he had been raised
notes.why: Trephō means to nourish, to feed, to bring up a child. Tethrammenos (perfect passive) means the place where he had been formed and raised — where the whole shape of his life was built. Nazareth is not just his hometown; it is where he became who he is.

notes.original: ptōchois
notes.rendering: the poor
notes.why: Ptōchōs means the truly destitute — one who crouches or cowers, who has nothing. Not the modestly poor (penēs) but the beggar, the utterly without resources. Luke uses this word throughout his gospel with consistent economic and social specificity. The good news is for those with nothing to bring.

notes.original: aichmalōtois aphesis
notes.rendering: release to the captives
notes.why: Aichmalōtos is a prisoner of war, a captive. Aphesis is release, liberation — the same word used for forgiveness of sins (3:3), because both are forms of being set free. The Jubilee resonance (Leviticus 25) is unmistakable: every fiftieth year, debts were cancelled, slaves freed, land returned. Jesus announces a new Jubilee.

notes.original: tethrausmenōus en aphesei
notes.rendering: the crushed in release
notes.why: Thrauo means to break in pieces, to crush. The crushed are those ground down by life, by oppression, by systems larger than themselves. En aphesei — in release, in freedom. This phrase appears to draw on Isaiah 58:6 rather than Isaiah 61 — Luke has conflated two Isaiah passages to construct the composite quotation. The effect is to broaden the scope: physical captivity, spiritual debt, and systemic oppression are all in view.

notes.original: eniauton kyriou dekton
notes.rendering: the year of the Lord’s favor
notes.why: Dektos means acceptable, welcome, received with favor. The year of the Lord’s favor is the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10 LXX). But Jesus stops the quotation at a strategic point — Isaiah 61:2 continues ‘and the day of vengeance of our God.’ Jesus reads the scroll and stops before the judgment. He is proclaiming the day of favor, not yet the day of wrath. The truncation is deliberate and noticed by anyone who knows the text.

notes.original: atenizontes
notes.rendering: every eye is fixed on him
notes.why: Atenizō means to stare intently, to gaze without blinking — the eyes locked on a single point. The whole synagogue goes still. Luke gives us the physical silence before the most important sentence in the chapter.

notes.original: sēmeron peplērōtai
notes.rendering: Today — this scripture has been fulfilled
notes.why: Sēmeron — today — is one of Luke’s signature words. He uses it at the angel’s announcement to the shepherds (2:11), at Zacchaeus’s house (19:9), on the cross to the thief (23:43). Each time it marks a moment of decisive divine action happening right now, in this present moment, not in a future age. The kingdom of God is not coming eventually — it is arriving today, in this room, in your hearing.

notes.original: emartyroun / ethaumazon
notes.rendering: speak well of him / astonished
notes.why: Two reactions simultaneously: martyroun (they bear witness positively, speak well of him) and thaumazon (they are astonished). The crowd’s initial response is favorable wonder. The turn comes in v.23 when Jesus anticipates their demand for proof. The rejection is not immediate — it builds.

notes.original: ophrys
notes.rendering: the edge of the hill
notes.why: Ophrys means the brow — an eyebrow, or the brow of a hill. It is the jutting edge, the cliff-face. Nazareth sits on hilly terrain; there are limestone ridges nearby. The crowd intends to throw him off. The word is precise: not a slope but a sheer drop.

notes.original: diēlthen dia mesou autōn
notes.rendering: walks straight through the middle of them
notes.why: Dierchomai dia mesou: to go through the midst. Luke offers no explanation. The crowd is there; then Jesus is through them and gone. The quiet miracle of it — no drama, no fight, just passage — is more unsettling than a confrontation would be. He goes on his way.

notes.original: en exousia
notes.rendering: his word carries authority
notes.why: Exousia means authority, the right and power to act. The scribes taught by citing predecessors: ‘Rabbi so-and-so said...’ Jesus teaches as one who has the authority in himself. The astonishment is not at his eloquence but at the source of his words. He speaks as if he owns the text.

notes.original: pneuma daimoniou akathártou
notes.rendering: a spirit of an unclean demon
notes.why: Luke’s phrase is unusual and precise: not just an unclean spirit (Mark’s language) but a spirit of an unclean demon — stacking the terms. The redundancy emphasizes contamination, otherness, something that does not belong in the holy assembly. The synagogue is supposed to be a clean place. This is a confrontation.

notes.original: Ea
notes.rendering: Ha!
notes.why: Ea is a Greek exclamation of surprise or protest — something like ‘Ah!’ or ‘Ha!’ or ‘Hey!’ It is a startled outcry. Most translations render it as ‘Leave us alone!’ (taking it as an imperative from eao) but ea as an exclamation is the better reading here — the demon’s first reaction is a cry of recognition and alarm before it speaks.

notes.original: oida se tis ei
notes.rendering: I know who you are
notes.why: The demon knows before the disciples know, before the crowds know, before anyone in the synagogue knows. The spiritual world recognizes Jesus immediately. The irony is thick: the people who should know — the teachers of Israel in the synagogue — are still asking questions, while the unclean spirit announces the answer.

notes.original: erripen auton
notes.rendering: throws the man down
notes.why: Riptō means to hurl, to fling. The demon’s exit is violent — it throws the man to the ground on its way out. But Luke immediately adds: without harming him at all. The exit is dramatic; the man is uninjured. Both details matter.

notes.original: synechomenē pyretō megalō
notes.rendering: in the grip of a severe fever
notes.why: Sunechō means to hold together, to press, to seize — to grip something so tightly it cannot move. Simon’s mother-in-law is not merely feverish; she is held in the fever’s grip. Luke the physician uses clinical language. And in v.39, Jesus rebukes the fever using the same word (epitiman) used for the demon in v.35. Luke is making a point: fever and demon are addressed with the same authority.

notes.original: heni hekastō
notes.rendering: each one of them
notes.why: Heis hekastos means every single one — not a mass healing but individual, personal attention. The crowd is large; Jesus lays hands on each one. This is one of Luke’s consistent emphases: the particular person, not just the crowd.

notes.original: katechon auton
notes.rendering: try to hold him back
notes.why: Katecheō means to hold back, to restrain, to detain. The crowds find him in the deserted place and physically try to stop him from leaving. The word is strong — not ‘they asked him to stay’ but ‘they tried to hold him there.’ He cannot be held.

notes.original: dei me euangelisasthai
notes.rendering: I must proclaim
notes.why: Dei means it is necessary, it must happen — a word of divine compulsion in Luke. Jesus uses it at key moments to express the necessity driving his mission: he must be in his Father’s house (2:49), he must proclaim the good news (4:43), he must go to Jerusalem (13:33), the Son of Man must suffer (9:22). The dei is not external obligation but the inner logic of his calling.

outro: Note on the Isaiah quotation (4:18–19): The text Jesus reads does not correspond exactly to any single passage in Isaiah. It draws primarily on Isaiah 61:1–2 (LXX), but the line ‘to send away the crushed in release’ (apostellai tethrausmenous en aphesei) appears to come from Isaiah 58:6 LXX. This is a deliberate composite — a reading that weaves together two Isaianic visions of liberation. Jesus, or Luke, or both, are constructing a programmatic text from the Isaiah scroll that encompasses physical, economic, and spiritual freedom simultaneously.

Note on the three temptations in Luke vs. Matthew: Matthew’s order is stones-to-bread, pinnacle of the temple, mountain with all kingdoms. Luke’s order is stones-to-bread, all the kingdoms, pinnacle of the temple. Luke’s sequence ends in Jerusalem — and Jerusalem is where Luke’s entire gospel is heading. The final temptation in Luke takes place in the holy city, on the holy temple. This is not an accident. Luke’s narrative geography is theological: everything moves toward Jerusalem.

intro: Luke 5 introduces four scenes that will define Jesus’ ministry in Galilee: a calling, a cleansing, a controversy, and a feast. The Greek of each is precise and worth attending to closely.
I. The Catch of Fish and the Calling of Simon (5:1–11)

notes.original: limnēn Gennesaret
notes.rendering: Lake Gennesaret
notes.why: The body of water Luke calls Limnē Gennesaret — Lake Gennesaret — is known in other gospels as the Sea of Galilee or Sea of Tiberias. Limnē means lake, not sea (thalassa). Luke, writing for a Hellenistic audience, uses the more geographically accurate term. It is a large freshwater lake. Calling it a sea was local hyperbole. Luke does not indulge it.

notes.original: epí to bathos
notes.rendering: the deep water
notes.why: Bathos means depth — the deep part, the open water away from the shallows where the fish are in daylight. Simon has just spent all night working the shallows and caught nothing. Jesus tells him to go out to the deep and try again, in full daylight, when experienced fishermen would not expect a catch. The command is counterintuitive. Simon’s obedience is therefore the more striking.

notes.original: epití sō rhēmati
notes.rendering: on your word
notes.why: Rhēma again — a specific spoken word, a particular utterance. Simon does not say ‘because you told me to’ or ‘since you asked.’ He says: on your word. He is staking his professional judgment on a single utterance from a carpenter-teacher who has just been using his boat as a pulpit. The phrase is an act of faith rendered in the most understated possible way.

notes.original: prosepeêten tois gonasin
notes.rendering: falls down at Jesus’ knees
notes.why: Prospiptō means to fall toward, to throw oneself down. The specific detail — at his knees, not at his feet — is Luke’s alone. Simon is on the boat, in the middle of a haul that is sinking the vessel, and he collapses to his knees in front of Jesus. The physical posture is worship and terror at once.

notes.original: anēr hamartolos
notes.rendering: I’m a sinful man
notes.why: Anēr hamartolos — a sinful man. Not ‘I have committed sins’ but ‘this is what I am.’ Simon’s response to holiness is not gratitude or amazement but self-knowledge. He sees himself clearly for the first time and it undoes him. The same pattern appears in Isaiah 6:5 (‘Woe to me, I am ruined, for I am a man of unclean lips’) and Job 42:5–6. The encounter with the holy produces not comfort but exposure.

notes.original: anthrōpous esē zōgrōn
notes.rendering: you will be catching people
notes.why: Zōgreō means to catch alive — to take living. It is used of capturing animals or prisoners without killing them. The word is deliberate: Simon will not be collecting the dead but catching the living. The fishing metaphor is transformed: the point is not to bring in a haul but to bring in living people. The present tense periphrastic (esē zōgrōn) suggests an ongoing activity, not a one-time event.

notes.original: aphentes panta
notes.rendering: they leave everything
notes.why: Panta means everything — not most things, not what they can spare. The nets, the boats, the fish (the largest haul of their careers, still in the water), the business, the life. Luke’s version of the calling has the greatest cost because the call comes after the greatest abundance. They are not abandoning failure. They are abandoning success.

notes.heading: II. The Man Covered in Leprosy (5:12–16)

notes.original: plērēs lepras
notes.rendering: covered all over with leprosy
notes.why: Plērēs means completely full — the same word used of Jesus being full of the Spirit (4:1). This man is full of leprosy, utterly consumed by it. Luke the physician uses clinical language: this is not a mild case. The man is at the extreme end of the disease and therefore of ritual uncleanness. He should not be in a town at all. He should be calling out ‘Unclean!’ (Leviticus 13:45–46). His approach to Jesus is a double transgression: entering a populated area and approaching a teacher.

notes.original: ean theleis
notes.rendering: if you are willing
notes.why: The leper does not doubt Jesus’ power. He doubts whether Jesus will choose to exercise it on someone like him. This is one of the most theologically piercing moments in the chapter: the man is certain of the ability and uncertain of the willingness. Jesus’ answer — thelō, I am willing — is therefore the answer to the deepest question, not just the medical one.

notes.original: ēpsato
notes.rendering: touches him
notes.why: Touch is the transgression. Leviticus 13–14 makes touching a leper a source of ritual contamination. Jesus does not heal at a distance, does not speak from across the room. He reaches out and makes contact. By the rules of the purity system, the uncleanness should transfer to Jesus. Instead, the cleanness transfers to the man. The direction of contagion has reversed.

notes.original: hypēn en tais erēmois kai proseuchomenos
notes.rendering: withdraws to deserted places and prays
notes.why: An imperfect periphrastic — a repeated, habitual action. This is not one withdrawal; it is a pattern. The more the crowds press in, the more consistently Jesus retreats to deserted places to pray. Luke’s Jesus is the most consistently prayerful of the four gospels. The withdrawals are not reluctance but discipline — the source is being replenished.

notes.heading: III. The Man Let Down Through the Roof (5:17–26)

notes.original: dynamis kyriou ēn eis to iasthai
notes.rendering: the power of the Lord is present for him to heal
notes.why: A remarkable phrase. The power of the Lord is present — present, actively available, here in this room. The infinitive eis to iasthai (for the purpose of healing) indicates the power is directed and purposeful. Luke signals to the reader that what is about to happen is not accidental. The room is charged before the paralyzed man arrives.

notes.original: dia tōn keramidōn
notes.rendering: take off the tiles
notes.why: Keramis means a roof tile — a fired clay tile. Luke’s roofing material is different from Mark’s version (2:4), where they dig through a flat earthen roof. Luke’s house has tiled roofing, which is consistent with a more Hellenistic setting. The detail is not incidental: Luke is writing for readers who know what a tiled roof is.

notes.original: anthrōpe, apheontai soi hai hamartiai sou
notes.rendering: Friend — your sins are released
notes.why: Anthrōpe is simply ‘man’ or ‘human being’ — but used as a form of address it is warm and direct: friend, fellow. Jesus does not say ‘your sins are forgiven’ in the passive voice of divine action at a distance. He speaks the release himself, in the present tense, to the man’s face. The scribes immediately understand the claim being made. They are not wrong about what he has said; they are wrong about who he is.

notes.original: epignōs tous dialogismous
notes.rendering: knows what they are thinking
notes.why: Epiginōskō means to know fully, to perceive clearly. Dialogismos means an internal reasoning, a turning-over of arguments in the mind. Jesus perceives their interior debate before they have spoken. Luke uses this verb to signal that Jesus’ knowledge is not inference from facial expressions — it is direct perception of what is happening inside them.

notes.original: exousia… epi tēs gēs
notes.rendering: authority on earth
notes.why: The phrase ‘on earth’ is doing real theological work. The scribes’ objection was correct on one level: releasing sins is a divine prerogative. Jesus does not dispute this. Instead he claims that the Son of Man has this authority — here, on earth, in a room in Galilee, not only in heaven. The miracle is the proof of the claim: if he can do one, he can do the other.

notes.original: paradoxa
notes.rendering: extraordinary things
notes.why: Paradoxos means contrary to expectation, incredible, beyond the ordinary — the root of the English ‘paradox.’ The crowd does not say they have seen miracles or signs or wonders. They say they have seen things outside the category of the expected. Luke’s word choice is precise: these events do not fit into any existing framework.

notes.original: etheasato
notes.rendering: notices
notes.why: Theaomai means to gaze at, to observe carefully — to really look at someone. Jesus does not merely glance at Levi. He looks at him. The word is used of deliberate, attentive seeing — the kind that takes someone in fully. Levi is noticed, truly seen, before a word is spoken.

notes.original: telōnēn
notes.rendering: tax booth
notes.why: Tēlōnēs is a tax collector; the tēlōnion is his booth or office — the place of business where he sits and collects. Levi is at his post, at work. The call does not come during a moment of spiritual seeking or personal crisis. He is simply doing his job.

notes.original: katalipōn panta
notes.rendering: leaves everything
notes.why: The same phrase as 5:11 — aphentes panta (the fishermen) and here katalipōn panta (Levi). Luke is deliberate: both the fishermen and the tax collector leave everything. But there is a difference. Simon, James, and John can go back to fishing — their boats and nets will still be there. Levi cannot go back. A tax franchise once abandoned cannot be reclaimed. His leaving is irreversible.

notes.original: dochēn megalēn
notes.rendering: a great banquet
notes.why: Dochē means a reception, a feast given in someone’s honor. Megalēn means great, large, lavish. Levi’s first act after being called is to throw a party for Jesus — and to fill it with his own people: other tax collectors, other social outcasts. The feast is an act of witness. He brings his world to Jesus the only way he knows how.

notes.original: iatrós
notes.rendering: a doctor
notes.why: Iatros is a physician — Luke’s own profession according to tradition (Colossians 4:14). The doctor illustration may be the one moment in the gospel where we hear Luke’s own vocation echoed in the words of Jesus. Whether coincidence or not, the image is exactly right: a doctor goes to the sick, not to demonstrate affinity with sickness but because the sick are the ones who need him.

notes.original: huioi tou nymphonos
notes.rendering: wedding guests
notes.why: Literally: sons of the bridal chamber — the close companions of the bridegroom, the wedding party. The idiom is Semitic: ‘sons of’ often indicates membership in a category or sharing in a quality. These are people defined by their proximity to the bridegroom and by the joy of the occasion. Fasting during a wedding feast would be a contradiction in terms.

notes.original: apathēē
notes.rendering: taken away
notes.why: Apairō means to take away by force, to remove — it is a violent word. The bridegroom is not simply absent; he is taken. This is the first hint in Luke’s gospel of a violent end. The shadow falls across the wedding feast image just for a moment, then passes. The disciples would not have understood it yet. The reader of the full story does.

notes.original: oudemeis … epiblema
notes.rendering: Nobody tears a patch
notes.why: The parable of the garments is about incompatibility — not just impracticality. The new patch and the old garment belong to different worlds. Putting them together destroys both. Jesus is not saying the old is bad or the new is good; he is saying they cannot be mixed without mutual destruction.

notes.original: ho palaios chrēstos estin
notes.rendering: The old is good
notes.why: Chrēstos means good, pleasant, agreeable — comfortable, even. This last saying is quietly devastating. Nobody who has been drinking old wine wants new — because the old wine is good, it is pleasant, it is familiar. The resistance to Jesus is not primarily moral failure; it is the deep human preference for what is known and comfortable over what is new and disruptive. The parable does not condemn this preference. It simply names it.

outro: Note on ‘releasing sins’ vs. ‘forgiving sins’ (5:20–24): Throughout Luke 5, the word for what Jesus does with sins is aphíemi — to release, to let go, to send away. The noun form is aphesis (used in 3:3 and 4:18). The consistent translation here is ‘release’ rather than ‘forgive’ — not because forgiveness is wrong, but because release is more concrete. A prisoner is released. A debt is released. A captive goes free. The forgiveness metaphor has become so familiar that it can lose its force; ‘release’ restores the physical, legal, and Jubilee dimensions of what Luke’s Jesus is doing.

Note on the three callings in Luke 5 (Simon/James/John, and Levi): Luke has arranged these two calling scenes so that they bracket the healing of the leper and the paralyzed man. The structure is calling — healing — calling. And in both callings, everything is left behind. Luke is building a picture of what it means to follow Jesus: it means the complete reorientation of a life, not a supplemental religious commitment. The fishermen leave their catch. The tax collector leaves his franchise. Both leave what defines them.

intro: Luke 6 is the Sermon on the Plain — shorter and more concentrated than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount, and in some ways harder. The Beatitudes are followed immediately by Woes. The love-your-enemies teaching is addressed to people who actually have enemies. The chapter ends not with comfort but with a choice. The Greek rewards close attention throughout.
I. Lord of the Sabbath and the Withered Hand (6:1–11)

notes.original: psōchontes tais chersin
notes.rendering: rubbing them in their hands
notes.why: Psōchō means to rub, to crush between the fingers. Luke’s detail is specific: the disciples are rubbing the grain in their hands to separate the kernels from the husks. This is what triggers the Pharisaic objection — rubbing grain is a form of threshing, and threshing is work, and work is prohibited on the Sabbath. The physical detail makes the controversy concrete rather than abstract.

notes.original: paretrēroun
notes.rendering: watching him closely
notes.why: Paratēreō means to watch narrowly, to observe with intent, to keep under surveillance. It is not casual observation; it is calculated watching designed to catch something. The imperfect tense suggests they were doing this continuously. The synagogue has become a trap.

notes.original: psychēn sōsai ē apolasai
notes.rendering: to save a life or to destroy it
notes.why: Psychē means soul, self, life — the living person. Sōzō means to save, to rescue, to preserve. Apollymi means to destroy, to ruin, to cause to perish. Jesus frames the Sabbath question as a binary: the law either permits saving life or it permits destroying it. There is no neutral ground. Inaction in the presence of suffering is not the same as keeping the Sabbath; it is a choice to destroy.

notes.original: anoia
notes.rendering: fury
notes.why: Anoia literally means mindlessness, lack of reason — but in this context it means rage, senseless fury. It is the anger that has shut down rational thought. The Pharisees are not calculating; they are seething. Luke’s word strips away any pretense of principled objection: what fills them is not theology but rage.

notes.heading: II. The Choosing of the Twelve (6:12–16)

notes.original: en tē proseuche tou theou
notes.rendering: in prayer to God
notes.why: The phrase is unusual — literally ‘in the prayer of God.’ Some read it as an intensive: the prayer of/to God, as opposed to routine prayer. It underlines that this is not a human decision. The choosing of the Twelve follows a whole night of prayer. The apostolate is the result of divine deliberation, not political calculation.

notes.original: apostolous
notes.rendering: apostles
notes.why: Apostolos means one who is sent — a commissioned agent, an envoy sent with full authority to represent the sender. Jesus names the Twelve both as disciples (mathētais — learners, students) and as apostles (sent ones). The two roles are related but distinct: they are still learning, but they are also already being deployed.

notes.original: prodotēs
notes.rendering: who becomes a traitor
notes.why: Prodotēs means a betrayer, one who hands over — from prodidōmi, to give over into the hands of another. Luke’s use of the present participle here is striking: ‘who became a traitor’ or ‘who was to become a traitor.’ The word is not a prediction inserted after the fact; it is Luke alerting his reader to what is coming from the very first time the Twelve are listed. Judas is named and named truly.

notes.original: makarios
notes.rendering: Blessed
notes.why: Makarios in classical Greek describes the blessed state of the gods — those who are beyond the reach of human misery. In the LXX it is used to describe the person whom God favors, the one who is in a right relationship with God and therefore flourishing. It is not a command (‘be happy’) or a wish (‘may you be happy’) but a declaration: this person is in a state of genuine well-being, regardless of appearances. The Beatitudes are not aspirational; they are announcements of a reality already in motion.

notes.original: hoi ptōchoi
notes.rendering: you who are poor
notes.why: Luke’s Beatitudes are addressed in the second person — ‘you who are poor’ — not the third person (‘blessed are the poor in spirit,’ Matthew 5:3). Luke’s poor are the economically destitute, standing in front of Jesus. Matthew’s spiritualising addition (‘in spirit’) is absent. The kingdom of God is declared to belong to people who have nothing. The directness of the second person makes it impossible to spiritualise away.

notes.original: gelasete
notes.rendering: you will laugh
notes.why: Gelao means to laugh — actual laughter, not merely ‘rejoicing.’ The promise to those who weep now is not that they will feel better or find peace; it is that they will laugh. The word is physical, audible, socially visible. The eschatological reversal is not a spiritual recalibration but a genuine turn of events that will produce real laughter.

notes.original: ekbalōsin to onoma hymōn hōs ponēron
notes.rendering: throw your name out as evil
notes.why: Ekballō means to throw out, to expel, to cast aside. The phrase is vivid: they will throw out your name — expel it from respectable discourse, treat it as something to be discarded. The social ostracism here is not subtle exclusion but active expulsion. Your name becomes refuse.

notes.original: apechete tēn paraklēsin hymōn
notes.rendering: you have received your comfort in full
notes.why: Apechō is a technical commercial term meaning to have received payment in full — the word used on ancient receipts: ‘paid in full.’ The rich have already cashed their check. Their comfort is not coming — it has already been paid out. This is not a prediction of future punishment so much as a statement about the present: those whose comfort is in present wealth have already received everything they are going to get.

notes.original: kalōs hymas eipōsin pantes
notes.rendering: when everyone speaks well of you
notes.why: The fourth Woe mirrors the fourth Beatitude. The Beatitude: blessed when people hate you for the Son of Man’s sake. The Woe: woe when everyone approves of you. The implication is that faithfulness to Jesus produces friction with the world. Universal approval is therefore a warning sign, not an achievement. The prophets who received universal approval were the false ones.

notes.original: agapate tous echthrous
notes.rendering: love your enemies
notes.why: Agapaō is not the same as liking, enjoying, or feeling warmly toward. It is a word for deliberate, chosen, active goodwill — the will to seek another’s genuine good regardless of feeling. Echthrós means an enemy, a hated one — not a mild annoyance or a rival but someone actively opposed to you, someone who wishes you harm. Jesus is not asking his listeners to feel fond of their enemies. He is asking them to choose their enemies’ good anyway.

notes.original: kalōs poieite
notes.rendering: Do good
notes.why: Kalōs poieō means to do beautifully, to act in a way that is genuinely good and admirable. The word kalōs carries aesthetic as well as moral weight — there is something excellent and whole about this action. Doing good to those who hate you is not merely tolerant or patient; it is, in Luke’s vocabulary, beautiful.

notes.original: ton chitōna
notes.rendering: your shirt
notes.why: The chiton is the undergarment — the basic inner tunic worn next to the skin. The himation (cloak) is the outer garment, also used as a sleeping blanket — which is why Exodus 22:26–27 prohibited taking someone’s cloak as collateral overnight. Jesus says: if someone takes the outer garment, give the inner one too. The escalation strips the person completely. The point is not a legal formula but the posture of radical non-grasping.

notes.original: hupsistou
notes.rendering: sons of the Most High
notes.why: Hypsistos — the Most High — is the divine title used by Gentiles and in LXX passages addressed to a non-Jewish world. Luke uses it in Gabriel’s announcement (1:32, 35) and here. The people who love their enemies, who are kind to the ungrateful, who do good without expecting return — these people resemble God. They become recognizable as his children because they act like him.

notes.original: oiktermōn
notes.rendering: compassionate
notes.why: Oiktermōn means full of compassion, merciful — from oiktos, pity, the visceral response to another’s suffering. Matthew’s parallel has ‘perfect’ (teleios, Matthew 5:48). Luke’s word is relational and emotional: be moved by what moves your Father. The standard is not abstract perfection but the concrete compassion of a God who is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

notes.heading: V. Judging, Tree and Fruit, Two Builders (6:37–49)

notes.original: apolyete
notes.rendering: Release
notes.why: Apolyo means to release, to set free, to let go. The three commands in v.37–38 form a sequence: don’t judge, don’t condemn, release. The third word is often translated ‘forgive’ — but apolyete is release, not aphiete (which is the forgiveness word). The image is of unclenching a hand, of letting something go rather than holding it. The mercy asked for is not grudging forgiveness but genuine letting go.

notes.original: metron kalōn pepiesmenon
notes.rendering: A good measure — pressed down, shaken together, running over
notes.why: Three agricultural participles describing a measure of grain filled to absolute capacity: pressed down so it settles and compacts, shaken together so no air pockets remain, and then heaped until it runs over the brim. The image is of extravagant, impossible-to-contain generosity. What you give out will come back in a measure that exceeds what any container should hold.

notes.original: karphos / dokos
notes.rendering: splinter / beam
notes.why: Karphos is a chip of wood, a splinter, a speck — something tiny. Dokos is a roof beam — a structural timber. The comic disproportion is the point: the person trying to remove a splinter from someone else’s eye is walking around with a ceiling joist in their own. The humor is deliberate and pointed. Jesus is not being merely metaphorical; he is being absurd on purpose.

notes.original: ek tou perisseumatōs tēs kardias
notes.rendering: from what overflows in the heart
notes.why: Perisseuma means abundance, overflow, surplus — what spills over because the container is full. The mouth does not produce what the will selects; it produces what overflows from what the heart is actually full of. Speech is not a performance of character; it is a symptom of it. What comes out under pressure is what is really inside.

notes.original: ethemēliosen epi tēn petran
notes.rendering: laid the foundation on rock
notes.why: Themelioo means to lay a foundation, to establish on a base. Luke’s version of the parable is different from Matthew’s (7:24–27): in Matthew, one man builds on rock and the other on sand. In Luke, one man digs down deep and lays a foundation on rock; the other builds directly on the ground, without digging at all. Luke’s contrast is between the man who does the hard, invisible work of digging and the man who doesn’t bother. The foundation is not visible from the street. The difference is only revealed when the flood comes.

notes.original: euthys epesen
notes.rendering: immediately it collapsed
notes.why: Euthys means immediately, at once — without delay. The house built without a foundation does not gradually weaken; it collapses at once. And the ruin — to rhēgma — is great. Luke’s version of the parable ends harder than Matthew’s. There is no softening. The collapse is sudden and total.

outro: Note on the Beatitudes and Woes as a unit: Luke’s four Beatitudes and four Woes are structurally parallel — each Beatitude has a matching Woe that inverts it exactly. Poor/rich. Hungry/full. Weeping/laughing. Hated for the Son of Man’s sake/praised by everyone. The parallelism is not incidental; it is the argument. The kingdom of God reverses the present order. What looks like blessing now — wealth, satiation, laughter, universal approval — is not the final word. What looks like misery now — poverty, hunger, grief, social exclusion — is not the final word either. The Woes are not curses or condemnations; they are warnings issued to people who are in danger of mistaking their present comfort for their ultimate security.

Note on Luke’s Sermon vs. Matthew’s: Luke’s Sermon on the Plain (6:17–49) and Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (5:1–7:29) share substantial material but differ in setting, length, and tone. Matthew’s sermon contains 107 verses; Luke’s contains 30. Luke’s version is more compressed, more concrete, and more economically specific. The poor in Luke are the economically destitute; in Matthew they are the ‘poor in spirit.’ Luke’s Sermon is delivered on a level place (epi topou pedinou) to a crowd that includes sick people and those tormented by demons. Matthew’s is delivered on a mountain to the disciples. Whether these are two versions of one sermon or two different sermons has been debated for centuries. For this paraphrase, Luke’s version stands on its own terms.

intro: Luke 7 is the chapter of outsiders who get it right. A Roman soldier understands authority better than Israel’s teachers. A dead boy’s mother is seen by Jesus before anyone asks. John asks the hardest possible question from prison. A sinful woman weeps on Jesus’ feet while a Pharisee watches and misses everything. The Greek is at its most precise in all four scenes.
I. The Centurion’s Servant (7:1–10)

notes.original: entimos
notes.rendering: dear to him
notes.why: Entimos means held in honor, prized, valued — precious to someone. The servant is not merely useful property; he is dear to the centurion. Luke establishes the personal stake before establishing the desperation. The miracle is asked for out of love, not merely necessity.

notes.original: ou gar hikanos eimi
notes.rendering: I am not worthy
notes.why: Hikanos means sufficient, adequate, fit for the task — the same word John used of himself in relation to Jesus (3:16). The centurion places himself in the same posture as the Baptist: not fit. And yet this is the man Jesus calls the greatest example of faith in Israel. The posture of unworthiness and the reality of extraordinary faith are held together without contradiction.

notes.original: tassomenos hypo exousian
notes.rendering: a man under authority
notes.why: The centurion’s argument is precise: he understands how authority works because he is both under it and over others. He does not say ‘I am a powerful man’ but ‘I am a man under authority.’ His power derives from submission to a higher command. He recognizes in Jesus the same structure: a word from this man carries the force of the authority behind him. This is the theological insight that astonishes Jesus.

notes.original: ethaumasen
notes.rendering: he is astonished
notes.why: Thaumazo means to be amazed, to marvel, to be struck with wonder. Luke uses this word of the crowds throughout the gospel — but here it is used of Jesus. Jesus is astonished at the centurion. This is one of only two places in the gospels where Jesus is said to marvel (the other is Mark 6:6, where he marvels at unbelief in Nazareth). The centurion’s faith produces in Jesus the same response that Jesus’ miracles produce in the crowds.

notes.original: esplagchnisthē
notes.rendering: his heart breaks for her
notes.why: Splagchnizomai is one of the most important words in Luke’s gospel and one of the hardest to translate. It derives from splagchna — the intestines, the viscera, the gut. To be splagchnistheis is to be moved in your innermost parts, to feel another’s suffering as a physical sensation in your own body. ‘Compassion’ is the standard translation, but it has become so domesticated it no longer registers the physical force of the Greek. ‘His heart breaks for her’ attempts to restore the visceral quality. This is the first of three times Luke uses this verb: for Jesus here, for the father in the Prodigal Son parable (15:20), and for the Good Samaritan (10:33). In each case it is the moment of encounter that generates action.

notes.original: sorou
notes.rendering: the bier
notes.why: Soros is a bier — the open wooden frame on which a body was carried for burial in Jewish practice. Jesus touches it. This is a second deliberate touching of the ritually unclean (the first was the leper in 5:13). A corpse and everything associated with it conveyed the highest degree of ritual impurity (Numbers 19:11). Jesus does not avoid the unclean; he makes contact with it and the contagion runs the other direction.

notes.original: edōken auton tē mētri autou
notes.rendering: gives him back to his mother
notes.why: The phrase echoes 1 Kings 17:23 LXX almost word for word — Elijah restoring the widow’s son: ‘and he gave him to his mother.’ Luke is deliberate. The crowd’s response confirms it: ‘A great prophet has risen among us!’ Jesus is being placed in the succession of Elijah and Elisha — the wilderness prophets who brought the dead back to the living. But the echo also underlines the difference: Elijah labored over the boy three times; Jesus speaks one sentence.

notes.original: epeskepsato ho theos
notes.rendering: God has visited his people
notes.why: Episkeptomai — to visit, to come and look after with intent to help. This is the same verb Zechariah used in the Benedictus (1:68): ‘he has visited and accomplished redemption for his people.’ The crowd at Nain uses the same word. They recognize that what is happening in front of them is a divine visitation — God coming to his people the way he came in the Exodus, the way the prophets announced he would come again.

notes.original: ho erchomenos
notes.rendering: the one who is to come
notes.why: Ho erchomenos — the coming one — is a specific messianic title drawing on Psalm 118:26 (‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’) and the prophetic expectation of one who would inaugurate the age of divine intervention. John is not expressing personal doubt about Jesus’ character; he is asking a precise theological question: are you the eschatological figure I announced, or is someone else still to come? The question is pastoral and urgent — John is in prison, possibly facing death.

notes.original: nekroi egeirontai
notes.rendering: the dead are raised
notes.why: Jesus answers John not with a theological argument but with a list of events drawn almost entirely from Isaiah 35:5–6 and 61:1 — the same passage he read in the Nazareth synagogue. The list is the answer: look at what is happening and match it against what Isaiah said would happen when God came. The widow’s son at Nain has just been raised. The answer to John’s question is walking around Galilee.

notes.original: skandalisthē
notes.rendering: tripped up by me
notes.why: Skandalizō means to cause to stumble, to trip, to be caught in a trap. The skandalon was originally the triggering stick of an animal trap — the thing you catch your foot on. Jesus says: blessed is the one who does not catch their foot on me. The word acknowledges that he is, in fact, a tripping hazard — that his manner of being the Messiah is not what most people expected, and that the gap between expectation and reality can be a trap. This is a word of gentleness toward John, not rebuke.

notes.original: meizōn en gennētois gynaikōn
notes.rendering: no one is greater than John
notes.why: The superlative claim is absolute: among all who have been born of women, none is greater. And yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. This is not a demotion of John but a statement about the nature of the kingdom: it represents such a radical new order that even its least member stands in a position John could not reach from outside it. John stands at the threshold but not yet inside.

notes.original: tēn boulēn tou theou
notes.rendering: the purpose of God
notes.why: Boulē means counsel, deliberate plan, considered purpose — the word for a resolved divine intention. The Pharisees and lawyers did not merely miss an opportunity; they rejected the purpose of God. Luke’s language is strong: their refusal of John’s baptism was a rejection of God’s considered plan for them. The verb is aorist — they definitively set it aside.

notes.original: apo tōn teknōn authēs
notes.rendering: by all her children
notes.why: Sophia — wisdom — is vindicated by her children: those who respond to her, who are shaped by her, who produce her fruit. The children of wisdom include both John (ascetic, fasting) and Jesus (eating and drinking) — two completely different styles, both expressing the same divine wisdom. The generation that rejects both is not discerning; it is simply contrary. They want neither the dirge nor the dance.

notes.heading: IV. The Woman with the Alabaster Jar (7:36–50)

notes.original: hamārtolos
notes.rendering: who is a sinner
notes.why: Hamārtolos — a sinner — is used here without qualification. Luke does not tell us what her sin is. Speculation about prostitution is ancient but not textual. What Luke tells us is that the town knows her, that the Pharisee knows her, and that she knows herself. She carries a public identity as a sinner. Whatever her story, it has been decided for her by others.

notes.original: tē thrichi tēs kephalēs
notes.rendering: with her hair
notes.why: For a Jewish woman to let down her hair in public was considered deeply improper — a sign of immodesty or grief. She is unraveling social convention at the Pharisee’s table. The gesture is not calculated for effect; it is an overflow. She has run out of the right tools (she brought perfume, not a towel) and uses what she has. The intimacy is both scandalous and disarming.

notes.original: Triple contrast
notes.rendering: You gave me no... but she
notes.why: Three parallel contrasts build in intensity: no water for feet / wet with tears; no kiss / hasn’t stopped kissing my feet; no oil on my head / perfume on my feet. Each contrast moves downward — from head to feet, from the expected hospitality gesture to its extravagant excess. Simon gave Jesus the minimum obligatory welcome of a dinner guest. The woman gave what she had, applied where it cost her most. The contrasts are not a rebuke of Simon’s morality but of his poverty of perception: he could not see what was in front of him.

notes.original: hoti ēgapēsen poly
notes.rendering: because she loved much
notes.why: The causality in this verse has generated centuries of debate: are her sins released because she loved, or did she love because her sins were released? The Greek hoti can mean ‘because’ or ‘with the result that’ — and the parable of the two debtors (vv.41–42) makes the logic clear: the one forgiven more loves more. The release came first; the love is the evidence and the response. She loved much because she had been released from much. The scene in the Pharisee’s house is not the moment of her release; it is the visible fruit of a release that has already happened.

notes.original: hē pistis sou sesōken se
notes.rendering: Your faith has saved you
notes.why: Sōzō means to save — but in Luke it carries the full semantic range from physical rescue to eschatological salvation. Jesus says this to the woman who has just been told her sins are released. The saving is comprehensive: she leaves this room released from her sins, seen by Jesus, spoken to directly, and sent into peace (eis eirēnēn). The word shalom is behind eirēnē — wholeness, completeness, the restoration of everything that should be.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 7: The chapter is organized around the theme of faith in unexpected places. The centurion — a Gentile soldier — displays greater faith than anyone in Israel. The widow of Nain asks for nothing; Jesus acts out of his own compassion before she can speak. John — the greatest of the prophets — asks the hardest question and receives the most gracious answer. The sinful woman — unnamed, socially disgraced — performs the most extravagant act of worship in the chapter while the host watches and judges. Luke is building a consistent pattern: the kingdom is visible to those who are poor, desperate, or disgraced, and hidden from those who are comfortable, credentialed, and certain they can already see.

Note on the alabaster jar scene and its relationship to the anointing accounts in other gospels: This scene (7:36–50) is frequently conflated with the anointing at Bethany in Matthew 26:6–13, Mark 14:3–9, and John 12:1–8. They share the elements of a woman, an alabaster jar of perfume, and a dinner with a man named Simon. But Luke’s account is in Galilee, early in the ministry, and involves a sinful woman whose story is about release and love. The Bethany accounts are in Jerusalem, at the end of the ministry, and are explicitly about preparation for burial. They are almost certainly different events. Luke’s scene stands on its own and should not be read through the lens of the later accounts.

intro: Luke 8 moves from parable to escalating miracle in a single sustained arc. The Sower establishes the question of how the word is received. Then the chapter answers it with four demonstrations of power that leave even the disciples asking: who is this? The Greek rewards close reading in almost every scene.
I. The Women Who Followed (8:1–3)

notes.original: diekonoun autois
notes.rendering: providing for them out of their own means
notes.why: Diakoneō means to serve, to minister, to provide for — the same root as diakonos (deacon, servant). The imperfect tense indicates an ongoing, habitual practice: these women were continuously providing for the group from their own resources (hyparchōntōn, their own possessions). Luke names them — Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna, and many others — before any of the male disciples are named in the narrative. They are not background figures; they are the material infrastructure of the mission.

notes.original: Chouzas epitropos Hērōdou
notes.rendering: Herod’s household manager
notes.why: Epitropos means a steward, a manager, one entrusted with the administration of an estate or household. Chuza manages Herod Antipas’s household. Joanna — a woman connected directly to the Galilean court — is among those funding Jesus’ ministry. This is socially remarkable. Luke is noting that the movement draws support from within the very household of the man who imprisoned and beheaded John.

notes.heading: II. The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation (8:4–15)

notes.original: ho speirōn
notes.rendering: A sower goes out to sow
notes.why: The Greek present participle — the sowing one, the one who sows — keeps the action present and ongoing. In ancient Palestinian agriculture, sowing preceded ploughing in many regions: seed was broadcast over unbroken ground, then ploughed in. This explains how seed falls on the path, on rock, among thorns — the field has not yet been prepared. The sower is not careless; this is simply how broadcasting works.

notes.original: ta mustēria
notes.rendering: the mysteries of the kingdom
notes.why: Mustērion — mystery — in Greek usage refers to something that has been hidden and is now being disclosed to the initiated. It is not simply something difficult to understand; it is something that was concealed and is now being revealed to those inside. The disciples are being given access to the hidden structure of God’s kingdom. The parables do not hide this structure — they reveal it to those with ears, and pass over those without.

notes.original: pros kairon pisteuousin
notes.rendering: they believe for a while
notes.why: Pros kairon: for a season, for a time. The word is not chronos (measured time) but kairos (a season, a period defined by its quality). These people’s faith has a season — it flourishes while conditions are favorable and collapses under pressure. The word for falling away is aphistantai — they stand away from, they withdraw, they defect. It is the word for apostasy.

notes.original: hypo merimnōn kai ploutou kai hēdonōn
notes.rendering: cares and riches and pleasures
notes.why: Three things choke the word. Merimna means anxiety, worry, the divided mind — Martha’s condition in 10:41. Ploutos is wealth. Hēdonē is pleasure, enjoyment — the root of the English ‘hedonism.’ None of these three are inherently evil; they become deadly when they crowd out the word. The fruit ‘never matures’ — it doesn’t die, it just never comes to completion. A half-formed life.

notes.original: en hypomonē
notes.rendering: with patient endurance
notes.why: Hypomonē means the capacity to remain under a heavy load without collapsing — steadfast endurance, not passive resignation. It is an active, muscular word. The good soil produces fruit not just by receiving the word but by holding it through everything that comes. Hypomonē is one of Luke’s key discipleship words: it appears again in 21:19 (‘by your endurance you will gain your lives’).

notes.original: blepete oun pōs akouete
notes.rendering: pay attention to how you hear
notes.why: Not simply whether you hear but how you hear. The quality and posture of hearing determines what you receive. Luke’s version of this saying is more pointed than Mark’s (‘pay attention to what you hear’). The content matters, but so does the orientation of the hearer. Two people can hear the same word and receive entirely different things.

notes.heading: III. The Calming of the Storm (8:22–25)

notes.original: lailaps anemou
notes.rendering: a squall
notes.why: Lailaps is specifically a sudden violent squall or whirlwind — not a steady storm but a violent downburst. The Sea of Galilee (here called the lake, limnē) is notorious for these: cold air funnelling down from the surrounding hills can produce sudden, violent conditions with almost no warning. The disciples’ terror is not timidity; they are experienced fishermen.

notes.original: epetimēsen
notes.rendering: rebukes
notes.why: Epitimaō means to rebuke, to censure, to command with authority. Jesus uses the same word to silence the demon in 4:35, to rebuke the fever in 4:39, and now to rebuke the wind and water. Luke uses it consistently: Jesus exercises the same authority over sickness, over demons, and over the natural order. The storm is addressed as though it were a disobedient agent, and it responds accordingly.

notes.original: tis ara houtos estin
notes.rendering: Who then is this?
notes.why: Ara — then, therefore, in that case — signals that the question arises from what they have just witnessed. This is not an idle theological question; it is the forced conclusion of an experience they have no category for. They have seen exorcisms and healings. But wind and water do not respond to human commands. The question ‘who is this?’ is the structural question of the entire central section of Luke. It will be answered at Caesarea Philippi (9:20) and fully only at the resurrection.

notes.original: en tois mnēmasin
notes.rendering: in the tombs
notes.why: Tombs were cut into rock outside towns — they were unclean places, beyond the boundary of community life, where the dead were kept. The man lives among the dead. He has been expelled from the living. He has no clothes, no house, no community. Luke accumulates the details to paint the complete picture of a human life destroyed: naked, homeless, homeless among graves, unable to be restrained even by chains. When Jesus restores him, he is clothed, seated, and in his right mind — the exact reversal of each detail.

notes.original: Legiōn
notes.rendering: Legion
notes.why: A Roman legion consisted of approximately six thousand soldiers. The name is both a statement of quantity and, almost certainly, a political resonance Luke’s readers would have caught: the land is occupied by Legion — Roman military power. The demons bear the name of the occupying force. The exorcism has overtones of liberation that a first-century Palestinian audience would not have missed.

notes.original: abysson
notes.rendering: the abyss
notes.why: Abyssos — the bottomless deep, the place of confinement for demonic powers (see Revelation 9:1–2, 11). The demons do not fear destruction; they fear premature confinement. Their request — send us into the pigs rather than the abyss — is a negotiation for delay. They know their ultimate destination.

notes.original: parà tous podas tou Iēsou
notes.rendering: sitting at Jesus’ feet
notes.why: To sit at someone’s feet is the posture of a disciple — the learner at the feet of the teacher (Acts 22:3, Paul at the feet of Gamaliel). The man who was naked and living among tombs is now clothed, seated, and in the posture of a disciple. The restoration is complete and its form is deliberate. He is not merely sane; he is oriented toward Jesus.

notes.original: kath’ hōlen tēn polin
notes.rendering: through the whole town
notes.why: The man Jesus sends away becomes the first missionary in Gentile territory. Jesus tells him to proclaim what God has done; he goes and proclaims what Jesus has done. Luke notes both — without comment on the substitution. The equation between what God does and what Jesus does is allowed to stand without explanation.

notes.heading: V. Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding (8:40–56)

notes.original: Two twelves
notes.rendering: The interwoven twelves
notes.why: Luke’s interweaving of the two stories contains a hidden symmetry: Jairus’s daughter is twelve years old (v.42); the woman has been bleeding for twelve years (v.43). The girl has lived her entire life in the shadow of the woman’s suffering. The woman has suffered for as long as the girl has been alive. Luke places these two figures — one at the threshold of death, one at the threshold of restoration — in deliberate parallel. Both are addressed as ‘daughter’ (v.48, v.54 in some manuscripts).

notes.original: tou kraspedou
notes.rendering: the fringe of his garment
notes.why: Kraspedon means the edge or border of a garment — specifically the tassels (tzitzit) worn by Jewish men on the corners of their outer garment as commanded in Numbers 15:38–40. To touch the fringe is to touch the sign of covenant faithfulness. The woman reaches for the visible marker of Jewish piety and receives healing. The detail is not accidental: what she touches is the outward sign of the very covenant under which she has lived as an outcast for twelve years.

notes.original: dynamin exēlthousan
notes.rendering: power has gone out from me
notes.why: Dynamis — power, force, ability. Jesus knows something has happened not by sight but by sensation: power has left him. The healing is not a performance or a decision; it is a transaction. Something real has passed from him to her. This is one of the most physically immediate statements Jesus makes about his own body in any gospel.

notes.original: thygatēr
notes.rendering: Daughter
notes.why: This is the only time in the gospels that Jesus directly addresses a woman as ‘daughter.’ The word is tender, relational, and elevating: she who has been ritually unclean for twelve years, who touched him in a crowd without permission, is addressed by Jesus as family. The healing of her body and the restoration of her social identity happen in the same sentence.

notes.original: katheudei / apedhanen
notes.rendering: She is sleeping / she is dead
notes.why: Jesus says the child is sleeping (katheudei). The crowd laughs — knowing (eidotes) she is dead (apedhanen). Both statements are true from their respective vantage points. For them, death is the final word; for Jesus, it is a condition he can reverse, and therefore functionally equivalent to sleep. The laughter is not cruel; it is the honest response of people whose experience has given them no category for what is about to happen.

notes.original: epestrepsen to pneuma autēs
notes.rendering: her spirit returns
notes.why: Pneuma — spirit, breath, the animating principle. It returns: the verb implies it had genuinely departed. This is not a misdiagnosis of death; it is a reversal of it. Luke, characteristically precise, records both the spirit’s return and the immediate physical response — she gets up. And then, with disarming practicality: Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. The girl is alive. She is hungry. Feed her.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 8 as a theology of power: The four miracle accounts in 8:22–56 form a deliberate sequence of escalating domains. The storm (8:22–25): power over the natural order. The demoniac (8:26–39): power over the demonic realm. The bleeding woman (8:43–48): power over chronic illness. The dead girl (8:49–56): power over death itself. Each miracle is harder than the last; each produces a deeper astonishment. The structural question ‘who then is this?’ (8:25) hangs over all four. Luke is not yet ready to answer it fully — that answer comes in chapter 9.

Note on the women in 8:1–3: Luke’s list of women who traveled with Jesus and funded his ministry is without parallel in the other gospels at this point in the narrative. Mary Magdalene, Joanna (wife of Herod’s household manager), and Susanna are named; ‘many others’ are noted. The word for their financial support — diekonōun — is the same word used for the ministry of deacons and for the service of angels (4:39 uses the same root). These women are not peripheral to the mission; they are sustaining it from their own resources. Luke places this passage immediately before the Sower parable — a parable about how the word is received and carried. The women are the first demonstration of good soil.

intro: Luke 9 is the structural center of the gospel. The first half builds to Peter’s confession and the Transfiguration — the twin peaks of the Galilean ministry. The second half begins the long descent toward Jerusalem. The Greek in this chapter carries a weight that rewards close attention at nearly every verse.
I. The Sending of the Twelve (9:1–6)

notes.original: dynamin kai exousian
notes.rendering: power and authority
notes.why: Luke distinguishes two words: dynamis (inherent power, force, ability) and exousia (authority, the right to exercise power). Jesus gives both. The disciples are not merely permitted to act; they are equipped to act. Exousia without dynamis is an empty warrant; dynamis without exousia is raw force without sanction. The Twelve receive both together.

notes.original: mēde ana dyo chitōnas echein
notes.rendering: don’t have two tunics apiece
notes.why: The instruction is not to travel light for practical reasons but as a theological statement: the mission depends on God’s provision, not stockpiled resources. The disciples are to be radically dependent — on hospitality, on the generosity of those they serve, on the kingdom they proclaim. No backup plan. The vulnerability is the point.

notes.original: ton koniorton apo tōn podōn
notes.rendering: shake the dust off your feet
notes.why: Jewish travelers returning from Gentile territory would shake the dust from their feet before re-entering the land — a symbolic gesture of separation from ritual impurity. Jesus instructs the disciples to perform this gesture against Jewish towns that reject the kingdom. The implication is stark: a town that refuses the kingdom of God has become, in relation to that kingdom, like foreign territory.

notes.heading: II. The Feeding of the Five Thousand (9:10–17)

notes.original: dote autois hymeis phagein
notes.rendering: You give them something to eat
notes.why: The emphasis falls on hymeis — you, plural, emphatic. Not ‘someone should feed them’ or ‘send them to find food’ but: you do it. The command is direct and seemingly impossible. The disciples’ response — we have only five loaves and two fish — is not faithlessness but honesty about what they can see. What they cannot see is that the one commanding them is the one who will supply.

notes.original: eulogēsen / kateklasen / edidou
notes.rendering: blesses / breaks / gives
notes.why: Three verbs in sequence — the same three used at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus (24:30). Luke is deliberate: the feeding in the wilderness is eucharistic in form. The crowd of five thousand is fed with the same gestures that will define the meal Jesus shares with his disciples on the night of his arrest, and the meal that opens the eyes of the Emmaus disciples. The loaves connect all three scenes.

notes.original: dōdeka kophinoi
notes.rendering: twelve baskets
notes.why: Twelve baskets of leftovers — one for each tribe of Israel, one for each apostle. The abundance exceeds the need by exactly the number that represents the whole people of God. This is not waste; it is a sign. The kingdom produces more than enough.

notes.original: proseuchesthai auton kata monas
notes.rendering: while he is praying alone
notes.why: Luke alone notes that Jesus is praying when he asks the identity question. As at the baptism (3:21), the Twelve (6:12), and the Transfiguration (9:28), Luke’s Jesus prays at every hinge moment. The most important theological conversation in the Galilean ministry happens while Jesus is at prayer. The disciples are present — kata monas does not mean physically isolated but engaged in solitary prayer — and the question comes out of that prayerful state.

notes.original: ton Christon tou Theou
notes.rendering: The Messiah of God
notes.why: Peter’s answer in Luke is ton Christon tou Theou — the Messiah of God, God’s anointed. Matthew has ‘the Christ, the Son of the living God’; Mark has simply ‘the Christ.’ Luke’s form is the most Jewish of the three — the Messiah belonging to God, God’s own anointed agent. The genitive tou Theou (of God) anchors the title in God’s ownership and commissioning of this particular figure.

notes.original: dei ton Huion tou anthrōpou
notes.rendering: the Son of Man must
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary, it must happen — appears here for the first time in connection with the passion. The suffering is not an accident or a political miscalculation; it is a divine necessity. The same dei drove Jesus to proclaim in 4:43; it will drive him toward Jerusalem throughout the travel narrative. The passion prediction is not a prophecy of disaster but a statement of vocation.

notes.original: apoktanthēnai kai tē tritē hēmera
notes.rendering: be killed — and on the third day be raised
notes.why: Luke’s first passion prediction includes the resurrection from the beginning. Matthew and Mark also include it, but its placement is significant: Peter confesses Jesus as Messiah; Jesus immediately redefines what Messiah means. Not conquest, not throne, not the expulsion of Rome. Rejection, suffering, death — and then resurrection. Peter has the right title and the wrong picture.

notes.original: kath’ hēmeran
notes.rendering: every day
notes.why: Luke alone adds kath’ hēmeran — every day — to the cross-bearing instruction. Matthew and Mark have ‘take up your cross and follow me.’ Luke has ‘take up their cross every day.’ The cross is not a single dramatic moment of decision but a daily practice of self-denial. This is Luke’s characteristic emphasis on discipleship as a sustained way of life, not a one-time commitment.

notes.original: psychēn / apoleses
notes.rendering: life / lose
notes.why: Psychē means soul, self, the living person — the whole of who you are, not merely biological life. Apollymi means to destroy, to lose, to cause to perish. The saying turns on a paradox that cannot be resolved by cleverness: the very act of protecting the self destroys it. The self is only truly found when it is given away. Luke’s addition of ‘for my sake’ specifies the direction: the losing is not random self-sacrifice but oriented toward Jesus.

notes.original: epaiscynthei
notes.rendering: is ashamed of
notes.why: Epaischynomai means to be ashamed of, to be embarrassed by, to disown in public. The social pressure being named is real: in a world where honor and shame structure all social relationships, being associated with a crucified criminal is genuinely costly. Jesus names the temptation precisely: the person who is ashamed of him in front of others will find the Son of Man equally unable to acknowledge them.

notes.original: to eidos tou prosōpou autou heteron
notes.rendering: the appearance of his face becomes different
notes.why: Luke does not use the word metamorphoo (to be transfigured, transformed) that Matthew and Mark use. He says the appearance (eidos) of his face becomes other, different (heteron). This is Luke the physician’s precision: he describes the visible phenomenon without importing the theological interpretation embedded in the word ‘transfiguration.’ The reader sees what the disciples see — something they have no word for.

notes.original: tēn exodon autou
notes.rendering: his departure
notes.why: Exodos — exodus, departure, going out. Moses and Elijah appear in glory and discuss Jesus’ exodos, which he is about to accomplish (plēroun — to fulfill, to bring to completion) at Jerusalem. The word is not incidental: it is the Exodus word, the word of Israel’s liberation from Egypt. Jesus’ death is being framed from within the glory of the mountain as an Exodus event — a departure that accomplishes liberation. Luke is the only gospel writer who tells us what Moses and Elijah are talking about.

notes.original: diagrēgorēsantes
notes.rendering: when they wake fully
notes.why: Diagrēgoreō means to be fully awake, to rouse completely from sleep — the intensive dia- prefix indicating thoroughness. The disciples were heavy with sleep and then fully awake. This detail anticipates Gethsemane (22:45–46), where the same disciples will again be overcome by sleep at a moment of divine intensity. At the Transfiguration they rouse in time to see the glory. At Gethsemane they will not.

notes.original: mē eidōs ho legei
notes.rendering: He does not know what he is saying
notes.why: Luke’s editorial aside is gentle but clear. Peter’s impulse to build shelters — to institutionalise the moment, to make the mountain into a permanent dwelling — misunderstands what is happening. The Transfiguration is not a destination; it is a commissioning for the road to Jerusalem. The cloud and the voice interrupt Peter’s proposal before it can develop.

notes.original: ho eklelgmenos
notes.rendering: my Chosen
notes.why: The voice at the Transfiguration differs slightly from the voice at the baptism (3:22). At the baptism: ‘You are my Son, the Beloved.’ Here: ‘This is my Son — my Chosen.’ The word is eklelegmenos — the chosen one, the elect. This title draws on Isaiah 42:1 (‘my servant whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights’) — the first Servant Song. The mountain voice identifies Jesus as the Isaianic Servant: the one chosen for suffering, not despite his glory but as the expression of it.

notes.heading: VI. The Second Passion Prediction and the Turn Toward Jerusalem (9:43–62)

notes.original: thesthe hymeis eis ta ōta
notes.rendering: let these words sink into your ears
notes.why: Tithemi eis ta ōta — literally: place these words into your ears. It is an idiom for attentive, careful hearing — to receive something so deliberately that it goes all the way in. Jesus is not merely saying ‘pay attention.’ He is asking the disciples to do active work with what they are about to hear. The urgency signals that what follows — the second passion prediction — is the most important thing he has said since Peter’s confession.

notes.original: kekrymmenon ap’ autōn
notes.rendering: It is hidden from them
notes.why: The passive kekrymmenon — it has been hidden, it remains concealed — implies a divine agent. The disciples’ incomprehension is not simply obtuseness; it is a veiling permitted or enacted by God.
