The full meaning of the passion prediction cannot be received until after the resurrection has provided the interpretive key. Their fear to ask is also noted — they sense the weight of what they don’t understand.

notes.original: to prosōpon estērisen tou poreuesthai
notes.rendering: he sets his face resolutely to go
notes.why: Sterizo to prosōpon — to harden the face, to set the face like flint — is a Hebrew idiom for determined, irreversible resolve. It echoes Isaiah 50:7: ‘I have set my face like flint.’ This is the Servant again. From this verse, everything in Luke moves toward Jerusalem. The travel narrative (9:51–19:44) is the longest section of the gospel and takes place entirely under the shadow of this set face.

notes.original: tēn analempseos autou
notes.rendering: his being taken up
notes.why: Analēmpsis — taking up, assumption. The days of his analēmpsis are being completed — a word that points forward to the ascension (Acts 1:2 uses the same root). The journey to Jerusalem is not merely toward death; it is toward a taking up. Luke frames the cross and the ascension as a single movement: going up to Jerusalem in order to be taken up to God.

notes.original: ouk echei pou tēn kephalēn klinē
notes.rendering: nowhere to lay his head
notes.why: The image is precise and concrete: every animal has a burrow or a nest — a place to put its head down. The Son of Man has no such place. The one who created the world has no corner of it to call his own. This is the cost named to the would-be follower who volunteers enthusiastically before counting it.

notes.original: aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous
notes.rendering: Leave the dead to bury their own dead
notes.why: One of the most jarring sayings in the gospels. Burying a parent was among the most sacred obligations in Jewish life — even the high priest was permitted to become ritually unclean to bury a close relative (Leviticus 21:1–3). Jesus does not dispute the obligation; he names something more urgent. The ‘dead’ who bury their own dead are the spiritually dead — those who have not yet heard the call of the kingdom. The living must go and proclaim. The urgency of the kingdom supersedes even the most sacred family duty.

notes.original: euthetos tē basileia tou theou
notes.rendering: fit for the kingdom of God
notes.why: Euthetos means fit for use, suitable, serviceable. A ploughman who looks back cannot plough a straight furrow — the line wanders wherever the eyes go. The kingdom requires a single-minded orientation forward. The person who follows Jesus while keeping one eye on the life being left behind is not equipped for the work of the kingdom. The image is agricultural and unsparing.

outro: Note on Luke 9 as the structural hinge of the gospel: Luke’s gospel divides into three major sections. The Galilean ministry (4:14–9:50) culminates in the Transfiguration and the second passion prediction. The travel narrative (9:51–19:44) begins with the set face toward Jerusalem and contains the bulk of Luke’s unique material — the parables of the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Rich Man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus, and much of the teaching material found only in Luke. The Jerusalem narrative (19:45–24:53) covers the final week, the passion, and the resurrection. Chapter 9 contains the transition between the first and second sections: the confession, the Transfiguration, and the set face. Everything pivots here.

Note on the Transfiguration and Exodus: The connections between the Transfiguration and the Sinai theophany (Exodus 24–34) are extensive. Moses appears on the mountain. A cloud overshadows. A divine voice speaks. The disciples are heavy with sleep, as were the elders who accompanied Moses (Exodus 24:9–11). The word exodos in v.31 clinches the typology. Luke is presenting the Transfiguration as a new Sinai: the place where the divine glory is revealed, the covenant is renewed, and the way forward is commissioned. The difference is that Moses received the Law on the mountain; the disciples are told simply to listen to Jesus.

intro: Luke 10 moves from commissioning to confrontation to revelation to parable to domestic scene — five completely different registers in a single chapter. The Good Samaritan alone would justify a chapter’s worth of notes. The Greek throughout is precise and rewards the closest attention.
I. The Sending of the Seventy-Two (10:1–12)

notes.original: hebdomēkonta [dyo]
notes.rendering: seventy-two
notes.why: The manuscript tradition is divided between seventy (P75, B, and some others) and seventy-two (P45, א, A, C, and others). The NA28 follows seventy-two. Both numbers carry resonance: seventy evokes the seventy elders of Israel (Numbers 11:16–25) and the seventy nations of Genesis 10; seventy-two is the number of nations in the LXX version of Genesis 10 and also the number of elders in some traditions. Either way, Luke signals a mission that extends beyond Israel. The Twelve were sent to Israel; this larger group goes ahead into every place Jesus is about to enter.

notes.original: therismos polys
notes.rendering: The harvest is plentiful
notes.why: Therismos — harvest — is an eschatological image throughout the Hebrew prophets: the final gathering of God’s people at the end of the age (Joel 3:13, Isaiah 27:12). Jesus is not using a pleasant agricultural metaphor; he is announcing that the end-time harvest has begun. The workers are few not because the task is modest but because the harvest is happening now and the labourers have not yet arrived.

notes.original: mēdena kata tēn hodon aspasesthe
notes.rendering: Greet no one on the road
notes.why: Ancient Near Eastern greetings were elaborate, time-consuming, and socially obligatory. To pass someone without greeting them was offensive; to greet properly required stopping, inquiring about family and health, and often accepting hospitality. Jesus’ instruction is not rudeness but urgency: the mission cannot be delayed by the social conventions of the road. The kingdom is coming and there is no time for the full ceremonial of normal life.

notes.original: huios eirēnēs
notes.rendering: a son of peace
notes.why: Huios eirēnēs — a son of peace — is a Semitic idiom meaning a person who embodies or belongs to peace, one who is receptive to the peace the disciples carry. The phrase does not refer to a peaceful personality but to spiritual readiness — someone in whom the shalom of the kingdom can take root. If such a person is in the house, the peace settles and stays. If not, it returns to the one who offered it, unused but not wasted.

notes.original: hē basilēia tou theou ēggiken
notes.rendering: the kingdom of God has come near
notes.why: Eggizō means to draw near, to approach, to come close — but not necessarily to arrive. The kingdom’s nearness is announced even to the town that rejects the missionaries. The proclamation is not withheld from those who refuse it; it is given and then the dust is shaken off. The rejection of the messengers does not prevent the announcement; it only changes its character from invitation to testimony against.

notes.heading: II. The Return of the Seventy-Two (10:17–24)

notes.original: Satan hōs astrapēn pesonta
notes.rendering: Satan fall like lightning from heaven
notes.why: The aorist participle pesonta — having fallen — and the imperfect ethēroum — I was watching — are debated. Is Jesus reporting a past cosmic vision (Satan’s original fall from heaven, as in Isaiah 14:12)? Or a present reality being accomplished through the mission of the seventy-two? Most likely both: the exorcisms performed by the missionaries are manifestations of a defeat already accomplished in the heavenly realm. The kingdom’s advance on earth reflects a prior, decisive victory above.

notes.original: ta onomata hymōn engegraptài en tois ouranois
notes.rendering: your names are written in heaven
notes.why: Engegraptài is a perfect passive — your names have been written and remain written. The register of heaven is a standing document in which their names already appear. This is the ground of joy that exceeds even the joy of effective ministry: not what you have accomplished but that you are known. The verb is perfect: the writing is done and permanent.

notes.original: ēgalliasāto en tō pneumati tō hagiō
notes.rendering: he rejoices in the Holy Spirit
notes.why: Agalliao — to leap for joy, to exult — the same word used of John leaping in Elizabeth’s womb (1:44) and of Mary’s spirit exulting (1:47). Luke notes that this joy is specifically in the Holy Spirit: it is not merely human happiness but Spirit-prompted exultation. This is the only place in the gospels where Jesus is explicitly described as rejoicing. The occasion is the revelation of the kingdom to the simple and its concealment from the sophisticated.

notes.original: nēpiois
notes.rendering: little children
notes.why: Nēpios means an infant, a small child — one too young to speak clearly, one entirely dependent. It is not a compliment to childlike spiritual qualities; it is a description of social and intellectual status: the uneducated, the simple, those without the credentials of the wise and understanding (syneton). The kingdom’s hiddenness from the credentialed and its revelation to the simple is, Jesus says, what the Father found pleasing. The Greek eudokia here echoes the voice at the baptism (3:22).

notes.original: ekpeirazōn
notes.rendering: to test him
notes.why: Ekpeirazō — the compound form of peirazō, to test, used of the devil’s testing of Jesus in the wilderness (4:2). The lawyer is not seeking enlightenment; he is setting a trap. Luke tells us his motive before he speaks. The question ‘what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ is formally pious but functionally adversarial. Jesus’ response — turning the question back on the questioner — is the first move in a contest the lawyer does not win.

notes.original: ex holēs tēs kardias… psychēs… ischyos… dianoias
notes.rendering: heart… soul… strength… mind
notes.why: The lawyer’s answer combines Deuteronomy 6:5 (the Shema) with Leviticus 19:18 (love your neighbour). He cites four faculties: kardia (heart, the seat of will and emotion), psychē (soul, the living self), ischys (strength, physical and vital energy), and dianoia (mind, understanding, the thinking faculty). The Shema in Hebrew has three; the LXX has three in a different combination; Luke’s version has four. The point is totality: every faculty, without remainder, directed toward God.

notes.original: dikaiōsai heauton
notes.rendering: wanting to justify himself
notes.why: Dikaioō means to justify, to declare righteous, to vindicate. The lawyer wants to justify himself — to establish that he has already been doing what is required. His second question (‘who is my neighbour?’) is not intellectual curiosity; it is a request for a definition narrow enough to confirm that he has already satisfied it. Jesus’ parable refuses to give him that definition.

notes.original: katabainōn apo Hierousalēm
notes.rendering: going down from Jerusalem to Jericho
notes.why: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho descends approximately 900 metres over 27 kilometres through the Judean wilderness — rocky, exposed, notorious in antiquity for bandits. Jesus’ first listeners knew this road. The setting is not generic; it is a specific, dangerous stretch of road that every traveller to Jericho knew. The parable is grounded in a real place before the characters are introduced.

notes.original: antipar0113lthen
notes.rendering: passes by on the other side
notes.why: Antiparerchomai — to go past on the opposite side, to cross to the other side of the road and continue. The verb is used twice: for the priest (v.31) and the Levite (v.32). It is not that they fail to notice the man; it is that they actively move to the other side to avoid him. Their avoidance is deliberate. The standard explanation — that a priest could not touch a corpse without becoming ritually unclean — is plausible but not stated. Jesus does not excuse them; he simply records what they did.

notes.original: Samaritēs… esplagchnisthē
notes.rendering: a Samaritan… his heart breaks for him
notes.why: The third traveller is introduced without a title or profession — simply a Samaritan, a member of the people regarded by Jews as half-breed schismatics, ritually unclean, theologically deviant. And then: splagchnizomai. The gut-word. His heart breaks. The word that Luke uses for Jesus at Nain (7:13), for the father of the Prodigal Son (15:20), appears here for the Samaritan. Luke places the most Jewish of visceral-compassion words in the body of the most despised outsider.

notes.original: epichēon elaion kai oinon
notes.rendering: pouring on oil and wine
notes.why: Oil and wine were standard first-century wound treatments: wine as an antiseptic (its acidity killed bacteria), oil as a soothing agent to reduce inflammation. Luke the physician notes the specific treatment. The Samaritan does not merely gesture at the man’s need; he applies what he knows will help. The care is informed, practical, and costly — he uses his own supplies, his own animal, his own money, his own time.

notes.original: tis toutōn tōn triōn plēsion
notes.rendering: Which of these three proved to be a neighbour
notes.why: Jesus does not answer the lawyer’s question (‘who is my neighbour?’) directly. He inverts it. The lawyer asked: who qualifies as my neighbour, whom I am obligated to love? Jesus asks: which of these three acted as a neighbour? The question shifts from the identity of the recipient to the character of the one who acts. The neighbour is not a category of person to be defined; it is a role to be performed. And the one who performed it was the one the lawyer would have least expected.

notes.original: ho poiēsas to eleos
notes.rendering: the one who showed him mercy
notes.why: The lawyer cannot bring himself to say ‘the Samaritan.’ He answers with a circumlocution: the one who showed mercy (eleos — compassion, loving-kindness, the covenant word hesed). Jesus does not press him on it. He simply says: go and do likewise. The command is in the same form as 4:23 and 7:50 — a sent person, a direction, no further instruction. Do what you have seen.

notes.original: parà tous podas tou kyriou
notes.rendering: sits at the Lord’s feet
notes.why: As at 8:35 (the Gerasene demoniac restored to his right mind, sitting at Jesus’ feet) and Acts 22:3 (Paul educated at the feet of Gamaliel), sitting at someone’s feet is the posture of a disciple receiving instruction. Mary takes the posture of a male student in a rabbinic learning relationship. In first-century Judaism, women were not expected or typically permitted to be taught Torah as disciples. Luke notes it without comment — which is itself a comment.

notes.original: periespa to
notes.rendering: pulled in every direction
notes.why: Perispao means to be dragged around, to be distracted by being pulled in multiple directions — the prefix peri- (around) combined with spao (to pull, to drag). Martha is not simply busy; she is being pulled apart by the demands of the serving. The image is of a person at the centre of multiple competing claims, each pulling outward. It is a sympathetic word — Luke is not condemning Martha’s work but describing her experience of it.

notes.original: merimnas kai thorybazē
notes.rendering: anxious and troubled
notes.why: Two words. Merimnaō — to be anxious, to have the divided mind (from merizō, to divide, and nous, mind) — the word used in the Sower parable for the thorns that choke the word (8:14). Thorybazō — to be troubled, to be thrown into an uproar (from thorybos, noise, tumult). Martha’s inner state is both divided and turbulent. Jesus names it precisely and without contempt: he uses her name twice — Martha, Martha — a form of address that is tender even when corrective.

notes.original: henos de estin chreia
notes.rendering: one thing is necessary
notes.why: The manuscript tradition offers variants: ‘one thing is necessary’ (NA28), ‘few things are necessary, or only one’ (some manuscripts). The NA28 reading is preferred. The one necessary thing is not identified explicitly — but the context makes it clear: it is what Mary is doing. Not a particular religious exercise, but the orientation of the whole self toward Jesus, receiving what he gives. The ‘one thing’ is not a task; it is a posture.

notes.original: tēn agathēn merida
notes.rendering: the good part
notes.why: Meris means a portion, a share, a part — as in an inheritance divided among heirs. Mary has chosen her portion: the part that belongs to her in this moment. Agathēn — good, beautiful, the genuine article. And it will not be taken from her (ouk aphairethhsetai) — the future passive: no one will take it away. What Mary has received in this moment is permanent. The food Martha is preparing will be eaten and gone; what Mary is receiving will remain.

outro: Note on the structure of the Good Samaritan parable: The parable is constructed in three movements with an escalating reversal at its centre. Two figures who should act (priest, Levite) do not. One figure who should not act (Samaritan) does — and does so with comprehensive, costly, ongoing care. The reversal is not merely moral (‘even Samaritans can be good’); it is structural. The parable demolishes the lawyer’s question by refusing to answer it. He asked who counts as a neighbour so he could locate the boundary of his obligation. Jesus gives him a story that removes the boundary entirely and replaces the question with a commission: go and do likewise. The parable does not answer the lawyer’s question; it makes that question impossible to ask in good faith.

Note on Mary and Martha as a continuation of the Good Samaritan: The two stories are often read in isolation, but Luke places them in sequence for a reason. The Good Samaritan insists on active service: go and do. The Mary-and-Martha scene insists on attentive reception: sit and listen. Read together, they form a complete picture. Neither active service without receptivity nor receptivity without active service is the whole thing. Martha’s problem is not that she serves; it is that her service has become anxious and divided, cut off from the source. Mary’s chosen portion is the foundation that makes genuine service possible.

intro: Luke 11 moves from the most intimate moment in the gospel — a disciple asking Jesus how to pray — to some of its most confrontational. The Lord’s Prayer, the persistent neighbour, the Beelzebul controversy, and the seven woes each make distinct demands on the translator. The Greek is precise and often surprising.
I. The Lord’s Prayer (11:1–4)

notes.original: Pater
notes.rendering: Father
notes.why: Luke’s version of the prayer is significantly shorter than Matthew’s (6:9–13) and more direct. Matthew opens with ‘Our Father in heaven’; Luke has simply Pater — Father, the Aramaic Abba reduced to its Greek equivalent. The intimacy is stark. No qualification, no preamble, no honorific beyond the name. Jesus teaches his disciples to address God the way he addresses God: directly, personally, as a child to a father.

notes.original: hagiasthētō to onoma sou
notes.rendering: may your name be hallowed
notes.why: An aorist passive imperative — a petition that God’s name be treated as holy, be set apart, be regarded with the weight it deserves. The passive implies that God himself is the one who hallows his own name (as in Ezekiel 36:23: ‘I will sanctify my great name’). The petition is both a request for God to act and a commitment on the part of the one praying to participate in that hallowing.

notes.original: ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion
notes.rendering: bread for the coming day
notes.why: Epiousios is one of the rarest words in Greek literature — it appears almost nowhere outside this prayer and its parallel in Matthew 6:11. Its derivation is disputed: from epi + ousia (the bread of substance, the essential bread) or from epi + iousan (hēmeran — the coming day’s bread). The second derivation is more linguistically sound. ‘Bread for the coming day’ — the bread we need for tomorrow, asked for today — captures the petition’s daily, concrete quality. This is not a request for spiritual sustenance; it is a request for actual food, one day at a time.

notes.original: aphes hēmin tas hamartias hēmōn
notes.rendering: release us from our sins
notes.why: Luke uses aphes and hamartias where Matthew uses opheilēmata (debts). Luke’s version names sins directly; Matthew’s uses the debt metaphor. Both are present in Luke’s prayer, however: the basis for asking release from sins is that we ourselves release (aphiōmen) those indebted to us. The present tense aphiōmen is significant: we are releasing, habitually, as an ongoing practice — not ‘we have already released’ but ‘we are the kind of people who release.’

notes.original: mē eisenenkeis hēmas eis peirasmon
notes.rendering: do not bring us into testing
notes.why: Peirasmos means testing, trial, temptation — the same root as the testing of Jesus in the wilderness (4:2). The petition is not asking God to prevent all difficulty but to not lead us into the kind of testing that overwhelms — the trial that breaks rather than refines. The negative aorist subjunctive (mē eisenenkeis) is a petition for divine guidance away from the path that ends in apostasy. Luke’s version does not include Matthew’s ‘but deliver us from evil/the evil one.’

notes.original: anaideia
notes.rendering: shamelessness
notes.why: Anaideia is one of the most important and most mistranslated words in this parable. It means shamelessness, impudence, the absence of shame — not persistence or importunity (the traditional translations). The word is used negatively in Greek literature: it describes someone who has thrown off the social restraint of shame and makes demands regardless of the embarrassment involved. The parable says: even a reluctant neighbour will get up and give because of the asker’s shamelessness. Some scholars apply anaideia to the host rather than the petitioner: the neighbour gives in order to avoid the shame of being seen as inhospitable. Either way, the word is stronger and more specific than ‘persistence.’ ‘Shamelessness’ is retained here because it is what the Greek says.

notes.original: aitei… zētei… krouei
notes.rendering: ask… seek… knock
notes.why: Three present imperatives — ongoing, continuous actions. Not ‘ask once’ but ‘keep asking.’ Not ‘seek once’ but ‘keep seeking.’ Not ‘knock once’ but ‘keep knocking.’ The parable of the neighbour has just illustrated what persistent asking looks like. The commands that follow it are in the same continuous mode: the posture of prayer is ongoing, habitual, unrelenting.

notes.original: pneuma hagion
notes.rendering: the Holy Spirit
notes.why: Luke’s version of this saying differs from Matthew’s (7:11) in one significant word. Matthew has ‘good gifts’ (agatha); Luke has ‘the Holy Spirit.’ For Luke, the supreme gift the Father gives to those who ask is the Spirit — consistent with his emphasis throughout Luke-Acts. The good gifts of Matthew become, in Luke’s hands, a single surpassing gift: the presence and power of God himself.

notes.original: Beelzeboul archonti tōn daimōniōn
notes.rendering: Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons
notes.why: Beelzebul (the Greek form) derives from a Semitic name meaning ‘lord of the flies’ or possibly ‘lord of the high place.’ It is used as a title for Satan, the chief of the demonic realm. The accusation is precise: Jesus is not merely operating with demonic assistance; he is operating under the authority of the demonic commander-in-chief. The charge is the most serious possible: that his power is satanic in origin.

notes.original: diameristheisa kath’ heautēs
notes.rendering: divided against itself
notes.why: Diamerizō means to divide thoroughly, to split apart. Jesus’ argument is logical and devastating: if Satan is casting out his own demons, he is dismantling his own kingdom. No military commander sabotages his own forces. The accusation of Beelzebul is self-refuting: it implies a Satan so confused he is fighting himself.

notes.original: en daktylō theou
notes.rendering: by the finger of God
notes.why: Matthew’s parallel (12:28) has ‘by the Spirit of God.’ Luke alone has ‘the finger of God’ — an Exodus image. When the Egyptian magicians could not replicate the plague of gnats, they said to Pharaoh: ‘This is the finger of God’ (Exodus 8:19). The same finger that wrote the Law on stone tablets at Sinai (Exodus 31:18) is now driving out demons. Luke is drawing a direct line from the Exodus to the ministry of Jesus: the same divine power that acted in the liberation from Egypt is acting now.

notes.original: ischyros… ischyroteros
notes.rendering: a strong man… someone stronger
notes.why: The parable of the strong man answers the Beelzebul charge directly. Jesus is not working for the strong man; he is the stronger one who has overpowered him. The armour the strong man trusted in — his defenses, his security — has been stripped away. Jesus is describing what his exorcisms mean cosmically: not collaboration with Satan but conquest of him. The ministry of healing and liberation is a sustained assault on an occupied house.

notes.original: anydron topōn
notes.rendering: waterless places
notes.why: In Jewish tradition, demons were associated with desert and wilderness places — the dry, uninhabited margins of the world (cf. Isaiah 13:21, 34:14; the wilderness where Jesus was tested). The expelled demon searches for rest in the waterless places and finds none. The image implies that a demon’s natural habitat is a human being; it is at rest only when inhabiting a person. The warning of vv.24–26 is stark: exorcism without genuine renewal leaves the house swept clean and available for a worse occupation.

notes.original: sēmeion Zōna
notes.rendering: the sign of Jonah
notes.why: Matthew’s version (12:39–40) explains the sign of Jonah as the three days in the belly of the fish — a type of the resurrection. Luke does not give this explanation. In Luke, Jonah himself was the sign to Nineveh: his arrival, his preaching, the improbable fact of his presence was the sign. The Son of Man will similarly be a sign — his presence, his preaching, the fact of who he is will be the thing that calls this generation to account. Luke’s version points to the ministry; Matthew’s points to the resurrection.

notes.original: basilissa notou
notes.rendering: the queen of the South
notes.why: The queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–13) who traveled from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom. She is invoked as a Gentile witness who responded to a lesser revelation with greater seriousness than this generation responds to Jesus. The comparison is deliberately humiliating: a foreign queen outshines the generation that hosts the one greater than Solomon.

notes.original: pleiōn Iōna hōde
notes.rendering: something greater than Jonah is here
notes.why: Pleiōn is comparative: greater, more. The neuter form (not ‘someone’ but ‘something’) may be deliberate — pointing to the kingdom itself, not merely its representative. Both comparisons in vv.31–32 use the same structure: the Gentile outsider responded; the insider generation will not. And what is here is greater than what they responded to.

notes.heading: V. Woes Against the Pharisees and Lawyers (11:37–54)

notes.original: harpage kai ponerías
notes.rendering: greed and wickedness
notes.why: Harpage means plunder, rapacity, greed that seizes what belongs to others. Poneria means wickedness, moral corruption. Jesus names the inside of the Pharisees’ cup with two concrete words: they have taken what is not theirs and they are morally corrupt. The external ritual cleansing of cups and dishes is a practiced performance of purity that conceals these realities.

notes.original: ta enonta dote eleemōsynen
notes.rendering: give what is inside as generosity
notes.why: A famously difficult phrase. Ta enonta means ‘the things within’ — the contents of the cup, or the inner disposition. Eleemōsynen means almsgiving, generosity to the poor. The saying may mean: give the contents of the cup as alms (give your food to the poor); or: give from your inner life in acts of generosity. Either way, the contrast is between external ritual washing and the transformation of the inside that produces genuine generosity. Jesus offers a path: the inside can be made clean, but not by washing the outside.

notes.original: parerchesthe tēn krisin kai tēn agapēn tou theou
notes.rendering: you pass over justice and the love of God
notes.why: Parerchomai means to go past, to bypass, to neglect by passing by — the same word used of the priest and Levite in the Good Samaritan (10:31–32). The Pharisees tithe their herb garden with meticulous care and walk straight past justice and the love of God. The verb is the same: they pass by on the other side.

notes.original: tà mnēmeia tà adela
notes.rendering: unmarked graves
notes.why: An unmarked grave was a source of ritual pollution: walking over one, even unknowingly, conveyed corpse-impurity (Numbers 19:16). In the dry season in Palestine, graves could be invisible under the dust. Jesus says the Pharisees are like unmarked graves — those who interact with them contract impurity without knowing it. The image is the inverse of the whitewashed tombs in Matthew 23:27: those are visibly impressive but inwardly full of death; Luke’s version is invisible, unseen, all the more dangerous for it.

notes.original: phortizete… daktylō hymōn ou prospsauete
notes.rendering: load people down… won’t touch with one of your fingers
notes.why: The lawyers are specialists in the interpretation of the Law. They elaborate its requirements into detailed regulations that bind ordinary people, and then find legal workarounds for themselves. The image is vivid: they pile loads onto others’ backs that they would not touch with a fingertip. The finger of God drove out demons (v.20); the fingers of the lawyers won’t lift a burden.

notes.original: tēn klein tēs gnōseōs
notes.rendering: the key of knowledge
notes.why: The lawyers hold the key of knowledge — the interpretive authority to unlock the meaning of Scripture and open the way to God. They have not used it to enter; they have used it to lock the door and stand outside it, blocking those who want to go in. The image is of a key that has been used as a barrier rather than an opener. Knowledge that excludes rather than includes has become the opposite of what it was meant to be.

outro: Note on Luke’s Lord’s Prayer vs. Matthew’s: Luke’s version (11:2–4) is shorter and more direct than Matthew’s (6:9–13). It lacks ‘who art in heaven,’ ‘your will be done on earth as in heaven,’ and the doxology (‘for yours is the kingdom’), which is a later liturgical addition absent from the best manuscripts of Matthew as well. Luke’s version is probably closer to what Jesus actually taught on a particular occasion; Matthew’s may represent a more developed liturgical form used in Matthew’s community. Both are canonical; neither is more ‘original’ in any theologically meaningful sense. Luke’s brevity and directness, however, have their own theological weight: this is a prayer stripped of ceremony and given to ordinary disciples who asked how to pray.

Note on the seven woes and their structure: Jesus delivers three woes against the Pharisees (vv.42–44) and three against the lawyers (vv.46–52), with a seventh embedded in the accusation about the prophets (vv.47–51). The woes mirror the Beatitudes of chapter 6 in form but reverse their content: where the Beatitudes announce blessing to the marginalised, the woes announce judgment on the religiously privileged. The recurring structure — you do X but neglect Y — exposes a consistent pattern: external performance masking internal vacancy. The climax is v.52: the lawyers have taken the key of knowledge and locked the door. The most serious charge against religious authority is not corruption but obstruction.

intro: Luke 12 is a long sustained discourse, moving from hypocrisy through wealth through anxiety through watchfulness through fire. The thread running through it is the question of where a person’s real life is located — in possessions, in security, in reputation, or in God. The Greek is consistently precise and rewards close reading.
I. Fear God, Not People (12:1–12)

notes.original: hypokrisis
notes.rendering: hypocrisy
notes.why: Hypokrisis in classical Greek means the playing of a theatrical role — performance for an audience. A hypokritēs is an actor. The Pharisees’ hypocrisy is not merely dishonesty; it is the performance of a religious role for public approval, a life lived for the audience rather than for God. The yeast metaphor is important: a little hypocrisy works its way through the whole character, as yeast works through dough. It is not an isolated failure but a corrupting principle.

notes.original: Geennan
notes.rendering: Gehenna
notes.why: Gehenna — transliterated directly rather than rendered as ‘hell’ — is the Valley of Hinnom (ge-hinnom) south of Jerusalem, where child sacrifice had been practiced in the time of the kings (2 Kings 23:10) and which became in Jewish tradition a symbol of divine judgment and destruction. The word ‘hell’ carries centuries of later theological freight; Gehenna is the specific Jewish image Jesus uses, rooted in a real geographical place with a real historical horror attached to it.

notes.original: assaria dyo
notes.rendering: two pennies
notes.why: Two assaria — the assarion being a small Roman copper coin, one sixteenth of a denarius, worth approximately what a labourer might earn in an hour. Five sparrows for two of these coins: the cheapest possible unit of food in the marketplace, sold in bulk to the poor. The sparrow is the most economically negligible creature Jesus could have named. And not one of them is forgotten before God.

notes.original: hai triches tēs kephalēs
notes.rendering: even the hairs of your head are all numbered
notes.why: A form of rabbinic argument from the lesser to the greater: if the most trivial and unnoticed details of creation are known to God, how much more the people made in his image. The hair is not merely counted (arithmēmenai) but numbered — each one has a number, a designation. The image is of a God whose knowledge is not general and approximate but specific and exhaustive.

notes.original: tō pneumati tō hagiō blasphēmēsanti
notes.rendering: blasphemes against the Holy Spirit
notes.why: One of the most debated sayings in the gospels. In context, the blasphemy against the Spirit refers to the persistent, deliberate attribution of the Spirit’s work to demonic agency — the accusation made in 11:15. It is the settled choice to call light darkness and darkness light, the hardening of the perceptual faculty that distinguishes God’s action from evil. Speaking against the Son of Man — misunderstanding, misjudging, opposing Jesus in his earthly ministry — can be released, because fuller understanding may come. But the deliberate, sustained rejection of the Spirit’s testimony has no corrective available.

notes.original: pleonexia
notes.rendering: greed
notes.why: Pleonexia means the desire for more — pleon (more) + echein (to have). It is not simply wanting things but the compulsive, restless desire for more than one has, which is never satisfied by acquisition. Jesus names it as something to guard against in every form (pasēs pleonexias): greed comes in multiple varieties and disguises. The warning comes before the parable, not after: the listeners should already be examining themselves as the story unfolds.

notes.original: dialogizeto en heautō
notes.rendering: he reasoned to himself
notes.why: Dialogizomai — to reason, to deliberate, to turn over in one’s mind. The rich man conducts an internal conversation with himself about his problem. The problem he identifies is storage: where will he put his surplus? He never asks who else might need it, what it is for, or what God thinks of it. The internal monologue is the character study: a man whose entire horizon is bounded by his own accumulated goods.

notes.original: tē psychē mou
notes.rendering: to my soul
notes.why: The rich man speaks directly to his own soul — an unusual and revealing construction. He addresses his psychē as though it were a separate entity: Soul, you have plenty. Take your ease. Eat, drink, be merry. But the soul he is addressing is the very thing about to be demanded of him. In addressing his soul as a passive beneficiary of his wealth, he misunderstands what the soul is. It is not a consumer of stored goods; it is the living self that stands before God.

notes.original: apaitoōsin tēn psychēn sou
notes.rendering: your soul is being demanded of you
notes.why: Apaiteo means to demand back, to require the return of something — the word used when a loan is called in. The soul is not taken arbitrarily; it is demanded back, as though it were always a loan. The passive voice and the plural implied subject (they are demanding — an impersonal plural, possibly referring to angels or divine agents) make the statement solemn and impersonal. Tonight. The loan is being called in.

notes.original: eis theon ploutōn
notes.rendering: rich toward God
notes.why: The contrast is between storing up for oneself (heautō thesaurizōn) and being rich toward God (eis theon ploutōn). Rich toward God does not mean donating to religious causes; it means orienting one’s wealth — one’s life, energy, and resources — in the direction of God and what God values. The parable does not condemn abundance; it condemns the redirection of the self inward, toward the stockpile, away from God and neighbour.

notes.original: mē merimnate
notes.rendering: don’t be anxious
notes.why: Merimnaō means to be anxious, to have the divided mind (from merizō, to divide, and nous, mind — a mind pulled in multiple directions at once). The present imperative with mē means: stop doing this, cease this ongoing practice. The disciples are already anxious; Jesus is calling them out of it. The word appears five times in this passage (vv.22, 25, 26, 29 — the noun form in v.22): anxiety is the subject being dismantled.

notes.original: katanoesate tous korakas
notes.rendering: Consider the ravens
notes.why: Katavoeo means to observe carefully, to contemplate, to fix the mind on. Jesus does not say ‘glance at the birds.’ He says: fix your attention on them, think about what you are seeing. Luke uses ravens (korakas) where Matthew has ‘birds of the air.’ Ravens in Jewish tradition were unclean birds (Leviticus 11:15) — yet God feeds them. The argument is sharper than it first appears: if God feeds even the ritually unclean raven, how much more the disciples?

notes.original: prostheinai epi tēn hēlikian autou pēchyn
notes.rendering: add a single hour to their lifespan
notes.why: Hēlikia means either stature (physical height) or lifespan. Pēchyn means a cubit — approximately half a metre. The phrase is debated: does it mean add a cubit to one’s height, or add a small span to one’s life? The lifespan reading fits the context better — Jesus is addressing anxiety about survival, not about height. The smallest unit of time or measure added to a life is beyond the anxious person’s control.

notes.original: ta krina
notes.rendering: the lilies
notes.why: Krinon means lily — almost certainly the wild anemone or poppy of the Galilean hillsides, which blooms brilliantly in spring and is gone within weeks. The point is their absolute dependence on God’s provision combined with their extraordinary, fleeting beauty. They do nothing to produce their glory; it is simply given. Solomon at his most magnificent could not match what God does effortlessly for a wildflower. The argument moves from the economically negligible (ravens) to the aesthetically surpassing (lilies).

notes.original: oligopistoi
notes.rendering: You of little faith
notes.why: Oligopistos — little-faithed — is a compound word: oligos (little, small) + pistis (faith). It is a gentle rebuke, not a condemnation: the disciples have faith, but it is small relative to the provision of the God they are trusting. The word is always used of people who are in relationship with Jesus — not outsiders. It is the word used when someone almost trusts enough but holds back a corner of their anxiety.

notes.original: to mikron poimnion
notes.rendering: little flock
notes.why: Mikron poimnion — little flock — is a term of extraordinary tenderness. The disciples are a small, vulnerable group in a large and often hostile world. Jesus does not minimize the vulnerability; he names it, and then speaks the assurance directly into it: your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Eudokēsen — the aorist of divine good pleasure (the word from the baptism and Transfiguration voices) — has already settled this. The kingdom is a gift already decided.

notes.original: estōsan hymōn hai osphyes periezōsmenai
notes.rendering: Let your loins be girded
notes.why: Periezōsmenai — having been belted, girded up. A long robe gathered up and tucked into a belt so the legs are free for movement — the posture of the Israelites eating the Passover meal in Exodus 12:11 (‘with your belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, your staff in your hand’). Jesus invokes the Exodus posture of readiness: dressed to move, lamps lit, waiting for the signal. The disciples are to be perpetually in the posture of Passover night.

notes.original: perizōsetai kai anaklinei autous
notes.rendering: he will gird himself and have them recline
notes.why: The reversal is astonishing. The master comes home to find his servants awake and waiting — and instead of being served, he serves them. He girds himself (takes the servant posture), has them recline (takes the position of the served), and waits on them. This is the only place in the gospels where Jesus describes the master serving the servants at table — a direct anticipation of 22:27 (‘I am among you as the one who serves’) and of the foot-washing in John 13.

notes.original: panti dōthēsetai poly
notes.rendering: From everyone to whom much is given, much will be required
notes.why: One of the most quoted sentences in Luke, often misapplied to talent or ability. In context it is specifically about knowledge of the master’s will. The servant who knows and does not act is more culpable than the servant who does not know. The principle is about moral and spiritual knowledge: greater revelation creates greater accountability. The disciples, who have been given the mysteries of the kingdom (8:10), are the ones to whom much has been given.

notes.original: pyr elthon balein epi tēn gēn
notes.rendering: I came to cast fire on the earth
notes.why: Ballo means to throw, to cast, to hurl. Jesus did not come to kindle fire gently; he came to hurl it. The fire here is not the fire of judgment alone but the fire of the Spirit — John announced baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire (3:16). The fire Jesus casts is the same fire that will fall at Pentecost: purifying, dividing, consuming what cannot survive it. The anguish in ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ is real: Jesus is eager for what his death will release.

notes.original: synechomai
notes.rendering: I am hemmed in
notes.why: Synecho means to hold together, to press, to constrain — the same word used of Simon’s mother-in-law gripped by fever (4:38) and of the crowd pressing in on Jesus (8:45). Here Jesus uses it of himself: he is hemmed in, constrained, pressed on all sides until his baptism — his death — is accomplished. The word is visceral: it describes a person under pressure that will not release until something decisive happens.

notes.original: dianerismōn
notes.rendering: division
notes.why: Diamerismos means a splitting apart, a thorough division. Luke’s version of this saying uses dianerismōn where Matthew (10:34) uses machairan — a sword. Luke’s word is more abstract but no less sharp: the effect of Jesus’ coming is a cleaving of households, a division that runs through the most intimate relationships. The kingdom’s arrival does not produce social harmony; it produces the crisis of decision, and decisions divide.

notes.original: tōn kairon touton
notes.rendering: this present time
notes.why: Kairos — not merely chronos (clock-time) but the season defined by its character, its significance, its opportunity. The crowds can read weather signs with perfect accuracy but cannot read the kairos: the decisive, unrepeatable moment in which God is acting. The meteorological competence and the theological blindness are held in contrast. The irony is that the signs of the kingdom are at least as visible as a cloud in the west.

notes.original: ep’ archonta
notes.rendering: to the magistrate
notes.why: Archōn means a ruler, a magistrate, one with authority. The legal illustration in vv.58–59 has a double register: it is practical wisdom about settling disputes before they reach court, and it is an eschatological warning about settling one’s account with God before the final judgment. The urgency of the road — settle now, while there is still time — mirrors the urgency of the entire chapter.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 12: The chapter is a single sustained discourse addressed first to the disciples (vv.1–12), then to a crowd member who interrupts (vv.13–21), then back to the disciples (vv.22–53), then to the crowds (vv.54–59). The thread running through every section is the question of where a person’s actual life is located. The hypocrite locates it in reputation; the rich fool in possessions; the anxious person in security; the unfaithful servant in the master’s absence; the crowd in the weather forecast rather than the moment. Each section names a different displacement of the self from its proper centre. The positive counterpart to all of them is stated twice: ‘Seek his kingdom’ (v.31) and ‘be rich toward God’ (v.21).

Note on ‘I came to cast fire’ (12:49) and its place in Luke’s theology: This verse is one of the most startling in the gospel and one of the most neglected. Jesus expresses longing — ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ — for the fire his death will release. The baptism of v.50 is unmistakably the baptism of suffering (a usage found in Mark 10:38 as well). Between these two verses Jesus describes the tension of the liminal period: the fire he came to ignite has not yet been kindled; the baptism he must undergo has not yet been accomplished. He is hemmed in by what has not yet happened. The anguish is genuine and Luke does not smooth it over. This is one of the moments in the gospel where the cost of the incarnation is most nakedly visible.

intro: Luke 13 gathers several of the travel narrative’s most urgent threads: the randomness of death as a call to repentance, a woman released from bondage on the Sabbath, two small parables about unstoppable growth, the narrow door, and the lament over Jerusalem that makes the reader feel the weight of everything that is coming. The Greek in each section is worth close attention.
I. Repent or Perish (13:1–9)

notes.original: haimati emixen
notes.rendering: whose blood Pilate had mixed
notes.why: The event — Pilate killing Galileans while they were offering sacrifice — is not recorded elsewhere in ancient sources, but Pilate’s brutal suppression of Jewish religious gatherings is historically well-attested (Josephus describes multiple such incidents). The phrase ‘mixed their blood with their sacrifices’ is vivid and horrifying: Pilate killed them at the altar, so that their blood literally mingled with the blood of the animals they were offering. The listeners come to Jesus expecting him to explain why this happened to those particular people. He refuses.

notes.original: metanoēte
notes.rendering: unless you repent
notes.why: Metanoeō — to change one’s mind and direction, to turn. The aorist subjunctive mē metanoēte carries a condition of urgency: the time for turning is now, before the catastrophe arrives. Jesus refuses the question of comparative guilt (were those people worse sinners?) and replaces it with a universal call: everyone needs to turn. The tower’s randomness and Pilate’s violence are not windows into the victims’ guilt; they are mirrors showing every listener their own mortality and the urgency of repentance.

notes.original: katargō
notes.rendering: wasting the soil
notes.why: Katargeō means to render idle, to make useless, to waste — to cause something to produce no return on the investment made in it. The fig tree is consuming soil, water, and space while producing nothing. The word is economic: the owner’s complaint is not aesthetic but practical. The tree is occupying resources that could be producing fruit elsewhere. The vinedresser’s intercession — one more year — is the parable’s theological heart: the mercy that delays judgment to allow one more chance.

notes.original: eis to mellon
notes.rendering: next year
notes.why: Literally: into the coming time. The vinedresser does not promise the tree will bear fruit; he promises effort and one more season. The parable ends without resolution. The owner agrees, the year begins, and we never learn the outcome. Luke leaves the ending open deliberately: the reader is the fig tree, and the year is still running.

notes.original: pneuma astheneias
notes.rendering: a spirit of weakness
notes.why: Luke names both a spiritual and a physical dimension: a spirit of weakness (pneuma astheneias) causing her physical condition. He does not separate them or explain how they relate. The woman is bent double (synkyptousa) and cannot straighten up — cannot anakyptein, cannot raise herself up. The word anakyptein — to lift the head, to look up — will reappear in 21:28 (‘lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near’). Luke’s healing vocabulary and his eschatological vocabulary share a root.

notes.original: apolelyai
notes.rendering: you are released
notes.why: Apolyo — to release, to set free, to loose — the same root as aphesis (release/forgiveness). Jesus does not say ‘you are healed’ but ‘you are released from your weakness.’ The language is liberation language: she has been held and now she is let go. And in v.16 the bondage is made explicit: Satan has kept her bound (dedemenin) for eighteen years. The Sabbath is the day of liberation — the seventh day, the day of rest from bondage, the day pointing toward Jubilee. Releasing her on the Sabbath is not a violation of the Sabbath’s meaning; it is its fulfillment.

notes.original: hypokritài
notes.rendering: Hypocrites
notes.why: The plural is striking — Jesus addresses the synagogue ruler but uses the plural. The hypocrisy is not individual but systemic: the whole religious apparatus that objects to healing on the Sabbath while routinely untying animals on the Sabbath. The argument is a fortiori — from the lesser to the greater. If you untie an ox for water — a purely practical action for an animal — how much more should this daughter of Abraham be untied from eighteen years of bondage?

notes.original: thygatera Abraam
notes.rendering: a daughter of Abraham
notes.why: The title is rare and deliberate. Luke uses ‘son of Abraham’ for Zacchaeus (19:9) and ‘daughter of Abraham’ here — only twice in the gospel. The title confers full covenant membership and dignity on people the religious establishment has marginalised. This woman is not an object of charity; she is a full heir of the covenant promise, bound in its own house by Satan for eighteen years. The indignation of the synagogue ruler is not merely wrong; it is a failure to see who is standing in his own building.

notes.original: katedaischynonto
notes.rendering: were put to shame
notes.why: Kataischynō means to put to shame thoroughly, to humiliate — the kata- prefix intensifying the effect. The opponents are not merely silenced or corrected; they are shamed. In a honour-shame culture, this is decisive: the public argument has been lost and everyone in the synagogue knows it. And the crowd’s response — rejoicing over all the glorious things being done — forms the counter-image. Two reactions to Jesus in a single verse.

notes.heading: III. The Mustard Seed and the Leaven (13:18–21)

notes.original: ebalen eis kēpon heautou
notes.rendering: throws into his garden
notes.why: Ballo — to throw, to cast — the same energetic verb Jesus used of casting fire on the earth (12:49). The mustard seed is not placed gently in prepared soil; it is thrown. The kingdom arrives with the same irreverence for careful human planning. And the result is disproportionate: the smallest of seeds becomes a tree large enough for birds to nest in — echoing Daniel 4:12, where the great tree shelters all the nations. The kingdom’s growth from negligible beginnings to universal shelter is the parable’s arc.

notes.original: enekrypsen eis aleurou sata tria
notes.rendering: hides in three measures of flour
notes.why: Enkryptō means to hide, to conceal within — to bury the leaven in the flour so it disappears. Three measures (sata tria) is approximately forty litres — enough to feed a hundred people, the quantity Abraham prepared for his divine visitors (Genesis 18:6 LXX uses the same measure). The leaven works invisibly, pervasively, until the whole batch is transformed. The kingdom does not announce its progress; it simply works until everything is leavened. The hiddenness and the totality are both part of the image.

notes.original: agonizesthe
notes.rendering: Strive
notes.why: Agonizomai — to struggle, to compete, to fight for something with everything you have. The word is used of athletic contest (1 Corinthians 9:25) and military combat. It is not a gentle encouragement to make an effort; it is a call to exert oneself fully, to treat entry into the kingdom as something that demands the whole self. The narrow door (steias thyras) is not simply narrow in the sense of exclusive; it is narrow in the sense that you cannot get through it sideways, carrying everything you brought, without turning and going through directly.

notes.original: apokleiseē tēn thyran
notes.rendering: has shut the door
notes.why: The aorist subjunctive: once the master has got up and shut the door, the situation is changed. The shutting is a single completed action, and after it the outside is the outside. The people knocking on the door are not strangers; they are people who ate and drank in his presence, who heard him teach in their streets. Familiarity with Jesus is not the same as being known by him. The door closes on acquaintances.

notes.original: ouk oida pothen este
notes.rendering: I don’t know where you are from
notes.why: The repeated phrase — first in v.25, then in v.27 — is not a statement of geographical ignorance. It is a statement of relational non-recognition: I do not know you, you do not belong to my household, there is no bond between us. The Greek pothen (from where) asks about origin, identity, belonging. The locked-out people do not belong to this household — not because they were excluded by divine decree but because they never truly entered.

notes.original: apo anatolōn kai dysmōn… borra kai notou
notes.rendering: from east and west, from north and south
notes.why: The four directions encompass the whole world. Those reclining at table in the kingdom of God come from every compass point — the universal gathering of the nations anticipated in Isaiah 43:5–6, 49:12. Immediately after the warning about those who thought proximity to Jesus guaranteed them a seat comes the announcement that those from the farthest reaches of the earth will be seated. The first-and-last reversal of v.30 applies in both directions.

notes.original: tē alōpeki taytē
notes.rendering: that fox
notes.why: Alōpēx means fox. In Jewish tradition the fox was a symbol of the cunning and destructive but ultimately minor threat — not the lion (a symbol of Rome or genuine power) but the skulking, opportunistic predator. Jesus dismisses Herod’s threat with contempt: this fox does not control the timeline of his mission. The Pharisees’ warning may or may not be genuine; Jesus treats it as irrelevant regardless.

notes.original: tē tritē teleioumai
notes.rendering: on the third day I reach my goal
notes.why: Teleioo means to complete, to bring to its intended end, to perfect — the cognate of teleios (perfect, complete). The third day — whatever its precise reference here — points toward the resurrection: the day on which Jesus’ mission reaches its telos, its completion. He is not fleeing from Herod toward safety; he is moving toward Jerusalem and toward the accomplishment of everything he was sent to do. The verb is active and directional: he is reaching his goal, not being caught.

notes.original: ouk endechetai propheten apolesthai exo Hierousalēm
notes.rendering: a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem
notes.why: A grimly ironic observation: Jerusalem kills its prophets, so Jesus must go there to die. The must (dei) of divine necessity governs even the location of his death. He cannot be stopped by Herod in Galilee; the script requires Jerusalem. The bitterness in the statement is real — Jerusalem is not the destination of triumph but of execution, and Jesus knows it.

notes.original: Ierousalēm Ierousalēm
notes.rendering: Jerusalem, Jerusalem
notes.why: The doubled name is a Hebrew form of lament: ‘Jerusalem, Jerusalem’ carries the same emotional weight as ‘Martha, Martha’ (10:41) and ‘Simon, Simon’ (22:31) — a cry of urgent, anguished address. But here the addressee is a city, and the grief is proportionally vast. Jesus is not yet in Jerusalem when he says this — he is still on the road. The lament precedes the arrival. He weeps for the city before he sees it.

notes.original: hōs ornis tà heautēs nossion
notes.rendering: the way a hen gathers her chicks
notes.why: The image of God as a bird gathering and sheltering appears in Deuteronomy 32:11 (an eagle), Psalm 17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 61:4, 91:4 (wings). Jesus applies the image to himself: he is the one who has been trying to gather Jerusalem’s children. This is a claim of divine identity embedded in a maternal image — Jesus using feminine imagery for his own longing. The tenderness of the image makes the ‘you were not willing’ (ouk ēthelēsate) all the more devastating. The failure is not the hen’s; it is the chicks’ refusal to come.

notes.original: aphietai hymōn ho oikos
notes.rendering: your house is left to you desolate
notes.why: Aphietai — is released, is left, is abandoned. The word is aphiemi again — the release word, the forgiveness word, the Jubilee word. But here it turns in a direction no one expects: the house is released, left, abandoned. The divine presence departs. This is the language of the Shekhinah’s departure from the Temple — the prophetic imagery of Ezekiel 10–11, where the glory of the Lord rises from the temple and departs. Jesus announces the Temple’s abandonment before its destruction.

notes.original: ho erchomenos en onomati kyriou
notes.rendering: Blesséd is he who comes in the name of the Lord
notes.why: Psalm 118:26 — the great Hallel psalm sung at Passover. The crowd will shout these words at the triumphal entry (19:38). Jesus quotes it here as the condition of Jerusalem’s seeing him again: you will not see me until you say this. Whether this refers to the triumphal entry, to the second coming, or to the eschatological recognition of Israel is debated. Luke may intend all three as a single movement: the entry that precedes the passion, the passion that precedes the resurrection, the resurrection that precedes the parousia. The psalm binds them together.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 13 as a chapter of compressed urgency: Every section in chapter 13 carries the same underlying pressure: time is running out, the door is open now but will not always be, the tree has one more season, the woman has been bound long enough, the journey to Jerusalem is under way and cannot be diverted. The chapter opens with sudden death (Pilate’s victims, the tower of Siloam) and closes with a lament over a city that will be destroyed. Between them, Jesus heals, teaches, argues, and moves. The Greek sustains a consistent note of urgency — dei (must), nun (now), eti (still) — that accumulates through the chapter until it breaks into grief in the final verses.

Note on the lament over Jerusalem and its placement: Luke places the Jerusalem lament here, still on the road (13:22), long before the triumphal entry. Matthew places a parallel lament later (23:37–39), during Jesus’ final week in the city. Luke’s placement is theologically significant: Jesus laments the city he has not yet reached, weeps for people who have not yet rejected him in the final, public way. The grief precedes the events that would justify it. This is not retrospective sorrow but prophetic mourning — the sorrow of one who knows what is coming and cannot prevent it because the city will not be gathered.

intro: Luke 14 is structured as a single extended dinner scene in a Pharisee’s house, with teaching that moves outward in concentric rings from the table itself to all of society to the radical demands of discipleship. The Greek in each section repays close attention — particularly in the parable of the banquet and the cost-of-discipleship sayings, where the language is at its most unsparing.
I. Healing on the Sabbath (14:1–6)

notes.original: paratethrēmenoi auton
notes.rendering: watching him carefully
notes.why: Paratēreō — to observe narrowly, to watch with intent — the same word used of the scribes and Pharisees in 6:7 who watched whether he would heal on the Sabbath in order to find grounds for accusation. The scene is set before anyone speaks: Jesus is under surveillance at the dinner table of a man who has invited him. The hospitality is a trap.

notes.original: hydrōpikos
notes.rendering: whose body is swollen with fluid
notes.why: Hydrōpikos means someone suffering from dropsy — the accumulation of fluid in body cavities and tissues, producing severe swelling. Luke the physician uses the clinical term. The man’s presence in the house is unexplained: was he invited, or did he simply appear? Luke’s ‘right there in front of him’ suggests the encounter is staged — possibly by those watching. The silence of the Pharisees when Jesus asks his question (v.4) is its own answer.

notes.original: epilabomenos iasato
notes.rendering: takes hold of the man, heals him
notes.why: Epilambanomai means to take hold of, to grasp, to lay hands on with firm intention. Jesus does not gesture toward the man or speak a word across the room; he takes hold of him. The physical contact in a room full of lawyers watching for a violation is itself a statement. Then iaomai — he heals — and apolyo — he releases him, sends him on his way. Three verbs in immediate sequence: grasp, heal, release. The whole encounter is compressed into a single decisive movement.

notes.original: huios ē bous
notes.rendering: your son or your ox
notes.why: The manuscript tradition is divided between ‘son’ (huios) and ‘donkey’ (onos) in the first position. The NA28 follows ‘son,’ which creates a more powerful argument: you would pull out your own child without hesitation. Either way, the logic is the same a fortiori argument Jesus used in 13:15: if you do this for an animal or a child, how much more for a human being bound by disease? The silence of v.6 is the answer: they cannot refute it.

notes.original: tous keklemenous… tàs prōtoklisias
notes.rendering: the guests choosing the places of honour
notes.why: Prōtoklisia means the first reclining place — the position of greatest honour at the table, closest to the host. In a Greco-Roman triclinium, the seating arrangement was a precise social map: where you reclined announced your rank and the host’s estimation of you to everyone present. Jesus observes the guests jockeying for position and responds not with a reprimand but with a parable. The parable is simultaneously practical social wisdom and a theological statement about the kingdom’s inversions.

notes.original: meta aischynēs
notes.rendering: in shame
notes.why: Aischynē is shame — the public exposure of having overreached, of having claimed more than one is due. In a culture structured by honour and shame, this is not a mild embarrassment; it is social humiliation witnessed by everyone at the table. The person who grabbed the best seat and was made to move to the worst has not merely lost a seat; they have lost face in front of the entire company. The calculated risk of self-promotion carries this specific penalty.

notes.original: pas ho hypsōn heauton tapeinōthēsetai
notes.rendering: Every one who exalts himself will be humbled
notes.why: A maxim that appears in three places in Luke (here, 18:14, and the Magnificat’s ‘he has brought down the powerful’ in 1:52). The passive verbs — will be humbled, will be exalted — are divine passives: God is the agent of both movements. The kingdom’s social structure is not merely the inverse of the world’s; it is the world’s structure corrected by the one who sees clearly.

notes.original: antiklēthēs
notes.rendering: repayment
notes.why: Antikaleō means to call back in return — to invite someone who will then invite you, completing a social transaction. The dinner party circuit of mutual obligation is precisely what Jesus names and instructs the host to break. Inviting friends, brothers, relatives, and rich neighbours produces antiklēthēs — a return invitation. The social economy of favour-trading keeps wealth and honour circulating among those who already have them. Jesus proposes a feast that breaks the circuit entirely.

notes.original: ptōchous, anapeirous, chōlous, typhlous
notes.rendering: the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind
notes.why: The same four categories that the servant gathers from the streets and lanes of the city in v.21. The host’s guest list and the banquet’s eventual attendees are identical. Luke is deliberate: the teaching about who to invite is immediately illustrated by the parable of who actually attends. The people who cannot repay are the ones the kingdom fills its table with. Luke’s Jesus returns to this list repeatedly throughout the gospel (4:18, 7:22, 14:13, 14:21): it is the consistent description of the kingdom’s constituency.

notes.original: en tē anastasi tōn dikaiōn
notes.rendering: at the resurrection of the righteous
notes.why: Luke’s phrase is precise: not simply ‘at the resurrection’ but at the resurrection of the righteous. This reflects a Jewish tradition of two resurrections — one for the righteous and one for the wicked — found in Daniel 12:2 and developed in Second Temple Judaism. The repayment Jesus promises is not merely delayed; it is eschatological. It will happen at the great reckoning, when the accounts that could not be settled in this age are settled in the next.

notes.heading: IV. The Parable of the Great Banquet (14:15–24)

notes.original: makarios hostis phagetai arton en tē basileia
notes.rendering: Blessed is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of God
notes.why: The pious exclamation from one of the guests triggers the parable. It is a genuinely Jewish hope: the messianic banquet, the great feast at the end of the age (Isaiah 25:6–8). The man who says it is reclining at the table with Jesus, in the house of a leading Pharisee, presumably confident that he is exactly the kind of person who will be at that table. Jesus’ parable is a response to that confidence.

notes.original: erchou, hoti ēdē hetoima estin
notes.rendering: Come — everything is ready now
notes.why: The invitation has two stages in this culture: an advance invitation (which the guests have already accepted), and then a final summons when the meal is actually ready. The guests have already said yes. The servant’s message is not the original invitation but the call that it’s time to come. Their refusals at this stage are therefore a withdrawal from a prior commitment, not a polite decline of an unexpected invitation. The offence to the host is compounded.

notes.original: apò miàs pantes
notes.rendering: one after another
notes.why: Literally: from one — all of them. The phrase indicates unanimity and sequence: they all begin making excuses, one by one, starting from the first. The three excuses that follow are each implausible in different ways. No one buys a field without inspecting it first. No one buys oxen without testing them first. The newly-married man’s excuse doesn’t even have a polite formula attached — he simply says he can’t come. The escalating casualness of the refusals reflects escalating contempt for the host.

notes.original: ōrgisthē
notes.rendering: is angry
notes.why: Orgizō — to be angry, to be provoked to wrath. The master’s anger is not petulance; it is the appropriate response to having extended honour to those who have treated it with contempt. In a culture of honour and obligation, the refusals are a public insult. The anger drives the second invitation — not as consolation but as determined fulfillment: the banquet will happen, the house will be filled, and it will be filled with people the originally invited guests would never have expected to see there.

notes.original: anankason eiselthein
notes.rendering: compel them to come in
notes.why: Anankazō means to compel, to constrain, to press urgently — not physical force but insistent, persuasive urging that overcomes reluctance. The people on the roads and hedges — outside the city entirely, the most marginalised — are not simply invited; they are pressed to come. Their reluctance may arise from disbelief that the invitation is genuine, from awareness of their own social unworthiness, or from simple unfamiliarity with banquets. The servant’s task is to overcome that reluctance with insistence.

notes.original: oudēis tōn keKlEménōn
notes.rendering: not one of those who were invited
notes.why: The final statement is absolute and irrevocable. The originally invited guests — those who received the advance invitation, who said yes, who then declined when the moment came — will taste nothing. Their refusal at the moment of fulfillment is permanent. The parable does not leave room for a late arrival; the door is shut by the fullness of the house. Every seat has been taken by someone who came.

notes.original: misei ton patera heautou
notes.rendering: hates his own father and mother
notes.why: Miseō means to hate — but in Semitic idiom, to hate often means to love less, to prefer less, to give lower priority to. The parallel in Matthew 10:37 uses the language of ‘love more’ rather than ‘hate.’ Luke preserves the stronger Semitic form. The saying does not require emotional hatred of family; it requires a commitment to Jesus that relativizes every other loyalty — including the most primal ones — so thoroughly that by comparison they look like hatred. The addition of ‘and even his own life’ (kai eti tēn psychēn heautou) extends the requirement to self-regard: even the instinct for self-preservation must be subordinated.

notes.original: ton stauron heautou
notes.rendering: their own cross
notes.why: The cross is not a metaphor for hardship or difficulty in first-century Palestine. It is the instrument of execution by the occupying power. A person carrying their cross is walking to their own execution, in public, having been condemned by Rome. Jesus is asking his followers to take on that posture: publicly committed to him, publicly marked as belonging to a movement that Rome may find subversive, willing to go where that commitment leads regardless of the cost. Luke’s version (as in 9:23) adds the daily quality: each day this cross is picked up again.

notes.original: psephistai tēn dapanēn
notes.rendering: counts the cost
notes.why: Psephizō means to count with pebbles — psephos is a pebble used as a counting stone. The image is of a builder sitting down with a pile of pebbles, moving them one by one as he calculates the total expense. Dapanē means cost, expense — the full financial outlay required to complete the project. Jesus is not discouraging people from following him; he is insisting that they reckon clearly what they are signing up for. Naive enthusiasm that collapses under pressure is worse than honest assessment that leads to a genuine commitment.

notes.original: prēsbeian apostellas
notes.rendering: sends a delegation
notes.why: Prēsbeia means an embassy, a delegation of envoys sent to negotiate. The king with ten thousand men, facing twenty thousand, sends diplomatic representatives to ask for terms of peace while the enemy is still at a distance. The military illustration is paired with the building illustration: both are about honest assessment of resources versus demands. The application to discipleship is the same: count what you have, assess what is required, and make a genuine decision — rather than beginning what you cannot finish.

notes.original: to halas kalon
notes.rendering: Salt is good
notes.why: Salt in the ancient world was essential for preserving food, seasoning, and ritual purity (Leviticus 2:13 required salt on all grain offerings). A disciple without genuine commitment is like salt that has lost its saltiness: it looks like salt, it occupies the space of salt, but it performs none of salt’s functions. The Greek word for ‘loses its taste’ is moōranthē — becomes foolish, becomes insipid — from mōros (fool). Saltless salt is not merely useless; it is a kind of folly.

notes.original: oute eis gēn oute eis koprian
notes.rendering: neither for the soil nor for the manure pile
notes.why: Salt that has lost its saltiness cannot even serve as fertilizer or be mixed into the compost. It is completely without use — fit only to be thrown out. The image is deliberately extreme: the disciples who attach themselves to Jesus without genuine commitment are not merely ineffective; they are less useful than refuse. The sharp ending — ‘whoever has ears to hear, let them hear’ — signals that what has just been said is something many people will not want to hear.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 14 as a single banquet scene: The entire chapter unfolds at and around the Pharisee’s dinner table. Jesus heals a man (vv.1–6), teaches the guests (vv.7–11), teaches the host (vv.12–14), responds to a pious comment with a parable (vv.15–24), and then turns to address the crowds following him (vv.25–35). The movement from the intimate space of a dinner table to the crowds on the road mirrors the movement in the parable itself: from the originally invited guests to the streets and lanes and roads and hedges. The banquet that begins in a Pharisee’s house ends with the whole world invited.

Note on the three excuses in the parable (vv.18–20): Each excuse involves a prior acquisition or commitment that takes precedence over the banquet. A field, five pairs of oxen, a new wife. None of these are intrinsically wrong. The point is not that the things themselves are evil but that they have become the reason for declining the most important invitation ever extended. Luke’s Jesus consistently presents the danger of the kingdom’s good things — land, property, family — becoming the obstacle to the kingdom itself. The parable of the rich fool (12:16–21), the cost-of-discipleship sayings in this chapter (vv.26–33), and the rich ruler in chapter 18 all turn on the same axis: what you legitimately have can become what keeps you from what is offered.

intro: Luke 15 is the most concentrated expression of Luke’s theology of grace. Three parables, each longer than the last, each pressing deeper into the question of what God does when something is lost. The Greek of the Prodigal Son in particular is among the most carefully crafted prose in the New Testament — every verb, every detail, every silence is deliberate.
I. The Setting (15:1–2)

notes.original: engizontēs autō
notes.rendering: drawing near to him
notes.why: Engizō — to draw near, to approach — carries theological weight in Luke. It is the word used of the kingdom drawing near (10:9, 11), of Jesus drawing near to Emmaus (24:15), of the prodigal’s return when the father sees him ‘still a long way off.’ The tax collectors and sinners are not merely attending a lecture; they are approaching Jesus in the same way the kingdom approaches people. Their movement toward him mirrors his movement toward them.

notes.original: diegoggyzon… hoti hamartolous prosdechetai
notes.rendering: grumbling… welcomes sinners
notes.why: Diagoggyzo — to grumble thoroughly, to murmur persistently. The dia- prefix intensifies: this is not a passing complaint but a sustained, ongoing objection. The word echoes the LXX’s description of Israel grumbling against Moses in the wilderness (Exodus 16:2, Numbers 14:2). The accusation prosdechetai — he receives them, welcomes them, accepts them — is the very thing Jesus is about to defend and illustrate through all three parables. The Pharisees’ charge is his text.

notes.original: epi tō apolōloti
notes.rendering: goes after the lost one
notes.why: Apollymi — to lose, to destroy, to perish. The same verb runs through all three parables: the lost sheep (apolēsas, v.4), the lost coin (apolese, v.8), the lost son (apolōlota, v.24 and 32). The word is not merely ‘misplaced’ but genuinely lost — in danger, without direction, unable to find its own way back. The shepherd does not wait for the sheep to return; he goes after it. The initiative is entirely his.

notes.original: epitithēsin epi tous ōmous autou chairōn
notes.rendering: lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing
notes.why: The found sheep is not driven back or led; it is lifted and carried. The shepherd takes the full weight of the sheep onto his own body. The present participle chairōn — rejoicing — means the joy begins at the moment of finding, before the return home, before the party, before any celebration. The joy is in the finding itself. He walks home under the weight of what was lost, rejoicing.

notes.original: epi heni hamartōlō metanoounti
notes.rendering: over one sinner who repents
notes.why: The ninety-nine righteous who have no need of repentance are not condemned — but they do not generate the particular joy that one returning sinner does. Heaven’s arithmetic is counterintuitive: the one lost and found outweighs the ninety-nine never lost. This is not because the ninety-nine matter less but because the recovery of what was perishing produces a specific, distinctive joy that the sustained safety of the never-lost does not.

notes.original: drachmēn mian
notes.rendering: one silver coin
notes.why: A drachma was roughly equivalent to a day’s wage for a labourer — not an insignificant sum for a woman who has only ten. The ten coins may represent her entire savings, a dowry, or ceremonial coins worn as a headdress — each reading gives different weight to the loss. What matters is the proportion: one in ten, lost, and she lights a lamp, sweeps the whole house, and searches carefully until she finds it. The effort is comprehensive and the stakes are real.

notes.original: epimelōs zētei
notes.rendering: searches carefully
notes.why: Epimelos means carefully, diligently, with thorough attention. The woman does not glance around and give up; she lights a lamp (even in daylight, to see into corners and under furniture), sweeps every surface, and searches with sustained attention until she finds it. The three actions — light, sweep, search — are the human analogy to what God does when something belonging to him is lost.

notes.original: enōpion tōn agelōn tou theou
notes.rendering: in the presence of the angels of God
