notes.why: Luke does not say ‘the angels rejoice’ but that there is joy in the presence of the angels — a reverent circumlocution for God’s own joy. The joy is God’s, witnessed by the angels. This is the second of three graduated statements about heaven’s joy over one repentant sinner: in heaven (v.7), in the presence of the angels (v.10), and the father’s own running and kissing and feasting (vv.20–24). Each parable intensifies what the previous one stated.

notes.original: dos moi to epiballon meros tēs ousias
notes.rendering: give me my share of the estate
notes.why: The request is shocking in its cultural context. A son asking his father for his inheritance while the father is still alive was, in the ancient Near East, the equivalent of saying: I wish you were dead. The father would normally have the right — and would be expected by all social convention — to refuse, to rebuke, even to cut the son off. Instead, he divides his property between them. The father’s compliance is itself the first staggering act of grace in the parable.

notes.original: eis chōran makran
notes.rendering: a distant country
notes.why: Makran — far off, a long way away. The same word used in v.20 when the father sees him ‘still a long way off’ (eti autou makran apechontos). The parable measures distance in both directions: how far the son went, and how far away he still is when the father runs to meet him. The father’s vision reaches across the entire distance the son has put between them.

notes.original: asotos
notes.rendering: reckless living
notes.why: Asōtos means without saving, without keeping anything back — the adverb of asotos, one who cannot be saved or rescued, one who is past recovery. The word describes a mode of living that consumes everything without restraint or prudence. It is translated variously as ‘prodigal,’ ‘wild,’ ‘dissolute.’ The cognate noun appears in Ephesians 5:18 and Titus 1:6. ‘Reckless’ captures the heedless, consuming quality without the archaic flavour of ‘prodigal.’

notes.original: ekeràtiōn… oudēis edidou
notes.rendering: he longs… no one gives
notes.why: Epithumeo — to desire intensely, to long for — is the word used of sinful desire in many contexts (it is the word used in the tenth commandment’s LXX translation). Here it describes desperate hunger: he longs for the pods the pigs eat. The pigs — unclean animals in Jewish law — are being fed while he starves. He has sunk below the level of animals considered impure. And oudēis edidou — no one gave him anything. The passive abandonment of the sentence lands quietly and completely.

notes.original: eis heauton dē elthōn
notes.rendering: coming to himself
notes.why: Erchomai eis heauton — to come to oneself, to return to one’s senses, to come back inside oneself. The phrase is used in Greek literature for recovering from a trance, a fever, or a state of madness. The far country is not merely geographic; it is a state of being outside oneself, lost to one’s own identity. The return begins not on the road but in this moment of self-recognition in the pigsty. He comes to himself before he goes to his father.

notes.original: hēmarton eis ton ouranon kai enōpion sou
notes.rendering: I have sinned against heaven and before you
notes.why: The double confession — against heaven and before you — is both vertical and horizontal. The sin is against God (heaven is a Jewish circumlocution for God’s name) and it is done in the presence of his father. The son’s prepared speech is theologically precise: he names what the sin is, who it is against, and what it means for his status (‘no longer worthy to be called your son’). He has thought this through in the pigsty. The speech is the product of genuine self-knowledge.

notes.original: esplagchnisthē kai dramōn
notes.rendering: his heart breaks for him — and he runs
notes.why: Splagchnizomai again — the gut-word, the visceral compassion that Luke uses for Jesus at Nain (7:13) and for the Good Samaritan (10:33). Here it is the father’s. And the response is immediate and physical: dramōn — he runs. Running was considered undignified for an elderly Middle Eastern man of means; it required gathering up one’s robe and exposing one’s legs. The father does not maintain his dignity and wait for the son to complete his walk of shame to the door. He runs. He covers the distance that shame would have required the son to cross alone.

notes.original: epepesen epi ton trachylon autou kai katephilesen auton
notes.rendering: falls on his neck and kisses him again and again
notes.why: Epipiptō — to fall upon, to throw oneself on. The father throws himself on the son’s neck — an embrace so complete the son can barely speak his prepared speech. Kataphileo — the kata- prefix intensifying phileo — means to kiss repeatedly, tenderly, fervently. Not a formal greeting kiss but an outpouring of physical affection. The son’s speech (v.21) is nearly identical to what he rehearsed (vv.18–19) — but he is never able to finish it. The request to be made a hired servant is cut off before it can be spoken. The father’s embrace pre-empts the negotiation.

notes.original: stōlēn tēn prōtēn
notes.rendering: the best robe
notes.why: Stōlē tēn prōtēn — the first robe, the chief robe, the most honourable garment in the household. Not a servant’s clothing but the robe of a son restored to full standing. The three gifts — robe, ring, sandals — are each markers of restored status. The robe signals honour. The ring (daktyliou) is a signet ring, conferring authority to act on the father’s behalf. Sandals distinguish a free person from a slave, who went barefoot. The son asked to be made a servant; the father makes him a son again with each gift.

notes.original: nekros ēn kai anezēsen
notes.rendering: was dead and has come back to life
notes.why: Nekros — dead. Anazao — to live again, to come back to life. The language is not metaphorical here; it is the father’s own declaration. His son was dead — genuinely, in the father’s experience, dead — and now he lives. The parable’s language anticipates the resurrection: the same verb anazao is used in Revelation for the risen life. Luke allows the father to speak in terms that reach beyond the merely psychological recovery of a wayward son.

notes.original: ōrgisthē kai ouk ēthelen eiselthein
notes.rendering: is furious and will not go in
notes.why: Two verbs in sharp sequence: ōrgisthē (was enraged, aorist — the anger arrives suddenly) and ouk ēthelen eiselthein (imperfect — he was continuously refusing to go in, kept refusing). The older son’s anger is not momentary; it settles into a sustained refusal. He is outside the feast in the same way the self-righteous are outside the kingdom — not because they were excluded but because they will not enter.

notes.original: oudépote entolēn sou parēlthon
notes.rendering: I never once disobeyed your orders
notes.why: Oudepote — never, not once. Parēlthon — I transgressed, I went past. The older son’s self-description is that of perfect obedience — and the word for disobeying is parerchesthai, to pass by, to go around. It is the same verb used for the priest and Levite passing by the wounded man (10:31–32) and for the Pharisees passing over justice (11:42). The older son has never passed by his father’s commands — but in his furious refusal to go in, he is now passing by his father’s joy.

notes.original: sy pantote met’ emou ei
notes.rendering: you are always with me
notes.why: The father’s response to the older son is one of the most tender sentences in the parable. You are always with me. The older son has been in the field; the father has been in the house. But the father does not concede the older son’s implicit claim that proximity equals possession. ‘Everything I have is yours’ — panta ta ema sa estin — is the father’s acknowledgment that the older son’s inheritance is secure, unaffected by the celebration. The banquet has not cost him anything.

notes.original: ēdei de euphranthēnai
notes.rendering: we had to celebrate
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary, it must happen, the same word of divine compulsion used throughout Luke (2:49, 4:43, 9:22, 13:33). Celebrating the return of the dead-and-living, lost-and-found son is not an optional indulgence; it is a necessity. The father does not ask the older son to understand or agree. He states a fact: we had to. And the parable ends there — the older son standing outside, the father having spoken, the music still playing inside, the question of whether the older son will enter left entirely open.

outro: Note on the three parables as a single argument: Luke 15 is the longest and most sustained response to a single objection in the entire gospel. The Pharisees’ grumble in v.2 — ‘this man welcomes sinners and eats with them’ — is the occasion for all three parables. Jesus does not argue against the charge; he defends it. Yes, I welcome sinners. And here is why: because heaven rejoices when one lost person is found. The three parables are a graduated argument: a sheep (1 in 100), a coin (1 in 10), a son (1 in 2). The proportion grows. The personalness grows. The joy grows. And the third parable adds what the first two do not: the older son, who stands for the Pharisees themselves, is not condemned but invited. The parable ends with the father outside, the music inside, and the door open. Luke does not tell us whether the older son enters.

Note on the Prodigal Son and the father’s running: In the social world of the parable, a father of means running down the road was a spectacle. Kenneth Bailey’s research into Middle Eastern village culture suggests the father may also have been running to intercept the son before the village could shame him — the kezazah ceremony, by which a Jewish community formally cut off a son who had squandered his inheritance among Gentiles, involved breaking a pot before him and declaring him cut off. If the father reaches the son first, publicly embraces him, publicly claims him, the village cannot perform the kezazah. The running is not merely emotional; it is protective. He covers the son with his own honour before the village can strip it away.

intro: Luke 16 is structured around money and its ultimate inadequacy as a foundation for life. The shrewd manager teaches a lesson about using wealth wisely before it runs out. The interlude on the Law and the Pharisees names the deeper problem. The rich man and Lazarus shows what it looks like when the lesson is not learned. The Greek throughout is precise, and the connections between the two parables are more deliberate than they first appear.
I. The Shrewd Manager (16:1–13)

notes.original: diaballō
notes.rendering: reports come to him
notes.why: Diaballō means to throw accusations across, to slander, to make reports against someone — the root of the word diabolos (the devil, the accuser). The manager is accused to his master, but Luke does not tell us whether the accusation is true. We never learn whether he was actually squandering the wealth or whether the reports are malicious. The parable begins in ambiguity and stays there. What matters is the manager’s response to being caught in a crisis, not the precise nature of his prior guilt.

notes.original: skaptein ouk ischyo, epaitein aischunomai
notes.rendering: I’m not strong enough to dig, and I’m ashamed to beg
notes.why: Two confessions in five words each. The first is physical: he lacks the strength for manual labour. The second is social: he lacks the capacity for shame — or rather, he is too full of it to beg. He is a man caught between his incapacity and his pride, and he knows it. His self-assessment is completely clear-eyed. The manager’s great virtue in the parable is not his honesty but his lucidity about his own situation.

notes.original: hekatòn batous elaiou… hekatòn korous sitou
notes.rendering: a hundred measures of oil… a hundred measures of wheat
notes.why: A batos of olive oil was approximately 37 litres; a hundred batos was roughly 3,700 litres — the yield of many olive trees, worth a substantial sum. A koros of wheat was approximately 370 litres; a hundred koros was a large grain harvest. The debts being reduced are not trivial adjustments; they represent significant commercial obligations. Reducing them by 50% and 20% respectively is a substantial, costly act. The question of whether the manager is cutting the interest component (which would have been illegal under Jewish law) or reducing his own commission has been debated for centuries.

notes.original: epainesen ho kyrios ton oikonomon tēs adikias
notes.rendering: the master commends the dishonest manager
notes.why: One of the most debated verses in Luke. Who is ‘the master’ here — the rich man of the parable, or Jesus commending the example? Most likely the rich man of the parable: even he acknowledges the shrewdness. The commendation is not of the dishonesty but of the phronímōs — the shrewdness, the practical wisdom of using what you have before it runs out. The manager saw his crisis coming, assessed his resources, and acted decisively. Jesus holds this up not as a moral model but as an example of urgent, resourceful action in the face of an approaching reckoning.

notes.original: phronimōteros… hoi huioi tou aiōnos
notes.rendering: shrewder… the children of this age
notes.why: Phronimos means practically wise, shrewd, clear-headed about how to act in a given situation. The children of this age — those whose values and strategies are shaped by the present world order — are more phronimos in their own sphere than the children of light are in theirs. The observation is not a compliment to worldliness; it is a rebuke to the disciples. The energy, creativity, and urgency that people deploy in pursuit of worldly advantage should be at least matched in the pursuit of the kingdom.

notes.original: mamōna tēs adikias
notes.rendering: dishonest wealth
notes.why: Mamōnas is an Aramaic loanword meaning wealth, property, possessions. The genitive tēs adikias — of unrighteousness, of dishonesty — does not necessarily mean money obtained dishonestly; it may simply characterise all worldly wealth as belonging to the realm of the unrighteous age, morally compromised by nature. The instruction to make friends by means of it is not an endorsement of corruption but a radical repurposing: use the money of this age — before it runs out — in ways that build relationships in the coming age.

notes.original: eis tas aiōnious skēnas
notes.rendering: into the eternal dwellings
notes.why: Aiōnioi skēnai — eternal tents, eternal tabernacles. The word skēnē evokes the wilderness Tabernacle, the dwelling place of God with his people. But it also evokes the temporary nature of all earthly shelter: a tent is not a house. The eternal dwellings are the permanent shelter that outlasts the wealth used to obtain them. The money runs out; the welcome into those dwellings does not.

notes.original: oiketēs… dusi kyriois douleuein
notes.rendering: No servant can serve two masters
notes.why: Oiketēs is a household slave — one whose entire existence belongs to the master’s household. The saying is not about divided attention or competing priorities; it is about the impossibility of total loyalty to two owners. A slave belongs to one master. The word mamōnas appears here for the final time: you cannot be God’s property and money’s property simultaneously. The chapter has been moving toward this statement since v.1.

notes.heading: II. The Law, the Kingdom, and Divorce (16:14–18)

notes.original: philargyroi… exemyktērizon
notes.rendering: lovers of money… sneer at him
notes.why: Philargyros means a lover of silver, a money-lover — the compound of philos (lover) and argyros (silver). Luke names the Pharisees’ specific vice before describing their reaction. Ekmyktērizō means to turn up the nose at, to sneer with contempt — from myktēr, the nose. The gesture is physical: the curled lip, the upturned nostril. They are showing contempt for Jesus’ teaching about wealth because it exposes something they do not want named.

notes.original: bdelygma enōpion tou theou
notes.rendering: an abomination before God
notes.why: Bdelygma is a strong word — abomination, something detestable, the word used in the LXX for idols and for things that violate the covenant (Daniel 9:27, 11:31; the ‘abomination of desolation’). What is exalted among people — the public display of wealth, honour, religious prestige — is before God an abomination. Luke places this indictment directly against the Pharisees who have just sneered at the teaching about money. Their contempt for Jesus’ words reveals the idol.

notes.original: biazētai
notes.rendering: everyone is pressing forcefully into it
notes.why: Biazō means to press, to force, to enter with urgency and energy. The kingdom of God is being proclaimed and people are pressing forcefully into it — thronging to enter, pushing their way in with the same energy the manager used to secure his future. The form is either middle voice (everyone forces their way in) or passive (everyone is being pressed in by it). Either way the image is of a great surge of entry — the tax collectors and sinners of 15:1 pressing toward Jesus, the kingdom advancing irresistibly.

notes.original: mian keraian
notes.rendering: one stroke of a letter
notes.why: Keraia means the tiny horn or serif of a Hebrew letter — the decorative stroke that distinguishes one letter from another. The smallest possible unit of written text. Jesus says it is easier for the entire created order to collapse than for one of these to fall out of the Law. The statement immediately follows the announcement that the kingdom era has begun with John: the new age does not abolish the Law; it fulfills and intensifies it.

notes.heading: III. The Rich Man and Lazarus (16:19–31)

notes.original: porphyran kai byssion
notes.rendering: purple and fine linen
notes.why: Porphyra is purple cloth — the most expensive dye in the ancient world, extracted from murex shellfish and worth more than its weight in gold. Byssos is fine Egyptian linen, another luxury fabric. The rich man is clothed in the two most expensive materials available. He does not merely wear fine clothes; he wears the markers of extreme, conspicuous wealth. And he feasts every day — not on special occasions but habitually, as a daily expression of his abundance.

notes.original: ptōchos… Lazaros
notes.rendering: a poor man named Lazarus
notes.why: This is the only named character in any of Jesus’ parables. Every other parable character is anonymous: a man, a father, a Samaritan, a king. Lazarus is named. The rich man — despite centuries of tradition calling him Dives (the Latin for ‘rich man’) — is not named. The reversal is deliberate: the one who was invisible in life is known by name in death; the one who was prominent in life is known only by his wealth.

notes.original: heilōmenos helkē
notes.rendering: covered with sores
notes.why: Helkoo — to be covered with sores, to be ulcerated. The perfect passive participle heilōmenos indicates a condition long established and ongoing. Lazarus is not merely hungry; his body is failing. He is placed (ebeblēto — cast, laid, thrown) at the gate — someone has brought him there and left him. He is entirely dependent, entirely passive, entirely without resources or advocates.

notes.original: alla kai hoi kynēs… epeleikhon
notes.rendering: The dogs come and lick his sores
notes.why: The detail is carefully placed. In Jewish culture dogs were unclean scavengers, not household pets. Their licking of his sores is not comfort but an additional humiliation — he is so low that even unclean animals attend him. But Luke’s kai (even) may carry a trace of irony: even the dogs come to him, while the rich man does not. The animals show more attention to Lazarus than his neighbour does.

notes.original: apēnechthē hypò tōn angelōn
notes.rendering: carried by the angels to Abraham’s side
notes.why: Apophero — to carry away, to transport. The angels carry Lazarus — he who could not carry himself, who was laid at the gate and left there, is now borne aloft. The contrast with the rich man is total: the rich man ‘is buried’ (etaphe — a single verb, no angels, no ceremony described beyond the interment). Lazarus’ death receives a sentence of transport and arrival; the rich man’s receives a sentence of burial.

notes.original: eis ton kolpon Abraam
notes.rendering: Abraham’s side
notes.why: Kolpos means bosom, chest, the fold of a garment — the intimate place of reclining beside someone at a feast, as a beloved disciple would recline at the teacher’s side. To be in Abraham’s bosom is to be at the place of highest honour at the great feast, the messianic banquet. Lazarus, who longed for scraps from the rich man’s table, now reclines in the place of honour at the table of the father of all Israel.

notes.original: odynōmai en tē phlogí taytē
notes.rendering: I am in agony in this flame
notes.why: Odynaomai means to be in acute pain, to suffer intensely — the same word used of Mary and Joseph’s anguish searching for the boy Jesus (2:48) and of the rich man’s plea being mirrored in Abraham’s reply (v.25: odynasai). The word appears only four times in Luke-Acts: twice here. The physical specificity — a tongue that needs cooling, a finger dipped in water — makes the scene visceral and immediate.

notes.original: apelaben ta agatha sou… nun dē parakAleitai
notes.rendering: you received your good things… now he is comforted
notes.why: Apelaben — you received, you took, you collected in full. The word apechō (from which apelaben comes) is the commercial receipt word used in 6:24: the rich have already received their comfort in full. The account has been settled. Now (de nun) Lazarus is being comforted (parakaleitai — present passive, ongoing comfort). And you are in agony (odynasai — present, continuous). The reversal is complete and permanent.

notes.original: chasma mega
notes.rendering: a great chasm
notes.why: Chasma is a chasm, a gulf, an unbridgeable gap — from the verb chainō, to gape open. It has been fixed (estēriktai — perfect passive, permanently established) between the two sides. The fixity is the theological point: the reversal that has occurred in death is not provisional or temporary. The rich man asks for Lazarus to cross to him; Abraham says the structure of reality does not permit it. This is not cruelty but consequence: the chasm is the permanent form of the choices made in life.

notes.original: Mousēa kai tous prophētas
notes.rendering: Moses and the Prophets
notes.why: The Hebrew Scriptures — the Torah (Moses) and the Prophets — are sufficient. Abraham does not say they are insufficient and a miracle would help; he says they are the appointed means of hearing God’s word. The rich man’s brothers have access to everything needed to understand how to live and what awaits them. The problem is not lack of information but unwillingness to hear what they already have.

notes.original: oudē ean tis ek nekrōn anastē
notes.rendering: not even if someone rises from the dead
notes.why: The parable’s final line reaches beyond the story and touches the reader directly. Luke’s audience knows that someone has risen from the dead. The warning is not hypothetical; it is the condition of the reader’s own world. The question the parable leaves is whether, in the face of the resurrection that has actually occurred, the reader is listening to Moses and the Prophets — or whether the heart is still closed.

outro: Note on the connection between the two parables in Luke 16: The two parables are more tightly linked than they first appear. The shrewd manager uses wealth shrewdly to secure a welcome in ‘eternal dwellings’ (v.9). The rich man fails entirely to use his wealth in a way that secures any welcome anywhere. The manager sees the crisis coming and acts; the rich man does not see, or will not see, the crisis at his own gate. Both parables turn on the same axis: what you do with wealth before it runs out determines what happens when it does. The manager’s commendation and the rich man’s torment are two sides of the same lesson.

Note on the rich man and Lazarus as not primarily a geography of the afterlife: The parable is not a topographical description of what happens after death. Its detail — the chasm, the flame, the water — is parabolic imagery, not cartography. The parable’s primary purpose is the final verse: they have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen. The afterlife imagery is the frame that makes the urgency of that conclusion inescapable. The point is not to describe Hades but to insist on the moral weight of the present moment: what you do with the Lazarus at your gate, while Moses and the Prophets are available to you, determines everything.

intro: Luke 17 moves through four distinct registers: ethical instruction on stumbling blocks and forgiveness, a parabolic corrective about servanthood, the ten lepers, and an extended discourse on the coming of the kingdom. The Greek throughout rewards close attention, particularly in the leper account and in the kingdom sayings, where several key words carry more weight than standard translations convey.
I. Stumbling Blocks, Forgiveness, and Faith (17:1–6)

notes.original: anendekton estin tou mē elthein ta skandala
notes.rendering: Stumbling blocks are bound to come
notes.why: Anendektos means impossible, inadmissible, not able to be otherwise. The coming of skandala — stumbling blocks, traps, causes of falling — is inevitable in the present age. Jesus does not say they can be prevented; he says woe to the one who becomes the instrument of them. The inevitability of the stumbling block does not remove the culpability of the one through whom it comes. Both things are simultaneously true.

notes.original: lithos mylikos
notes.rendering: a millstone
notes.why: Lithos mylikos means a millstone — specifically the large upper stone of a donkey-powered mill, weighing hundreds of kilograms. This is not a small hand-grinding stone but an industrial weight. The image of being thrown into the sea wearing such a stone is not merely death but absolute, irreversible submersion — a drowning from which there is no surfacing. Jesus says this is preferable to causing a child of the kingdom to stumble.

notes.original: heptakis tēs hēmeras
notes.rendering: seven times in a day
notes.why: Seven times in a single day. Not over a lifetime, not across a relationship — in one day. The demand is not merely patience but an active practice of release that refuses to keep accounts even when every accounting instinct says the limit has been reached. The apostles’ response — ‘increase our faith’ — is entirely understandable. What Jesus is describing requires something beyond ordinary human willingness.

notes.original: sykaminos
notes.rendering: mulberry tree
notes.why: Sykaminos is specifically a mulberry tree — known for its exceptionally deep and extensive root system, making it extraordinarily difficult to uproot. Matthew’s parallel (21:21) uses a mountain. Luke’s mulberry tree is more specifically chosen: the image is of faith addressing the most deeply rooted, most stubbornly fixed obstacle imaginable and commanding it to move. The mustard seed of faith is not contrasted with a pebble but with a tree that takes years to remove.

notes.original: douloi achreioi esmen
notes.rendering: We are unworthy servants
notes.why: Achreios means useless, unworthy, of no profit — literally without use (a- privative + chreia, use, need). The word is strong and deliberately so. A servant who has done everything required has not done anything extraordinary; they have simply fulfilled the terms of their service. There is no surplus of merit to claim, no extra credit to accumulate. The posture Jesus calls the disciples to is not false modesty but accurate self-assessment: we have only done what was owed.

notes.original: dia meson Samareias kai Galilaias
notes.rendering: along the border between Samaria and Galilee
notes.why: The geographical detail is precise and significant. Jesus is travelling through the borderland between Samaria and Galilee — a liminal zone, inhabited by people of mixed identity, where the social and ritual boundaries between Jewish and Samaritan communities were porous. It is exactly the right setting for a story in which a Samaritan and nine Jews share the same condition, receive the same healing, and respond in opposite ways.

notes.original: hoi estasan porrōthen
notes.rendering: they are standing at a distance
notes.why: Porrōthen — from a distance, from far off. The Mosaic law required lepers to keep their distance from the healthy population and to call out ‘Unclean!’ (Leviticus 13:45–46). These ten are obeying the law even as they cry for mercy. They do not rush Jesus; they stand at the prescribed distance and lift their voices. The discipline of the marginalized: following the rules that mark you as outside while begging to be let in.

notes.original: Epistāta
notes.rendering: Master
notes.why: Epistatēs means overseer, commander, the one who stands over — a title of authority used by the disciples for Jesus in Luke (5:5, 8:24, 8:45, 9:33, 9:49). It is specifically a Lukan word; the other gospels use Rabbi or Teacher in equivalent moments. All ten lepers — including the Samaritan — use this title. They address him with the same word as the disciples. Their need has made them his community before they even know what he will do.

notes.original: en tō hypagein autous
notes.rendering: As they are going
notes.why: The healing does not happen at the moment of the command. Jesus says ‘go’ and they go — and en tō hypagein, in the going, in the act of obedience while the healing has not yet occurred, they are cleansed. This is the narrative present tense at its most precise: the cleansing happens while they are walking, not before they set out and not after they arrive. Obedience and healing are simultaneous. Faith is already in motion before the evidence arrives.

notes.original: idōn hoti iatthē
notes.rendering: seeing that he is healed
notes.why: One of the ten notices. The Greek is precise: he sees (eidōn, aorist — a moment of recognition) that he has been healed (iatthē, aorist passive — it has been done to him). The recognition precedes the turning. He does not decide to go back and then notice; he sees, and turning is the immediate consequence. Gratitude here is not a duty performed but the natural motion of a person who has just seen something extraordinary and cannot keep walking away from the source of it.

notes.original: meta phōnēs megalēs doxazōn ton theon
notes.rendering: glorifying God at the top of his voice
notes.why: Phōnē megalē — a great voice, a loud cry. The same phrase used of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33), of the woman who blessed Jesus’ mother (11:27), and of Jesus on the cross (23:46). It is the sound of something that cannot be contained in normal conversational volume — something too large for ordinary speech. The healed Samaritan is not quietly thankful; he is loud with it, publicly, uncontrollably.

notes.original: autos ēn Samaritēs
notes.rendering: And he is a Samaritan
notes.why: Luke saves the identification for the end of the scene, after the prostration and the giving of thanks. The sentence falls like a stone. The reader already expects it — the Samaritan in the story is always the one who does what the others don’t — but the placement makes it land with full force. Everything has been described: the turning, the voice, the prostration, the thanks. And then: and he is a Samaritan. Luke does not explain. The contrast with the nine is left entirely to the reader to feel.

notes.original: ouch hoi deka ekatharisthēsan
notes.rendering: Were not ten cleansed?
notes.why: The rhetorical question is not anger but grief — a lament in question form. Jesus is not punishing the nine or rescinding their healing; he is naming the wound of ingratitude. The word katharizō — to cleanse — is used for the healing of leprosy throughout the gospel (5:12, 7:22, 17:14). All ten were cleansed. The cleansing was not conditional on gratitude. The nine received the gift and kept walking. That is what makes the question so quietly devastating.

notes.original: allà ouch heurethēsan… ei mē o allogenes
notes.rendering: except this foreigner
notes.why: Allogenes means one of another race, a foreigner, a person from outside the covenant people — from allos (other) and genos (race, kind). It is a stronger word than ‘stranger’ or ‘outsider’; it marks ethnic and religious otherness explicitly. The nine who did not return were presumably Jewish — the ones with the most reason, by covenant expectation, to know how to respond to God’s gift. The one who returned was the one with the least claim. Luke has been making this observation since chapter 4 (Elijah and the widow of Sidon; Elisha and Naaman the Syrian). It does not get easier to hear.

notes.original: hē pistis sou sesōken se
notes.rendering: Your faith has saved you
notes.why: Sōzō again — the full word, save, rescue, make whole. The nine were cleansed (katharisthēsan); the one is saved (sesōken). The distinction is not a punishment for the nine but a statement about what has happened to the one who returned. Cleansing addressed the body; salvation addresses the whole person. The Samaritan received more than he came for. He came asking for mercy on his diseased body and went away with something that outlasts the body entirely.

notes.heading: IV. The Coming of the Kingdom (17:20–37)

notes.original: metà paratrēseōs
notes.rendering: with things to be observed
notes.why: Paratērēsis means observation, watching for signs — from paratēreō, the same word used of the Pharisees watching Jesus for violations (6:7, 14:1). The kingdom does not come with the kind of observable, sign-readable arrival that people are watching for. It cannot be tracked and predicted by those who know how to read such things. The irony is precise: the Pharisees who are expert watchers are told that watching is exactly the wrong approach to the kingdom.

notes.original: entos hymōn
notes.rendering: in your midst
notes.why: Entos can mean either ‘within you’ (inside you, an interior reality) or ‘in your midst’ (among you, in your presence). The interpretive tradition is divided. The ‘within you’ reading has fuelled centuries of inward, mystical readings of the kingdom. But the context — Jesus addressing Pharisees, not disciples — makes the interior reading less likely. ‘In your midst’ is almost certainly the right reading: the kingdom is already present in the person and ministry of Jesus, standing in front of the Pharisees who are asking when it will come. The question presupposes a future arrival; the answer announces a present reality they have been failing to see.

notes.original: hē astrapē… lampousa
notes.rendering: lightning flashes
notes.why: Astrapē is lightning — instantaneous, total, unmissable. Lampoo means to shine, to blaze. The Son of Man’s coming will be like lightning that illuminates the whole sky from one edge to the other — not a secret arrival in a particular place that must be sought out, but an event so total and immediate that no corner of the world is unaffected. The contrast with the careful, location-specific signs people are watching for could not be sharper.

notes.original: dei auton polla pathein
notes.rendering: he must suffer many things
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary, the divine must. The suffering is not an interruption of the Son of Man’s coming but the path through which it arrives. Luke inserts this verse — absent from Matthew’s parallel discourse — as a characteristic reminder: the glory of the kingdom comes through and not around the cross. Every reference to the coming of the Son of Man in Luke is accompanied by the shadow of the passion.

notes.original: mnēmoneuete tēs gynaikos Lot
notes.rendering: Remember Lot’s wife
notes.why: Three words in Greek. The shortest verse in Luke. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26) and became a pillar of salt — she turned toward the city she was leaving instead of forward toward the life she was being given. In context, Jesus has just said: on that day, don’t go back into the house for your belongings, don’t turn back from the field. The one who turns back to preserve what they are leaving is the one who loses everything. Three words. No elaboration needed.

notes.original: peripoioēsai… zoogonēsei
notes.rendering: tries to preserve… will keep
notes.why: Peripoieo means to preserve, to make safe around oneself — to hold onto by surrounding with protection. Zoogoneō means to keep alive, to preserve in life. The paradox of verse 33 is the same as 9:24 but in different vocabulary: the grip that tries to hold life loses it; the open hand that releases it finds it kept. The same truth appears three times in Luke — at the cost-of-discipleship teaching, here, and implicitly in the Prodigal Son’s far country — because it is the truth that most needs repeating.

notes.original: hoi aetoi episynachthēsontai
notes.rendering: there the vultures will gather
notes.why: Aetos means eagle or vulture — the word covers large birds of prey that gather at carcasses. The disciples ask ‘where?’ and Jesus answers with a proverb: where the body is, the birds gather. He refuses to give a map or a timetable. The coming of the Son of Man is not a destination to be plotted on a journey; it will be as unmistakable and as inevitable as vultures over a carcass. You will not need to ask where — it will be obvious to everyone, everywhere, at once.

outro: Note on the ten lepers and Luke’s consistent pattern of the returning outsider: The story of the ten lepers is the third time in Luke that a Samaritan appears as the exemplary respondent. In 10:33 the Samaritan is the one who shows mercy when the Jewish religious officials pass by. In 17:16 the Samaritan is the one who returns with gratitude when the nine Jewish lepers keep walking. In both cases Luke does not explain or editorialize; he simply places the Samaritan in the position of the one who gets it right and lets the contrast speak. The pattern goes back to chapter 4: Elijah was sent to a Sidonian widow, not an Israelite; Elisha cleansed Naaman the Syrian, not an Israelite. Jesus’ own ministry follows the same pattern. Those with the least expectation of inclusion are the ones who respond most fully when the kingdom arrives.

Note on ‘your faith has saved you’ vs. ‘you were cleansed’ (17:14 vs. 17:19): The distinction between the cleansing of the ten (katharisthēsan, v.14) and the saving of the one (sesōken, v.19) is one of the most theologically loaded details in the chapter. All ten received the healing they asked for. The Samaritan received something more — not because he earned it by returning, but because his returning was the expression of a faith that was oriented not merely toward healing but toward the Healer himself. He fell at Jesus’ feet. He gave glory to God. In Luke’s theology, to give glory to God and to fall at Jesus’ feet are the same act — as the equation in 7:16 and 8:39 has already shown. The Samaritan’s faith recognised something in Jesus that the nine, for all their obedience, did not pause to see.

intro: Luke 18 is structured around the question of who is actually able to enter the kingdom of God. A widow with nothing but persistence. A tax collector with nothing but self-knowledge. Infants who have not yet developed the confidence that makes entry difficult. A rich ruler who has everything and cannot let go of it. A blind man who sees more clearly than anyone around him. The chapter reads as a sustained dismantling of the assumption that the qualified are the ones who get in.
I. The Persistent Widow (18:1–8)

notes.original: mē enkakein
notes.rendering: not lose heart
notes.why: Enkakeō means to lose heart, to grow weary, to give up — from en + kakos, to be in the bad place, to let the badness win. Luke states the parable’s purpose before telling it, which is unusual: Jesus wants the disciples to understand from the beginning that this is a parable about persistence in prayer, not a description of God as a reluctant judge. The comparison is an argument from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge eventually yields, how much more will God act for those he loves.

notes.original: ekdikēson me
notes.rendering: Give me justice
notes.why: Ekdikeō means to do justice for, to vindicate, to avenge — from ek (out of) + dikē (justice). The widow is not asking for revenge in a petty sense; she is asking for her legal rights to be upheld, for the justice that is owed to her to be rendered. In the ancient world a widow without a male advocate was extraordinarily vulnerable to exploitation. Her adversary (antidikos — one opposed in a legal case) has a structural advantage she cannot overcome except by sheer persistence.

notes.original: hypōpiazen
notes.rendering: wear me out
notes.why: Hypōpiazō is a boxing term — to strike under the eye, to give a black eye, to beat continually about the face. The judge is not saying he is tired; he is saying she is pummelling him into submission. The image is deliberately physical and slightly comic: a powerful judge brought to his knees not by force or argument but by the relentless, tireless returning of a woman with nothing but her cause. This is the quality of prayer Jesus is commending: not eloquence or merit but the refusal to stop coming.

notes.original: makrothymei ep’ autois
notes.rendering: Will he keep putting them off?
notes.why: Makrothymeō means to be patient, to delay, to bear long with something. The question is genuinely difficult to translate: is God being long-suffering toward his elect (patient with them, bearing with their weakness) or is he delaying on their behalf (holding back judgment while giving time for the elect to come in)? The most natural reading in context is the latter: God is not indifferent but is exercising restraint. The vindication is certain; its timing is in his hands. The final question — will the Son of Man find faith when he comes? — turns the question back on the reader.

notes.heading: II. The Pharisee and the Tax Collector (18:9–14)

notes.original: pepoithōtas eph’ heautois
notes.rendering: confident in their own righteousness
notes.why: Pepoithō means to trust, to rely on, to have confidence in. The Pharisees’ problem is not that they have righteousness but that they are trusting in their own — eph’ heautois, in themselves, on their own account. The preposition is precise: they are resting their weight on their own record. The parable does not condemn the Pharisee’s religious practice; it diagnoses the fatal orientation of that practice toward the self rather than toward God.

notes.original: pros heauton… tauta
notes.rendering: prays about himself
notes.why: The Greek is ambiguous: pros heauton can mean ‘to himself’ (praying silently, or praying to himself rather than to God) or ‘about himself’ (his prayer is a self-description). Either reading condemns the same thing: a prayer that has the self as both subject and audience. The content confirms it — the prayer is a list of the Pharisee’s accomplishments, offered to God as evidence of his superiority. He is not asking for anything; he is reporting.

notes.original: apodekatō panta hosa ktaōmai
notes.rendering: I give tithes of everything I get
notes.why: The Pharisee’s religious practice is genuinely exemplary by any external standard. Fasting twice a week exceeded what the Law required (the Law mandated fasting only on the Day of Atonement). Tithing everything he acquired went beyond the basic requirements. He is not lying or exaggerating. The problem is not the practice but the posture: he stands before God and presents this as the basis of his standing. He is comparing upward (to God’s standard, which he believes he has met) and downward (to others, whom he has surpassed).

notes.original: ho de telōnēs makrothen hestōs
notes.rendering: the tax collector, standing far off
notes.why: The spatial contrast is precise. The Pharisee stands (estōs, perfect — in his established position) and prays. The tax collector stands far off (makrothen — at a distance, the same word used of the ten lepers in 17:12). He has placed himself at the margin of the sacred space. He will not lift his eyes. He beats his chest — a gesture of grief and contrition, the physical expression of a person striking themselves in self-accusation. His prayer is five words in Greek: ho theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō. God, be merciful to me, the sinner.

notes.original: hilasthēti moi
notes.rendering: have mercy on me
notes.why: Hilaskomai means to propitiate, to make atonement, to cover over — the word of the mercy seat (hilastērion) in the LXX, the place where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The tax collector is not asking for general kindness; he is asking for the specific act of atonement that covers sin. He knows precisely what his condition is and what he needs. The definite article in tō hamartōlō — the sinner, not a sinner — is significant: he is not claiming a category but owning a position. He is the sinner in this room.

notes.original: dedikaiōmenos
notes.rendering: justified
notes.why: Dikaioō — to justify, to declare righteous, to acquit. The perfect passive participle: he has been justified and goes home in that state. This is the only use of the verb dikaioo in Luke’s gospel (the noun dikaiosynē appears more frequently). The word is at home in Paul’s letters; here Jesus uses it of a tax collector whose prayer lasted five words. The Pharisee who came to the temple justified in his own eyes goes home otherwise.

notes.original: ta brephe
notes.rendering: infants
notes.why: Brephos means an infant, a newborn, a baby still in arms — Luke’s word for the infant Jesus in the manger (2:12, 16) and for the baby John leaping in the womb (1:41, 44). These are not children who can understand a teaching; they are babies being brought for a touch. The disciples’ rebuke is protective and entirely reasonable. Jesus’ overruling of it is therefore the more radical: the kingdom belongs to those who have not yet developed the self-sufficiency that makes entry hard.

notes.original: hos an mē dexetai tēn basileian tou theou hōs paidion
notes.rendering: whoever does not receive the kingdom like a child
notes.why: The child (paidion) who receives the kingdom is slightly older than the infant (brephos) — but the quality being named is the same: receptivity without prior qualification, acceptance without the condition of having earned the right to be there. The kingdom must be received (dexetai — welcomed, accepted) not achieved. The verb is passive in its orientation: the child does not take the kingdom; the child receives what is given.

notes.original: archōn tis
notes.rendering: A certain ruler
notes.why: Archōn means a ruler, a leader, a person of authority — possibly a synagogue ruler or a member of the local aristocracy. Luke’s version of this encounter differs from Matthew’s (‘a young man’, 19:20) and Mark’s (‘a man’, 10:17). Luke alone identifies him as a ruler. He has religious observance, social position, wealth, and the right question. He is the most credentialed person to approach Jesus in the gospel, and he goes away sad.

notes.original: ti me legeis agathon
notes.rendering: Why do you call me good?
notes.why: Jesus does not deflect the title to avoid praise; he probes the assumption behind it. If good belongs to God alone, calling Jesus good either means the ruler is using the word loosely — as a flattery — or it means he is saying more than he knows. The question forces the ruler to examine what he means. It is also, characteristically, a question that turns back on the one who asked: you have called me good; now let’s see what that means for what I ask of you.

notes.original: pōleson panta hosa echeis
notes.rendering: Sell everything you have
notes.why: Panta — everything. Not most things. Not the surplus. Everything. The command is absolute and individual — Jesus does not give this instruction to everyone he meets; he gives it to this man, in this moment, because he has seen precisely what the obstacle is. The ruler’s wealth is not incidental to his life; it is the foundation of his identity and security. The one thing he lacks is the willingness to stand before God with nothing in his hands. That is what ‘come and follow me’ requires of him.

notes.original: perilypos… plousios sphodra
notes.rendering: very sad — for he is extremely rich
notes.why: Perilypos means deeply grieved, surrounded by grief — the same word used of Jesus in Gethsemane (Mark 14:34, ‘my soul is deeply grieved’). The ruler is not callous or defiant; he is genuinely sorrowful. He wanted to follow. The sadness makes the scene more devastating, not less: he is a man who can see what he is losing by not following, and still cannot let go. Plousios sphodra — extremely, intensely rich. The adverb intensifies the obstacle.

notes.original: kamelos dia trēmatos belenēs
notes.rendering: a camel through the eye of a needle
notes.why: The image is deliberately absurd — the largest animal in the Palestinian world passing through the smallest possible opening. Various attempts to soften the saying (a ‘rope’ instead of a ‘camel,’ a small gate called the ‘needle’s eye’) have no textual or historical support. The point is the impossibility: it cannot be done. The disciples’ response — ‘then who can be saved?’ — is the correct response. Jesus intends to be heard as saying: by human means, the wealthy cannot enter. The next verse explains why this is not the final word.

notes.original: ta adynata para anthrōpois dynata parà tō theō estin
notes.rendering: What is impossible with people is possible with God
notes.why: Adynatos — impossible, without power (a- privative + dynatos, powerful). The salvation of the wealthy is impossible with human means — no religious effort, no moral achievement, no act of will can produce the transformation required. But parà tō theō, with God, beside God, in God’s presence — the impossible becomes possible. The grammar is not merely consoling; it is precise: with people, no. With God, yes. The distinction is not small.

notes.original: telesthsetai panta ta gegrammena
notes.rendering: everything that is written… will be fulfilled
notes.why: Telestēsetai — will be brought to completion, will reach its telos. The passion is not an accident or a political miscalculation; it is the fulfillment of everything written about the Son of Man in the prophets. Luke emphasises this more than any other gospel: the cross is a scripturally necessary event, the completion of a pattern laid down across centuries of prophetic writing. The disciples cannot grasp it (v.34) because they have no framework yet for a Messiah whose completion comes through death.

notes.original: kekrymmenon ap’ autōn
notes.rendering: the meaning is hidden from them
notes.why: The same phrase as 9:45 — it has been hidden, it remains concealed, a divine passive. The third passion prediction is the most detailed of the three: handed over to Gentiles, mocked, insulted, spat on, flogged, killed, raised. And still they do not understand. Luke is not criticising the disciples; he is noting a mercy: the full weight of what is coming cannot be received before the interpretive key of the resurrection has been given. Understanding comes after, not before.

notes.heading: VI. The Blind Beggar at Jericho (18:35–43)

notes.original: typhlos tis ekatheto parà tēn hodon epaitōn
notes.rendering: a blind man is sitting by the road begging
notes.why: Three present participles that place the scene in continuous motion: sitting, begging, existing in this condition as his ongoing state. He is not passing through; this road is his life. Jericho is eighteen kilometres from Jerusalem — Jesus is almost at the end of the journey he set his face to complete in 9:51. The blind man at the road’s edge is the last person he heals before entering the holy city.

notes.original: Huie Dauid
notes.rendering: Son of David
notes.why: The blind man uses a title no one else uses to address Jesus in Luke until the triumphal entry (19:38). Son of David is the royal messianic title — the one descended from David who would restore the kingdom. The blind man cannot see Jesus but he has heard who is passing and draws the theological conclusion that the disciples are still struggling with. He calls out the messianic title and asks for mercy. His sight is spiritual before it is physical.

notes.original: ekrazen… megà màllon
notes.rendering: he cries out all the more
notes.why: Krazeō — to cry out, to scream, to shout. The crowd rebukes him; he cries louder. The imperfect tense (ekrazen) means he keeps crying out — continuously, repeatedly. The rebuke does not silence him; it increases his volume. This is the persistent widow’s quality applied to a single desperate moment: the refusal to be quieted when the need is real and the source of help is within range.

notes.original: ti soi thelēs poiēsō
notes.rendering: What do you want me to do for you?
notes.why: Jesus stops and asks. The question is not redundant — a blind beggar calling for mercy might want money, food, or any number of things. Jesus asks the man to name his specific need. The question gives the man his dignity back: he is not assumed, not categorised, not given what someone else has decided he needs. He is asked. And he answers with precision: Lord — let me see again. Anablepsai: to see again, to regain sight. The verb implies he could see before.

notes.original: hē pistis sou sesōken se
notes.rendering: Your faith has saved you
notes.why: The same words spoken to the sinful woman (7:50), to the hemorrhaging woman (8:48), to the Samaritan leper (17:19) — and now to a blind beggar at the gate of Jericho. Each time, the person has reached toward Jesus in some form of desperate, specific faith. Each time, the word is sōzō — not merely healed but saved, the whole word. The blind man’s faith is his crying out against the crowd’s rebuke, his refusal to be silenced, his persistent naming of Jesus as Son of David. That is what the faith looks like.

notes.original: akolouthōn autō doxazōn ton theon
notes.rendering: follows him, glorifying God
notes.why: The healed man does not go home. He follows — present participle, continuous action — and glorifies God as he goes. The last scene before Jerusalem is a man who received his sight and immediately joined the procession. The crowd that had been rebuking him joins the praise. The chapter that began with a widow refusing to stop crying out ends with a man who refused to stop crying out, now with his eyes open, walking into the holy city.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 18 as a chapter about entry and exclusion: Each scene in chapter 18 circles the question of who gets in. The widow gets justice through persistence, not standing. The tax collector goes home justified, not the Pharisee. The kingdom belongs to infants who cannot qualify. The rich ruler cannot enter because he will not let go. The disciples cannot understand. The blind man receives sight and follows. The chapter builds a consistent picture: entry into the kingdom is not achieved by the qualified but received by the desperate, the empty-handed, and those who will not stop asking.

Note on ‘your faith has saved you’ as a refrain in Luke: The phrase hē pistis sou sesōken se appears four times in Luke — to the sinful woman (7:50), the hemorrhaging woman (8:48), the Samaritan leper (17:19), and the blind man (18:42). In each case, the faith expressed is not doctrinal precision or moral achievement but a reaching toward Jesus that refuses to accept the barriers between them: social disgrace, uncleanness, ethnic difference, physical blindness and crowd hostility. Each person has identified something in Jesus worth everything and has acted on that identification. Luke uses the repeated phrase to show that this quality — whatever its form — is what Jesus calls faith, and it is always met with the same word: saved.

intro: Luke 19 is the arrival chapter — the end of the long journey set in motion at 9:51. Zacchaeus is the last person Jesus encounters before Jerusalem; the weeping over the city is the first thing he does when he sees it. Between them stand a parable about a king who goes away and returns to judge, a crowd throwing cloaks, and the stones that will cry out if the disciples go silent. The Greek throughout is charged with the weight of everything converging.
I. Zacchaeus (19:1–10)

notes.original: diērcheto
notes.rendering: is passing through
notes.why: Dierchomai — to pass through, to travel across, to go on the way. The imperfect tense: he is in the process of passing through Jericho, not stopping. This is the narrative tension of the scene: Zacchaeus wants to see a man who is not stopping. Everything that follows — the running ahead, the tree, the looking up — happens because Jesus is passing through and time is short.

notes.original: architelōnēs
notes.rendering: chief tax collector
notes.why: Architelōnēs is a word found nowhere else in ancient Greek literature — a hapax legomenon in the entire known corpus. Luke apparently coins or records a unique term: the arch- prefix indicates Zacchaeus is not merely a tax collector but a superintendent of tax collectors, the head of the regional taxation operation. Jericho was a major customs post on the trade route between Peraea and Judea. Zacchaeus runs the whole system. His wealth is proportional to his authority over it.

notes.original: sykomorean
notes.rendering: sycamore tree
notes.why: The sycamore fig (Ficus sycomorus) — not the European sycamore — is a large, low-branching tree common in the Jordan valley. Its branches spread wide and low, making it easily climbable. Zacchaeus does not merely perch at the edge of the crowd; he runs ahead (prodramōn — running before) and climbs. The chief tax collector, the most powerful economic figure in the region, is running and climbing a tree. Luke records this without comment. The desperation to see Jesus transcends dignity.

notes.original: dei me… sēmeron
notes.rendering: I must stay at your house today
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary, divine compulsion, the same word Luke uses for Jesus going to Jerusalem (9:22), for the Son of Man suffering (9:44), for the crippled woman being released (13:16). The visit to Zacchaeus’ house is not a social choice; it is a necessity of the mission. And sēmeron — today, Luke’s signature word of immediate divine action (2:11, 4:21, 13:32, 23:43). The kingdom does not arrive eventually at Zacchaeus’ house; it arrives today.

notes.original: hystās de Zakchaios… idou
notes.rendering: Zacchaeus stands there and says
notes.why: The standing (stas — aorist participle, taking a deliberate posture) and the idou (look, behold — a particle of formal declaration) give Zacchaeus’ speech the quality of a public announcement. He is not whispering to Jesus privately; he is making a declaration before the grumbling crowd. The present tense didomi (I give) and apodidoō (I restore) are debated: are these habitual present tenses (this is what I already do) or instantaneous presents (this is what I am doing now)? Either way, the declaration is public and binding.

notes.original: tetraplaōn apodidōmi
notes.rendering: I pay it back fourfold
notes.why: The fourfold restoration echoes Exodus 22:1 and 2 Samuel 12:6 — the restitution required for theft beyond what was taken. Zacchaeus does not merely return what he took; he pays the penalty of a thief who has been caught. The half-of-possessions to the poor and the fourfold restitution together represent a comprehensive economic reckoning. Jesus does not instruct him to do this; Zacchaeus announces it. The salvation comes to the house (v.9) because something has already happened in the man before the declaration.

notes.original: sēmeron sōtēria tō oikō toutō egeneto
notes.rendering: Today salvation has come to this house
notes.why: Sēmeron again. Sōtēria — salvation, the comprehensive rescue word. The house is the unit of salvation here — not just Zacchaeus individually but his household. The son of Abraham title restores Zacchaeus to full covenant membership: the man who had sold himself to the Roman taxation system is declared, by Jesus, to belong to the family of promise. This is the last use of sēmeron in the travel narrative. The next will be on the cross (23:43).

notes.original: zētēsai kai sōsai to apolōlos
notes.rendering: to seek and to save the lost
notes.why: The three verbs of Luke 15 — seek, find, rejoice — are compressed here into the mission statement of the Son of Man. Zēteō (to seek), sōzō (to save), apollŭmi (to lose, perish — the word running through all three parables of chapter 15). Zacchaeus is the culminating example of the lost being found: a chief tax collector, publicly shamed, economically compromised, unable to see over the crowd — and found by Jesus before he could be found by anyone else.

notes.heading: II. The Parable of the Ten Minas (19:11–27)

notes.original: parachrēma… anādeiknysthai
notes.rendering: about to appear at once
notes.why: Parachrēma means immediately, at once, right now. The crowd supposes the kingdom is about to appear immediately because they are near Jerusalem and have just witnessed the Zacchaeus episode. The parable is a direct corrective: the king goes away to a distant country before returning to reign. There is an interval — the interval of the disciples’ faithful or faithless stewardship — between the departure and the return. The kingdom does not arrive on the schedule the crowd is expecting.

notes.original: pragmateusasthe
notes.rendering: Do business with these
notes.why: Pragmateuomai means to engage in business, to trade, to put capital to work. The command is active and specific: the servants are not to preserve the money but to deploy it. The mina (approximately one hundred days’ wages for a labourer) is not a gift to be enjoyed but a trust to be invested. The servant who wraps his in a cloth and returns it unchanged has not been cautious; he has been faithless to the entire purpose of the entrusting.

notes.original: austeros
notes.rendering: a severe man
notes.why: Austeros means harsh, exacting, severe — one who demands full return without flexibility. The servant’s characterisation of the master may be accurate, may be a projection of his own fear, or may be both simultaneously. What it cannot be is a justification for inaction: if he truly believed the master was this exacting, the logical response was to work harder, not to hide the money. His fear produces the very outcome he claims to have been avoiding. The master’s response — I will judge you by your own words — turns his self-description into his condemnation.

notes.original: tous echthrous mou… katasphaxate
notes.rendering: slaughter them in front of me
notes.why: The parable ends with a sentence of extraordinary violence. The enemies who sent the delegation refusing the king’s reign (v.14) are brought before him and executed. Luke does not soften this. Many readers find it disturbing and try to separate it from the rest of the parable. But it is part of the parable’s structure: the king’s return brings both reward for the faithful and judgment for those who refused his kingship. The violence echoes the historical reality Luke’s audience knew: the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, when those who rejected the coming of the King faced exactly this outcome.

notes.original: pōlon… eph’ hon oudeis pōpote anthrōpōn ekathisen
notes.rendering: a colt on which no one has ever sat
notes.why: An animal on which no one has ridden was considered ritually appropriate for sacred use (Numbers 19:2, Deuteronomy 21:3). The detail is not incidental: Jesus enters Jerusalem on a colt set apart for sacred purpose, never broken to ordinary use. The entry is a consecrated act from its first element. Zechariah 9:9 lies behind the scene: ‘your king comes to you… mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’ The crowd does not quote Zechariah, but Luke’s readers familiar with the prophets hear it.

notes.original: ho erchomenos ho basileus
notes.rendering: Blessed is the King who comes
notes.why: Luke’s version of the crowd’s acclamation adds a word that the other gospels do not: basileus — King. The crowd shouts: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord. This is Psalm 118:26 with the royal title inserted. Luke’s crowd is making the claim explicit: this is the royal arrival, the Davidic king entering his city. The Pharisees’ request that Jesus silence them (v.39) is a request that he suppress a politically dangerous messianic acclamation. He refuses.

notes.original: hoi lithoi kraxousin
notes.rendering: the stones will cry out
notes.why: Krazō — to cry out, to scream — the same word used of the blind man at Jericho who refused to be silenced (18:38–39). If the disciples go silent, the stones take up their cry. The creation itself cannot be prevented from acclaiming the arrival of its Lord. The image reaches back through Habakkuk 2:11 (‘the stone will cry out from the wall’) and forward to Romans 8:19 (the creation groaning in eager expectation). The whole created order is already responding to what the Pharisees want hushed.

notes.original: eklauen ep’ autēn
notes.rendering: he weeps over it
notes.why: Klaiō means to weep, to cry — the word of audible grief, not merely moist eyes. Luke uses it for the widow of Nain (7:13), for Peter after the denial (22:62), for the women on the Via Dolorosa (23:28). Here it is Jesus weeping — and not for a person but for a city. He sees Jerusalem and the sight breaks him. The lament of 13:34 was spoken from the road before the city was visible; now he sees it and the grief becomes tears. The city does not know he is weeping for it.

notes.original: ei egnōs en tē hēmera taytē
notes.rendering: If you — even you — had known on this day
notes.why: The conditional is a second-class condition in Greek — contrary to fact: if you had known (but you did not). The emphatic kai sy — even you, you of all cities — makes the lament more devastating: Jerusalem, the city of God’s presence, the place toward which all the prophets pointed, the city that should of all cities have known. And it did not. The things that make for peace (ta pros eirēnēn — the things belonging to peace, the shalom-things) are named but not listed. Their absence is the tragedy.

notes.original: charaka… perikiyklosousin
notes.rendering: throw up a barricade… surround you
notes.why: The military imagery is precise and historical. Charax is a palisade, a siege wall — the kind of encircling earthwork a Roman army would build to prevent escape from a besieged city. Perikykloō means to encircle completely. The description matches the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70 with striking accuracy: Titus’ forces built a wall of circumvallation around the city before the final assault. Luke writes after AD 70; his readers knew what had happened. Jesus’ prophecy and its fulfillment are in the same frame.

notes.original: ton kairon tēs episkopēs sou
notes.rendering: the time of your visitation
notes.why: Kairos — the appointed time, the season of divine action. Episkopē means visitation, oversight, the coming of God to look after his people — the same root as episkeptomai used in the Benedictus (1:68) and at Nain (7:16). The city that kills the prophets did not recognise when God himself visited it. The lament ends here: the destruction comes not as arbitrary punishment but as the consequence of a failure to see. Jerusalem was visited and did not know it.

notes.heading: V. The Cleansing of the Temple (19:45–48)

notes.original: ērxato ekballein
notes.rendering: begins to drive out
notes.why: The imperfect periphrastic: he begins and continues driving out. Luke’s account of the temple cleansing is the most compressed of the four gospels — two verses where Mark devotes six. Luke omits the overturning of tables and the detail of the money-changers. What he keeps is the quotation: my house shall be a house of prayer (Isaiah 56:7), and you have made it a den of robbers (Jeremiah 7:11). The prophetic charge is the point, not the physical disruption.

notes.original: spēlaion lēstōn
notes.rendering: a den of robbers
notes.why: Jeremiah 7:11 — the temple sermon in which Jeremiah accuses Israel of treating the temple as a hideout for those who have oppressed the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner. A spēlaion lēstōn is not merely a market with inflated prices; it is the refuge of those who commit injustice and then retreat to the sacred space as though it protects them. Jesus quotes Jeremiah to name what the temple has become: a place of transaction and refuge for the commercially exploitative, not a house of prayer for all nations.

notes.original: exekremato autou akouon
notes.rendering: hang on his words
notes.why: Ekkrmanōmai means to hang from, to be suspended from — as a pendant hangs from a chain. The people are hanging on his words in the most physical sense the metaphor allows: they are suspended from what he is saying, unable to let go. The chief priests and scribes want to destroy him but cannot find a way to act because the people will not release him. The whole of Jerusalem is between them and their target.

outro: Note on Zacchaeus as the culmination of the travel narrative: The journey from 9:51 to 19:10 — the longest single section of Luke’s gospel — ends with Zacchaeus. The travel narrative has been a sustained exploration of what the kingdom of God looks like when it arrives in a human life: the lost found, the last made first, the outsider welcomed, the self-righteous exposed. Zacchaeus gathers all of these threads. He is lost (the architelōnēs who has sold himself to Rome), small (literally unable to see over the crowd), and the object of communal contempt. Jesus seeks him before he can be found, names him before he can introduce himself, and declares salvation over his house before he has even come down from the tree. The mission statement of v.10 — the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost — is the thesis of the entire travel narrative, stated on its last page.

Note on the weeping over Jerusalem and its placement: Luke places the weeping (19:41–44) between the triumphal entry (19:28–40) and the cleansing of the temple (19:45–48). The crowd is shouting blessed is the King; the Pharisees are demanding silence; Jesus says the stones will cry out. And then — before he enters the temple, before any confrontation with the authorities, before a single act in Jerusalem — he weeps. The arrival that looked like triumph from the road looks, from the moment he sees the city, like grief. The tears are not a contradiction of the acclamation; they are its deepest expression. He is arriving as King in a city that will not receive its King, and he knows it, and he weeps.

intro: Luke 20 is a day of open debate in the temple courts. Every major faction — the chief priests and elders, the scribes and Pharisees, the Sadducees — takes a turn attempting to trap Jesus, and each one withdraws having been outmanoeuvred on their own ground. The debates are not merely clever; they are theologically decisive. The Greek of each exchange is precise and worth attending to closely.
I. The Question of Authority (20:1–8)

notes.original: en poia exousia
notes.rendering: by what authority
notes.why: Exousia — authority, the right and power to act. The question is not about Jesus’ competence or ability but about his credentials: who authorized him? The religious establishment has a system of authorization — rabbinic ordination, priestly lineage, scribal training. Jesus operates outside all of it. The question is designed to force him either to name an authority they can dismiss or to claim divine authorization they can call blasphemy. He refuses both options by turning the question back on them.

notes.original: dialogizonto pros heautous
notes.rendering: they discuss it among themselves
notes.why: The inner deliberation is reported in direct speech — a device Luke uses to reveal the calculation behind the public response. They are not seeking truth; they are doing political risk assessment. Answer A produces outcome X; Answer B produces outcome Y. Both outcomes are bad for them. Their silence is not intellectual humility but strategic evasion — and Jesus names it by refusing to answer a question from people who have just demonstrated they will not answer one honestly themselves.

notes.heading: II. The Parable of the Wicked Tenants (20:9–19)

notes.original: ampelon… apedemēsen chronous hikanous
notes.rendering: a vineyard… goes abroad for a long time
notes.why: The vineyard is an unmistakably Isaianic image: Isaiah 5:1–7, the Song of the Vineyard, where Israel is the vineyard God planted and which produced only wild grapes. Jesus’ audience recognises the image immediately — the scribes’ fury in v.19 confirms it. The long absence (chronous hikanous — sufficient times, a considerable period) creates the narrative space for the servants’ repeated mistreatment: this is a vineyard that has been ungoverned for long enough that the tenants have forgotten who owns it.

notes.original: ton huion mou ton agapēton
notes.rendering: my beloved son
notes.why: The vocabulary is unmistakable: agapētos — beloved, only — the word used by the voice at the baptism (3:22) and the Transfiguration (9:35). The owner sends his beloved son as the last resort after the servants have been beaten and killed. The parable is an allegory whose key is already in the reader’s hands from the earlier chapters. Perhaps they will respect him — the perhaps (isos) is the word of a father who hopes against evidence.

notes.original: apokteinomēn auton, hina hēmōn genētai hē klēronomia
notes.rendering: Let’s kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours
notes.why: The tenants’ logic is legally coherent in one specific scenario: if the owner dies without heirs, the tenants as occupants might claim the land under certain Roman property laws. By killing the son — the heir — they eliminate the claim and potentially gain possession. The plan is not irrational; it is a calculated act of violent greed dressed in legal reasoning. The parable diagnoses the exact crime that is being planned against Jesus in the very room where he tells it.

notes.original: lithos hon apedokimasan hoi oikodomountes
notes.rendering: The stone the builders rejected
notes.why: Psalm 118:22 — the same Hallel psalm the crowd quoted at the triumphal entry (118:26). The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner (kephalēn gōnias — cornerstone or capstone). Jesus quotes the psalm the crowd just sang and turns it from a royal acclamation into a statement about his rejection and vindication. The builders are the religious establishment who have just tried to trap him. Their rejection is the precondition of the stone’s exaltation.

notes.original: pas ho pesōn ep’ ekeinon ton lithon synthlasthēsetai
notes.rendering: Every one who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces
notes.why: Two images of destruction: falling on the stone and being broken (synthlao — to shatter, to crush together), and the stone falling on someone and grinding them to powder (likmao — to winnow, to scatter like chaff). The first may describe the stumbling of those who encounter Jesus in his earthly ministry and are broken by the encounter; the second, the eschatological judgment that falls on those who resist him. Both are irreversible.

notes.original: hypokrinomenous heautous dikaioys einai
notes.rendering: pretend to be sincere
notes.why: Hypokrinomai — to play a role, to act, to pretend. The spies are performing sincerity — deliberately presenting a false face of genuine inquiry. Dikaioys — righteous, upright, sincere. They are acting the role of the righteous questioner while calculating how to deliver Jesus to the governor’s jurisdiction. Luke names the performance before the flattery begins: the reader sees through the mask before the dialogue starts.

notes.original: katanonesas… tēn panourgia
notes.rendering: he sees through their cunning
notes.why: Katanoeō means to observe carefully, to perceive fully. Panourgia means cunning, craftiness — from pan (all) + ergon (work): one who uses every means available, who will do anything to achieve their end. The word is used of the serpent’s cunning in 2 Corinthians 11:3. Jesus does not respond to the flattery; he looks past it and sees the mechanism underneath. His response dismantles the trap without engaging its terms.

notes.original: eikōna kai epigraphēn
notes.rendering: image and inscription
notes.why: Eikōn means image, likeness — the word used in Genesis 1:26 LXX for humanity made in the image of God. Epigraphē is inscription, the name written on the coin. The denarius bore the image of Tiberius and the inscription Tiberius Caesar Divi Augusti Filius Augustus — Tiberius Caesar, Son of the Divine Augustus. Jesus’ question is apparently simple; his answer is theologically explosive. Give Caesar what bears his image. Give God what bears his image. The implication — that the human person, made in the image of God, belongs entirely to God — is left for the listener to complete.

notes.original: ta Kaisaros apodote Kaisari kai ta tou theou tō theō
notes.rendering: Give back to Caesar… and to God
notes.why: Apodidomi means to give back, to return what is owed — not merely to give but to render what belongs to someone. The verb is the same as Zacchaeus’ ‘I restore’ (apodidōmi, 19:8). Caesar’s coin bears Caesar’s image and belongs to Caesar’s realm. But the question of what belongs to God — and what bears God’s image — is the question Jesus leaves ringing in the air. The answer silences his questioners completely.

notes.heading: IV. The Question About the Resurrection (20:27–40)

notes.original: Saddoukaioi… hoi antilegontes anastasin mē einai
notes.rendering: Sadducees — those who say there is no resurrection
notes.why: Luke identifies the Sadducees by their defining theological position before they speak. The Sadducees accepted only the Pentateuch as authoritative and rejected the resurrection as a later development not found in the Torah. Their question is a reductio ad absurdum designed to make the resurrection doctrine look ridiculous by applying it to a case of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). They assume they are on unassailable ground: seven marriages, one woman, absurd heavenly polygamy. Jesus’ response dismantles their premise entirely.

notes.original: tēs anastaseōs tēs ek nekrōn
notes.rendering: the resurrection from the dead
notes.why: Jesus distinguishes between the present age (ho aiōn houtos) and the coming age (ho aiōn ekeinos) in which the resurrection occurs. The resurrection life is not an extension of present life with its reproductive necessities; it is a different mode of existence, characterised by being equal to angels (isangeloi — a word found nowhere else in Greek literature before Luke) and by the impossibility of death. The Sadducees’ question assumes the resurrection is just present life continued into another realm. Jesus corrects the assumption before answering the question.

notes.original: hōs legei Kyrion ton theon Abraam
notes.rendering: when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham
notes.why: The argument is exegetical and devastating. Exodus 3:6 — the burning bush passage, squarely in the Pentateuch the Sadducees accept — has God introducing himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in the present tense.
