Not ‘I was’ but ‘I am.’ If God is presently the God of Abraham, Abraham must presently exist. The resurrection is implied by the most foundational moment of divine self-revelation in the Torah. The Sadducees have been refuted by their own scripture.

notes.original: pantes gar autō zōsin
notes.rendering: for all are alive to him
notes.why: The conclusion is comprehensive: all — pantes — are alive to God. Not just the patriarchs, not just the righteous, but all. The phrase to him (autō) is the key: from God’s perspective, in God’s present, everyone who has lived is alive. The statement reaches beyond the immediate argument about the resurrection into a profound affirmation about the nature of God’s relationship with those he has made: they do not cease to be present to him.

notes.heading: V. Whose Son Is the Messiah (20:41–44)

notes.original: Psalm 110:1
notes.rendering: The Lord said to my Lord
notes.why: Psalm 110:1 was the most cited Old Testament text in the early church and the most used by Jesus himself. The argument turns on the two uses of ‘Lord’: the Lord (YHWH) addresses my Lord (the Davidic king — but the text says ‘adoni,’ my lord, a title used of someone of higher status than the speaker). If David calls the Messiah his lord, how can the Messiah be merely David’s son — a descendant, who would be subordinate to his ancestor? The question is not a denial of Davidic descent but an insistence that the Messiah is something more than a human king in David’s line. Jesus leaves the puzzle open — for those who have ears to hear.

notes.original: stolais peripatein
notes.rendering: walk around in long robes
notes.why: Stolē is a long, flowing robe — a garment of distinction, immediately recognisable as the dress of the educated religious class. Peripateo means to walk around — the walking is public and deliberate, the robe a costume of status worn for the viewing of others. Jesus does not object to the learning or the office; he objects to the performance of them for social reward. The triad that follows — greetings in marketplaces, best seats, places of honour — maps exactly onto the Pharisee’s prayer posture from 18:11.

notes.original: katēsthiousin tàs oikias tōn chērōn
notes.rendering: devour widows’ houses
notes.why: Katesthio means to eat down, to consume completely — to devour. The scribes who perform elaborate religious devotion are simultaneously consuming the estates of widows — possibly by acting as financial trustees or estate managers for vulnerable women and exploiting that position. The juxtaposition is deliberately savage: lengthy prayers and devoured widows in the same sentence. The heavier judgment (perissoteron krima) falls on those whose religious performance conceals economic predation. The next scene — a widow giving her last two coins at the temple — is the immediate illustration.

outro: Note on the structure of Luke 20 as a day of debate: The chapter presents four consecutive challenges to Jesus in the temple, each from a different group, each on different ground. The chief priests and elders challenge his authority (vv.1–8). The scribes and Pharisees challenge him on Roman taxation (vv.20–26). The Sadducees challenge him on the resurrection (vv.27–40). Jesus then turns and challenges all of them on the identity of the Messiah (vv.41–44). The pattern is military: each faction sends its best argument and each retreats in defeat. By v.40 they no longer dare to ask him anything. He has exposed the bad faith of the priests, the cunning of the spies, the false premise of the Sadducees, and the inadequacy of the purely Davidic conception of Messiah — using their own texts against them at every turn.

Note on ‘Give to Caesar’ and the image of God (20:24–25): The saying about Caesar and God is often read as a statement about the separation of political and religious obligations. This reading is not wrong but it is incomplete. The key word is eikōn — image. The coin bears Caesar’s image and belongs to Caesar. What bears God’s image belongs to God. In the Hebrew tradition, the human person is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27). Jesus’ answer does not merely divide the tax question from the religious question; it implies that the human person, as the image-bearer of God, belongs entirely to God — which subordinates all political obligation to that prior, total claim. The questioners are silenced not because the answer is clever but because it is devastating.

intro: Luke 21 opens with the most economically precise act of worship in the gospel and closes with the most urgent call to wakefulness. Between them stands the Olivet discourse — Jesus’ extended prophecy about the destruction of Jerusalem, the persecution of his followers, and the coming of the Son of Man. Luke’s version of the discourse is notably more historically specific than Matthew’s or Mark’s, and the Greek reflects that precision throughout.
I. The Widow’s Offering (21:1–4)

notes.original: lepta dyo
notes.rendering: two small copper coins
notes.why: Lepta — lepton is the smallest coin in circulation, a thin copper piece worth half a quadrans, which was itself the smallest Roman coin. Two lepta together amount to approximately one sixty-fourth of a denarius — perhaps two minutes of a labourer’s wages. Luke does not give the equivalent value in larger coins as Mark does (Mark 12:42: ‘which is a quadrans’). The amount is simply named: two lepta. The smallness stands without conversion.

notes.original: panta ton bion hon eichen
notes.rendering: everything she had to live on
notes.why: Bios means life, livelihood, the means of sustaining life — not merely money but the material foundation of existence. She has given her entire bios — everything that stood between her and destitution. The rich gave from their perisseuma (their surplus, their overflow); she gave from her hystērema (her lack, her deficit). The contrast is not merely quantitative; it is the difference between giving from what you do not need and giving what you cannot spare. Jesus places this scene immediately after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47). The juxtaposition is the commentary.

notes.original: mē poreēthēte
notes.rendering: Don’t follow them
notes.why: Poreuomai means to go, to travel, to follow a path — the word of deliberate journeying. Don’t set out after them. Don’t begin the journey that leads to them. The command is about the direction of the whole life, not merely about intellectual scepticism. Many will come claiming to be the Messiah or announcing the imminent end; the disciples are not to be moved by these claims at all.

notes.original: apobēsetai hymin eis martyrion
notes.rendering: This will be your opportunity to bear witness
notes.why: Apobainō means to step off, to disembark, to turn out — here: it will turn out for you as a testimony. Martyrion — testimony, witness, the word from which martyr derives. Persecution and trial are not obstacles to the mission; they are the mission’s occasion. The suffering becomes the opportunity for witness before kings and governors who would otherwise never hear. Luke’s Acts narratives (Paul before Felix, Festus, Agrippa) are the fulfilment of this promise in narrative form.

notes.original: stoma kai sophian
notes.rendering: words and wisdom
notes.why: Stoma is mouth — literally: I will give you a mouth and wisdom. The image is of speech itself as a gift: the organ of testimony will be supplied, along with the sophia (wisdom, understanding, the capacity to speak rightly) that makes the testimony compelling. The promise is that the disciples will not have to prepare — because what they need will be given at the moment it is needed. This is not a permission to be unprepared in general; it is a specific assurance for the specific context of persecution.

notes.original: thrix ek tēs kephalēs hymōn ou mē apolētai
notes.rendering: not a hair of your head will perish
notes.why: The promise is placed immediately after ‘some of you will be put to death’ (v.16). The apparent contradiction is the point: physical death does not constitute the perishing of the person. Apollymi — to perish, to be destroyed — is the word of ultimate, final loss. Jesus distinguishes between being killed and perishing: the body can be killed; the person, in the deepest sense, cannot be lost. The hair of the head that will not perish echoes 12:7 (‘even the hairs of your head are all numbered’) — God’s specific, exhaustive knowledge of each person persists beyond death.

notes.original: en tē hypomonei hymōn
notes.rendering: By your endurance
notes.why: Hypomonē — patient endurance, the capacity to remain under a heavy load without collapsing, the same word from the Sower parable (8:15). The disciples gain their lives (psychàs) not by escaping suffering but by enduring it. Ktàomai means to acquire, to win, to gain — as a soldier gains ground or a merchant gains profit. Endurance is the means by which the self is acquired, secured, made truly one’s own. The paradox is consistent with everything Luke has said about losing and finding life (9:24, 17:33).

notes.original: kukloumenēn hypò stratopedōn
notes.rendering: surrounded by armies
notes.why: Kykloō means to encircle, to surround on all sides. Stratopedon is an army camp, a military force in battle array. The sign Jesus gives for the desolation of Jerusalem is not supernatural but military and historical: when armies surround the city, flee. This is notably different from Mark’s version (13:14), which speaks of ‘the abomination of desolation.’ Luke’s version is more historically explicit, which is why many scholars believe Luke writes after AD 70 and shapes the discourse in light of what actually happened.

notes.original: hēmerai ekdikēseōs
notes.rendering: days of vengeance
notes.why: Ekdikēsis means justice, vengeance, the righting of wrongs — the same root as the widow’s cry in 18:3 (give me justice). The days of vengeance are days when God’s justice is executed — not arbitrary destruction but the fulfillment of everything written (pantà ta gegrammēna). The fall of Jerusalem is framed as a scripturally necessary event, the consequence of the city’s rejection of its visitation (19:44). Luke draws a direct line from the weeping over Jerusalem to its destruction.

notes.original: kairoi ethnōn
notes.rendering: the times of the Gentiles
notes.why: Kairoi ethnōn — the seasons of the nations, the appointed period during which the Gentiles exercise dominion over Jerusalem. The phrase implies a limit: these times will be fulfilled (plērōthōsin), completed, brought to their appointed end. Luke’s gospel and Acts together frame the entire period between the fall of Jerusalem and the final coming of the Son of Man as the era of the Gentile mission — the time during which the good news goes to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8) before the end.

notes.heading: IV. The Coming of the Son of Man (21:25–28)

notes.original: synochē ethnōn en aporia
notes.rendering: distress of nations in perplexity
notes.why: Synochē means constriction, being hemmed in, anguish that comes from being trapped — related to synechō (the word Jesus used of himself being hemmed in, 12:50). Aporia means being at a loss, having no way out, perplexity in the face of something that cannot be resolved. The nations are not merely afraid; they are constricted and without a path forward. The roaring of the sea (hēchos thalassēs) reaches back to the Psalms and the prophets where the churning sea represents chaos threatening the created order.

notes.original: erchomenon en nephēlē meta dynameōs kai doxēs pollēs
notes.rendering: coming in a cloud with power and great glory
notes.why: The cloud is the cloud of the divine presence — the Shekinah cloud of the Exodus, the cloud of the Transfiguration (9:34–35), the cloud of the ascension (Acts 1:9). The Son of Man’s coming reverses the sequence of departure: he left in a cloud; he returns in a cloud. Daniel 7:13–14 lies behind the image — the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive everlasting dominion. What Daniel saw in vision, Jesus announces as coming reality.

notes.original: anakyptete kai eparate tas kephalàs hymōn
notes.rendering: stand up and lift your heads
notes.why: Anakyptō — to raise oneself up, to lift the head, to look up — the same root as the word for the crippled woman who could not straighten up (anakuptein, 13:11). When the signs of cosmic dissolution appear, the disciples are not to cower or flee; they are to raise their heads. The redemption (apolytrosis — a liberation word, the buying-back of a captive) is drawing near. The signs that produce terror in the nations produce expectation in those who belong to the Son of Man.

notes.heading: V. The Fig Tree and the Call to Watchfulness (21:29–38)

notes.original: hē genea hautē ou mē parethē
notes.rendering: this generation will not pass away
notes.why: One of the most discussed sayings in the Olivet discourse. Genea can mean a biological generation (approximately thirty to forty years), a type of people (the faithless generation), or an era. The most natural reading — that the events Jesus describes will occur within the lifetime of his contemporaries — fits the historical destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 precisely. Luke’s audience, reading after that event, would recognise the fulfilment. Whether ‘all these things’ refers to the Jerusalem events only, or to the Son of Man’s coming as well, has been debated since the second century.

notes.original: ho de logos mou ou mē parelthōsin
notes.rendering: my words will never pass away
notes.why: Parerchesthai — to pass away, to pass by, to come to an end. The word used twice in the same verse: heaven and earth will pass away (pareleusōntai), but my words will absolutely not pass away (ou mē parelthōsin — the strongest possible Greek negation). The cosmos is more temporary than the word of Jesus. This is the claim that establishes the authority of everything in the discourse: not because Jesus is a reliable forecaster but because his words have the permanence of the divine word.

notes.original: baretōsin… mēpote epistē eph’ hymàs aiphnidios hē hēmera
notes.rendering: your hearts are not weighed down… catch you off guard
notes.why: Bareō means to weigh down, to burden, to make heavy — the same word used of the disciples heavy with sleep at the Transfiguration (9:32). Aiphnidios means sudden, unexpected, coming without warning. The trap image (pagis) is precise: a trap closes on an animal precisely when the animal is not watching for it. The three threats — dissipation (kraipale, the headache and nausea of overindulgence), drunkenness (methe), and the anxieties of life (merimna biōtike, the same word from the Sower parable) — are not dramatic vices but ordinary dullings of attention.

notes.original: agrypneite… deomenoi
notes.rendering: stay awake… praying
notes.why: Agrypneō means to be sleepless, to keep vigil, to stay awake through the night. It is a stronger word than grēgoreō (to watch, to be alert) — it implies the active effort of fighting off sleep when the body wants to yield to it. The companion command is deomenoi — praying, petitioning, asking. Watchfulness and prayer are not two separate activities but a single discipline: alert waiting that expresses itself in constant asking. The chapter that began with a widow who gave everything ends with a command to stay awake and keep asking.

notes.original: tàs dē nyktas… tò prōi
notes.rendering: every night… early in the morning
notes.why: The closing verses establish the daily rhythm of the final days in Jerusalem: teaching in the temple by day, sleeping on the Mount of Olives by night, the crowds coming early to hear him. The mountain where he sleeps is the mountain from which he will be taken to his arrest (22:39). The people coming early in the morning are hanging on the words of a man who will be dead before the week is out. Luke places this quiet daily rhythm directly before the passion narrative as a final portrait of Jesus in his last days: present, teaching, accessible, sleeping under the open sky.

outro: Note on Luke’s Olivet discourse versus Matthew’s and Mark’s: Luke’s version (21:5–38) is notably more historically grounded than Matthew’s (24:1–51) or Mark’s (13:1–37). Where Mark speaks of ‘the abomination of desolation’ (13:14), Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies (21:20). Where Matthew and Mark use apocalyptic language that is harder to locate historically, Luke’s version reads almost as a description of the Roman siege of AD 70 — the surrounding armies, the trampling of Jerusalem, the captivity among the nations. Most scholars believe Luke wrote after the destruction of Jerusalem and shaped the discourse in light of that event, while preserving the substance of Jesus’ teaching. The result is a discourse that operates on two levels simultaneously: the historical judgment on Jerusalem and the eschatological coming of the Son of Man.

Note on the widow’s offering and its placement: The widow who gives her last two lepta (21:1–4) is the immediate counterpart to the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47). Luke places them in direct sequence without comment. The scribes perform religion for public reward while consuming the resources of the vulnerable; this unnamed widow performs the most extravagant act of worship in the temple without any audience except Jesus. She gives her bios — her entire livelihood — into the treasury of an institution that, Jesus will announce in the next sentence, is about to be destroyed stone by stone. She gives everything to something that will not last. And Jesus declares her gift the greatest in the room. The chapter’s movement from this scene to the cosmic dissolution and the call to stand and lift your heads forms a quiet theological arc: the one who gives everything now is the one who will have nothing to lose when the shaking comes.

intro: Luke 22 is the most emotionally concentrated chapter in the gospel. Every scene carries enormous weight: the Passover meal where Jesus redefines the covenant, the garden where he sweats blood, the courtyard where Peter weeps, the council chamber where the question is finally put directly. The Greek in each scene is among the most carefully crafted in the New Testament.
I. The Plot and Judas (22:1–6)

notes.original: eisēlthen de Satanas
notes.rendering: Satan enters into Judas
notes.why: Luke names the agent behind Judas’ defection with stark directness: Satan enters into him. The same Satan who tested Jesus in the wilderness (4:2–13) and withdrew until an opportune time (4:13) has found his kairos. The act of betrayal is simultaneously Judas’s choice and Satan’s entry — Luke holds both without resolving the tension. The verb eiserchomai (to enter into) is used elsewhere of demons entering the Gerasene’s pigs (8:33). The comparison is deliberate and sombre.

notes.original: ater ochlou
notes.rendering: without a crowd being present
notes.why: Ater means without, in the absence of. The entire plot turns on this condition: the authorities want Jesus eliminated, but they cannot act publicly because of the people’s devotion (19:48, 20:19, 21:38). Judas’s value is precisely his knowledge of where Jesus can be found when the crowd is absent. The arrest in the garden — at night, in a private place — is the fulfilment of this condition.

notes.original: epithymia epethēmesa
notes.rendering: I have longed and longed
notes.why: A Hebrew-style emphatic construction using the noun and verb from the same root: epithymia epethŭmesa — with desire I have desired, I have intensely longed. The same construction appears in Luke 15:16 (the Prodigal Son longing for the pigs’ food) and in the LXX for strong desire. Jesus’ longing to eat this Passover with his disciples is the deepest personal desire he expresses in the gospel. He is about to suffer; he wants this meal first, with these people.

notes.original: eis tēn emēn anamnēsin
notes.rendering: in remembrance of me
notes.why: Anamnēsis means remembrance, memorial, the active recalling of a person or event into present reality. In the LXX it is used for the memorial portions of sacrifices offered before God — not merely mental recollection but a making-present of the past act. When the disciples do this in remembrance of Jesus, they are not simply thinking about him; they are performing the act that makes his sacrifice present in the room. The word carries cultic weight the English ‘remembrance’ can lose.

notes.original: hē kainē diathēkē
notes.rendering: the new covenant
notes.why: Kainē means new in kind, qualitatively new — not merely recent but of a new order. Diathēkē means covenant, will, testament — a binding agreement establishing a relationship with defined terms. The new covenant in Jesus’ blood fulfills and supersedes the Sinai covenant, exactly as Jeremiah 31:31–34 promised: a covenant written on the heart rather than on stone, with forgiveness of sins at its centre. The cup is the enacted sign of that covenant.

notes.original: kata to hōrismenon
notes.rendering: as it has been determined
notes.why: Horizō means to mark off, to define, to determine — from which comes our word ‘horizon.’ The Son of Man goes according to what has been marked out, defined in advance. The same verb is used in Acts 2:23 (‘delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God’) and Acts 10:42 (‘appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead’). The passion is not an accident or a defeat; it is the fulfilment of a defined divine purpose. The woe on the betrayer stands alongside this without contradiction: divine necessity and human culpability coexist.

notes.heading: III. Dispute About Greatness and Peter’s Denial Foretold (22:24–34)

notes.original: euergetēs
notes.rendering: Benefactors
notes.why: Euergetes — Benefactor — was an actual royal title used by Hellenistic rulers including Ptolemy III Euergetes of Egypt. The title was a piece of self-congratulatory propaganda: rulers who exercised coercive power over their subjects styled themselves as those who did good to them. Jesus names the hypocrisy embedded in the title and says: it must not be so with you. The kingdom inverts this structure entirely: the greatest serves, the leader becomes like the youngest.

notes.original: egō de en mesō hymōn eimi hōs ho diakonōn
notes.rendering: I am among you as the one who serves
notes.why: Diakonōn — the servant, the one who waits at table, the one who carries and pours. Jesus does not say he will serve or that he has served; he says I am, present tense, the serving one among you. The meal they are eating — which he has prepared and is hosting — is the enacted demonstration of the claim. The foot-washing in John 13 is the same statement in physical form.

notes.original: exetēsato hymàs tou siníiàsai
notes.rendering: Satan has demanded to have you all
notes.why: Exaiteōmai means to ask for, to demand for oneself — with the force of a legal petition. Satan has filed a claim against the disciples, demanding to have them. The plural hymàs — you all — is significant: Satan’s demand is for all of them, not just Peter. The sifting (siniasai — to put through a sieve) is an image of violent testing that separates what is genuine from what is not. The prayer for Peter specifically is the one act standing between Peter and destruction.

notes.original: epistrephas
notes.rendering: when you have turned back
notes.why: Epistrepho means to turn around, to return, to convert — the same verb used throughout Luke for repentance and return to God (1:16–17). Jesus does not say ‘if you turn back’ but ‘when’ — the restoration is assumed. The denial is predicted; the turning back is equally predicted. Peter’s weeping in v.62 is the turning beginning. The word ‘strengthen’ (stērison) places on Peter, once restored, the task of being the support for others who will face the same testing.

notes.original: mē to thelēma mou alla to son ginestho
notes.rendering: Not my will but yours be done
notes.why: The most important sentence Jesus speaks. Two wills named and distinguished: his own (to thelēma mou) and the Father’s (to son). The genestho — let it happen, let it be done — is an optative of will, a genuine expression of choice. This is not a performance of submission for the disciples’ benefit; it is a real internal contest between what the human nature of Jesus recoils from (the cup) and what his deepest self wills (the Father’s purpose). The prayer is the hinge on which everything turns.

notes.original: thromboi haimatos
notes.rendering: drops of blood
notes.why: Verses 43–44 — the angel strengthening Jesus and the sweat becoming like drops of blood — are absent from some early manuscripts (P75, א, A, B and others) and present in others. The NA28 includes them with brackets indicating uncertainty. Whether original or an early addition, the content is theologically consistent with Luke’s portrait of a Jesus who is genuinely, physically agonized. Thrombos means a clot, a thick drop — the sweat is not merely heavy; it falls in clots like blood. The agony (agōnia — the word of athletic contest pushed to the extreme) is physiological as well as spiritual.

notes.original: apo tēs lypēs
notes.rendering: from grief
notes.why: The disciples sleep from grief — apo tēs lypēs. Luke alone gives this explanation. They are not merely weary or indifferent; they are overcome by sorrow. Luke is the only gospel writer who names grief as the reason for their sleep — consistent with his characteristically sympathetic portrait of the disciples throughout the passion.

notes.heading: V. The Arrest and Peter’s Denial (22:47–62)

notes.original: philēmati
notes.rendering: with a kiss
notes.why: Philema — a kiss, the gesture of affection and greeting between friends or teacher and disciple. In the ancient world a student greeted his rabbi with a kiss; it was a sign of devotion and honour. Judas uses the most intimate gesture of discipleship as the signal for arrest. Jesus’ question — are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss? — names the specific enormity: not merely betrayal but betrayal using the very sign of love.

notes.original: hautē estin hymōn hē hōra kai hē exousia tou skotous
notes.rendering: This is your hour — and the power of darkness
notes.why: Hōra — hour, the appointed time, the kairos. The power of darkness (exousia tou skotous) is the authority of the dark realm — the domain Jesus identified as Satan’s in 4:6. This is the moment from which Satan withdrew in 4:13 — the opportune time finally arrived. Jesus does not resist; he names what is happening with absolute clarity and walks into it. The arrest is not a defeat; it is a deliberate entry into the hour.

notes.original: epistraphteis ho kyrios eneblepsen tō Petrō
notes.rendering: the Lord turns and looks at Peter
notes.why: Emblepo means to look directly at, to fix the gaze on — the word of a searching, penetrating look. At the moment the rooster crows, Jesus — somehow visible from where he is being held — turns and finds Peter’s face in the courtyard. No word is spoken. The look is everything. Peter remembers the word. And he goes outside and weeps bitterly. The bitterness (pikrōs) is the word for intense, cutting grief — grief that stings.

notes.heading: VI. The Trial Before the Council (22:66–71)

notes.original: ean hymin eipō, ou mē pisteusete
notes.rendering: If I tell you, you will not believe
notes.why: Jesus refuses to give them what they are asking for — a direct messianic claim that could serve as grounds for a charge. He names the futility: they will not believe, they will not answer. The question is not a genuine inquiry; it is a procedural mechanism for producing a confession. Jesus sees through the procedure and declines to participate in it on their terms.

notes.original: apo tou nyn de estai ho Huios tou anthrōpou kathēmenos
notes.rendering: from now on the Son of Man will be seated
notes.why: Apo tou nyn — from now on, from this very moment. Not at some future eschatological date but beginning now, from this interrogation room. The session at the right hand of the power of God (Psalm 110:1, the psalm Jesus cited in 20:42–44) begins from this moment of apparent defeat. The council has Jesus in their hands; Jesus announces that the sequence of events they are initiating is the very sequence that will result in his exaltation.

notes.original: hymēis legete hoti egō eimi
notes.rendering: You say that I am
notes.why: The answer is neither a direct yes nor a denial. Hymēis legete — you say it, you yourselves are saying it. It is an affirmation that turns the claim back on the speakers: the words are true, and you are the ones who have just said them. The council takes it as a confession (v.71: we have heard it from his own mouth). Whether the Greek formula is evasive or affirmative has been debated since antiquity. Luke’s context makes clear the council receives it as a yes — and they are not wrong.

outro: Note on Luke’s Last Supper and its unique elements: Luke’s account of the Last Supper (22:14–23) contains several elements absent from Matthew and Mark. The doubled cup — one before the bread (v.17) and one after (v.20) — reflects the Passover seder’s sequence more precisely than the other accounts. The saying about not drinking the fruit of the vine (v.18) is placed before the institution of the Eucharist, not after. And the announcement of the betrayer comes after the institution (vv.21–23), not before — meaning Judas receives the bread and cup before being named. Whether this is historically deliberate or a different tradition from Matthew and Mark is debated; what is clear is that Luke’s arrangement places the gift before the naming of the betrayer, making the grace more radical.

Note on the look (22:61): The detail that the Lord turns and looks at Peter is unique to Luke. Jesus is inside the high priest’s house; Peter is in the courtyard. The look happens at the precise moment the rooster crows — implying either that Jesus is visible through a doorway or window, or that the tradition preserves the memory of a glance that destroyed and reconstituted a man. Luke offers no explanation of the mechanics. He simply says: the Lord turns, looks, and Peter remembers. Three verbs, one sentence, a whole life changed. It is one of the most powerful moments in the gospel, and Luke tells it in the most restrained possible way.

intro: Luke 23 is the passion narrative — the chapters toward which the entire gospel has been moving since Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem in 9:51. Luke’s account is distinctive in several ways: three declarations of innocence by Pilate, the weeping women on the Via Dolorosa, the criminal who defends Jesus, and the centurion who glorifies God rather than expressing pagan awe. The Greek throughout is spare and precise.
I. The Trials (23:1–25)

notes.original: diastrophonta to ethnos hēmōn
notes.rendering: misleading our nation
notes.why: Diastrephō means to twist, to pervert, to turn away from the right path. The charge is precisely framed for Pilate: this man is a political subversive who is turning the Jewish people away from proper order. The three charges — misleading the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, claiming to be king — are all political in framing. The religious charge (blasphemy before the council) is translated into the only terms that matter to a Roman governor: sedition and treason.

notes.original: ouден aition heurískō
notes.rendering: I find no guilt in this man
notes.why: Aition means cause, ground, reason for a charge — the legal basis for a conviction. Pilate uses this word or its equivalent three times in the chapter (vv.4, 14, 22). Three declarations of innocence by the Roman authority constitute Luke’s clearest statement that the crucifixion is a judicial murder: Rome’s own representative finds no legal basis for the death sentence, and capitulates to political pressure anyway.

notes.original: Philíoi dē egenonto… en autē tē hēmera
notes.rendering: become friends… that very day
notes.why: The detail is peculiar and precise: Herod and Pilate were previously enemies; they become friends on the day they collaborate in the trial of Jesus. Luke does not explain the prior enmity or comment on the irony. Acts 4:27 will cite this as a fulfilment of Psalm 2:1–2 (‘the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’). The friendship sealed in the condemnation of the innocent is Luke’s quiet indictment of both men.

notes.original: paredoken auton tō thelēmati autōn
notes.rendering: he hands Jesus over to their will
notes.why: Paradidōmi — to hand over, to deliver up — the word used throughout the passion predictions (9:44, 18:32) for the delivering of the Son of Man into human hands. Here Pilate delivers Jesus not to Roman justice but to the will (thelēma) of the crowd. The word thelēma — will, desire — echoes the Gethsemane prayer: not my will (thelēma) but yours. In the garden Jesus surrendered to the Father’s will; here he is delivered into the crowd’s will. Both acts are part of the same determined purpose.

notes.original: Kranion
notes.rendering: The Skull
notes.why: Kranion — skull, cranium. Luke uses the Greek anatomical term; Mark and Matthew use the transliterated Aramaic Golgotha. The place of execution is named for its appearance — a skull-shaped hill or a place associated with death. Luke’s clinical term is consistent with his physician’s vocabulary throughout the gospel.

notes.original: Pater, aphes autois
notes.rendering: Father — forgive them
notes.why: Verse 34a is absent from some important manuscripts (P75, א, B, D and others) but present in others. The NA28 includes it with brackets. Whether original or very early, the prayer is entirely consistent with Luke’s theology: Jesus forgives from the cross using the same aphiemi (release, forgive) that has been his characteristic word throughout the gospel (5:20–24, 7:47–48, 11:4). The ‘they don’t know what they are doing’ is not an excuse but an explanation that makes the forgiveness more rather than less extraordinary.

notes.original: sēmeron met’ emou esē en tō paradeisōi
notes.rendering: today you will be with me in paradise
notes.why: Sēmeron — today — Luke’s signature word of immediate divine action (2:11, 4:21, 19:9) appears for the last time, from the cross, to a dying criminal. Paradise (paradeisos) is a Persian loanword meaning an enclosed garden or park, used in the LXX for the Garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8–9) and in Jewish tradition for the dwelling place of the righteous after death. The criminal asked to be remembered when Jesus comes into his kingdom; Jesus gives him something more immediate: today, with me. The promise precedes the resurrection.

notes.original: diemerizanto ta himatia autou
notes.rendering: they cast lots to divide his clothing
notes.why: Psalm 22:18 — ‘they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.’ The soldiers carrying out the routine procedure of dividing the condemned man’s possessions are, without knowing it, enacting a psalm. Luke does not cite the psalm; he simply records the action. The reader who knows Psalm 22 hears the echo. The whole of Psalm 22 — the cry of abandonment, the mockery, the bones out of joint, the rescue at the end — hangs over the crucifixion scene.

notes.original: skotous… tou hēliou ekleipontos
notes.rendering: darkness… the sun failing
notes.why: Ekleipō means to fail, to leave off, to cease — the word from which ‘eclipse’ derives. Luke says the sun fails, not that it is eclipsed (a Passover full moon makes a solar eclipse astronomically impossible). The darkness is a sign — cosmic mourning, the withdrawal of light in the presence of the death of the Light of the world. The ninth hour is approximately 3pm; the darkness lasts three hours. The tearing of the temple curtain is simultaneous with the darkness: the inner sanctuary is laid open.

notes.original: to katapetasma tou naou eschisthē
notes.rendering: the curtain of the temple is torn in two
notes.why: The katapetasma was the great curtain separating the Holy of Holies from the rest of the temple — the veil behind which only the high priest entered, once a year, on the Day of Atonement. Its tearing (schizō — to split, to tear apart) at the moment of Jesus’ death signals the end of the sacrificial system as the means of access to God. The way into the presence of God is now open — torn open from top to bottom, in the moment of the one sacrifice that makes all others unnecessary.

notes.original: eis cheiras sou paratithemai to pneuma mou
notes.rendering: Father — into your hands I commit my spirit
notes.why: Psalm 31:5 — ‘into your hands I commit my spirit.’ Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips, as he has taught and lived throughout the gospel. The verb paratithemi means to place beside, to entrust, to deposit for safekeeping — as a traveller deposits valuables with a trusted host. The spirit is not merely given up; it is entrusted, placed in the Father’s hands. The final word Luke records from the cross is not despair but trust.

notes.original: ontōs ho anthrōpos houtos dikaios ēn
notes.rendering: Certainly this man was righteous
notes.why: The centurion’s declaration in Luke differs from Matthew and Mark (who have him say ‘Son of God’). Luke’s centurion says dikaios — righteous, innocent, just. The word is the same Pilate used in declaring no grounds for conviction (aition). A Roman soldier, having watched the crucifixion, arrives at the same verdict as the Roman governor: this man was innocent. And he glorifies God (edoxazen ton theon) — the response of those who witness divine action throughout Luke’s gospel (5:25, 7:16, 13:13, 17:15, 18:43).

outro: Note on Luke’s three declarations of innocence (23:4, 14, 22): Luke alone records three explicit declarations by Pilate that Jesus is innocent of the charges against him. The structural repetition is deliberate: the Roman justice system finds no case, three times over. The crucifixion is therefore unambiguously a judicial murder — not a legitimate execution of a genuine criminal but the capitulation of a compromised official to the pressure of a crowd. Luke’s legal precision throughout the passion narrative serves a theological purpose: Jesus dies not because he is guilty but precisely because he is innocent. His death is the death of the righteous one, the Isaianic Servant who is ‘cut off from the land of the living’ (Isaiah 53:8) though he has done no violence.

Note on the penitent criminal (23:40–43): Luke alone records the exchange between Jesus and the two criminals. The penitent criminal’s words are remarkable for their theological precision: he acknowledges his own guilt, acknowledges the justice of his sentence, declares Jesus’ innocence, and asks not for rescue but for remembrance. He does not say ‘save me’ but ‘remember me.’ Jesus gives him something greater than what he asked: not merely memory but presence — today, with me, in paradise. The last person Jesus speaks to before his death is a dying criminal. The first person to be promised paradise is someone with no religious credentials, no baptism, no discipleship record — only the recognition that Jesus is innocent and the request to be remembered. Luke ends the crucifixion scene with this exchange because it is the most complete expression of the gospel he knows.

intro: Luke 24 is one of the most carefully constructed chapters in all of Scripture. Three scenes — the empty tomb, the Emmaus road, the upper room — build progressively toward a recognition that the disciples cannot achieve by human means and cannot prevent once God grants it. The chapter opens in darkness and ends with the disciples in the temple, blessing God. The Greek throughout is among the most beautiful and precise in the gospel.
I. The Empty Tomb (24:1–12)

notes.original: en esthēti astraptousē
notes.rendering: in dazzling clothes
notes.why: Astraptō means to flash like lightning — the same verb used of lightning in 17:24 and of Jesus’ appearance at the Transfiguration (9:29: the appearance of his face became different, his clothing dazzling white). The two men in the tomb are clothed in the same radiance as the transfigured Jesus. The connection is deliberate: the empty tomb is being interpreted by figures who belong to the same order of reality as the Transfiguration. Their clothing declares what they are before they speak.

notes.original: ti zēteēte ton zōnta meta tōn nekrōn
notes.rendering: Why are you looking for the living among the dead?
notes.why: The question is the gospel in eight words. The women have come to tend a corpse; they are asked why they are looking for a living person in the place of the dead. Zōn — the living one, the one who is alive — is a present participle: he is actively, presently alive. The tomb is the wrong category for what Jesus now is. The angel’s question does not merely report the resurrection; it reorients the women’s entire frame of reference.

notes.original: lēros
notes.rendering: nonsense
notes.why: Lēros means idle talk, nonsense, drivel — what someone says when they are delirious or raving. The word is used in medical texts for the confused speech of a fever patient. The apostles do not merely doubt the women’s report; they classify it as the kind of thing a sick or irrational person says. The resurrection is received first as medical nonsense. This is the honest record of how the disciples initially responded.

notes.original: hoi de ophthalmoi autōn ekratountō
notes.rendering: their eyes are kept from recognising him
notes.why: Krateo means to seize, to hold, to overpower. Their eyes are being held — kept in a grip that prevents recognition. The passive voice implies a divine agent: something is actively preventing them from seeing who is walking beside them. This is not psychological projection or wishful thinking; it is a deliberate veiling. Recognition will come, but not on their terms or schedule.

notes.original: skēthropoloi
notes.rendering: their faces downcast
notes.why: Skythrōpos means with a gloomy, sad, downcast face — from skythrō (sullen, dark) and ops (face). The word appears only here in the New Testament. The two disciples stop walking when Jesus asks his question. Their stopping and their faces tell the whole story before they speak: they are people for whom everything has gone wrong.

notes.original: hēmeis de ēlpizomen hoti autos estin
notes.rendering: we were hoping
notes.why: The imperfect tense ēlpizomen — we were hoping, we used to hope — is the sound of hope in the past tense. They speak of their hope for redemption as something that was and is no longer. The crucifixion has made the hope past tense. This is the condition of the whole world before the resurrection is received: hope that was, extinguished. The two disciples do not know they are describing themselves to the one who is about to give their hope back to them.

notes.original: ō anoetoi kai bradeis
notes.rendering: Oh, how foolish you are
notes.why: Anoetos means without nous, without understanding, foolish in the sense of failing to use the mind one has. Bradeis means slow, sluggish. Jesus’ rebuke is not harsh but it is direct: you have the scriptures, you have the words of the prophets, and you have been too slow to put it together. The rebuke is immediately followed by the most comprehensive act of scriptural interpretation in the gospel — from Moses and all the Prophets, everything concerning himself.

notes.original: diermēneusen autois en pasais tais graphais
notes.rendering: he interprets to them in all the scriptures
notes.why: Diermeneuō means to interpret, to explain thoroughly, to translate from one register to another. The dia- prefix indicates thoroughness: he goes through all of them. The word is related to Hermes — the divine messenger, the interpreter. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus becomes the definitive interpreter of his own story, reading the entire canon of Scripture as a text about himself. The disciples’ hearts burn not because of emotion but because the scriptures are being read correctly for the first time.

notes.original: klasas epídidou… dienoichthēsan hoi ophthalmoi
notes.rendering: breaks and gives… their eyes are opened
notes.why: The three eucharistic verbs from 9:16 (the feeding of the five thousand) — takes, blesses, breaks, gives — appear again. At the moment of the breaking and giving, the eyes are opened (dienoichthēsan — divine passive, opened from outside themselves). Recognition comes in the same gesture that the feeding and the Last Supper used. The Emmaus disciples recognise the risen Jesus in the breaking of bread — the first eucharistic recognition of the resurrection. And then he vanishes. He is known in the moment of breaking; the moment is enough.

notes.original: ouchi hē kardia hēmōn kaiomentē ēn
notes.rendering: Weren’t our hearts burning within us?
notes.why: Kaio means to burn, to be on fire. The present participle kaiomentē describes an ongoing burning — not a flash but a sustained heat. They did not know at the time what was producing the heat; now they name it. The burning was the risen Jesus interpreting the scriptures beside them on the road. What felt like inexplicable warmth in the conversation was the resurrection making itself known through the word before it made itself known through the bread.

notes.heading: III. Jesus Appears to the Disciples (24:36–49)

notes.original: pneuma theoreōsin
notes.rendering: a ghost
notes.why: Pneuma here means a spirit, a disembodied spirit, an apparition — not the Holy Spirit but a shade or ghost. The disciples’ first response to the risen Jesus is to classify him as a ghost — a spiritual apparition of the dead man they knew. Jesus’ response is physical and deliberate: see my hands and feet, touch me, watch me eat. The risen body is not a ghost; it has flesh (sarx) and bones (ostea) — the most physical terms possible. The resurrection is bodily; Luke insists on this.

notes.original: eti de apistountōn autōn apo tēs charàs
notes.rendering: while they still cannot believe for joy
notes.why: One of the most psychologically acute observations in the resurrection narratives. They cannot believe — not from scepticism but from joy. The joy is too large; it overwhelms the capacity to process what is happening. Apisteō apo tēs charàs — disbelieving from joy, overcome by the very emotion the good news produces. Luke names this as a recognisable human state: there is a kind of joy so complete that it prevents belief precisely because the thing being believed is too good.

notes.original: en tō nomō Mōseōs kai tois prophētais kai psalmois
notes.rendering: the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms
notes.why: The threefold division of the Hebrew canon — Torah, Prophets, Writings (here represented by the Psalms, the first and most important book of the Writings) — is the most comprehensive formula Luke could use for ‘the entire Scripture.’ The risen Jesus declares that all three divisions of the Hebrew Bible must be fulfilled in him. The resurrection is not a surprise ending; it is the conclusion the entire scriptural narrative has been moving toward.

notes.original: dienōixen autōn ton noun
notes.rendering: he opens their minds
notes.why: Dianoigo means to open thoroughly, to open wide — the same verb used of the tomb being opened (24:2), of the scriptures being opened on the Emmaus road, and of Lydia’s heart being opened in Acts 16:14. The risen Jesus opens the disciples’ nous — their mind, their capacity to understand — to receive what the scriptures have been saying all along. Understanding is a gift, not an achievement. It is received, like the kingdom, like the breaking of bread, like the recognition at Emmaus.

notes.original: epàggelian tou patros mou
notes.rendering: the promise of my Father
notes.why: The promise — epàngelia — is the Holy Spirit, the fulfilment of the Father’s promised gift (see Acts 1:4–5, 2:33). Power from on high (ex hypsous) — from the heights, from heaven — is the Spirit’s gift descending. The disciples are told to wait in Jerusalem until this clothing (endysesthe — dressed in, enveloped in) with power arrives. The gospel ends with the disciples waiting for the next beginning.

notes.original: epàras tas cheiras autou eulogēsen autous
notes.rendering: lifting up his hands, he blesses them
notes.why: The priestly gesture of blessing with raised hands (Numbers 6:24–26, the Aaronic blessing) is Jesus’ final act. He leaves his disciples not with a command, not with a summary of doctrine, but with a blessing in the priestly posture. The last thing his hands do in Luke’s gospel is bless. Those hands that touched lepers and took children and broke bread and were shown to the disciples as proof of resurrection — they are raised in blessing at the end.

notes.original: diestē ap’ autōn kai anaphereto eis ton ouranon
notes.rendering: he parts from them and is carried up into heaven
notes.why: Diistemi means to stand apart, to separate, to depart. Anaphero means to carry up, to lift up — used in the LXX of offerings brought up to the altar, and here of the Son being carried up to the Father. The ascension is a passive construction: he is carried up, received into heaven. The departure is real and physical, as the appearance had been real and physical. But the blessing continues through the departure — he blesses them while being taken up, so that the last thing they receive from him is the blessing.

notes.original: hypestrepsan… meta charas megalēs… eulogountes ton theon
notes.rendering: return… with great joy… blessing God
notes.why: The gospel ends where it began: in the temple, with people blessing God. Zechariah was struck silent in the temple in chapter 1; the disciples are speaking — blessing God — in the temple in chapter 24. The journey from the silenced priest to the joyful community of witnesses is Luke’s full arc. The great joy (chara megalē) echoes the angel’s announcement to the shepherds (2:10: I bring you good news of great joy). The joy that was promised at the beginning has arrived at the end, and it is great.

outro: Note on the Emmaus road as the interpretive key to Luke 24: The Emmaus account (24:13–35) is the longest and most theologically developed resurrection appearance in any gospel. Its structure is a model for how the risen Jesus is known: through the opened scriptures and through the breaking of bread. Both modes of recognition are given to the disciples in the upper room (24:44–47 for the scriptures; the eating together in 24:41–43 for the meal). The church’s two central practices — the reading and interpretation of Scripture and the eucharistic breaking of bread — are established by Luke as the means by which the risen Jesus makes himself known to those who cannot see him face to face. The Emmaus disciples do not see the risen Jesus and then believe; they encounter him in the word and the bread and then see. Recognition comes through the practices, not before them.

Note on Luke’s ending and its connection to Acts: Luke 24 ends with the disciples in the temple, continually blessing God, waiting for the promise of the Spirit. Acts 1 begins with the same waiting, the same Jerusalem, the same promise. The two volumes are one continuous narrative. The ascension is the hinge: Luke 24:51 and Acts 1:9 describe the same event from slightly different angles. The joy at the end of the gospel is not the joy of completion but the joy of a beginning: the disciples are waiting for the next chapter, which is the story of the Spirit-powered mission to the ends of the earth. Luke’s gospel does not end; it opens into Acts.

notes.original: archē
notes.rendering: where it all begins
notes.why: Archē means beginning, origin, the first principle of a thing. Mark’s opening word echoes Genesis 1:1 in the LXX. He signals new creation from the first syllable.

notes.original: Hēsaïā tō prophētē
notes.rendering: the prophet Isaiah
notes.why: The attribution is to Isaiah alone, but the quotation is composite: Malachi 3:1 appears in v. 2, Isaiah 40:3 in v. 3. Mark attributes both to Isaiah because Isaiah is the dominant prophetic frame — the new exodus, the voice in the wilderness, the prepared way.

notes.original: aphesis hamartiōn
notes.rendering: release of sins
notes.why: Aphesis means release, liberation, the cancellation of a debt or bondage. The word carries the Jubilee resonance of prisoners set free. John’s baptism announces liberation.

notes.original: hikanos
notes.rendering: not fit
notes.why: Hikanos means sufficient, adequate, up to the task. Untying sandals was slave’s work. John says he is not sufficient even for the lowliest service to the one coming after him.

notes.original: en pneumati hagiō
notes.rendering: in the Holy Spirit
notes.why: The phrase is anarthrous — no article. Literally: in holy spirit, in the raw pneumatic power of the divine breath. The lack of the article presents the Spirit as elemental power, like wind and fire.

notes.original: schizomenous tous ouranous
notes.rendering: the heavens are ripped open
notes.why: Schizō is a violent verb — to split, to tear apart. Not opened as a door opens. Mark uses this verb again at 15:38 for the tearing of the temple curtain at Jesus’ death. These are the only two uses of schizō in Mark. The two moments frame the entire gospel.

notes.original: su ei ho huios mou ho agapētos
notes.rendering: You are my Son — the Beloved
notes.why: The pronoun su is emphatic: you, specifically you, this one. The voice addresses Jesus directly and personally. At the Transfiguration (9:7) the voice shifts to third person. Here it speaks to him. The distinction is deliberate and tender.

notes.original: eudokēsa
notes.rendering: I delight
notes.why: Eudokeō means to be well pleased, to set one’s good favor on. The aorist may point to a moment of divine choice or function as a statement of the Father’s abiding relation to the Son.

notes.original: ekballei auton
notes.rendering: drives him out
notes.why: Ekballō is the same verb Mark uses throughout for casting out demons. The Spirit does not lead Jesus gently — it thrusts him out. The Spirit does to Jesus what Jesus will do to unclean spirits.

notes.original: meta tōn thēriōn
notes.rendering: with the wild animals
notes.why: Mark alone mentions the wild animals. In Isaiah 11:6–9 and 65:25 the messianic age is described in terms of harmony between wild animals and the redeemed. The enmity of Genesis 3:15 is already being reversed.

notes.original: paradothēnai
notes.rendering: handed over
notes.why: Paradidōmi — to hand over, to deliver up — is the shadow-word of Mark’s gospel. John is handed over to prison here; Jesus will be handed over in the passion. Mark plants the word early. The shape of John’s story is the shape of Jesus’ story.

notes.original: peplērōtai ho kairos
notes.rendering: the moment has come
notes.why: Peplērōtai is a perfect passive — the moment has been filled up, brought to its full measure, and remains in that state. Kairos is not clock time (chronos) but the appointed season, the ripened moment.

notes.original: ēggiken hē basileia tou theou
notes.rendering: drawn near — and it’s staying near
notes.why: Eggizō in the perfect tense: has drawn near and remains in proximity. The kingdom is not approaching — it has arrived at nearness and holds its position.

notes.original: aphēken autēn ho pyretos
notes.rendering: the fever releases her
notes.why: Aphiēmi — the release-word used for sins throughout the gospel. The fever releases her as sin releases its captive when forgiven.

notes.original: opsia…ote edū ho hēlios
notes.rendering: when evening comes — when the sun sets
notes.why: A double time marker. The Sabbath ended at sundown. The whole city has been waiting since the synagogue scene and comes the moment it ends.

notes.original: ennychon lian
notes.rendering: while it is still deep dark
notes.why: Together they indicate something more intense than “early morning” — Jesus goes out while it is still thoroughly, deeply dark. The contrast with the city full of need makes the withdrawal more striking.

notes.original: katedíōxen
notes.rendering: hunted for him
notes.why: Katadiōkō means to pursue intently, to hunt down. Simon does not look; he hunts. He can only be found in the place of prayer.

notes.original: splagchnistheis / orgistheis
notes.rendering: moved in his very gut
notes.why: The most significant textual variant in Mark. The majority of manuscripts read splagchnistheis — moved with visceral compassion from the intestines. But ancient witnesses including Codex Bezae read orgistheis — he was angry. The principle of the harder reading applies. The translation follows the majority text; the note preserves the question.

notes.original: embrimēsamenos
notes.rendering: warning him sternly
notes.why: Embrimaomai means to snort with intensity — used in classical literature for warhorses. It indicates barely contained feeling expressed through a guttural charge.

notes.original: mēdeni mēden eipēs
notes.rendering: say nothing to anyone
notes.why: A double negative — the strongest possible Greek prohibition: to absolutely no one, nothing at all.

notes.original: kēryssein
notes.rendering: proclaim it
notes.why: Kēryssō is the herald’s word — the verb used for Jesus’ own proclamation of the good news (v. 14). The man begins doing what Jesus does: proclaiming. He has become, inadvertently, a herald.

notes.original: exoruxantes
notes.rendering: having dug through it
notes.why: Exoryssō means to dig out, to excavate — a violent, physical act. Mark’s roof is an earthen Palestinian roof of packed mud, clay, and thatch over wooden beams. They dig through it. The scene is physically chaotic.

notes.original: teknon
notes.rendering: Child
notes.why: Not huios — the formal word for son — but teknon, a term of intimate warmth: little child, dear one. Before anything else happens — before the healing, before the controversy — Jesus names the paralyzed man as his own.

notes.original: aphiontai…hamartiai
notes.rendering: your sins are released
notes.why: The present passive — they are being released, right now, by an action not the man’s own. This is not declaration of a past forgiveness but a release happening in the moment of speech.

notes.original: exousian…epi tēs gēs
notes.rendering: authority on earth
notes.why: The phrase is deliberately ambiguous in Greek. It can modify who has authority (the Son of Man has authority here on earth) or where release happens (release of sins on earth, not only in heaven). Both senses are present.

notes.original: telōnion
notes.rendering: tax booth
notes.why: The toll station — a fixed collection post at which tariffs were levied on goods passing through the region. Levi collects for Herod Antipas, not Rome directly, but the stigma is the same: collaboration, extraction, uncleanness by association with Gentile money.

notes.original: ēlthon kalein
notes.rendering: I did not come to call
notes.why: The aorist ēlthon points to the purpose of the incarnation itself — not just this meal, but the whole mission. The call is the vocation of the Messiah stated plainly over a dinner table.

notes.original: huioi tou nymphōnos
notes.rendering: wedding guests
notes.why: Literally: sons of the bridal chamber. A Semitic idiom for the close companions of the groom, those who organize and celebrate the wedding. They belong to the feast by their very identity.

notes.original: epirraptei…epiblema
notes.rendering: sews a patch
notes.why: The image is practical and domestic. Unshrunk cloth will contract with washing and tear the old garment further. The point is not that the old is bad but that the new and the old operate on incompatible principles.

notes.original: hodōn poiein
notes.rendering: to make their way
notes.why: Literally: to make a road. The disciples are not just walking but forging a path through the grain. The idiom suggests purposeful progress, perhaps even a slightly aggressive passage.

notes.original: dia ton anthrōpon
notes.rendering: for the sake of the human
notes.why: The Greek uses anthrōpos — the human being generically, not a specific person. The Sabbath was given as a gift to humanity, not as a test. Its telos is human flourishing, not compliance.

notes.original: xēran echōn tēn cheira
notes.rendering: a withered hand
notes.why: Xēros means dry, withered — the opposite of living and moist. The hand has lost its vital capacity. The word is clinical in its precision, and the healing will be equally precise.

notes.original: paretēroun
notes.rendering: watching him closely
notes.why: Paratēreō means to watch narrowly, to observe under surveillance. The imperfect tense: they kept watching him, continuously and intently. The synagogue has become a trap.

notes.original: egeire eis to meson
notes.rendering: Stand up in the middle
notes.why: Jesus does not heal quietly, in a corner. He calls the man to the center of the room. He refuses to be secretive about what he is doing or why.

notes.original: psychēn sōsai ē apokteinai
notes.rendering: to save a life — or to kill
notes.why: The binary is absolute: there is no neutral option. In the presence of a need that can be met, inaction is a choice. The Pharisees’ silence is their answer.

notes.original: met’ orgēs, syllypomenos epi tē pōrōsei
notes.rendering: with anger — grieved at the hardness
notes.why: Two emotions held simultaneously. Pōrōsis: the medical term for the callous that forms on a bone after repeated fracture. Their hearts are not merely stubborn — they have undergone a hardening process.

notes.original: meta tōn Hērōdianōn
notes.rendering: with the Herodians
notes.why: An unusual alliance. Pharisees were religious purists; Herodians were political collaborators. Their joining against Jesus signals that his ministry threatens both religious and political structures.

notes.original: ploiarion
notes.rendering: a small boat
notes.why: The diminutive — a little boat. Not a ship, but a small craft kept close to shore as a crowd-management tool. The detail is precise and eyewitness in texture.

notes.original: epipiptosin autō
notes.rendering: press in on him
notes.why: Epipíptō means to fall upon, to press against with force — almost violent in its urgency. The crowd does not wait in an orderly line. They surge.

notes.original: hous ēthelen autos
notes.rendering: those he himself wants
notes.why: The pronoun autos is emphatic: he himself, he specifically. These twelve did not apply or volunteer. He wanted them. The initiative is entirely his.

notes.original: hina ōsin met’ autou
notes.rendering: so that they might be with him
notes.why: The first and governing purpose of the appointment is not proclamation or exorcism but being with him. Presence comes before function throughout the gospel.

notes.original: hos kai paredōken auton
notes.rendering: who also handed him over
notes.why: Paradidōmi — the shadow-word again. Mark introduces Judas with this verb at the moment the Twelve are named. The betrayal is not an afterthought; it is written into the appointment itself.

notes.original: hoi par’ autou
notes.rendering: his own people
notes.why: Those belonging to him — most naturally his family, the same group that arrives in v. 31. The verb kratēsai — to seize — is used for arresting a criminal. They come to take him into custody.

notes.original: dēsē ton ischyron
notes.rendering: binds the strong man
notes.why: Deō means to tie, to bind. Jesus presents his exorcisms as acts of warfare — entering enemy territory, binding the strong man, plundering his house. The kingdom comes through combat.

notes.original: ouk echei aphesin eis ton aiōna
notes.rendering: does not have release into the age
notes.why: Aphesis — the liberation word — appears here in its negative form. It is not that God refuses to forgive; it is that the person who calls the Holy Spirit’s work demonic has placed themselves outside the frame of recognition within which release can be received.

notes.original: tous peri auton kyklō kathēmenous
notes.rendering: those sitting in a circle around him
notes.why: Kyklō — in a circle. His look takes in everyone before he speaks. What he is about to define as family is already physically arranged around him in the shape of belonging.

notes.original: to thelēma tou theou
notes.rendering: the will of God
notes.why: Thelēma — the deliberate, considered will of God. The family of Jesus is not defined by bloodline or ethnicity but by shared orientation toward the Father. The circle is open to anyone who enters it.

notes.original: idou
notes.rendering: Look
notes.why: Idou is an exclamation demanding attention — look, behold, fix your eyes on this. Jesus uses it to arrest the hearing before the story begins.

notes.original: ho echōn ōta akouein akouetō
notes.rendering: whoever has ears to hear — let them hear
notes.why: The saying assumes that having ears and hearing are two different things. Physical hearing is given; the hearing Jesus calls for is a disposition of the whole person toward the word.

notes.original: to mystērion
notes.rendering: the mystery
notes.why: Mark alone uses the singular: to mystērion, the mystery. Matthew and Luke have the plural. In Jewish usage mystērion refers to the hidden counsel of God that has now been disclosed to the insiders.

notes.original: hina blepontes blepōsin kai mē idōsin
notes.rendering: so that looking they may look and not see
notes.why: The hina — so that — is the word that has troubled interpreters for two thousand years. Mark’s version is harder than Matthew’s and Luke’s. The parables are not merely illustrations; they are a mode of judgment as well as revelation.

notes.original: aphethē autois
notes.rendering: be released
notes.why: Aphiēmi — the release word, the forgiveness word — appears here in its most unsettling form: lest they turn and be released. The word carries its full Jubilee weight even in this alarming application.

notes.original: proskairoí eisin
notes.rendering: they are temporary
notes.why: Proskairoi — for a season, for a fixed time only. Their faith is not shallow in depth of feeling but in duration. It has no root in eternity.

notes.original: hē apatē tou ploutou
notes.rendering: the seduction of wealth
notes.why: Apatē means deception, seduction — the power to mislead by making something appear to be what it is not. Wealth presents itself as the answer to every question. That is the lie.

notes.original: paradechontai
notes.rendering: receive
notes.why: Paradechomai means to receive alongside, to welcome in, to embrace. The good-soil hearers do not merely register the word — they welcome it as a guest and let it stay.

notes.original: Unique to Mark
notes.rendering: The only parable found only in Mark
notes.why: Of the approximately thirty parables in the Synoptic Gospels, this is the one Mark alone preserves. Its central emphasis is the hiddenness and inevitability of growth — the kingdom comes whether human beings understand it or not.

notes.original: ouk oiden autos
notes.rendering: he does not know
notes.why: The farmer’s ignorance is not incidental — it is the point. The growth of the kingdom does not depend on human understanding or effort. It proceeds by a power internal to the seed.

notes.original: automatē
notes.rendering: by itself
notes.why: Automatos — by itself, of its own accord, spontaneously. The root of the English automatic. The earth produces without human agency. So does the kingdom.

notes.original: hotan de paradoi ho karpos
notes.rendering: when the grain delivers itself up
notes.why: Paradidōmi — the passion word. John was handed over; Jesus will be handed over. And here the grain delivers itself up to the harvest. The handing-over is not only betrayal — it is also the final surrender that makes the harvest possible.

notes.original: lailaps megalē anemou
notes.rendering: a great squall of wind
notes.why: Lailaps is a specific meteorological term: a sudden violent downburst or whirlwind squall. The Sea of Galilee is notoriously subject to these. The disciples are experienced fishermen — this is not an ordinary storm.

notes.original: epi to proskephalāion
notes.rendering: on the cushion
notes.why: The proskephālaion was the leather headrest kept at the helmsman’s station in the stern. This is the kind of detail that comes from someone who was there.

notes.original: siōpa, pephiōso
notes.rendering: Silence. Be muzzled.
notes.why: Two commands. Siōpā — be silent. And pephiōso — be muzzled, stay muzzled. The same word used for the demon in 1:25. Jesus addresses the storm the way he addresses unclean spirits. The implication is not lost on the disciples.

notes.original: galēnē megalē
notes.rendering: a great calm
notes.why: Not simply calm — a great calm. The same adjective used for the great squall. The greatness of the storm is matched and exceeded by the greatness of the peace.

notes.original: tis ara houtos estin
notes.rendering: who then is this?
notes.why: Ara — therefore, in consequence of this. The question is structural: they have seen too much to ask it casually. It is the central question of the entire gospel.

notes.original: katakopton heauton lithois
notes.rendering: cutting himself with stones
notes.why: Katakoptō means to cut down, to slash. The man is not scratching himself; he is actively, repeatedly cutting himself. The picture of extreme torment is deliberate and unsparing.

notes.original: horkizō se ton theon
notes.rendering: I adjure you by God
notes.why: Horkizō means to put under oath, to bind by solemn adjuration. The demon uses against Jesus the very vocabulary of binding and release that runs through the gospel.

notes.original: Leōn onoma moi
notes.rendering: My name is Legion
notes.why: A Roman legion comprised approximately six thousand soldiers. The name is simultaneously a statement of quantity and an evocation of occupation. The man is colonized by a military force.

notes.original: sōphronoūnta
notes.rendering: in his right mind
notes.why: Sōphronēo means to be of sound mind — from sōs (safe, whole) and phrēn (mind). The man’s restoration is described as a wholeness of the self, not merely the absence of symptoms.

notes.original: hosa ho kyrios soi pepoiēken
notes.rendering: how much the Lord has done for you
notes.why: Jesus tells the man to report what the Lord — kyrios — has done. In v. 20, the man proclaims what Jesus has done. Mark quietly equates the two. The identification is implicit but unmistakable.

notes.original: eschatōs echei
notes.rendering: at the point of death
notes.why: Eschatōs echei means to be in the last extremity — from eschatos, the last. Jairus is saying his daughter has reached the final boundary. The word is precise and devastating.

notes.original: sōthēsomai
notes.rendering: I will be saved
notes.why: Sōzō — not merely healed but saved, the full word. The woman does not say she will be cured. She uses the word for final deliverance. Jesus confirms her usage in v. 34.

notes.original: pēgē tou haimatos
notes.rendering: source of her blood
notes.why: Pēgē means a spring, a source — the origin point of a flow. Mark uses this precise anatomical image: the source itself dries up, not just the symptom.

notes.original: tēn ex autou dynamin exerchousan
notes.rendering: power has gone out from him
notes.why: Jesus does not perform a healing; something leaves him. The power goes out from him — a present participle describing an event he experiences in his body before anyone tells him what has happened.

notes.original: thygatēr
notes.rendering: Daughter
notes.why: The only time in any of the four gospels that Jesus directly addresses a woman as daughter. The word confers belonging. She came as a stranger in the crowd; she leaves as family.

notes.original: Talitha koum
notes.rendering: Aramaic preserved
notes.why: Mark transliterates Jesus’ exact words into Greek characters and then provides a translation. These are the sounds Jesus made. The intimacy of the Aramaic — talitha is a term of endearment for a young girl — is preserved by the act of transcription.

notes.original: dothēnai autē phagein
notes.rendering: give her something to eat
notes.why: After the Aramaic, after the astonishment, after the command to silence — give her something to eat. The practical tenderness of this instruction is characteristic of Mark’s Jesus. Resurrection requires feeding.

notes.original: ho tektōn
notes.rendering: the craftsman
notes.why: Tektōn refers to a craftsman who works in wood and stone — a builder, joiner, or carpenter in the broadest ancient sense. The word identifies Jesus by his trade. In Nazareth, they think they already know him.

notes.original: eskandalizonto en autō
notes.rendering: they are tripped up by him
notes.why: Skandalizō — the trap word. The congregation at Nazareth have caught their foot on him. The familiarity that should produce recognition produces offense instead.

notes.original: ouk edynato ekei…dynamin
notes.rendering: he is not able
notes.why: Mark uses the unqualified word: he could not. Matthew softens this. Mark does not. The connection between faith and the possibility of healing is stated plainly and without apology.

notes.original: ethaumazen
notes.rendering: he marvels
notes.why: Thaumazō — the marvel-word, used of the crowds throughout the gospel in response to Jesus. Here it is used of Jesus himself, in response to the crowd. The reversal is striking.

notes.original: eneichen autō hē Hērōdias
notes.rendering: Herodias had it in for him
notes.why: Enechō means to hold against someone, to have a grievance lodged inside oneself. Herodias carries a sustained, internal hostility. It is not a passing anger but a permanent posture.

notes.original: syn etērei auton
notes.rendering: kept him safe
notes.why: Syntēreō means to keep together, to preserve, to protect. Herod is John’s captor and simultaneously his protector. The moral incoherence of the man is on full display.

notes.original: perilypos
notes.rendering: deeply grieved
notes.why: Perilypos means surrounded by grief. Mark uses this word only twice: here for Herod at the banquet, and in 14:34 for Jesus in Gethsemane. The verbal echo is deliberate.

notes.original: esplagchnisthē
notes.rendering: his heart breaks for them
notes.why: Splagchnizomai — the gut-word — appears for the third time in Mark. The compassion is never merely felt; in Mark it always produces action. Here it produces teaching; later it will produce feeding.

notes.original: hōs probata mē echonta poimena
notes.rendering: like sheep without a shepherd
notes.why: Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34: God indicts the false shepherds of Israel and promises to come himself and shepherd his people. Mark applies the image to Jesus without comment.

notes.original: eulogēsen kai kateklasen
notes.rendering: blesses and breaks
notes.why: The eucharistic sequence — takes, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, gives — appears here as it will at the Last Supper. The feeding in the wilderness anticipates the table in the upper room.

notes.original: ēthelen parelthein autous
notes.rendering: he intends to pass by them
notes.why: Parerchesthai — to pass by — carries specific weight in the Hebrew scriptures. When God passes by Moses in Exodus 33–34, and by Elijah in 1 Kings 19, it is a theophanic act. Jesus’ passing-by is of the same order.

notes.original: egō eimi
notes.rendering: it is I
notes.why: Literally: I am. The same construction as the divine self-declaration in Exodus 3:14. Mark places egō eimi on the lips of Jesus walking on water in a storm, and the disciples miss the reference entirely.

notes.original: pepōrōmenē ēn hē kardia autōn
notes.rendering: their hearts were hardened
notes.why: Pōrōō — the medical callous-word. Mark used this in 3:5 for the Pharisees. Now he uses it for the disciples. The disciples are not immune to the hardening that afflicts the opponents of Jesus.

notes.original: pygmē
notes.rendering: with the fist
notes.why: Pygmē literally means fist, clenched hand. It is a hapax legomenon — found nowhere else in the New Testament. It describes a particular manner of hand-washing, perhaps rubbing one fist against the other.

notes.original: akyrountes ton logon tou theou
notes.rendering: nullifying the word of God
notes.why: Akyroō is the legal term for invalidating a contract or abrogating a legally binding agreement. The tradition does not merely supplement the word of God; it legally overrides it.

notes.original: koinōsai
notes.rendering: defile
notes.why: Koinoō means to make common, to render profane. Jesus is relocating the boundary: not at the surface of the body but at the center of the will.

notes.original: katharizōn panta ta brōmata
notes.rendering: declaring all foods clean
notes.why: This is Mark’s own editorial intrusion — a parenthetical comment in the narrator’s voice. Mark steps in and draws out the implication that the original audience apparently needed stated.

notes.original: prōton
notes.rendering: first
notes.why: The single word that opens the space for everything that follows. Let the children first be satisfied. If there is a first, there is a second. The woman hears the word that matters.

notes.original: ta kynaria
notes.rendering: the little dogs
notes.why: The diminutive of kyōn — a term of contempt used for Gentiles. The woman does not flinch. She takes the metaphor on its own terms and turns it. Her response is neither offense nor submission but wit.

notes.original: dia touton ton logon
notes.rendering: because of this word
notes.why: Not because of her persistence alone, not because of her faith alone — Mark does not use the word pistis here. It is the word she has spoken. Her argument has prevailed.

notes.original: mogilalon
notes.rendering: speaks with difficulty
notes.why: Mogilalos is one of the rarest words in the New Testament — found here and in one other place: Isaiah 35:6, where the tongue of the mute will sing for joy in the age of salvation.

notes.original: anastenaxas
notes.rendering: sighs deeply
notes.why: Anastenazō — to groan upward, to sigh from the depths. The word occurs only here in the New Testament. The groan precedes the healing. It is not explained.

notes.original: Ephphatha
notes.rendering: Aramaic preserved
notes.why: As in 5:41 (Talitha koum), Mark transliterates Jesus’ exact words. These are the sounds that came out of his mouth. The intimacy of Aramaic is preserved as a mark of authenticity.

notes.original: hyperperissōs
notes.rendering: beyond all measure
notes.why: A compound superlative found nowhere else in the New Testament. Hyper — beyond — combined with perissōs — exceedingly. Mark runs out of normal superlatives.

notes.original: kalos panta pepoiēken
notes.rendering: he has done all things well
notes.why: The perfect tense: has done, and the doing stands. And kalos — well, beautifully, rightly. This is the language of Genesis 1, where God sees that what he has made is good.

notes.original: spyridon
notes.rendering: baskets” (spyris)
notes.why: The basket word here is spyris — a large rope or wicker basket, used for carrying heavy loads. In the feeding of the five thousand, kophinos was used — a smaller Jewish traveling basket. The different baskets may signal the different ethnic settings of the two feedings.

notes.original: anastenaxas tō pneumati
notes.rendering: sighing deeply in his spirit
notes.why: The sigh is located: in his spirit, in himself. The word group appears only twice in Mark — the deaf man’s healing (7:34) and here. There, healing follows. Here, refusal follows. The same depth of feeling produces opposite responses to opposite situations.

notes.original: ei dothēsetai…sēmeion
