notes.rendering: no sign will be given
notes.why: The Greek is an oath form — a conditional without an apodosis, which in Hebrew idiom means the consequence is too severe to state. It functions as an absolute refusal underwritten by divine oath.

notes.original: pepōrōmenēn echete tēn kardian
notes.rendering: do you have hardened hearts?
notes.why: Pepōrōmenēn — the medical callous-word, appearing for the third time in Mark (3:5; 6:52; here). The disciples’ hardness is now named directly. The blindness about to be healed in vv. 22–26 is their blindness.

notes.original: dōdeka / hepta
notes.rendering: twelve / seven
notes.why: Twelve and seven. The disciples remember the numbers but do not yet understand what the numbers mean. Twelve: the tribes of Israel. Seven: the fullness of the Gentile mission. The two feedings are not repetition; they are two halves of one proclamation.

notes.original: hōs dendra horō peripatountas
notes.rendering: I see them as trees, walking
notes.why: The most precise description of partial sight in any ancient text. He can tell they are people because they are walking. But they look like trees. The detail is clinical, specific, and irreducible to symbol.

notes.original: dieblepsen
notes.rendering: looks intently
notes.why: Diablepō — to look through, to look clearly, to see all the way. The result is entelōs hapanta — clearly, everything. The two-stage healing is not a failure; it is the shape of restoration.

notes.original: en tē hodō
notes.rendering: on the road
notes.why: The confession happens on the road — not in a synagogue, not in a house. En tē hodō: in the way, traveling. From here to the passion, they are always on the road.

notes.original: sy ei ho Christos
notes.rendering: You are the Messiah
notes.why: Mark’s version of the confession is the most stripped of the three Synoptics. Nothing added. No blessing follows. And immediately the charge to silence. The answer is right, but the understanding behind it is not yet adequate.

notes.original: dei ton Huion tou anthrōpou
notes.rendering: the Son of Man must
notes.why: Dei — it is necessary, the word of divine compulsion. The suffering is not an accident. It is the plan. The dei of God runs through the passion narrative as a kind of grammar.

notes.original: parrēsia ton logon elalei
notes.rendering: speaks this word openly
notes.why: Parrēsia means openness, boldness, frank speech. After chapters of parables and commands to silence — here, for the first time, he says plainly what is coming. Peter cannot receive it.

notes.original: hypage opisō mou, Satana
notes.rendering: Get behind me, Satan
notes.why: Opisō mou — behind me, after me — the exact phrase of the call to discipleship in 1:17. Peter is being sent back to his proper position: not in front, setting the agenda, but behind, following.

notes.original: aparnēsasthō heauton
notes.rendering: deny themselves
notes.why: Aparneomai — to deny, to disown. The same verb used for Peter’s three denials in 14:30–72. The disciple is called to do to themselves what Peter will do to Jesus. The irony is structural.

notes.original: elēlythyëan en dynamei
notes.rendering: having come in power
notes.why: The perfect participle elēlythyëan — having come, standing arrived. En dynamei — in power — distinguishes this from other manifestations of the kingdom. What some present will see is the kingdom not merely announced but demonstrated with power.

notes.original: metemorphōthē
notes.rendering: he is transfigured
notes.why: Metamorphoō — to be transformed in form from the inside out. The change is a disclosure of what is already the case. The glory is not added to Jesus; it is revealed from within him.

notes.original: episkiazousa
notes.rendering: overshadowing
notes.why: Episkiazō — used in the LXX for the glory-cloud settling on the Tabernacle (Exodus 40:35). The cloud is the Shekinah. The Transfiguration is a Tabernacle event.

notes.original: akouete autou
notes.rendering: Listen to him
notes.why: Two words — the entire content of the voice from the cloud. The Transfiguration ends not with a blessing but with a command. The disciples are to be students of what he will now teach them about the road to Jerusalem.

notes.original: pisteuō, boēthei mou tē apistia
notes.rendering: I believe — help my unbelief!
notes.why: The cry arrives without deliberation. The father says what is true: both things at once. The simultaneous presence of faith and its absence is not hypocrisy — it is the condition of every honest believer.

notes.original: en proseuche
notes.rendering: except prayer
notes.why: Prayer is not a method or technique. It is the orientation of total dependence on the source of power. The disciples’ failure is a failure of orientation, not of effort.

notes.original: paradidotai
notes.rendering: is being handed over
notes.why: Present passive — not will be handed over, but is being handed over, right now, in the ongoing purpose of God. The handing-over is not a future event Jesus dreads; it is a present reality he inhabits.

notes.original: hē skōlēx…kai to pyr
notes.rendering: their worm…the fire
notes.why: An echo of Isaiah 66:24 — the final verse of Isaiah, describing the fate of the rebellious. Mark’s Jesus quotes the darkest eschatological image in the Hebrew prophets without softening.

notes.original: emblepas autō ēgapēsen auton
notes.rendering: looking at him, Jesus loves him
notes.why: Emblepō — to look directly at, to look into. And then: ēgapēsen — loved him. This is the only place in Mark where Jesus is explicitly said to love an individual he encounters. The love precedes the demand.

notes.original: proagōn autous ho Iēsous
notes.rendering: Jesus is going ahead of them
notes.why: Proagō — to go before, to lead the way. Jesus is out ahead of the group, walking toward Jerusalem while they follow in fear. The image is of a general leading troops into battle they do not yet understand.

notes.original: lytron anti pollōn
notes.rendering: a ransom for many
notes.why: Lytron means a ransom — the price paid to release a prisoner. Anti pollōn — in place of many, as the substitution price. This is the only explicit statement of atonement theology in Mark, and it comes as the climax of the servant-greatness teaching.

notes.original: apobalōn to himation autou
notes.rendering: throwing off his cloak
notes.why: The himation was the outer garment — a large cloak used as wrap by day and blanket by night, the beggar’s only real possession. He throws it away before he even reaches Jesus. The gesture is total.

notes.original: Rabbouni
notes.rendering: Aramaic preserved
notes.why: Rabbouni — my great teacher, my master — is a more intimate and elevated form than the simple Rabbi. It is the word Mary Magdalene uses in John 20:16 at the resurrection. Bartimaeus reaches for the highest title he knows.

notes.original: ēkolouthei autō en tē hodō
notes.rendering: he follows him on the road
notes.why: En tē hodō — on the road. The final verse before Jerusalem. The blind man who now sees is the last figure Mark shows us following Jesus. He is the model disciple: healed, called, and on the road.

notes.original: periblepsámenos panta
notes.rendering: looking around at everything
notes.why: Periblepō — the searching, circular look Jesus uses at decisive moments. He enters the temple and looks at everything. He is making an inventory. He will return the next day with a verdict.

notes.original: ērxato ekballein
notes.rendering: begins to drive out
notes.why: Ekballō — the exorcism word. Jesus drives out the sellers and buyers with the same verb used for driving out demons. The temple has become a place requiring exorcism.

notes.original: pasin tois ethnesin
notes.rendering: for all the nations
notes.why: The Isaiah quotation in its full form — which Mark alone preserves — includes pasin tois ethnesin: for all the nations. The court that has been commercialized was the court of the Gentiles, the only space in the temple complex where non-Jews could pray.

notes.original: aphete
notes.rendering: release it
notes.why: Aphiēmi — the liberation word. Forgiveness and releasing debts are the same act in the vocabulary of the gospel. The prayer teaching is embedded in the language of Jubilee.

notes.original: ouk oidamen
notes.rendering: we do not know
notes.why: The most dishonest statement in the chapter. They know. They have calculated exactly what each answer means and chosen the only option that protects them. Jesus accepts their answer and closes the conversation.

notes.original: eikōna kai epigraphēn
notes.rendering: image and inscription
notes.why: Eikōn means image, likeness — the word used in Genesis 1:26 LXX for humanity made in the image of God. What bears the image of God belongs to God. Jesus’ answer encompasses both politics and theology in a single word.

notes.original: pantes autō zōsin
notes.rendering: all are alive to him
notes.why: All — pantes — are alive to God. The phrase to him (autō) is the key: from God’s perspective, in God’s present, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are living. Death is not the final category in the grammar of God.

notes.original: ho polys ochlos ēkouen autou hēdeōs
notes.rendering: the large crowd hears him gladly
notes.why: Hēdeōs — gladly, with pleasure. The same word used in 6:20 for Herod hearing John gladly. Both Herod and the crowd hear with pleasure and without transformation. Gladness is not the same as obedience.

notes.original: lepta dyo, ho estin kodrantēs
notes.rendering: two lepta — which is a quadrans
notes.why: Mark translates for his Roman audience: two lepta (the smallest Jewish coin) equals one quadrans (the smallest Roman coin). The translation is Mark’s own explanation, confirming the Roman provenance of his gospel.

notes.original: holon ton bion autēs
notes.rendering: her whole livelihood
notes.why: Bios — life, livelihood, the means by which life is sustained. She has put in everything that stood between her and destitution. The word bios carries more weight than “money.” She has given her life.

notes.original: blepete mē tis hymas planēsē
notes.rendering: see to it that no one leads you astray
notes.why: Blepete — the watching word, making its first appearance in the discourse. It will appear four more times (vv. 9, 23, 33, 35). The entire chapter is organized around the command to watch.

notes.original: ho de hypomeinas eis telos
notes.rendering: the one who endures to the end
notes.why: Hypomonē — endurance, the capacity to remain under a heavy load without collapsing. Here it is given its goal: salvation. Endurance is not passive suffering; it is active, sustained faithfulness under pressure.

notes.original: to bdelygma tēs erēmōseōs
notes.rendering: the desolating sacrilege
notes.why: The phrase echoes Daniel 9:27, 11:31, 12:11. In Daniel it refers to the desecration of the temple by Antiochus IV in 167 BCE. Jesus applies it to a future desecration. Mark’s parenthetical — let the reader understand — is addressed to us.

notes.original: oude ho huios
notes.rendering: not even the Son
notes.why: The most theologically startling admission in Mark. The Son does not know the day or the hour. Only the Father knows. Mark does not soften this. The limitation of the Son’s knowledge is presented as fact.

notes.original: opsé ē mesonyktiou ē alektorophōnías ē prōi
notes.rendering: evening or midnight or the crowing of the rooster or morning
notes.why: The four watches of the Roman night. The passion narrative will be structured around exactly these four watches: the Last Supper (evening), Gethsemane (midnight), Peter’s denial (cockcrow), and the trial before Pilate (morning).

notes.original: grēgoreite
notes.rendering: Watch
notes.why: The word grēgoreite — Watch — is addressed to everyone who will ever read this gospel. The discourse ends by pulling the reader into the imperative. The command is for all.

notes.original: syntripsa sa tēn alabastron
notes.rendering: breaking the jar
notes.why: Syntribō — to break thoroughly, to shatter. She does not open the jar carefully and pour a measured amount. She breaks it entirely. The act is irreversible. Nothing is held back.

notes.original: kalon ergon
notes.rendering: a beautiful thing
notes.why: Kalon — beautiful, good, fine. The word of Genesis 1. What the woman does is placed in the vocabulary of creation. Jesus calls her act beautiful in the same register that God called creation good.

notes.original: eulogēsas eklasen
notes.rendering: blessing it he broke it
notes.why: The eucharistic sequence — takes, blesses, breaks, gives — for the final time in Mark. It appeared at both feedings in the wilderness. Now it appears in the upper room. The three scenes form a triptych.

notes.original: to haima mou tēs diathēkēs
notes.rendering: my blood of the covenant
notes.why: The blood of the covenant echoes Exodus 24:8, where Moses sprinkled the people with the blood of the sacrificial animals and said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant.’ Jesus identifies his own blood as the fulfillment of that act.

notes.original: Abba ho patēr
notes.rendering: Abba — Father
notes.why: Mark preserves the Aramaic Abba and then translates it. Abba is the intimate address of a child to its father — not formal address but the language of the family table. In the garden, facing the cross, this is what Jesus says.

notes.original: all’ ou ti egō thelō alla ti sy
notes.rendering: yet not what I want — but what you want
notes.why: Two wills named and placed in sequence. The conjunction all’ — but, yet — is the hinge. The prayer does not deny the reality of what Jesus wants; it places what God wants above it. The submission is genuine, not performed.

notes.original: Simon, katheudeis
notes.rendering: Simon — are you sleeping?
notes.why: The name is significant. Jesus does not say Peter — the rock-name. He says Simon — the name he had before the call. In the moment of failure, the old name returns. The gap between who Peter is called to be and who he is in this moment is contained in the single word.

notes.original: egō eimi
notes.rendering: I am
notes.why: The words Jesus used when walking on the water (6:50) — the echo of Exodus 3:14 — are now spoken in the highest court of the land, in response to the highest-stakes question. This is the only place in Mark where Jesus answers the Messianic question directly and without qualification.

notes.original: epibalōn eklaien
notes.rendering: he breaks down and wept
notes.why: The word suggests a body responding before the mind has finished processing: he breaks. Then he weeps. The moment is physical before it is emotional. Mark does not explain what Peter felt. He describes what his body did.

notes.original: allous esōsen, heauton ou dynatai sōsai
notes.rendering: he saved others — he cannot save himself
notes.why: The most theologically compressed statement in the crucifixion narrative, spoken in mockery. He cannot save himself precisely because he is saving others. The taunt is truer than those who speak it know.

notes.original: skotos egeneto eph’ holēn tēn gēn
notes.rendering: darkness falls over the whole land
notes.why: Egeneto — came into being. The same verb as ‘let there be light’ in Genesis 1 — and now its reversal. The darkness at the cross is a de-creation event. The sixth hour to the ninth hour: the hours of highest light become hours of darkness.

notes.original: Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani
notes.rendering: Aramaic preserved
notes.why: As with Talitha koum and Ephphatha, Mark preserves the Aramaic. This is Psalm 22:1. The cry is not a loss of faith; it is the prayer of Psalm 22, which ends in vindication. Jesus dies praying a psalm that the Father will answer.

notes.original: to katapetasma tou naou eschisthē eis dyo
notes.rendering: the curtain of the temple is torn in two
notes.why: Schizō — used only twice in Mark: at 1:10 when the heavens are ripped open at the baptism, and here at the death. The two schizō moments frame the gospel. What opened at the beginning is answered at the end.

notes.original: alēthōs houtos ho anthrōpos huios theou ēn
notes.rendering: Truly this man was the Son of God
notes.why: The confession that the whole gospel has been building toward since 1:1 is finally spoken by a human being, correctly — by a Roman soldier, a Gentile, at the moment of death. Not in the triumph of the Transfiguration but at the foot of the cross.

notes.original: ton estaurōmenon
notes.rendering: the crucified
notes.why: The title ton estaurōmenon — the crucified one — is carried forward into the announcement of resurrection. He does not shed the cross on the way to the empty tomb. The risen one is identified by his wounds.

notes.original: kai tō Petrō
notes.rendering: and Peter
notes.why: The specification of Peter — singled out by name — is one of the most tender details in the gospel. The last word about Peter before the resurrection is that he broke down and wept. The first word after it is: make sure Peter knows.

notes.original: proagei hymas eis tēn Galilaian
notes.rendering: he is going ahead of you into Galilee
notes.why: Proagō — to go before, to go ahead. The same word used in 10:32 when Jesus walks ahead of the disciples on the road to Jerusalem. He was ahead of them then; he is ahead of them now. The story continues.

notes.original: ephobounto gar
notes.rendering: for they are afraid
notes.why: The gospel ends with gar — for, because. A sentence ending with gar is grammatically irregular in Greek. Whether this is deliberate or accidental, the effect is the same: the story breaks off mid-sentence, leaving the fear and the empty tomb and the message undelivered — until the reader carries it forward.

notes.original: The Longer Ending
notes.rendering: Not in earliest manuscripts
notes.why: The Longer Ending is absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, the Sinaitic Syriac, and other early witnesses. Eusebius and Jerome note its absence from most manuscripts known to them. It draws on material from Matthew 28, Luke 24, and John 20. It is included here as part of the received canonical tradition, clearly marked as a secondary addition.

intro: Matthew 1 opens the Gospel with two of its most distinctive features: the genealogy and the birth narrative. Where Luke's genealogy goes backward from Jesus to Adam, Matthew's goes forward from Abraham to Jesus — tracing the royal and covenantal line. Where Luke's birth narrative centres on Mary, Matthew's centres on Joseph. Both chapters establish who Jesus is before the story begins.

notes.original: biblos geneseos Iēsou Christou huiou Dauid huiou Abraam
notes.rendering: the book of the origin of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham
notes.why: Biblos geneseos — book of origin, book of genesis, book of genealogy. The phrase appears only twice in the Greek Bible: here and in Genesis 5:1 (LXX: haute he biblos geneseos anthrōpōn — this is the book of the origin of human beings). Matthew opens his Gospel in the register of Genesis — this is a new genesis, a new beginning of the human story. Son of David — the royal lineage, the Messianic claim. Son of Abraham — the covenant lineage, the promise of blessing to all nations (Genesis 12:3). The two titles together place Jesus at the intersection of Israel's two greatest covenants: David's throne and Abraham's blessing.

notes.original: ek tes Thamar… ek tes Rhachab… ek tes Rhouth… ek tes tou Ouriou
notes.rendering: by Tamar… by Rahab… by Ruth… by the wife of Uriah
notes.why: Matthew includes four women in the genealogy — unusual in ancient Jewish genealogies, which traced through the male line. All four are in some way irregular: Tamar (Genesis 38) conceived by disguising herself as a prostitute; Rahab was a Canaanite prostitute; Ruth was a Moabite foreigner; Bathsheba ('the wife of Uriah') is named by her relationship to a man David had killed rather than by her own name. The pattern has been debated: they may signal Gentile inclusion (three of the four are non-Israelites), or divine grace working through irregular means, or the pattern of women through whom the messianic line was unexpectedly preserved. All four anticipate the greatest irregularity of all: the fifth woman in the lineage, Mary, through whom the Messiah is born without a human father.

notes.original: ex hes egennethe Iesous ho legomenos Christos
notes.rendering: from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ
notes.why: The genealogical formula throughout has been X egennesen Y — X fathered Y. At verse 16, the pattern breaks: Jacob fathered Joseph the husband of Mary, from whom (ex hes — feminine singular, referring to Mary alone) was born Jesus. The passive construction is deliberate: the genealogy has been tracing the line of fathering, and at the end the verb goes passive and the mother replaces the father as the agent. The break in the pattern is the break in the biological chain — announcing, without explanation, that something different has happened here.

notes.original: kaleseis to onoma autou Iēsoun, autos gar sōsei ton laon autou apo tōn hamartiōn autōn
notes.rendering: you shall call his name Jesus — for he will save his people from their sins
notes.why: Iēsous is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua (Joshua) — a name meaning YHWH saves, YHWH is salvation. The name is given with its explanation: the name is the mission. He will save (sōsei — from sōzō, the salvation word) his people from their sins. The Gospel that opens with a genealogy proving descent from David and Abraham ends with the Great Commission going to all nations (28:19) — the salvation that begins as 'his people' (Israel) expands to encompass the world. The name Jesus is the Gospel's first and most compressed theological claim.

notes.original: kalesousin to onoma autou Emmanouel, ho estin methermēneuomenon Meth' hēmōn ho theos
notes.rendering: they will call his name Emmanuel — which means, God with us
notes.why: Emmanuel (Immanuel, from Isaiah 7:14) — the name that bookends the Gospel. Matthew opens with Emmanuel (1:23: God with us) and closes with the promise of Jesus: 'I am with you always, to the end of the age' (28:20: ego meth' hymōn eimi). The Gospel is structurally held together by the presence of God: announced in the birth, fulfilled in the person, promised beyond the resurrection. The Emmanuel of chapter 1 becomes the 'I AM with you' of chapter 28. Matthew's Jesus is not merely a teacher or a Messiah-king; he is the abiding presence of God himself.

intro: Matthew 2 is structured around three fulfillment quotations — Micah 5:2 (Bethlehem), Hosea 11:1 (out of Egypt), and Jeremiah 31:15 (Rachel weeping). Together they narrate the birth of Jesus as the recapitulation of Israel's story: as Israel was called out of Egypt, as Bethlehem was the origin of David's line, as Rachel wept for the exiled children, so Jesus enacts and fulfils all three moments simultaneously. The chapter also introduces Matthew's pattern of divine communication through dreams — Joseph receives three dream-warnings in this chapter alone.

notes.original: magoi apo anatolōn… eidomen gar autou ton astera en te anatolē
notes.rendering: Magi from the east… we saw his star when it rose
notes.why: Magoi — Magi, wise men, astrologers-priests from the Persian or Babylonian tradition. Matthew does not say there are three (tradition added this from the three gifts); he does not say they are kings (a later tradition). He says only: Magi from the east (apo anatolōn — from the rising, from the east), who have seen a star en te anatolē (at its rising, in the east). The irony Matthew constructs in chapter 2 is precise: Gentiles from the east come to worship the King of the Jews, while Herod — the Jewish king — seeks to destroy him, and the Jewish religious leadership knows exactly where the Messiah should be born but does not go to find him.

notes.original: ex Aigyptou ekalesa ton huion mou
notes.rendering: out of Egypt I called my son
notes.why: The quotation is from Hosea 11:1 — where it refers to Israel being called out of Egypt in the Exodus. Matthew applies it to Jesus, not as a prediction of Jesus (Hosea was writing about Israel's history) but as typological fulfilment: Jesus recapitulates Israel's story. As Israel went down to Egypt and was called out, so Jesus goes down to Egypt as an infant and is called out. Jesus is the new Israel — embodying in his own life the history of the people he comes to represent and redeem. Matthew's use of Old Testament quotations is consistently typological rather than merely predictive: the past pattern is repeated and fulfilled at a deeper level in Jesus.

notes.original: tote Hērōdēs idōn hoti enepaichthē hypo tōn magōn ethumōthē lian
notes.rendering: when Herod sees that he has been outwitted by the Magi, he is in a furious rage
notes.why: Enepaichthē — he was mocked, outwitted, tricked (from empaizō — to play with, to mock). Ethumōthē lian — he was exceedingly angry, furious. Matthew's Herod is a figure of the Egyptian Pharaoh: a king threatened by the birth of Israel's deliverer who responds with the slaughter of infant boys. The parallel is structural and deliberate — as Moses escaped Pharaoh's infant slaughter (Exodus 1–2), so Jesus escapes Herod's. Matthew is narrating not merely the historical birth of Jesus but the new Exodus: the new Moses has arrived, and the new Pharaoh rages.

notes.original: Rhachel klaiōusa ta tekna autes, kai ouk ēthelen paraklēthenai, hoti ouk eisin
notes.rendering: Rachel weeping for her children… she refuses to be comforted, because they are no more
notes.why: The Jeremiah quotation (31:15) is the most haunting of Matthew's fulfillment citations. In Jeremiah's context, Rachel represents the northern tribes going into Babylonian exile — the matriarch of Joseph and Benjamin weeping at Ramah (a staging point for the deportation). Matthew applies it to the mothers of Bethlehem whose infant sons Herod has slaughtered. The connection is grief — the grief of mothers over lost children, whether to exile or to a tyrant's sword. Matthew does not explain away the suffering; he places it in the long tradition of Israel's grief that reaches back through exile to the patriarchs. The children die; the lament is real; and the one who escapes to Egypt will one day embody the answer to the lament.

intro: Matthew 3 introduces John the Baptist and narrates the baptism of Jesus. Matthew's account is shorter than Luke's but adds two elements absent from Mark: John's confrontation with the Pharisees and Sadducees (vv.7–12) and the brief exchange between John and Jesus about the propriety of the baptism (vv.14–15). Both additions are characteristic of Matthew's theological interests: the coming judgment and the fulfilment of all righteousness.

notes.original: metanoeite, engiken gar he basileia tōn ouranōn
notes.rendering: repent — for the kingdom of heaven is at hand!
notes.why: Metanoeite — repent, change your mind and direction, turn around. The same opening word as Jesus' own proclamation in 4:17: from that time Jesus began to preach and say, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.' John and Jesus begin with the same word. The kingdom of heaven (basileia tōn ouranōn) is Matthew's consistent circumlocution for 'kingdom of God' — using heaven (ouranōn) instead of God (theou) in the reverential Jewish manner that avoids using the divine name unnecessarily. Matthew uses it 32 times; Mark and Luke prefer 'kingdom of God.' Engiken — has come near, has drawn close, the perfect tense indicating completed action with present effect: the nearness is already accomplished.

notes.original: gennemata echidnōn, tis hypedeixen hymin phygein apo tes mellouses orges
notes.rendering: you brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
notes.why: Gennemata echidnōn — offspring of vipers, brood of snakes. The address is shocking — John does not moderate his language for the religious elite who have come to his baptism. The question — who warned you? — implies that they have not come out of genuine repentance but to perform the appearance of it, as if baptism were an insurance policy against divine judgment rather than a public declaration of changed life. Matthew includes both Pharisees and Sadducees together here (unusual, since they were rivals); they represent the entire religious establishment. John's confrontation with them in chapter 3 anticipates Jesus' even more sustained confrontation in chapter 23.

notes.original: houtōs gar prepon estin hēmin plērōsai pasan dikaiosynēn
notes.rendering: it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness
notes.why: Plērōsai pasan dikaiosynēn — to fulfil all righteousness. The phrase is uniquely Matthean and characteristically theological: where Mark and Luke simply narrate the baptism, Matthew pauses to explain why Jesus — who has no sin to repent of — submits to a baptism of repentance. The answer is given in the language of Matthew's central category: righteousness (dikaiosynē). Jesus' baptism is an act of solidarity — identifying with the sinners John has been baptising, taking the position of the one who needs what John offers, fulfilling the full range of what God requires. The 'us' is significant: both Jesus and John are included in the fulfilment.

notes.original: idou hoi ouranoi ēnoichthēsan… houtos estin ho huios mou ho agapētos en hō eudokēsa
notes.rendering: the heavens are opened… this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased
notes.why: Two differences from Mark's account: where Mark says the heavens were 'torn' (schizomenous — the violent word), Matthew uses the gentler ēnoichthēsan — were opened. And where Mark addresses Jesus directly ('you are my Son'), Matthew addresses the crowd ('this is my Son') — the baptism in Matthew is a public declaration, not merely a private commissioning. Eudokēsa — I am well pleased, I have delighted in, I have found good pleasure in. The word echoes Isaiah 42:1 (the first Servant Song): 'Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights.' The baptismal voice identifies Jesus as the Isaianic Servant — not only the royal Messiah (Son of David) and the covenantal heir (Son of Abraham) but the suffering Servant of Isaiah's vision.

outro: Note on Matthew 1–3 as the Gospel's opening movement: These three chapters establish who Jesus is (Son of David, Son of Abraham, Emmanuel, the Isaianic Servant) before he has spoken a word or performed a single act. The genealogy proves his lineage; the birth narrative proves his divine origin; the flight to Egypt proves his recapitulation of Israel's story; the Baptist's preaching frames the urgency of his arrival; the baptism declares his identity from heaven. Matthew front-loads the theology so that everything that follows — every teaching, every healing, every controversy — is heard in the light of what has already been declared. The reader knows who this is before the story begins; the characters in the story will spend the rest of the Gospel discovering it.

intro: Matthew 4 presents Jesus as the new Israel in the wilderness — the forty days echoing Israel's forty years. Where Israel failed each test (bread, testing God, idolatry), Jesus passes each one by quoting Deuteronomy. The pattern is deliberate: Jesus is reliving the wilderness story as the faithful son that Israel was called to be.

notes.original: Deut. 8:3, 6:16, 6:13 — all three temptation responses
notes.rendering: Three Deuteronomy quotations
notes.why: All three of Jesus' responses to the devil come from Deuteronomy — the book of Moses' wilderness speeches to Israel. Deuteronomy 8:3 (man does not live by bread alone) was spoken about Israel's hunger in the wilderness and the manna. Deuteronomy 6:16 (do not test the Lord) was spoken about Israel's testing at Massah. Deuteronomy 6:13 (worship the Lord alone) was the command against the golden calf and Canaanite idolatry. Jesus quotes the exact texts that Israel failed to embody. He is not merely defeating the devil; he is living what Israel could not. This is Matthew's new-Moses, new-Israel Christology at its most concentrated. The teaching language here is almost certainly Aramaic — these are Scripture-citation debates in the rabbinic tradition of the wilderness.

notes.original: metanoeite, engiken gar he basileia tōn ouranōn
notes.rendering: repent — for the kingdom of heaven is at hand!
notes.why: Identical to John's proclamation in 3:2 — word for word. Matthew places the same opening announcement on the lips of both the forerunner and the one who follows. The kingdom that John announced is arriving; the one who embodies it has now begun to preach it. Metanoeite — repent — is the Greek rendering of the Hebrew/Aramaic shuv or tuv: turn, return, change direction. In the tradition of Jesus' teaching, the call to repentance (teshuvah in Hebrew) is not primarily a call to feel sorry but a call to turn — to reorient the whole self toward God and the coming kingdom.

intro: Matthew 5 is the opening chapter of the Sermon on the Mount — the first and greatest of Matthew's five discourses. Jesus sits (the posture of a teacher, kathedra, from which our word 'cathedral'), opens his mouth (a solemn introductory formula), and delivers what amounts to a new Torah from the mountain. The Beatitudes are the preamble; the antitheses are the exposition. Both are almost certainly preserved from Aramaic teaching tradition, with significant Hebrew idiom throughout.

notes.original: hoi ptōchoi tō pneumati — likely Aramaic anawim
notes.rendering: the poor in spirit
notes.why: Ptōchoi tō pneumati — the poor in spirit. This is almost certainly a Greek rendering of a Hebrew/Aramaic expression. In the Hebrew Psalms and prophets, the anawim (the poor, the humble, the lowly) are those who have nothing to offer God except their need — they are the opposite of the self-sufficient. 'Poor in spirit' does not mean spiritually deficient; it means those who are genuinely empty before God, without pretension or self-reliance. The Psalms of the Anawim (34, 37, 69, 147) are the background. Isaiah 61:1 (which Jesus will quote in Luke 4:18) announces good news to the anawim. These are the first people Jesus pronounces blessed — and they are not the spiritually accomplished but the spiritually empty.

notes.original: hoi praeis — Aramaic miskene / Hebrew anawim
notes.rendering: the meek
notes.why: Praeis — meek, gentle, humble. The word does not mean weak or timid but controlled strength — the powerful person who chooses not to assert power. The background is Psalm 37:11: 'the meek (anawim) will inherit the land.' In the context of first-century Palestine under Roman occupation, the promise that the meek will inherit the earth (ten gen — the land/earth) carries enormous political resonance. The anawim will possess what the Romans think they own. Jesus is not promising pie-in-the-sky compensation; he is making a political-eschatological claim about who will be vindicated when the kingdom comes.

notes.original: Rhaka — Aramaic rēqā preserved raw
notes.rendering: Raca
notes.why: Rhaka — the Aramaic word preserved untranslated in the Greek text (rēqā — empty, worthless, hollow). It is an insult directed at a person's intelligence or worth: 'empty-head.' Only Matthew preserves this Aramaic term — one of the strongest signals in the Gospel that we are very close to the actual Aramaic words of Jesus. The progression in verse 22 moves from anger (judgment) to Raca (council) to 'fool' (Gehenna) — a graduated scale of contempt for persons that Jesus treats with graduated seriousness. The preservation of the Aramaic word Raca in the Greek text is almost certainly evidence that this saying was transmitted in Aramaic before it was translated, and that translators preserved the original word because they couldn't find an adequate Greek equivalent.

notes.original: ho ophthalmos sou ho dexios / he dexia sou cheir
notes.rendering: your right eye… your right hand
notes.why: The specification of the right eye and right hand reflects Semitic idiom in which 'right' signifies the more valued, more responsible member. In Hebrew and Aramaic culture, the right hand is the hand of power and covenant (oaths are sworn with the right hand); the right eye is the dominant eye. Jesus is not describing self-mutilation; he is using hyperbole in the Semitic wisdom tradition to make a point about radical moral priority. The hyperbole is recognisably a teaching device — the rabbis used similar forms. What is remarkable is that the offending member is the most valued one: not the left eye or the left hand but the right. The valued thing, if it becomes an occasion for sin, must go. The idiom almost certainly originates in Aramaic and is preserved somewhat woodenly in Greek.

notes.original: 'you shall hate your enemy' — not in Torah
notes.rendering: love your enemies
notes.why: The sixth antithesis pairs 'love your neighbour' (Leviticus 19:18, genuine Torah) with 'hate your enemy' — which is not in the Torah. Jesus appears to be quoting a popular interpretation or tradition that added the second clause to the first. The command to love enemies (agapate tous echthrous hymōn) is the most radical of the six antitheses and the most distinctively Jesus. It has no parallel in Jewish or Greco-Roman ethics at the same level of generality. The grounding he gives — God makes his sun rise on evil and good alike — is a theological argument from the character of the Father: as the Father is indiscriminate in his provision, so the children of the Father are to be indiscriminate in their love. The word agapate may be rendering the Aramaic achavu or rāchēm — the love that chooses an object regardless of its worthiness.

notes.original: teleios — Aramaic šālēm / Hebrew tamim
notes.rendering: perfect — as your heavenly Father is perfect
notes.why: Teleios — complete, whole, mature, fully formed. The word does not mean morally flawless in the modern perfectionist sense; it means whole, undivided, having integrity. The Aramaic or Hebrew background is šālēm (complete, whole — from which shalom) or tamim (blameless, complete — used of Noah in Genesis 6:9 and of the requirement for sacrificial animals). Be teleios as your heavenly Father is teleios: be whole as God is whole — undivided in love, consistent in generosity, complete in your treatment of all people without the partial love that loves only those who love back. Luke's parallel (6:36) uses 'merciful' instead of 'perfect': be merciful as your Father is merciful — which may be closer to the Aramaic original (rachamana, merciful one, is one of the Aramaic names for God).

intro: Matthew 6 is the practical heart of the Sermon on the Mount — three acts of Jewish piety (giving, prayer, fasting) radically reoriented away from public performance and toward the Father who sees in secret. The Lord's Prayer sits at the centre. Several verses in this chapter carry strong Hebrew and Aramaic idiom that the Greek preserves without explanation.

notes.original: ton arton hēmōn ton epiousion dos hēmin sēmeron — epiousios unique in Greek
notes.rendering: give us this day our daily bread
notes.why: Epiousios — the bread word — is one of the most debated terms in the New Testament. It appears only twice in the entire Greek corpus (Matthew 6:11 and Luke 11:3) — nowhere else in ancient Greek literature. Its meaning is genuinely uncertain. Three proposals: (1) bread for today, for this day (epi + ousia = for the day's substance); (2) bread for tomorrow, for the coming day (epi + iousa hemera = for the coming day); (3) the supersubstantial bread, the bread of the age to come (in the eucharistic reading of some early church fathers). Jerome, when he translated into Latin, rendered it as quotidianum (daily) in the Lord's Prayer and supersubstantialem (supersubstantial) in Matthew — acknowledging both possibilities. The very uniqueness of the word suggests it may be a coinage from an Aramaic original — a translator reaching for a Greek word for something that had no exact Greek equivalent.

notes.original: ta opheilēmata — Aramaic choba = both debt and sin
notes.rendering: forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors
notes.why: Opheilēmata — debts (not trespasses or sins — those are different Greek words). Luke's version uses hamartias (sins). Matthew's use of debts is almost certainly a more literal rendering of the Aramaic choba, which means both financial debt and moral obligation/sin. In Aramaic, the same word covers both concepts — a sin is a debt owed to God. This double meaning was natural in Aramaic but required a choice in Greek. Matthew chooses the more literal term (debts), Luke the more theological one (sins). The Aramaic background illuminates both: sin is understood as a debt that can be forgiven or released, and forgiveness is understood as debt-cancellation. The petition asks God to cancel our moral debts as we cancel what others owe us — a radical economic and spiritual claim.

notes.original: ho ophthalmos haplous / ponēros — Hebrew ayin tovah / ayin ra'ah
notes.rendering: if your eye is generous… if your eye is stingy
notes.why: This is perhaps the clearest example of Hebrew idiom preserved in Greek translation in the entire Sermon on the Mount. The Greek haplous (single, simple) and ponēros (evil, bad) make little obvious sense as descriptions of an eye — how can an eye be 'single' or 'evil'? But in Hebrew, the ayin tovah (good eye) and ayin ra'ah (evil eye) are well-established idioms for generosity and stinginess respectively. To have a good eye toward someone is to be generous toward them (Deuteronomy 15:9, Proverbs 22:9); to have an evil eye is to be stingy or greedy (Proverbs 23:6, 28:22). The Fireside Gospel renders haplous as 'generous' and ponēros as 'stingy' to make the idiom intelligible — returning the saying to the meaning it would have had in Jesus' Aramaic or Hebrew original. The verse is about money and generosity, not ophthalmology.

notes.original: Mamōna — Aramaic māmōnā preserved
notes.rendering: you cannot serve God and Mammon
notes.why: Mamōnas — another Aramaic word preserved raw in the Greek text, as Raca was in chapter 5. Māmōnā in Aramaic means wealth, property, money — but with a slightly different register than the neutral Greek chrēmata (wealth). It carries the connotation of money as an object of trust and reliance — wealth as a rival god, wealth as that in which one puts one's security. The very preservation of the Aramaic word (Matthew could have translated it) is itself a signal that this saying circulated in Aramaic before Greek and that the Aramaic term had a resonance translators chose not to lose. Jesus is not merely saying you cannot serve two employers; he is naming wealth as a spiritual power capable of becoming a master — a master that competes directly with the Father who provides daily bread.

notes.original: arketon te hemera he kakia autes — sufficient for the day is its evil
notes.rendering: sufficient for the day is its own trouble
notes.why: The final verse of the chapter has the rhythm and form of an Aramaic proverb — a pithy wisdom saying with the kind of compression that characterises Jesus' teaching. 'Its own evil' (he kakia autes) is rendered 'its own trouble' in the Fireside Gospel because in the context of the passage, kakia clearly means the hardships and difficulties of the day rather than moral evil. The saying is structurally similar to many Aramaic wisdom proverbs: short, balanced, slightly paradoxical. Don't borrow tomorrow's trouble; today has enough of its own. The whole anxiety passage (vv.25–34) has the cadence of Aramaic wisdom poetry — the repeated 'therefore do not be anxious,' the carefully balanced observations about birds and lilies, the rhetorical questions. This is teaching that was meant to be memorised, and it was almost certainly first memorised in Aramaic.

outro: Note on the Sermon on the Mount and Hebrew/Aramaic idiom: Matthew 5–7 contains the highest concentration of identifiable Aramaic and Hebrew idiom in any sustained passage of the New Testament. The Beatitudes, the antitheses, the Lord's Prayer, the eye passage, the Mammon saying, and the closing parable of the two builders all show signs of originating in Semitic speech — whether Aramaic or Hebrew — and being rendered into Greek with varying degrees of transparency. The Fireside Gospel's translator's notes flag these moments not to undermine the Greek text but to honour the teaching tradition behind it: these are the words of a Galilean rabbi who taught in Aramaic, whose teaching was preserved by communities that had to translate it, and whose idioms occasionally shine through the Greek like the original language asserting itself. To read the Sermon on the Mount with awareness of its Aramaic substrate is to hear it more fully, not less.

intro: Matthew 7 closes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of shorter sayings and a final extended parable. The chapter moves from judgment to discernment to persistence to the two ways to prophetic testing to the terrifying 'I never knew you' — and lands on the image of two builders. Jesus ends where he began: the one who hears and does is the one whose house stands.

notes.original: me krinete, hina me krithete — Hebrew / Aramaic din / dun
notes.rendering: do not judge — so that you may not be judged
notes.why: Krinete — judge. The Hebrew and Aramaic background is significant: the word din (to judge, to litigate, to render a verdict) is also the word for legal judgment and for the divine judgment of the last day. In the rabbinic tradition, the saying has a close parallel: 'Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place' (Mishnah Avot 2:4). Jesus radicalises it: not just 'judge carefully' but 'do not judge' — because the measure you use comes back to you. The saying is not a prohibition of all discernment (the same passage immediately asks us to recognise false prophets by their fruit), but a warning against the posture of judgment that fails to account for one's own standing before God.

notes.original: me dote to hagion tois kysin — possibly Aramaic wordplay lost in Greek
notes.rendering: do not give dogs what is holy
notes.why: This verse has long puzzled commentators because the pairing — holy things/dogs and pearls/pigs — seems asymmetrical. Some scholars have proposed that behind the Greek lies an Aramaic wordplay: in Aramaic, the word for 'holy thing' (qaddisha) and the word for 'earring/nose-ring' (qedasha) are close, which would give a tighter A-B / A-B structure: don't give an earring to dogs, don't throw a nose-ring before pigs — both being images of precious things wasted on those who cannot value them (cf. Proverbs 11:22: a beautiful woman without discretion is like a gold ring in a pig's snout). If so, the Greek has lost the wordplay in translation. Whatever the precise original, the saying uses strong Semitic hyperbole: holy things and pearls represent what is precious and sacred; pigs and dogs represent those who cannot receive it.

notes.original: houtos gar estin ho nomos kai hoi prophetai — cf. Hillel's summary
notes.rendering: this is the Law and the Prophets
notes.why: The Golden Rule in its positive form ('do to others what you wish they would do to you') is Jesus' summary of the entire Law and Prophets — the same phrase used in 5:17 when he said he came not to abolish but to fulfil them. This is almost certainly a deliberate bookend. The negative form of the rule ('do not do to others what you would not have them do to you') appears in Tobit 4:15, and the Talmud records that Rabbi Hillel gave the same negative summary to a Gentile enquirer: 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour — that is the whole Torah, and all the rest is commentary. Go and learn.' Jesus gives the positive form and places it at the summit of the Sermon. Both Hillel and Jesus are doing the same interpretive work: identifying the heart of Torah in a single principle of reciprocal regard.

notes.original: oudepote egnon hymas — Hebrew yada, intimate knowing
notes.rendering: I never knew you
notes.why: Egnon — I knew, from ginōskō. But in the Hebrew background, knowing (yada) is far more than intellectual recognition. To know someone in the Hebrew sense is to be in covenant relationship with them, to be intimately bound to them. When God says 'I know you by name' (Exodus 33:17) or 'before I formed you I knew you' (Jeremiah 1:5), the knowing is relational and elective. When Jesus says 'I never knew you,' he is not saying 'I was unaware of your existence' — he is saying 'you were never in relationship with me, never truly mine.' The prophesying, the exorcisms, the mighty works were done in his name without being done in his relationship. The name was used; the person was never known. This is the most terrifying sentence in the Sermon — and it hinges on a Hebrew word.

notes.original: pas oun hostis akouei… kai poiei — hearing and doing as a unit
notes.rendering: everyone who hears… and does them
notes.why: The concluding parable turns entirely on the contrast between hearing-and-doing and hearing-without-doing. In Hebrew, the word shema (hear) is not passive reception but active response — to hear is to obey, to take in and act upon. The Shema Israel ('Hear, O Israel') is not a call to listen but a call to take up a way of life. Jesus ends the Sermon with a parable that enacts this Hebrew understanding of hearing: the wise builder is not the one who processes the words intellectually but the one whose house is built on them. The storm tests not belief but foundation. Everything in the Sermon — the Beatitudes, the antitheses, the Lord's Prayer, the not-judging, the narrow gate — is the rock. The fool hears every word of it and builds on sand anyway.

intro: Matthew 8 is a chapter of ten miracles in rapid succession — healings, an exorcism, and a nature miracle — each one raising the question the disciples voice at the end of the storm scene: what kind of man is this? The chapter moves outward from Jewish Israel (the leper, Peter's mother-in-law) to the margins (the Gentile centurion, the country of the Gadarenes) — previewing the Gospel's arc toward all nations.

notes.original: ethaumasen… par' oudeni tosauten pistin en to Israel heuron
notes.rendering: he marvels… with no one in Israel have I found such faith
notes.why: Ethaumasen — he marvels, is astonished, wonders. The word is striking because the Gospels rarely record Jesus being amazed — usually it is others who marvel at him. Mark records only two instances of Jesus marveling: here (in Matthew's parallel) and at the unbelief of his hometown in Mark 6:6. What astonishes Jesus is not a miracle but a theological insight: the centurion understands the nature of authority — that words, properly backed by authority, accomplish things at a distance. He does not need Jesus physically present; he needs Jesus' word. This Gentile soldier understands something about the way Jesus' authority operates that the religious establishment has missed. The faith Jesus finds in a Roman officer what he has not found in Israel.

notes.original: hoi huioi tes basileias ekblethesontai eis to skotos to exōteron
notes.rendering: the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness
notes.why: Huioi tes basileias — sons of the kingdom: those who by birth and covenant should be first to enter. The phrase is a Hebrew idiom — 'son of X' meaning 'one who belongs to X, one characterised by X.' The reversal Jesus announces is radical: Gentiles from east and west recline at the patriarchal table while the covenant heirs are cast out. The outer darkness with its weeping and gnashing of teeth is Matthew's vivid image for exclusion from the messianic banquet. The warning in this context is pastoral, not ethnic — it is addressed to those following Jesus, who presumably know the covenant. Having the right lineage does not guarantee the seat. The centurion's faith does.

notes.original: ho huios tou anthrōpou — Aramaic bar enasha
notes.rendering: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head
notes.why: Ho huios tou anthrōpou — the Son of Man. This is almost certainly a direct rendering of the Aramaic bar enasha (or bar nash), which in ordinary Aramaic simply means 'a human being,' 'the man,' or 'someone.' Jesus uses it as his characteristic self-designation throughout the Synoptic Gospels — always in the third person, always in contexts that are either humble (foxes have holes, but the Son of Man has no home) or exalted (the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven, Daniel 7:13). The Aramaic ambiguity may be intentional: bar enasha can mean 'a human being' (humble register) while simultaneously evoking the Danielic figure (exalted register). Jesus' self-title is deliberately double-layered, and it only works fully in Aramaic. The Greek 'Son of Man' preserves the phrase but loses the idiomatic register.

notes.original: aphes tous nekrous thapsai tous heautōn nekrous
notes.rendering: leave the dead to bury their own dead
notes.why: One of the most radical and deliberately startling sayings of Jesus. Burying one's father was among the highest obligations in Jewish law — it superseded almost every other duty, including Torah study. The disciple's request (let me first go and bury my father) is entirely reasonable by Jewish standards. Jesus' response is a provocation: let the dead bury their own dead. In Aramaic, 'the dead' can refer both to the physically dead and to those who are spiritually dead — not alive to the kingdom. The double meaning is part of the saying's force: let those who are dead to the kingdom attend to the physically dead; you, follow me into life. The saying is not an attack on family duty but a declaration about the urgency and absoluteness of the kingdom call.

intro: Matthew 9 accelerates the narrative — healing, calling, controversy, and more healing tumble over each other in rapid succession. The chapter contains Matthew's own calling (verse 9, told with characteristic brevity), the first quotation of Hosea 6:6 ('I desire mercy and not sacrifice'), and the closing image of the harassed crowds that will motivate the mission discourse of chapter 10.

notes.original: kai legei autō, akolouthei moi. kai anastas ēkolouthēsen autō
notes.rendering: he says to him: 'Follow me.' And he rises and follows him.
notes.why: The calling of Matthew is told in two sentences — the most compressed of the four disciple-calls in Matthew (compare 4:18–22). The brevity is itself the point: Matthew, a tax collector (telōnēs — a collector of Roman taxes, despised as a collaborator and a cheat), is sitting at his toll booth and Jesus says follow me. Full stop. He rises and follows. No deliberation, no question, no farewell. The immediacy of the response is the narrative's declaration: the call of Jesus creates its own urgency. What is remarkable is that Matthew, alone among the evangelists, names himself and preserves his own disreputable profession without softening it. Luke calls the same man 'Levi'; Matthew calls himself by his Gospel name and identifies himself as what he was.

notes.original: eleos thelō kai ou thysian — Hosea 6:6, Hebrew chesed
notes.rendering: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice" — Hosea 6:6
notes.why: The quotation is from Hosea 6:6 — the first of two times Matthew quotes this verse (the second is 12:7). The Hebrew chesed (lovingkindness, covenant loyalty, mercy — translated eleos in the LXX) is one of the richest words in the Hebrew Bible. It describes the quality of God's character and the primary obligation of covenant life: loyal, faithful, steadfast love that shows itself in action. 'Mercy, not sacrifice' is a prophetic critique of religious performance that substitutes ritual for the relational quality God actually desires. Jesus quotes it here in defence of eating with sinners — and the application is precise: the mercy (chesed) he shows by sitting with tax collectors and sinners is exactly what Hosea's God desired over the clean observances of the Temple. Go and learn what this means is an invitation to reread Hosea.

notes.original: oinos neos eis askous kainous — new wine, new wineskins
notes.rendering: new wine is put into fresh wineskins
notes.why: The paired images of unshrunk cloth and new wine announce that what Jesus brings cannot be contained in the old structures. The Aramaic background is relevant here: the word translated 'new' in 'new wine' (neos — chronologically recent) and 'fresh' in 'fresh wineskins' (kainos — new in kind) are distinct in Greek but may both render the Aramaic chadath (new, fresh). The images are wisdom proverbs in form — compressed, concrete, memorable. Jesus is not rejecting the old but announcing that what he brings is so alive and expanding that it will burst whatever cannot grow with it. The wineskin that cannot expand destroys both itself and the wine. This is the Sermon on the Mount's 'I came not to abolish but to fulfil' translated into domestic economy.

notes.original: esplanchnisthē — Aramaic rachem / Hebrew rahamim
notes.rendering: he has compassion on them
notes.why: Esplanchnisthē — he was moved with compassion, from splagchna (the internal organs, the bowels, the gut). In Greek physiology the splagchna were the seat of deep emotion — what we might call 'gut-feeling.' But the word almost certainly renders the Aramaic rachem (compassion, from the root for womb — rechem) or the Hebrew rahamim (mercies, compassions — also from rechem). The compassion Jesus feels is visceral, physical, internal — not a distant benevolence but something that moves in him when he sees the harassed and helpless crowds. The word will appear again at key moments of healing throughout Matthew (14:14, 15:32, 20:34). Each time, the compassion precedes the action: he sees, he is moved in his gut, he acts. This sequence — seeing, being moved, responding — is the pattern of the incarnation itself.

notes.original: ho men therismos polys, hoi de ergatai oligoi
notes.rendering: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few
notes.why: The harvest image draws on the Hebrew prophetic tradition of the final ingathering — Joel 3:13, Isaiah 27:12, Jeremiah 51:33 — where the harvest of the last days is the gathering of God's people. Jesus looks at the harassed crowds and sees not a problem to manage but a harvest waiting to be gathered. The labourers (ergatai — workers, agricultural labourers) are to be prayed for, not recruited by human strategy: pray to the Lord of the harvest to send them out. The word for send out (ekbalē — to cast out, expel, thrust out) is forceful — the same word used for casting out demons. The Lord of the harvest does not gently invite workers; he thrusts them into the field. The harvest image connects to the mission discourse that begins immediately in chapter 10.

outro: Note on Matthew 7–9 as the authority movement: These three chapters demonstrate the authority that the crowd recognised in Jesus' teaching (7:29: he taught as one having authority) expressed across three registers — the authority of his words in the Sermon (chapters 5–7), the authority of his deeds in the miracles (chapter 8), and the authority to forgive sins and call sinners (chapter 9). The question 'what kind of man is this?' (8:27) is the question that drives all three chapters. Matthew's answer is given in the accumulation of the evidence, not in a single declaration: this is the kind of man whose words stand the storm and whose touch cleanses the untouchable and who eats with tax collectors because that is where the sick are.

intro: Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses — the Mission Discourse. Jesus sends the Twelve with authority, instructions for the road, and warnings about what reception they should expect. The discourse quickly outgrows its original setting (a mission within Israel) and addresses the post-resurrection mission of the church — the language of verse 18 (dragged before governors and kings) and verse 22 (hated by all for my name) anticipates the entire Gentile mission of Acts.

notes.original: phronimoi hōs hoi opheis kai akeraioi hōs hai peristerai
notes.rendering: shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves
notes.why: A paired wisdom saying in classic Semitic form — two comparisons, each carrying its own weight. Phronimoi (shrewd, prudent, wise in practical matters) echoes the serpent of Genesis 3:1 (arum in Hebrew — shrewd, clever), now rehabilitated as a quality disciples need rather than an attribute of the tempter. Akeraioi (unmixed, pure, innocent — literally 'without horn,' unadulterated) echoes the dove, the symbol of the Spirit (3:16) and of peace. The pairing is deliberately paradoxical: be as clever as the creature that deceived, as pure as the creature that descended at the baptism. In Aramaic proverbial form, such paradoxical pairings were common teaching devices — the student held both together rather than choosing between them.

notes.original: ouk elthon balein eirenen alla machairan — cf. Luke 12:51, diamerismon
notes.rendering: not peace but a sword
notes.why: Luke's parallel to this saying (12:51) has diamerismon — division — rather than machairan (sword). This divergence is one of the strongest arguments for an Aramaic original behind both: in Aramaic, the word pachda or machloqet (division, strife) could have been rendered by two different translators as 'sword' (Matthew, choosing the more vivid concrete term) and 'division' (Luke, choosing the more abstract sense). If Jesus spoke in Aramaic, his hearers heard a word that meant conflict, splitting apart — Matthew's sword and Luke's division are both attempts to render the same teaching. The quotation in verse 35–36 is from Micah 7:6, a text about family division in the last days — Jesus is applying an eschatological text to the immediate effects of his mission.

notes.original: ho heurōn ten psychen autou apolesei auten — the life/soul paradox
notes.rendering: whoever finds his life will lose it — and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it
notes.why: Psyche — life, soul. The paradox appears six times across the four Gospels in various forms — it is one of Jesus' most repeated sayings, suggesting it was a cornerstone of his teaching. In Aramaic, the word naphsha means both life (the biological fact of being alive) and self (the inner person, the ego). The paradox works at both levels: whoever clings to their biological life will lose it; whoever surrenders their self-definition to Jesus will find true selfhood. The saying is deliberately impossible to hold in one's head — it requires sitting with the tension. Holding both clauses simultaneously is itself the practice the saying recommends.

intro: Matthew 11 is one of the most theologically rich chapters in the Gospel — a chapter of questions (John's from prison, Jesus' about the crowds), a chapter of paradoxes (the greatest born of women is lesser than the least in the kingdom), and a chapter containing the two most extraordinary passages in Matthew: the Johannine thunderbolt (vv.25–27) and the yoke invitation (vv.28–30).

notes.original: ptōchoi euangelizontai — the anawim / Isaiah 61
notes.rendering: the poor have good news proclaimed to them
notes.why: Jesus' answer to John's question is a mosaic of Isaiah texts: 35:5–6 (blind see, deaf hear, lame walk), 26:19 (dead raised), and 61:1 (good news to the poor). The final item — the poor (ptōchoi, the Greek for the Hebrew anawim) have good news proclaimed to them — is placed last and climactically. In Luke 4:18, Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1 in the Nazareth synagogue and declares it fulfilled. Here he lists it as the capstone of messianic evidence. The anawim — the humble, the lowly, the economically and socially marginalised — are not an afterthought in the messianic agenda; they are its proof of authenticity. The one who is to come is recognised by who receives the good news.

notes.original: he basileia tōn ouranōn biazetai — one of the most debated sentences in the NT
notes.rendering: the kingdom of heaven has been forcing its way forward
notes.why: Biazetai — is pressing forward violently, is forcing its way, is being seized by force. This is one of the most debated verses in the entire New Testament. The verb biazetai is middle or passive — 'forces its way' or 'is being forced/seized.' Two main readings: (1) the kingdom is violently pressing forward (middle voice) — it is breaking through with force since the days of John; (2) the kingdom is being violently attacked/seized (passive voice) — it suffers violence from its opponents. The parallel biazomenoi (those who press in/seize) can mean either earnest seekers forcing their way in or violent opponents forcing their way against it. The Aramaic original probably had ithar (press forward) or a similar word that carried both senses. The Fireside Gospel renders it as the kingdom pressing forward, but holds the ambiguity in this note.

notes.original: edikaióthe he sophia apo tōn ergōn autes — Wisdom personified, Hebrew Hokhmah
notes.rendering: wisdom is vindicated by her deeds
notes.why: Sophia — Wisdom, feminine in Greek as in Hebrew (Hokhmah). The personification of Wisdom as a feminine figure who acts in the world and whose children reflect her character draws directly on Proverbs 8, Sirach 24, and Wisdom of Solomon 7–8. Jesus has just described himself and John as figures who cannot win with this generation — one too ascetic, one too social — and concludes that Wisdom is vindicated (literally justified, dikaiōthē) by what she produces. The children of Wisdom (Luke's version, 7:35) or her deeds (Matthew's version) prove her right. The personification of Wisdom in this context suggests Jesus is implicitly aligning himself with Wisdom — a move made more explicit in verses 25–30, where the invitation to take his yoke closely echoes Wisdom's invitation in Sirach 51:26.

notes.original: panta moi paredothē hypo tou patros mou — the Johannine thunderbolt
notes.rendering: all things have been handed over to me by my Father
notes.why: This passage has been called the 'Johannine Thunderbolt in the Synoptics' since the 19th century — because its theological register sounds almost exactly like John's Gospel (compare John 3:35, 10:15, 17:2). The mutual knowledge of Father and Son (oudeis epiginōskei ton huion ei me ho patēr — no one knows the Son except the Father, and vice versa) is John's theology of mutual indwelling in compressed Synoptic form. Its presence in Matthew (and Luke) suggests this theological tradition about Jesus predates John's Gospel and was not invented by the Fourth Evangelist. The saying almost certainly has an Aramaic original — the structure of 'no one... except' (oudeis... ei me) is a Semitic formula for exclusive relationship. This is the closest Matthew gets to Johannine Christology — and it is followed immediately by the yoke invitation, which is the practical consequence of who Jesus has just declared himself to be.

notes.original: deute pros me pantes hoi kopiōntes — the yoke of Torah, cf. Sirach 51:26
notes.rendering: come to me, all who are weary… take my yoke
notes.why: The yoke (zygos in Greek, ol in Hebrew/Aramaic) is a central image in Jewish wisdom and legal tradition. In rabbinic literature, the 'yoke of Torah' (ol Torah) is the obligation of observance — gladly taken on by the devout. Sirach 51:26 (150 BCE) uses almost identical language: 'put your neck under her yoke and let your soul receive instruction.' Jesus inverts the invitation: instead of Wisdom's yoke, take mine. The burden the scribes and Pharisees have loaded on the people (23:4: they tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear) is contrasted with Jesus' yoke, which is chrēstos (easy, kind, gracious — possibly a play on Christos, though the wordplay is clearer in Aramaic). The promise — anapausin tais psychais hymōn (rest for your souls) — quotes Jeremiah 6:16: 'Ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls.' Jesus is the ancient path, the good way — the fulfilment of what Jeremiah's invitation was pointing toward.

intro: Matthew 12 is the chapter of escalating conflict — two Sabbath controversies, the Beelzebul accusation, the demand for a sign, and the closing redefinition of family. It is also the chapter where Matthew quotes the longest of his fulfillment texts — the first Servant Song of Isaiah (42:1–4) — in its fullest form, making explicit that Jesus is the Servant Isaiah described.

notes.original: eleos thelō kai ou thysian — Hosea 6:6, second quotation
notes.rendering: I desire mercy and not sacrifice" — Hosea 6:6
notes.why: The second quotation of Hosea 6:6 in Matthew (the first was in 9:13). Both times it is quoted in defence of Jesus' table fellowship or Sabbath practice against Pharisaic criticism. Matthew's repeated use of this verse is deliberate — it is his interpretive key to these controversies. The Hebrew chesed (lovingkindness, covenant loyalty) that God desires over sacrifice is being embodied in Jesus' ministry: healing on the Sabbath is chesed; eating with sinners is chesed. The Pharisees who know the text (you would not have condemned the guiltless) are being shown that they do not understand what they are reading. Hosea's God who desires chesed over sacrifice is the same God Jesus is enacting — and they are opposing him in the name of the God who sent him.

notes.original: ephthasen eph' hymas he basileia tou theou — kingdom has arrived
notes.rendering: the kingdom of God has come upon you
notes.why: Ephthasen — has arrived, has come, has reached. The verb phthano in this form (aorist) indicates completed action: the kingdom has already come. This is Matthew's most explicit statement of realised eschatology — the kingdom is not merely approaching (engiken — is at hand) but has arrived (ephthasen). The exorcisms are the evidence: if Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit of God (and not by Beelzebul), then the strong man has already been bound, the plundering has already begun, and the kingdom is already present in the acts of liberation Jesus is performing. The Beelzebul controversy forces the question: whose power is at work here? And the answer — the Spirit of God — carries the conclusion that the age to come has broken into the present age.

notes.original: he tou pneumatos blasphemia ouk aphethesetai — the unforgivable sin
notes.rendering: blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven
notes.why: One of the most feared passages in the Gospels. The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (blasphemia tou pneumatos) that cannot be forgiven needs to be read in its context: Jesus has just been accused of casting out demons by the prince of demons (Beelzebul) when in fact he casts them out by the Spirit of God. To call the Spirit's work demonic — to so thoroughly invert good and evil that the Holy Spirit's activity is attributed to Satan — is to close off the very faculty by which one could recognise and receive forgiveness. It is not a particular sin that God is unwilling to forgive; it is a condition in which the possibility of recognising what needs forgiving has been destroyed. The unforgivable sin is the final refusal to see clearly. In the Aramaic tradition, this would be the sin of calling light darkness and darkness light — precisely what Isaiah 5:20 warns against.

notes.original: hōsper gar en Ionas en te koilia tou ketous treis hemeras kai treis nyktas
notes.rendering: just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish
notes.why: The sign of Jonah is Matthew's first explicit passion prediction embedded in typology. Jonah in the fish's belly for three days (Jonah 2:1) is the pattern for the Son of Man in the heart of the earth — the Hebrew lev ha'aretz (heart of the earth/land) being a vivid image for the tomb or Sheol. The Jonah typology is rich: Jonah preached repentance to Gentiles (Nineveh), was swallowed and then released, and his preaching produced the repentance that this generation is refusing. Something greater than Jonah is here — and they are demanding a sign from the one who is the sign. Luke's parallel (11:30) does not have the belly of the fish elaboration and simply says 'Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites' — suggesting Matthew's version has developed the typology more explicitly.

notes.original: ek gar tou perisseuatos tes kardias to stoma lalei
notes.rendering: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks
notes.why: Ek tou perisseuatos tes kardias — from the overflow, the surplus, the excess of the heart. The lev (heart) in Hebrew thought is not the seat of emotion but of thought, will, and intention — the whole inner person. The mouth speaks what the heart holds in surplus — it is not conscious choice but overflow that reveals character. The saying is in the tradition of Hebrew wisdom proverbs about the relationship between inner life and outer speech (Proverbs 4:23: above all else guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it). The application here is devastating: the Pharisees who accused Jesus of demonic power have revealed by that accusation what their hearts hold. The brood of vipers (gennemata echidnōn, the same phrase John used in 3:7) produce poison because they contain poison.

outro: Note on Matthew 10–12 as the conflict and revelation movement: These three chapters move between Jesus' sending out of the Twelve (chapter 10) and the escalating conflict with the religious establishment (chapters 11–12). The mission discourse ends with the promise that receiving the disciples is receiving Jesus. Chapter 11 records the puzzlement of John — the forerunner who wonders from prison whether he bet on the right one — and Jesus' answer that the blind see and the poor hear good news. Chapter 12 records the accusation that what they see is demonic. Between the Johannine thunderbolt (all things have been handed over to me) and the Beelzebul controversy (they said he casts out by the prince of demons) is the gap between what Jesus is and what his opponents see — and that gap is the defining drama of these chapters.

intro: Matthew 13 is the Parable Discourse — the longest sustained collection of parables in any Gospel, built around the central question of why Jesus teaches in parables at all. Eight parables in one chapter — the Sower, the Wheat and Weeds, the Mustard Seed, the Leaven, the Hidden Treasure, the Pearl, the Net, and the Trained Scribe — each one a different facet of the kingdom of heaven.

notes.original: en parabolais — Hebrew mashal / Aramaic mathla
notes.rendering: in parables
notes.why: Parabolē — parable, comparison, analogy. The Greek word translates the Hebrew mashal (proverb, parable, riddle, allegory, taunt-song) and the Aramaic mathla. The Hebrew mashal is a far broader category than the English 'parable' — it includes proverbs (Proverbs 1:1), allegories (Ezekiel 17), riddles (Judges 14:10–18), and extended comparisons. When Jesus speaks en parabolais, he is working in the tradition of the wisdom teachers and prophets who used indirect speech to engage the imagination before the intellect. The parable is not a simple illustration of a point already known; it is an invitation to discover something by the process of the comparison. The listener who hears does not simply receive information — they enact understanding by making the connection.

notes.original: ta mysteria tes basileias tōn ouranōn — Hebrew/Aramaic raz
notes.rendering: the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven
notes.why: Mysteria — mysteries, secrets. In the Greek world, mysteria referred to the secret teachings of the mystery religions, available only to initiates. But Jesus' use almost certainly renders the Hebrew or Aramaic raz (secret, mystery) — the word used in Daniel 2 for the secrets of God revealed to the wise. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, the rāzê 'ēl (mysteries of God) are the hidden purposes of God being disclosed to the community of the covenant. Jesus says these mysteries — God's hidden purposes now being enacted in the kingdom — have been given to the disciples to know. The parables are not obstacles to understanding; they are the appropriate form for mysteries that can only be received, not deduced.

notes.original: kokkō sinapeōs — 'smallest of all seeds' — rabbinic comparison
notes.rendering: the smallest of all seeds — but when grown, a tree
notes.why: The mustard seed (kokkos sinapeōs) was proverbial in Jewish tradition as the smallest measurable quantity — rabbis used it as the benchmark for the smallest volume in legal rulings (Mishnah Niddah 5:2: as small as a mustard seed). Jesus takes the familiar comparison and inverts it: the kingdom begins at the scale of what everyone agrees is negligibly small and grows to what everyone can see — a tree large enough for birds to nest in. The birds nesting in the branches echo Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12, where they represent nations finding shelter under a great kingdom. The eschatological overtones are deliberate: the kingdom that begins in obscurity becomes the sheltering tree of the nations.

notes.original: tria sata aleurou — three seahs, echoing Genesis 18:6
notes.rendering: three measures of flour
notes.why: Tria sata — three seahs (a seah is about seven litres). Three seahs of flour makes enough bread to feed well over a hundred people — this is not a household loaf but a feast quantity. The specific amount echoes Genesis 18:6, where Abraham tells Sarah to take three seahs of fine flour (shalosha se'im qemach solet) to make bread for the three visitors who bring the promise of Isaac. The quantity in the parable is not incidental detail; it places the kingdom's hidden working in the register of Abraham's hospitality — the founding act of covenantal welcome from which Israel's story flows. The leaven hidden in three seahs of flour is the kingdom hidden in the founding meal of the covenant.

notes.original: hypo tes charas autou — out of his joy, he sells everything
notes.rendering: in his joy he goes and sells everything he has
notes.why: The two short parables of the Hidden Treasure and the Pearl make the same point from two different characters — one who stumbles on the kingdom by accident (the treasure hidden in a field) and one who searches for it deliberately (the merchant seeking fine pearls). But both share the same response: they sell everything (panta hosa echei — everything, all that he has). The critical phrase in the treasure parable is hypo tes charas autou — out of his joy. The selling is not a sacrifice; it is the consequence of joy. This is Matthew's clearest statement of the economics of the kingdom: you don't give up everything to get the kingdom; you discover the kingdom and then find that everything else is worth less than what you have found. The selling follows from the joy, not the other way round.

notes.original: grammateus matheteutheis te basileia tōn ouranōn
notes.rendering: every scribe trained for the kingdom of heaven
notes.why: The final parable — if it is a parable — may be Matthew's self-description. Grammateus matheteutheis — a scribe who has become a disciple of the kingdom, or a disciple who has become a kingdom-scribe. The master of a house who brings out of his treasure new things and old (kaina kai palaia) is the interpreter who knows the tradition (palaia — the old inheritance, the Torah and Prophets) and recognises the new thing God is doing in Jesus (kaina — what the parables have been announcing). Matthew's Gospel is itself this treasure — it brings the old (five discourses mirroring five books of Moses, fourteen genealogy quotations, eleven fulfillment formulas) and the new (the kingdom of heaven, the Son of Man, the Great Commission) out of the same storeroom.
