intro: Matthew 14 pairs two feeding stories — the grotesque feast of Herod (a head on a platter) and the abundant feast of Jesus (five thousand fed) — then narrates the sea crossing that follows. The chapter contains Matthew's unique account of Peter walking on water, and the disciples' first explicit confession of Jesus as Son of God.

notes.original: labōn… eulogēsen kai klasas edōken — the fourfold eucharistic action
notes.rendering: taking… he blesses and breaks and gives
notes.why: The four verbs — took (labōn), looked up and blessed (eulogēsen), broke (klasas), gave (edōken) — are the same four actions that will appear at the Last Supper (26:26: taking bread, Jesus blessed and broke it and gave it to the disciples). The deliberate parallel is Matthew's signature: the feeding of the five thousand is a eucharistic scene, and the Last Supper will be a feeding scene. Between the two, the same gestures over bread interpret each other. The disciples who distribute the bread are the church distributing what Jesus gives. In Aramaic, the blessing (birkat ha-mazon — the blessing over bread) was the standard opening of any meal: Baruch Atah Adonai Eloheinu melech ha'olam hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz. Jesus performs this familiar act over five loaves and two fish — and the familiar becomes miraculous.

notes.original: tharseite, ego eimi — I AM on the sea
notes.rendering: Take heart — I AM. Do not be afraid.
notes.why: Ego eimi — I AM, without predicate. As in John's sea-crossing (John 6:20), the disciples on the storm-tossed sea hear the divine name spoken by the one walking on the water. The sea in Hebrew cosmology is the domain of chaos (tehom — the deep of Genesis 1:2), the place of the uncontrollable. YHWH's mastery over the sea is one of the defining images of his power in the Psalms (Psalm 77:19: your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; Psalm 107:29: he made the storm be still). Jesus walking on the water and saying I AM is placing himself in the position of YHWH who walks through the sea. Peter's request — command me to come to you — is unique to Matthew and tests whether the I AM extends to Peter. It does, until he looks at the wind.

notes.original: kyrie, sōson me — Lord, save me
notes.rendering: Lord, save me!
notes.why: Kyrie, sōson me — Lord, save me. Two words in Greek, but in the Hebrew liturgical tradition they are the cry of the Psalms (Psalm 118:25: Hoshia na — save now, from which Hosanna comes; Psalm 69:1: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck). Peter sinking in the sea and crying Lord save me is Psalm 69:1 enacted — the righteous sufferer calling to YHWH from the water. Jesus' response is immediate: he reaches out his hand and takes hold of him. The gesture echoes Isaiah 41:10 (I will uphold you with my righteous right hand) and Psalm 18:16 (he reached down from on high and took hold of me; he drew me out of mighty waters). The whole scene is saturated in the Psalms of rescue.

notes.original: alēthos theou huios ei — truly you are the Son of God
notes.rendering: Truly you are the Son of God
notes.why: The disciples' confession here precedes Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi (16:16) — and it is collective, not individual. The whole boatload of disciples worships (prosekynesan) and confesses. In Matthew's structure, the sea-crossing confession is the first fruits of the disciples' recognition, and the Caesarea Philippi confession is its deepening. Both use the phrase Son of God (huios theou) rather than Messiah alone — and both come after demonstrations of power over the elements (the sea) or after the disclosure of supernatural knowledge. The disciples in the boat have seen Jesus walk on water, calm the storm, and hold Peter up — and their response is worship. This is the posture Matthew has been building toward since the Magi knelt in chapter 2.

intro: Matthew 15 is structured around the question of clean and unclean — what the tradition defines as defiling (unwashed hands, forbidden foods) versus what Jesus identifies as truly defiling (what comes from the heart). The chapter moves from the Jerusalem Pharisees' challenge to the Canaanite woman's faith — two encounters that together redefine the boundaries of who belongs to the people of God.

notes.original: Korbanas — Aramaic qorban preserved raw
notes.rendering: what you would have gained from me is Korban
notes.why: Korbanas — the Aramaic word qorban (offering, that which is devoted to God) preserved untranslated, as Raca and Mammon were preserved before it. In Jewish law, a korban declaration made property ceremonially dedicated to God — technically it could not be used for any other purpose, including supporting one's aging parents. The legal loophole Jesus exposes is devastating: by saying 'korban' over what would have gone to support parents, a son could evade the fifth commandment (honour your father and mother) while appearing pious. Jesus names it precisely what it is — using the word of God (korban) to void the commandment of God. The preservation of the Aramaic term is almost certainly evidence that the saying circulated in Aramaic before Greek translation.

notes.original: ou to eiserchomnon eis to stoma koinoi ton anthrōpon — not what enters but what exits
notes.rendering: not what goes into the mouth defiles — but what comes out
notes.why: This is among the most radical sayings in the Jesus tradition — a direct challenge to the purity system that governed Jewish table fellowship. Mark's version (7:19) adds the parenthetical note 'thus he declared all foods clean' — making the implication explicit. Matthew omits that editorial comment, leaving the saying to work without the explanation. The principle — defilement is interior, not exterior; it comes from the heart, not from the food — overturns centuries of practice while simultaneously recovering the prophetic critique embedded in Hosea, Amos, and Isaiah: what YHWH desires is not ritual purity but the purity of the heart. The teaching almost certainly originates in Jesus' Aramaic teaching, where tuma (impurity) and taha (purity) are heart-categories in the wisdom tradition.

notes.original: Kyrie eleison, huie David — the Canaanite woman's threefold address
notes.rendering: Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David
notes.why: The Canaanite woman's address combines three titles: Kyrie (Lord), huie David (Son of David — the Messianic title used by those seeking healing in Matthew: 9:27, 20:30–31), and the plea eleison (have mercy — from the Greek eleos, translating Hebrew chesed). She is a Gentile woman crying out to a Jewish Messiah using the language of the Jewish Psalms of petition. The story's movement — silence, dismissal, kneeling, a difficult saying, a brilliant answer, and then commendation — is the most dramatically compressed conversation in Matthew. Her response to the dog/children saying ('even the dogs eat the crumbs from the table') is not an argument about rights but about belonging: if I am among the dogs of the household, I am still in the household. Jesus' response — O woman, great is your faith — is one of only two explicit commendations of faith by name in Matthew (the other is the centurion in 8:10).

notes.original: ou kalon labein ton arton tōn teknōn kai balein tois kynarion
notes.rendering: it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs
notes.why: The exchange is one of the most difficult in the Gospels — Jesus apparently dismissing a desperate mother with a diminishing comparison. Several things are significant: (1) kynarion (dogs) is the diminutive — small dogs, household pets, not the scavenging street dogs of the insult; (2) the woman's reply picks up the diminutive and runs with it: yes, but even the household dogs eat the crumbs that fall from the master's table; (3) Jesus' entire response to her — the initial silence, the Israel-first statement, the dog saying — may be a testing of her faith rather than a statement of settled policy. Whatever the interpretive decision, what is undeniable is that a Gentile woman's wit, persistence, and faith overturn the limitation Jesus initially states. The crumbs from the table become the point of entry for the Gentile mission that Matthew's Gospel is building toward.

outro: Note on Matthew 13–15 as the parable and boundary movement: These three chapters move between the interior (the parables — seeds, yeast, treasure, pearl, net, the trained scribe) and the exterior (the miracles — five thousand fed, Peter on water, Canaanite woman, four thousand fed). The parable discourse defines the kingdom in terms of hidden growth and total commitment. The miracle chapters test the boundaries of who belongs in the kingdom: a Gentile centurion in chapter 8, a Canaanite woman in chapter 15, and now two feedings — one for Israel (five thousand, twelve baskets), one suggesting the Gentiles (four thousand, seven baskets, the number of Gentile nations). Matthew is quietly expanding the circle while the story is still ostensibly limited to Israel.

intro: Matthew 16 is the pivot chapter of the Gospel — the hinge between the Galilean ministry and the journey to Jerusalem. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is the human high point of the first half; the rebuke of Peter three verses later is its immediate undoing. The chapter contains the most theologically loaded exchange in Matthew and two of the strongest arguments for an Aramaic original anywhere in the Gospels.

notes.original: Simōn Bar-Iōna — Aramaic patronymic preserved raw
notes.rendering: Simon Bar-Jonah
notes.why: Bar-Iōna — Son of Jonah. An Aramaic patronymic preserved untranslated in the Greek text — one of the clearest signals in the Gospel that this saying circulated in Aramaic before being written in Greek. The Greek equivalent would be Simōn huios Iōna — Simon son of John/Jonah — but Matthew preserves the Aramaic Bar form. Only three Aramaic words are preserved raw in Matthew's Gospel: Raca (5:22), Korban (15:5), and here Bar-Jonah. Each time, the Aramaic appears because the translators either could not or chose not to translate it — and each time, it is a strong indication that the saying originated in Aramaic speech.

notes.original: Petros… petra — Greek wordplay rendering Aramaic Kepha/kepha
notes.rendering: you are Peter — and on this rock I will build my church
notes.why: The Greek text has a wordplay: sy ei Petros (you are Peter/Rock, masculine) kai epi tautē tē petra (and on this rock, feminine). The two words are grammatically different but semantically the same — Peter is the rock and the rock is Peter. The wordplay works better in Aramaic, where kepha (rock, stone) functions as both a personal name (Cephas, the name Jesus gives Simon in John 1:42) and a common noun — there is no gender distinction, no awkward shift from masculine Petros to feminine petra. In Aramaic the sentence would be: ant kepha, ve'al de'na kepha evneh qehali — you are the Rock, and on this Rock I will build my assembly. Many scholars regard this as the strongest single argument for an Aramaic original of this particular saying: it works perfectly in Aramaic and slightly awkwardly in Greek.

notes.original: ha an desēs epi tes ges estai dedemenon en tois ouranois — binding and loosing
notes.rendering: whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven
notes.why: The binding and loosing (dēō/lyō in Greek, asar/shara in Aramaic) is the halakhic terminology of the rabbinic tradition — a rabbi's authoritative ruling on what is forbidden (asar — bound) or permitted (shara — loosed) in matters of Torah observance. The Mishnah uses this language regularly for legal decisions. Jesus gives Peter (and later the community, 18:18) the authority to make binding halakhic decisions about the life of the kingdom community. The saying only makes full sense against the rabbinic background — in Greek, 'binding and loosing' is opaque; in the Aramaic context of first-century Jewish legal discourse, it is a precise technical delegation of interpretive authority.

notes.original: hypage opisō mou, satana — Get behind me, Satan
notes.rendering: Get behind me, Satan!
notes.why: The address to Peter as Satan (satana — the Hebrew/Aramaic satan, the adversary, the one who obstructs) is the most jarring reversal in the Gospel. Three verses after being declared the rock on which the church will be built and given the keys of the kingdom, Peter is called Satan — the adversary. The word satan in Hebrew/Aramaic means obstacle, adversary, the one who stands in the way (Numbers 22:22: the angel of YHWH stood in the road as a satan against Balaam). Peter has become the obstacle — exactly what the name means. He is setting his mind on the things of man (ta tōn anthrōpōn — human interests, human expectations of what the Messiah should be) rather than the things of God (ta tou Theou — the divine necessity of suffering and resurrection). The rock has become a stumbling block (skandalon) in four verses.

intro: Matthew 17 moves through three scenes that together interpret who Jesus is after the confession at Caesarea Philippi: the Transfiguration (the divine confirms what Peter said), the discussion about Elijah (the eschatological timetable), and the failed exorcism (the disciples' inadequacy without prayer and faith). The chapter is bracketed by the two passion predictions that are reshaping the disciples' understanding of what kind of Messiah they are following.

notes.original: metemorphōthē emprosthen autōn — metamorphōsis, glory revealed
notes.rendering: he is transfigured before them
notes.why: Metemorphōthē — was transfigured, transformed in form (from metamorphoō — to change the form). The word appears only here and in the parallel Mark 9:2 in the Gospels, and in Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18 for the transformation of believers. The Transfiguration is the momentary lifting of the veil over Jesus' glory — what was always there becomes visible. Matthew specifies the details: his face shining like the sun (hōs ho hēlios), his garments white as light (leuka hōs to phōs). The imagery deliberately echoes the description of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 (his garment white as snow) and Moses' shining face after the Sinai encounter (Exodus 34:29–35). Jesus' transfiguration on the mountain is a Sinai moment — glory descending, the divine voice speaking, the disciples prostrated.

notes.original: Mōysēs kai Ēlias — the Law and the Prophets
notes.rendering: Moses and Elijah appear to them
notes.why: Moses and Elijah represent the Law (Torah) and the Prophets (Neviim) — the two great divisions of the Hebrew Bible that Jesus said he came not to abolish but to fulfil (5:17). Their appearance on the mountain with Jesus is Matthew's visual statement of fulfilment: the two representatives of everything that came before are now in conversation with the one they anticipated. Moses received Torah on Sinai in fire and cloud; Elijah heard the still small voice on Horeb in fire and wind. Now both appear on the mountain where Jesus is transfigured in light. Peter's offer of three tents (three sukkot — booths, possibly evoking the Feast of Tabernacles) is a human attempt to prolong and domesticate the visionary moment. The cloud cuts him off.

notes.original: akouete autou — Listen to him — Deuteronomy 18:15
notes.rendering: Listen to him
notes.why: The voice at the Transfiguration repeats the baptismal declaration (this is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — 3:17) and adds one word: akouete autou — listen to him, hear him, obey him. The addition quotes Deuteronomy 18:15: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you — you shall listen to him (shema'u elav / akouete autou).' The prophet-like-Moses promise has been waiting since Sinai; the voice at the Transfiguration declares its fulfilment. Jesus is the prophet Moses promised — and the command to the disciples (and to all readers of Matthew) is: listen to him. After six chapters of Sermon on the Mount and eight parables and five miracles, the divine voice gives the interpretive instruction: hear what he says and do it.

notes.original: erei tō orei toutō, metaba enthen ekei — move this mountain
notes.rendering: say to this mountain, 'Move from here to there'
notes.why: Moving mountains is an established Aramaic idiom for accomplishing something extraordinarily difficult or seemingly impossible. The Talmud uses it: 'An uprooter of mountains' (aqar harim) is a title for a scholar who can resolve impossibly difficult questions (Babylonian Talmud Berachot 64a). Rabbinic teachers could be described as 'moving mountains' when they made difficult rulings. Jesus uses the idiom — which his Aramaic-speaking hearers would have immediately recognised as hyperbole — to describe the effect of genuine faith. He is not teaching levitation; he is saying that faith of even the smallest genuine kind can accomplish what seems categorically impossible. The mustard seed (the benchmark of smallness from 13:31) applied to faith: even that much real faith moves mountains. The disciples' failure to cast out the demon was not a question of technique but of the quality of their trust.

intro: Matthew 18 is the Community Discourse — the fourth of the five great discourses, addressed not to crowds but to the disciples, and concerned with life together in the kingdom community. It moves from greatness (who is greatest?) through the protection of the vulnerable (little ones) to the discipline of the straying (the church process of 18:15–17) to forgiveness (seventy-seven times) to the parable that makes forgiveness non-negotiable.

notes.original: ean me strephēte kai genēsthe hōs ta paidia — turning / teshuvah
notes.rendering: unless you turn and become like children
notes.why: Strephēte — turn, be converted, change direction. The verb renders the Hebrew/Aramaic shuv (return, turn) — the word for repentance in the Hebrew prophetic tradition. Teshuvah (turning) is not primarily an emotional experience but a directional one: you are going one way and you turn to go another. The disciples have just been arguing about who is greatest in the kingdom — jockeying for position in the very order of things that Jesus is upending. He tells them to turn — to reverse the entire direction of the question. The child placed in their midst is not a symbol of innocence but of social insignificance: in the ancient world, children had no status, no rights, no standing in the community. To become like a child is to abandon the claim to status altogether.

notes.original: ho an desēte… ho an lysēte — binding/loosing in community; two or three — Mishnah Avot 3:2
notes.rendering: whatever you bind on earth… wherever two or three are gathered in my name
notes.why: The binding and loosing authority given to Peter alone in 16:19 is here given to the community — the gathered church (ekklēsia, 18:17). The movement from individual to communal authority is deliberate: the halakhic discernment that Peter exercises is also exercised by the community in agreement. The promise of verse 19 (if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask) and verse 20 (where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I) almost certainly echoes Mishnah Avot 3:2: 'If two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Shekinah rests between them.' Jesus replaces 'words of Torah' with 'in my name' — he himself is the Torah-presence, the Shekinah that gathers and dwells in the community. The rabbinic form is preserved; the centre has shifted.

notes.original: heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta — seventy-seven times — Genesis 4:24 inverted
notes.rendering: seventy-seven times
notes.why: Hebdomēkontakis hepta — seventy-seven times (or seventy times seven — the Greek is ambiguous, as is the underlying Aramaic shiv'im v'shiv'a). The number deliberately inverts Genesis 4:24, where Lamech boasts: 'If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold.' Lamech's song is the founding charter of unlimited vengeance — the escalation of retaliation without limit. Jesus takes the same number and makes it the charter of unlimited forgiveness. Where Lamech multiplied vengeance to seventy-seven, Jesus multiplies forgiveness to the same count. The Aramaic background makes the inversion crisp: the same phrase (shiv'im v'shiv'a) that licence vengeance in Genesis becomes the measure of forgiveness in the kingdom. The parable that follows is the exegesis of the number.

notes.original: myria talanta — ten thousand talents; splanchnistheis — moved with compassion
notes.rendering: ten thousand talents… moved with compassion, he releases him
notes.why: Ten thousand talents (myria talanta) is a deliberately absurd sum — the largest number (myria) combined with the highest unit of currency (talanton). It has been estimated at approximately 200,000 years' wages for a day labourer — a debt so vast it could never be repaid by any conceivable means. The contrast with the hundred denarii (roughly one hundred days' wages) owed by the fellow servant is equally absurd in the other direction: the forgiven servant was forgiven an astronomically unpayable debt and refused to forgive a trivially manageable one. Splanchnistheis — moved with compassion in his gut, the same word used of Jesus when he sees the crowds (9:36) and when he heals the sick (14:14). The king's compassion is the image of God's compassion; the unforgiving servant's refusal is the image of the community member who has received everything and gives nothing.

notes.original: aph' tōn kardiōn hymōn — from your hearts
notes.rendering: if you do not forgive your brother from your heart
notes.why: The parable closes with the word that the community discourse has been building toward: heart (kardia — lev in Hebrew). The forgiveness Jesus requires is not merely procedural or verbal but from the heart — from the lev, the centre of thought and will and intention. The servant performed the right gestures (fell on his knees, pleaded) but did not receive the forgiveness into his heart and therefore could not extend it from his heart. In the Hebrew wisdom tradition, the heart is not the seat of emotion but of character — what a person is in their core. Forgiveness from the heart is forgiveness that has changed the forgiver. The heavenly Father's treatment of those who do not forgive (v.35: delivered to the jailers) is not a separate threat added to the parable but the parable's own logic: the one who does not forgive has not received forgiveness. You cannot hold what you refuse to give.

outro: Note on Matthew 16–18 as the turning-point movement: These three chapters are the Gospel's pivot — the moment when the Galilean ministry of preaching and healing gives way to the explicit announcement of the cross and the formation of the community that will survive it. Peter's confession names Jesus correctly; his rebuke reveals that he does not yet understand what the name means. The Transfiguration confirms the confession from heaven and adds the command to listen. The Community Discourse (chapter 18) is the charter for the community of people who have turned, become like children, refused to cause the little ones to stumble, exercised binding and loosing in agreement, and forgiven from the heart seventy-seven times. It is a community shaped by the cross before the cross has happened.

intro: Matthew 19 opens the journey toward Jerusalem with three teaching encounters — divorce, children, and wealth — each one pressing against a different kind of hardness: the hardness of heart that breaks covenant, the hardness that excludes the small, and the hardness that cannot let go of possessions. Jesus appeals to the beginning (the created order) against the Mosaic accommodation, receives the children the disciples want to send away, and asks the rich young man to do the one thing he cannot do.

notes.original: kata pasan aitian — for any cause — Hillel/Shammai debate
notes.rendering: is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?
notes.why: The phrase kata pasan aitian (for any cause) is the key: it places the question directly in the context of the famous rabbinic debate between the schools of Shammai and Hillel about the grounds for divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1 speaks of a man finding 'some indecency' (erva davar — literally 'a matter of nakedness') in his wife. Shammai interpreted this narrowly: only sexual immorality. Hillel interpreted it broadly: anything the husband found displeasing, including burning his food. The Pharisees are asking Jesus to adjudicate between two rabbinic positions. Jesus refuses both and goes behind Moses entirely — to the created order, to the before of Mosaic law. The question was about legal grounds for divorce; Jesus reframes it as a question about what marriage is.

notes.original: kamēlon dia trēmatos rhaphidos — camel through needle's eye
notes.rendering: easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle
notes.why: One of the most discussed sayings in the Gospels. Two textual/interpretive notes: (1) Some manuscripts read kamilon (rope, cable) rather than kamēlon (camel) — which would make the image a rope through a needle's eye, equally impossible but slightly less vivid. The earliest and best manuscripts support kamēlon (camel). (2) The 'needle's gate' theory — that there was a small gate in Jerusalem called 'the needle's eye' through which a camel could pass with difficulty — has no historical support and was invented to soften the saying. The context makes the impossible image the point: the disciples ask 'who then can be saved?' (v.25) — the right question. Jesus is not suggesting that rich people can enter the kingdom if they try hard enough; he is saying that with human effort it is categorically impossible. The answer is 'with God all things are possible' — not a strategy but a theology. The camel is meant to be absurd.

notes.original: ei theleis teleios einai — if you would be teleios
notes.rendering: if you would be perfect
notes.why: Teleios — complete, whole (the same word as 5:48: be teleios as your Father is teleios). The rich young man has kept all the commandments from his youth — an impressive achievement, and Jesus does not dispute it. What he lacks (v.20: ti eti hystero — what am I still short of?) is the teleios condition: the undivided wholeness that cannot be achieved while one's wealth remains the unmoving centre of one's life. The sell-everything-give-to-the-poor command is not a universal rule for all disciples (Jesus does not say this to everyone he calls). It is the specific diagnosis of this man's specific incompleteness: his possessions are the one thing standing between him and the wholeness he seeks. He goes away sorrowful — the only person in the Gospels who is explicitly called to follow Jesus and declines.

notes.original: en te palingenesia — in the new creation/regeneration
notes.rendering: in the new world
notes.why: Palingenesia — new birth, regeneration, new creation. The word appears only twice in the NT: here and Titus 3:5 (the washing of regeneration). In Stoic philosophy it described the periodic renewal of the cosmos. In Jewish eschatology it resonates with the new creation expected at the end of the age (Isaiah 65:17: I am creating a new heavens and a new earth; Isaiah 66:22). Jesus uses it for the eschatological renewal when the Son of Man sits on his throne — the regeneration of all things. The Fireside Gospel renders it 'the new world' to capture the cosmic scope without importing the later Christian sense of personal spiritual rebirth. The twelve thrones for the twelve disciples judging the twelve tribes is the image of the renewed Israel in the age of completion.

intro: Matthew 20 holds together the parable of the vineyard labourers, the third and most detailed passion prediction, the Sons of Zebedee request (and the dispute it causes), and the healing of two blind men at Jericho. The chapter is a study in contrasts: the labourers who grumble at the master's generosity, the disciples who argue about greatness while Jesus describes his coming death, and the two blind men who see more clearly than anyone.

notes.original: ho ophthalmos sou ponēros estin hoti egō agathos eimi — the evil eye idiom again
notes.rendering: is your eye evil because I am generous?
notes.why: Ponēros — evil (eye). The evil eye (ayin ra'ah) idiom appears here for the third time in Matthew (6:23: the eye passage in the Sermon; 9:4: the scribes thinking evil in their hearts; and here). The master's question to the grumbling labourer is literally: 'Is your eye evil because I am good?' In the Hebrew/Aramaic idiom, an evil eye means stinginess — you begrudge what others receive, you are contracted around your own entitlement. The labourers who worked all day are stingy toward the ones who worked an hour — not because they themselves received less (they got exactly what they agreed to) but because others received the same. The evil eye is the eye that cannot bear others' good fortune. The parable ends on this question rather than an answer: the reader is left to decide whether their own eye is evil.

notes.original: ho huios tou anthrōpou ouk elthen diakonēthēnai alla diakonēsai kai dounai ten psychen autou lytron anti pollōn
notes.rendering: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many
notes.why: Lytron anti pollōn — a ransom for many. Lytron is the price paid to release a prisoner or slave; anti means 'in place of, in exchange for.' The saying is the closest the Synoptic Gospels come to an explicit atonement theology — Jesus giving his life as the price that releases the many. The phrase anti pollōn (for many) almost certainly renders the Aramaic saggin (many, the multitude) and echoes Isaiah 53:11–12 (LXX: he bore the sins of many — tas hamartias pollōn ēnenken; he was delivered up for their sins — paredothē dia tas hamartias autōn). The Isaianic Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and 'bore the sin of many' is the background for Jesus' self-description. The Son of Man who is the Danielic figure of eschatological authority (7:13) is simultaneously the Servant who gives his life: the two figures are merged in Jesus' self-understanding.

notes.original: to poterion ho egō mellō pinein — the cup I am to drink
notes.rendering: the cup that I am to drink
notes.why: To poterion — the cup. In the Hebrew prophetic tradition, the cup is the cup of YHWH's wrath — the judgment that nations must drink (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15–17, Ezekiel 23:31–33). Jesus speaks of 'his cup' — the suffering appointed for him — the same cup he will pray about in Gethsemane (26:39: if it is possible, let this cup pass from me). The sons of Zebedee confidently say 'we are able' — and Jesus says they will indeed drink it (the martyrdom tradition about James is confirmed by Acts 12:2, and tradition records John's suffering). But they do not yet know what the cup contains. The request for seats of honour is immediately followed by the cup of suffering — Matthew's structural point: the seats at the right and left hand of the king are the crosses at Golgotha.

notes.original: splanchnistheis de ho Iesous — moved with compassion
notes.rendering: Jesus, moved with compassion, touches their eyes
notes.why: Splanchnistheis — the gut-compassion word, from the same Aramaic rachem/rahamim root as before (9:36, 14:14). Matthew's use of this word for Jesus is always at the moment of healing or feeding — it marks the visceral, internal movement that precedes action. Two blind men crying out are rebuked by the crowd (the social pressure to silence the marginalised) but Jesus stops, asks what they want, and touches their eyes. The detail that he touches their eyes (hēpsato tōn ommatōn autōn) is tender and specific — not a command from a distance but the laying of hands. And they follow him: the blind who receive sight become disciples. The chapter that began with labourers and greatness ends with two men who see for the first time, walking behind Jesus toward Jerusalem.

intro: Matthew 21 is the most event-dense chapter in the Gospel — the triumphal entry, the Temple cleansing, the fig tree, the authority debate, and two parables, all in one day's narrative. The chapter arrives in Jerusalem and immediately generates conflict at every turn. Jesus enters as the humble king of Zechariah 9:9, cleanses the Temple with Isaiah and Jeremiah on his lips, and tells the religious leadership two parables that make unmistakably clear what he thinks of them — and what God will do about it.

notes.original: epi onon kai epi pōlon — on a donkey and on a colt (Matthew's two animals)
notes.rendering: mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden
notes.why: Matthew's account of the triumphal entry is unique in having two animals — a donkey and a colt — where Mark, Luke, and John have only the colt. This has puzzled readers since antiquity. The explanation is almost certainly Matthew's close following of the LXX of Zechariah 9:9: epi hypozygion kai pōlon neon (on a beast of burden and a young colt). Hebrew poetry uses parallelism (the same thing said twice in different words), and Zechariah's couplet describes one animal in two ways. Matthew, reading the Hebrew parallelism as two separate animals, produces a scene where Jesus sits on both — which is logistically awkward but theologically precise about what Matthew is doing throughout his Gospel: reading the Old Testament with meticulous literalness to show fulfilment.

notes.original: Hōsanna — Hebrew Hoshia na, Psalm 118:25
notes.rendering: Hosanna
notes.why: Hōsanna is the transliteration of the Hebrew hoshia na (Psalm 118:25: O Lord, save now, O Lord, grant us success). In its original liturgical context it was a petition — 'save, we pray!' By the first century it had become an acclamation of praise, still carrying its petitionary force but used to greet the arrival of a pilgrim or king. The crowds crying 'Hosanna to the Son of David' are both acclaiming Jesus and appealing to him: save us now, son of David! The full quotation — 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (Psalm 118:26) — was the standard greeting for pilgrims arriving in Jerusalem for the feasts. Jesus is arriving as both the feast pilgrim and the messianic king of Psalm 118, the king the builders rejected who becomes the cornerstone.

notes.original: oikos proseuchēs… spēlaion lēstōn — Isaiah 56:7 + Jeremiah 7:11
notes.rendering: my house shall be called a house of prayer… but you are making it a den of robbers
notes.why: Two prophetic texts in one sentence. Isaiah 56:7 (in full: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples) is the great universalist vision of the Temple as the gathering point for all nations — not just Israel. Jeremiah 7:11 (den of robbers — me'arat paritsim) comes from Jeremiah's Temple sermon, where he condemns those who treat the Temple as a sanctuary for continued injustice: you come to the Temple, do your ritual, and go back out to oppress the poor. The Temple cleansing is not primarily about commercial activity disrupting worship; it is about the prophetic indictment that the institution has become a cover for injustice while failing its universal vocation. Jesus' action and words together perform Jeremiah's Temple sermon.

notes.original: ampelōna… kai phrygmon autō periethen — Isaiah 5:1–2, the song of the vineyard
notes.rendering: planted a vineyard and put a fence around it
notes.why: The parable of the wicked tenants opens with an unmistakable quotation of Isaiah 5:1–2 — the Song of the Vineyard: 'My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it and hewed out a wine vat in it.' Isaiah's song ends with YHWH removing the hedge and letting the vineyard be destroyed because it produced wild grapes (injustice). Jesus takes Isaiah's vineyard and adds tenants — and the parable becomes a history of Israel's response to the prophets (the servants beaten and killed) and now to the Son (the heir thrown out and killed). The religious leaders understand perfectly (v.45: he is speaking about them) — which is exactly what the parable intends.

notes.original: lithos hon apedokimasan hoi oikodomountes — Psalm 118:22, the rejected cornerstone
notes.rendering: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone
notes.why: Psalm 118:22 — ho lithos hon apedokimasan hoi oikodomountes, houtos egenēthē eis kephalēn gōnias (the stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner). The same psalm that provided 'Hosanna' (v.25) and 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (v.26) now provides the rejected cornerstone. Jesus applies it to himself explicitly: the builders (the religious authorities) have rejected the stone (Jesus/the Son of the parable); God has made him the cornerstone (kephalē gōnias — head of the corner, the stone that holds the whole building together). The parable ends with the cornerstone imagery: to fall on this stone is to be broken; to have it fall on you is to be crushed. Jesus is both the stone the builders rejected and the stone that cannot be evaded.

outro: Note on Matthew 19–21 as the Jerusalem approach movement: These three chapters narrate the final approach to the city — teaching on the road (chapter 19), the last signs of the kingdom outside Jerusalem (chapter 20), and the arrival in the city that immediately becomes confrontation (chapter 21). The camel through the needle's eye and the labourers in the vineyard are the final teaching parables before the passion parables of chapters 21–25 take over. The blind men who cry 'Son of David' and follow Jesus are the last healing narrative before Jerusalem. And the triumphal entry — Jesus arriving as the humble king, not the conquering general — sets the terms for everything that follows: this is not the Messiah the city expected, and its rejection of him is the subject of the two parables with which chapter 21 closes.

intro: Matthew 22 is the chapter of controversies — four disputes in rapid succession, each one initiated by a different group (Pharisees and Herodians, Sadducees, a lawyer, and finally Jesus himself). Each dispute turns on a question about authority: whose authority governs payment of taxes, whose authority defines the resurrection, which authority stands highest in the Law, whose authority defines the Messiah. Jesus answers the first three and the fourth silences everyone.

notes.original: apodote oun ta Kaisaros Kaisari kai ta tou Theou tō Theō
notes.rendering: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's — and to God the things that are God's
notes.why: The answer is so elegant it has been quoted for two thousand years. The trap was designed to be inescapable: say yes to the tax and lose the crowd's sympathy; say no and face charges of sedition against Rome. Jesus asks whose image (eikōn) and inscription is on the coin — and the answer immediately suggests the counter-question: whose image is on you? Genesis 1:26 says human beings are made in the image (tselem, LXX: eikōn) of God. The coin bears Caesar's image and belongs to Caesar; the human person bears God's image and belongs to God. The answer does not resolve the question of church and state — it radicalises it by reframing what belongs to God. In Aramaic, the word for image (tsalma) and the word for likeness (deyumna) used in Genesis are both preserved in the targums. Jesus may be making a Genesis allusion his Aramaic-speaking hearers would catch.

notes.original: egō eimi ho theos Abraam… ouk estin ho theos nekrōn alla zōntōn
notes.rendering: I am the God of Abraham… he is not God of the dead but of the living
notes.why: Jesus' argument for resurrection from the Torah is elegant in the extreme — and the Sadducees who reject the resurrection but accept only the Torah are defeated on their own ground. The argument turns on tense: God says to Moses 'I AM the God of Abraham' (present tense), not 'I was.' If Abraham were simply dead and gone, the past tense would be appropriate. The present tense implies ongoing relationship — Abraham is still in relationship with the God who speaks. He is not God of the dead (nekrōn) but of the living (zōntōn). The argument reflects a rabbinic style of scriptural reasoning — the present tense of the divine name as evidence of ongoing covenant relationship. Whatever one thinks of the logic, the crowd is astonished (v.33) and the Sadducees are silenced.

notes.original: agapēseis kyrion ton theon sou… agapēseis ton plēsion sou — Deut. 6:5 + Lev. 19:18
notes.rendering: love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind… love your neighbour as yourself
notes.why: The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5) and Leviticus 19:18 joined as the double summary of Torah. The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:5 reads: love YHWH your God with all your lev (heart/mind/will), with all your nefesh (soul/self/life), and with all your me'od (strength/muchness/intensity). The LXX renders these as dianoia (understanding/mind), psychē (soul), and dynamis (strength). Matthew's version has kardia (heart), psychē (soul), and dianoia (mind) — slightly different from the LXX, possibly reflecting an Aramaic version of the Shema (lev/naphsha/kol hayilach) that Jesus used in teaching. The triple structure — heart, soul, mind — is Matthew's way of conveying the totality of the Shema's demand: the whole person, from every direction. And Jesus does what Hillel did: condenses the entire Torah into a single principle — love — and adds the neighbour command as co-equal with the love of God.

notes.original: kyrios eipen tō kyriō mou — YHWH / Adoni — Psalm 110:1
notes.rendering: the Lord said to my Lord
notes.why: Psalm 110:1 is the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament. In Hebrew: ne'um YHWH la'adoni (the utterance of YHWH to my lord/Adoni). The two Hebrew words YHWH and Adoni (my lord) are both rendered kyrios in the LXX — giving the Greek the appearance of 'the Lord said to my Lord.' Jesus' argument turns on the attribution: if David wrote Psalm 110 (as was assumed) and he calls his son 'lord' (Adoni/kyrios), then the Messiah-as-David's-son is an inadequate category. A father does not call his own son 'my lord.' Therefore the Messiah must be something greater than merely David's biological descendant. The question — how is he David's son? — is not a denial of Davidic descent but a demand for a more adequate Christology. The crowd cannot answer because the question requires them to say that the Messiah is also David's Lord — which is exactly what the disciples confessed at Caesarea Philippi.

intro: Matthew 23 is the most sustained prophetic denunciation in the Gospels — seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees, followed by the lament over Jerusalem. It has no parallel in length or intensity anywhere in the NT. The woes are not anti-Semitic polemic; they are the language of the Hebrew prophetic tradition — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel — turned against the religious leadership of Jerusalem by a Jewish teacher from Galilee. The chapter closes with one of the most beautiful and heartbreaking lines in Matthew.

notes.original: epi tes Mōyseōs kathedras ekathisan — Moses' seat, kathedra Mōyseōs
notes.rendering: sit on Moses' seat
notes.why: The kathedra Mōyseōs (Moses' seat) is not merely a metaphor — it is an actual stone seat found in ancient synagogues, from which the authorised interpreter would read and expound Torah. Archaeological examples have been found at Chorazin and Delos. The one who sat in Moses' seat had the authority to make halakhic rulings on behalf of the community — the binding and loosing authority of 16:19 and 18:18. Jesus does not deny the authority of the seat; he affirms it in verse 3 (practise and observe whatever they tell you). What he condemns is the gap between the authority claimed and the life lived: they teach from Moses' seat without living what they teach. The chair is legitimate; the occupants are not.

notes.original: phyllaktēria — tefillin; kraspedon — tzitzit
notes.rendering: phylacteries… fringes
notes.why: Phyllaktēria — the Greek word for tefillin (the small black leather boxes containing Torah passages, worn on the arm and forehead during prayer, based on Deuteronomy 6:8). Kraspedon — fringes, the Greek for tzitzit (the ritual fringes on the corners of the garment, commanded in Numbers 15:38–40 and Deuteronomy 22:12). Both are legitimate practices of Jewish piety — the same fringes (kraspedon) the woman with the haemorrhage touched in 9:20, and Jesus himself wore them (14:36). The condemnation is not the practice but the widening and lengthening for display: the enlarging of the phylacteries and the lengthening of the fringes to be seen by others. The act of Torah is turned into a performance of piety.

notes.original: ta barutera tou nomou — mishpat, chesed, emunah — justice, mercy, faithfulness
notes.rendering: the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness
notes.why: Ta barutera tou nomou — the heavier things of the Law, the things that carry more weight. The three terms Jesus names — krísin (justice), éleon (mercy), pístín (faithfulness) — almost certainly translate the Hebrew mishpat, chesed, emunah: the three great categories of prophetic ethics. Micah 6:8 asks: 'What does the Lord require of you but to do justice (mishpat), love mercy (chesed), and walk humbly with your God?' Hosea 2:19 lists mishpat, chesed, and emunah as the terms of the renewed covenant. Zechariah 7:9 commands mishpat and chesed. The 'weightier matters' are not Jesus' invention — they are the prophets' consistent diagnosis of what Torah requires at its heart. The Pharisees have kept the letter (tithing spices) and missed the substance (justice, mercy, faithfulness).

notes.original: tōn kōnōpa... tēn kamēlon — gnat and camel: Aramaic gamla/galma wordplay
notes.rendering: straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel
notes.why: This is almost certainly the clearest Aramaic wordplay in the entire New Testament. In Aramaic, the word for camel is gamla and the word for gnat is galma — mirror images of each other, distinguished only by the reversal of two consonants. The pun would be immediately audible in Aramaic: you strain out the galma (gnat) and swallow the gamla (camel). The saying is already absurd as an image — no one literally swallows a camel — but the wordplay makes it also memorable as sound. Both animals are levitically unclean (Leviticus 11:4, 11:23): you filter out one unclean creature and gulp down the largest unclean creature available. The pun is lost in Greek translation and completely lost in English — but it almost certainly means that this saying was composed and first taught in Aramaic.

notes.original: Ierousalem Ierousalem… hosakis ēthelēsa episynagagein ta tekna sou — the hen and her chicks
notes.rendering: how often would I have gathered your children as a hen gathers her brood
notes.why: The lament over Jerusalem is the most tender moment in a chapter of fury. The image of the hen (ornis — a bird, specifically a hen) gathering her chicks under her wings draws on the Hebrew imagery of YHWH's wings as shelter and protection (Psalm 91:4: he will cover you with his feathers, under his wings you will find refuge; Psalm 17:8: hide me in the shadow of your wings; Deuteronomy 32:11: like an eagle stirring up its nest, hovering over its young). Jesus uses the same image for himself — the one gathering Jerusalem's children under his wings — and the double name ('Jerusalem, Jerusalem') is the form of anguished address used for the dying (2 Samuel 18:33: Absalom, Absalom; Genesis 22:11: Abraham, Abraham). The lament closes the Temple teaching and the Jerusalem ministry: your house is left to you desolate.

intro: Matthew 24 is the first part of the Olivet Discourse — the fifth and final great discourse, delivered not in the Temple or on a mountain but on the Mount of Olives, across the valley from the Temple, overlooking it. The discourse addresses two questions that Matthew's community could not easily separate: when will the Temple be destroyed, and when will the Son of Man return? The discourse does not fully separate them either — which is part of its interpretive difficulty.

notes.original: to bdelygma tes eremōseōs — Daniel's shiqqutz hashomem
notes.rendering: the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel
notes.why: Bdelygma tes eremōseōs — abomination of desolation. The phrase translates the Hebrew shiqqutz meshomem (Daniel 9:27, 11:31, 12:11) — Daniel's term for the desecration of the Temple by Antiochus Epiphanes IV in 168 BCE, when he erected a pagan altar and sacrificed a pig in the holy place (1 Maccabees 1:54). Daniel uses the phrase for a historical event; Jesus applies it to a future crisis. The parenthetical 'let the reader understand' (ho anaginōskōn noeitō) is directed at the reader of Daniel as well as the reader of Matthew — an invitation to do the interpretive work of applying the Danielic language to the new situation. The abomination that Daniel described has become a template for the ultimate sacrilege that will mark the crisis before the end.

notes.original: hopou ean ē to ptōma, ekei synagchthēsontai hoi aetoi — Aramaic proverb
notes.rendering: wherever the corpse is, there the vultures will gather
notes.why: The saying has the compressed form of an Aramaic proverb — three words in the Aramaic original would express it: ayka d'givra, taman nishrayya (where the body is, there the eagles/vultures gather). The image is used as a criterion of recognition: as vultures mark the location of a corpse without needing to be told where it is, so the coming of the Son of Man will be self-evident rather than requiring insider information or rumour. The proverb answers the false alarm verses 26: 'he is in the wilderness, he is in the inner rooms' — don't go look. The real event will be as unmistakable as vultures circling. The idiom is common in ancient wisdom literature; its Aramaic substrate is evident.

notes.original: he genea haute ou me parelthe heōs an panta tauta genētai
notes.rendering: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place
notes.why: One of the most debated sentences in Matthew. Genea haute — this generation — the same phrase used in 11:16, 12:41, 12:42, 12:45, 16:4, 17:17, 23:36 for the contemporaries of Jesus. If the natural meaning is kept, Jesus is saying that the events he describes — including the coming of the Son of Man — will happen within the lifetime of his contemporaries. Three main interpretations: (1) the fulfilment refers to the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, which is the 'all these things' Jesus has in view; (2) genea means 'race/people' (Israel will not pass away); (3) Jesus was mistaken about the timing. The first reading is the strongest: much of the discourse (particularly vv.15–22) fits the events of 66–70 CE closely. The coming of the Son of Man (v.30) may be the vindication of Jesus in those events rather than the final parousia.

notes.original: peri de tes hēmeras ekeinēs… oude ho huios — not even the Son
notes.rendering: nor the Son, but the Father alone
notes.why: The most theologically remarkable limitation in Matthew — Jesus explicitly including himself among those who do not know the day and the hour of the end, placing his own knowledge below the Father's. Oude ho huios — not even the Son. Some manuscripts omit the phrase 'nor the Son,' but it is present in the most reliable witnesses and is far more likely to have been dropped by scribes uncomfortable with it than added by scribes comfortable with limitation. The early church wrestled with this verse extensively — how can the Son not know what the Father knows? — and found various solutions. But the verse as written is clear: in his incarnate state, Jesus does not have this knowledge. It is the strongest statement of kenotic limitation in the Synoptics — the Son who knows all things (11:27: all things have been handed over to me by my Father) does not know the hour of his own return.

outro: Note on Matthew 22–24 as the Jerusalem controversy movement: These three chapters are set entirely in and around the Temple in Jerusalem — the final week of Jesus' ministry before the passion. Chapter 22 is controversy inside the Temple (four disputes). Chapter 23 is denunciation of the Temple's leadership (seven woes) followed by the lament that closes with 'your house is left to you desolate.' Chapter 24 is the discourse across the valley from the Temple about the Temple's coming destruction. The movement is from engagement (22) to condemnation (23) to lamentation and departure (24). The Temple that was supposed to be a house of prayer for all nations (21:13) has become the place from which Jesus departs, whose desolation he announces, and whose stones — not one left on another — he predicts. The lament over Jerusalem (23:37–39) is the hinge: he would have gathered her children, and she would not.

intro: Matthew 25 closes the Olivet Discourse with three parables — the virgins, the talents, and the sheep and goats — each one pressing on a different dimension of readiness. The sheep and goats is the most universalist and the most socially demanding passage in the entire Gospel: judgment is rendered entirely on the basis of how the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick, and the imprisoned were treated — and Jesus identifies himself with all of them.

notes.original: ouk oida hymas — I do not know you
notes.rendering: I do not know you
notes.why: The bridegroom's response to the locked-out virgins echoes the judge's response in 7:23 ('I never knew you, depart from me'). The word oida — I know — is the knowledge of recognition and relationship, not merely information. The foolish virgins had lamps and were at the right place for the right event. But when the moment came they were absent — and absence from the decisive moment is, in the logic of the parable, what constitutes not being known. The warning 'watch therefore — you know neither the day nor the hour' connects directly back to 24:36: the limitation of knowledge about the hour is the ground of the command to be constantly ready.

notes.original: talanton — enormous monetary unit, not a 'talent' in the modern sense
notes.rendering: five talents… two talents… one talent
notes.why: A talanton was approximately six thousand denarii — about twenty years' wages for a day labourer. The servant given one talent has been entrusted with what amounts to two decades of earnings. The parable is not about small gifts; it is about enormous ones. The master's distribution 'according to ability' (kata ten idian dynamin) is significant: the servant given one talent was not given less because he was loved less but because his capacity was assessed as appropriate for one. The wickedness of the one-talent servant is not failure to multiply it but fear that produced paralysis and burial — treating the gift as a threat rather than an opportunity.

notes.original: eph' hoson epoiēsate heni toutōn… emoi epoiēsate — the identification with the least
notes.rendering: as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me
notes.why: The theological shock of the sheep and goats is the identification: Jesus is not saying 'serve the poor because God rewards you for it' but 'when you served the hungry and naked and imprisoned, you were serving me.' The least of these (elachistōn — the very smallest, the least significant) are identified with the King who is judging. The righteous are astonished (vv.37–39) — they had no idea they were serving Jesus. The unrighteous are equally astonished (v.44) — they would have served him if they had known. The parable exposes the insufficiency of conditional charity (I'll help if I know who I'm helping) against the unconditional claim: the hungry stranger is Jesus. The identification of Jesus with the suffering poor is the most demanding Christological statement in Matthew.

intro: Matthew 26 is the longest chapter in the Gospel — the Passover preparation, the Last Supper, Gethsemane, the arrest, the trial before Caiaphas, and Peter's denial. The chapter moves from the intimacy of the upper room to the darkness of the garden to the courtyard fire where Peter stands and denies. Everything Jesus has been moving toward since 16:21 ('from that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem') arrives in this chapter.

notes.original: touto estin to sōma mou… touto gar estin to haima mou tes diathekes
notes.rendering: this is my body… this is my blood of the covenant
notes.why: The words of institution at the Last Supper are the most theologically freighted sentences in Matthew — the words over which the church has debated for two thousand years. Touto estin to sōma mou (this is my body) and touto estin to haima mou tes diathekes (this is my blood of the covenant). The covenant language (diatheke) echoes Exodus 24:8: 'Behold the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you.' Moses sprinkled the covenant blood; Jesus gives his covenant blood to drink. The addition 'for the forgiveness of sins' (eis aphesin hamartiōn) is unique to Matthew — it connects the eucharist directly to the purpose of Jesus' name (1:21: he will save his people from their sins) and to John the Baptist's baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (3:6). Matthew's eucharist is explicitly the enacted forgiveness that the whole Gospel has been announcing.

notes.original: hymnesantes — singing the Hallel
notes.rendering: when they have sung a hymn
notes.why: Hymnesantes — they sang a hymn. At the Passover seder, the Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118) were sung in two groups: Psalms 113–114 before the meal, and Psalms 115–118 after. 'When they have sung a hymn' refers to the second group — the post-meal Hallel. These are the psalms of the Exodus, of the Red Sea crossing, of YHWH's steadfast love that endures forever. They are also the psalms that provided 'Hosanna' (118:25) and the rejected cornerstone (118:22) and 'blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord' (118:26). Jesus goes to Gethsemane with these words of praise and trust still on his lips — and in the garden will sweat blood as he prays 'not as I will, but as you will.'

notes.original: Gethsemani — Aramaic gath shemanim, oil press
notes.rendering: Gethsemane
notes.why: Gethsēmani — the Aramaic name preserved in Greek transliteration. Gath shemanim means 'oil press' — the place where olives were crushed to extract their oil. Jesus is pressed in the place of pressing. The name is one of the most quietly significant details in the passion narrative: the garden on the Mount of Olives where the disciples sleep and Jesus prays is named for the crushing of what grows there. The Aramaic name, preserved raw without translation (unlike Emmanuel in 1:23, which Matthew immediately glosses), is another signal that the passion tradition reached Matthew through Aramaic-speaking communities who remembered the name.

notes.original: to men pneuma prothumon, he de sarx asthenēs — spirit willing, flesh weak
notes.rendering: the spirit is willing — but the flesh is weak
notes.why: To pneuma prothumon — the spirit eager, ready, willing (prothumos — from pro + thymos, forward-spirited, zealous). He de sarx asthenēs — the flesh weak, fragile, unable. The antithesis is characteristic of Aramaic wisdom teaching: two opposed nouns, each with a single descriptive word, balanced against each other. The saying functions as pastoral acknowledgment rather than condemnation: Jesus does not rebuke the sleeping disciples for moral failure but names the structure of human experience — the inner person that genuinely wants and the body that cannot sustain the want. He himself is about to live out both sides: the spirit willing (not as I will, but as you will) and the flesh in anguish (he began to be sorrowful and troubled, v.37).

notes.original: ton huion tou anthrōpou… ek dexiōn kathemenon tes dynameōs — Psalm 110 + Daniel 7
notes.rendering: the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven
notes.why: Two texts joined in a single sentence: Psalm 110:1 (sit at my right hand — kathōu ek dexiōn mou, here rendered as seated at the right hand of Power) and Daniel 7:13 (one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven — erchomenos epi tōn nephelōn). Jesus combines the two at the moment of maximum crisis — before the high priest who has put him under oath. The two texts together describe a figure enthroned in divine glory and arriving in eschatological judgment. The high priest tears his robes because the claim is explicit: the one standing before you in chains will be the one you see enthroned and coming. This is the blasphemy charge — and the irony is precise: what the high priest calls blasphemy is what the Gospel has been declaring since the prologue.

intro: Matthew 27 is the passion narrative at full reach — Judas, Pilate, Barabbas, Golgotha, and the cross. The chapter contains the cry from the cross (in Aramaic, the only dominical saying preserved in Aramaic in Matthew's passion), the tearing of the Temple curtain, the raised saints (unique to Matthew), and the centurion's confession. It ends with the guard at the tomb — Matthew's concern with the resurrection claim and its opponents.

notes.original: dia Ieremiou tou prophētou — attributed to Jeremiah but from Zechariah
notes.rendering: what had been spoken through the prophet Jeremiah
notes.why: Matthew attributes the thirty pieces of silver quotation to Jeremiah — but the text is primarily Zechariah 11:12–13, with some influence from Jeremiah 32:6–9 (Jeremiah's purchase of a field) and Jeremiah 18:2–3 (the potter's house). The discrepancy has puzzled commentators since antiquity; Jerome noted it in the 4th century. Several explanations: (1) Matthew is conflating two texts and attributes to the more prominent prophet; (2) the attribution follows a rabbinic convention of citing a combined text under the name of the major prophet; (3) there was a tradition of a Jeremiah text now lost. What is significant theologically is Matthew's insistence that even the betrayal money and its disposal are the fulfilment of prophetic Scripture. The price of the Son of God is thirty silver pieces — the price of a gored slave (Exodus 21:32) — and every coin goes where the Scripture said it would go.

notes.original: to haima autou eph' hēmas kai epi ta tekna hēmōn
notes.rendering: his blood be on us and on our children
notes.why: This verse has the most terrible reception history of any sentence in the NT — used for nearly two thousand years to justify persecution and murder of Jewish people. The responsible reading requires several things: (1) the crowd in the narrative is a specific group in Jerusalem at a specific moment, not 'the Jewish people' across history; (2) accepting blood guilt in this form is an idiom of individual responsibility (cf. 2 Samuel 1:16), not a hereditary curse on all descendants; (3) Matthew himself is almost certainly Jewish and writing for a Jewish-Christian community, which makes anti-Jewish reading of his Gospel incoherent; (4) the verse appears nowhere else in the passion tradition — it is not in Mark, Luke, or John. Whatever Matthew intends, he does not intend what has been done with it.

notes.original: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani — Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic/Hebrew
notes.rendering: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
notes.why: The cry from the cross is preserved in its Aramaic (or Hebrew-Aramaic mixed) form — one of only two sayings of Jesus on the cross in Matthew, and the only one preserved in his actual language. Eli, Eli (my God, my God — Hebrew) lema sabachthani (why have you forsaken me — Aramaic). The mixed form may reflect the way the Psalm was known and recited in the first-century synagogue. It is a direct quotation of Psalm 22:1 — the psalm that opens in desolation ('my God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me?') and closes in vindication and praise ('he has not despised or scorned the suffering of the afflicted one; he has not hidden his face from him but has listened to his cry for help'). Whether Jesus cries only the opening or recites the whole psalm in his mind is a question of devotion more than exegesis. What is certain: the bystanders mishear Eli (my God) as Eliyahu (Elijah) — a misunderstanding only possible if the language is Aramaic/Hebrew, not Greek. The preserved original language is itself the evidence of authentic tradition.

notes.original: to katapetasma tou naou eschisthē ap' anōthen heōs katō — the Temple curtain torn
notes.rendering: the curtain of the Temple is torn in two, from top to bottom
notes.why: The Temple had two curtains: one at the entrance to the holy place, one between the holy place and the holy of holies. The torn curtain is almost certainly the inner one — the barrier between the world and the presence of God. Torn from top to bottom (ap' anōthen heōs katō) — from above downward, the direction of divine rather than human action. The tearing simultaneously signals the end of the barrier between God and humanity, the judgment on the Temple system, and the fulfilment of the prophecy of desolation (23:38). The earthquake and the opened tombs are Matthew's way of narrating the cross as a cosmic event — the death of Jesus is not a private tragedy but a moment that shakes the earth and opens the dead.

notes.original: alēthōs theou huios ēn houtos — truly Son of God he was
notes.rendering: Truly this was the Son of God!
notes.why: The centurion's confession closes a thread that began at the baptism (3:17: this is my Son), continued through the Transfiguration (17:5: this is my Son), was demanded at the trial (26:63: are you the Son of God?), and was mocked at the cross (27:40, 43: if you are the Son of God). Now, in the moment of death — the darkness, the earthquake, the cry from the cross — a Gentile soldier and his men see it: alēthōs theou huios ēn houtos. Truly this was the Son of God. Not the Jewish high priest, not the religious establishment, not the crowd that demanded crucifixion — but a Roman centurion at the foot of the cross. Matthew completes his Gospel's pattern: the Magi from the east, the centurion of Capernaum, and now this soldier — the Gentiles see what Israel's leaders cannot.

outro: Note on Matthew 25–27 as the judgment and passion movement: These three chapters move from the final judgment parables (who will be ready? who will invest? who will feed the hungry?) to the passion narrative where Jesus himself becomes the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the imprisoned. The sheep and goats parable (25:31–46) and the passion (chapters 26–27) are mirror images: in one, the nations are judged for what they did or did not do to the least; in the other, Jesus is delivered over, stripped, mocked, and killed by the nations. The one who will judge from the throne (25:31) is the one being spat on and crucified. The king who identifies himself with the least of these (25:40) is himself becoming the least — the one crucified between robbers, mocked by all, forsaken by God in Aramaic from a cross.

intro: Matthew 28 is the shortest chapter in the Gospel — twenty verses — and the most theologically concentrated. The resurrection is announced by an angel on a rolled-away stone. The risen Jesus meets the women on the road and then the eleven on the mountain. The Gospel closes with the Great Commission and with the final promise that answers the opening declaration of chapter 1. The Emmanuel who was promised is now the Presence who remains.

notes.original: seismos megas — great earthquake; he idea autou hōs astrapē — like lightning
notes.rendering: a great earthquake… his appearance like lightning, his clothing white as snow
notes.why: Matthew’s resurrection scene is the most dramatic in the four Gospels — unique in its earthquake (seismos megas — the same word as the earthquake at the crucifixion, 27:51), its angel descending from heaven, and the guards becoming like dead men (egenethēsan hōs nekroi). The imagery is theophanic — an appearance of divine power in the mode of Sinai. The soldiers who had been set to prevent the disciples from stealing the body are rendered useless by the very presence they were sent to guard against.

notes.original: kratēsasai autou tous podas kai prosekyēnesan autō — grasping his feet, worshipping
notes.rendering: they take hold of his feet and worship him
notes.why: The women grasping the feet of the risen Jesus and worshipping (prosekyēnesan) completes the posture of worship that runs through Matthew: the Magi who prostrate before the infant (2:11), the disciples who worship at the sea (14:33). Now the first witnesses of the resurrection fall at his feet. The physical detail — his feet — is significant: this is not a vision but a bodily encounter. The commission he gives them makes the women the first messengers of the resurrection.

notes.original: hoi de edistasan — but some doubted
notes.rendering: but some doubt
notes.why: Hoi de edistasan — but some doubted, hesitated, were uncertain (from distazō — to stand in two places, to be of two minds). The admission is remarkable: in the final resurrection appearance of the risen Jesus, on the mountain to which he had directed them, some of the eleven still doubt. Matthew does not resolve this or explain it away. The Great Commission is given to a group that includes doubters. Jesus does not wait for the doubt to be resolved before commissioning them.

notes.original: edothē moi pasa exousia en ouranō kai epi gēs — authority given, not seized
notes.rendering: all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me
notes.why: Edothē — was given, passive. The resurrection authority is received, not asserted by force. The contrast with Satan’s offer in 4:8–9 is precise: the devil offered all the kingdoms of the world if Jesus would worship him. Jesus refused — and here, through the cross and resurrection, receives the authority the devil offered. Pasa exousia — all authority, complete authority, in heaven and on earth. The Great Commission flows from this claim.

notes.original: eis to onoma tou patros kai tou huiou kai tou hagiou pneumatos — one name, three persons
notes.rendering: in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
notes.why: Eis to onoma — into the name, in the name. The word onoma is singular — one name — shared by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit together. This is Matthew’s most developed theological statement about the identity of the God into whose name disciples are baptised. The relational language — Father, Son, Holy Spirit — identifies the three not by their attributes but by their relationships to each other.

notes.original: egō meth’ hymōn eimi pasas tas hēmeras — the Emmanuel bookend
notes.rendering: I am with you always, to the end of the age
notes.why: The final words of Matthew’s Gospel answer the first theological declaration: in 1:23, the angel tells Joseph to name the child Emmanuel — ‘God with us.’ Now the risen Jesus says: I am with you all the days, to the completion of the age. The meth’ hymōn (with you) of 1:23 is now the meth’ hymōn eimi (I am with you) of 28:20. The Gospel that opened with Emmanuel closes with the risen God who promises to be with us always.

outro: Note on the mountains of Matthew: The Gospel is shaped by five mountains — each a scene of revelation and commission. The Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7), the Mount of Transfiguration (chapter 17), the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25), and now the mountain in Galilee (28:16). Matthew’s Jesus is the new Moses — but the difference is the closing promise: Moses died on the mountain; Jesus commissions from the mountain and then remains.

intro: Micah 1 opens with a cosmic theophany — YHWH descending, mountains melting like wax, valleys splitting — and applies it to the specific political situation of the eighth century. The prophet then performs a grief-march through the towns of the Shephelah, punning on each place name in a series of wordplays that is virtually untranslatable.

notes.original: Micha haMorashti — Micah the Morashtite
notes.rendering: Micah of Moresheth
notes.why: Moresheth was a town in the Shephelah — the agricultural lowlands between Jerusalem and the coastal plain. Micah is a rural prophet, not a court prophet. His social location shapes everything: the rulers and land-grabbers he attacks in chapters 2–3 are the Jerusalem elite; his perspective is the village farmer's. He is contemporary with Isaiah but sees the world from below rather than from the palace.

notes.original: mah pisha Ya'aqov halo Shomron — what is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria?
notes.rendering: what is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria?
notes.why: The question-and-answer format concentrates the accusation: the capital cities are the sources of the infection that has spread to the whole nation. Samaria for the north (Jacob/Israel), Jerusalem for the south (Judah). Both are idolatrous; both will fall. Micah levels his accusation at the centres of power, not the periphery.

notes.original: the Shephelah lament — place-name wordplays
notes.rendering: the series of town-names with punning accusations
notes.why: Micah performs a grief-march through towns of his home region, playing on each name: Gath (gat — tell; do not tell it in Tell-town); Beth-le-aphrah (house of dust — roll in the dust); Shaphir (beauty — pass on in nakedness and shame); Zaanan (yatza — go out; the going-out town will not go out); Maroth (bitter things — wait for good but disaster comes); Lachish (rechesh — swift horse; harness the horse); Achzib (achzav — deception; the houses of Deception will deceive); Mareshah (yoresh — heir/conqueror; a conqueror comes to Heir-town); Adullam (the cave where David fled). The wordplays are the lament's substance: each town's name becomes its epitaph.

intro: Micah 2 opens with the sharpest social indictment in the book: the powerful lie awake at night devising ways to seize the land. The Mosaic land theology is the background: each family's inheritance (nachalah) was given by YHWH and was not meant to be accumulated by the powerful. Micah is not a socialist avant la lettre but a Mosaic covenanter.

notes.original: choshvei aven u'po'alei ra al mishkevotam — those who devise wickedness on their beds
notes.rendering: woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds
notes.why: The indictment is precise about the planning: they think it through at night (on their beds) and execute it by morning. The sequence from intention to action is the definition of deliberate sin. What they seize is fields (sadot) and houses (batim) — the basic units of agricultural life — and specifically nachalah, inheritance, the covenanted portion of each family in the land YHWH gave. The land-grab violates not just property rights but covenant theology.

notes.original: poretz — the one who breaks through
notes.rendering: he who opens the breach will go up before them
notes.why: The sudden shift from judgment to salvation at 2:12 is one of Micah's characteristic structural moves: indictment, then promise. The Poretz — the Breacher, the one who breaks open the way — is the divine warrior going before his people as a shepherd leads a flock out through the gate. The image will be developed in 4:6–7 and 5:2–4. YHWH at their head (b'rosham YHWH) is the culmination: not just a human leader but the divine presence as vanguard.

intro: Micah 3 is the book's most concentrated indictment — rulers, priests, and prophets all named together as the triple corruption of Judah's leadership. The chapter closes with the most devastating prophetic utterance Micah speaks: Zion shall be ploughed as a field. This verse was remembered over a century later when Jeremiah faced a similar charge (Jeremiah 26:18).

notes.original: ochle she'er ami — those who eat the flesh of my people
notes.rendering: who eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them, and break their bones in pieces
notes.why: The imagery of cannibalism is a sustained metaphor for economic predation: the rulers are consuming the people they should protect. The sequence — tear the skin, strip flesh from bones, chop up like meat, cook in a cauldron — follows the stages of butchering an animal. Applied to human beings it is deliberately horrifying. Micah does not soften the accusation: the language is designed to make the listener recoil and then recognise what the polite language of 'taxation' and 'land acquisition' actually describes.

notes.original: v'ulam anochi male'ti koach et ruach YHWH — but as for me I am filled with power, with the Spirit of YHWH
notes.rendering: but as for me, I am filled with power, with the Spirit of YHWH, and with justice and might
notes.why: The contrast is absolute: the false prophets prophesy for pay and see nothing (v.6–7); Micah is filled (male'ti — I am full, I am filled) with power (koach), Spirit of YHWH, justice (mishpat), and might (gevurah). The fourfold endowment is the prophetic commission: not a special gift he sought but a filling he received. The declaration is the ground for the oracle that follows — the most radical Micah will speak.

notes.original: Tzion sadeh techaresh — Zion shall be ploughed as a field
notes.rendering: Zion shall be ploughed as a field
notes.why: The most radical verse in Micah. Jerusalem — the city of YHWH's choice, the site of the temple, the political and religious centre of Judah — will be reduced to agricultural land. Jeremiah 26:18 quotes this verse by name when Jeremiah faces a death sentence for his own temple speech, and the elders cite Micah's precedent to save him. The oracle was not just remembered but canonised as prophetic courage: Micah said what no court prophet would say, and it proved true.

intro: Micah 4 contains the swords-into-ploughshares oracle shared almost word-for-word with Isaiah 2:2–4. Whether Micah quotes Isaiah, Isaiah quotes Micah, or both draw on a common tradition is debated. What is certain is that the oracle was sufficiently important to be preserved in both collections. Chapter 4 also names Babylon explicitly (v.10) — an eighth-century prophet anticipating the Babylonian exile a century before it happened.

notes.original: v'chittu charvotam l'ittim — and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares
notes.rendering: they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning hooks
notes.why: The image is from agricultural metalwork: the same iron that makes a sword makes a ploughshare; the same bronze that makes a spear makes a pruning hook. The instruments of destruction are converted into instruments of cultivation — not destroyed but repurposed. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation (goy el goy cherev) is the negative formulation; neither shall they learn war anymore (v'lo yilmedu od milchamah) adds the educational dimension: the curriculum of violence ceases. The vision is not of armed peacekeeping but of transformed human community.

notes.original: v'yashvu ish tachat gapno v'tachat te'enato — they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree
notes.rendering: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid
notes.why: The image of the vine and fig tree is the Bible's recurring picture of secure agrarian life (cf. 1 Kings 4:25; Zechariah 3:10).
