Overlooking an offense is an act of magnanimity, not weakness.

intro: Proverbs 20 includes some of the collection's most quietly profound theological observations. Verse 5 on drawing out the deep purposes of the heart, verse 9 on the impossibility of perfect self-purification, verse 24 on the mystery of human direction, and verse 27 on the spirit as YHWH's lamp — these are not mere practical wisdom but reflections on the inner architecture of the human person.

notes.original: mayim amuqqim eitzah belev ish — a plan in a man's heart is deep water
notes.rendering: The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out
notes.why: Mayim amuqqim — deep waters, the water of the cistern's bottom or the well's source, not visible from the surface. Eitzah — counsel, purpose, the inner deliberation (the same root as in 19:21 — the counsel of YHWH that stands). The person of understanding (tevunah — the capacity for discernment) will draw it up (dalah — to draw water from a well; the effort of lowering a bucket into depth). The image is of the wise counselor who can probe beneath the surface presentation to find what is actually driving another person.

notes.original: mi yomar zikiti libbi — who can say I have made my heart clean
notes.rendering: Who can say, 'I have kept my heart pure; I am clean from my sin'?
notes.why: The question expects the answer: no one. It is one of Proverbs' rare moments of radical anthropological honesty. Zikiti libbi — I have made my heart pure (zakah — to be clean, to be pure, used for moral purity). The question is posed not to produce despair but to cut off the self-righteousness that the collection occasionally seems to encourage. Even the righteous are not purely righteous. The fear of YHWH is appropriate partly because of this.

notes.original: nishmat adam ner YHWH — the spirit of man is YHWH's lamp
notes.rendering: The spirit of man is YHWH's lamp, searching all his innermost parts
notes.why: Nishmat adam — the breath of man, the life-breath (neshamah — the breath breathed into Adam in Genesis 2:7; the animating presence of life). Ner YHWH — YHWH's lamp. YHWH searches the human interior using the human's own spirit as the light source. Chophes — searching (chaphas — to search, to seek out, to probe). The innermost parts (chadreh baten — rooms of the belly, the deepest inner chambers). The proverb suggests that the human capacity for self-examination is not autonomous; it is the divine light working from within.

intro: Proverbs 21 opens with a magnificent image of divine sovereignty (v. 1) and closes with an equally vivid one (v. 31). Between them it weaves together proverbs on justice, generosity, domestic life, and the limits of human power. Verse 3 is the prophetic tradition's claim in proverbial form: righteousness over sacrifice.

notes.original: palgei mayim lev melech — like channels of water is the heart of a king
notes.rendering: A king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of YHWH; he turns it wherever he will
notes.why: Palgei mayim — channels of water, the irrigation channels that a farmer digs and redirects to water different fields (peleg — a watercourse, an artificial channel). The king's heart — the most powerful individual will in the ancient world — is, in YHWH's hand, no more fixed than a water channel. Yattenu — he turns it (natah — to turn, to incline, to stretch out). The image does not erase the king's agency; it frames it within a sovereignty that moves all things as easily as a farmer redirects water.

notes.original: asot tzedaqah umishpat nivchar laYHWH mizevach — to do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to YHWH than sacrifice
notes.rendering: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to YHWH than sacrifice
notes.why: Tzedaqah — righteousness, right relationship (moral alignment with YHWH's character). Mishpat — justice, right judgment in the public sphere. Nivchar — is more chosen, is preferred (bachar — to choose, to elect, to prefer deliberately). The proverb places this in the same tradition as 1 Samuel 15:22 (obedience over sacrifice), Amos 5:21–24 (YHWH despising worship without justice), and Micah 6:8 (what YHWH requires). This is not a rejection of sacrifice per se but a clear ordering of priorities.

notes.original: hassus muchan leyom milchamah — the horse is prepared for the day of battle
notes.rendering: The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to YHWH
notes.why: The horse was the supreme military technology of the ancient world — the armoured tank of antiquity, requiring enormous resources to acquire and maintain. Prepare it you must (the proverb is not pacifist). But teshu'ah — the deliverance, the victory (yeshua — salvation, the noun that gives Jesus his name) — belongs to YHWH. The proverb closes the chapter at the boundary between what human preparation can do and what it cannot. Prepare well; do not trust the preparation.

intro: Proverbs 22 closes the great Solomonic collection (10:1–22:16) and opens a new section at verse 17: the 'Words of the Wise' — a distinct collection, likely related to Egyptian wisdom texts (the Instruction of Amenemope). The thirty sayings announced in verse 20 run from 22:17 to 24:22.

notes.original: shem tov livchar me'osher rav — a good name is more desirable than great wealth
notes.rendering: A good name is more desirable than great riches, and favor more desirable than silver or gold
notes.why: Shem tov — a good name, a good reputation (shem — name, but in the Semitic world the name is the person's essential identity and social standing; a name carries a family's honor across generations). Nivchar — more chosen, more desirable (bachar — to choose deliberately). The proverb does not say wealth is worthless; it says reputation is more worth choosing. Chen — grace, favor (the social quality of being welcomed by others). The ranking places character above capital.

notes.original: chanoch lana'ar al pi darko — train up a child in his way
notes.rendering: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it
notes.why: Chanoch — train, dedicate, initiate (chanak — to dedicate, to initiate; the same root as Hanukkah — the dedication of the temple). Al pi darko — according to the mouth of his way (the idiom means 'suited to his way,' 'according to his own path'). The phrase is ambiguous: it may mean 'train him in the right way' or 'train him according to his own particular bent.' Many commentators favor the second: wisdom is not one-size instruction but formation that attends to the individual child.

notes.original: halo katavti lecha shlishom — have I not written for you thirty sayings
notes.rendering: Have I not written for you thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge
notes.why: Shlishom — thirty (the word has been debated; some manuscripts read sheloshim — thirty; this is now widely accepted and corresponds to the thirty sections identifiable in 22:17–24:22). The number connects this section to Egyptian wisdom literature — specifically the Instruction of Amenemope, which also has thirty chapters. The parallels are close enough to suggest literary dependence, though the biblical text reframes the material theologically around the fear of YHWH. Israel did not refuse wisdom from Egypt; it baptized it.

intro: Proverbs 23 is the most varied chapter in the Words of the Wise section — moving through table manners, wealth, poverty, education, filial love, envy, and temperance before landing in the extended and darkly funny portrait of the drunkard (vv. 29–35). The latter is one of the most vivid pieces of comic writing in the Hebrew Bible.

notes.original: hata'uf einecha bo ve'einennu — when your eyes fly to it, it is gone
notes.rendering: When your eyes light on it, it is gone, for suddenly it sprouts wings, flying like an eagle toward heaven
notes.why: The image of wealth growing wings is one of the most memorable in the book. Kiy asoh ya'aseh lo kenafahim — for it will certainly make itself wings. The eagle (nesher — the great eagle or griffon vulture, the most powerful bird in the region) is the simile for how rapidly and effortlessly wealth departs. The lesson: before you wear yourself out acquiring it, understand its nature. It is not a stable possession. It is a bird.

notes.original: ki im yesh acharit — for surely there is a future
notes.rendering: For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off
notes.why: Acharit — a future, an end, an outcome (the same word used in 5:4 for the bitter end of the forbidden woman). Here it is positive: your acharit — your future, your ultimate outcome — is secure if you remain in the fear of YHWH. Tiqvatecha lo tikkaret — your hope will not be cut off. The verse answers the envious glance at sinners who appear to prosper: the righteous person has a secured future that the sinner does not. The perspective is eschatological, not immediate.

notes.original: lami oy lami avoy — who has woe? Who has sorrow?
notes.rendering: Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife?
notes.why: The poem is a tour de force of descriptive intoxication: the interrogation (six rhetorical questions in v. 29), the description of wine (v. 31 — looking, sparkling, smooth), the sting (v. 32 — the serpent bite arrives after the swallowing), the hallucinations (v. 33), the disorientation (v. 34 — lying on the mast top, on the open sea, the most dangerous posture), and the punchline (v. 35 — I feel no pain; where is the next drink?). It is simultaneously a warning and a portrait of addiction's logic that could have been written yesterday.

intro: Proverbs 24 concludes the Words of the Wise (vv. 1–22) and adds a shorter appendix (vv. 23–34). The chapter contains the book's most explicit call to social courage (vv. 11–12), one of its finest recovery proverbs (v. 16), and a brief meditation on mercy toward enemies (vv. 17–18) that anticipates the New Testament's logic of enemy-love.

notes.original: hatzeil lequchim lamaveth — rescue those being taken to death
notes.rendering: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter
notes.why: Lequchim — those being taken (passive participle — the ones being seized, the ones being led). The verse demands active intervention on behalf of the condemned. The follow-up (v. 12) cuts off the comfortable excuse 'we did not know.' Lo yadanu zeh — we did not know this. The response: does not he who weighs hearts see? The proverb will not allow bystander passivity to shelter behind ignorance. Social courage is not optional for the wise.

notes.original: ki sheva yipol tzaddik vaqam — for the righteous falls seven times and rises
notes.rendering: For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity
notes.why: The proverb is one of the most encouraging in the collection. Sheva — seven (the number of completeness: not merely multiple times but as many times as it takes). Yipol tzaddik — the righteous one falls (naphil — the same verb used for the fallen woman in Amos 5:2; here, the righteous is the one who falls but is not defined by the fall). Vaqam — and rises (qum — to arise, the resurrection word). The contrast: the wicked stumble only once (b'ra'ah — in calamity) and there is no rising. Seven falls and seven risings; the wicked do not rise.

notes.original: sephatayyim yishaq meshiv devarim nechochim — lips will be kissed for honest answers
notes.rendering: Whoever gives an honest answer kisses the lips
notes.why: The proverb is dense and vivid: an honest answer (devarim nechochim — right words, words that correspond to reality) is an act of intimacy — as close as a kiss. The image of a kiss on the lips is used elsewhere in the Song of Songs for erotic closeness. Here wisdom uses it for the intimacy of honesty. A true word given in the right moment creates the same closeness as a kiss: it is the right thing given at the right distance. The proverb is one of the most beautiful in the book.

notes.original: ʿaṯəqû / ʾanšê Ḥizqiyyāhû
notes.rendering: the men of Hezekiah copied out
notes.why: ʿtq means 'to transfer/move'; Hezekiah's scribal project (c. 715–686 BC) preserved these proverbs

notes.original: kāḇôḏ ʾĕlōhîm / kāḇôḏ mĕlāḵîm
notes.rendering: God's glory to conceal / king's glory to search
notes.why: Beautiful contrast: God hides; kings investigate. Pastoral rendering keeps the paradox intact

notes.original: dāḇār dāḇûr ʿal-ʾopnāyw
notes.rendering: a word well spoken at the right moment
notes.why: ʾopnāyw = 'its wheels/turnings' — idiom for the right occasion; golden apples = tapûaḥ, debated (quince? citrus?)

notes.original: ṣinnāṯ-šeleḡ bəyôm qāṣîr
notes.rendering: cool of snow at harvest time
notes.why: Not literal snow — likely snow-cooled water brought down from mountains; harvest = summer heat

notes.original: maʿădeh-beged bəyôm qārāh
notes.rendering: like pouring vinegar on a wound
notes.why: MT: 'removing a garment on a cold day'; LXX and context suggest wound/natron reading; most scholars prefer wound

notes.original: gāḥālîm ʾattāh ḥōṯeh ʿal-rōʾšô
notes.rendering: heap burning coals on his head
notes.why: Ambiguous: shame/conviction (Egyptian ritual), or warmth/kindness melting hostility. Paul cites it in Romans 12 — likely the latter

notes.original: Verses 4–5 (answer/don't answer)
notes.rendering: Don't answer… Answer…
notes.why: Deliberately paradoxical pair — the tension is the teaching: wisdom knows which moment calls for which response

notes.original: ṣərôr ʾeḇen bəmargēmāh
notes.rendering: tying a stone in a sling
notes.why: The stone can't be thrown — it's locked in uselessly. Honoring a fool is similarly self-defeating

notes.original: raḇ məḥôlēl kōl / śōḵēr kəsîl
notes.rendering: archer who wounds / hires a fool
notes.why: MT is difficult; raḇ can mean 'archer' or 'master.' Best reading: whoever hires randomly wounds everyone

notes.original: kəkeḇel šāḇ ʿal-qēʾô
notes.rendering: dog returns to its vomit
notes.why: Visceral image retained — 2 Peter 2:22 quotes this directly

notes.original: bəʾeyn ʿēṣîm tiḵbeh-ʾēš
notes.rendering: no wood, no fire
notes.why: A two-word proverb in Hebrew; the parallel with gossip/quarrel is explicit and devastating

notes.original: kesep siḡîm
notes.rendering: cheap glaze on an earthen pot
notes.why: siḡîm = slag/dross; the word plays on silver (kesep) — this is fake silver coating. Modern: paint over rot

notes.original: ʾal-titəhalēl bəyôm māḥār
notes.rendering: don't boast about tomorrow
notes.why: James 4:13–15 echoes this. māḥār = 'tomorrow'; the limitation is human — God knows; we don't

notes.original: tôḇāh tôkaḥaṯ məguллāh
notes.rendering: open rebuke is better than hidden love
notes.why: məgullāh = uncovered/exposed; the rebuke you can see and feel is more valuable than love that stays quiet

notes.original: neʾĕmānîm piṣṣê ʾôhēḇ
notes.rendering: wounds of a friend can be trusted
notes.why: neʾĕmānîm = faithful/trustworthy; nəšîqôṯ śônēʾ = kisses of an enemy. The enemy's affection is deceptive excess

notes.original: barzel bəḇarzel yiḥad
notes.rendering: iron sharpens iron
notes.why: One of the most-quoted proverbs in the book. yiḥad = 'sharpens'; the image is friction producing an edge

notes.original: kamayim happānîm lappānîm
notes.rendering: as water reflects a face
notes.why: Literally 'as water face to face, so the heart of a man to man' — a remarkable insight into empathy and mirroring

notes.original: niḵbāḏ bəhallĕlô
notes.rendering: a man is tested by his praise
notes.why: How does a man handle praise? That reveals him. Alternate: 'tested by what he praises' — both readings valid

notes.original: kəḵapîr yiḇṭaḥ
notes.rendering: bold as a lion
notes.why: ḵapîr = young lion at full strength; the righteous don’t startle because they have nothing to hide

notes.original: tōm dərāḵāyw
notes.rendering: walking in integrity / twisted in his ways
notes.why: tōm = wholeness/completeness; ʾiqqēš = perverse/crooked. The contrast is totality: integrated vs. fractured character

notes.original: bənešeḵ ûḇəṯarḇîṯ
notes.rendering: interest and profit
notes.why: Both terms refer to lending at interest (prohibited from Israelite to Israelite in Torah); what’s exploited returns to those who give freely

notes.original: məkasseh pəšāʿāyw
notes.rendering: conceals / confesses and forsakes
notes.why: One of Proverbs’ clearest grace-notes: confession + abandonment = mercy. Luther loved this verse

notes.original: ʿōšēq bəḏam-nāpeš
notes.rendering: weighted down by bloodguilt
notes.why: A fugitive murderer; the command not to help is not cruelty but justice — don’t shield the guilty

notes.original: maṣṭîr ʿênāyw
notes.rendering: shut your eyes to them
notes.why: Literally ‘hides his eyes’ from the poor — willful blindness; not ignorance but refusal

notes.original: maqšeh-ʿorpô
notes.rendering: stiff-necked
notes.why: Classic OT idiom for stubborn refusal; yiššāḇēr = ‘will be shattered’ — the image is a ceramic vessel, not a tree

notes.original: rûḥô yəšallēaḥ
notes.rendering: gives full vent to his spirit
notes.why: yəšallēaḥ = sends it out completely; contrast with the wise man who ‘stills’ it. Full emotional discharge vs. regulation

notes.original: ḥāzôn / tôrāh
notes.rendering: vision / law
notes.why: ḥāzôn = prophetic revelation; tôrāh = instruction/law. The verse pairs prophetic word with covenant law — both needed for ordered community

notes.original: mənunnāq menoʿar
notes.rendering: pamper from childhood / ungrateful
notes.why: Final word (mānôn) is obscure — hapax legomenon; ancient translators disagreed. Context suggests an ungrateful/insolent outcome

notes.original: ḥerdaṯ-ʾādām môqēš
notes.rendering: fear of man is a snare
notes.why: môqēš = trap/snare; the proverb cuts both ways: it’s not just cowardice but misplaced ultimate trust. Cf. 1:7

notes.original: tôʿăḇaṯ rəšāʿîm
notes.rendering: abomination to the wicked
notes.why: The word tôʿēḇāh (abomination) appears in reverse: the righteous man is an abomination to the wicked. The feeling is mutual and cosmic

notes.original: nəʾum haggeber / wəʾiyṯāl
notes.rendering: Agur / oracle
notes.why: Agur is otherwise unknown; some MSS read these as common nouns (‘I am weary’ / ‘I have been consumed’) rather than names — both are valid

notes.original: mah-šəmô ûmah-šem-bənô
notes.rendering: what is his name / his son’s name
notes.why: This rhetorical question anticipates NT Christology to many readers; in context it’s a humble ‘we cannot know’ about the Creator

notes.original: kol-ʾimraṯ ʾĕlôah ṣərûpāh
notes.rendering: every word of God is pure
notes.why: ṣārûp = refined metal; Ps 12:6 uses the same image for God’s words as silver refined seven times

notes.original: leḥem ḥuqqî
notes.rendering: bread I need / my allotted bread
notes.why: ḥuqqî = portion/statute; this is the OT precedent for the Lord’s Prayer petition ‘give us this day our daily bread’

notes.original: lāʿălûqāh šətê ḇānôṯ
notes.rendering: leech has two daughters: Give! Give!
notes.why: lāʿălûqāh = leech (hapax); the bloodsucker’s children are insatiable demand — a dark proverb that opens a series of ‘never-enough’ observations

notes.original: derek geber bəʿalmāh
notes.rendering: way of a man with a young woman
notes.why: ʿalmāh = young woman of marriageable age (same word as Isa 7:14); the ‘wonder’ here is intimacy — it leaves no trace, like the others in the list

notes.original: diḇrêLəmûʾēl melek maśśāʾ
notes.rendering: Lemuel king of Massa
notes.why: Lemuel is unknown in other OT texts; Massa may be an Arabian tribe (cf. 30:1). Some ancient tradition identified Lemuel with Solomon, and his mother as Bathsheba

notes.original: tənû-šēkār ləʾôḇēḏ
notes.rendering: give strong drink to the one who is perishing
notes.why: Not a general endorsement of alcohol; the contrast with the king (vv. 4–5) is deliberate: what ruins a ruler may mercifully numb the dying

notes.original: ʾēšeṯ ḥayil
notes.rendering: woman of valor
notes.why: ḥayil = strength, valor, military might (same word used of mighty warriors); this is not a gentle domestic portrait — she is formidable

notes.original: kappāh pārəśāh leʿānî
notes.rendering: opens her hand to the poor
notes.why: The hand that works (v. 19, distaff) opens to the poor (v. 20) — the sequence is intentional: productivity enables generosity

notes.original: wattişḥaq ləyôm ʾaḥărôn
notes.rendering: she laughs at the time to come
notes.why: Not mocking anxiety but fearless confidence; the same verb (śḥq) used of Sarah’s laughter — here it is trust, not disbelief

notes.original: ʾiššāh yirʾaṯ-YHWH
notes.rendering: a woman who fears the Lord
notes.why: The entire book begins (1:7) with ‘the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ and ends here with a woman who embodies it. The frame is intentional and glorious

intro: Psalm 1 functions as a preface to the entire Psalter. It sets out the fundamental contrast — the righteous man rooted like a tree, the wicked like windblown chaff — and introduces the governing question of the book: What does it look like to live before God? The psalm has no title and no named author, which is likely deliberate: it speaks for everyone.

notes.original: ashrei ha’ish — happy/blessed is the man
notes.rendering: Blessed is the one who does not walk...
notes.why: Ashrei is not the word for divinely bestowed blessing (barukh); it is the wisdom-literature word for the happiness of the one whose life is rightly ordered. The threefold descent — walk, stand, sit — traces increasing entanglement with the wicked. Each posture is more settled than the last.

notes.original: uvtoroto yeh’geh yomam valayla — and in his Torah he meditates day and night
notes.rendering: his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night
notes.why: Hagah — to meditate, mutter, murmur (the sound of quiet recitation). Torah study in the ancient world was done aloud. The righteous man’s lips are always moving. The word is also used of a lion growling over prey (Isa. 31:4) and a dove cooing (Isa. 38:14): full, absorbed attention.

notes.original: k’etz shatul — like a tree transplanted/planted
notes.rendering: He is like a tree planted beside streams of water
notes.why: Shatul — transplanted rather than self-seeded; deliberately placed where the water is. The image is of intentional rootedness. The streams (peleg — irrigation channels, the man-made channels that distribute river water) are not the chaos of a flood but the steady supply of ordered nourishment.

intro: Psalm 2 is a royal enthronement psalm — probably used at coronations in Jerusalem — and became one of the most cited psalms in the New Testament. It opens in the political theater of rebelling nations and closes with a beatitude: blessed are those who take refuge in the king. The structural movement — from chaos to coronation to decree to warning — is perfectly shaped.

notes.original: al YHWH v’al m’shikho — against the LORD and against his anointed
notes.rendering: against the LORD and against his anointed
notes.why: Mashiach — anointed one. The anointing of the king with oil made him the LORD’s representative on earth. In later tradition this term became the title for the ultimate Davidic king (the Messiah). Acts 4:25–27, Heb. 1:5, and Rev. 2:27 all read this psalm as fulfilled in Jesus.

notes.original: yoshev bashamayim yiskhak — the one sitting in heaven laughs
notes.rendering: The one enthroned in heaven laughs
notes.why: Sakhak — to laugh, to mock. The divine laughter is not comedy but cosmic disdain: the rebels’ conspiracy against the LORD is so absurd that the appropriate response is derision. The contrast between the frantic plotting of the nations (v.1) and the serene laughter of the enthroned God is one of the great tonal contrasts in the Psalter.

notes.original: nashku bar — kiss the son (or: pay homage to purity)
notes.rendering: Pay homage to the son
notes.why: The phrase is famously difficult: bar in Hebrew can mean son (an Aramaic form) or purity/cleanliness. Most modern translations read "kiss the son" (a gesture of submission). The ambiguity may be deliberate. The verse ends with the psalm’s surprise: blessed are all who take refuge in him — the same word used of sheltering from storms. The threatening king becomes the refuge.

intro: Psalm 3 is the first of the lament psalms and the first psalm with a superscription (mizmor l’David). It establishes the pattern of the individual lament: crisis, confidence in God, appeal, and assurance. The superscription linking it to Absalom’s rebellion (2 Samuel 15–17) gives it a specific historical gravity, though the psalm can be prayed by anyone who wakes to enemies they cannot number.

notes.original: magen ba’adi — shield around/before me
notes.rendering: you, LORD, are a shield around me
notes.why: Magen — a small round shield, the personal combat shield (distinct from the full-body tzinnah). The around is ba’adi — about/around me, encircling. The progression in v.3 is striking: shield (protection), glory (honor restored), and lifter of my head (dignity — the bowed-head posture of the humiliated man is reversed).

notes.original: shakhavti va’ishah — I lay down and slept
notes.rendering: I lie down and sleep; I wake again, because the LORD sustains me
notes.why: The perfect tense here functions as a testimony: I lay down (when surrounded by armies) and I slept. The miracle is the sleep, not the waking. The one who sustains (samakh — to support, undergird, hold up) makes the rest possible. Sleep in the midst of enemies is a theological statement.

notes.original: l’YHWH hayeshu’ah — to the LORD belongs deliverance/salvation
notes.rendering: From the LORD comes deliverance
notes.why: The psalm’s thesis in four words. Yeshu’ah — salvation, deliverance, rescue (the same root as the name Yeshua/Jesus). The psalm moves from “many” (foes) in v.1 to “many” (people) in v.8: the enemies who threatened are answered by the community that receives blessing.

intro: Psalm 4 is an evening counterpart to Psalm 3 (which is a morning prayer). It moves from urgent appeal to quiet confidence, ending with one of the most serene closing lines in the Psalter. The psalm addresses two audiences: God (vv.1, 6–8) and the powerful who oppress (vv.2–5). The middle passage is closest to Wisdom literature — the psalmist rebukes and instructs.

notes.original: Elohei tzidki — God of my righteousness
notes.rendering: O God of my righteousness
notes.why: The phrase is unusual — not God who is righteous, but God who is the source and vindicator of the psalmist’s righteousness, the God who makes his case right. This is forensic language: the psalmist’s cause is in God’s hands, and he is the defendant seeking acquittal.

notes.original: rigzu v’al tekhet’u — tremble/be angry and do not sin
notes.rendering: Tremble and do not sin
notes.why: Ragaz — to tremble, to be agitated (with anger or fear). The Septuagint reads “be angry,” which Paul quotes in Ephesians 4:26. The Hebrew is ambiguous in the best way: both anger and trembling before God can be starting points for either sin or restraint. The command is: whatever you feel, do not sin. Silence on your beds is the path to discernment.

notes.original: l’vadad YHWH labetach toshiveni — for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety
notes.rendering: for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety
notes.why: L’vadad — alone, only (the word of singularity and sufficiency). The peace of the final verse is not the peace of favorable circumstances — the troubles mentioned in the psalm are still present — but the peace of the one who has entrusted those circumstances to the only one who can actually secure them.

intro: Psalm 5 is a morning lament — the psalmist prays at dawn, then waits. Its structure contrasts the worshipper who enters the temple by grace with the wicked who cannot stand in God’s presence. The middle section (vv.9–10) contains some of the most visceral speech in the Psalter, quoted by Paul in Romans 3 as evidence of universal sinfulness.

notes.original: boqer tishma’ qoli — in the morning you will hear my voice
notes.rendering: In the morning, LORD, you hear my voice
notes.why: The morning context is structural: Psalm 3 is flight, Psalm 4 is evening rest, Psalm 5 is morning prayer. Erukhh l’kha — I arrange/lay out (the word for laying out the showbread, the wood on the altar). The prayer is prepared and offered like a sacrifice, then the posture shifts: wait (tzapah — to watch, to keep watch, the watchman’s posture of alert expectation).

notes.original: qiram pelakh elim — their throat is an open grave
notes.rendering: Their throat is an open grave
notes.why: Paul cites this in Romans 3:13 as part of his catena of Old Testament texts demonstrating universal sinfulness. The Hebrew is precise: an open grave is what waits, gapes, swallows. The throat of the liar is the entrance to destruction. The anatomy of deceit: throat (devouring), tongue (lies), lips (flattery).

notes.original: v’tze’nat’ra k’tzinnah tit’rot’nu — like a shield you surround him with favor
notes.rendering: you surround them with your favor as with a shield
notes.why: Ratzon — favor, delight, good will (the same word used of God’s pleasure in worship, and of the acceptable year of the LORD in Isaiah 61:2). The final image mirrors the shield of Psalm 3:3: the righteous man is encircled not by armor but by divine favor. The poem that opened with groaning closes with being surrounded by blessing.

intro: Psalm 6 is the first of the seven traditional Penitential Psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143). It opens in physical and spiritual extremity — illness, weakness, weeping through the night — and then pivots sharply at verse 8. The turn is not explained: the psalmist simply knows, mid-psalm, that the LORD has heard. The confidence is not the result of circumstances changing but of prayer received.

notes.original: amlal ani — I am languishing/fading
notes.rendering: I am faint
notes.why: Amlal — to droop, fade, wither (used of plants wilting in drought, Isa. 24:4; Joel 1:10). The psalmist uses the vocabulary of vegetative collapse: the irrigated tree of Psalm 1 has become the withering plant. The bones are in agony (nivhalu — terrified, dislocated) — the body itself is in disorder.

notes.original: ad matai — until when / how long?
notes.rendering: How long, LORD, how long?
notes.why: The question ad matai is the lament’s central cry, appearing more than twenty times in the Psalter. It is not an accusation but a complaint born of trust: only the one who believes the LORD can act asks when he will. The repetition — how long, LORD, how long? — doubles the urgency. The silence of God is the deepest pain.

notes.original: suru mimeni kol po’alei aven — depart from me all workers of iniquity
notes.rendering: Away from me, all you who do evil
notes.why: The pivot verse. The enemies have not departed; they are presumably still present. But the psalmist’s inner reality has shifted: shama YHWH qol bik’hiy — the LORD has heard the voice of my weeping. The weeping itself was the prayer. The certainty of the perfect tense (heard, has accepted) enacts the faith that prayer has been received before circumstances confirm it.

intro: Psalm 7 is a psalm of innocence — the psalmist invites judgment, wagering his own life on his integrity. The form is an oath of innocence followed by a summons of the divine judge. The closing trap-imagery (vv.14–16) is one of the Psalter’s finest examples of lex talionis as cosmic principle: the pit dug for another becomes the digger’s own grave.

notes.original: shiggayon l’David — a shiggayon of David
notes.rendering: A shiggaion of David
notes.why: Shiggayon (plural: shigionoth, Hab. 3:1): the term’s meaning is uncertain — possibly from shagah (to wander, to reel), suggesting a wild, irregular poetic form. The psalm has a passionate, almost breathless energy that fits the idea of an impassioned outpouring.

notes.original: bochen libot ukh’layot — testing hearts and kidneys
notes.rendering: who searches hearts and minds
notes.why: Kidneys (k’layot — literally the organ) was the Hebrew locus of emotion and desire, as the heart (lev) was the seat of thought and will. Together they encompass the whole inner life. The divine search reaches both the reasoning mind and the feeling core.

notes.original: bor kara vayakhp’rehu — he dug a pit and hollowed it out
notes.rendering: He digs a pit and scoops it out and then falls into the hole he has made
notes.why: The image appears in Proverbs 26:27 and Ecclesiastes 10:8. It is the retributive principle embedded in creation: evil is structurally self-defeating. The trap-digger always risks being the first to fall in.

intro: Psalm 8 is a creation hymn structured as a perfect frame: the refrain of v.1 returns in v.9, enclosing a meditation on the paradox of human dignity — tiny against the cosmos, yet crowned. Hebrews 2:6–8 reads vv.4–6 as fulfilled in Jesus, the true human who brings creation back under human stewardship.

notes.original: mipiy olelim v’yoneqim — from the mouths of children and nurslings
notes.rendering: Through the praise of children and infants you have established a stronghold
notes.why: Jesus quotes this verse (Matt. 21:16) when the children shout hosanna in the temple and the chief priests object. The divine strength perfected in infant praise is the ultimate inversion of power: the stronghold against enemies is not an army but the babbling of children.

notes.original: ma enosh ki tizk’renu — what is a mortal that you remember him
notes.rendering: what is a human being that you think of him
notes.why: Enosh — the frail, mortal human (distinct from adam, the earthly one, and ish, the social person). The verb zakar — to remember, to keep in mind — carries covenantal weight: God’s remembering is always active, always saving (as in Noah, Gen. 8:1; Rachel, Gen. 30:22).

notes.original: vatekhas’rahu m’at me’Elohim — you made him lack a little from God/divine beings
notes.rendering: You have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings
notes.why: The word is Elohim — God, or divine beings/angels. The ambiguity is deliberate: humanity is not divine, but the gap between human dignity and the divine is only a little. The Septuagint reads angelous — angels — which the author of Hebrews uses Christologically.

intro: Psalms 9 and 10 form an acrostic pair in Hebrew (the aleph-beth runs across both), which is why many ancient manuscripts and the LXX treat them as one psalm. Psalm 9 is the praise half: past victories rehearsed, the enthroned judge celebrated. Psalm 10 is the lament half: where is God now?

notes.original: misgav l’dakh — a stronghold for the crushed
notes.rendering: YHWH is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble
notes.why: Dakh — crushed, beaten down (from dakhah, to crush). The word is rare and forceful. The oppressed are not merely disadvantaged but ground down. Misgav — a high place of refuge, an inaccessible stronghold (the same word in Psalm 46:7). The theological claim: the one who is lowest finds the highest refuge.

notes.original: yode’ei sh’mekha — those who know your name
notes.rendering: Those who know your name trust in you
notes.why: The name of God in Hebrew thought is not a label but a declaration of character. To know the name is to have experienced who God is. The verse makes the logic explicit: knowledge of God’s character produces trust. The psalmist can pray boldly because he knows who he is praying to.

intro: Psalm 10 is the lament pair to Psalm 9. It opens with the most direct possible challenge to God: Why do you hide? Then it catalogues the predatory wicked in devastating detail before turning, in vv.12–18, to confident appeal. The wicked man’s inner monologue (vv.6, 11, 13) is a portrait of practical atheism: God sees nothing, forgets, will not call to account.

notes.original: lamah YHWH ta’amod b’rakhok — why, YHWH, do you stand in the distance
notes.rendering: Why do you stand far off, YHWH? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?
notes.why: The two questions frame the theology of divine hiddenness. The psalm does not deny God’s existence or power — it assumes both. The anguish is precisely that the all-powerful God appears absent. Hester panim — the hiding of the face — is a recurring theme in Psalms and prophets (Isa. 8:17; 45:15).

notes.original: ein Elohim kol mizmotav — God is not in all his schemes
notes.rendering: in all his thoughts there is no room for God
notes.why: This is the biblical definition of the fool (nabal — Ps. 14:1). Not intellectual atheism but practical atheism: life planned, conducted, and justified without reference to God. The wicked man is not an agnostic; he actively excludes God from his calculations.

notes.original: atah ra’ita ki ata amal va’kheas — you have seen, for you look at trouble and grief
notes.rendering: But you, God, see the trouble of the afflicted; you consider their grief
notes.why: The turn. Against the wicked man’s claim (God has forgotten, v.11) stands the psalmist’s counter-claim: you have seen. The invisible God sees the invisible victims. Natun — to give into the hand: to take personal responsibility for. God takes the victim’s cause into his own hands.

intro: Psalm 11 is a short, concentrated psalm of trust in the face of collapse. The dramatic structure is a refusal: the psalmist has been advised to flee (the counsel of practical fear), and he rejects that counsel with a counter-vision of God enthroned. If the foundations shake, the answer is not flight but sight — seeing the one who sits above the chaos.

notes.original: ki hashatatot yeharesun — for the foundations are being torn down
notes.rendering: When the foundations are being destroyed, what can the righteous do?
notes.why: Shahath — foundations, bases (the structural underpinnings of social and moral order). The question is the counsel of despair. The psalm’s answer is implied by the framing: if you know that YHWH is on his throne (v.4), the question changes. The righteous can do what they always do: trust.

notes.original: YHWH b’heikhal kodsho — YHWH in his holy temple
notes.rendering: YHWH is in his holy temple; YHWH is on his heavenly throne
notes.why: The temple and the throne are the same reality: the earthly temple is the footstool of the heavenly throne. The eyes that examine (bkhn — test, examine as a refiner tests metal) miss nothing. The contrast with the practical atheism of Psalm 10 (God has forgotten) is total.

notes.original: pana’mo yikhzu — his face they will see / the upright will see his face
notes.rendering: the upright will see his face
notes.why: The vision of God’s face is the supreme beatitude of the Psalter (cf. Ps. 17:15; 27:4, 8). It is the goal of worship, the hope of the righteous, and the final answer to the hiding of the face (Ps. 10:1). The psalm that opened with the question of what the righteous can do ends with what they will have.

intro: Psalm 12 sets two kinds of speech against each other: the hollow, inflated speech of the powerful (flattery, boasting, manipulation) and the pure, refined words of YHWH. The contrast is metallurgical: human speech is dross, the divine word is silver seven times purified. The psalm ends in paradox — protected by God’s word while the wicked still strut.

notes.original: shav’ yidabru — they speak emptiness/falsehood
notes.rendering: Everyone lies to their neighbor; they flatter with their lips
notes.why: Shav’ — emptiness, vanity, worthlessness (the same word as the third commandment: do not take the LORD’s name in shav’). The lips that speak smoothness (khalaqot — smooth, slippery things) are the lips that say exactly what the listener wants to hear. Flattery in the Psalter is always predatory.

notes.original: mishod aniyim me’anqat evyonim — from the plundering of the poor, from the groaning of the needy
notes.rendering: Because the poor are plundered and the needy groan, I will now arise
notes.why: The divine speech in v.5 is the psalm’s hinge: YHWH himself speaks. The word that rises in response to the plundering and groaning is the same word that cannot be corrupted (v.6). God answers hollow speech with flawless speech. Atah aqum — now I will arise — is the language of the warrior stirring for battle.

notes.original: k’sef tzaruf ba’alil la’aretz m’zuqqaq shiv’atayim — silver purified in a crucible of earth, refined seven times
notes.rendering: like silver purified in a crucible, like gold refined seven times
notes.why: The purification image answers the hollow speech of vv.2–4. Human words are inflated and empty; divine words have been through the fire until nothing remains but pure metal. Seven times — the number of completeness — means fully, finally, without remainder of dross.

intro: Psalm 13 is the perfect compressed lament: six verses that move from the pit to praise. The four-fold “how long” covers every angle of the abandonment — God hiding, the psalmist’s own anguish, the enemy’s triumph. Then the pivot: but I. The darkness does not dissolve; the trust is chosen inside it.

notes.original: ad anah YHWH tishkacheni netzach — how long, YHWH, will you forget me — forever?
notes.rendering: How long, YHWH? Will you forget me forever?
notes.why: The four ad anah — how long — questions are the lament’s engine. They do not deny God’s existence; they insist he is not presently acting. Netzach — forever, perpetually (from the root meaning victory or endurance). The question is whether divine forgetting could be permanent. The rest of the psalm answers: no.

notes.original: va’ani b’khasd’kha vatakhti — but I in your hesed I have trusted
notes.rendering: But I trust in your unfailing love
notes.why: The pivot is the word hesed — covenant love, steadfast loyalty, the love that does not let go. The psalmist does not appeal to his own merit but to the character of God. Hesed is the word for the love that exists precisely because it is not deserved and cannot be forfeited.

intro: Psalm 14 (nearly identical to Psalm 53) is a prophetic indictment of universal moral corruption. Paul quotes vv.1–3 in Romans 3:10–12 as his Old Testament proof of universal sinfulness. The nabal (fool) is not an intellectual atheist but someone whose practical denial of God produces moral ruin.

notes.original: amar naval b’libo ein Elohim — the fool has said in his heart: there is no God
notes.rendering: The fool says in his heart, “There is no God.
notes.why: Naval — the fool, the morally bankrupt (not the intellectually puzzled). The classic example is Nabal in 1 Samuel 25, whose name means fool and whose character confirms it. The denial is not philosophical but existential: I will live as though God does not see, judge, or act. The consequence is systematic corruption of every relationship.

notes.original: YHWH mishhamayim hishqif — YHWH from the heavens has looked down
notes.rendering: YHWH looks down from heaven on all mankind
notes.why: The divine survey (hishqif — to look down from a height, to peer over) answers the practical atheism of v.1. The fool says God does not see; the psalm shows God looking. The survey finds no one who understands (maskil — the person with discernment), no one who seeks. The conclusion is universal: all have turned aside.

intro: Psalm 15 is a liturgical entrance psalm — likely used in conjunction with temple entry, asking who qualifies to worship. Its answer is an ethical portrait rather than a ritual checklist: the one who enters the presence of God is the one whose inner and outer lives are aligned. The psalm ends not with sacrifice but with social ethics.

notes.original: mi yagur b’ohalekha — who will sojourn in your tent
notes.rendering: YHWH, who may dwell in your sacred tent? Who may live on your holy mountain?
notes.why: The question uses two images: ohal (tent — the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary) and har qodsh’kha (your holy mountain — Zion). Both point to the divine dwelling. The gate liturgy reflects a real practice: approaching worshippers were examined (cf. Psalm 24:3–6; Isaiah 33:14–16).

notes.original: nishba l’hara v’lo yamir — who swears to his own hurt and does not change
notes.rendering: who keeps an oath even when it hurts, and does not change their mind
notes.why: This is perhaps the hardest ethical requirement in the psalm: keeping a commitment that has become costly. The culture of the ancient Near East expected oath-keeping to be absolute; Israel’s law specifically prohibited breaking vows (Num. 30:2; Deut. 23:21). The psalm identifies this as the mark of someone who genuinely fears God.

notes.original: lo yitein b’neshekh — who does not give on interest
notes.rendering: who lends money to the poor without interest
notes.why: The prohibition on interest-bearing loans to fellow Israelites (Exod. 22:25; Deut. 23:19–20) protected the poor from debt spirals. Neshekh — interest (literally: a bite). The psalm places this economic practice at the heart of the ethical life required for worship. Justice and worship cannot be separated.

intro: Psalm 16 is a psalm of trust with an extraordinary conclusion: the confident hope that God will not abandon his servant to Sheol. Peter quotes vv.8–11 at Pentecost (Acts 2:25–28) and Paul at Antioch (Acts 13:35) as prophecy of resurrection. Whether the psalmist himself understood this scope is debated; the language reaches further than any individual deliverance from illness.

notes.original: amartI l’YHWH Adonai ata — I say to YHWH: you are my Lord
notes.rendering: I say to YHWH, “You are my Lord; apart from you I have no good thing.
notes.why: The confession is total: YHWH is not one good among others but the ground of all good. Tovati bal alekha — my good is not apart from/above you. The psalmist’s inheritance, portion, and joy are all located in the divine person, not in gifts or circumstances.

notes.original: YHWH m’nat chelqi v’kosi — YHWH is the portion of my share and my cup
notes.rendering: YHWH, you are my portion and my cup
notes.why: The image is from the land distribution: each tribe and family received their chelekh (portion, allotment). The Levites received no land because “YHWH is their portion” (Num. 18:20; Deut. 10:9). The psalmist applies this to himself: his inheritance is not property but a person.

notes.original: ki lo ta’azov nafshi l’sheol — for you will not abandon my soul to Sheol
notes.rendering: because you will not abandon me to the realm of the dead, nor will you let your faithful one see decay
notes.why: Chasid — the faithful one, the object of hesed, the covenant-loyal servant. Shachat — pit, decay (the physical corruption of death). Peter and Paul both read this as pointing beyond any individual deliverance: no human psalmist could remain incorrupt; only the resurrection of Jesus fulfills the claim completely (Acts 2:31; 13:37).

intro: Psalm 17 closes with one of the Psalter’s most haunting lines: “when I awake, I will be satisfied with seeing your likeness.” The context is immediate — waking from sleep, as opposed to the enemies who have their reward in this life. But the line reaches toward the beatific vision. To see the divine face is the goal toward which all the psalms press.

notes.original: ishon bat ayin — the pupil, daughter of the eye
notes.rendering: Keep me as the apple of your eye
notes.why: The apple of the eye (ishon — literally: the little man, the tiny reflection of oneself seen in another’s pupil) is the most sensitive and protected part of the body. The image appears in Deuteronomy 32:10 of YHWH’s care for Israel in the wilderness. The two images together — pupil and sheltering wings — express absolute divine care and protection.

notes.original: ani b’tzedeq ekhezeh panekha — I in righteousness will see your face
notes.rendering: I will be vindicated and will see your face
notes.why: The final verse sets the psalmist against the worldly people of v.14. Their portion is this world; his is the vision of God. The seeing of the divine face (pana’mo — Ps. 11:7) is the supreme reward. Whether this refers to temple worship, morning prayer, or eschatological hope, it locates the psalmist’s ultimate satisfaction not in circumstances but in God himself.

intro: Psalm 18 is one of the longest psalms and one of the most cosmically dramatic: a personal deliverance narrated as a divine warrior’s theophany. The poem appears also in 2 Samuel 22 with minor variants, where it closes David’s memoirs. The imagery (smoke from nostrils, riding cherubim, parting heavens) draws on ancient Near Eastern warrior-deity traditions and applies them to the LORD’s rescue of his king.

notes.original: YHWH sali um’tzudati um’palti — YHWH is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer
notes.rendering: YHWH is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer
notes.why: The accumulation of seven titles in vv.1–2 (strength, rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, stronghold) is deliberate excess: no single image captures the divine rescue. Sela — the bedrock cliff, the bare limestone outcrop (contrast with even — a smaller stone). The rock is geological permanence against the torrents of death.

notes.original: vayirkav al k’ruv vayaf — and he rode upon a cherub and flew
notes.rendering: He mounted the cherubim and flew; he soared on the wings of the wind
notes.why: The warrior-god riding the storm cherub draws on Canaanite imagery of Baal as the storm-rider, radically reapplied to YHWH. The poem is not mythological borrowing but ideological conquest: the powers attributed to the storm deity belong to YHWH alone. The wings of the wind (khanfei ruakh) appear also in Ps. 104:3.

notes.original: migdol yeshu’ot malko v’oseh khesed limshikho — great victories to his king and showing hesed to his anointed
notes.rendering: He gives his king great victories; he shows unfailing love to his anointed, to David and to his descendants forever
notes.why: The final verse ties the whole psalm to the covenant with David (2 Samuel 7). The personal deliverance described throughout the poem is also dynastic: the king who is rescued is the bearer of the eternal promise. Mashikho — his anointed, the messianic king through whom the divine hesed will flow to all generations.

intro: Psalm 19 is a diptych: the speech of creation (vv.1–6) and the speech of Torah (vv.7–11), joined by a prayer for cleansing (vv.12–14). C.S. Lewis called it the greatest poem in the Psalter. The two revelations are complementary: the heavens speak without words; the Torah speaks with them. Both testify to the same God.

notes.original: hashamayim m’saperim k’vod El — the heavens are recounting the glory of God
notes.rendering: The heavens declare the glory of God
notes.why: Sapper — to count, recount, tell (the same root as sefer — a book). The heavens are narrating. The irony of v.3 is precise: they have no speech (ein omer, there is no utterance), yet their voice (qol) goes to all the earth. The silent testimony of the cosmos is louder than any sermon.

notes.original: torat YHWH t’mimah m’shivat nafesh — the Torah of YHWH is perfect, restoring the soul
notes.rendering: The law of YHWH is perfect, refreshing the soul
notes.why: Six synonyms for the Torah are deployed in vv.7–9, each paired with an effect: perfect/restoring, trustworthy/wise, right/joyful, radiant/enlightening, pure/enduring, righteous altogether. The accumulation is itself a kind of praise — no single word is adequate.

notes.original: l’ratzon imrei fi v’hegyon libi — for acceptance: the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart
notes.rendering: May these words of my mouth and this meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight
notes.why: The closing prayer ties the two halves of the psalm together: the psalmist who has heard creation speak and has meditated on Torah now offers his own speech and meditation. Hegyon — meditation, murmuring (from hagah, the word of Psalm 1:2). The goal is that human speech might rise to the level of creation’s testimony.

intro: Psalm 20 is a liturgical intercession for the king before battle, likely spoken by the priests or congregation. Psalm 21 is its thanksgiving counterpart after victory. Together they frame the royal liturgy. The heart of the psalm is v.7: the contrast between trust in military hardware and trust in the name of YHWH.

notes.original: eleh varekev v’eleh vasusim — these in chariots and these in horses
notes.rendering: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of YHWH our God
notes.why: Chariots (rekev) and horses (susim) were the heavy weaponry of ancient Near Eastern armies. Israel’s kings were explicitly warned against multiplying horses (Deut. 17:16). The contrast is not between military and non-military but between what is trusted: hardware or the divine name. The name of YHWH (shem YHWH) carries all the weight of the divine character and covenant.

notes.original: YHWH hoshia hamelekh — YHWH, save the king
notes.rendering: YHWH, give victory to the king! Answer us when we call!
notes.why: The final cry is liturgical: the congregation prays for their king and for themselves in the same breath. Hoshia — save, deliver (the root of Hosanna). The king’s salvation and the people’s answer to prayer are intertwined. In later messianic reading, the king who is both the subject of prayer and the object of divine answer becomes a type of the anointed one.

intro: Psalm 21 is the thanksgiving to Psalm 20’s prayer: the king who was prayed for has been answered. The list of divine gifts in vv.1–7 mirrors the list of requests in Psalm 20. Length of days forever and ever (v.4) reaches past any individual king toward the eternal dimension of the Davidic covenant.

notes.original: khayyim sha’al mimkha — life he asked from you
notes.rendering: He asked you for life, and you gave it to him — length of days, for ever and ever
notes.why: The gift of life (khayyim) and its extension to arekh yamim l’olam va’ed (length of days for ever and ever) exceeds any human lifespan. The statement is either hyperbolic royal praise — a common form in the ancient Near East — or it gestures toward the eternal reign promised to the Davidic house (2 Sam. 7:13, 16). The NT sees both fulfilled in the resurrection of Jesus.

notes.original: t’shitem l’varekha la’ad — you place blessings on him forever
notes.rendering: Surely you have granted him unending blessings
notes.why: The joy of divine presence (b’et panekha — with the light/joy of your face) in v.6 anticipates the beatific vision of Psalm 17:15. The king who trusts (v.7) is the king who is sustained by the hesed of the Most High: the human virtue and the divine attribute correspond to each other.

intro: Psalm 22 is the most cited psalm in the New Testament Passion accounts. Jesus quotes its opening cry from the cross (Matt. 27:46; Mark 15:34). The mockers’ taunt (v.8), the casting of lots for garments (v.18), the piercing of hands and feet (v.16) — all are echoed in the crucifixion narrative. The psalm moves from the abyss of abandonment to the widest possible praise: all the ends of the earth, all generations yet unborn.

notes.original: eli eli lamah azavtani — my God, my God, why have you forsaken me
notes.rendering: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
notes.why: Azav — to abandon, forsake (used of a parent abandoning a child, a husband leaving a wife, God leaving his people in exile). The cry is not a theological statement that God has abandoned the psalmist permanently but the raw speech of felt absence. The double “my God” preserves relationship even in the scream of loss.

notes.original: v’anokhi tolaat v’lo ish — and I am a worm and not a man
notes.rendering: But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by everyone
notes.why: The descent from human dignity (Psalm 8: crowned with glory) to worm is the full arc of humiliation. The mockers’ taunt in vv.7–8 echoes the Wisdom of Solomon’s description of the suffering righteous man (Wisd. 2:17–18) and is quoted almost verbatim in Matt. 27:43.

notes.original: y’challeku v’gadai lahem — they divide my garments among them
notes.rendering: They divide my clothes among them and cast lots for my garment
notes.why: John 19:24 quotes this verse and notes its fulfillment precisely: the soldiers divided the outer garments and cast lots for the seamless tunic. The detail that John isolates — the distinction between divided clothes and the single garment for which they gamble — is already present in the Hebrew (begadim, plural; lebush, singular garment).

notes.original: ki asah — that he has done
notes.rendering: He has done it
notes.why: The final two words in the Hebrew are ki asah — that he has done (it). They are the last words of the psalm. They have no object. The subject is God; the deed is the deliverance described. The ambiguity is perhaps intentional: the deed is whatever YHWH did that turned abandonment into praise. In John’s Gospel, Jesus’ last word from the cross is tetelestai — it is finished/accomplished — which is the Greek equivalent.

intro: Psalm 23 is perhaps the most beloved piece of poetry in the world’s literature. Six verses that move from the shepherd’s field to the host’s table, from Psalm 22’s desolation to rest. The structure shifts from metaphor (shepherd, vv.1–4) to direct address (you, vv.2–5) to declaration (I will dwell, v.6). The movement from third person to second is the movement of trust becoming intimacy.

notes.original: YHWH ro’i lo ekh’sar — YHWH is my shepherd; I shall not want
notes.rendering: YHWH is my shepherd; I lack nothing
notes.why: Ro’eh — shepherd, the one who tends, leads, feeds, and guards (the same word used of Moses and David, and applied to YHWH in Ezek. 34). Lo ekh’sar — I shall not lack (khasar — to be in want, to be without). The claim is not that the shepherd makes life easy but that he makes it complete: nothing that is truly needed is absent.

notes.original: gei tzalmavet — valley of deep darkness / death-shadow
notes.rendering: through the darkest valley
notes.why: Tzalmavet — the shadow of death, or deep darkness (from tzal — shadow, and mavet — death; or from a root meaning deep darkness). Many modern scholars favor deep darkness; the traditional reading death-shadow persists because it captures both the physical (ravines where predators lurk) and metaphorical (the approach to death) dimensions. Either way, the point is the same: in the worst place, you are there.

notes.original: v’shavti b’veit YHWH l’orekh yamim — and I will dwell in the house of YHWH for length of days
notes.rendering: I will dwell in the house of YHWH forever
notes.why: The final verb is debated: shavti (I will dwell) or shavti (I will return). The context supports dwell. The house of YHWH (the temple, the divine dwelling) as the destination of the psalm’s journey turns the shepherd poem into a pilgrimage poem: the flock is being led home. L’orekh yamim — for length of days, for many days, for ever — the temporal horizon opens into eternity.

intro: Psalm 24 is an entrance liturgy for the ark procession into Jerusalem — likely the ceremony commemorating David’s bringing of the ark to Zion (2 Samuel 6). The structure moves from cosmic claim (vv.1–2) to ethical entrance requirement (vv.3–6) to dramatic gate-opening (vv.7–10). The ethical gatekeeping of Psalm 15 and the cosmic Lord of Psalm 19 meet here in one ceremony.

notes.original: l’YHWH ha’aretz um’lo’ah — to YHWH the earth and its fullness
notes.rendering: The earth is YHWH’s, and everything in it
notes.why: Paul quotes this verse twice (1 Cor. 10:26, 28) regarding food offered to idols: the earth’s produce belongs to YHWH; nothing in creation is inherently defiled. The cosmic claim grounds the liturgical drama: the one who enters the gates is not a local deity but the owner of everything.

notes.original: n’ki khapayim uvar levav — clean of hands and pure of heart
notes.rendering: The one who has clean hands and a pure heart
notes.why: The ethical requirements for temple entry (cf. Psalm 15) focus here on the two centers of human action: hands (outward deeds) and heart (inward intention). The rabbinic tradition read this as the minimum requirements for any worshipper. Jesus reads the pure heart eschatologically (Matt. 5:8 — blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God).

notes.original: mi zeh melekh hakavod — who is this king of glory
notes.rendering: Who is this King of Glory? YHWH strong and mighty, YHWH mighty in battle
notes.why: The antiphonal exchange — question and answer, twice — is the psalm’s dramatic climax. The gates are addressed as if they are sentinels who must verify the identity of the one seeking entry. The answer names the warrior-deity: YHWH Sabaoth (the LORD of armies). The divine warrior who defeats chaos (v.2, founding the earth) is the same who enters through the gates in triumph.

intro: Psalm 25 is an acrostic — in Hebrew each verse begins with a successive letter of the alphabet (aleph through taw). This formal constraint produces an unusual range of moods within a single psalm: petition, instruction, confession, lament, and communal intercession. The acrostic says: whatever letter you are at in your own experience, there is a word here for it.

notes.original: haderikheini va’amiteikha — lead me in your truth
notes.rendering: Guide me in your truth and teach me
notes.why: The prayer for guidance (darakh — to lead, make tread a path, as a guide leads a traveler) is also a prayer for formation. Truth here is emet — faithfulness, reliability, the quality of God’s word that makes it worth following. The psalmist does not know the way; he needs both direction and companionship.

notes.original: sod YHWH l’yere’av — the counsel/secret of YHWH is for those who fear him
notes.rendering: YHWH confides in those who fear him; he makes his covenant known to them
notes.why: Sod — the intimate counsel, the inner circle, the divine confidence (the same word in Amos 3:7 for the prophetic council). The fear of YHWH is not terror but the reverence that creates intimacy: those who truly stand before God are drawn into his confidence. The covenant (b’rit) is what he shares with them.

intro: Psalm 26 is a psalm of innocence: the psalmist invites divine examination and protests his integrity. It is not self-righteousness (the appeal in v.3 grounds everything in hesed and emet) but the speech of the falsely accused who has no recourse but to lay his life before the only judge who sees all.

notes.original: b’khaneni YHWH v’naseni — test me, YHWH, and try me
notes.rendering: Test me, YHWH, and try me; examine my heart and my mind
notes.why: The three verbs (test, try, examine/refine) are the vocabulary of metallurgical testing — the same testing of silver in Psalm 12:6. The psalmist submits to the full refiner’s examination. Kidneys and heart (kiliyot v’libi — my kidneys and my heart) together cover the emotional and rational inner life (cf. Psalm 7:9).

notes.original: erkhaltz b’niqayon kappai — I will wash in innocence my hands
notes.rendering: I wash my hands in innocence, and go about your altar, YHWH
notes.why: The ritual hand-washing before approaching the altar (Exod. 30:17–21) becomes the psalmist’s metaphor for moral purity. The washing declares: my hands are clean. Pilate’s hand-washing (Matt. 27:24) uses the same gesture in reverse: a declaration of innocence that is in fact an abdication of justice.

intro: Psalm 27 holds together confident praise and urgent lament in a single poem — the structure that Luther called “the faith that fights.” The one request (v.4) is not safety but presence: to dwell in the house of YHWH and see his beauty. The psalm ends with two commands that are also a prayer: wait. Wait for YHWH.

notes.original: YHWH ori v’yishi — YHWH is my light and my salvation
notes.rendering: YHWH is my light and my salvation — whom shall I fear?
notes.why: Light (or) is unusual as a divine attribute in the Psalms (cf. Ps. 36:9; Isa. 60:19–20; Mic. 7:8). It suggests illumination in darkness, orientation in confusion. Salvation (yishi — my Yeshua, the same root as the name of Jesus) and stronghold together constitute the full defense. The double rhetorical question (whom? of whom?) challenges any counter-claim to authority.

notes.original: akhat sha’alti me’et YHWH — one thing I have asked from YHWH
notes.rendering: One thing I ask from YHWH, this only do I seek
notes.why: The single petition in a psalm full of dangers is not deliverance or victory but laz’ot — this: to dwell (sheveti — to sit, to settle, to stay), to see (likhzot — to gaze, the word of absorbed contemplation), and to inquire (l’vaqer — to seek out early in the morning, to meditate). The one thing is not an activity but a relationship.

notes.original: qaveh el YHWH — hope for/wait for YHWH
notes.rendering: Wait for YHWH; be strong and take heart and wait for YHWH
notes.why: The doubled qaveh (wait for/hope in) frames the command. Kavah — to wait with tense expectation (the word of a watchman or a hunter in alert stillness). The psalm that began with bold assertion (I will not fear) ends with an exhortation to wait: confidence and waiting are not opposites but complements. Strength and courage (khazaq v’ametz libbekha) are the posture of hope, not the absence of fear.

intro: Psalm 28 follows the lament pattern precisely: urgent cry (vv.1–2), petition regarding enemies (vv.3–5), then praise at the pivot (v.6). The transition at v.6 is abrupt and unexplained: the psalmist goes from cry to “praise be!” without narrating what changed. The shift is the act of faith.

notes.original: el YHWH aqra tzuri — to YHWH I call; my Rock
notes.rendering: To you, YHWH, I call; you are my Rock, do not turn a deaf ear to me
notes.why: The fear underlying the psalm is spelled out: if you are silent (tekherash — remain deaf, silent), I will be like those going down to the pit (bor — the cistern, the underworld). The rock who could shelter becomes, if silent, the rock that entombs. The whole petition is suspended on the possibility of divine silence.

notes.original: libbi vatakh bo vane’ezarti — my heart trusted in him and I was helped
notes.rendering: my heart trusts in him, and he helps me. My heart leaps for joy
notes.why: The pivot: vatikkon (past perfect — it trusted, and was helped) grounds the present leap of joy. The word for leaping/exulting (alatz) is the same as in Psalm 5:11 and 68:4 — the joy that breaks into song. The one who trusted and found help can praise with confidence.

intro: Psalm 29 is a storm theophany hymn — the closest thing in the Psalter to Canaanite Baal poetry in its imagery, deliberately redeploying the attributes of the storm-god for YHWH. The sevenfold qol YHWH (voice of YHWH) hammers through the poem like thunder. The psalm ends in complete contrast: the cosmic storm becomes a blessing of peace for the psalmist’s people.

notes.original: havu l’YHWH bnei elim — give to YHWH, O sons of gods/divine beings
notes.rendering: Ascribe to YHWH, you heavenly beings
notes.why: Bnei elim — sons of the gods/divine beings (the heavenly council). The psalm opens by summoning the divine assembly to worship: even the divine beings must acknowledge YHWH’s supremacy. The same council that was assumed in Job 1–2 and Psalm 82 is here called to give the tribute that belongs to the LORD of the storm.

notes.original: qol YHWH — the voice/thunder of YHWH
notes.rendering: The seven-fold voice of YHWH
notes.why: The sevenfold qol YHWH (over waters, powerful, majestic, breaking cedars, striking lightning, shaking desert, twisting oaks) maps the storm’s geography from the Mediterranean Sea to the northern mountains (Lebanon/Sirion — Hermon) to the southern desert (Kadesh). YHWH’s voice covers the entire land.

notes.original: YHWH oz l’amo yiten YHWH y’varekh et amo vashalom — YHWH will give strength to his people, YHWH will bless his people with peace
notes.rendering: YHWH gives strength to his people; YHWH blesses his people with peace
notes.why: The juxtaposition is deliberately astonishing: the God whose voice shatters cedars and shakes deserts gives his people not earthquakes but shalom — the complete well-being that the storm cannot destroy. The cosmic power of YHWH is placed in service of the smallest human need: peace.

intro: Psalm 30 is a thanksgiving psalm for a personal healing that became the dedication song for the temple (perhaps used at the rededication of the Maccabean era). Its central verse (v.5) is one of the most quoted in the entire Psalter: the night of weeping, the morning of joy. The psalm’s candor about the psalmist’s prior complacency (v.6) is unusual and disarming.

notes.original: ki rega b’apo khayyim birtzonao — for a moment in his anger, life in his favor
notes.rendering: For his anger lasts only a moment, but his favor lasts a lifetime
notes.why: The contrast is temporal: rega (a moment, an instant) against khayyim (life, a lifetime). Weeping (bekhi — weeping as a guest) may lodge for the evening, but joy (rinah — a joyful shout, a ringing cry) comes in the morning. The image is of sorrow as a temporary lodger who has stayed the night but will not stay forever.

notes.original: hapakhta misp’di l’makhol li — you turned my wailing into dancing for me
notes.rendering: You turned my wailing into dancing; you removed my sackcloth and clothed me with joy
notes.why: The transformation is total and physical: mourning clothes (sackcloth — the coarse garment of grief and repentance) become joy. The image of divine re-dressing appears also in Isaiah 61:3 (a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair). God’s restoration is not just internal but embodied: the whole body changes posture, from prostration to dance.

intro: Psalm 31 is one of the most emotionally varied psalms: it moves from confidence (vv.1–8) to the depths of social humiliation (vv.9–13) to trust and exhortation (vv.14–24). Jesus quotes v.5 from the cross (Luke 23:46): “Into your hands I commit my spirit.” The verse becomes the paradigm of entrusting oneself to God at the moment of greatest vulnerability.

notes.original: b’yadkha afkid rukhi — into your hand I commit my spirit
notes.rendering: Into your hands I commit my spirit; deliver me, YHWH, my faithful God
notes.why: Paqad — to commit, to deposit as a trust, to hand over for safekeeping (the same word used of leaving valuables in someone’s custody). The spirit (ruakh) is the life-breath, the person. The prayer entrusts the whole self to the divine hand. Luke 23:46 records Jesus praying this at the moment of death, transforming it into the model prayer of total surrender.

notes.original: b’yadkha itotai — in your hand are my times
notes.rendering: My times are in your hands
notes.why: Ittot — my times, my appointed seasons, the moments and periods of my life. The affirmation is that the psalmist’s time — not just his spirit but the very schedule of his life — is in divine custody. This is trust at its most comprehensive: not just the crisis moment but the whole arc.

notes.original: ani amartI b’khofsizi — I said in my haste/alarm
notes.rendering: In my alarm I said, “I am cut off from your sight!
notes.why: The word translated alarm (khofzi) is the same as in Psalm 116:11 (“In my alarm I said, all men are liars”). It is the speech of panic, the feeling-conclusion that misreads the situation. The psalmist confesses that this was wrong: you heard my cry. The false conclusion (cut off from your sight) was refuted by the actual answer.

intro: Psalm 32 is the second of the Penitential Psalms and Paul’s favorite: he quotes vv.1–2 in Romans 4:7–8 to demonstrate that justification is a matter of non-imputation, not of earned righteousness. The psalm is a confession story — what it felt like to not confess, what it felt like to confess, and what followed. Augustine had this psalm inscribed on his wall.

notes.original: ashrei n’sui pesha k’sui khata’ah — blessed of the lifted-up transgression, the covered sin
notes.rendering: Blessed is the one whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered
notes.why: Three synonyms: nasa (lifted, carried away — the same word as the scapegoat carrying the sins into the desert, Lev. 16:22), kasah (covered), and lo yakhshov (not reckoned, not counted). Three dimensions of forgiveness: removal, concealment, and non-imputation. Paul uses the non-reckoning as his proof that Abraham’s justification was credited, not earned (Rom. 4:6–8).

notes.original: ki hekhesharti — for when I kept silent
notes.rendering: When I kept silent, my bones wasted away
notes.why: The psychosomatic effect of unexpressed guilt: the bones (the skeletal structure, the frame of the self) decay as if consumed. The body keeps the score of the spirit. The groaning (sh’agah — a lion’s roar, applied here to involuntary physical sound) is the body’s protest at what the will refuses to confess.

notes.original: atah seter li — you are my hiding place
notes.rendering: You are my hiding place; you will protect me from trouble and surround me with songs of deliverance
notes.why: The imagery of hiding (seter — shelter, concealment, the same root as the secret place of Ps. 91:1) reverses the concealment of sin: the psalmist who could not cover his own guilt is now hidden by God. The songs of deliverance (rannei pallet — shouts of rescue) surround him like a wall.

intro: Psalm 33 is an untitled hymn of creation and history. Its theological logic runs from the creative word (vv.6, 9 — he spoke and it stood firm) to the sovereign word that overrules the nations’ plans (v.10) to the watching eye of YHWH (vv.13–15) to the only reliable hope: not armies or horses, but the divine hesed.

notes.original: bidvar YHWH shamayim na’asu — by the word of YHWH the heavens were made
notes.rendering: By the word of YHWH the heavens were made, their starry host by the breath of his mouth
notes.why: The creation-by-word theology of Genesis 1 (and he said... and it was so) is here made explicit as praise: the one who speaks creation into being is the one now addressed in song. Breath of his mouth (rukh piv) links creative speech and the divine spirit/breath.

notes.original: atzat YHWH l’olam ta’amod — the counsel of YHWH stands forever
notes.rendering: But the plans of YHWH stand firm forever, the purposes of his heart through all generations
notes.why: The contrast with v.10 (YHWH foils the plans of nations) is structural: human plans are foiled, divine plans stand. Mahsh’vot libo — the thoughts of his heart, the deliberated purposes of the divine will. The word machshavah (thought, plan) is the same used of the wicked’s schemes in earlier psalms, now applied to God: his plans, unlike theirs, cannot be thwarted.

intro: Psalm 34 is an acrostic thanksgiving and wisdom psalm. Its center is the invitation in v.8: taste and see. The psalm moves from personal testimony to public teaching — the psalmist who has experienced YHWH’s goodness now teaches the young. V.20 (not one of his bones will be broken) is applied to Jesus in John 19:36.

notes.original: ta’amu ur’u ki tov YHWH — taste and see that YHWH is good
notes.rendering: Taste and see that YHWH is good
notes.why: The invitation is experiential, not merely cognitive: ta’amu — taste, try, test with the palate. The goodness of YHWH is not just an idea but a flavor. The invitation echoes Isaiah 55:1–2 (come, taste, eat) and is the background to the Eucharist. 1 Peter 2:3 quotes it directly in the context of craving spiritual nourishment.

notes.original: qarov YHWH l’nishb’rei lev — near is YHWH to the broken of heart
notes.rendering: YHWH is close to the brokenhearted and saves those who are crushed in spirit
notes.why: Nishb’rei lev — the shattered of heart, the one whose inner life has been broken (from shavar — to break, the same word as the breaking of the nation in Amos). Dakkai ruakh — crushed in spirit (from dakah — to be crushed, ground fine). The paradox: divine closeness is greatest at the point of human collapse.

notes.original: shomer kol atzomotav — he guards all his bones
notes.rendering: he protects all their bones, not one of them will be broken
notes.why: The bones-intact image may refer to Passover (Exod. 12:46 — do not break any of its bones). John 19:36 applies this verse to Jesus on the cross, where the soldiers did not break his legs because he was already dead. The preservation of the Passover lamb’s bones and the preservation of the righteous man’s bones meet in the Johannine passion account.

intro: Psalm 35 is one of the most extended imprecatory psalms — a legal complaint brought before the divine judge against those who have attacked the psalmist without cause. The key phrase “without cause” (khinnam) appears three times. Jesus echoes it of his own persecutors (John 15:25). The intensity of the imprecation is proportional to the treachery described: those who received the psalmist’s compassion (vv.13–14) have returned malice.

notes.original: rivah YHWH et yorivai — contend, YHWH, with those who contend with me
notes.rendering: Contend, YHWH, with those who contend with me
notes.why: The legal and military imagery overlaps: riv (contend, plead a case, argue) is the vocabulary of the law court; the following verse shifts to military shield and spear. God is both advocate and warrior. The psalmist has no human defense; he calls the divine attorney to take his case.

notes.original: ki khinom titm’nu li shet r’shtam — for without cause they hid their net for me
notes.rendering: Since they hid their net for me without cause
notes.why: Khinnam — without cause, for nothing, freely (the same word used in Job 1:9 — “Does Job fear God for nothing?” and in John 15:25 — they hated me without cause, quoting either Ps. 35:19 or 69:4). The innocence of the psalmist is what makes the divine appeal possible: the one who pleads must not be guilty of what he charges against others.

intro: Psalm 36 is structured as a sharp diptych: the portrait of the wicked who have no fear of God (vv.1–4) followed by the portrait of the God whose love reaches the heavens (vv.5–9). The contrast is total. The two most theologically charged phrases in the psalm are mirror images: no fear of God (v.1) and fountain of life / in your light we see light (v.9).

notes.original: n’um pesha la’rasha b’qerev libi — the oracle of transgression/sin to the wicked in the midst of my heart
notes.rendering: I have a message from God in my heart concerning the sinfulness of the wicked
notes.why: The verse is striking: the psalmist receives an oracle (n’um — the prophetic declaration, the divine utterance, normally “thus says YHWH”) concerning the wicked. He has inside knowledge of their inner life because God has revealed it. The phrase no fear of God before their eyes is quoted by Paul in Romans 3:18 as the climax of his catena on universal sinfulness.

notes.original: ki immkha m’kor khayyim b’orkha nireh or — for with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light
notes.rendering: For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light
notes.why: The most theologically dense verse in the psalm. M’kor khayyim — the spring/source of life (the same image in Jer. 2:13 — YHWH is the spring of living water). In your light we see light: the divine light is not just what we see but what makes all seeing possible. John 1:4–9 (the light that enlightens everyone) works in the same conceptual space.

intro: Psalm 37 is an acrostic poem — each two-verse unit begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The Hebrew אלף (aleph) through ריש (resh/shin) sequence structures what is otherwise a flowing meditation on divine justice and patient trust.
