notes.why: The divine desire (avvah) matches David’s desire. The covenant of place is mutual: David longed to give God a home; God desired this precise location above all others.

notes.original: atsmiah qeren le-David
notes.rendering: I will make a horn to sprout for David
notes.why: The sprouting horn is a messianic image — the dynasty growing like a plant from the ground (cf. Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8). Luke 1:69 applies this directly to Jesus.

intro: Psalm 133 is a celebration of communal unity in three verses and two images. The anointing oil on Aaron’s head and the dew of Hermon falling on Zion seem incongruous — one is a southern ceremony of priestly consecration, the other a northern mountain’s famous moisture falling on the southern hills of Jerusalem. But both images are about abundant, overflowing blessing that exceeds its container: oil running beyond the beard to the robe-collar, dew traveling hundreds of miles to descend on Zion. Unity is similarly extravagant and improbable. Where it exists, God commands blessing.

notes.original: shevet akhim gam-yakhad
notes.rendering: brothers dwell in unity
notes.why: Gam-yakhad: also together, in unity. The adverb gam (also, even) adds an element of surprise or emphasis: even together, genuinely together — not merely in proximity but in real unity.

notes.original: ka-shemen ha-tov
notes.rendering: like the precious oil
notes.why: The anointing oil of Exodus 30:22–25 — a specific, expensive, sacred compound. Its flowing down from Aaron’s head to beard to robe-collar enacts a visible, lavish blessing.

notes.original: tal-Khermon she-yored al-harei Tsion
notes.rendering: the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion
notes.why: Hermon (9,000 ft) receives heavy moisture; Zion is 150 miles south. The image is of blessing flowing beyond all natural boundaries. God’s commanded blessing similarly exceeds geography.

intro: Psalm 134 closes the Songs of Ascents with a nighttime exchange of blessings between the pilgrims departing for home and the temple servants who remain. The three verses form a chiasm of blessing: the pilgrims call the night-watchmen to bless God (vv. 1–2), and the priests respond by blessing the pilgrims from Zion (v. 3). The journey that began in Psalm 120 with the pilgrim far from home in hostile territory ends here with this reciprocal blessing — a liturgical embrace at the gate as the community disperses to carry Zion’s blessing back to their ordinary lives.

notes.original: ha-omddim be-veit YHWH ba-leilot
notes.rendering: who stand by night in the house of the LORD
notes.why: The Levitical night-watch kept vigil in the temple after the pilgrims slept. Their nocturnal ministry is honored by the departing congregation’s call to bless.

notes.original: se'u yedeikhem qodesh
notes.rendering: lift up your hands to the holy place
notes.why: Raised hands were the posture of blessing and prayer (cf. 1 Tim 2:8). The holy place (qodesh) may refer to the sanctuary or simply to the sacred orientation of worship.

notes.original: yevarekh-kha YHWH mi-Tsion
notes.rendering: May the LORD bless you from Zion
notes.why: The Aaronic blessing formula (Num 6:24) compressed to its essence: Zion as the source and God as the giver of blessing that follows the pilgrim home.

intro: Psalm 135 is a liturgical anthology, drawing freely on earlier psalms: the idol polemic from Psalm 115:4–8, the historical review from Psalms 105–106 and 136, the doxology of Psalm 113. This is not literary borrowing but liturgical practice — the congregation sings its way through the canon of praise. The idol polemic (vv. 15–18) gains additional force from its context: immediately after celebrating the God who controls weather, history, and nations, the contrast with mute and blind idols is total. The fourfold closing doxology (vv. 19–20) mirrors Psalm 115:9–11.

notes.original: ki Ya'aqov bakhar lo Yah
notes.rendering: the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself
notes.why: The election of Israel is not based on Israel’s merit but on divine freedom: the LORD chose. The word “for himself” (lo) emphasizes that God’s choosing is personal, relational, possessive.

notes.original: kol asher-khafets YHWH asah
notes.rendering: whatever the LORD pleases, he does
notes.why: Khafets: to delight in, to desire, to take pleasure in. Divine sovereignty is not mechanical compulsion but the freedom of one who acts in accord with his own deepest desires.

notes.original: shimkha YHWH le-olam zikhrekha le-dor va-dor
notes.rendering: your name endures forever; your renown throughout all ages
notes.why: Zekher: renown, memory, the name that is remembered and spoken across generations. God’s identity is not forgotten but actively preserved in communal worship.

notes.original: ke-mohem yihyu oseihem
notes.rendering: those who make them become like them
notes.why: Repeated from Ps 115:8. The idol-maker’s spiritual formation: to make an image is to be shaped by it. Worship is always transformative — the question is only what one worships.

intro: Psalm 136 is the Great Hallel — sung at the Passover seder after Psalms 113–118. Its defining feature is the antiphonal refrain: every half-verse is answered by the congregation with “for his steadfast love endures forever” (ki le-olam khasdo), 26 times without interruption. The three movements cover creation (vv. 4–9), the Exodus and conquest (vv. 10–22), and universal providence (vv. 23–26). The refrain is the theological key: whatever the event — the making of stars, the plagues of Egypt, the wilderness years, the feeding of all creatures — khesed is the constant. Every act of God, from cosmic to mundane, is an expression of the one covenant love that never ends.

notes.original: ki le-olam khasdo
notes.rendering: for his steadfast love endures forever
notes.why: The refrain. Le-olam: to eternity, without end. Khasdo: his khesed, his covenantal steadfast love. The repetition is not monotony but accumulation — each event adds another piece of evidence for the same inexhaustible reality.

notes.original: le-oseh ha-shamayim bi-tvunah
notes.rendering: to him who by understanding made the heavens
notes.why: Tevunah: understanding, intelligence, skill. Creation is not brute power but wise artistry. The heavens are the product of divine intelligence, not arbitrary force.

notes.original: she-be-shif'elenu zakhar lanu
notes.rendering: who remembered us in our low estate
notes.why: Shif'elenu: our lowness, our abasement. God’s memory of his people at their lowest point is the act of khesed most needed — and least expected. This verse may refer to the Babylonian exile.

notes.original: noten lekhem le-khol-basar
notes.rendering: he who gives food to all flesh
notes.why: The final act before the closing doxology: God who struck down Pharaoh also feeds every living creature. The warrior is also the provider. Power and care belong to the same God.

intro: Psalm 137 is one of the most emotionally complex poems in Scripture. It opens with unforgettable beauty — exiles weeping by Babylon’s rivers, their lyres hanging silent on the willows — and closes with a verse that has troubled readers for centuries. The psalm must be held in its full historical context: the exiles have witnessed the slaughter of children in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 25:7; Lam 4:4; 5:13). The prayer of verse 9 is not a policy recommendation but the raw, unfiltered cry of those who have seen their own children destroyed. The Psalter’s honesty includes this: the God who hears prayer hears even the prayer that cannot be theologically domesticated.

notes.original: al naharot Bavel sham yashavnu gam-bakhinu
notes.rendering: By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept
notes.why: The geographical precision makes the grief specific and real: not abstract exile but this river, this weeping, this moment. The opening is among the most poignant in world literature.

notes.original: al-aravim be-tokhah talinu kinnorotenu
notes.rendering: on the willows there we hung up our lyres
notes.why: The lyre is the instrument of praise (Ps 33:2; 150:3). Hung silent in a foreign tree, it is the image of worship suspended — praise impossible in the face of devastation.

notes.original: eikh nashir et-shir YHWH al admat nekhar
notes.rendering: how shall we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land?
notes.why: The theological question at the heart of exile: is YHWH a local deity whose song belongs only in Zion? The rest of the psalter answers: no. But the anguish of the question is real.

notes.original: ve-nippets et-olalayikh el-ha-sela
notes.rendering: who dashes them against the rock
notes.why: The most disturbing verse in the Psalter. Ancient warfare included this atrocity (2 Kgs 8:12; Isa 13:16; Nah 3:10). The exiles had seen it done to their children. The imprecation echoes the crime. The Psalter preserves it without editorial softening.

intro: Psalm 138 opens the final Davidic collection (138–145), the last sustained block of psalms attributed to David in the Psalter. The psalm moves from personal thanksgiving (vv. 1–3) to universal vision (vv. 4–5) to confident trust in trouble (vv. 6–8). Verse 6 is the characteristic Psalter reversal: God is high yet regards the lowly; the haughty he knows only from a distance. The closing declaration — “do not forsake the work of your hands” — is one of the most tender endings in the Psalter: God has made this person; he cannot abandon his own handiwork.

notes.original: neged elohim azammereka
notes.rendering: before the gods I sing your praise
notes.why: Before other divine beings — perhaps the heavenly council. The psalm’s thanksgiving is declared publicly in the realm where God’s supremacy is asserted.

notes.original: ki-higdalta al-kol shimkha imratekha
notes.rendering: you have exalted above all things your name and your word
notes.why: A stunning claim: God has placed his word and name above everything else, even above his own prior reputation. His word commits him more fully than any prior self-disclosure.

notes.original: ki ram YHWH ve-shapal yir'eh
notes.rendering: though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly
notes.why: The divine paradox: transcendence and condescension held together. Ram (high, exalted) and shapal (low, humble) are set in deliberate tension that the psalm refuses to resolve away.

notes.original: YHWH yigmor ba'adi
notes.rendering: the LORD will fulfill his purpose for me
notes.why: Gamar: to complete, to bring to an end, to perfect. God’s purpose is not abandoned halfway. What he begins, he finishes — including the work of human beings he has fashioned.

intro: Psalm 139 is among the greatest poems in any language — a meditation on divine omniscience and omnipresence that is simultaneously a confession, a lament, and a prayer. The structure is precise: God’s knowledge of the psalmist (vv. 1–6), God’s inescapable presence (vv. 7–12), God’s creative work in the womb (vv. 13–16), the psalmist’s response (vv. 17–22), and the closing self-offering (vv. 23–24). The imprecatory section (vv. 19–22) has troubled readers, but it flows logically: one who has grasped that God knows everything cannot be indifferent to those who oppose him. The psalm ends where it began: “search me and know me.”

notes.original: tzartani akhor va-qedem
notes.rendering: you hem me in, behind and before
notes.why: Tsar: to press in on all sides, to besiege, to enclose. The all-knowing God is also all-surrounding. The knowledge is not surveillance but embrace.

notes.original: im-esaq shamayim sham-attah ve-atsiah she'ol hinnekha
notes.rendering: if I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, you are there
notes.why: The two extremes of the vertical cosmos — heaven above, Sheol below — are equally filled with the divine presence. There is no altitude or depth where God is absent.

notes.original: ki-attah qanitah kilyotai tsesakhtani be-veten immi
notes.rendering: you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb
notes.why: Kilyotai: kidneys, inner organs — the seat of emotion and deep feeling. Tsesakhtani: wove, knitted together (used of embroidery). The body is intricate divine weaving.

notes.original: niflaytah ma'asekha
notes.rendering: wonderful are your works
notes.why: Niflaytah: awe-inspiring, beyond human explanation. The psalmist places himself within the category of God’s wonders — my own existence is a marvellous act of God.

notes.original: khaqreni El ve-da lev
notes.rendering: Search me, O God, and know my heart
notes.why: The circle closes: the psalm that opened with “you have searched me and known me” ends with a voluntary invitation to the same searching. Divine knowledge is welcomed, not feared.

intro: Psalm 140 is one of the most focused enemy-psalms in the Psalter: the enemies are characterized entirely through their speech — serpent-tongue, asp-venom, the mischief of their lips (v. 9). The danger is verbal: slander, false accusation, the kind of social violence done with words rather than weapons. Paul quotes verse 3 in Romans 3:13 as part of his catena of texts demonstrating universal sin. The psalm’s confidence builds through the petition: from urgent plea (vv. 1–5) through declarative trust (vv. 6–7) to certain knowledge of divine justice (v. 12).

notes.original: sharpu leshonkha ke-nakhash
notes.rendering: they make their tongue sharp as a serpent's
notes.why: The serpent’s tongue is the instrument of deception since Genesis 3. Paul quotes this verse in Rom 3:13 as evidence of universal human corruption through the misuse of speech.

notes.original: taphsu ragelai
notes.rendering: who have planned to trip up my feet
notes.why: The hunting imagery is precise: hidden trap, spread net, set snares. The enemy has prepared the ground for the psalmist’s downfall long before the encounter.

notes.original: sakkota le-roshy be-yom nesheq
notes.rendering: you have covered my head in the day of battle
notes.why: The LORD as battlefield helmet — a specific, physical, military image of divine protection at the moment of maximum danger.

notes.original: yadin YHWH din ani
notes.rendering: the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted
notes.why: Din: to judge, to plead the legal case. God as defense attorney for the afflicted, executing mishpat (justice) on their behalf against the verbal violence of the powerful.

intro: Psalm 141 is a prayer of the evening — matched to the incense offering and the evening sacrifice (v. 2). Its central petition is unusual: not for escape from enemies but for a guard over the psalmist’s own mouth (v. 3) and heart (v. 4). The danger of prolonged exposure to evil is that one begins to adopt its habits and share its table. The willingness to receive correction from the righteous (v. 5) is a mark of extraordinary spiritual health: the faithful rebuke is received as anointing oil, not as assault.

notes.original: tekkon tefillati qetoret lefanekha
notes.rendering: Let my prayer be counted as incense before you
notes.why: The incense offering rose continuously in the temple; the prayer of the absent worshiper is offered as its equivalent. Prayer as liturgical substitute, equally acceptable to God.

notes.original: shitah YHWH shomrah le-phi nitsrah al-delet sefatai
notes.rendering: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips
notes.why: The mouth as a city-gate that requires a posted watchman. The guard is not merely self-discipline but a requested divine appointment.

notes.original: yehlemeni-tsaddiq khesed ve-yokhikheni shemen rosh
notes.rendering: Let a righteous man strike me — it is a kindness; let him rebuke me — it is oil for my head
notes.why: One of the most counter-intuitive petitions in the Psalter: the psalmist welcomes correction as anointing. Faithful rebuke is a gift, not an assault.

intro: Psalm 142 comes from David’s cave years — the period of fugitive exile when Saul pursued him (1 Sam 22; 24). The cave is both a literal hiding place and a metaphor for the constriction of the psalmist’s life. Verse 4 is one of the loneliest lines in the Psalter: “look to the right and see — there is none who takes notice of me.” In ancient Israel, one’s advocate stood at the right hand; to look there and find no one is to be utterly without human support. The only one left is God himself: “you are my refuge.”

notes.original: eshpokh lefanav sikhi
notes.rendering: I pour out my complaint before him
notes.why: Shaphakh: to pour out, to spill — used of blood, water, and soul. The complaint is not controlled speech but a pouring-out of everything that has been contained under pressure.

notes.original: habbet yamin ur'eh ve-ein li makkir
notes.rendering: look to the right and see: there is none who takes notice of me
notes.why: The right side is where one’s legal advocate stood. Total abandonment: no advocate, no refuge, no one who cares. The desolation is complete and specific.

notes.original: atta makhsi khelqi be-erets ha-khayyim
notes.rendering: You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living
notes.why: The pivot: from absolute human loneliness (v. 4) to exclusive divine sufficiency (v. 5). God replaces every human advocate and becomes the psalmist’s entire inheritance.

intro: Psalm 143 is the last of the seven Penitential Psalms and one of the most theologically precise. Its opening declaration — “no one living is righteous before you” (v. 2) — is quoted by Paul in Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16 as the foundation of his argument that justification cannot come through works of the law. What grounds the prayer is not the psalmist’s merit but God’s faithfulness (emunah) and righteousness (tsedeqah) — both covenant qualities. The petition for the good Spirit to lead on level ground (v. 10) is the closest the Psalter comes to a pneumatological prayer.

notes.original: al-tavo be-mishpat et-avdekha ki lo yitsddaq lefanekha kol-khay
notes.rendering: Enter not into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you
notes.why: Paul quotes this in Rom 3:20 and Gal 2:16. The universal verdict — no one righteous — is the premise from which the gospel of grace is the only possible conclusion.

notes.original: zakharti yamim mi-qedem
notes.rendering: I remember the days of old
notes.why: Memory of past divine action is again the therapy for present despair (cf. Ps 77:5–11). The psalmist’s response to spiritual darkness is to rehearse what God has done.

notes.original: hashmieni ba-boqer khasdekha
notes.rendering: Let me hear in the morning of your steadfast love
notes.why: The morning as the time of renewed hope (cf. Ps 5:3; 30:5; 59:16; 88:13; 130:6). Khesed heard in the morning reorients the whole day.

notes.original: rukhakha tovah tankheni be-erets mishor
notes.rendering: let your good Spirit lead me on level ground
notes.why: Ruakh tovah: your good Spirit. One of the clearest OT references to the Spirit as a personal guide — leading, not driving. The level ground (mishor) is the path of security and uprightness.

intro: Psalm 144 is a royal prayer that weaves together two contrasting moods: the warrior’s urgency (vv. 1–11) and the farmer’s vision of shalom (vv. 12–15). The centrepiece question — “what is man that you regard him?” (v. 3) — echoes Psalm 8:4, but here the context is military vulnerability: the king is aware that his life, like all human life, is a breath and a shadow. The closing beatitude is the psalm’s theological centre: not “blessed are the people with many cattle” but “blessed are the people whose God is the LORD.” The material blessings are real; God is better.

notes.original: ha-melammedh yadai la-qrav
notes.rendering: who trains my hands for war
notes.why: The divine warrior trains the human warrior — military skill is a gift, not merely a human acquisition. The acknowledgment is theologically significant for a soldier-king.

notes.original: YHWH mah-adam va-teda'ehu
notes.rendering: O LORD, what is man that you regard him?
notes.why: The question of Ps 8:4, here in a military context: the king is as fragile as any mortal. Divine regard for such ephemeral creatures is the ground of wonder.

notes.original: adam la-hevel damah yamav ke-tsel over
notes.rendering: man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow
notes.why: Hevel and tsel (passing shadow) together: Ecclesiastes’ vocabulary in the mouth of a warrior-king. Military power does not exempt one from mortality.

notes.original: asher banenu ke-neti'im
notes.rendering: May our sons be like plants full grown
notes.why: The closing vision of shalom: sons growing tall, daughters like carved palace pillars, full granaries, multiplying flocks. The warrior’s prayer is ultimately for peace, not more war.

notes.original: ashrei ha-am she-YHWH Elohav
notes.rendering: Blessed are the people whose God is the LORD
notes.why: The climactic beatitude. Not blessed are the rich, the strong, the fruitful — but blessed are the people who belong to YHWH. Covenant identity surpasses every material gift.

intro: Psalm 145 is the only psalm explicitly titled tehillah — praise — and it is an acrostic (one verse per Hebrew letter; the nun verse is missing in the MT but preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls). In rabbinic tradition, this psalm is recited three times daily. It is David’s final psalm in the Psalter, and it pivots the entire collection toward the five Hallelujah psalms that close the book. Verse 8 is the Exodus formula of divine self-disclosure once more (Exod 34:6) — the bedrock of Israel’s theology, quoted for the last time. The psalm ends where the Psalter is going: “let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever.”

notes.original: aromimkha Elohai ha-melekh
notes.rendering: I will extol you, my God and King
notes.why: The double address — my God, my King — frames the psalm as both personal devotion and royal doxology. David the king praises the divine King who outranks him.

notes.original: Exod 34:6 echo
notes.rendering: gracious and merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love
notes.why: The Exodus formula appears for the last time in the Psalter. Every subsequent use in Israel’s worship traces back to this self-disclosure at Sinai.

notes.original: malkhutekha malkhut kol-olamim
notes.rendering: your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom
notes.why: The kingdom claim is unqualified: no historical dynasty, no earthly empire can outlast God’s reign. All human kingdoms are bounded; God’s is eternal.

notes.original: potei'akh et-yadekha u-masbia le-khol-khay ratson
notes.rendering: you open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing
notes.why: One of the most universal statements of divine provision in the Bible. Not just Israel, not just humans — every living thing receives its desire from God’s open hand.

notes.original: qarov YHWH le-khol-qore'av
notes.rendering: the LORD is near to all who call on him
notes.why: Qarov: near, close. The transcendent God of the previous verses is also the near God — proximity and transcendence are not opposites but partners in the divine character.

intro: Psalm 146 opens the five-psalm Hallelujah finale of the Psalter. The contrast at its heart is stark: princes whose plans perish with their dying breath (vv. 3–4) against the LORD who keeps faith forever (v. 6). The catalogue of divine actions in verses 7–9 is remarkable — justice for the oppressed, food for the hungry, freedom for prisoners, sight for the blind, lifting of the bowed-down, love for the righteous, care for the sojourner, widow, and fatherless. Jesus reads this list in Luke 4:18–19 and 7:22 as the program of his own ministry — he has come to do exactly what Psalm 146 declares God does.

notes.original: al-tivtekhu be-nedivim
notes.rendering: put not your trust in princes
notes.why: Nedivim: nobles, generous ones, princes. The most powerful humans cannot deliver — their breath departs, their plans die with them. Human patronage is unreliable at the deepest level.

notes.original: YHWH...YHWH...YHWH
notes.rendering: The LORD...the LORD...the LORD
notes.why: Seven actions of God in three verses, each introduced by YHWH as subject. The sevenfold enumeration mirrors creation’s completeness — God’s care for the vulnerable is total.

notes.original: YHWH poqeakh ivrim
notes.rendering: the LORD opens the eyes of the blind
notes.why: Jesus quotes and enacts this in Luke 4:18 (Isa 61:1) and Luke 7:22. The physical healing of blindness is the sign that the kingdom announced in Ps 146 has arrived.

notes.original: yimlokh YHWH le-olam Elohayikh Tsion le-dor va-dor
notes.rendering: the LORD will reign forever, your God, O Zion, to all generations
notes.why: The enthronement declaration closes the psalm. God’s reign is not seasonal or political; it is permanent, generational, and rooted in Zion as its earthly center.

intro: Psalm 147 holds together two scales of divine action that seem incompatible: the God who counts and names the stars (v. 4) is the same God who heals the brokenhearted (v. 3). Cosmic power and personal tenderness belong to the same LORD. The psalm’s closing section (vv. 15–20) personifies the divine word as a swift runner: it goes out, snow falls, frost scatters, ice forms, then the word goes out again and all thaws. The word of God governs the weather. Then, climactically: this same word has been given to Israel — the greatest privilege in the psalm’s vision.

notes.original: mone mispar la-kokhavim le-khulam shemot yiqra
notes.rendering: he determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names
notes.why: The God who names the billions of stars also heals individual broken hearts. The same intelligence that orders the cosmos attends to personal grief. Both are expressions of the same love.

notes.original: lo ve-gevurat ha-sus yakhpots...rotseh et-yir'av
notes.rendering: his delight is not in the strength of the horse...but in those who fear him
notes.why: Military and athletic power impress humans; God is pleased by reverence and hope. The reversal of human value systems is characteristic of the closing psalms.

notes.original: ha-sholeakh imrato arets ad-meherah yarutz devaro
notes.rendering: he sends out his command; his word runs swiftly
notes.why: Devaro yarutz: his word runs. The word of God is personified as a swift courier. Paul may be echoing this in 2 Thess 3:1: “that the word of the Lord may speed ahead.”

notes.original: lo asah khen le-khol-goy u-mishpatim bal-yeda'um
notes.rendering: he has not dealt thus with any other nation
notes.why: The extraordinary privilege of Israel: to have received God’s word, statutes, and ordinances is a grace given to no other people. The psalm ends with this election-consciousness, not arrogance.

intro: Psalm 148 is the cosmic liturgy: the entire creation called to praise from heaven downward to earth. The two movements — heavenly praise (vv. 1–6) and earthly praise (vv. 7–14) — mirror each other, descending through the hierarchy of being: angels, hosts, sun, moon, stars, waters, sea creatures, weather, mountains, trees, animals, humans of every age and rank. The ground of the praise is stated in verse 5: “he commanded and they were created.” Every creature praises by being what it was made to be. The closing verse adds the particular privilege of Israel: among all the praising creation, they are the people who are near to him.

notes.original: ki hu tsivvah ve-nivre'u
notes.rendering: for he commanded and they were created
notes.why: The entire creation came into existence by divine speech-act (Gen 1). To exist is to be an object of that creative command. Existence itself is a form of dependence on God’s word.

notes.original: tanninim ve-khol-tehomot
notes.rendering: you great sea creatures and all deeps
notes.why: Tanninim: the sea monsters (cf. Gen 1:21; Ps 74:13). Even the chaos creatures of the deep are summoned to praise. Nothing in creation is outside the scope of the cosmic liturgy.

notes.original: ki-nissa shemo levaddo hodo al-erets ve-shamayim
notes.rendering: for his name alone is exalted; his majesty is above earth and heaven
notes.why: Levaddo: alone, exclusively. God’s name is exalted above everything — the superlative of the whole psalm in a single declaration.

notes.original: va-yarem qeren le-ammo
notes.rendering: he has raised up a horn for his people
notes.why: The raised horn of Israel within the cosmic liturgy: the particular privilege of this people is not their superiority but their proximity. They are the people “near to him” (qerov lo).

intro: Psalm 149 is the most militarily charged of the five closing Hallelujahs — praise and sword in the same hand. The image has been interpreted variously across the centuries: as eschatological judgment (the godly participating in the final reckoning), as historical Israel’s role as God’s instrument of justice, or as spiritual warfare. What is consistent is the union of worship and active engagement: praise is not passive but the empowered response of those whom God has adorned with salvation (v. 4). The honor of verse 9 is the honor of participating in God’s own purposes in the world.

notes.original: ki-rotseh YHWH be-ammo ye-fa'er anavim bi-shu'ah
notes.rendering: the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation
notes.why: Ye-fa'er: to beautify, to adorn (as with a garland or crown). The humble are not merely saved but ornamented with salvation — made glorious by what God has done for them.

notes.original: ye'allzu khasidim be-khavod yranenu al-mishkevotam
notes.rendering: let the godly exult in glory; let them sing for joy on their beds
notes.why: The bed as a place of praise: even in rest, in the night watches, the godly break into song. The praise of Ps 149 is not only corporate but intimate and personal.

notes.original: romemot El be-geronnam ve-kherev pi-fiyyot be-yadam
notes.rendering: let the high praises of God be in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands
notes.why: The dual image has fueled debate. Most likely it is eschatological: the community that praises is the community that participates in God’s final righteous judgment on evil.

intro: Psalm 150 is the great doxological finale of the entire Psalter — thirteen imperative verbs of praise in six verses, answering the six questions of Where? Why? How? with the single overwhelming answer: Hallelujah. The where: God’s sanctuary and his mighty heavens (v. 1). The why: his mighty deeds and his excellent greatness (v. 2). The how: every instrument known to Israel — trumpet, lute, harp, tambourine, dance, strings, pipe, cymbals (vv. 3–5). The final verse is the Psalter’s last word: not a doctrine, not a law, not a lament — but a command addressed to every breathing creature. The book that began with the blessedness of the righteous person ends with everything that has breath in the act of praise. The journey from Psalm 1 to Psalm 150 is the journey from instruction to doxology.

notes.original: hallelu-El be-qodsho
notes.rendering: Praise God in his sanctuary
notes.why: Two locations: qodsho (his holy sanctuary) and raqia uzzo (his mighty heavens/firmament). The praise fills both the earthly meeting place and the cosmic temple simultaneously.

notes.original: halleluhu bi-gevurotav
notes.rendering: praise him for his mighty deeds
notes.why: The grounds of praise: gevurot (mighty deeds) and gudlo (his surpassing greatness). Both what God does and what God is are reasons for praise — action and being together.

notes.original: shofar...nevel ve-khinor...tof u-makhol...minim ve-ugav...tsiltselei-shama...tsiltselei teruah
notes.rendering: trumpet...lute and harp...tambourine and dance...strings and pipe...cymbals
notes.why: The full orchestration of temple worship: wind, string, and percussion, plus the body itself (dance). No instrument is excluded. The praise is as varied as creation.

notes.original: kol ha-neshamah tehalel Yah
notes.rendering: Let everything that has breath praise the LORD
notes.why: Ha-neshamah: the breath, the living breath (same word as Gen 2:7 — God breathed into Adam’s nostrils). Every breath is a loan from the Creator; returning it as praise is the Psalter’s final definition of human existence.

intro: Revelation 1 establishes the book’s triple genre (apocalypse, prophecy, letter) and its governing vision: the risen Christ standing blazing in the midst of his churches, clothed in imagery drawn from Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 1. Three Greek terms anchor the theological claims that will drive the entire book.

notes.original: apokalypsis Iēsou Christou — the revelation / uncovering of Jesus Christ
notes.rendering: The revelation of Jesus Christ — which God gives him to show his servants what must soon take place.
notes.why: Apokalypsis means an uncovering, a lifting of the veil (apo — away; kalypō — to cover). The book presents itself as disclosure, not encryption. The genitive Iēsou Christou is deliberately ambiguous: a revelation belonging to Jesus, about Jesus, and from Jesus. The chain of transmission (God → Christ → angel → John → the churches) establishes the book’s entire authority structure in its opening clause.

notes.original: ho ōn kai ho ēn kai ho erchomenos — the one who is and who was and who is to come
notes.rendering: from him who is and who was and who is to come
notes.why: The construction is grammatically unusual to the point of being deliberate error: the preposition apo (from) requires the genitive, but ho ōn is nominative — and John leaves it undeclined. The divine name refuses Greek grammar. Jewish tradition rendered the Tetragrammaton as ‘I am who I am’ (Exodus 3:14, LXX: egō eimi ho ōn); John expands it into three time-axes. Ho erchomenos is not merely ‘the future’ but the Coming One — the God who actively arrives, who acts in history. This name is what the whole book unpacks.

notes.original: homoion huion anthrōpou — one like a son of man
notes.rendering: one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe and with a golden sash around his chest
notes.why: The phrase echoes Daniel 7:13 (LXX: hōs huios anthrōpou). In Daniel the Son of Man comes before the Ancient of Days to receive dominion; here he already holds it, walking among the lampstands. The accumulated imagery — white hair (Daniel 7:9, the Ancient of Days), eyes of fire, feet of bronze, a voice like many waters (Ezekiel 43:2) — fuses human and divine registers. What looked like a man is clothed in the appearance of God. This is the book’s central christological image.

intro: Revelation 2 delivers the first four of seven letters. Each follows a fixed judicial pattern: address, self-identification of Christ drawn from chapter 1’s vision, ‘I know your works,’ commendation and rebuke, warning and promise, the conqueror promise, and the ear-call. The pattern is diagnostic rather than merely pastoral — Christ speaks as the one who walks among the lampstands and sees everything.

notes.original: tēn agāpēn sou tēn prōtēn aphēkes — you have sent away your first love
notes.rendering: you have abandoned the love you had at first
notes.why: The verb aphiēmi means to release, send away, let go — the same word used for forgiveness of sins (releasing the debt). The first love is not dimmed or forgotten but actively released. The double article (tēn…tēn) is emphatic: the love — the specific, original love — is what is gone. This to a church that is doctrinally rigorous and endurance-proven: orthodoxy without love is already a kind of apostasy. The remedy is disarmingly simple: remember, repent, return.

notes.original: psēphon leukēn — a white stone
notes.rendering: I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on it that no one knows except the one who receives it
notes.why: The white stone (psēphos leukē) is one of Revelation’s most contested images. Proposed referents include: the white voting stone (acquittal in Athenian courts, versus the black stone for condemnation); the tessera hospitalis (a hospitality token entitling the holder to welcome); the gladiatorial pass; the magical amulet inscribed with a hidden name of power. The detail that only the recipient knows the name makes the gift irreducibly personal — a secret between Christ and the one who overcomes.

notes.original: poimanei autous en rhabdō sidēra — he will shepherd them with an iron rod
notes.rendering: he will shepherd them with an iron rod, as when earthen pots are shattered in pieces
notes.why: The promise to Thyatira quotes Psalm 2:8–9 (LXX). The verb poimainō means to shepherd, to tend — but the instrument is a rod of iron and the image is smashed pottery. What Psalm 2 applies to the Messiah, John transfers to the conqueror who shares Christ’s authority. This is Revelation’s most radical participatory claim in these early chapters: the saints do not merely witness the reign of Christ — they exercise it.

intro: Revelation 3 completes the seven letters. Sardis is nearly dead. Philadelphia is small and faithful. Laodicea is wealthy, comfortable, and oblivious. The letter to Laodicea is the most extended rebuke of all seven, and it closes not with threat but with the most intimate image in the book: a figure standing at the door.

notes.original: hē archē tēs ktiseōs tou theou — the beginning / origin of God’s creation
notes.rendering: the beginning of God’s creation
notes.why: Archē carries a range of meaning: beginning (in time), origin (as source), ruler (as first in authority). The christological stakes are high: does this mean Christ is the first created being, or the constitutive source of all creation? Colossians 1:15–18 — where Christ is the prōtotokos pasēs ktiseōs (firstborn of all creation, in whom and for whom all things exist) — provides the lens: archē here does not mean ‘first made’ but ‘constitutive origin.’ The Amen who speaks is the one through whom creation is.

notes.original: chliaros — lukewarm
notes.rendering: because you are lukewarm — neither hot nor cold — I am about to spit you out of my mouth
notes.why: The city of Laodicea had no adequate water supply. Hierapolis (6 miles north) had famous hot medicinal springs; Colossae (10 miles east) had cold mountain water. Laodicea’s supply came by aqueduct and arrived tepid — useless for medicine, useless for refreshment. The rebuke is topographically precise: the Laodiceans would have known exactly what lukewarm meant every time they drew water. The verb emesai (to vomit, spit out) is visceral and deliberate.

notes.original: idō hestēka epi tēn thyran kai krouō — look, I have been standing at the door and I knock
notes.rendering: Look — I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me.
notes.why: Hestēka is perfect tense: I have taken my stand and continue to stand. This is not a momentary knock but a sustained, patient presence. The image is addressed not to outsiders but to a church — Christ knocking at the door of his own community. The shared meal (deipnēsō — I will dine) is covenant language: table fellowship as the fullness of restored relationship. The promise that follows — sitting together on the throne — is Revelation’s most extravagant participatory image. It arrives at the end of seven letters as both climax and invitation.

intro: Revelation 4 is the hinge of the whole book: the transition from earth to heaven, from letters to vision. The throne room John enters is built from the materials of Ezekiel 1, Isaiah 6, and Daniel 7, assembled into a new whole. Three elements anchor the chapter’s theology of worship and sovereignty.

notes.original: thyra ēneōgmenē — a door that has been opened and stands open
notes.rendering: there before me is an open door in heaven
notes.why: The perfect passive participle ēneōgmenē (from anoigō — to open) carries the force of a completed action whose effect continues: the door has been opened and remains open. John does not force his way through a reluctant barrier; he is invited through a door that God has already set ajar. The same form appears in 3:8 (I have set before you an open door) — the Philadelphia promise and the throne-room entry share the same grammar of divine initiative.

notes.original: tessara zōa — four living creatures
notes.rendering: four living creatures, covered with eyes in front and behind
notes.why: Zōon means living being, living creature — not the ‘beast’ of older translations (which confusingly echoes the beastly enemies of ch. 13). The four creatures draw from Ezekiel’s chariot-throne vision (ch. 1 and 10) — man, lion, ox, eagle — and from Isaiah’s seraphim (ch. 6) with their six wings and unceasing song. The eyes covering them suggest total awareness, complete perception. They are not decoration; they are the engine of heavenly worship, and everything that follows (the seals, the trumpets, the bowls) originates from their liturgical space.

notes.original: hagios hagios hagios — holy holy holy
notes.rendering: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!
notes.why: The trisagion comes from Isaiah 6:3, where the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy, YHWH of hosts. John keeps the triple repetition (the fullest superlative in Hebrew idiom) but adds the trinitarian time-formula from 1:4 and 1:8. The worship of the living creatures is thus both the oldest liturgy in scripture (Isaiah’s temple vision) and the newest (reshaped around the revelation of the Coming One). Pantokratōr — Almighty, the one who holds all things in his hand — is the LXX rendering of YHWH Sabaoth (Lord of hosts).

intro: Revelation 5 is the theological pivot of the entire book. The question ‘Who is worthy?’ governs not just this chapter but the cosmos. The answer — announced as a lion, revealed as a slain lamb — is Revelation’s central christological paradox: power exercised through self-giving, conquest achieved through death. The hymns that follow belong to the greatest liturgical poetry in the New Testament.

notes.original: ho leōn / arnion — the Lion / the Lamb
notes.rendering: the Lion of the tribe of Judah... has conquered” / “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain
notes.why: The pivot of the whole book: John is told to look at a Lion and sees a Lamb. Leōn (lion) invokes the messianic imagery of Genesis 49:9 and the warrior-king of Jewish expectation. Arnion (lamb) is a diminutive — a little lamb — and appears 28 times in Revelation (virtually nowhere else in the NT). The Lamb bears the marks of slaughter (hōs esphagmenōon — as having been slaughtered) yet stands. The grammar of conquest is rewritten here: the Lion conquers by becoming the Lamb. Everything that follows in the book’s violent imagery must be read through this lens.

notes.original: ōdēn kainēn — a new song
notes.rendering: And they sing a new song: Worthy are you to take the scroll…
notes.why: Kainos in Greek means new in quality or kind, not merely new in time (neos). The new song is the song that could not have been sung before the Lamb’s act — it is new because the reality it celebrates is new. The background is the Exodus song of Moses (Exodus 15) and the ‘new song’ of the Psalms (Pss. 96, 98, 149): Israel sang of redemption from Egypt; the elders sing of ransoming (egorasas — you bought, you redeemed) people from every tribe, language, people, and nation. The Exodus has gone universal.

notes.original: axios estin to arnion — worthy is the Lamb
notes.rendering: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!
notes.why: Axios — worthy, deserving, of appropriate weight (from agō — to weigh, to lead). In the Roman imperial context, worth and worthiness were the vocabulary of the emperor’s acclamation. The sevenfold list that follows (power, wealth, wisdom, might, honor, glory, blessing) is a counterimperial doxology: every attribute the empire claimed for Caesar is here ascribed to the slaughtered Lamb. The number seven signals completeness: all honor, without remainder, belongs to the Lamb.

intro: Revelation 6 opens the sealed scroll and releases what is inside: not predictions in sequence but a compressed portrait of the age between the Lamb’s victory and the final consummation. The four horsemen, the martyrs’ cry, and the cosmic unraveling are not future timetable items — they are the texture of history under judgment. The chapter closes with a question the book will spend sixteen more chapters answering.

notes.original: nikōn kai hina nikēsē — conquering and in order to conquer
notes.rendering: He rides out conquering and to conquer.
notes.why: The white horse rider is fiercely debated. Some identify him with Christ (cf. 19:11–16, where Christ rides a white horse). Others see Conquest or military aggression, the first of four progressive catastrophes. The crown (stephanos — victor’s wreath, not the diadem of royalty) is given (edothē — divine passive) — as are the sword and authority to the other riders. The passive ‘given’ is key: even the horsemen operate within the permission of the one who holds the scroll. History is not out of control.

notes.original: hypo to thysiatērion — under the altar
notes.rendering: I see under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the witness they had borne.
notes.why: The image is drawn from the Old Testament altar theology: the blood of a sacrifice was poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). The martyrs’ lives, poured out as blood, lie at the base of the heavenly altar. They are not forgotten casualties — they are offerings. The word for slaughtered (esphagmenōn) is the same used for the Lamb in 5:6 and 5:12: the martyrs share the Lamb’s own condition. Their cry ‘how long’ (heōs pote) echoes the psalms of lament (Ps. 6:3; 13:1; 79:5) and is the oldest prayer of the persecuted.

notes.original: hē hēmera hē megalē tēs orgēs — the great day of wrath
notes.rendering: For the great day of their wrath has come — and who is able to stand?
notes.why: The great day (hēmera megalē) is the Day of YHWH — the theme that runs through Amos 5:18–20, Joel 2:11, Zephaniah 1:14–15, and Malachi 4:5. Amos warned that the Day would be darkness and not light for the unjust. Here it arrives as the wrath of both the one on the throne and the Lamb — the only place in Revelation where wrath is attributed to the Lamb. The closing question (tis dynatai stathēnai — who is able to stand?) borrows from Malachi 3:2 and is answered immediately in chapter 7: the sealed.

intro: Revelation 7 is the great interlude — the pause between the sixth and seventh seals that answers the chapter 6 question: who is able to stand? Two visions respond: the 144,000 sealed on earth, and the innumerable multitude already before the throne. Together they form a diptych of the same people seen from two different angles: the church militant and the church triumphant.

notes.original: hoi esphragismenoi — the sealed ones
notes.rendering: And I hear the number of the sealed: 144,000, from every tribe of the sons of Israel
notes.why: Sphragizō — to seal, to mark with an owner’s mark (from sphragis — the signet ring or stamp). The seal protects: not from suffering but from apostasy (cf. Ezekiel 9:4, where the mark on foreheads protects the righteous). The number 144,000 is 12 × 12 × 1,000 — the tribes of Israel squared and multiplied by the number of completion. Revelation consistently uses numbers symbolically (seven spirits, seven churches, seven seals). The 144,000 here and in chapter 14 are the same as the innumerable multitude of 7:9 — the whole people of God seen from two vantage points.

notes.original: oi erchomenoi ek tēs thlipseōs tēs megalēs — the ones coming out of the great tribulation
notes.rendering: These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
notes.why: Erchomenoi is a present participle: not ‘those who came out’ (past and complete) but ‘those who are coming out’ (continuous). The great tribulation (thlipsis — pressure, affliction, the crushing weight of persecution) is not a single future event but the ongoing condition of faithful witness under empire — the same thlipsis John shares with his readers in 1:9. The paradox of the white robes washed in blood belongs to Revelation’s characteristic reversal logic: the blood of the Lamb purifies rather than defiles.

notes.original: exaleipsei ho theos pan dakryon — God will wipe away every tear
notes.rendering: and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes
notes.why: The promise quotes Isaiah 25:8 (LXX: apheilato ho kyrios ton dakryon — the Lord removed the tear). Isaiah’s banquet vision — the mountain feast, death swallowed up, every face’s tears wiped away — becomes the pastoral resolution of a chapter that began with angels holding back cosmic destruction. The verb exaleipho means to wipe out completely, to erase — the same word used for erasing a name from a list (3:5) or blotting out sin. God will erase every tear as thoroughly as a debt is cancelled. The promise will be repeated, word for word, at the new creation in 21:4.

intro: Revelation 8 opens the seventh seal and releases not immediate catastrophe but something more arresting: half an hour of silence. Then the prayers of the saints become the fuel for judgment. The first four trumpets echo the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7–10), resetting the Exodus pattern at cosmic scale.

notes.original: sigē en tō ouranō hōs hēmioron — silence in heaven for about half an hour
notes.rendering: When the Lamb opens the seventh seal, there is silence in heaven for about half an hour.
notes.why: The half hour of silence is one of Revelation’s most theologically loaded pauses. After the roar of the throne room, the living creatures’ ceaseless song, and the great multitude’s cry, everything stops. Jewish liturgical tradition held that the angels were silent during the morning offering so that the prayers of Israel might be heard. The silence here frames what follows: the prayers of the saints (v.4) rise into a heaven that has hushed to receive them. The scroll has been opened; the prayers have been heard; what comes next is the answer.

notes.original: prosphoraï sōn hagiōn — the prayers of the saints
notes.rendering: He is given a great quantity of incense to offer, with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne.
notes.why: The golden bowls of incense in 5:8 were already identified as the prayers of the saints. Here those prayers are offered directly before the throne, and what rises from the censer becomes the fire thrown to the earth. The theological claim is startling: the prayers of persecuted believers are not passive petitions waiting for divine notice — they are the mechanism by which judgment is released. The martyrs’ cry of 6:10 (‘how long?’) is being answered through the very incense that carried their words.

notes.original: Apsinthos — Wormwood
notes.rendering: The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters become wormwood, and many people die from the water because it has been made bitter.
notes.why: Apsinthos (wormwood, Artemisia absinthium) is an intensely bitter plant used in the Old Testament as an image of judgment and the bitter consequences of apostasy (Proverbs 5:4; Jeremiah 9:15; Lamentations 3:15, 19; Amos 5:7, where justice is turned to wormwood). The star that poisons the waters reverses the miracle of Marah (Exodus 15:23–25, where Moses sweetens bitter water). Here the sequence runs in the opposite direction: the waters of creation are made lethal. The Exodus pattern that gave life now signals judgment.

intro: Revelation 9 deploys two of the most nightmarish visions in the book — the locust-army from the abyss and the cavalry of two hundred million — and ends with an observation more devastating than any plague: they still do not repent. The chapter borrows freely from Joel’s locust army (Joel 1–2) and the Parthian cavalry that haunted Rome’s eastern frontier.

notes.original: astera ek tou ouranou peptōkota — a star fallen from heaven
notes.rendering: I see a star fallen from heaven to earth. The key to the shaft of the bottomless pit is given to him.
notes.why: The star is a personal agent: he is given (edothē — divine passive again) the key. The perfect participle peptōkota (having fallen) echoes Isaiah 14:12 (how you have fallen from heaven, O Day Star) and Luke 10:18 (I saw Satan fall like lightning). The abyssos — bottomless pit, the abyss (from the LXX of Genesis 1:2, where it describes the formless deep) — is the reservoir of chaos and demonic power, the undoing of creation’s order.

notes.original: Abaddōn / Apollyōn — Destruction / Destroyer
notes.rendering: His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek he is called Apollyon — the Destroyer.
notes.why: Abaddon (from abad — to perish, to be destroyed) appears in Job 26:6, 28:22, and Proverbs 15:11 as the realm of the dead, the place of destruction. John gives the angel of the abyss both his Hebrew name and its Greek translation, Apollyon (from apollymi — to destroy, to ruin). The Greek name is almost certainly a pointed wordplay on Apollo — the god associated with Domitian’s imperial cult and with the locust as his sacred animal. Revelation names the destroyer, and the name is not the emperor’s god.

notes.original: ou metenoēsan — they did not repent
notes.rendering: The rest of humanity, who are not killed by these plagues, do not repent…
notes.why: The refrain echoes Amos 4:6–11 (yet you did not return to me) five times over. In Revelation it appears here and again after the bowl plagues (16:9, 11). The trumpets are not punishments designed to destroy but warnings designed to turn. When they fail to produce repentance (metanoia — a turning of mind and life), the failure lies not in the warnings but in the hardened will. The catalog of what they refuse to renounce — idol worship, murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, theft — is the mirror image of the new Jerusalem from which these things are excluded (21:8; 22:15).

intro: Revelation 10 is the second great interlude — a pause between the sixth and seventh trumpets that parallels the interlude of chapter 7. The mighty angel straddles sea and land; the sealed thunders withhold a revelation even from John; the eaten scroll commissions the prophet again. The chapter is saturated with Ezekiel.

notes.original: sphragison ha elalēsan — seal up what they said
notes.rendering: Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down.
notes.why: The command reverses the book’s opening instruction (1:11 — write what you see). Daniel was also told to seal his vision until the end (Daniel 12:4, 9). But the sealed thunders are more radical: John has heard them, has started to write, and is stopped. There is a revelation withheld even from the revealer — a boundary on apocalyptic disclosure. The apophatic silence at the center of the loudest book in scripture is deliberate: not everything that God does in history is given to prophets to announce.

notes.original: kataphage auto — eat it
notes.rendering: Take it and eat it. It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.
notes.why: The eating of the scroll comes directly from Ezekiel 2:8–3:3, where the prophet eats the scroll and it is sweet as honey in his mouth. Ezekiel’s scroll was filled with lamentations and mourning and woe — the sweetness was not its content but the privilege of receiving it. John adds the bitterness: the word of God is both gift (sweet) and burden (bitter). To prophesy is to carry what you have eaten, and what follows — the two witnesses, the dragon, the beast — is the taste of that bitterness.

notes.original: chronos ouketi estai — there will be no more delay
notes.rendering: There will be no more delay!
notes.why: Chronos here means not time in general but delay, interval, waiting period — as in the martyrs’ cry of 6:10 (how long?). The angel’s oath swears by the Creator and announces that the delay is over: the mystery of God (to mystērion tou theou) will be brought to completion (etelesthē — fulfilled, finished, completed) when the seventh trumpet sounds. The oath echoes Daniel 12:7, where the angelic figure swears that all will be accomplished after a time, times, and half a time. John is near the end of the delay.

intro: Revelation 11 compresses a dense theology of witness into two scenes: the two witnesses who prophesy, die, and are raised, and the seventh trumpet that announces the completion of God’s reign. The chapter is one of Revelation’s most allusive — Zechariah’s lampstands, Elijah’s drought, Moses’ plagues, Ezekiel’s measuring, and the Exodus all converge on a street in a city called Sodom and Egypt.

notes.original: hoi dyo martyres / hai dyo elaiai — the two witnesses / the two olive trees
notes.rendering: my two witnesses… the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth
notes.why: The two olive trees and two lampstands come from Zechariah 4 — the vision of the two anointed ones (Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the governor) who supply oil to the menorah. The witnesses have been identified as Moses and Elijah (fire, drought, plague), Enoch and Elijah, Peter and Paul, or as symbolic figures for the prophetic and priestly functions of the whole church. The 1,260 days (= 42 months = three and a half years) comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7 — the time, times, and half a time of tribulation. What matters is not the identity of the witnesses but their function: they testify, they are killed, they are raised.

notes.original: hē polis hē megalē — the great city
notes.rendering: the great city that is symbolically called Sodom and Egypt — where also their Lord was crucified
notes.why: The great city (hē polis hē megalē) is identified three ways: Sodom (depravity), Egypt (oppression and slavery), and the place where their Lord was crucified (Jerusalem). The Greek pneumatikōs (symbolically, spiritually, in a figure) signals that no single geography is meant. The great city is any city that combines luxury, oppressive power, and the murder of God’s witnesses. In 17:18 the same phrase identifies Babylon — Rome. The great city is Rome, Jerusalem, and every city that martyrs its prophets simultaneously.

notes.original: egeneto hē basileia tou kosmou tou kyriou hēmōn — the kingdom of the world became that of our Lord
notes.rendering: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever!
notes.why: The seventh trumpet is the announcement of completed sovereignty — not something that will happen but something declared as accomplished (egeneto — aorist: it became, it happened). The proclamation takes the language of imperial accession (the kingdom has become the possession of…) and transfers it entirely to the Lord and his Christ. Handel’s Messiah made this the climax of the oratorio for good reason: it is the climax of the trumpet sequence and the declaration that drives everything that follows. What remains is not the winning of the kingdom but the working out of a victory already announced.

intro: Revelation 12 pulls back the curtain on the cosmic dimension of the story the whole book has been telling. The dragon, the woman, and the child are not allegory overlaid on history — they are the history behind the history. The war in heaven has already been fought; the dragon has already lost; what remains is the earth-bound fury of a defeated power.

notes.original: sēmeion mega — a great sign
notes.rendering: A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun…
notes.why: Sēmeion — sign, portent, a meaning-laden event (the same word for Jesus’ signs in John’s Gospel). The woman has been read as Mary, as Israel (the twelve stars echoing Joseph’s dream in Genesis 37:9), as the church, and as the heavenly counterpart of all three. Her solar clothing, lunar footstool, and stellar crown draw from the imagery of the sky-goddess in ancient cosmology, deliberately appropriated and reshaped: this is no pagan deity but the faithful community from which the Messiah emerges. She embodies the whole story of Israel in labor toward its fulfillment.

notes.original: ho drakon ho megas, ho ophis ho archaios — the great dragon, the ancient serpent
notes.rendering: The great dragon is hurled down — that ancient serpent who is called the Devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world.
notes.why: John stacks four names: dragon (drawing on Leviathan and the chaos-monster of the Hebrew Bible, Job 41; Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:14), serpent (ophis archaios — the ancient snake of Genesis 3, identifying the tempter with this cosmic enemy), Diabolos (Devil — the slanderer, the one who throws accusations across), and Sat0101n0101s (the adversary, the prosecuting angel of Job 1–2). The identification is total and deliberate: every force of chaos, accusation, and deception in the biblical story is the same enemy, and he has been hurled down.

notes.original: dia to haima tou arniou — by the blood of the Lamb
notes.rendering: And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, for they did not love their lives even in the face of death.
notes.why: The victory hymn identifies three instruments of conquest: the Lamb’s blood, the witnesses’ testimony (martyria — the word that gives us martyr), and the willingness to die. The conquered dragon is not defeated by force but by the same logic as the cross: self-giving overcomes accusation because the accuser’s power is the threat of death, and those who no longer fear death cannot be controlled. The pattern of 5:5–6 (Lion/Lamb) is repeated here at the level of the saints’ own lives.

intro: Revelation 13 gives the dragon his earthly instruments: two beasts, one from the sea (political-military power), one from the earth (the propaganda apparatus that enforces worship). Together they form an unholy trinity parodying Father, Son, and Spirit. The chapter’s famous conclusion — the number 666 — is almost certainly a gematria, not a prediction schedule.

notes.original: hōs esphagmenēn eis thanaton — as having been slaughtered to death
notes.rendering: One of its heads seems to have a mortal wound, but the mortal wound is healed.
notes.why: The beast’s wounded-and-healed head directly parodies the Lamb who was slaughtered (esphagmenon, 5:6). The beast mimics resurrection. The Nero redivivus legend — the belief that Nero, who died in 68 CE, would return leading a Parthian army — was circulating in the 90s. But John’s target is broader than one emperor: any imperial power that survives what should have killed it and demands worship is the beast. The imitation of the Lamb’s death and return is the most satanic possible parody: the same pattern, the opposite allegiance.

notes.original: to biblion tēs zoēs tou arniou — the book of life of the Lamb
notes.rendering: all who dwell on the earth will worship it — everyone whose name has not been written before the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain
notes.why: The book of life appears in Exodus 32:32–33 (Moses’ offer to be blotted out), Psalm 69:28, Daniel 12:1, and throughout Revelation (3:5; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27). That it belongs to the Lamb and that names were inscribed before the foundation of the world establishes a pre-temporal election that runs counter to the beast’s claims. Those whose names are in the book do not belong to the beast, however much it controls the marketplace. The choice of who controls the book is the deepest political question of the chapter.

notes.original: arithmos anthrōpou — the number of a man / a human number
notes.rendering: Here is wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666.
notes.why: Gematria assigns numerical values to letters (in both Hebrew and Greek each letter has a number). NERON KAISAR in Hebrew letters (nun=50, resh=200, waw=6, nun=50, qoph=100, samek=60, resh=200) = 666. The variant reading 616 in some manuscripts corresponds to the Latin spelling NERO CAESAR. The identification is strong. But John’s point is not to encode a single name — it is to say that the beast’s number is human (anthrōpou): it falls short of seven (the divine number), triple-six being the maximum of human pretension, always one short of divine completion.

intro: Revelation 14 is a chapter of previews and announcements: the 144,000 already standing with the Lamb, the gospel still flying in midheaven, Babylon’s fall pre-announced, and the double harvest — grain and vintage — as the shape of the end. The beatitude of verse 13 is the second of the book’s seven blessings.

notes.original: hoi meta gynaikōn ouk emolynthēsan — those who have not defiled themselves with women
notes.rendering: These are the ones who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins.
notes.why: The sexual language is almost certainly symbolic, following the Old Testament tradition of using adultery and prostitution as images for idolatry (Hosea, Ezekiel 16 and 23, Jeremiah 2–3). The 144,000 are parthénoi (virgins — the word applies to both sexes in Greek) who have not ‘defiled themselves’ with the porneia of Babylon — the empire’s idolatrous commerce and worship. The following clause (they follow the Lamb wherever he goes) defines their identity positively: undivided allegiance.

notes.original: Epesen Babylon hē megalē — Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great
notes.rendering: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who made all nations drink the wine of the passion of her sexual immorality.
notes.why: The double fallen (epesen, epesen) quotes Isaiah 21:9, where a watchman announces the fall of historical Babylon. In Revelation, Babylon is the code name for Rome (as in 1 Peter 5:13 and the Sibylline Oracles) — the city that sits on seven hills (17:9), drunk on the blood of saints (17:6), whose merchants grew rich on her luxury trade (18:3). The announcement here in ch. 14 is proleptic: the fall is declared before the detailed account of chapters 17–18. The prophetic perfect tense announces as certain what has not yet visibly occurred.

notes.original: makarioi hoi nekroi hoi en Kuriō apothnēskontes — blessed are the dead who die in the Lord
notes.rendering: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on… for their deeds follow them.
notes.why: The second of Revelation’s seven beatitudes (cf. 1:3; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7, 14). It is spoken into the context of the third angel’s warning about the consequences of beast-worship: blessed, in that context, are those who choose to die rather than compromise. Ap’ arti — from now on — marks a turning point: after the announcement of judgment, death in the Lord has a particular blessedness. Their works (erga) follow them as witnesses, as evidence, as the freight of a life faithfully lived.

intro: Revelation 15 is the shortest chapter in the book and one of its most liturgically rich. It is also a threshold — the vestibule of the bowl judgments. Before the wrath is poured out, the conquerors stand on the glassy sea and sing. The pattern is deliberate: worship precedes judgment, just as Exodus 15’s song followed the sea’s crossing.

notes.original: tēn ōdēn Mōysēos … kai tēn ōdēn tou arniou — the song of Moses… and the song of the Lamb
notes.rendering: They sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb.
notes.why: The song of Moses is Exodus 15 — the victory hymn after the Red Sea crossing, the first great song of redemption in Israel’s story. Here it is also the song of the Lamb: the two songs are one. The Exodus is not superseded but fulfilled — the same God who drowned Pharaoh’s army has now defeated the dragon’s empire by the blood of the Lamb. The words of the hymn (vv. 3–4) are woven from Psalm 111:2, Amos 4:13, Psalm 86:9–10, and Psalm 98:2: the conquerors sing the whole library of scripture in one breath.

notes.original: hoti monos hosios — for you alone are holy
notes.rendering: For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed.
notes.why: Hosios — holy, devout, set apart in a moral sense (distinct from hagios, which is cultic holiness). YHWH alone is hosios — the only one whose holiness is entirely internal, requiring nothing outside itself for validation. The universalism of ‘all nations will come’ (panta ta ethnē) quotes Psalm 86:9 and anticipates Revelation’s final vision (21:24–26, where the nations walk by the light of the new Jerusalem and bring their glory into it). The bowl judgments that follow this hymn are not the opposite of this vision but its painful approach.

notes.original: edoxēs tou theou kai ek tēs dynameōs autou — the glory of God and from his power
notes.rendering: The sanctuary is filled with smoke from the glory of God and from his power, and no one is able to enter the sanctuary until the seven plagues are finished.
notes.why: The filling of the sanctuary with the cloud of glory (doxa) echoes the dedication of the Mosaic tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35, where Moses cannot enter because the glory fills it) and the Solomonic temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). The parallel signals that what follows is as momentous as those foundational acts of covenant. The temporary inaccessibility of the sanctuary — no intercession possible until the bowls are finished — is itself part of the theological claim: this sequence of judgment is complete and will not be interrupted.

intro: Revelation 16 pours out the seven bowls in rapid sequence — the most compressed of the three judgment series. Unlike the trumpets, which affected a third of things, the bowls are total and final. Yet the human response is the same as in chapter 9: they curse God and do not repent. The chapter’s judgment raises the same moral question the whole series has raised: what is the purpose of a wrath that hardens rather than turns?

notes.original: ou metenoēsan dounai autōi doxan — they did not repent to give him glory
notes.rendering: They do not repent and give him glory” / “They do not repent of their deeds.
notes.why: The double non-repentance (vv. 9 and 11) forms a deliberate bracket around the fifth bowl. The language echoes 9:20–21 — the same refusal after the trumpets. Metanoia — repentance, a turning of mind and will — is what the bowls are designed to produce. That they do not produce it is not a failure of the warnings but a revelation of the will: those who have organized their lives around the beast’s system cannot unbind themselves from it. The bowls do not create hardness; they reveal it.

notes.original: makarios ho grēgorōn — blessed is the one who stays awake
notes.rendering: Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps their garments, so as not to go about naked and be seen in shame.
notes.why: The fourth of Revelation’s seven beatitudes, dropped without transition into the middle of the bowl sequence. Its voice is the same as the letters’ promises — the risen Christ speaking directly to the reader across the visions. The nakedness recalled (cf. Laodicea’s naked poverty in 3:17) is both literal (the shame of public exposure) and spiritual (the unpreparedness of the soldier caught off guard). The word for keeps (tērōn) is the same used for keeping Christ’s word in the letters: watchfulness and obedience are the same act.

notes.original: Gegonen — It is done
notes.rendering: It is done!
notes.why: Gegonen (perfect tense of ginomai — to become, to happen) announces completion: it has happened, it is accomplished, it stands done. The word echoes the tetelestai of John 19:30 (It is finished) — the same grammar of accomplished reality. Both words are spoken from a throne: there, from the cross as throne of suffering; here, from the throne of heaven as judgment completes what the cross began. The seventh bowl poured into the air affects the very medium of life — there is nowhere left that is untouched.

intro: Revelation 17 unveils the ideological architecture behind the beast: the great prostitute who is Rome — the city on seven hills, drunk on martyrs’ blood, seducing nations with the wine of her commercial and imperial power. The chapter is John’s most extended political analysis, encoded in the visionary idiom of Jewish apocalypticism.

notes.original: Babylon hē megalē, hē mētēr tōn pornōn — Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes
notes.rendering: Babylon the great, mother of prostitutes and of earth’s abominations
notes.why: Babylon is the code name for Rome used in Jewish texts of the period (1 Peter 5:13; 4 Ezra 3:1–2; 2 Baruch 10:1–3; the Sibylline Oracles). The seven hills (v. 9) confirm the identification — Rome’s seven hills were famous throughout the ancient world. Pornē (prostitute) is the Old Testament image for a city or nation that has sold itself to idolatry and economic exploitation (Isaiah 23:15–17 on Tyre; Nahum 3:4 on Nineveh; Ezekiel 16 and 23 on Jerusalem). The mother of prostitutes is not merely immoral — she is the generative source of the imperial idolatry system.

notes.original: hēn kai ouk estin kai parestai — was and is not and is to come
notes.rendering: The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to rise…
notes.why: The beast’s identity formula (was / is not / is to come) is a deliberate inversion of the divine name (who is and who was and who is to come, 1:4; 4:8). The beast parodies God’s eternal being: its version of ‘to come’ is parestai (is about to be present) — leading to destruction. The Nero redivivus legend fits here: Nero was, then died (is not), and was rumored to return. But the structure is theological as well as political: any imperial power that mimics divine eternity will ultimately face the same verdict — hupagei eis apoleian (goes to destruction).

notes.original: Kyrios kyriōn kai Basileus basileōn — Lord of lords and King of kings
notes.rendering: the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings
notes.why: The title appears in Deuteronomy 10:17 (YHWH as God of gods and Lord of lords), Daniel 2:47, and 1 Timothy 6:15. In Revelation it is applied first to the Lamb here, then to the rider on the white horse in 19:16. The order of titles is significant: the Lamb conquers not by being more powerful in the world’s terms but by being the ground of all power. Those with him (hoi met’ autou) are klētoi kai eklektoi kai pistoi — called, chosen, and faithful: the threefold identity of the saints in a single clause.

intro: Revelation 18 is the great dirge over the fallen empire — a sustained piece of prophetic poetry drawing from the laments over Tyre (Ezekiel 26–28) and Babylon (Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50–51). The three mourning groups (kings, merchants, sailors) weep from a safe distance. The single line that most haunts the chapter is buried in the cargo list: ‘human souls.’

notes.original: Exelthe ex autes ho laos mou — Come out of her, my people
notes.rendering: Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues
notes.why: The call to exodus echoes Isaiah 48:20 (Go out from Babylon; flee from Chaldea) and Jeremiah 51:45 (Come out of her, my people). The command is not primarily geographical but ethical: the people of God living within the empire’s economic system are called not to emigrate but to disentangle — to stop participating in the violence and idolatry that undergird Rome’s prosperity. The same call is implicit in the letters: Thyatira’s problem with Jezebel, Pergamum’s eating of idol food, Laodicea’s wealth — all are forms of remaining inside Babylon.

notes.original: psycas anthrōpōn — souls of human beings
notes.rendering: …slaves — human souls
notes.why: The cargo list of Revelation 18 ends with soma (bodies, slaves) kai psychas anthrōpōn (and souls of human beings). The chiastic pair is devastating: first the economic category (bodies for sale), then the theological correction (but they are human souls). Rome’s economy ran on approximately two million slaves in Italy alone. The empire that demanded worship had built its prosperity on the reduction of persons to property. Revelation names what the merchants refuse to name: what they are trading in the last item on the list is not cargo but people.

notes.original: phōnē nymphiou kai nymphēs — the voice of bridegroom and bride
notes.rendering: The voice of the bridegroom and bride will be heard in you no more
notes.why: The litany of silenced sounds (harps, music, craft, millstone, lamp, voices) draws from Jeremiah 7:34 and 16:9, where the silencing of the voice of the bridegroom and bride is the sign of utter desolation. Each sound represents a dimension of human life: music (culture), craft (labor), millstone (food), lamp (shelter), wedding voice (covenant love and new life). When Babylon falls, what falls with it is the entire fabric of human flourishing it had commodified. The same sounds will return, transformed, in the new Jerusalem.

intro: Revelation 19 moves from lament to liturgy to combat: the fourfold Hallelujah, the marriage of the Lamb, and the appearance of the rider whose only weapon is a word. The chapter is one of the most misread in scripture — the warrior-king’s violence is entirely verbal, and the bride’s garments are woven from deeds.

notes.original: Hallēlouiā — Hallelujah (praise YHWH)
notes.rendering: Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God
notes.why: Hallēlouiā is a direct transliteration of the Hebrew hallēlū Yāh (praise YHWH) — the only place in the New Testament where the Hebrew doxological formula appears untranslated. It occurs four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 3, 4, 6) — nowhere else in the NT. The great Hallel psalms (Psalms 113–118, sung at Passover) form the background: Revelation’s Hallelujah chorus is the eschatological Passover song, sung now that the true Passover Lamb has brought final deliverance.

notes.original: ta dikaiōmata tōn hagiōn — the righteous deeds of the saints
notes.rendering: for the fine linen is the righteous deeds of the saints
notes.why: The bride’s garment (byssinos lampros katharos — fine linen, bright and pure) is given to her (edothē — divine passive) yet is identified as her own righteous acts (dikaiōmata). Both are simultaneously true: the garment is grace and it is the woven texture of a life lived faithfully. The passive gift and the active weaving are not in tension. This is the same logic as the martyrs’ works that follow them (14:13) and the conqueror promises of the letters: faithfulness under pressure is both given and achieved.

notes.original: ho Logos tou Theou — the Word of God
notes.rendering: the name by which he is called is The Word of God
notes.why: The only place in Revelation where the rider is named The Word of God (ho Logos tou Theou). The connection with John 1:1–14 (the Logos who was with God and was God, who became flesh) is unmistakable — especially given the shared Johannine idiom. The sword from the rider’s mouth (v. 15) is thus not a literal weapon but the Word itself in its full judicial force: the one who spoke creation into existence now speaks the final judgment. His robe is dipped in blood before the battle begins (v. 13) — it is the blood of the cross, not of the slaughtered, that marks his garment.

intro: Revelation 20 is the most contested chapter in the book and perhaps in all of Christian eschatology. The thousand years (millenium) has generated millenialist movements across twenty centuries of interpretation. The chapter’s more certain theological achievement is its account of the last judgment: death itself is destroyed, and what remains is the book of life.

notes.original: chilia etē — a thousand years
notes.rendering: They come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years.
