notes.why: The thousand years appears only in this chapter (six times in vv. 2–7) and nowhere else in the New Testament. Chilioi (thousand) in Revelation is consistently symbolic: 144,000 = 12 x 12 x 1,000; a thousand years = the complete and full extent of Christ’s reign between his resurrection and the final consummation. Three major interpretations exist: premillennialism (Christ returns before a literal 1,000-year reign), postmillennialism (Christ returns after a golden age produced by the church), and amillennialism (the thousand years is the current age, the reign is already underway). The text itself does not resolve this; it asserts the reign’s completeness and the certainty of its end.

notes.original: thronon megan leukon — a great white throne
notes.rendering: Then I see a great white throne and the one who is seated on it. From his presence earth and sky flee away.
notes.why: The great white throne (contrast with the scarlet beast-throne of ch. 17) is the final judgment seat. White (leukos) throughout Revelation signals purity, victory, and divine character. The fleeing of earth and sky (from the presence — apo prosōpou, from the face) echoes Psalm 114:3–7 (the sea fled at YHWH’s presence, the mountains skipped). Creation itself cannot stand before the final judgment; what is left is only persons and the record of their deeds. The books and the book of life together hold both the comprehensive account and the decisive word.

notes.original: ho thanatos kai ho Hades eblēthēsan — Death and Hades were thrown
notes.rendering: Then Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death.
notes.why: Death and Hades have been paired throughout Revelation (1:18, where the risen Christ holds their keys; 6:8, the fourth horseman). Now they are destroyed. The abolition of death is the promise of Isaiah 25:8 (he will swallow up death forever) and 1 Corinthians 15:26 (the last enemy to be destroyed is death). By throwing death into the lake of fire, John enacts Paul’s eschatology in visionary form. After this, nothing that was before the throne is any longer subject to death’s power — which makes the new creation possible.

intro: Revelation 21 is the destination the whole book has been traveling toward. The new creation is not the annihilation of the old but its transformation: the same twelve tribes, the same twelve apostles, the same nations — but no sea (the ancient symbol of chaos), no temple (because God’s presence is total), no night, no tears. The new Jerusalem descends; it is not the flight of souls upward but the arrival of God downward.

notes.original: kainos ouranos kai kainē gē — a new heaven and a new earth
notes.rendering: Then I see a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth have passed away.
notes.why: Kainos — new in quality, not merely new in time (neos). The new creation is not replacement but transformation, fulfillment: Isaiah 65:17–25 and 66:22 provide the background. The sea is no more (he thalassa ouk estin eti) — the sea in Jewish cosmology was the reservoir of chaos, the source of the beasts (13:1), the abyss. Its absence is not the elimination of ocean but the elimination of everything chaotic, threatening, and uncontrollable. The creation that began with the Spirit moving over the deep (Genesis 1:2) ends with no deep remaining.

notes.original: hē skēnē tou theou meta tōn anthrōpōn — the dwelling place of God with humanity
notes.rendering: Look — the dwelling place of God is with humanity. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people
notes.why: Skēnē (tent, dwelling, tabernacle) deliberately echoes the Mosaic tabernacle (skēnē in the LXX) and John 1:14 (the Word skēnoo-ed among us — tabernacled, pitched his tent). The covenant formula ‘they will be his people and he will be their God’ (Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27) is now fully and finally realized: not in the temple courts but in the new creation itself. The whole history of temple, tabernacle, and incarnation arrives here at its end: God with humanity, directly and permanently.

notes.original: naon ouk eidon — I see no temple
notes.rendering: I see no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb… the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it.
notes.why: The absence of a temple is the most radical statement in the chapter: the entire sacrificial-mediatorial system that structured Israel’s worship is no longer needed because unmediated divine presence is total. The nations (ta ethnē) walking by its light and kings bringing their glory into it — their doxa (not the doxa of military conquest but the genuine glory of human cultural achievement) — fulfills Isaiah 60’s vision of the nations streaming to Zion. Not destruction of the nations but their transformation and inclusion: the new Jerusalem is the city that receives what every city was meant to be.

intro: Revelation 22 brings the book full circle — back to the garden, back to the tree of life, back to the face of God — and then pivots to the present tense with an urgency that is the whole point of the book: Come. The visions are not entertainment or prediction; they are the ground of a present call to faithfulness. The last word is grace.

notes.original: xylon zōēs — the tree of life
notes.rendering: On either side of the river is the tree of life with its twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit each month. The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.
notes.why: The tree of life (xylon zōēs) was planted in Eden (Genesis 2:9) and barred to humanity after the fall (Genesis 3:22–24). Now it stands accessible on both sides of the river — its barrier removed, its fruit perpetual (twelve kinds, month by month), its leaves for the healing (therapeia — therapeutic, healing, health-restoring) of the nations (ta ethnē — the Gentile nations, who walked in darkness in the old age, now healed in the new). The tree of life promised to the conqueror in Ephesus (2:7) is now available to all. The exclusion of Eden’s garden is undone by the inclusion of the city’s garden.

notes.original: opsontai to prosōpon autou — they will see his face
notes.rendering: They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.
notes.why: The beatific vision — seeing God face to face — was the ultimate promise of the Psalms (Psalm 17:15; 27:4; 42:2) and the deepest longing of the covenant relationship. Moses could not see God’s face and live (Exodus 33:20); the beatitudes promised it to the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8). Here it is simply stated as fact: they see his face. The name on the forehead (cf. 3:12, the new name written on the conqueror; 7:3, the seal on the foreheads of the 144,000) is the mark of complete belonging, complete identity — the reversal of the beast’s mark (13:16). To bear the name of God on your forehead is to be entirely and finally known.

notes.original: ho thelōn labētō hydōr zōēs dōrean — let the one who desires take the water of life without price
notes.rendering: let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price
notes.why: Dōrean — freely, as a gift, without cost (from dōron — gift; the same word as grace-gift). Isaiah 55:1 (Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat… without money and without price) underlies the invitation. The final open invitation of the book is universal in form: any thirsty one, any desiring one, may come. After twenty-one chapters of sealed scrolls, judgments, and numbers of the elect, the book ends with an open door and a free gift. The last word of invitation is grace, as the last word of the letter is grace (v. 21).

intro: Romans 1 opens with one of Paul's most complex sentences — vv.1–7 are a single Greek period — then states the letter's governing thesis (vv.16–17) before anatomising the consequences of idolatry (vv.18–32). The argument about idolatry draws heavily on Wisdom of Solomon 13–14 and is directed, in its original rhetorical context, at Gentile religion — not at Jews. The three-fold repetition of paredōken ('gave them over,' vv.24, 26, 28) structures the passage as a deliberate descent: from idolatry to sexual disorder to general moral collapse.

notes.original: doulos Christou Iesou — slave of Christ Jesus
notes.rendering: a servant of Christ Jesus
notes.why: Doulos means slave, not merely servant — the one who is owned. Paul opens by relinquishing status: the apostle to the nations is first the Messiah's property. Kletos apostolos — called as an apostle — indicates the calling is prior to the commission. Paul did not volunteer; he was apprehended (Phil. 3:12).

notes.original: Ioudaio te proton kai Helleni — to the Jew first, and also to the Greek
notes.rendering: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek
notes.why: This phrase is the structural key to the entire letter and the primary guardrail against supersessionist misreading. 'First' is not a statement of privilege without accountability — it recurs at 2:9–10 applied to judgment, showing covenantal priority runs in both directions. The gospel comes through Israel's scriptures and Israel's Messiah; it does not bypass or replace Israel. Paul returns to this with full force in chapters 9–11.

notes.original: dikaiosynē theou — righteousness of God
notes.rendering: the righteousness of God is being revealed
notes.why: Dikaiosynē theou is the letter's central concept and its most debated. Is it (a) God's own covenant faithfulness — the attribute by which he is true to his promises — or (b) a status of righteousness that God confers on those who believe? The Reformation tradition read it primarily as (b). The New Perspective on Paul emphasises (a). Paul may intend the ambiguity: God is righteous and makes the people of faith righteous. The source verse is Habakkuk 2:4 — itself a word of patience to those waiting for God to act on covenant promises.

notes.original: paredōken — gave them over (three times)
notes.rendering: God gave them over" (vv. 24, 26, 28)
notes.why: The triple repetition structures the passage as a deliberate theological descent: idolatry produces sexual disorder; sexual disorder produces general moral collapse. This is not a condemnation of same-sex attraction as the supreme sin — it is an analysis of how the disruption of the knowledge of God cascades into disorder at every level of human life. The argument is drawn from Wisdom of Solomon 13–14, where Gentile idolatry produces exactly this unravelling. It is a diagnosis of paganism's internal logic, not a universal ranking of sins.

intro: Romans 2 is consistently misread as a condemnation of Jews. It is not. Paul's argument is architectural: chapter 1 anatomised Gentile idolatry; 2:1–16 turns on the generic human judge (anthrōpe — 'O human being,' not 'O Jew'); the Jewish-specific section begins only at 2:17. The rhetorical structure mirrors Amos 1–2: indict the nations, then spring the trap. But Paul's trap is not ethnic condemnation — it is the universality of moral accountability before a God who shows no favouritism. He will insist in chapter 9 that Israel's election is irrevocable.

notes.original: dio anapologētos ei, ō anthrōpe — you are without excuse, O human being
notes.rendering: you have no excuse, whoever you are
notes.why: The address is anthrōpe — 'O human being,' not 'O Jew.' Paul is making a universal case in 2:1–16 before narrowing to the Jewish interlocutor at 2:17. The move echoes Amos 1–2: condemn the nations in turn, then spring the trap. But the trap here is not ethnic — it is the universality of self-knowledge: the one who judges does the same things. This is addressed to anyone who has ever used moral categories for condemnation without self-examination.

notes.original: Ioudaio te proton kai Helleni — to the Jew first, and also to the Greek
notes.rendering: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" — for both judgment and honour
notes.why: The same phrase from 1:16 returns applied now to both wrath (v.9) and peace (v.10). This symmetry is Paul's point: covenantal priority means prior accountability, not exemption. The logic is identical to Amos 3:2 — 'you only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you.' Israel's election intensifies the moral demand; it does not dissolve it. Critique from within the covenant, not abolition of the covenant.

notes.original: su Ioudaios onomazē — you who call yourself a Jew; epanapauesai nomō — and rest in the Torah
notes.rendering: if you identify yourself as a Jew and rest your confidence in the Torah
notes.why: Paul's target is the person who uses covenant identity as a shield against self-examination — a type his own scriptures know well (Jer. 7:4 — 'the temple of the LORD'; Isa. 58 — fasting that bypasses justice; Amos 5 — worship that coexists with the trampling of the poor). This is internal prophetic critique. Paul is not attacking Jews; he is standing in the tradition of Amos, Isaiah, and Jeremiah, arguing that covenant membership requires covenant faithfulness.

notes.original: ou gar ho en tō phanerō Ioudaios estin — it is not the outwardly Jewish person who is truly Jewish; peritomē kardias — circumcision of the heart
notes.rendering: it is not the person who is outwardly Jewish who is truly Jewish... real circumcision is of the heart
notes.why: This passage has been used to argue that Paul abolishes Jewish identity. He does not. He is drawing on Deuteronomy 30:6 ('YHWH your God will circumcise your heart'), Jeremiah 4:4 ('circumcise yourselves to YHWH, remove the foreskin of your hearts'), and Jeremiah 9:25–26 — an internal biblical tradition about the heart's orientation within the covenant. Paul in Romans 9:4–5 will explicitly name Israel's adoption, glory, covenants, Torah, worship, promises, and patriarchs as still-valid and still-Israel's. 'Inward Jew' does not mean 'Christian replacing Jew.' It means what the prophets always meant: the person whose heart is aligned with what the covenant requires.

intro: Romans 3 is perhaps the most theologically consequential chapter in the letter. It opens with Paul emphatically affirming Jewish advantage (vv.1–2) before addressing the problem of universal sin, and closes with the declaration that God is the God of both Jews and Gentiles and that faith upholds rather than abolishes the Torah. The misreading of this chapter as a demotion of Judaism has caused centuries of harm; the translation notes below attempt to restore what Paul actually argues.

notes.original: ti to perisson tou Ioudaiou — what is the advantage of the Jew? poly kata panta tropon — much in every way
notes.rendering: much in every way! First of all, the Jewish people were entrusted with the oracles of God
notes.why: This passage is chronically underdiscussed. Paul opens chapter 3 by emphatically affirming Jewish advantage. The Jewish people are uniquely entrusted with ta logia tou theou — the oracles, the divine utterances, the scriptures that contain the covenant promises. This is not revoked. It will be made even more explicit in 9:4–5. Those who read Romans as an argument for Jewish demotion must reckon with the fact that Paul himself spends the first two verses of this chapter saying the opposite.

notes.original: proechometha? ou pantōs — do we have a preeminence? not at all
notes.rendering: Do we Jews have an advantage here? No, not in this respect at all
notes.why: The key phrase is 'in this respect' (pantōs here is restrictive, not absolute). Paul is not reversing 3:1–2 — he has just said Jews have much advantage in every way. Here he is making the point that in the specific matter of sin's dominion, no one is exempt. The catena of scripture quotations that follows (vv.10–18) draws on Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Ecclesiastes — texts from Israel's own scriptures describing the condition of the wicked. Paul does not quote them to condemn Jews but to establish universal human need for the redemption he is about to announce.

notes.original: ex ergōn nomou — from works of the Torah; epignōsis hamartias — knowledge of sin
notes.rendering: by works of the Torah no human being will be found righteous in his sight
notes.why: Erga nomou — 'works of the Torah' — is the passage's most debated phrase. The Reformation tradition read it as 'moral effort' or 'meritorious deeds.' The New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, Wright) argues convincingly that in context it refers specifically to Torah-identity markers — circumcision, food laws, Sabbath observance — the practices that defined the boundary between Jew and Gentile. Paul's point is that these ethnic-boundary works do not constitute the basis for standing before God; faith does. This is not an attack on Jewish law-keeping as such — it is an argument that Gentiles do not need to become Jews in order to belong to the people of God.

notes.original: hilastērion — mercy-seat, place of atonement; propitiation
notes.rendering: whom God set forth publicly as the mercy-seat — the place of atonement — through his blood
notes.why: Hilastērion in the LXX is the word for the kapporet — the mercy-seat or atonement cover on the Ark of the Covenant (Lev. 16:2, 13–15), the place where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Paul is drawing a deliberate and dense connection to Yom Kippur: Jesus's death is the act of divine atonement that the Levitical system anticipated. This is not the abolition of the Temple cult — it is Paul reading Jesus through the Temple's logic. The imagery presupposes the validity of what it fulfils.

notes.original: ē Ioudaiōn ho theos monon — is God the God of Jews only? nomon histanomen — we uphold the Torah
notes.rendering: Is he not also the God of Gentiles? Yes, of Gentiles also... we uphold the Torah
notes.why: Verses 29–31 contain two of the most important anti-supersessionist statements in the chapter. First: God is the God of Gentiles too — this is expansion, not replacement. Gentiles are being included in what was always Israel's God's domain. Second: nomon histanomen — we uphold, establish, confirm the Torah. Faith does not abolish the Torah. Paul will develop this in chapters 7–8 and reach his fullest statement on Israel's irrevocable election in chapters 9–11.

intro: Romans 4 is Paul's extended exegesis of Genesis 15:6 — Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. The argument turns on the sequence of events in Abraham's life: faith came before circumcision, which means circumcision sealed an existing relationship rather than constituting it. This makes Abraham the father of two groups: believing Gentiles (who share his pre-circumcision faith) and believing Jews (who share both his faith and his circumcision). The argument is expansive — it enlarges the family — not replacive. Abraham is not taken from the Jews and given to the Gentiles; he is shown to have been the father of a larger family all along.

notes.original: Abraam ton propatora hēmōn — Abraham our forefather; kata sarka — according to the flesh
notes.rendering: Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh
notes.why: The 'our' here is Paul identifying with Israel. Paul is a Jewish writer addressing a mixed community, speaking of Abraham as his own ancestor. The phrase kata sarka (according to the flesh) signals that Paul is aware there are multiple ways Abraham is 'father' — biological descent is one; the faith-relationship he will develop in vv.11–12 is another. Both matter. The argument is not that ethnic descent from Abraham is meaningless but that it is insufficient on its own.

notes.original: patera pantōn tōn pisteuontōn — father of all who believe; patera peritomēs — father of the circumcised
notes.rendering: father of all who believe without being circumcised... and father of the circumcised who also walk in the steps of the faith
notes.why: The structure is additive, not substitutive. Abraham is father of two groups: (a) uncircumcised believers — Gentiles who share his pre-circumcision faith; and (b) the circumcised — Jews who are not merely circumcised but who walk in Abraham's faith. The Jewish group is not erased or replaced; they remain Abraham's children in the fuller sense: they share both the sign and the faith the sign sealed. This is expansion of the family, not displacement of its original members.

notes.original: patēra pantōn hēmōn — the father of us all; tois ek nomou — those who hold to the Torah; tō ek pisteōs Abraam — those who share Abraham's faith
notes.rendering: he is the father of us all — not only to those who hold to the Torah, but also to those who share Abraham's faith
notes.why: The syntax is critical: 'not only... but also.' Torah-holders are the primary group; faith-holders are the added group. The argument is about expansion, not about Torah-holders being replaced. 'The father of us all' — hēmōn — is a Jewish writer speaking inclusively. Abraham's fatherhood is enlarged to embrace Gentile believers; it is not transferred away from his Jewish children.

notes.original: paredothē dia ta paraptōmata hēmōn — handed over for our trespasses; ēgerthē dia tēn dikaiōsin hēmōn — raised for our justification
notes.rendering: handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification
notes.why: The parallel structure — death for trespasses, resurrection for justification — is carefully constructed. Dikaiōsis (justification, acquittal, being-put-right) is not merely a legal status; in Paul's usage it carries the sense of God's covenant faithfulness being vindicated and the people being set right within the relationship. The resurrection is not incidental to justification — it is its ground. The chapter that began with Abraham's faith in the God 'who gives life to the dead' (v.17) ends with the resurrection of Jesus as the event in which that faith becomes historically concrete.

intro: Romans 5 pivots from the argument about justification to the argument about the new human situation — what has changed cosmically through Christ. The Adam-Christ typology (vv.12–21) is the scaffolding: Paul is not attacking the Torah in v.20 but explaining its role in a larger narrative. The Torah was not a mistake; it was the clarifying instrument that named what sin was — making it possible for grace to be seen for what it is.

notes.original: dikaiōthentes ek pisteōs — having been put right by faith; eirēnēn echomen — we have peace
notes.rendering: since we have been put right by faith, we have peace with God
notes.why: The Greek manuscripts are divided between echomen (we have peace — indicative) and echōmen (let us have peace — subjunctive). The difference is a single letter. Most modern scholars prefer the subjunctive ('let us enjoy the peace we have'), but the indicative has equally strong manuscript support. The meaning is close either way: peace with God is the existing situation of those who have been justified, and Paul calls his readers to inhabit it. The word eirēnē carries the full weight of the Hebrew shalom — completeness, right ordering, flourishing.

notes.original: di' henos anthrōpou hē hamartia — through one human being sin; eph' hō pantes hēmarton — because all sinned
notes.rendering: sin entered the world through one human being... death spread to all people, because all sinned
notes.why: The phrase eph' hō pantes hēmarton has been translated two ways: (a) 'in whom all sinned' (Augustine's Latin reading, which underpins original sin as inherited guilt) and (b) 'because all sinned' (most modern scholarship). The Greek phrase eph' hō means 'on the basis of which' or 'because' — the latter reading makes better sense of Paul's parallel argument: death spread not because Adam's guilt was imputed but because death created the conditions in which all human beings in fact sin. Paul's concern is not inherited guilt but universal mortality and the human tendency to sin within it.

notes.original: nomos de pareisēlthen hina pleonasē to paraptōma — the Torah came in alongside so that the trespass might increase
notes.rendering: the Torah came in so that the trespass might increase
notes.why: Pareisēlthen — came in alongside, entered secondarily (the prefix para implies a secondary entry into the stage already occupied by sin and death). Paul is not saying the Torah is evil or was a mistake. He is making a narrative point about sequence: sin was already in the world (v.13); the Torah's function was to make transgression explicit, nameable, measurable — which is why grace could then overflow in precisely the opposite direction. The Torah serves the drama of grace by identifying what grace overcomes.

intro: Romans 6 answers the antinomian inference Paul knows will be drawn from chapter 5: if grace abounds where sin increases, why not sin more? The answer is baptismal — those who have been incorporated into the Messiah's death and resurrection have changed ontological status. They belong to a different master. The slavery metaphor in vv.15–23, uncomfortable as it is, serves a specific purpose: no human being is truly autonomous. The question is not freedom from all masters but which master one serves.

notes.original: ebaptisthēmen eis Christon Iesoun — baptised into Christ Jesus; eis ton thanaton autou ebaptisthēmen — baptised into his death
notes.rendering: all of us who were baptised into Christ Jesus were baptised into his death
notes.why: Eis with the accusative expresses incorporation into — not merely 'in reference to' but 'into the sphere of.' Baptism in Paul is not a symbol of an inner experience; it is the moment of transfer into the Messiah's story. The believer is not just remembering Christ's death — they are placed within it. This makes the argument of vv.5–11 possible: having died with Christ, they are genuinely dead to sin's jurisdiction. The logic is sacramental before it is ethical.

notes.original: logizesthe heautous nekrous men tē hamartia zōntas de tō theō — reckon yourselves dead to sin but alive to God
notes.rendering: count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus
notes.why: Logizesthe — count, reckon, calculate (the same accounting verb used of Abraham's faith in 4:3–5). Paul is not calling for a feeling but a reckoning — a deliberate cognitive act of taking seriously what is objectively true. The believer's death to sin and life to God is a fact established by union with Christ; the imperative is to reason from that fact. Ethics in Paul is not effort-to-become but reckoning-on-what-is.

notes.original: ou gar este hypo nomon alla hypo charin — you are not under law but under grace
notes.rendering: you are not under law but under grace
notes.why: This verse has been used to argue that Christians are exempt from Torah. Paul does not mean that. In the context of vv.12–14, 'under law' means under sin's jurisdiction that operates through the law (see 7:7–11 and 3:20). Being 'under grace' does not mean licence — the very next verse (6:15) shuts that door immediately. The contrast is between two modes of existence: one where sin names and exploits transgression through the law, and one where grace has broken sin's dominion. The Torah itself is not abolished — it is the dominion of sin that is broken.

intro: Romans 7 is the passage most frequently used to mischaracterise Paul's view of the Torah — and arguably the most carefully constructed trap in the letter. Paul is not describing his current Christian experience (in ch.8 the Spirit has resolved what ch.7 describes). He is performing the logic of life under sin's exploitation of the Torah from the perspective of one who has been liberated from it. Crucially, at the centre of the performance stands v.12: the Torah is holy. The villain of the piece is sin, not Torah.

notes.original: ho nomos hamartia — is the Torah sin? mē genoito — absolutely not!
notes.rendering: That the Torah is sin? Absolutely not!
notes.why: Mē genoito — Paul's strongest negation, used when he anticipates someone drawing a logical conclusion he regards as catastrophic. His argument has gone: the Torah arouses sinful passions (7:5), the Torah gives sin its opening (7:8), so — is the Torah sin? The answer is violent: absolutely not. The Torah is the innocent party. Sin is the exploiter. This distinction is the interpretive key to all of chapters 7–8.

notes.original: hōste ho men nomos hagios — so then the Torah is holy; kai hē entolē hagia kai dikaia kai agathē — and the commandment is holy and righteous and good
notes.rendering: the Torah is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good
notes.why: This is the theological anchor of chapter 7 and must not be buried. Paul uses three adjectives: holy (hagios — belonging to God's domain), righteous (dikaios — aligned with right ordering), good (agathos — genuinely beneficial). The same Torah that has been 'killed by' (7:10) and 'exploited by' sin (7:11) is, in itself, holy. Sin is the problem; the Torah is sin's victim, not its source. Any reading of Paul that treats Torah as the enemy of grace has misread this chapter at its centre.

notes.original: egō sarkinos eimi — I am made of flesh; talaipōros egō anthrōpos — wretched man that I am
notes.rendering: I am made of flesh, sold under sin's ownership... what a wretched man I am!
notes.why: Who is the 'I' of 7:14–25? Three major readings: (a) Paul's pre-Christian life under Torah; (b) Adam, representing the human condition; (c) Israel's experience under Torah, which is the experience of unregenerate humanity generally. The overwhelming consensus of recent Pauline scholarship rejects the reading that Paul is describing his current Christian experience — because in chapter 8 the Spirit resolves precisely this situation. The 'I' is performing a voicing of what life under sin's dominion of the Torah feels like. The escape from it, announced in v.25 and fully developed in ch.8, is through Jesus Christ our Lord.

intro: Romans 8 is widely considered the summit of Paul's theological argument — the destination toward which the tortuous path of chapters 1–7 has been leading. The chapter moves from the liberation of the individual through the Spirit, to the adoption of God's children, to the redemption of all creation, to the climactic doxology that nothing in the cosmos can sever the relationship between God and his people. The Aramaic Abba in v.15, and the citation of Psalm 44 in v.36, are both preserved.

notes.original: peri hamartias — for sin; as a sin-offering
notes.rendering: by sending his own Son... as a sin-offering, he condemned sin in the flesh
notes.why: Peri hamartias in the LXX regularly translates the Hebrew asham or chatat — sin-offering (Lev. 5:6–7; Ps. 40:6). The phrase almost certainly carries sacrificial weight here: God sent his Son in the form of sinful flesh and as a sin-offering. The consequence is that sin was condemned in the flesh — the sphere where sin had been operating. The Torah could not do this because it lacked the power to deal with sin from the inside; it could only name transgression from the outside. God dealt with sin at its source.

notes.original: Abba ho patēr — Abba, Father (Aramaic + Greek translation)
notes.rendering: we cry out, 'Abba — Father!'
notes.why: Abba is Aramaic — the intimate address a Jewish child used to a father. Paul preserves it in both its Aramaic form and Greek translation (the same combination appears in Gethsemane, Mark 14:36, and Galatians 4:6). The preservation of the Aramaic is significant: it roots the Christian experience of prayer in the Jewish family vocabulary of intimacy with God. The Spirit does not invent a new category; it grants access to the relational vocabulary already embedded in Israel's covenant life.

notes.original: hē apokaradokia tēs ktiseōs — the eager expectation of creation; eleutherōthēsetai — will be liberated
notes.rendering: the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay
notes.why: Apokaradokia — eager expectation with neck outstretched (kara — head, dokeuō — to watch for). The image is vivid: creation straining forward like someone watching for a distant figure to appear. Paul's eschatology is cosmic: the redemption in Christ is not the rescue of individual souls from a doomed physical world. It is the liberation of the whole creation — including matter, nature, animals, and land — from the corruption that has held it. This is the prophetic vision of Isaiah 11 and 65 expressed in Paul's Greek idiom.

notes.original: tois agapōsin ton theon panta synergei eis agathon — in all things he works together for good with those who love God
notes.rendering: in all things God works together for good with those who love him
notes.why: The verb synergei — works together — is the source of 'synergy.' The question is who works with whom: 'all things work together for good' (classical reading) or 'God works together with those who love him in all things' (alternative). The second reading makes God the active subject throughout, which fits the chapter's emphasis on God's initiative. Either way, the promise is not that everything that happens is good, but that God is active in all circumstances to bring about good for those who love him.

intro: Romans 9–11 is the theological heart of the letter's second half and the passage that controls everything else Paul has said about Jews and Gentiles. Paul opens chapter 9 with personal grief: he would wish himself accursed for Israel's sake. This is not the posture of someone who believes Israel has been abandoned or replaced. The argument of the chapter is about the character of God's sovereign election — it has always been more specific than ethnic descent — but Paul never concludes that election has been transferred from Israel to the Church. That conclusion is explicitly rejected in chapter 11.

notes.original: hōn hē huiothesia kai hē doxa kai hai diathēkai... — theirs is the adoption, the glory, the covenants...
notes.rendering: theirs is the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the Torah, the worship, the promises — theirs are the patriarchs, and from their lineage comes the Messiah
notes.why: Eight privileges listed in the present tense: they are — not were — Israel's. Paul is writing this after the resurrection, after Pentecost, after his missions to the Gentiles, and he still describes these realities as presently belonging to Israel. The adoption (huiothesia), the glory (doxa — the shekinah), the covenants (hai diathēkai — plural), the Torah-giving, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and the Messiah in the flesh — all of these are Israel's. Any theology that claims these have been transferred to the Church must deal directly with Paul's present tense here. He says nothing of the kind.

notes.original: ouch hoion de hoti ekpeptōken ho logos tou theou — it is not as though the word of God has failed
notes.rendering: It is not as though the word of God has failed
notes.why: This sentence is Paul's thesis for chapters 9–11 and the sharpest possible rejection of supersessionism. The premise that raises the problem is: if Israel has not believed, has God's covenant word to Israel collapsed? Paul's answer is an unequivocal no. The argument he makes — that election was never simply ethnic — is designed not to explain away Israel but to demonstrate that God's word stands. The chapter ends with the remnant preserved (vv.27–29); chapter 11 will end with all Israel saved.

notes.original: ton Iakōb ēgapēsa, ton de Ēsau emisēsa — Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated
notes.rendering: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated
notes.why: From Malachi 1:2–3, where YHWH addresses the nations of Israel and Edom — not the individual patriarchs. 'Hated' in Semitic idiom means 'loved less' (compare Luke 14:26 — 'hate your father and mother' means 'love me more'). Paul is making a point about God's sovereign freedom in election, not about God's antipathy toward Esau personally. The argument is about the character of election: it is not automatically conferred by birth. This principle applies to ethnic Israel too — but see chapter 11 for what Paul actually concludes from it.

intro: Romans 10 addresses the question of how Israel, given every advantage, came not to believe. Paul answers with sorrow rather than condemnation: they have zeal for God (v.2), they heard (v.18), they understood (v.19) — and yet they have not believed. The chapter ends with the devastating image of God holding out his hands all day long. This is not a God who has given up on Israel. It is a God who refuses to stop reaching. The resolution comes in chapter 11.

notes.original: hē eudokia tēs emēs kardias kai hē deēsis pros ton theon hyper autōn eis sōtērian — the desire of my heart and my prayer to God on their behalf is for salvation
notes.rendering: the desire of my heart and my prayer to God on Israel's behalf is for their salvation
notes.why: Paul prays for Israel's salvation. This single verse demolishes the notion that Paul regarded Israel as irrevocably rejected or that Jewish people have no need of what he proclaims. He is not indifferent to Israel's condition. He is anguished by it and actively interceding for it. The prayer of 10:1 echoes the anguish of 9:1–3 — Paul's pastoral concern for Israel is not perfunctory but existential.

notes.original: telos gar nomou Christos — for Christ is the telos of the Torah
notes.rendering: Christ is the goal of the Torah — so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes
notes.why: Telos is the most contested word in the verse. It means: (a) termination, end (as in: the Torah's validity is over); or (b) goal, purpose, destination (as in: the Torah always pointed toward Christ). Modern scholarship strongly favours (b): telos in Greek philosophical usage typically means the purpose or aim of a thing, its proper end-point in the sense of what it was for. The Torah is not abolished; it is fulfilled in its intended direction. Reading (a) has been used to justify anti-Torah theology and contributed to supersessionism; reading (b) maintains the Torah's ongoing validity as scripture while affirming Christ as its culmination.

notes.original: ou gar estin diastolē Ioudaiou te kai Hellenos — there is no distinction between Jew and Greek
notes.rendering: there is no distinction between Jew and Greek
notes.why: This statement of equality in access must not be read as the erasure of Jewish identity. Paul's argument is that the same Lord (ho autos kyrios) is the Lord of both, and equally generous to both who call on him. Equal access is not the same as identical identity. The phrase echoes 3:22 ('for there is no distinction') — both are about equal standing before God in receiving salvation, not about the abolition of the particular covenant with Israel. Jewish people remain Jewish; the good news reaches them as it reaches everyone.

notes.original: holēn tēn hēmeran exepetasa tas cheiras mou — all day long I have held out my hands
notes.rendering: All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and obstinate people
notes.why: From Isaiah 65:2, where YHWH speaks of Israel. The image is not of a God who has retracted his hands but of one who keeps extending them against refusal. Paul places this at the end of chapter 10 precisely so that chapter 11's opening question — 'Has God rejected his people?' — lands with full force. The hands are still outstretched. The answer to the question is coming.

intro: Romans 11 is the theological climax of the argument begun in chapter 9, and it is one of the most consequential chapters in the New Testament for Jewish-Christian relations. Paul structures the chapter as a series of questions and emphatic denials. His opening mē genoito — 'absolutely not!' — sets the tone: the entire chapter is a refutation of the idea that God has abandoned Israel. The olive tree metaphor in 11:17–24 explicitly warns Gentile believers against arrogance toward Israel, and Paul's closing declaration in 11:29 — that God's gifts and calling are irrevocable — is perhaps the single most important anti-supersessionist statement in the entire New Testament.

notes.original: mē apōsato ho theos ton laon autou; mē genoito — has God rejected his people? absolutely not!
notes.rendering: Has God rejected his people? Absolutely not!
notes.why: The double mē — question and answer — is Paul's strongest rhetorical form. He uses mē genoito ('by no means / absolutely not') fourteen times in Romans, always to repudiate a theological error. Here it repudiates the idea of divine rejection of Israel. Paul then offers himself as immediate counter-evidence: he is an Israelite, a Benjaminite, and a believer. The remnant has always been Israel's story; the remnant does not replace Israel.

notes.original: mē eptaisan hina pesōsin; mē genoito — did they stumble so as to fall? absolutely not!
notes.rendering: Did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery? Absolutely not!
notes.why: A second emphatic mē genoito. The stumble (ptaiō) is distinguished from a catastrophic fall (piptō). Paul explicitly rejects a reading of Israel's unbelief as final or total. Their stumble has opened a door for the Gentiles — and the Gentile mission is itself intended to provoke Israel's 'envy' and return (11:11, 14). This is a missionary strategy of inclusion, not a theology of replacement.

notes.original: agrialaios — wild olive; kallielaios — cultivated olive; enkentrizō — to graft
notes.rendering: You do not support the root — the root supports you
notes.why: The olive tree is Israel, rooted in the covenantal promises to the patriarchs. Gentile believers are wild olive shoots grafted into — not replacing — this existing tree. Paul's agricultural metaphor makes Gentile belonging dependent on and derivative from Israel's root. He explicitly warns Gentile readers against boasting (11:18) and arrogance (11:20) toward the natural branches. The natural branches can and will be regrafted (11:23–24). This is the opposite of supersessionism.

notes.original: mustērion — mystery; pōrōsis apo merous — hardening in part
notes.rendering: A hardening in part until the full number of the Gentiles has come in
notes.why: Mustērion in Pauline usage means a previously hidden purpose of God now being disclosed. The mystery has two coordinates: (1) the hardening is partial (apo merous — 'in part'), not total; and (2) it is temporal ('until' — achri hou). The hardening is neither permanent nor encompassing all of Israel. Paul has already spoken of a believing remnant (11:5) and warns against misreading the hardening as God's final word.

notes.original: kai houtōs pas Israēl sōthēsetai — and in this way all Israel will be saved
notes.rendering: And in this way all Israel will be saved
notes.why: Houtōs means 'in this manner/way,' not 'and then afterward.' The salvation of all Israel is the telos of the mystery: through the Gentile mission provoking Israel's envy (11:11, 14), through the Deliverer coming from Zion (Isa 59:20–21, LXX), through the covenant that removes sins (Jer 31:33–34). 'All Israel' is a covenantal formula (kol-Yisra'el in rabbinic literature) meaning Israel as a corporate whole, the full number — not every individual without exception. The point is comprehensive national restoration, not a spiritual synonym for the Church.

notes.original: agapētoi dia tous pateras — beloved on account of the patriarchs; ametamelēta — irrevocable
notes.rendering: Beloved for the sake of the patriarchs — for the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable
notes.why: These two verses are the theological foundation of the entire argument. Israel is simultaneously 'enemies with respect to the gospel' (for Gentile benefit) and 'beloved with respect to election' (on account of the patriarchs). Paul holds both in tension without collapsing either. The word ametamelēta means 'not to be repented of, not revocable.' God's gifts (charismata — the privileges of 9:4–5) and his calling (klēsis — the election of Israel) remain in force permanently. Supersessionism requires Paul to be wrong about this verse, or to mean something different by 'irrevocable' than any normal reading would suggest.

intro: Romans 12 opens the letter's final major section, pivoting from the theological argument of chapters 1–11 to the practical and ethical implications for the messianic community. The pivot word is 'therefore' (oun): everything that follows flows from the mercies described in chapters 9–11 — including the irrevocable calling of Israel. Paul's ethics here are deeply rooted in Jewish tradition: the body as an offering to God (cf. Lev 1–7), transformation of mind (cf. Jer 31:33), and the gift-lists that echo Jewish models of communal charism. The love-ethics of 12:9–21 parallel the Sermon on the Mount and reflect Paul's formation in Pharisaic ethical teaching.

notes.original: logikēn latreian — reasonable/spiritual/logical worship
notes.rendering: Your true and proper worship
notes.why: Logikēn is from logos — it can mean 'rational,' 'spiritual,' or 'word-consistent.' The NRSV has 'spiritual worship,' the ESV 'spiritual worship,' the NIV 'true and proper worship.' Paul is describing the presentation of one's embodied life to God as the equivalent of temple sacrifice — but the temple here is the body and the community, not a building. This is consistent with Second Temple Jewish reflection on prayer and righteous living as substitutes for sacrificial cult when the Temple was inaccessible.

notes.original: metamorphousthe tē anakainōsei tou noos — be transformed by the renewal of the mind
notes.rendering: Be transformed by the renewing of your mind
notes.why: Metamorphousthe is a present-tense passive imperative: 'keep being transformed' — ongoing, not a single event. The anakainōsis (renewal) of the nous (mind/consciousness) echoes Jeremiah 31:33 ('I will put my Torah within them, written on their hearts') — the new covenant is a transformation of interiority, not an abolition of the covenant itself.

notes.original: ekdikēsin — vengeance; anthrax pyros — burning coals (Prov 25:21–22)
notes.rendering: Leave room for God's wrath" / "heap burning coals on his head
notes.why: Both quotations come from Jewish scripture: Deut 32:35 (vengeance belongs to God) and Prov 25:21–22 (the 'burning coals' image). The 'burning coals' likely refers to the Egyptian practice of carrying a pan of coals on one's head as a public sign of contrition — an act of shaming that leads to reconciliation, not retaliation. Paul's ethics here are not innovations but applications of Torah wisdom.

intro: Romans 13:1–7 is one of the most frequently misused passages in the history of Christian ethics. It has been invoked to justify submission to totalitarian regimes, including Nazi Germany. Its context is crucial: Paul is writing to a small community of Jesus-followers in the capital of the Roman Empire — a city where political resistance carried lethal consequences. His counsel is prudential and pastoral, not a blank theological endorsement of every state action. Notably, 13:8–10 immediately qualifies the political argument with an ethical one: love of neighbour — rooted in Torah — is the governing principle. Paul never counsels obedience to authorities that would require disobeying God.

notes.original: exousiais hyperechousais hupotassesthō — let every soul submit to governing authorities
notes.rendering: Let everyone submit to the governing authorities
notes.why: Hupotassesthō is a middle/passive imperative of 'arrange under' — not 'obey unconditionally.' The word implies a voluntary ordering of oneself within a social structure for the sake of peace, not an absolute moral duty of compliance with all commands. The political theology here is constrained by the theological claim: authorities are God's servants (diakonos) — when they act against God's purposes, the servant relationship is severed. Compare Acts 5:29: 'We must obey God rather than human beings.'

notes.original: plērōma nomou hē agapē — love is the fullness/fulfilment of the Torah
notes.rendering: Love is the fulfilment of the Torah
notes.why: Plērōma here means 'fullness, completion, bringing to its intended end' — the same root as plēroō. Paul is not saying Torah is abolished; he is saying love enacts what Torah always intended. This is consistent with Jewish tradition: Rabbi Akiva called 'love your neighbour' (Lev 19:18) the great principle of Torah. Jesus uses the same summary (Matt 22:37–40). Paul's ethics remain Torah-shaped — love is how Torah finds its fullest expression, not its replacement.

notes.original: endysasthe ton kyrion Iēsoun Christon — clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Messiah
notes.rendering: Clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus, the Messiah
notes.why: Endyō — to clothe, put on — is a baptismal metaphor (cf. Gal 3:27). The 'putting on' of Messiah is not replacement of identity but transformation of orientation: one's allegiances, desires, and conduct are now shaped by the Messiah rather than by the 'flesh' (sarx), which here means the self-centred drives of the old age rather than the physical body.

intro: Romans 14–15 addresses a concrete conflict within the Roman house-churches between those Paul calls 'strong' (those who believe all foods are permitted) and the 'weak' (those who observe food restrictions and special days). The most plausible reading is that the 'weak' are Jewish believers — and possibly Gentile sympathisers — who maintain Jewish dietary practice and Sabbath observance as covenantal commitments. Paul's response is remarkable: he does not tell the 'weak' they are wrong. He tells the 'strong' to bear with them in love. This is not about Torah being obsolete — it is about communal love across difference.

notes.original: ton de asthenunta tē pistei proslambanethe — welcome the one who is weak in faith
notes.rendering: Accept the one whose faith is weak — without quarrelling over disputable matters
notes.why: Proslambanethe means 'welcome, receive into your company' — the same verb used in 15:7 ('accept one another as Christ accepted you'). The 'weak in faith' is not morally deficient; their faith is strong in its commitments. The weakness is in the freedom they have not yet experienced. Paul consistently requires the 'strong' to move toward the 'weak' in welcome, not the reverse.

notes.original: hēmera par' hēmeran — day compared to day
notes.rendering: One person considers one day more sacred than another
notes.why: The 'special days' almost certainly include the Sabbath and Jewish festival calendar. Paul does not declare these wrong. He says each person should be 'fully convinced in their own mind' — this is the language of adiaphora, things morally indifferent, where the community must make room for difference without judgment. Jewish believers who keep Sabbath are keeping it 'for the Lord' (14:6), which Paul acknowledges as valid.

notes.original: ouden koinon di' heautou — nothing is common (unclean) in itself
notes.rendering: Nothing is unclean in itself
notes.why: Koinon (common, defiled) is the ritual purity term — not a Mosaic category but a Second Temple elaboration. Paul's claim is that no food is intrinsically defiling — echoing Jesus's teaching in Mark 7:15–19. However, Paul immediately qualifies: 'if anyone regards something as unclean, then for that person it is unclean' (14:14b). The strong person's freedom does not override the weak person's conscience. This is not an abolition of kashrut for Jewish believers — it is a statement about the governing principle of communal love.

notes.original: dikaiosynē kai eirēnē kai chara en pneumati hagiō — righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit
notes.rendering: The kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit
notes.why: This is one of Paul's few direct references to 'the kingdom of God' (basileia tou theou). The kingdom's substance is dikaiosynē (right relationship/justice), eirēnē (peace/shalom), and chara (joy) — all eschatological realities, all rooted in Jewish apocalyptic hope. Food practices are 'disputable matters'; shalom within the community is not.

intro: Romans 15 contains one of the most theologically significant — and consistently underemphasised — verses in Paul's letters: verse 8. Paul declares that the Messiah became a diakonos of the circumcised (i.e., of Israel) in order to confirm the promises to the patriarchs. This is Paul's understanding of the Messiah's primary mission: the confirmation of Israel's covenant. The Gentile inclusion follows from, and is secondary to, that primary covenant faithfulness. Paul's 'collection' for the Jerusalem poor (15:25–27) also reflects his theology: Gentile believers owe a material debt to the Jewish community from which their spiritual blessings flow.

notes.original: Christon diakonon gegenēsthai peritomēs — the Messiah has become a servant of the circumcision
notes.rendering: The Messiah has become a servant of the circumcised on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs
notes.why: This verse is the ecclesiological foundation of the whole letter. Diakonon peritomēs — 'servant of the circumcision' — means the Messiah came to serve Israel's covenant, to confirm (bebaiōsai) the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Gentile mission in v.9 is an extension of this, not a replacement: 'and also [kai] in order that the Gentiles might glorify God.' The 'and also' (kai) preserves the additive structure. Israel is not displaced; the nations are included alongside.

notes.original: opheiletai eisin autōn — they are their debtors
notes.rendering: They owe it to the Jews to share with them their material blessings
notes.why: Paul's collection for Jerusalem is not charity — it is debt repayment. The word opheiletai (debtors) is deliberate: Gentile believers have received Israel's spiritual heritage — the scriptures, the Messiah, the promises, the apostles — and they owe material reciprocity. This is Paul embodying his own theology: the relationship between Jewish and Gentile communities is one of mutual dependence, not Gentile supersession.

intro: Romans 16 is more than a list of names — it is a window into the social world of the early messianic movement. Paul greets at least twenty-six individuals by name, including numerous women in significant roles. Phoebe is a deacon (diakonos) and benefactor (prostatis); Priscilla is named before her husband; Junia is called 'outstanding among the apostles.' The diversity of the community — Jewish and Gentile, slave and free, male and female — is the living embodiment of the theology Paul has argued across sixteen chapters.

notes.original: diakonon — deacon; prostatin — benefactor/patron
notes.rendering: A deacon of the church in Cenchreae" / "the benefactor of many
notes.why: Phoebe holds two formal titles: diakonos (the same word used of male church officers in Phil 1:1, 1 Tim 3:8–13) and prostatis (benefactor, patron — a term of civic honour for one who used personal resources to support a community). Paul is asking the Romans to support someone with recognised ministerial and patronal authority. There is no grammatical or contextual reason to translate diakonos as 'servant' here while translating it as 'deacon' elsewhere.

notes.original: Iounian... episēmoi en tois apostolois — Junia, outstanding among the apostles
notes.rendering: Outstanding among the apostles
notes.why: Iounian is the accusative of the female name Junia — a common Latin name attested in hundreds of inscriptions. The masculine reading 'Junias' is unattested in the ancient world and appears to be a scribal correction motivated by discomfort with a female apostle. The church fathers (Chrysostom, Origen, Jerome) consistently read this as female. Episēmoi en tois apostolois means 'outstanding among the apostles' — Junia and Andronicus are themselves apostles, not merely well-regarded by apostles.

notes.original: mustērion... chronois aiōniois sesigēmenou, nyn de phanerōthentos — mystery hidden for eternal ages, now disclosed
notes.rendering: The mystery hidden for long ages past, but now disclosed
notes.why: The closing doxology ties together the letter's central themes: the gospel, the Messiah, the mystery disclosed through the prophets, and the obedience of faith among all nations. The 'mystery' (mustērion — as in 11:25) is the inclusion of the Gentiles within Israel's covenant story — not the replacement of Israel, but the expansion of the family. The letter ends where it began: 'to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles' (1:5 / 16:26) — a bracket holding the entire argument.

intro: Ruth 1 is set up with extraordinary economy. In five verses Naomi's entire world is stripped away: home, husband, sons, security. In eight verses the return journey is described with what amounts to a character test: both daughters-in-law are urged to go back; only one refuses. The chapter closes with Naomi naming her own emptiness — and the narrator immediately noting that the barley harvest has just begun.

notes.original: ya'as YHWH imachem chesed — may YHWH deal with you in chesed
notes.rendering: may YHWH deal kindly with you
notes.why: Chesed — the master word of the book of Ruth, appearing three times at key moments (1:8, 2:20, 3:10). It is the most important word in the book and one of the richest in the Hebrew Bible: steadfast love, covenant loyalty, lovingkindness, faithful devotion. It describes the quality of YHWH's relationship with Israel (Psalm 136 uses it 26 times: his chesed endures for ever) and the quality of the human relationships in Ruth that mirror it. Here Naomi invokes chesed from YHWH on behalf of the daughters-in-law who have shown chesed to the dead and to her. The word begins the book's theology: chesed is what YHWH does, and what the faithful characters in this story embody.

notes.original: ki el asher telchi elech — where you go I will go
notes.rendering: where you go I will go
notes.why: Ruth's declaration is one of the most celebrated passages in the Hebrew Bible — quoted at weddings, at funerals, as a statement of friendship, of love, of loyalty. Its context is important: Ruth is making this declaration to her mother-in-law, in a culture where the obligation ran the other way (a mother-in-law had obligations to her daughters-in-law, not vice versa). Ruth is committing to someone from whom she has nothing to gain — whose people are not her people, whose God is not her God, who has explicitly said she has nothing to offer. The declaration is pure chesed: covenant loyalty that gives without calculating return. The covenant formula — your people shall be my people and your God my God — is the language of the covenant itself applied by a Moabite woman to YHWH.

notes.original: Naomi — pleasant; Mara — bitter; shaddai hemi meod
notes.rendering: do not call me Naomi — call me Mara
notes.why: Naomi means pleasant (from na'em — pleasant, lovely, sweet). Mara means bitter (from marar — to be bitter, to embitter). Naomi is doing what the lament tradition always does: naming her condition truthfully before YHWH and the community rather than maintaining the fiction that all is well. The Almighty (Shaddai — the same divine name used in the Joel wordplay with shod, destruction) has dealt her bitterness; she will be named for it. The name-change is not permanent — by the book's end, 'Naomi' will be given back her full meaning. But the narrator's art is subtle: even as Naomi renames herself Mara, she is walking into Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest, with Ruth beside her. The bitterness is real. The harvest has also just begun.

intro: Ruth 2 is the chapter of providential coincidence — the word 'happen' in verse 3 signals that the narrator is winking at us. It is also the chapter that introduces Boaz and establishes the quality of chesed in him through his treatment of Ruth — before the plot has revealed his role as redeemer.

notes.original: vayiqer migreh'a chelqat hasadeh l'Vaz — it happened to chance
notes.rendering: it happens that she comes to the part of the field belonging to Boaz
notes.why: Vayiqer migreh'a — and it chanced to chance, and her chance chanced, and as it happened it happened. The Hebrew uses the root qrh (to happen, to chance, to befall) twice in rapid succession — a deliberate doubling that creates an almost comical emphasis on the coincidence. The narrator is signalling something: this is not really chance; this is providence wearing the costume of coincidence. The word qrh appears in Ecclesiastes for the random events that befall all people alike (qereh echad — one chance/fate for all). Here the same word is used for Ruth's arrival in exactly the right field. The book of Ruth does not use direct divine intervention; YHWH is named in prayers and blessings but never appears in the narrative. What YHWH does, he does through the ordinary: a woman walking into a field, a man arriving to check on his harvest.

notes.original: tachat k'nafav — under whose wings you have come to take refuge
notes.rendering: under whose wings you have come to take refuge
notes.why: K'nafav — his wings (plural, the wings of YHWH). The image of YHWH's wings as shelter appears throughout the Psalms (17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 61:4, 63:7, 91:4). In Psalm 91:4: 'he will cover you with his feathers; under his wings you will find refuge.' Ruth has left her own land, her own people, her own gods and has come to shelter under YHWH's wings — the wings of the God of Israel. The image will be repeated in chapter 3 (verse 9) when Ruth asks Boaz to 'spread his garment over her' — using the same word k'naf (wing/corner of garment). What YHWH does (shelter under his wings), Boaz is asked to enact (spread his garment-wing over Ruth). The human kinsman-redeemer's action mirrors the divine Redeemer's posture.

notes.original: asher lo azav chasdo — whose chesed has not forsaken
notes.rendering: whose kindness has not forsaken the living or the dead
notes.why: The second chesed of the book — and its subject is ambiguous in the Hebrew. Asher lo azav chasdo — whose chesed has not forsaken. The 'whose' could refer to Boaz (whose kindness to Ruth is not forsaking the family of the dead) or to YHWH (whose covenant faithfulness has not forsaken Naomi through this provision). The ambiguity is almost certainly intentional: Boaz's chesed and YHWH's chesed overlap so completely in this moment that the narrative refuses to separate them. This is the theology of Ruth in miniature: human faithfulness and divine faithfulness are different in degree but not in kind, and sometimes human chesed is the form YHWH's chesed takes.

intro: Ruth 3 is the book's most intimate chapter — a nighttime scene at the threshing floor where Ruth approaches Boaz in a way the narrator describes with careful ambiguity. What is unambiguous is the theology: Ruth's action is identified explicitly as chesed (v.10), and Boaz's response is immediate, honouring, and protective.

notes.original: ufaresat k'nafcha al-amatcha ki go'el atah — spread your wing over your servant
notes.rendering: spread your wings over your servant — for you are a redeemer
notes.why: K'nafcha — your wing, your garment's corner (k'naf — wing, corner, hem of garment). The word is identical to the k'nafav of 2:12 — the wings of YHWH under which Ruth has taken refuge. Ruth is now asking Boaz to enact with his garment-wing what Boaz prayed YHWH would do with his wings. The request is a legal action (spread your garment over a woman = take her under your protection, enter into a marriage bond with her — cf. Ezekiel 16:8 where YHWH spreads his garment over Jerusalem in a marriage covenant) and a theological statement: the human redeemer is being asked to embody the divine redeemer's posture. Go'el — redeemer, kinsman-redeemer — the legal institution by which a near relative could redeem land, free enslaved kin, and marry a childless widow to continue the family line (Deuteronomy 25:5–10, Leviticus 25:25–55).

notes.original: heitivat chasedech ha'acharon min-harishon — this last chesed is greater than the first
notes.rendering: this last kindness is greater than the first
notes.why: The third chesed of the book — and this time it is Boaz naming Ruth's chesed. The first chesed was Ruth's loyalty to Naomi on the road (1:8 — the chesed shown to the dead and to Naomi). The second was Boaz's chesed toward Ruth and Naomi (2:20 — whose chesed has not forsaken the living or the dead). Now the third: this last chesed is greater than the first. Ruth has not married for personal advantage (going after young men, whether poor or rich) but has come to Boaz as the kinsman-redeemer who can continue Elimelech's family line. The chesed word has now passed between all three central characters — Naomi, Ruth, and Boaz — each one naming it in the other.

notes.original: ki yodea kol sha'ar ami ki eshet chayil at — a worthy woman
notes.rendering: all my fellow townspeople know that you are a worthy woman
notes.why: Eshet chayil — woman of worth, woman of valour, capable woman. The same phrase that opens Proverbs 31 (eshet chayil mi yimtsa — a worthy woman who can find?). Boaz is not merely being polite; he is applying to Ruth a title of the highest honour in the wisdom tradition — the woman of chayil (strength, ability, worth, valour). The word chayil is also used for military strength and for the 'worthy man' of 2:1 — the same word describes both Boaz and Ruth, placing them on equal terms of moral character before the plot of redemption unfolds. A foreigner, a widow, a gleaner is recognised by the whole town as an eshet chayil.

intro: Ruth 4 resolves every thread the story has left open — the land, the name, the line of Elimelech, and Naomi's emptiness. The gate scene is legal precision and human drama simultaneously. The chapter closes with a ten-generation genealogy that places Obed between Boaz and Jesse, and Jesse between Boaz and David. A Moabite woman's chesed is in the bloodline of Israel's greatest king.

notes.original: v'hineh hago'el over — and look, the redeemer passes by
notes.rendering: and look — the redeemer of whom Boaz had spoken comes by
notes.why: V'hineh — and look, and behold, and suddenly. The word hinneh (behold) marks moments of narrative surprise throughout the Hebrew Bible — Abraham lifting his eyes and seeing a ram (Genesis 22:13), Joseph's brothers seeing the caravan (Genesis 37:25). Here, Boaz has just sat down at the gate and immediately, without any apparent arrangement, the nearer redeemer happens to walk by. The same providence that brought Ruth to Boaz's field (the double vayiqer migreh'a of 2:3) now brings the nearer redeemer past the gate at exactly the moment Boaz is there. The unnamed man — he is never named in the narrative, referred to only as 'so-and-so' (peloni almoni) — is the obstacle that providence removes without drama: he removes himself.

notes.original: lo uchal lig'ol li — I cannot redeem for myself
notes.rendering: I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I damage my own inheritance
notes.why: The nearer redeemer's refusal is not cowardice but self-interest: acquiring Ruth would complicate his own inheritance, since any child born to Ruth would be counted as Mahlon's, not his, and would inherit the redeemed land. His calculation is rational and legal. What he cannot see — or will not — is what Boaz can see: that Ruth is worth the complication. The contrast between the two men is not legal but characterological. Both know the law; Boaz acts with chesed inside the law. The unnamed redeemer acts within his legal rights. The story does not condemn him — the sandal ceremony is an honourable legal transaction — but by leaving him unnamed in a book that names everything else, the narrator renders a quiet verdict.

notes.original: ki chamatecha asher ahavtecha — your daughter-in-law who loves you
notes.rendering: your daughter-in-law who loves you, who is more to you than seven sons
notes.why: The women's blessing to Naomi names what the whole book has enacted: Ruth loves Naomi (ahavtecha — the love word, not the chesed word, but the personal devotion that gives chesed its warmth). More to you than seven sons — seven being the number of completeness in Hebrew symbolism. A daughter-in-law from Moab who chose to stay when she could have gone is worth more to Naomi than the fullness of sons. The book that began with Naomi losing her husband and both sons ends with her holding a grandson, surrounded by women blessing her, with her daughter-in-law named as worth more than seven sons. The emptiness of 1:21 (YHWH has brought me back empty) is filled — not by reversing the losses but by the new life that arrived alongside them.

notes.original: vayiqre'u lo hashecheinot shem — the women named him; Oved, avi Yishai, avi David
notes.rendering: they name him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.
notes.why: The genealogy's purpose is visible in its brevity: ten generations from Perez to David, and in that line: Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed. A Moabite woman is the mother of the grandfather of David. Matthew 1:5 places her in the genealogy of Jesus: 'Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth.' The book of Ruth, which begins with a Judahite family going to Moab and losing everything, ends with the Moabite woman who refused to leave becoming the ancestral link in the chain that leads to David — and, in the NT genealogy, to the one whom David's line was always pointing toward. The chesed of a foreign woman is woven into the foundation of Israel's greatest dynasty.

outro: Note on Ruth as a whole: The book is constructed with the precision of a master craftsman. Three scenes of departure (Bethlehem for Moab, Moab for Bethlehem, Bethlehem for the threshing floor) are answered by three arrivals. The three occurrences of chesed (1:8, 2:20, 3:10) mark the book's progress: YHWH's chesed invoked over the daughters-in-law, Boaz's chesed acknowledged toward the living and the dead, and Ruth's chesed named by Boaz as the greatest of the three. The emptiness of Naomi (1:21: I went away full and came back empty) is filled not by restoring what was taken but by giving what was not expected. And throughout, YHWH acts not through dramatic intervention but through the ordinary: the coincidence of a field, the routine of gleaning, the hospitality of a meal, the custom of a sandal, the birth of a child. The book of Ruth is the Hebrew Bible's most sustained argument that faithfulness is its own kind of miracle — and that sometimes the foreigner, the widow, and the gleaner are the ones through whom the story of YHWH's people is secretly being written.

intro: The Song opens mid-desire — no introduction, no narrative frame, just the woman's voice and her longing. The book is unlike anything else in the Hebrew canon: pure love poetry, with no explicit theology, no named God, no history, no law. Its inclusion in the canon was debated at the end of the first century CE and was secured by Rabbi Akiva's insistence that it is the Holy of Holies of Scripture.

notes.original: Shir hashirim asher liShlomo — Song of Songs, the greatest song
notes.rendering: the Song of Songs, which is Solomon's
notes.why: Shir hashirim — the superlative: Song of Songs = the greatest, the best, the most excellent of songs, just as Kodesh Hakodashim (Holy of Holies) = the most holy place. The superlative is achieved in Hebrew by placing the noun in construct with its own plural: the song of songs, the holy of holies, the servant of servants, the vanity of vanities (Ecclesiastes). The attribution to Solomon (liShlomo — of/for/belonging to Solomon) may indicate authorship, dedication, or association with the tradition of Solomonic wisdom literature. Solomon's name appears seven times in the book; references to his wealth and court appear throughout. Whether historical Solomonic authorship or a later literary association, the attribution places the book in the tradition of Israel's greatest wisdom king.

notes.original: shechorah ani v'navah — I am dark AND lovely
notes.rendering: I am dark and lovely
notes.why: Shechorah ani v'navah — I am dark and I am lovely. The conjunction v' (and) not the adversative ki (but). The common translation 'I am dark but lovely' (KJV, many others) imports a concession that is not in the Hebrew: as if darkness required an apology. The woman is making a double declaration: I am dark — and I am lovely. Both are simply true. The darkness comes from working in the vineyards under the sun (v.6); it is the mark of outdoor labour, of a woman who has worked. She is not apologising for it; she is naming herself fully. The daughters of Jerusalem — presumably the indoor, sheltered women of the court — are cautioned not to gaze upon her with the condescension of the privileged. She owns her appearance.

intro: Song of Songs 2 contains the most famous passage in the book — the springtime invitation of verses 10–13, among the most beautiful nature poetry in any language. The chapter also establishes the book's first refrain: do not awaken love until it pleases — a phrase that will appear three times, marking the book's rhythm of longing and restraint.

notes.original: v'diglo alai ahavah — his banner over me was love
notes.rendering: his banner over me was love
notes.why: Diglo — his banner, his standard, his flag (from degel — a military standard, a rallying banner). The image is of a military banner planted to mark territory or to signal a gathering point. The woman's territory is marked by love; the banner planted over her is the man's love. The verse has been variously interpreted: some read it as the banner of a victorious army (his love claims me), some as the sign above the entrance to the banquet hall (the house of wine, v.4a — the banner over this feast is love). Either way, love is not private or hidden; it is publicly displayed, made visible, claimed.

notes.original: qumi lach rayati yafati ul'chi-lach — arise, my love, come away
notes.rendering: arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away
notes.why: The springtime invitation is the Song's most celebrated passage — quoted in poetry, set to music, read at weddings across three millennia. The sequence of natural images (rain gone, flowers appearing, turtledove's voice, fig tree ripening, vines in blossom) is the Hebrew poetic equivalent of the renewal of the world. The invitation is doubled — spoken at v.10 and repeated word for word at v.13 — so the whole passage is enclosed in the same call: arise and come away. The Hebrew qumi lach — arise for yourself, arise in your own interest — uses the reflexive lach (for you/yourself) to give the invitation an intensely personal quality: this invitation is specifically, particularly for you.

notes.original: im ta'iru v'im te'oreru et-ha'ahavah ad shetech'patz — do not awaken love
notes.rendering: do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases
notes.why: The refrain appears three times: 2:7, 3:5, and 8:4 — marking the book's three main movements. Ad shetech'patz — until it pleases, until it desires, until it wishes of itself. The subject of 'please' is love itself — love has its own timing, its own will. The adjuration by gazelles and does of the field (the fleet, graceful animals associated with the beloved throughout the Song) is addressed to the daughters of Jerusalem — the chorus who witness the love and are asked not to rush what has its own season. The refrain is not a prohibition of love but a recognition that love cannot be forced or rushed: it awakens when it wishes.

intro: Song of Songs 3 gives us the book's most urgent and most narrative passage — the night search — followed by the royal procession that introduces the wedding setting. The repetition in the search (I sought him, but found him not — twice) gives the passage its aching quality, and the sudden resolution (scarcely had I passed them when I found him) its relief.

notes.original: et she'ahavah nafshi — him whom my soul loves
notes.rendering: him whom my soul loves
notes.why: Et she'ahavah nafshi — the one my soul loves, the one my whole self (nefesh — soul, self, being) loves. The phrase appears four times in four verses: vv.1, 2, 3, 4. The repetition is not redundancy but obsession — the woman's mind keeps returning to the same object, the same person. Nefesh is not merely emotional; it is the whole person (as the Shema commands love of YHWH with all your nefesh — your whole self). The woman's love is total-self love: she is looking for him with everything she is. The city-search at night — asking the watchmen, pushing past them — has the quality of a dream, and some interpreters have read it as a dream sequence (v.1: on my bed by night). Whether dream or reality, the emotional truth is the same.

intro: Song of Songs 4 contains the first wasf — the Hebrew term for a descriptive poem that praises the beloved's body through extended natural and architectural comparisons. The form is well attested in ancient Near Eastern love poetry, particularly in Egyptian love songs from the New Kingdom period. What sounds strange in English (hair like goats, teeth like ewes) was a familiar and beautiful poetic convention in its original cultural context.

notes.original: the wasf form — hair, eyes, teeth, lips, cheeks, neck, breasts
notes.rendering: The descriptive poem from head to (partially) downward
notes.why: The wasf (from Arabic — description) is a poem that moves through the body of the beloved, comparing each part to natural or architectural images. The comparisons are drawn from the landscape: goats descending Gilead, ewes coming up from washing, towers of Jerusalem. The image of teeth like washed ewes each with its twin — meaning all the teeth are present and symmetrical, a sign of youth and health — is a comparison that makes perfect sense once the cultural context is supplied. The architectural comparisons (neck like a tower hung with shields) suggest power and dignity, not rigidity. The wasf form appears again in 5:10–16 (the woman describes the man) and 7:1–9 (a second wasf of the woman). Together they form the book's most explicitly physical passages — and they are thoroughly mutual: both lovers are described with equal care and intensity.

notes.original: gan na'ul achoti challah — a garden locked, my sister, my bride
notes.rendering: a garden locked is my sister, my bride — a spring locked, a fountain sealed
notes.why: Na'ul — locked, bolted shut (from na'al — to bolt, to lock). The garden locked and the sealed fountain are images of the beloved's privacy and exclusivity — she belongs to him alone. The repeated address achoti challah (my sister, my bride) appears five times in chapters 4–5. 'Sister' (achoti) in this context is not a biological relationship but the language of intimate companionship — a term of deep affection in ancient Near Eastern love poetry, equivalent to 'my darling' in modern usage. The combination 'sister-bride' collapses the categories of friendship and marriage into a single person: she is both companion and beloved.

intro: Song of Songs 5 contains the book's most dramatic reversal: the woman almost misses her beloved, the door is opened too late, and the second search begins — this time with violence from the watchmen. It also contains the most extraordinary verse in the book: 'I slept, but my heart was awake.'

notes.original: ani yeshena v'libbi er — I slept but my heart was awake
notes.rendering: I slept, but my heart was awake
notes.why: The most psychologically acute line in the book — and one of the most resonant in all of Hebrew poetry. Ani yeshena — I was sleeping, I was asleep.
