outro: Note on Jacob’s deathbed as the gathering of all threads: Genesis 49 is the chapter in which every unresolved thread of the Jacob narrative is gathered and addressed. Reuben’s defilement of Bilhah (35:22), silently passed over, is finally named and judged. Simeon and Levi’s massacre at Shechem (chapter 34), defended by a question that Jacob left unanswered, is finally condemned. Judah’s transformation — from the brother who calculated Joseph’s price to the man who offered himself for Benjamin — is rewarded with the royal blessing. Joseph’s suffering is acknowledged and transcended. The dying father gives each son what his life has earned. The blessings are not arbitrary; they are the accumulated verdict of a father who has watched all of them for their entire lives.

intro: Genesis 50 is the book’s last chapter, and it contains the last word of the entire Genesis narrative — a coffin in Egypt, and a promise. The chapter moves from grief to reassurance to death to hope. The last sound in the book is not the coffin closing but Joseph’s oath about what God will do.

notes.original: shiv’im yom
notes.rendering: seventy days
notes.why: Egypt mourns Jacob seventy days — the same number as the souls who descended to Egypt (46:27), the same number as the nations of the Table of Nations (chapter 10). The symmetry is not accidental: the patriarch who brought seventy souls to Egypt is mourned by Egypt for seventy days. The most powerful nation in the world weeps for a Hebrew shepherd. The Abrahamic promise — ‘I will bless those who bless you’ — has been at work in Egypt.

notes.original: hatachat Elohim ani
notes.rendering: Am I in the place of God?
notes.why: Joseph’s response to his frightened brothers is not reassurance based on his own generosity but a question that puts the entire situation in theological perspective. Am I in the place of God? The same question he asked Rachel when she demanded children (30:2) — the question that names the limits of human agency and points to the divine. Joseph is not saying he has no power over his brothers; he is saying that vengeance belongs to God, and since God has been using their evil for good, there is nothing to avenge.

notes.original: atem chashavtem alai ra’ah Elohim chashavah l’tovah
notes.rendering: You intended harm… God intended it for good
notes.why: The theological summary of the entire Joseph narrative in one sentence. Chashav means to plan, to intend, to reckon — the same root as the accounting term in 15:6 (he counted it to him as righteousness). The brothers planned (chashav) evil; God planned (chashav) good. The same verb, the same event, two intentions running simultaneously. Joseph does not say God caused their evil or that their evil was not evil. He says: you meant it one way, God meant it another. Both are true. The theological grammar is double agency, and it is the most important statement in Genesis after the call of Abram.

notes.original: paqod yifqod etchem Elohim
notes.rendering: God will surely visit you
notes.why: Paqod yifqod — visiting he will visit, an emphatic infinitive absolute. The same verb (paqad — to visit, to attend to with purpose) that runs through the salvation history: God visited Sarah (21:1), God visited his people in the Exodus (Exodus 3:16, 4:31). Joseph’s dying word is a promise about a visitation that has not yet happened. He will not live to see it. He dies in Egypt. But the promise of paqad goes with the bones that the sons of Israel will carry out of Egypt four hundred years later. Exodus 13:19 records that Moses takes Joseph’s bones: ‘Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, God will surely visit you (paqod yifqod), and you shall carry up my bones with you from here.’ The last word of Genesis is the first word of Exodus.

notes.original: vayitten b’aron b’Mitzrayim
notes.rendering: he is put in a coffin in Egypt
notes.why: The book of Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt. The family of Abraham, after 215 years in Canaan, is now in Egypt. The promise of the land is entirely unfulfilled: the seed is multiplying, but the land is not possessed. The last image of Genesis is a coffin — and the last spoken words are a promise. The coffin is not the end; it is a placeholder, waiting for the visitation Joseph promised. Genesis ends in Egypt because the story is not over. The book that began with creation and covenant ends with a coffin and a promise, because the covenant has not yet been kept in full. The rest of the Torah is the next chapter.

outro: Note on Joseph’s final speech (50:19–21) as the theological capstone of Genesis: Joseph’s words to his brothers after Jacob’s death are the last substantial theological statement in the book. They bring together everything the Joseph narrative has been building toward: the double agency of human evil and divine good, the refusal of vengeance, the naming of God as the one in whose place Joseph refuses to stand, and the word of reassurance spoken tenderly to frightened men. The phrase ‘he spoke kindly to them’ (vayidabber al-libbam — he spoke to their hearts) is the same phrase used of a man comforting a woman in distress (see the same idiom in Hosea 2:14, where God speaks to the heart of Israel in the wilderness). Joseph speaks to his brothers’ hearts. The book ends with the sound of tenderness.

Note on Genesis as a book with an unfinished ending: Genesis 50:26 — ‘he is put in a coffin in Egypt’ — is one of the most deliberately unresolved endings in Scripture. The promise to Abraham (the land, the offspring, the blessing of all nations) is only partially fulfilled by the end of the book. The offspring have multiplied; the land is not possessed; the blessing of all nations is barely begun. The coffin of Joseph in Egypt is the image of a promise waiting to be fulfilled. When Moses, four hundred years later, takes Joseph’s bones out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19), he is completing what the end of Genesis leaves incomplete. The Torah is a single narrative in five volumes, and Genesis is its first chapter. The story is not over when the book closes.

intro: Joshua 1 opens with death and commission simultaneously: Moses is dead (v.1 — the first words of the book), and YHWH speaks immediately to Joshua. The book will not pause to mourn. The commission is centred on a command — be strong and courageous — repeated four times in nine verses (vv.6, 7, 9, 18), three times by YHWH and once by the people themselves.

notes.original: lo arpecha v'lo eshqevecha — I will not leave you or forsake you
notes.rendering: I will not leave you or forsake you
notes.why: Lo arpecha — I will not let go of you (from raphah — to let drop, to release, to relax one's grip). Lo eshqevecha — I will not forsake you (from azav — to leave, abandon; the same verb used in Hosea 4:10 of Israel forsaking YHWH). The double negative is absolute: YHWH commits to both holding on (not releasing) and staying present (not departing). The phrase is quoted in Hebrews 13:5 as the basis of contentment without love of money. It becomes one of the OT's most quoted covenant promises.

notes.original: rak chazaq ve'ematz me'od lishomor la'asot k'chol ha-Torah asher tzivkha Moshe avdi... v'hagita bo yomam va-layla — only be strong and very courageous to do according to all the law... you shall meditate on it day and night
notes.rendering: only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law... this Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night
notes.why: The commission is not primarily military but Torahic. Joshua's strength and courage are not about battlefield tactics; they are about not deviating from the Book of the Law — not turning to the right or to the left (lo tasur mimenu yamin u-smol — do not turn from it right or left). Lo yamush sefer ha-Torah ha-zeh mipicha — this book of the law shall not depart from your mouth. Higita bo — you shall meditate on it (from hagah — to mutter, to murmur, to ponder aloud; the word for the lion's growl in Isaiah 31:4 and the dove's moaning in Isaiah 38:14; meditation is a physical, audible practice). The leader's primary qualification is not military skill but sustained engagement with Torah.

intro: Joshua 2 introduces Rahab — a Canaanite prostitute who becomes one of the most celebrated figures in all of Scripture. She has heard the reports about YHWH; she has drawn a theological conclusion that the spies themselves have not yet stated; and she acts on it at personal risk. Her confession of faith (v.11) is among the most theologically precise in the Former Prophets.

notes.original: ki YHWH Eloheichem hu Elohim ba-shamayim mima'al v'al ha-aretz mitachat — for YHWH your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath
notes.rendering: for YHWH your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath
notes.why: Rahab's confession is the Shema from outside the covenant: a Canaanite woman who has never stood at Sinai confesses the exclusive sovereignty of YHWH over all territory — above and below. The formula ba-shamayim mima'al v'al ha-aretz mitachat (in the heavens above and on the earth beneath) is as comprehensive as possible: no space is excluded from YHWH's domain. Matthew 1:5 includes Rahab in the genealogy of Jesus. Hebrews 11:31 names her among the heroes of faith. James 2:25 cites her as an example of faith working through action. The NT honours her precisely as the one who acted on what she heard before she had any standing to do so.

notes.original: et-tiqvat chut ha-shani ha-zeh — this scarlet cord
notes.rendering: you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down
notes.why: Tiqvat chut ha-shani — the cord of scarlet thread (tiqvah — cord; also hope, expectation — the same word as the hope of Israel in Jeremiah 31:17 and the festival name Tikvah). The double meaning of tiqvah — both the physical cord hanging in the window and the hope that sustains the household — has generated extensive interpretive reflection. The scarlet cord that marks Rahab's house echoes the blood on the doorposts of the Exodus (Exodus 12:7): in both cases a marking on a threshold saves those inside from death. The cord is the sign of the covenant she has made; it stays in the window until salvation comes.

intro: Joshua 3 is the Jordan crossing — the moment that establishes Joshua's authority before all Israel and enacts a new Exodus. The book insists on the parallel: as YHWH dried up the Red Sea so that Israel left Egypt on dry ground, so he dries up the Jordan so that Israel enters the land on dry ground.

notes.original: lo-yedetem et ha-derech asher telkhu vah ki lo avar'tem baderech mitemol shilshom — you have not passed this way before
notes.rendering: you have not passed this way before
notes.why: Ki lo avar'tem baderech mitemol shilshom — for you have not passed in this way before yesterday and the day before (the Hebrew idiom for 'previously, ever before'). The instruction to keep distance from the ark (two thousand cubits — roughly a kilometre) is explicitly grounded in unfamiliarity: this is new territory, and the ark is the navigational instrument. What the people cannot know from experience must be known from following the presence of YHWH. The sentence is as much theological as geographical.

notes.original: v'raglei ha-kohanim noshe ha-aron nitbelu b'qtze ha-mayim — the feet of the priests bearing the ark are dipped in the brink of the water
notes.rendering: as soon as those bearing the ark come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark are dipped in the brink of the water... the waters coming down from above stand and rise up in a heap
notes.why: The waters do not stop before the priests enter; they stop when the priests enter. The miracle is triggered by the step of faith, not announced in advance of it. The Jordan is at flood stage (overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest — the most dangerous possible crossing conditions). The priests step into the flooding river and the water stops. The theology is consistent with Exodus: YHWH parts the water; human obedience is the occasion of the parting.

intro: Joshua 4 is about memory: the twelve stones are a monument to the crossing, designed to generate the question that will carry the story to the next generation. The pedagogy of the stones — children ask, parents answer — is the book's model of how covenant memory is transmitted.

notes.original: ki yish'alun beneichem machar lemor mah ha-avanim ha-eleh lachem — when your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?'
notes.rendering: when your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them...
notes.why: Ki yish'alun beneichem machar lemor — for your children will ask tomorrow (machar — tomorrow, in the future; the same word as in Exodus 13:14 — when your son asks you tomorrow). The stones are designed to provoke a question. Uninstructed curiosity draws out the story: the children see the rocks and ask; the parents answer with the Exodus-echo narrative. The monument is not self-explanatory — it requires a community that knows the story and will tell it. The pedagogy is the same as Passover: the ritual generates the question; the question generates the teaching.

notes.original: ka'asher asah YHWH Eloheichem l'Yam-Suf asher hevishenu milfaneinu ad-avarenu — just as YHWH your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over
notes.rendering: YHWH your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as YHWH your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over
notes.why: The narrative explicitly draws the parallel: Jordan = Red Sea. The verb is the same (hevish — to dry up, to cause to be dry; from yavesh — dry). The generation standing at Gilgal is a generation removed from the Exodus, but the pronoun shifts: the Red Sea is what he dried up for us (lanu — for us). They are invited into the story of the generation before them. The Jordan crossing is not a separate miracle; it is the Exodus continuing into the land.

intro: Joshua 5 contains two moments of transition — the reinstatement of circumcision (the covenant sign not practised in the wilderness) and the first Passover in the land — and one mysterious encounter that does not conclude: the commander of YHWH's army, whose drawn sword is neither sheathed nor explained.

notes.original: galoti et cherpat Mitzrayim me'aleichem — today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you
notes.rendering: today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you
notes.why: Galoti — I have rolled (from galal — to roll; the wordplay gives the place its name: Gilgal = the rolling). Cherpat Mitzrayim — the reproach of Egypt (cherpah — reproach, shame, disgrace). What the reproach of Egypt specifically means is debated: it may refer to the shame of slavery (the uncircumcised condition in which they wandered being a kind of spiritual vulnerability), or to Egypt's mockery of Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 32:12), or to the sense of incompleteness that forty years of delayed promise carried. Whatever its precise content, YHWH declares it rolled away at the moment the covenant sign is restored and the land is entered. Gilgal becomes Israel's base camp for the entire first phase of the campaign.

notes.original: lo ki ani sar-tzeva YHWH atah vati — no; but I am the commander of YHWH's army
notes.rendering: no; but I am the commander of the army of YHWH. Now I have come
notes.why: Joshua's question — are you for us or for our adversaries? — receives neither answer: the figure is not on either human side. Lo — no (a refusal of the binary). Ki ani sar-tzeva YHWH — but I am the commander (sar — prince, commander, chief officer) of YHWH's army. The encounter echoes Moses at the burning bush: Joshua falls on his face, worships, and is told to remove his sandals because the place is holy (compare Exodus 3:5). The drawn sword is neither sheathed nor explained; the chapter ends without a battle plan being given. The encounter establishes who is in command: not Joshua but the commander of YHWH's army. Joshua is the human commander under a divine one.

intro: Joshua 6 is the fall of Jericho — the book's most famous military engagement, which is not a military engagement at all. There is no siege equipment, no assault, no battle formation. There is marching, silence, trumpets, and a shout. The walls fall without any human weapon touching them.

notes.original: re'eh natati v'yadcha et-Yericho — see, I have given Jericho into your hand
notes.rendering: see, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valour
notes.why: Natati — I have given (the perfect tense of natan — to give; but in a context where Jericho still stands and the battle has not begun). The perfect of prophetic certainty: the event is so certain from YHWH's perspective that it is spoken of as already accomplished. This is the grammar of divine promise throughout the OT: what YHWH decrees is spoken of as done. Joshua and the army march around a city that has already fallen in the divine announcement, and only then falls in visible fact.

notes.original: va-yipol ha-choma tachteyha — the wall falls down flat
notes.rendering: the wall falls down flat, so that the people go up into the city, every man straight before him
notes.why: Tachteyha — under itself, beneath itself, flat (tahat — beneath, under). The wall does not fall outward or inward; it collapses straight down. Every man straight before him (ish neged panav — a man opposite his face): the entire circumference of the city becomes a breach simultaneously, so that every soldier can enter directly without funnelling through a gate. The tactical genius of the strategy, if it can be called that, is that a fallen-flat wall creates no defensive advantage for the defenders. The archaeological evidence for a destruction of Jericho in the Late Bronze Age is debated; what the narrative insists on is that the mechanism was divine, not human.

notes.original: ki hitspi'ah et ha-malakhim asher shalach Yehoshua laragel et Yericho — because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho
notes.rendering: she dwells in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho
notes.why: Rahab's integration into Israel is stated simply: hi yoshevet b'kerev Yisrael ad ha-yom ha-zeh — she dwells in the midst of Israel to this day. The Canaanite prostitute who confessed the sovereignty of YHWH (2:11) is not merely spared; she becomes part of the covenant community. Matthew 1:5 includes her in the genealogy of Jesus as the mother of Boaz and ancestor of David. Her story is one of the book's clearest testimonies that the covenant people is defined by faith and covenant loyalty, not by ethnic origin.

intro: Joshua 7 is the book's crisis chapter — the defeat at Ai exposing a hidden sin. The juxtaposition is deliberate: Jericho falls without Israel lifting a sword; Ai repels Israel with thirty-six casualties. The difference is not military but covenantal. The theological logic is corporate: one man's sin, Achan's, becomes the community's defeat. This is one of the most difficult passages in the book for modern readers shaped by individual ethics.

notes.original: va-yim'alu vnei Yisrael ma'al ba-cherem — the people of Israel break faith in regard to the devoted things
notes.rendering: the people of Israel break faith in regard to the devoted things
notes.why: Ma'al — broke faith, acted unfaithfully, committed a trespass (from ma'al — to be unfaithful, to act treacherously in a covenant context; the word used for spousal unfaithfulness and covenant violation). Ba-cherem — in regard to the devoted things (cherem — the ban, the devotion to destruction; what belongs wholly to YHWH and cannot be appropriated for human use). The verse names the sin before it names the sinner: Israel has broken faith, and only then is Achan identified. The corporate dimension is built into the grammar: the people's faithlessness is YHWH's experience before Achan's identity is disclosed.

notes.original: va-ere ba-shalal aderet Shin'ar achat tovah — when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar
notes.rendering: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a bar of gold... then I coveted them and took them
notes.why: Va-ere... va-echmod... va-ekach — I saw... I coveted... I took. The three verbs trace the trajectory of temptation: seeing (passive), coveting (internal desire), taking (external act). The sequence echoes the garden: Eve saw, desired, took (Genesis 3:6). Achan's confession is not an excuse but a precise self-analysis. The aderet Shin'ar — the cloak from Shinar (Babylon; shinar is the word for Babylon in Genesis 10:10 and 11:2, and Daniel 1:2) — is an irony: Babylon has already entered the camp of Israel through desire for Babylonian luxury before Babylon ever becomes a political threat.

intro: Joshua 8 is two things: the successful campaign against Ai (using the ambush strategy that Jericho's miraculous fall made unnecessary) and the covenant renewal ceremony at Mount Ebal. The second half of the chapter (vv.30–35) carries the book's theological weight: in the middle of the conquest, before many cities have been taken, Joshua pauses to read the entire Law before all the assembly.

notes.original: az yivneh Yehoshua mizbeach l'YHWH Elohei Yisrael b'Har Eval — at that time Joshua builds an altar to YHWH on Mount Ebal
notes.rendering: at that time Joshua builds an altar to YHWH, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of YHWH had commanded
notes.why: Az — at that time, then (the temporal marker of immediate fulfilment: as soon as Ai falls, Joshua acts on the command Moses gave in Deuteronomy 27:4–8). The altar at Ebal is built in the middle of enemy territory, not after the conquest is complete. The military campaign pauses for covenant ceremony. The uncut stones (avanim shelemot — whole stones, upon which no iron tool has been wielded) are the Mosaic specification: what is holy is not humanly shaped. The altar is simple; the act is comprehensive.

notes.original: lo hayah davar mikol asher tzivah Moshe asher lo-qara Yehoshua — there is not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua does not read
notes.rendering: there is not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua does not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners
notes.why: The inclusion list is the chapter's most pointed theological statement: kol qehal Yisrael v'ha-nashim v'ha-taf v'ha-ger — all the assembly of Israel, the women, the little ones, and the sojourner (ger — the resident alien, the foreigner living among Israel). The Torah reading is for everyone in the community without exception. Moses commanded this (Deuteronomy 31:12 — assemble the people, men, women, little ones, and the sojourner). Joshua does it exactly. The covenant community is defined not by ethnicity but by presence under the word.

intro: Joshua 9 is the book's most theologically nuanced episode. The Gibeonites deceive Israel, obtain a peace treaty, and are then protected by the oath Israel swore — even after the deception is discovered. The oath made in YHWH's name holds regardless of the circumstances under which it was obtained. The principle is: an oath is an oath.

notes.original: v'lo sha'alu et-pi YHWH — but they do not ask counsel from the mouth of YHWH
notes.rendering: so the men take some of their provisions, but do not ask counsel from the mouth of YHWH
notes.why: The diagnostic verse of the chapter: the Israelite leaders are persuaded by the physical evidence (the stale bread, the cracked wineskins, the worn sandals) and do not consult YHWH. V'lo sha'alu et-pi YHWH — they did not ask from the mouth of YHWH (sha'al — to ask, to inquire; pi — mouth). The failure is not malice but complacency: the evidence seems convincing, the covenant terms seem clear, and they act on what they can see rather than seeking divine counsel. The lesson the narrative extracts is not that you cannot trust your eyes but that human wisdom operating without divine consultation is insufficient. Every subsequent leader of Israel who does not ask YHWH makes the same mistake.

notes.original: nishbanu lahem b'YHWH Elohei Yisrael v'atah lo nuchal lagaat bahem — we have sworn to them by YHWH the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them
notes.rendering: we have sworn to them by YHWH, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath come upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them
notes.why: The leaders' reasoning is theologically precise: the oath was sworn by YHWH's name (not by an idol or by their own honour). To break it would be to profane YHWH's name. The wrath they fear is not Gibeonite retaliation but divine anger at oath-breaking. Centuries later, when Saul violates this oath by killing Gibeonites, David must make amends (2 Samuel 21:1–14). The principle survives across generations: covenants made in YHWH's name bind across time.

intro: Joshua 10 is the longest battle chapter in the book — the southern campaign, triggered by Gibeon's appeal for help, culminating in the sun standing still. The chapter's theological summary (v.42) is the book's refrain: YHWH God of Israel fights for Israel.

notes.original: Shemesh b'Giv'on dom v'yareach b'Emeq Ayalon — sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon
notes.rendering: sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stands still, and the moon stops... there has been no day like it before or since, when YHWH heeded the voice of a man
notes.why: Dom — be still, be silent, cease (the same word used in Psalm 4:4 — be still and know; and Habakkuk 2:20 — let all the earth be silent before him). Joshua's command is addressed to the sun and moon as if they can hear him — and they do. The text says the sun stops in the midst of heaven (ba-chatzi ha-shamayim — in the middle of the sky) for about a whole day (k'yom tamim — like a complete day). The Book of Jashar (sefer ha-yashar — the book of the upright; also quoted in 2 Samuel 1:18) is cited as a prior source. The miracle's meaning is theological: YHWH heeds the voice of a man (shama YHWH b'qol ish). Joshua asks; YHWH responds. YHWH fights for Israel, and when a man asks him to extend the day for the battle, he does.

notes.original: v'et-kol-ha-melachim ha-eleh v'et-artzam laqach Yehoshua pa'am achat ki YHWH Elohei Yisrael nilcham l'Yisrael — Joshua captures all these kings and their land at one time, because YHWH God of Israel fights for Israel
notes.rendering: Joshua captures all these kings and their land at one time, because YHWH God of Israel fights for Israel
notes.why: Pa'am achat — at one time, in one campaign (pa'am — a stroke, a beat, an occasion; used of a single time or occurrence). The summary compresses the campaign to its theological core: the speed and totality of the conquest is not Joshua's military genius but YHWH's engagement. Ki YHWH Elohei Yisrael nilcham l'Yisrael — for YHWH God of Israel fought for Israel. The verb nilcham is the niphal of lacham (to fight, to do battle), suggesting a reflex, a fully engaged fighting. YHWH is not merely supervising the battle; he is in it.

intro: Joshua 11 completes the conquest narrative with the northern campaign against the coalition led by Jabin of Hazor — the largest force Israel faces, as numerous as the sand on the seashore. The chapter ends with the book's first great summary: Joshua takes the whole land, and the land has rest from war.

notes.original: ka'asher tzivah YHWH et-Moshe avdo ken tzivah Moshe et-Yehoshua v'ken asah Yehoshua — just as YHWH had commanded Moses, so Moses commands Joshua, and so Joshua does
notes.rendering: just as YHWH had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commands Joshua, and so Joshua does. He leaves nothing undone of all that YHWH had commanded Moses
notes.why: The chain of obedience: YHWH → Moses → Joshua → action. And the completeness: lo hesir davar mikol asher tzivah YHWH et-Moshe — he does not remove (turn aside) a single word from all that YHWH commanded Moses. This is the Joshua of chapter 1 fulfilled: the one who was commanded not to turn to the right hand or to the left from the Book of the Law (1:7) has not turned. The summary verse connects the commission of chapter 1 to the execution of chapters 2–11.

notes.original: va-tishqot ha-aretz min-ha-milchamah — and the land has rest from war
notes.rendering: so Joshua takes the whole land, according to all that YHWH had spoken to Moses. And the land has rest from war
notes.why: Va-tishqot ha-aretz min-ha-milchamah — and the land rested from war (shaqat — to be quiet, to be at rest, to have peace from; the word for the Sabbath-like quietness of a land no longer convulsed by conflict). This is the first of four occurrences of this phrase in Joshua (11:23; 14:15; 21:44; 22:4) — each marking a milestone of completion. The land resting from war is the land being given its Sabbath, its shalom. The conquest is not celebrated as a military achievement but as the arrival of rest — the fulfilment of the promise of a place where Israel can dwell with YHWH.

intro: Joshua 12 is the conquest's balance sheet — a list of thirty-one kings defeated, closing the first half of the book. It functions as both a summary of chapters 1–11 and a transition to the second half, which concerns the distribution of the land rather than its capture. The list format is the book's way of counting the promise as kept.

notes.original: kol melachim shloshim v'echad — in all, thirty-one kings
notes.rendering: in all, thirty-one kings
notes.why: The list of thirty-one kings is the account of the conquest's scope. Verse 9 begins: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, one — and the word echad (one) follows each name like a drumbeat for fifteen verses. The repetition is deliberate: each king is counted, each defeat named. The book keeps careful record of what was promised and what was delivered. The transition from chapters 1–12 (taking the land) to chapters 13–24 (distributing the land) turns on this summary. The land now belongs to Israel by right of conquest and divine gift; the question is how it shall be apportioned among the tribes.

intro: Joshua 13 opens the land allotment section with an arresting honesty: Joshua is old, and there remains yet very much land to possess. The conquest is declared complete in theological terms (11:23 — Joshua takes the whole land) while the geographical reality is that significant territories remain unconquered. The book holds both together.

notes.original: v'Yehoshua zaqen ba ba-yamim va-yomer YHWH elav atah zaqenta ba-yamim v'ha-aretz nish'arah harbeh me'od l'rishtah — Joshua is old and advanced in years, and YHWH says: you are old, and there remains yet very much land to possess
notes.rendering: you are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess
notes.why: Nish'arah harbeh me'od l'rishtah — there remains, is left over, a very great amount to possess (rishtah — possession, to possess as an inheritance; from yarash — to inherit, possess, dispossess). The gap between theological declaration (all the land taken) and geographical reality (much land remaining) is the book's honest acknowledgement that the fulfilment of the promise is partial and progressive. YHWH's response is not to contradict the remaining task but to say: divide what has been taken and I will drive out the rest. The inheritance is given; the possession is incremental.

notes.original: YHWH Elohei Yisrael hu nachalatam — YHWH God of Israel is their inheritance
notes.rendering: YHWH God of Israel is their inheritance
notes.why: The tribe of Levi receives no land inheritance in the division (stated twice, in vv.14 and 33). Their inheritance is YHWH himself — the offerings by fire (ishei YHWH — the fire-offerings of YHWH) and, in v.33, simply YHWH God of Israel himself. The Levites are distributed among all the tribes (ch.21) rather than concentrated in a territory. The theology is pointed: what all Israel possesses in the land (a relationship with YHWH mediated through the land), the Levites possess in a different register — YHWH himself is what they inherit. Levi's dispossession of land is their greatest possession.

intro: Joshua 14 introduces the land distribution with Caleb's claim — one of the most vivid character moments in the book. Caleb is eighty-five years old and still asking for the hardest territory: the hill country held by the Anakim, the giants who made the other spies feel like grasshoppers. His faith has not diminished in forty-five years.

notes.original: v'atah hineni hayom shmonim v'chamesh shanah — behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me
notes.rendering: behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me
notes.why: Od anochi hayom chazaq — I am still strong today (od — still, yet; chazaq — strong, firm; the same word as the repeated command to Joshua: be strong and courageous). Caleb has waited forty-five years for this moment. He is not diminished by the waiting. The hill country he asks for is Hebron — the location of the Anakim — the very giants whose presence caused the other spies to despair (Numbers 13:33 — we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers). Caleb's request is the faith of chapter 2 (the spies who trusted) lived to its full conclusion: after forty-five years, still strong, still asking for the hardest promise.

intro: Joshua 15 is the most detailed single tribal allotment in the book — Judah's territory, boundary descriptions and city lists occupying 63 verses. It includes the Caleb and Achsah narrative (vv.13–19) — one of the book's finest character vignettes — and closes with the honest admission that Jerusalem was not taken (v.63).

notes.original: vat'si-ehu lish'ol me-et aviha sadeh vatitz-nach me-al ha-chamor — she urges him to ask her father for a field, and she gets off her donkey
notes.rendering: when she comes to him, she urges him to ask her father for a field. And she gets off her donkey, and Caleb says to her: 'What do you want?' She says: 'Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water.'
notes.why: Achsah is one of the few women in Joshua who speaks and acts with initiative. She urges her husband to ask for the field; when that is not enough, she goes herself to her father and asks. The getting off the donkey (vatitz-nach — and she got down, alighted) is a formal gesture of petition — the one approaching a superior dismounts as a sign of humility. Her request is practical: the Negeb without water is unusable. Caleb gives her both upper and lower springs. The episode shows the land distribution is not merely tribal assignment but a living process of inheritance claimed, negotiated, and secured.

notes.original: v'et ha-Yevusi yoshev Yerushalayim lo yakhlu vnei Yehudah l'horishim — the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out
notes.rendering: but the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day
notes.why: The honest footnote: Jerusalem is inside Judah's allotment but not Judah's possession. Lo yakhlu — they could not (not: they did not try; the verb yakhol — to be able, to manage to do). The Jebusites hold the city until David takes it in 2 Samuel 5:6–9, long after Joshua. The book does not hide the gap between allotment and possession. The inheritance is given by divine decree; the full possession is achieved over generations of obedience and faithfulness — and sometimes fails entirely.

intro: Joshua 16 assigns Ephraim's territory — the central hill country — and closes with the same honest note as Judah's chapter: the Canaanites of Gezer are not driven out. The pattern of partial possession is recurring.

notes.original: v'lo horishu et ha-Kena'ani ha-yoshev b'Gezer — they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer
notes.rendering: however, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day
notes.why: The refrain of incomplete possession: lo horishu — they did not drive out (horishu — the hiphil of yarash, to dispossess, drive out). The Canaanites of Gezer become vassals (forced labour — lemas oved — a tribute-worker). This repeated pattern (Judah cannot drive out the Jebusites of Jerusalem, Ephraim cannot drive out the Canaanites of Gezer) is the book's honest reckoning with the gap between what was commanded and what was accomplished. The book of Judges will develop the consequences of this gap.

intro: Joshua 17 includes two notable episodes: the daughters of Zelophehad claiming their father's inheritance (v.4), and the tribe of Joseph complaining that their allotment is too small. Joshua's response to the complaint is characteristically direct.

notes.original: uve-not Tzelofchad... ben-Chipher ben-Gilad ben-Machir ben-Menashe hayu banot v'lo banim — Zelophehad had no sons, but only daughters
notes.rendering: Zelophehad... had no sons, but only daughters... They come before Eleazar the priest and Joshua and say: 'YHWH commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers'
notes.why: The daughters of Zelophehad are the second instance in Joshua of women claiming and receiving their inheritance rights (after Achsah in ch.15). Their case is precedent from Numbers 27:1–11, where Moses ruled that in the absence of male heirs, daughters inherit. They cite the commandment of YHWH — ki tzivah YHWH et-Moshe latet lanu nachala b'toch acheinu — and the ruling is upheld. The inheritance system has a mechanism for women's rights built into it by divine command. Their names (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, Tirzah) are preserved in the text.

notes.original: yesh lecha yaar bila a'ela v'berata lecha sham b'eretz ha-Perizi v'ha-Refaim — go up to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves
notes.rendering: go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves... the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it
notes.why: Joshua's response to Joseph's complaint about insufficient land is not to give them more — it is to tell them to develop what they have. Bila — clear it, cut it down (from bala — to consume, to swallow up; used of clearing forest). The hill country is forest; the Canaanites have chariots of iron in the valley. Joshua's answer: the forest is your territory — clear it. The chariots of iron are formidable — ki-rechev barzel lo v'ki-chazaq hu — but you shall drive them out. The promise does not exempt from the work.

intro: Joshua 18 moves the distribution process to Shiloh — where the tent of meeting is set up for the first time in the land — and addresses the seven tribes that have not yet received their allotments. Joshua's question is pointed: how long will you put off going in to take possession?

notes.original: va-yiqahalu kol adat bnei Yisrael Shiloh va-yashkinu sham et-ohel moed v'ha-aretz nikh'besah lifneihem — the whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there. The land lies subdued before them
notes.rendering: then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembles at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there. The land lies subdued before them
notes.why: Nikh'besah lifneihem — the land is subdued before them (from kavash — to subdue, tread down, bring into subjection; the same verb as in Genesis 1:28 — fill the earth and subdue it). The tent of meeting is set up in the land for the first time: the centre of Israel's worship is now within the inheritance, not outside it. The movement from Gilgal (the entry camp) to Shiloh (the worship centre) marks a transition: the period of conquest gives way to the period of settlement. Shiloh will remain the central sanctuary until the time of Samuel.

notes.original: ad matai atem mitrapim lavo lareshot et ha-aretz asher natan lachem YHWH Elohei avoteichem — how long will you put off going in to take possession
notes.rendering: how long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which YHWH, the God of your fathers, has given you?
notes.why: Mitrapim — you are being slack, you are lingering, delaying (from raphah — to be slack, to let drop; the same root as the raphah in lo arpecha, I will not let go of you in 1:5, reversed: YHWH will not let go of them, but they are letting go of the promise). Seven tribes have not yet pursued their allotments. The land is available; the promise is given; and they are not going in. Joshua's rebuke is the same theology as the conquest narrative: the inheritance is YHWH's gift, but the possession requires human action.

intro: Joshua 19 completes the tribal distribution with the remaining six tribes (Simeon, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, Dan) and closes with Joshua himself receiving his inheritance — last of all. The narrative detail is theological: the leader takes his portion only after every tribe has theirs. The verse reverses the pattern of human leadership.

notes.original: nat'nu vnei Yisrael nachalah l'Yehoshua bin-Nun b'tocham al-pi YHWH — the people of Israel give an inheritance to Joshua the son of Nun in their midst, by the command of YHWH
notes.rendering: when they finish distributing the land for inheritance by its boundaries, the people of Israel give an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun. By the command of YHWH they give him the city that he asks
notes.why: B'tocham — in their midst, among them (toch — the middle, the inside). Joshua's inheritance is received as a gift from the people, not seized by right of office. The reversal is deliberate: Joshua led the conquest but is the last to take a portion. Al-pi YHWH — by the mouth of YHWH — the same phrase used for the daughters of Zelophehad's case in 17:4. Even the leader's inheritance is given by divine word, not personal claim. Timnath-serah (timnat-serach — portion of the abundance, or perhaps 'remaining portion') becomes Joshua's home and burial place (24:30).

notes.original: va-yechalu mechalek et ha-aretz — so they finish dividing the land
notes.rendering: so they finish dividing the land
notes.why: Va-yechalu — they finished, completed (kalah — to complete, to finish, to bring to an end). The verb signals closure of the entire distribution process (chapters 13–19). The land has been allotted in full. What was promised to Abraham, sworn to Moses, taken by Joshua's generation, has now been parcelled out tribe by tribe. The book's narrative of fulfilment has reached its formal completion in territory; the chapters that follow (cities of refuge, Levitical cities, farewell, covenant) consolidate what has been given.

intro: Joshua 20 institutes the six cities of refuge — three on each side of the Jordan, distributed so that no Israelite is more than a day's journey from sanctuary. The institution is mercy built into the legal structure: the unintentional manslayer is protected from blood vengeance while still answering to the congregation's judgment.

notes.original: arei ha-miqlat... lanus shamah rotzeach makeh-nefesh bishgagah bibli-da'at — the cities of refuge, that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there
notes.rendering: appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses, that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there
notes.why: Miqlat — refuge, place of receiving (from qalat, to take in, to harbour, to gather). The city does not hide the manslayer; it receives him for adjudication. Bishgagah — by error, unintentionally (shagag — to go astray, to err); bibli-da'at — without knowledge. The distinction is precise: a manslayer who acted in ignorance is not a murderer. The legal structure recognises gradations of culpability that pre-modern blood vengeance does not, while still acknowledging that blood has been shed and requires response. The city of refuge holds the manslayer until the death of the high priest — a kind of vicarious atonement; the priest's death ends the period of exile.

notes.original: go'el ha-dam — the avenger of blood
notes.rendering: they shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood
notes.why: Go'el ha-dam — the redeemer of blood (go'el from ga'al — to redeem, to act as next of kin; the same word for Boaz in Ruth and for YHWH himself as Israel's Redeemer). The go'el is not a vigilante but the legally recognised kinsman whose duty is to respond to the death of a relative. The cities of refuge regulate this institution: the go'el's response is not abolished but constrained. The unintentional manslayer is protected because the go'el's role is the response to murder, not to accident. The category 'avenger of blood' is one of Hebrew law's most precise expressions of communal moral economy.

intro: Joshua 21 distributes forty-eight cities to the Levites — the tribe with no territorial inheritance now receives habitation embedded within every other tribe's allotment. The Levites live everywhere; YHWH's worship and instruction are accessible from every region. And the chapter closes with what is arguably the theological climax of the entire book: the fulfilment formula in verses 43–45.

notes.original: va-yiten YHWH l'Yisrael et-kol-ha-aretz asher nishba latet la-avotam... va-yanach YHWH lahem misaviv k'chol asher nishba la-avotam — YHWH gives to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers... and YHWH gives them rest on every side, just as he swore to their fathers
notes.rendering: and YHWH gives to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers, and they take possession of it and dwell in it. And YHWH gives them rest on every side, just as he swore to their fathers
notes.why: The book's structural keystone. The double 'as he swore to their fathers' (k'chol asher nishba la-avotam) closes the loop opened at 1:6 (the land I swore to their fathers to give them). Va-yanach — he caused them to rest (nuach — to settle down, rest, find peace; the same root as Noach — Noah, the rest after the flood). The land has rest from war (11:23); now YHWH gives Israel rest from their enemies. The Sabbath theology of the promise is realised in the land.

notes.original: lo nafal davar echad mikol ha-davar ha-tov asher diber YHWH el-beit Yisrael ha-kol ba — not one word falls of all the good word that YHWH spoke to the house of Israel; all comes to pass
notes.rendering: not one word fails of all the good word that YHWH spoke to the house of Israel; all comes to pass
notes.why: Lo nafal davar — not a word fell (nafal — to fall, to fail; the same verb used of the walls of Jericho falling, ironically inverted here: the walls fell, but the word did not). This is the book's thesis statement: every promise made through Moses has been kept. Ha-kol ba — the whole has come (ba — came, arrived). The grammatical economy of those final three words — ha-kol ba — carries the entire weight of the conquest narrative. The phrase reappears in Joshua's farewell (23:14) as his last theological testimony before his death.

intro: Joshua 22 is the book's most carefully drawn narrative of misunderstanding and resolution. The eastern tribes, sent home with blessing, build an altar at the Jordan. The western tribes hear of it and assume the worst — a rival altar would be schism, idolatry, the sin of Peor repeated. Civil war nearly erupts. But the eastern tribes explain: the altar is not for sacrifice but for witness, that future generations will remember the eastern tribes' belonging to YHWH. The chapter teaches that misunderstanding is real, and that the discipline of asking before acting can prevent catastrophe.

notes.original: l'ahavah et-YHWH Eloheichem v'lalechet b'chol-drachav v'lishmor mitzvotav uledavqa-bo u'l'ovdo b'chol-l'vavchem u'b'chol-nafshechem — to love YHWH your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to cling to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul
notes.rendering: to love YHWH your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul
notes.why: Joshua's parting charge to the eastern tribes is pure Deuteronomic language — the same verbs and constructions that govern Moses's farewell in Deuteronomy. Ahavah — to love (love as the central covenant disposition, not affection but loyalty); davaq — to cling, to cleave, to be attached (the same word for marriage in Genesis 2:24). The five verbs (love, walk, keep, cling, serve) form a complete picture of covenant life. The eastern tribes are not exempt from Torah because they live across the Jordan; the Jordan is no theological boundary.

notes.original: El Elohim YHWH El Elohim YHWH hu yodea v'Yisrael hu yeda — The Mighty One, God, YHWH! The Mighty One, God, YHWH! He knows, and let Israel know!
notes.rendering: The Mighty One, God, YHWH! The Mighty One, God, YHWH! He knows; and let Israel itself know!
notes.why: The eastern tribes' opening invocation is among the most emphatic theological utterances in the OT: three divine names (El — the Mighty One; Elohim — God; YHWH — the covenant name) repeated twice, as if calling all three modes of God's identity to witness their innocence. Hu yodea — he knows (God's omniscient witness of their intentions); v'Yisrael hu yeda — and let Israel also know (their intent that the truth be public). The grammar is breathless, layered, and absolutely sincere. The accusation against them was rebellion against YHWH; their first words call YHWH himself as witness to the contrary.

notes.original: va-yiqr'u vnei Reuven u'vnei Gad la-mizbeach — the people of Reuben and the people of Gad call the altar Witness
notes.rendering: the people of Reuben and the people of Gad call the altar Witness, 'For,' they say, 'it is a witness between us that YHWH is God'
notes.why: Ed — witness (the same word used throughout the chapter; from the verb ud — to repeat, to bear witness). The altar's name is itself the explanation. The Hebrew text places the word ed (witness) where most translations supply a name; the altar simply is the witness. The theology recovers the original meaning of altars in the pre-Mosaic patriarchal period (Genesis 31:48 — Jacob's heap of witness with Laban) before centralised sacrifice was instituted. The eastern tribes have built a memorial, not a rival sanctuary.

intro: Joshua 23 is the first of two farewell addresses, given to the leaders. The aged Joshua, knowing his end is near, reprises the theological summary of 21:43–45 and warns that the same God who kept every good promise will, if the covenant is broken, keep the warnings as well. Faithfulness in giving is a guarantor of faithfulness in judgment.

notes.original: hineh anochi holech ha-yom b'derech kol ha-aretz — behold, I am going today the way of all the earth
notes.rendering: behold, this day I am going the way of all the earth
notes.why: B'derech kol ha-aretz — in the way of all the earth (the standard biblical euphemism for death; also used by David at his own farewell, 1 Kings 2:2). Joshua faces his death with composure, not denial. The phrase locates his death within the universal human condition: the way that all flesh goes. There is no claim to exemption. The leader who led Israel into the land now leaves it as every human does.

notes.original: lo nafal davar echad mikol ha-devarim ha-tovim asher diber YHWH Eloheichem aleichem ha-kol ba'u lachem — not one word has failed of all the good words that YHWH your God promised concerning you; all have come to pass for you
notes.rendering: you know in all your hearts and in all your souls that not one word has failed of all the good words that YHWH your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed
notes.why: Joshua repeats almost verbatim the summary of 21:45 — the book's structural keystone — with double emphasis: 'all have come to pass... not one has failed.' Lo nafal davar echad — not a single word has fallen. The doubling is a deathbed confession of God's faithfulness. What was said as narrative summary (21:45) is now said as personal testimony: I, Joshua, having led this people, declare to you that every promise has been kept. The repetition is the book's structural device: the same affirmation is made first by the narrator and then by the dying leader, sealing it from two directions.

intro: Joshua 24 is the book's climactic chapter — the covenant renewal at Shechem and the death of Joshua. The structure is itself a covenant ceremony: historical prologue (vv.2–13), call to commitment (vv.14–15), the people's response (vv.16–18, 21, 24), oath of witness (vv.22, 27), and conclusion. The chapter ends with three deaths: Joshua, the bones of Joseph (finally laid to rest in the land after four hundred years), and Eleazar. The age of conquest closes.

notes.original: bachru lachem ha-yom et-mi ta'avodun... v'anochi u'veiti na'avod et-YHWH — choose for yourselves today whom you will serve... but as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH
notes.rendering: choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH
notes.why: Bachru lachem ha-yom — choose for yourselves today (bachar — to choose; the same verb used of YHWH choosing Israel, now reversed: Israel choosing whom to serve). The choice is presented as genuine: the gods of the Mesopotamian past, the gods of the Canaanite present, or YHWH. Joshua does not assume the people's choice; he forces them to make it conscious. V'anochi u'veiti na'avod et-YHWH — but as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH (anochi — the emphatic 'I'; u'veiti — and my household). Joshua's testimony is personal and familial, not corporate. He does not say 'Israel will serve YHWH'; he says 'I and my house.' The corporate covenant is built from such individual confessions.

notes.original: lo tuchlu la'avod et-YHWH ki-Elohim qedoshim hu — you are not able to serve YHWH, for he is a holy God
notes.rendering: you are not able to serve YHWH, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins
notes.why: The most surprising line in the chapter. After the people have just pledged to serve YHWH, Joshua says: lo tuchlu — you are not able. Tuchlu (yakhol — to be able, to manage, to be capable). The grammar is not 'you should not' but 'you cannot.' The warning is theologically loaded: serving YHWH is not a matter of casual goodwill; it requires capacity the people do not naturally possess. Joshua's word here is a forerunner of the prophets' insistence that covenant faithfulness is not a human achievement but a divine gift — the new heart and new spirit promised by Ezekiel (Ezekiel 36:26). Joshua's warning is the question to which the rest of the OT writes its long answer.

notes.original: va-yamot Yehoshua bin-Nun eved YHWH — Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of YHWH, dies
notes.rendering: after these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of YHWH, dies, being a hundred and ten years old
notes.why: Yehoshua bin-Nun eved YHWH — Joshua son of Nun, the servant of YHWH. The title eved YHWH (servant of YHWH) belonged throughout the book to Moses (1:1, 7, 13, 15; 8:31, 33; 9:24; 11:12, 15; 12:6; 13:8; 14:7; 18:7; 22:2, 4, 5). Only now, in the verse announcing his death, is Joshua himself given that title. The book closes by elevating Joshua to the rank Moses held. He has finished his work and earned his name. The burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem (v.32) closes a loop opened in Genesis 50:25: Joseph asked his brothers to carry his bones up from Egypt when God would surely visit them. Four hundred years later the bones come home. The book of Joshua ends with the Exodus promise complete: Joseph is buried in the land of his fathers.

intro: Three threads run through this opening chapter: the verb to dispossess (yarash), the lex talionis poetry of Adoni-bezek, and the slow drumbeat of tribes who did not drive out. The book’s whole problem is already in place before a single judge appears.

notes.original: kaʼasher ʿasiti ken shillem-li elohim — “as I have done, so God has repaid me”
notes.rendering: As I have done, so God has repaid me.
notes.why: Lex talionis in the king’s own mouth. Adoni-bezek names himself the victim of his own grammar — and the book opens with a Canaanite ruler confessing the justice of Israel’s God. An unsettling overture for a story about Israel’s failures.

notes.original: mah-lakh — “what’s with you?”
notes.rendering: What is it you want?
notes.why: Caleb’s question to Achsah is two syllables in Hebrew — blunt, almost gruff. English versions tend to pad it (“What dost thou wish?”); the brevity is the point. He is her father; he is brief.

notes.original: lo l’horish et-yoshvei haʿemek — “not to dispossess the inhabitants of the valley”
notes.rendering: But they cannot drive out those who live in the plain.
notes.why: The verb yarash (dispossess, take possession, inherit) dominates Judges 1. From v.19 onward, the chapter becomes a litany — Manasseh did not, Ephraim did not, Zebulun did not, Asher did not, Naphtali did not. The whole book hangs on this single failed verb.

intro: The book’s whole engine is laid out in this chapter — a new generation, the verb to know (yadaʿ), and the slow grammar of repeated apostasy. Read these three notes together and you have the theology of Judges in miniature.

notes.original: Bokhim — “weepers”
notes.rendering: They name the place Bochim.
notes.why: From bakhah (to weep). The aetiology is literal: they wept, and so it is called Weeping-Place. Hebrew loves these site-name puns, and the choice is pointed — Bochim sits in the same hill country as Bethel (“house of God”). The proximity is uncomfortable.

notes.original: lo yadʿu et-YHWH — “they did not know YHWH”
notes.rendering: who do not know YHWH or the work he has done
notes.why: yadaʿ is intimate, relational knowledge — not information but acquaintance. This single phrase is the engine of the entire book. Everything that follows — Baals, apostasies, judges, civil war — flows from a generation that no longer knew.

notes.original: yinnachem YHWH min-naʺakatam — “YHWH is moved by their groaning”
notes.rendering: YHWH is moved to pity by their groaning
notes.why: nacham is the troubled verb: to relent, to be comforted, to grieve, to repent. Older translations soften it (“had compassion”). The Hebrew implies something stronger — a real shift in the divine, felt sorrow at human pain. The same verb is used in Genesis when YHWH grieves over making humanity.

intro: Ehud’s story is built on irony: a left-handed Benjaminite (Benjamin means “son of the right”), a sword on the right thigh that no one searches, and an untranslatable Hebrew word for what comes out of Eglon. Black comedy, but the theology is serious — YHWH delivers through the unexpected.

notes.original: ʿish itter yad-yemino — “a man restricted of his right hand”
notes.rendering: a left-handed man
notes.why: Literally “bound” or “impeded of the right hand.” Benjamin means “son of the right hand” — so a left-handed Benjaminite is a built-in contradiction. The same phrase recurs in 20:16 of Benjaminite slingers. The point: YHWH’s deliverer is the man Eglon’s guards never thought to check on the right side.

notes.original: vayetze ha-parshedonah — a hapax legomenon
notes.rendering: and the filth comes out
notes.why: A word that appears only here in the entire Hebrew Bible, and no one is sure what it means. Variously rendered “the dirt came out,” “it came out his back,” “his bowels emptied.” Most scholars take it as a scatological detail. The grossness is the point — Israel’s oppressor dies a humiliating death in a locked toilet.

notes.original: mesikh hu et-raglav — “he is covering his feet”
notes.rendering: He must be relieving himself
notes.why: A standard Hebrew euphemism for going to the toilet (also 1 Sam 24:3, of Saul in the cave). The servants assume the locked door means privacy. The joke is that Eglon is past privacy now.

intro: Two women frame this chapter — Deborah the prophetess at her palm, and Jael the Kenite at her tent. The phrase b’yad ishah, “into the hand of a woman,” in 4:9 is the line on which the whole story pivots.

notes.original: Deborah ishah n’vi’ah eshet lappidoth — “Deborah, a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth”
notes.rendering: Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth
notes.why: Hebrew names her twice — woman and prophetess — before identifying her marriage. Some read eshet lappidoth not as “wife of Lappidoth” but as “woman of torches” (lappid means torch). The ambiguity is probably deliberate — she lights the fight.

notes.original: b’yad ishah yimkor YHWH et-sisera — “into the hand of a woman YHWH will sell Sisera”
notes.rendering: YHWH will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman
notes.why: The line on which the whole story turns. Yad — hand — is the dominant military idiom of Judges (“given into the hand of...”). Here the idiom is inverted: the enemy commander is delivered not into Barak’s hand but into Jael’s. The same verb mkr (sell) is the verb YHWH uses of Israel’s own punishment in 2:14.

notes.original: yated haʺohel … ha-maqqevet — “the tent-peg … the hammer”
notes.rendering: a tent peg in her hand and a hammer in her other hand
notes.why: A woman’s domestic tools — the very things one uses to pitch a tent — become the instruments of Israel’s victory. The pairing of yad (hand) and yated (peg) sets up the language of Deborah’s song in chapter 5: “her hand to the peg, her right hand to the workman’s hammer” (5:26).

intro: Some of the oldest Hebrew in the Bible. The Song of Deborah is archaic poetry — possibly twelfth century BCE — and its grammar, vocabulary, and rhythm sit a little to the side of standard biblical Hebrew. Three notes on the song’s strangest moments.

notes.original: chadlu prazon b’yisrael chadelu — “the prazon ceased in Israel, they ceased”
notes.rendering: The villages were empty in Israel — empty
notes.why: prazon is rare and disputed. It probably means “unwalled villages” or “peasant warriors” — the open settlements outside the fortified towns, abandoned because of Canaanite raiding. The doubling chadlu … chadelu (they ceased … they ceased) gives the line its hollow, echoing feel.

notes.original: min-shamayim nilchamu ha-kokhavim — “from the heavens fought the stars”
notes.rendering: From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera
notes.why: The single most cosmic line in the Hebrew Bible’s war poetry. The stars are pictured as YHWH’s heavenly host fighting in formation (“from their courses” — m’silotam, their orbits). Older readers heard it as literal celestial combat; later readers as storm imagery — the rain that flooded the Kishon. Both are in the line.

notes.original: bein ragleha kara nafal shakhav — “between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still”
notes.rendering: Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still.
notes.why: The most discussed line in the song. Bein ragleha is literally “between her feet” — a euphemism elsewhere for the genital area (Deut 28:57). The verbs kara (sink, kneel) and nafal (fall) are pounded three times across the verse, an incantatory inversion of conqueror and conquered: the warlord ends up between a woman’s legs not in violence done to her but in violence done to him. The final word shadud — destroyed, plundered — closes the spell.

intro: Gideon is the most reluctant figure in the book — argumentative with the angel, evasive with YHWH, demanding signs even when the signs come fast. Three of his moments worth pausing on.

notes.original: chovet chittim ba-gat — “beating wheat in the winepress”
notes.rendering: is beating out wheat in a winepress
notes.why: Wheat is threshed in an open threshing floor — high ground, wind to carry off the chaff. A winepress (gat) is a sunken stone vat. Threshing wheat in a winepress is humiliating, hopeless, and hidden — a one-line picture of what Midian has done to Israel. The angel’s greeting “mighty warrior” lands on this absurd scene.

notes.original: ki ʿal-ken raʼiti et-malʼakh YHWH panim el-panim — “for on this account I have seen the angel of YHWH face to face”
notes.rendering: for I have seen the angel of YHWH face to face
notes.why: Old assumption: to see God’s face is to die (Exod 33:20). Gideon panics. YHWH’s answer — shalom lakh, “peace to you” — becomes the name of the altar (6:24, YHWH-Shalom). The naming pun runs across three verses: face-to-face, peace, peace-named-altar.

notes.original: Yerubbaʿal — “let Baal contend”
notes.rendering: Jerubbaal — let Baal contend with him
notes.why: Folk etymology built on the verb riv (contend, sue, prosecute). The naming is mockery on Baal’s behalf: “if Baal is a real god, let him bring the lawsuit himself.” Gideon will be called Jerubbaal for the rest of the book — the name his father gave him in the moment of religious defiance, even as Gideon himself will later make an idolatrous ephod.

intro: The 300 are a theological set-piece: YHWH whittles the army down so that no one can mistake the victory for human strength. The famous lapping test, the dream of the barley loaf, the smashing of jars — every detail is designed to make Israel’s hand small.

notes.original: pen-yitpaʺer ʿalai yisrael lemor yadi hoshiʿah li — “lest Israel boast against me, saying, my hand has saved me”
notes.rendering: for Israel might boast against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’
notes.why: The theological thesis of the chapter in a single verse. The verb tifaʺer (Hithpael of paʺar) means to glorify oneself, to boast. The whole army-shrinking exercise that follows exists to disable this verb.

notes.original: yalok b’lshono … ka’asher yalok ha-kelev — “laps with his tongue … the way a dog laps”
notes.rendering: Everyone who laps the water with his tongue as a dog laps
notes.why: The Hebrew is genuinely strange. The two stated postures — lapping like a dog vs. kneeling — sound like the lappers must be the alert, soldierly ones (eyes up, not vulnerable). But the very next verse describes them as “putting their hand to their mouth” — which is the opposite of lapping like a dog. The text leaves the test ambiguous. The point may simply be: YHWH chooses by an arbitrary mark, not by human readable merit.

notes.original: cherev l’YHWH ul’gidʿon — “a sword for YHWH and for Gideon”
notes.rendering: A sword for YHWH and for Gideon!
notes.why: The battle cry — and the only spoken words from the 300. Notice the order: YHWH first, Gideon second. In 8:22, when the men of Israel try to make Gideon king, this order is exactly the thing he will refuse: YHWH will rule. The cry holds the right hierarchy in place. Whether Gideon himself does, later, is another matter.

intro: Gideon’s arc bends. He refuses kingship in the right words (“YHWH will rule”) and then in the next breath builds an ephod that becomes a snare. The same hand that tore down Baal in chapter 6 sets up an idol in chapter 8.

notes.original: ha-lo tov ʿolelot efrayim m’batzir aviʿezer — “are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer”
notes.rendering: Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?
notes.why: Gideon’s diplomatic proverb. ʿolelot (gleanings) are the second-pass grapes left after the harvest; batzir is the full vintage. The line flatters Ephraim outrageously: “your leftovers are better than my whole harvest.” Tribal pride defused with a single line of agricultural poetry. The chapter that ends in idolatry begins with a moment of real political skill.

notes.original: YHWH yimshol bakhem — “YHWH will rule over you”
notes.rendering: YHWH will rule over you.
notes.why: The book’s deepest political claim, packed into three Hebrew words. Mashal — to rule, to govern, to have dominion — is the verb later used of Israel’s human kings. Gideon refuses it for himself and his line. Yet within four verses he makes the ephod that does to Israel what kingship would have done — bind their loyalty to the wrong place. The right theology, the wrong follow-through.

notes.original: vayehi l’moqesh l’gidʿon ul’veito — “and it becomes a snare to Gideon and to his house”
notes.rendering: it becomes a snare to Gideon and to his household
notes.why: Moqesh — a snare, a trap, especially a trap set for a bird. The same word the angel used in 2:3 of the Canaanite gods being a snare to Israel. The shape of the book is in this echo: what the angel warned about at Bochim is what Gideon now builds with his own hand.

intro: Abimelech’s story is the book’s bleakest. The first attempt at kingship in Israel is bought with seventy pieces of silver, paid for by seventy dead brothers, and ended by an unnamed woman with a millstone. Jotham’s parable warns of all of it before it happens.

notes.original: tiroshi ha-m’sameach elohim va’anashim — “my new wine that gladdens gods and humans”
notes.rendering: my new wine that gladdens gods and humans
notes.why: The vine’s refusal carries the parable’s theology. Tirosh is the fresh wine of harvest, and the phrase elohim va’anashim (gods and humans) is striking — wine is the one thing humans share with the divine. The olive, fig, and vine all refuse kingship because they have something better to give. Only the bramble — which produces nothing — accepts.

notes.original: vayizraʿeha melach — “and he sowed it with salt”
notes.rendering: and sows it with salt
notes.why: Salting a conquered city is a curse-act, not an agricultural step — the gesture means “may nothing grow here again.” Hebrew zaraʿ (to sow) is the same verb used for planting grain; Abimelech reverses the cycle of harvest with his own hand. The city that crowned him is sown with sterility by him.

notes.original: pen-yomru li ishah harag-tehu — “lest they say of me, a woman killed him”
notes.rendering: so they will not say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’
notes.why: The book’s second great inversion-by-woman, after Sisera. Abimelech sees what Sisera could not — the shame coming — and tries to outrun it through suicide-by-armor-bearer. He fails: the story remembers exactly what he was trying to bury. The narrator preserves the millstone, names her actions before his.

intro: A short chapter, but the theological hinge of the second half of the book: YHWH says he will not rescue Israel again — and then does. The change of heart is captured in a single Hebrew phrase that has troubled translators for centuries.

notes.original: lo osif l’hoshiaʿ etkhem — “I will not continue to rescue you”
notes.rendering: therefore I will rescue you no more
notes.why: YHWH’s most severe word to Israel in the book. The verb yasaf (to add, to continue) appears with negation — “I will not do it again.” Note how it sets up the surprise of v.16: YHWH says no, then changes. The book does not explain the reversal; it lets the two verses sit in tension.

notes.original: vatiqtsar nafsho baʿamal yisrael — “his soul grew short at Israel’s misery”
notes.rendering: his soul grows impatient at the misery of Israel
notes.why: One of the most striking divine-emotion phrases in the Hebrew Bible. The verb qatsar means to be short, cut off, impatient — used of human exasperation (“I am out of patience”) and of physical weariness. YHWH’s nefesh (soul, life-breath) shortens against Israel’s pain. The same word will be used of Samson’s soul shortening to death (16:16). Compassion is here pictured as something like inability to endure.

intro: Three Jephthah moments that the Hebrew handles with a precision English usually rounds off: the diplomatic Chemosh line, the grammar of the vow, and what exactly the daughter mourns on the mountains.

notes.original: halo et asher yorishekha kemosh elohekha — “do you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess”
notes.rendering: Do you not possess what your god Chemosh gives you to possess?
notes.why: A diplomatic and theologically peculiar line. Jephthah grants — at least rhetorically — that Chemosh gives the Ammonites their land, just as YHWH gives Israel theirs. (Chemosh is actually the Moabite god, not Ammonite — possibly Jephthah’s deliberate elision, possibly an old name-overlap.) Either way, the verse is read by some as henotheistic (other gods exist for other peoples) and by others as pure diplomacy.

notes.original: v’hayah ha-yotze asher yetze … v’haʿalitihu ʿolah — “whatever comes out … I will offer it up as a burnt offering”
notes.rendering: whoever comes out … I will offer him up as a burnt offering
notes.why: The Hebrew is ambiguous on purpose. Ha-yotze (“the one who comes out”) can be either an animal or a person — Hebrew uses the same masculine participle for both. Some traditions try to soften the vow by saying Jephthah expected a sheep; the text gives him no excuse. The narrator lets the ambiguity stand and then makes the door open.

notes.original: v’evkeh ʿal-betulay — “and I will weep over my maidenhood”
notes.rendering: and bewail my virginity
notes.why: Betulim is technically maidenhood — the state of being a young unmarried woman, but with the specific freight of a life never lived out: no marriage, no children, no continuation of her father’s line. The two months and the annual four-day lament are the chapter’s small, dignified resistance — the women of Israel keep telling this story when the men stop talking about it.

intro: The Shibboleth incident is the famous one, but the Ephraim threat at the beginning of the chapter rhymes with the same complaint Ephraim made to Gideon (8:1). Gideon disarmed them with a proverb; Jephthah does not. The chapter is what tribal grievance looks like when no one in charge has Gideon’s touch.

notes.original: beitkha nisrof ʿalekha ba-esh — “we will burn your house over you with fire”
notes.rendering: We will burn your house over you with fire!
notes.why: Compare 8:1, where Ephraim makes the same complaint to Gideon. Gideon defuses it with the gleanings/vintage proverb. Jephthah, with no such gift, answers with bluntness — and the result is forty-two thousand dead countrymen. The same complaint, two leaders, two outcomes.

notes.original: p’liṭei efrayim — “fugitives of Ephraim”
notes.rendering: You Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim
notes.why: An ethnic insult. Ephraim casts Gilead as runaways or refugees who never had their own territory — a deep slur in a tribal society where land was identity. The line is what makes the Gileadites pursue so ruthlessly: it’s personal.

notes.original: shibboleth … sibboleth — “flood” / “har of grain”
notes.rendering: Then say ‘Shibboleth.’ And he says ‘Sibboleth’
notes.why: The most famous dialect test in literature. Shibboleth can mean either an ear of grain or a stream/flood — a quietly ironic choice, given that the test happens at the river fords. The Ephraimite dialect apparently lacked the sh-sound. The point is not the word’s meaning but the sound: a single phoneme separating life and death. The first recorded use of an accent to kill.

intro: Samson’s birth narrative does what biblical birth narratives do (barren wife, angelic visit, child marked from the womb) — but it does them strangely. The mother is unnamed and the named father is the slower of the two. The angel’s name is wonderful. The child will be a Nazirite he never quite is.

notes.original: nazir elohim yihyeh ha-naʺar — “the boy shall be a Nazirite to God”
notes.rendering: the boy shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb
notes.why: Nazir comes from nzr — to separate, to consecrate. The Nazirite vow (Num 6) involves three signs: no wine or grape products, no haircut, no contact with the dead. Samson breaks the last two regularly (he handles a corpse in 14:8, kills with a jawbone in 15:15, gets his hair shaved in 16:19). The vow defines him by what he keeps and what he loses.

notes.original: lamah zeh tishʺal lishmi vehu peliʺi — “why do you ask my name, and it is wonderful”
notes.rendering: Why do you ask my name? It is wonderful.
notes.why: Peliʺi — from the root plʺ, wonder, marvel, the incomprehensible. Same root as Isaiah’s pele yoʿets, “Wonderful, Counselor” (Isa 9:6). The KJV rendered it “secret”; older Jewish tradition read it as “hidden.” The line works at two levels — the angel’s name is too holy to give, and the angel’s identity is itself a kind of wonder Manoah is only just beginning to recognize.

notes.original: vatachel ruach YHWH l’paʿamo — “the Spirit of YHWH began to stir him”
notes.rendering: begins to stir him
notes.why: Paʿam means to strike, to disturb, to drive — the same root as a beat or pulse. It is not the gentle indwelling of the Spirit in later texts; it is the Spirit goading, pushing, agitating. Samson’s Spirit-encounters all have this quality — they arrive like a blow, not a breath. The word will recur each time he tears something apart.

intro: The whole chapter turns on a riddle whose Hebrew is more compact than English can match. Samson’s violations of his Nazirite vow accumulate behind the storyline — he touches a corpse, he eats from it, he feasts.

notes.original: ki toʺanah hu m’vakeish — “for he was seeking an occasion”
notes.rendering: he is seeking an occasion against the Philistines
notes.why: Toʺanah — a pretext, opportunity, occasion (the only occurrence of the noun in the Hebrew Bible). The narrator interrupts to tell the reader what Samson does not know: the marriage is YHWH’s pretext for a fight. Samson thinks he is choosing; the verse says he is being used. This is the chapter’s deepest theological move — what looks like a young man’s appetite is, underneath, a divine setup.

notes.original: mei’okhel yatza maʼakhal umei’az yatza matok — “out of the eater came food, out of the strong came sweet”
notes.rendering: Out of the eater came something to eat, out of the strong came something sweet
notes.why: The Hebrew is six words. Two parallel lines, two matched verbs (yatza, yatza). The pun is structural: okhel/maʼakhal share a root (eater/eaten), and az (strong, fierce) is a near-rhyme for the verb. English versions can preserve the parallelism or the brevity, but rarely both.

notes.original: lulei charashtem b’eglati lo m’tza’tem chidati — “if you had not plowed with my heifer”
notes.rendering: If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have figured out my riddle
notes.why: A coarse proverbial expression — the wife is the heifer, the companions are the plowmen. It is the only place in the Hebrew Bible this idiom appears. Samson reaches for the agricultural insult because the Philistines have crossed into what was his: the woman who was supposed to be on his side.

intro: The jawbone song is one of the great untranslatable puns in the Hebrew Bible: chamor means donkey, and chomer means a heap. “With a donkey-jawbone, a donkey-heap, two donkey-heaps.” English has to choose between the rhythm and the joke.

notes.original: vayak otam shoq ʿal-yarekh — “he struck them, leg upon thigh”
notes.rendering: He strikes them hip and thigh — a great blow
notes.why: A puzzling Hebrew idiom that occurs only here. “Leg upon thigh” — possibly a wrestling image (pinning), possibly the slaughter of butchered animals (legs piled), possibly an idiom for total defeat.
